title: A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits
summary:
**Central idea.** Proposes a way to reverse-engineer transformers by rewriting them as sums of interpretable paths. The residual stream is treated as a linear communication channel that every layer reads from and writes to. Attention heads are independent, additive units, and each factors into a QK circuit (where to attend) and an OV circuit (what information moves). Studying attention-only models with zero, one and two layers, the paper builds intuitions meant to transfer to larger models.

**Experiments.** Mostly analytic decomposition of trained small attention-only transformers (no MLPs), reading weight products such as W_E W_QK W_E^T and W_U W_OV W_E directly, plus inspection of attention patterns. Eigenvalue analysis of OV and QK matrices is used to detect copying behavior.

**Key results.** (1) A zero-layer transformer models bigram statistics. (2) One-layer attention-only models are an ensemble of bigram and 'skip-trigram' predictors, which can be read off the weights, including copying heads and some characteristic bugs. (3) Two-layer models use composition between heads (Q-, K- and V-composition), and K-composition with a previous-token head produces *induction heads*, which give a general in-context copying algorithm. (4) Terms like 'virtual attention heads' and 'privileged basis' are introduced.

**Limitations / open questions.** Results are for attention-only toy models; MLP layers, which hold most parameters in real models, are explicitly left out. The independence and linearity framing is exact for these models but becomes an approximation once layer norm and MLPs are included. Whether the vocabulary scales to large models is posed rather than tested here.
provenance: claude-code-session:claude-opus-5-5 (seed draft from fetched text + model knowledge; unreviewed)

title: Thread: Circuits
summary:
**Central idea**

This is the landing/index page for Distill's *Circuits* thread. It is not a research article. The thread's premise is to take seriously the original narrative of deep learning, in which each neuron composes features from the previous layer into progressively more abstract, meaningful features. It then asks what can be learned by investing heavily in reverse-engineering a single network. The chosen target is **InceptionV1**, a classic vision model with roughly 10,000 unique neurons, a scale the authors consider tractable for a group effort.

The page argues that the natural unit of publication for this work is short papers on individual circuits or small families of features. It introduces the Distill "thread" format: a living collection of short, early-stage articles interleaved with critical commentary from experts in adjacent fields. Discussion is coordinated through an open #circuits Slack channel.

**Experiments**

The page itself reports no experiments. It lists and briefly summarizes the constituent articles:

- **Zoom In** proposes three claims: meaningful features, meaningful circuits between features, and universality.
- **Early Vision** gives a taxonomy of all neurons in InceptionV1's first five layers, organized into neuron groups.
- **Curve Detectors** reports that every vision model the authors explored contains curve detectors.
- **Naturally Occurring Equivariance** reports transformed copies of features connected by symmetric weights.
- **High-Low Frequency Detectors** describes early-vision neurons that respond to directional transitions from high to low spatial frequency.
- **Curve Circuits** reverse-engineers the curve algorithm from the weights and hand-crafts an artificial network that reimplements it.
- **Visualizing Weights** presents techniques for visualizing, contextualizing and understanding weights.
- **Branch Specialization** reports that neurons self-organize into coherent groupings across the branches of a layer.
- **Weight Banding** reports horizontal bands in the final-layer weights of common vision models.

**Key results**

As stated in the one-line blurbs:

- Curve detectors appear in every vision model examined in detail.
- Equivariant feature families with symmetric weights arise naturally.
- A learned curve-detection algorithm could be read from the weights and re-implemented by hand.
- Branched layers induce coherent neuron groupings.
- Final-layer weights of common vision models show banding.

The evidence for all of these lives in the linked articles, not on this page.

**Limitations / open questions**

- The authors explicitly frame the content as early-stage exploratory research.
- They call the thread format itself an experiment that may turn out "great" or "terrible", to be re-evaluated after two trial threads.
- The text available here is only the index. Methodological detail, quantitative results and critical commentary are in the individual articles and are not captured.
- Claims in this extraction are therefore recorded as premises ("assumes"), not as tested relations.

title: In-context Learning and Induction Heads
summary:
**Central idea.** Argues that induction heads may be the mechanism behind most in-context learning in transformers of any size, not only the small attention-only models where they were first described.

**Experiments.** Six complementary lines of evidence across small attention-only models and larger models with MLPs (up to about 13B parameters): (1) induction heads form during a phase change early in training, visible as a bump in the training loss, at the same time as a sharp improvement in in-context learning (loss on late versus early tokens); (2) architectural changes that shift when induction heads can form shift the phase change with them; (3) knocking out induction heads at test time in small models greatly reduces in-context learning; (4) concrete examples of induction heads performing more abstract, fuzzy or nearest-neighbor style copying, such as translation; (5) a mechanistic account of how they work in small models; (6) arguments for continuity from small to large models.

**Key results.** The co-occurrence of the induction-head phase change with the jump in in-context learning is robust across model sizes. The causal evidence (ablations) is strong for small attention-only models but only correlational for large ones.

**Limitations / open questions.** The authors present the large-model claim as a hypothesis with evidence of varying strength. Interference from MLPs and the many ways heads can compose make the mechanistic story in large models incomplete. 'In-context learning' is measured with a single token-index loss metric.

title: Visualizing Weights
summary:
**Central idea**

The article presents methods for inspecting hidden-layer weights as operations between interpreted features. It identifies three obstacles: weights lack semantic context, meaningful interactions can cross intermediate layers, and connection tensors are too large to inspect comprehensively. Feature visualizations supply provisional meanings for source and destination neurons; spatial diagrams and factorizations summarize their connections. The demonstrations concern convolutional vision networks, principally InceptionV1.

**Experiments**

The evidence consists of qualitative visualization demonstrations. One-sided nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF) reduces convolutional input-channel weights to three factors displayed through RGB channels: Figure 1 covers ten selected InceptionV1 `mixed4d_5x5` neurons, and Figure 2 covers eight `mixed5b_5x5` neurons. Other examples display connection grids among curve detectors, visualize weight directions at individual spatial positions of a car neuron, and factor weights connecting `conv2d2` to six high-low frequency detectors. Expanded weights compose intervening weight maps while replacing or ignoring nonlinear operations. Examples examine black-and-white center detector `mixed3b 208` and boundary detector `mixed3b 345`. No dataset-level benchmark, quantitative fidelity metric, uncertainty estimate, or controlled user study is reported.

**Key results**

The car-neuron visualization is interpreted as seeking window features above wheel features. The six frequency detectors receive a compact description involving high- and low-frequency factors in different spatial arrangements. NMF exposes horizontal banding in selected late InceptionV1 filters. Expanding weights reveals an aggregate absence-of-color pattern in the center of the black-and-white detector's inputs. Conversely, opposing pathways through high-low frequency detectors cancel in the boundary detector's expanded weights, obscuring the different context-dependent cases. The article also reports smooth multilayer spatial weight patterns whose interpretation remains unclear.

**Limitations / open questions**

These demonstrations illustrate visualization possibilities without establishing complete causal mechanisms. A single optimized image can omit response facets. Factorization can mix features, lose alignment with activation functions, and introduce neuron-specific bases that complicate global analysis. Expanded weights discard nonlinear gating; their stated expected-gradient interpretation is conditional on equal, independent firing probabilities and is not independently validated here. Inspecting the largest weights leaves the long tail unresolved, and the authors explicitly allow that small connections may contain important structure. The supplied rendering includes figure captions and explanatory prose but no inspectable figure images; conclusions here rely on those textual descriptions.

title: interpreting GPT: the logit lens
summary:
**Central idea**

GPT's output logits are a linear function (the transpose of the tied embedding matrix W, applied after the final layer norm) of its final-layer activations. The *logit lens* applies that same unembedding to the residual-stream activations of **intermediate** layers. The resulting next-token distributions are intuitively sensible. They converge gradually toward the final output distribution, often reaching a good guess well before the last layer. The author's reading is that GPT "thinks in predictive space": inputs are almost immediately converted into something resembling an output prediction, which is then iteratively refined. The post compares this to the iterative-refinement view of Universal Transformers.

**Experiments**

- Logit lens applied to GPT-2 1558M (48 layers, d=1600) on a passage of the GPT-3 abstract. Activations are block outputs after layer norm but before the learned pointwise affine transform.
- Three views: per-layer top-1 guess; rank of the final top-1 token at each layer; KL(final || layer).
- Case studies: copying a rare token ("plasma" repeated in a prompt), and extreme verbatim repetition loops.
- Addendum (after comments from Gurkenglas and algon33): KL(input || layer), plus the rank of the *input* token at each layer.
- A later edit mentions a follow-up Colab that applies the lens to 125M–2.7B models (GPT-Neo, CTRL), examines attention vs. MLP sub-blocks, and tries a modified decoder. Those results are not included in this text.

**Key results**

- The trajectory typically runs from nonsense, to shallow guesses (right part of speech or register), to better guesses. Rank of the final prediction drops sharply by the middle layers.
- Under KL(final || layer), the input embedding is very far from every later layer. Even after layer 0, activations look more like the final output than like the input, followed by smooth convergence.
- Rare-token copying ("plasma") is resolved only in the last few layers, even though the token must have been retained somehow.
- Repetition loops are "noticed" only in the upper half of the network.
- The addendum softens the "input discarding" claim. The jump in KL(input || layer) is much smaller, and input-token ranks often stay in the 100s–1000s out of a ~50K vocabulary. Preservation is contextual (commas differ), and rare tokens like the first "plasma" are strongly preserved.
- Proposed explanation for why the lens works at all: residual connections (identity is easy to learn) plus weight decay, which encourages small incremental changes spread across layers and so a shared basis.

**Limitations / open questions**

- Qualitative evidence from a few prompts on one main model, with no systematic metric over a dataset.
- The lens is partial: the post says information not expressible as vocabulary logits is likely present.
- KL is not a metric, so the "jump then smooth path" picture is misleading, as the author concedes.
- The discontinuous input discarding is unexplained. A hypothesized invertible token→next-token-prior mapping is considered and judged unconvincing.
- Why some tokens (e.g. "GPT") are not preserved while "plasma" is remains open. A speculated implication for better sampling is not developed.

title: A Primer in BERTology: What We Know About How BERT Works
Distill's Discussion Article experiment
https://alignmentforum.org/posts/eDicGjD9yte6FLSie
Toy Models of Superposition
abstract: Neural networks often pack many unrelated concepts into a single neuron - a puzzling phenomenon known as 'polysemanticity' which makes interpretability much more challenging. This paper provides a toy model where polysemanticity can be fully understood, arising as a result of models storing additional sparse features in "superposition." We demonstrate the existence of a phase change, a surprising connection to the geometry of uniform polytopes, and evidence of a link to adversarial examples. We also discuss potential implications for mechanistic interpretability.
summary:
**Central idea.** Polysemantic neurons can arise because networks store more sparse features than they have dimensions, encoding them as nearly-orthogonal directions: *superposition*. The paper builds toy models where this can be fully understood.

**Experiments.** Small ReLU autoencoder-style models (x -> ReLU(W^T W x + b)) trained to reconstruct synthetic sparse features with varying sparsity and importance. The authors vary the number of features relative to dimensions, the sparsity and the importance weights, then study the learned geometry (feature dimensionality, interference) and training dynamics. Extensions cover computation in superposition (|x|) and connections to adversarial vulnerability.

**Key results.** (1) Dense features get dedicated dimensions, while sufficiently sparse features are packed into superposition, and a nonlinearity is needed for this to pay off. (2) There is a sharp phase change between 'not represented', 'dedicated dimension' and 'superposition' as sparsity and importance vary. (3) Features in superposition arrange into uniform polytopes (antipodal pairs, triangles, pentagons, tetrahedra). (4) Models can do some computation while in superposition. (5) Evidence that superposition relates to adversarial vulnerability.

**Limitations / open questions.** Everything is shown in synthetic toy settings with features defined as known ground-truth directions. Whether real LLMs use superposition in the same way, and how to recover the features, is posed as the central open problem. The paper motivates dictionary learning / sparse autoencoders as one route, and 'privileged bases' as another.

title: Tracr: Compiled Transformers as a Laboratory for Interpretability
abstract: We show how to "compile" human-readable programs into standard decoder-only transformer models. Our compiler, Tracr, generates models with known structure. This structure can be used to design experiments. For example, we use it to study "superposition" in transformers that execute multi-step algorithms. Additionally, the known structure of Tracr-compiled models can serve as ground-truth for evaluating interpretability methods. Commonly, because the "programs" learned by transformers are unknown it is unclear whether an interpretation succeeded. We demonstrate our approach by implementing and examining programs including computing token frequencies, sorting, and parenthesis checking. We provide an open-source implementation of Tracr at https://github.com/google-deepmind/tracr.
summary:
**Central idea**

Tracr compiles human-readable Restricted Access Sequence Processing Language (RASP) programs into transformer weights with known variable encodings and computational structure. Elementwise operations become MLPs, and select–aggregate operations become attention heads. Each variable receives a dedicated orthogonal residual-stream subspace. Compilation requires a finite vocabulary and maximum context length, encoding annotations, and a BOS token. The implementation omits layer normalization. All main-paper models use non-causal attention, although causal compilation is supported. The proposed application is controlled experimentation and ground-truth evaluation of interpretability methods.

**Experiments**

The paper illustrates compiled forward passes for running token fractions and sorting, with additional programs described as parenthesis checkers. Compression experiments examine `frac_prevs` and `sort_unique`. They train one shared linear projection at every residual-stream read and write while freezing the original component weights. The objective combines output cross-entropy or mean-squared error with equally weighted layer-output matching. Appendix E specifies AdamW, 300,000 steps, batch size 256, and weight decay 0.1. Analyses examine output loss, sorting accuracy, feature overlaps, an eight-component PCA comparison, and average layer-output cosine similarity. Input-sampling distributions and evaluation sample counts are not specified.

**Key results**

The running-token-frequency model compresses from 14 residual dimensions to about six with essentially unchanged task performance. At eight dimensions, learned compression retains task-critical variables and discards unnecessary token identities more selectively than the displayed PCA solution. Sparse positional features become non-orthogonal, and the related `tokens:x` and `is_x` variables partially overlap. The compressed sorting model achieves nearly perfect accuracy while average layer-output cosine similarity remains around 0.8. Inspection suggests a change from categorical to numerical target-position encoding, showing that task success and layer-matching training do not ensure preservation of compiler annotations. Separately, Appendix F supplies constructions for selector negation and conjunction and a formal necessary condition restricting generic selector unions through a single bilinear attention operator over separate input subspaces.

**Limitations / open questions**

Compiled models are hand-engineered, unusually sparse, and axis-aligned. RASP uses binary selectors and lacks native probabilistic computation. The paper proposes interpretability evaluations but does not benchmark interpretability tools itself; successful evaluation on compiled models is presented as a minimum bar for validation. Compression may change mechanisms, and shared information is not independently manipulated to establish why features overlap. The sorting-encoding interpretation is tentative, with a compiled/compressed wording inconsistency in Section 5.3. The displayed multi-type parenthesis routine checks per-type prefix balance and final closure without explicitly checking cross-type nesting.

title: a number of open problems
Engineering Monosemanticity in Toy Models
abstract: In some neural networks, individual neurons correspond to natural ``features'' in the input. Such \emph{monosemantic} neurons are of great help in interpretability studies, as they can be cleanly understood. In this work we report preliminary attempts to engineer monosemanticity in toy models. We find that models can be made more monosemantic without increasing the loss by just changing which local minimum the training process finds. More monosemantic loss minima have moderate negative biases, and we are able to use this fact to engineer highly monosemantic models. We are able to mechanistically interpret these models, including the residual polysemantic neurons, and uncover a simple yet surprising algorithm. Finally, we find that providing models with more neurons per layer makes the models more monosemantic, albeit at increased computational cost. These findings point to a number of new questions and avenues for engineering monosemanticity, which we intend to study these in future work.
summary:
**Central idea**
Neuron monosemanticity can depend on training trajectory even when task performance is nearly unchanged. In synthetic feature-recovery networks, negative bias initialization followed by temporary bias-only weight decay encourages specialization in individual generating features, without retaining an activation-sparsity penalty in the final objective.

**Experiments**
The authors train two-layer networks comprising an affine map, usually ReLU, and a bias-free output map. All experiments use 512 generating features; defaults are a 64-dimensional random input projection and mean occurrence probability 1/64, giving eight active features per sampled nonnegative feature vector. Tasks recover these features, predict a second random projection, or recover the absolute difference between two independently sampled feature vectors. Fresh batches use uniform or power-law feature frequencies. Sweeps vary learning rate, hidden width, feature density, initial bias, bias decay, activation function, and activation-L1 regularization. Training uses LAMB; the negative-bias protocol typically starts near −1 and disables decay for the final half of training. Monosemantic neurons have an isolated-feature response-concentration ratio above 0.999; the absolute-value task combines responses to positive and negative feature inputs.

**Key results**
Feature decoders attain similar squared reconstruction losses with markedly different monosemantic-neuron counts. Negative initialization increases specialization across tested decoder learning rates and also works for random re-projection. Absolute-value recovery additionally benefits from slower bias decay or higher learning rates; its more monosemantic solutions have lower loss. Increasing hidden width increases monosemantic-neuron counts, with diminishing loss gains beyond 512 neurons, but the monosemantic fraction need not increase. Negative initialization slightly worsens loss at some intermediate widths. Fixed random sparse connectivity reportedly performs worse than dense layers at comparable compute.

Single-feature amplitude sweeps show one-threshold recovery with a single specialized neuron and complementary thresholds with two, consistent with interference suppression. In a selected decoder, residual positive-bias neurons contribute an approximately linear correction whose linearized feature map has singular values either zero or 0.99–1.03. The examined 64-dimensional LR3 decoder runs each contain 65 positive-bias neurons.

**Limitations / open questions**
These are synthetic networks without language-model validation. Isolated-feature selectivity does not establish selectivity across mixtures and amplitudes. Distinct loss basins and confidence-based interpretations remain partly conjectural. Bias decay must match learning speed; denser features reduce monosemanticity, GeLU requires different tuning, and SoLU results are inconclusive. Mechanistic analysis covers highly monosemantic feature decoders; predominantly polysemantic models remain unexplained. Plots are accessible here only through prose and captions, and some appendix table rows omit hidden widths.

title: Polysemanticity and capacity in neural networks
Superposition, Memorization, and Double Descent
summary:
**Central idea**

Superposition can support memorization of individual training examples as well as representation of reusable features. In a synthetic reconstruction model, small datasets produce orderly hidden-state geometries for training examples, whereas large datasets produce orderly geometries for input features. Test reconstruction loss exhibits double descent around this transition. Extension of this account to real-network memorization remains hypothetical.

**Experiments**

Inputs have 10,000 nonnegative coordinates, each zero with probability 0.999 and otherwise uniform on [0,1], followed by normalization to unit norm. A tied-weight bottleneck reconstructs inputs as ReLU(WᵀWx + b), minimizing uniformly weighted squared reconstruction error. Training ordinarily uses 50,000 full-batch AdamW updates, a 2,500-step warmup to learning rate 0.001, cosine decay, and weight decay 0.01. Geometric analyses emphasize two hidden dimensions. The main dataset-size loss curve averages four dataset seeds; joint dataset-size–hidden-width sweeps average four models per configuration. Four-dimensional ablations vary weight decay and training duration. Included researcher contributions report replications, feature-frequency and repeated-example experiments, and a preliminary MNIST analysis with one hidden layer of 512 units.

**Key results**

Small-data example embeddings form polygons while feature vectors appear scattered. Large-data two-dimensional solutions prominently represent five input features as a pentagon. Average test loss rises and falls between these regimes despite identical inputs and targets and no added label noise. Joint width–data sweeps contain regions where larger models worsen test loss. Longer training enlarges the bump; weight decay 1.0 removes it in the four-dimensional experiments.

An included extension finds approximately aligned generalization onsets near ten expected occurrences per feature, with weaker alignment at larger hidden widths. Its weight-decay sweep does not show the predicted onset shift from a decay-limited memorization explanation. Repeated examples can displace generalizing features. At larger T/N, a rough memorization boundary follows R ≈ 0.4T/N, where memorization means the repeated example ranks in the top 0.1% by example dimensionality. High maximal data dimensionality highlights unusual MNIST examples without establishing that they are memorized.

**Limitations / open questions**

The construction deliberately favors sparse, similarly sized, nearly orthogonal examples. Two-dimensional optimization is fragile and sometimes uses lowest-training-loss initialization selection. One replication preserves the qualitative regimes but reports different transition sizes and intermediate test losses reaching about 5,000 versus approximately 1.01 in the main results. Intermediate mechanisms and transfer to language models remain unresolved. Plots and linked notebooks are unavailable in the supplied rendering; numerical conclusions here rely on the prose.

title: https://lesswrong.com/posts/cgqh99SHsCv3jJYDS
Softmax Linear Units
summary:
**Central idea**

Softmax Linear Units (SoLU), defined as x ⊙ softmax(x), introduce competition among transformer MLP neurons to encourage features to align with individual neurons. The practical architecture adds LayerNorm after SoLU to recover language-model performance. The broader proposal is to choose architectures that make subsequent mechanistic reverse engineering easier.

**Experiments**

The authors compare baseline and SoLU-with-LayerNorm transformers from approximately 10 million to 50 billion parameters, spanning 1–64 layers. They measure language-model loss and performance on Lambada, ARC, OpenBookQA, TriviaQA, arithmetic, MMLU, and HellaSwag. Models share hyperparameters, without separate activation-specific tuning. The corpus is not fully specified here; models use 8,192-token contexts, rotary attention, mixed dense/sparse attention, and books and web data.

Randomized, blinded human evaluations examine 60 neurons per architecture at each of five depths—1, 16, 24, 40, and 64 layers—for 600 neurons total. Evaluators spend 1–2 minutes deciding whether one rule explains at least 80% of the strongest firings. Another 60 neurons come from a 16-layer LayerNorm-only control. Exploratory investigations inspect activation examples, vocabulary projections, and selected input edits. An informal, unblinded analysis categorizes around 1,000 pre- and post-LayerNorm examples for one left/right-associated neuron.

**Key results**

For 1–40-layer models, preliminary interpretability rises from roughly 35% to 60% of sampled neurons. At 64 layers, the observed rates are 33% versus 42%. LayerNorm alone yields an intermediate result in the 16-layer control. SoLU-with-LayerNorm loss corresponds to a 0.95–1.05 equivalent-model-size multiplier relative to baseline, usually about ±0.01 nats. Downstream performance is broadly similar, with arithmetic favoring SoLU and TriviaQA favoring baseline. SoLU alone reportedly performs like models 30–50% smaller. Reported training slowdown with suitable kernels is below 1%.

Selected neurons suggest early recognition of contextualized tokens and multi-token words, middle-layer abstract contextual features, and late promotion of constituent output tokens. Post-LayerNorm examples more often violate apparent neuron interpretations at low activation strengths, consistent with—but not establishing—amplification of suppressed distributed features.

**Limitations / open questions**

Strongest-example judgments establish ease of hypothesis generation, not validated monosemanticity or causal mechanisms. A later caveat explicitly questions this metric for architectural optimization. Evidence for hidden features and superposition remains circumstantial. Generalization beyond one architecture/data family, benefits beyond 50B parameters, and integration of neuron explanations into whole-model understanding remain unresolved.

title: Interpretability in the Wild: a Circuit for Indirect Object Identification in GPT-2 small
abstract: Research in mechanistic interpretability seeks to explain behaviors of machine learning models in terms of their internal components. However, most previous work either focuses on simple behaviors in small models, or describes complicated behaviors in larger models with broad strokes. In this work, we bridge this gap by presenting an explanation for how GPT-2 small performs a natural language task called indirect object identification (IOI). Our explanation encompasses 26 attention heads grouped into 7 main classes, which we discovered using a combination of interpretability approaches relying on causal interventions. To our knowledge, this investigation is the largest end-to-end attempt at reverse-engineering a natural behavior "in the wild" in a language model. We evaluate the reliability of our explanation using three quantitative criteria--faithfulness, completeness and minimality. Though these criteria support our explanation, they also point to remaining gaps in our understanding. Our work provides evidence that a mechanistic understanding of large ML models is feasible, opening opportunities to scale our understanding to both larger models and more complex tasks.
summary:
**Central idea.** Reverse-engineers how GPT-2 small does indirect object identification (IOI), e.g. completing 'When Mary and John went to the store, John gave a drink to' with 'Mary'. At the time this was the largest end-to-end circuit analysis of a natural behavior in a real language model.

**Experiments.** Uses causal interventions, chiefly *path patching* (patching activations along specific sender-to-receiver paths, taken from a counterfactual distribution with different names), together with attention-pattern analysis and ablations. The circuit is evaluated with three criteria: faithfulness (the circuit alone reproduces model performance), completeness (no important components are missing) and minimality (every component matters).

**Key results.** The circuit has 26 attention heads in 7 classes: duplicate-token heads, previous-token and induction heads, S-inhibition heads, name mover heads, negative name movers and backup name movers. Backup name movers take over when the primary name movers are ablated, an early documented case of self-repair. The circuit is fairly faithful, but completeness and minimality tests reveal gaps in the explanation.

**Limitations / open questions.** One task, one small model, a templated prompt distribution. Results depend on the choice of counterfactual (ablation) distribution. MLPs are mostly treated as part of the background. Self-repair complicates ablation-based attribution.
