title: has been suggested to have been missing important details
Transformers learn in-context by gradient descent
abstract: At present, the mechanisms of in-context learning in Transformers are not well understood and remain mostly an intuition. In this paper, we suggest that training Transformers on auto-regressive objectives is closely related to gradient-based meta-learning formulations. We start by providing a simple weight construction that shows the equivalence of data transformations induced by 1) a single linear self-attention layer and by 2) gradient-descent (GD) on a regression loss. Motivated by that construction, we show empirically that when training self-attention-only Transformers on simple regression tasks either the models learned by GD and Transformers show great similarity or, remarkably, the weights found by optimization match the construction. Thus we show how trained Transformers become mesa-optimizers i.e. learn models by gradient descent in their forward pass. This allows us, at least in the domain of regression problems, to mechanistically understand the inner workings of in-context learning in optimized Transformers. Building on this insight, we furthermore identify how Transformers surpass the performance of plain gradient descent by learning an iterative curvature correction and learn linear models on deep data representations to solve non-linear regression tasks. Finally, we discuss intriguing parallels to a mechanism identified to be crucial for in-context learning termed induction-head (Olsson et al., 2022) and show how it could be understood as a specific case of in-context learning by gradient descent learning within Transformers. Code to reproduce the experiments can be found at https://github.com/google-research/self-organising-systems/tree/master/transformers_learn_icl_by_gd .
summary:
**Central idea**

A Transformer can learn an optimization algorithm in its forward computation. The paper constructs a single-head linear self-attention layer whose token updates reproduce one gradient-descent step on squared-error regression. Updated targets and query predictions implicitly express the learned predictor. The broader claim that autoregressive in-context learning generally follows this mechanism remains a hypothesis.

**Experiments**

Small Transformers are trained with Adam on synthetic noiseless regression tasks. Most experiments use ten context examples, ten input dimensions, scalar outputs, Gaussian teacher weights, and uniform inputs in [−1,1]. Comparisons use 10,000 validation tasks, regression loss, prediction L2 differences, and cosine similarity and L2 differences between query-input derivatives. Tests include input and teacher rescaling, unfamiliar input distributions, interpolation of constructed and trained attention matrix products, and repeated application of trained layers. Architectures include single-layer, recurrent two-layer, and independent five-layer models. Sine regression uses ten examples, a 40-dimensional embedding, and a 160-hidden-unit GELU MLP. Another experiment presents inputs and targets in alternating tokens.

**Key results**

Single-layer linear attention closely matches tuned one-step GD, including effective weight products after scaling correction; Figure 2 reports five seeds. Dampening updates by 0.75 permits similar loss reduction over 50 repeated steps. Deeper models outperform equal-step plain GD and closely match GD++, which additionally transforms inputs by I−γXXᵀ. Recurrent models permit successful effective-weight interpolation; simple scaling correction generally fails for independent deeper layers. Sine-regression models resemble meta-learned representations with one readout update, although comparisons share initialization seeds. With alternating tokens, a two-layer model using softmax in its first layer reaches one-step GD performance; neighboring-token derivatives suggest pair assembly. Fully linear training did not succeed in that setting. A second softmax head improves regression performance and alignment, but the tested models still trail GD. LayerNorm also lowers in-distribution performance, while sometimes improving robustness to substantially enlarged inputs.

**Limitations / open questions**

Most training losses supervise only the final query, and no pretrained language model is tested. Deeper runs clip token values to [−10,10], and their OOD correspondence deteriorates away from training conditions. Nonlinear derivative agreement establishes local functional similarity rather than complete algorithmic equivalence. Small fixed task sets can fail to recover GD alignment. Noise, regularization, and deep MLP–attention interactions remain open. Proposition 3 incorrectly treats softmax of a one-hot selector as unchanged; exact finite-logit softmax copying is therefore not established by that construction. Plot images are unavailable in the supplied rendering, so numerical conclusions rely on prose and captions.

title: Transformer Circuit Exercises
summary:
**Central idea**
This document is a pedagogical problem set accompanying *A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits*. It asks readers to hand-write the weights of individual attention heads, in terms of W_Q, W_K, W_V and W_out (W_O), so that the heads implement specific algorithms. The aim is to build a full mechanistic understanding of transformers, all the way down to individual parameters. The exercises use the framework's view of a head as two low-rank bilinear maps:
- a QK circuit (W_Q^T W_K), which determines where the head attends;
- an OV circuit (W_out W_V), which determines what information is moved from one residual-stream subspace to another.

**Experiments**
There are no empirical experiments or trained models. The content consists of conceptual warm-up questions and three explicit weight constructions.
1. **Virtual attention head.** In a 16-dimensional residual stream with 4-dimensional heads, two previous-token heads in successive layers are composed. The layer-2 head copies three fresh dimensions plus one dimension written by the layer-1 head. The products W_net^2·W_net^1 (two-token copy) and W_net^2·Id + Id·W_net^1 (one-token copy) are then expanded.
2. **Pointer-arithmetic induction head.**
   - QK circuits are built from principal components of the content embedding and from sine/cosine positional-embedding components.
   - Attending to the previous position is achieved by applying a 2D rotation R_{-α} to each cos/sin pair.
   - A head attends to earlier same-content tokens while dispreferring itself, using a −β-weighted position term. It copies the positions of the tokens it attends to into a new subspace.
   - A later head rotates that stored position forward by one step, so it attends to the token after the previous occurrence.
3. **K-composition induction head.** A previous-token head copies content into a subspace. A second head then uses that subspace in its keys and matches it against the current token's content in its queries.

**Key results**
- The constructions show that small, explicit weight matrices suffice for these algorithms.
- In Exercise 1, the two heads devote 7/8 of their capacity to previous-token copying and 1/8 to a virtual two-tokens-back head. Head composition therefore lets heads share capacity across tasks.
- Any rotation composed into both W_Q and W_K yields a functionally equivalent head, so the weights are only identified up to this symmetry.
- The pointer-arithmetic algorithm is unavailable when positional information does not reach the W_V matmul, as with rotary attention. This motivates the K-composition variant.

**Limitations / open questions**
- These are hand constructions, not analyses of trained models. They show that such mechanisms can be expressed, not that trained transformers use them.
- The worked matrices for Exercise 1(a), (b) and (d) appear to be missing from the extracted text; only the commentary survives.
- The warm-up solutions defer to the framework paper.

title: Garcon
summary:
**Central idea**
Circuits-style mechanistic interpretability needs flexible access to model internals: reading activations at arbitrary layers, ablating or modifying components, and taking gradients. Notebook workflows built on PyTorch hooks do not carry over to models too large for a single GPU or node. Garçon is Anthropic's answer to this problem.

A researcher launches a server with a model path and a name. Model configuration and GPU count are autodetected. The researcher then connects remotely (`rmodel = garcon.connect(...)`) from notebooks or scripts. Servers launched from notebooks reuse existing instances and shut down automatically after one hour of inactivity.

The core abstraction is a set of named **probe points** inside the model. Users attach **probe functions**, which are arbitrary Python code serialized with cloudpickle and run on the server. A probe function receives a persistent per-connection save context and the tensor at that point. It returns either a replacement tensor or None, following the PyTorch hook convention. Probes work with forward passes and with backward passes against a user-supplied loss. Parameters are exposed through the same naming scheme.

**Experiments**
There are no controlled experiments. The document describes:
- Example usage patterns:
  - saving MLP post-activations;
  - zero-ablating a single neuron (mean ablation is mentioned as an alternative).
- Design motivations:
  - capture only the data requested;
  - compute reductions server-side, such as single positions or L2 norms, which saves bandwidth and exploits GPU parallelism;
  - keep state on the server, for example incrementally maintaining top-10 activating dataset examples per MLP neuron over potentially millions of training examples.
- Implementation:
  - about 1,000 lines of code;
  - one process per GPU running in lockstep;
  - rank 0 handles RPC and broadcasts requests, then gathers results;
  - large tensors are sent more directly than pickles.

**Key results**
The evidence is qualitative and from a single organization. Garçon is reportedly used for essentially all of Anthropic's interpretability work and has been adopted by other teams for ad-hoc exploration.

The authors report benefits even for small models:
- a consistent interface across models;
- higher throughput;
- long-running hosted servers that greatly reduce "time to first plot."

The authors say stateful server-side aggregation is "orders of magnitude" faster than returning full activations, but give no benchmarks. They see the main contribution as a workflow philosophy: every trained model is immediately available for interpretability, combining notebook flexibility with cluster scale.

**Limitations / open questions**
- No quantitative performance, latency or usability measurements are reported.
- The implementation is tightly coupled to Anthropic's internal infrastructure and has not been released.
- The probe interface is described as stateful and somewhat unwieldy.
- Higher-level abstractions are left to future work; one simpler wrapper, `easy_garcon`, exists for single-context analysis.

title: Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits
summary:
**Central idea**

This introductory essay for the Distill Circuits thread argues that interpretability can "zoom in". Individual neurons and weights can be treated as objects of serious study, much as cell biology treats cells. It puts forward three deliberately speculative claims, framed as both empirical and normative:

1. **Features.** Features are the fundamental unit of neural networks. They correspond to directions in activation space, often individual neurons, and they can be rigorously understood.
2. **Circuits.** Features are connected by weights into circuits, which are computational subgraphs that implement meaningful, readable algorithms.
3. **Universality.** Analogous features and circuits form across models and tasks.

It also argues that interpretability is pre-paradigmatic in Kuhn's sense. It proposes a natural-science standard of falsifiable claims about small circuits as a possible epistemic foundation for the field.

**Experiments**

The work is qualitative and based on case studies, almost entirely in InceptionV1 trained on ImageNet.

- **Curve detectors (mixed3b).** These are supported by seven lines of evidence:
  - feature visualization
  - ImageNet dataset examples
  - synthetic stimuli
  - joint tuning under rotation
  - the implementing weights
  - downstream use
  - a hand-written reimplementation of the circuit
- **High-low frequency detectors.** These are early-vision boundary heuristics.
- **A pose-invariant dog-head detector.**
- **Circuits:**
  - an early-curve to curve circuit with tangent-curve weight structure and rotational equivariance
  - a four-layer circuit with mirrored left- and right-facing dog-head pathways that inhibit each other and then are "unioned" into invariant units
  - a car detector in mixed4c whose feature is spread into dog-detecting neurons in the next layer

**Key results**

- With enough effort, neurons, including initially puzzling ones, usually have simple explanations.
- Weights between understood features are interpretable, so algorithms can be read off them.
- The essay identifies recurring **circuit motifs**: equivariance, unioning over cases, and superposition.
- It introduces **polysemantic neurons**, such as neuron 4e:55, which responds to cat faces, car fronts and cat legs.
- It names **superposition**, explained as packing features into nearly-orthogonal directions to save neurons. The car-into-dog example suggests polysemanticity is in some sense "deliberate".
- Universality evidence is explicitly anecdotal. Curve and high-low frequency detectors were seen in AlexNet, InceptionV1, VGG19 and ResNetV2-50, in Places365-trained models, and in vanilla conv nets trained from scratch.

**Limitations / open questions**

- The claims are stated as speculative, and the evidence is qualitative and limited to vision models, mostly a single model.
- There are no quantitative metrics, and the weight-editing tests of the circuit theories are deferred to future articles.
- Polysemanticity is acknowledged as a major obstacle, since connections between polysemantic neurons cannot be considered individually.
- A "long tail" of small weights is left unexplained.
- Multiplying the 1x1 and 5x5 convolution weights together ignores one ReLU.
- Whether universality is the rule or the exception for low-level features remains open.

title: https://transformer-circuits.pub/2022/phase-change
The Surprising Simplicity of the Early-Time Learning Dynamics of Neural Networks
Towards the Science of Security and Privacy in Machine Learning
Info-gan: Interpretable representation learning by information maximizing generative adversarial nets
Transformer Circuits Thread
Advances in Neural Information Processing
Analyzing Transformers in Embedding Space
abstract: Understanding Transformer-based models has attracted significant attention, as they lie at the heart of recent technological advances across machine learning. While most interpretability methods rely on running models over inputs, recent work has shown that a zero-pass approach, where parameters are interpreted directly without a forward/backward pass is feasible for some Transformer parameters, and for two-layer attention networks. In this work, we present a theoretical analysis where all parameters of a trained Transformer are interpreted by projecting them into the embedding space, that is, the space of vocabulary items they operate on. We derive a simple theoretical framework to support our arguments and provide ample evidence for its validity. First, an empirical analysis showing that parameters of both pretrained and fine-tuned models can be interpreted in embedding space. Second, we present two applications of our framework: (a) aligning the parameters of different models that share a vocabulary, and (b) constructing a classifier without training by ``translating'' the parameters of a fine-tuned classifier to parameters of a different model that was only pretrained. Overall, our findings open the door to interpretation methods that, at least in part, abstract away from model specifics and operate in the embedding space only.
summary:
**Central idea**
The paper proposes a zero-pass, input-independent framework for interpreting *all* parameters of a trained Transformer by projecting them into the embedding (vocabulary) space. It unifies Geva et al.'s projection of FF value vectors and Elhage et al.'s QK/OV interaction matrices for 2-layer attention-only models. Inner products in the model are rewritten as inner products in embedding space using a right-inverse E' of the embedding matrix E. This gives vocabulary-level readings of FF values (vE), FF keys (kE'^T), attention subheads, and e×e interaction matrices E'W_QK E'^T and E'W_VO E. In practice E' = E^T is used instead of the pseudo-inverse, justified by a new "keep-k robust invertibility" criterion. LayerNorm and biases are ignored. The framework requires a linear LM head (GPT family), and the main analyses use GPT-2 medium.

**Experiments**
- Qualitative inspection of top-k vocabulary pairs of W_VO and W_QK in GPT-2 base, medium, and large, and of FF key/value pairs. Heads were selected manually.
- Knowledge lookup: FF values are ranked by their dot product with averaged seed-token embeddings.
- R_k overlap test on GPT-2 medium over 60 IMDB examples (k=100). Top-k tokens of the most-activated parameter vectors (FF keys/values, W_V/W_O subheads) are compared with top-k tokens of the aligned hidden state and of a randomly sampled hidden state.
- The top 3 layers of GPT-2 base are fine-tuned on IMDB, and the parameter differences are projected into embedding space.
- Layer alignment between MultiBERTs seeds: embedding-space projections are correlated, then matched with the Hungarian algorithm.
- Zero-shot stitching: GPT-2 medium hidden states are mapped through E_A E_B^+ into the fine-tuned top layers of GPT-2 base.
- Keep-k comparison of E^T vs E^+ for GPT-2 base, medium, and large.

**Key results**
- Heads show interpretable relations: subword/name completion, gender, geography, British spelling, and related words.
- R_k for aligned hidden states exceeds the random-hidden-state baseline across layers.
- Corresponding key/value and subhead pairs share more top-k tokens (Jaccard) than shuffled pairs.
- Fine-tuning diffs in W_Q, W_K, W_V and FF keys project to sentiment words (e.g., 3–4 of 4 sampled vectors per layer). FF values showed 0 of 4 such vectors in each layer, and W_O also did not show this pattern.
- Same-index layers align across BERT seeds in embedding space, while the unprojected alignment looks random.
- Stitching gave about 70% IMDB accuracy for 3 of 11 runs when stitching from top layers; the others were near chance.
- For small k, E^T scores 0.83 vs 0.10 for E^+ on Gaussian vectors at k=1000, but the pattern reverses at large k. GPT-2 large shows erratic behavior.

**Limitations / open questions**
Evidence is largely qualitative and relies on manually selected heads. The framework ignores LayerNorm and nonlinear LM heads. Stitching is inconsistent across runs. The quantitative tests are small (60 examples). The provided text is truncated partway through Appendix D (W_K subheads).

title: Toward Transparent AI: A Survey on Interpreting the Inner Structures of Deep Neural Networks
Hidden Progress in Deep Learning: SGD Learns Parities Near the Computational Limit
Shifting machine learning for healthcare from development to deployment and from models to data
Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models
X-Risk Analysis for AI Research
Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT
abstract: We analyze the storage and recall of factual associations in autoregressive transformer language models, finding evidence that these associations correspond to localized, directly-editable computations. We first develop a causal intervention for identifying neuron activations that are decisive in a model's factual predictions. This reveals a distinct set of steps in middle-layer feed-forward modules that mediate factual predictions while processing subject tokens. To test our hypothesis that these computations correspond to factual association recall, we modify feed-forward weights to update specific factual associations using Rank-One Model Editing (ROME). We find that ROME is effective on a standard zero-shot relation extraction (zsRE) model-editing task, comparable to existing methods. To perform a more sensitive evaluation, we also evaluate ROME on a new dataset of counterfactual assertions, on which it simultaneously maintains both specificity and generalization, whereas other methods sacrifice one or another. Our results confirm an important role for mid-layer feed-forward modules in storing factual associations and suggest that direct manipulation of computational mechanisms may be a feasible approach for model editing. The code, dataset, visualizations, and an interactive demo notebook are available at https://rome.baulab.info/
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper asks where autoregressive transformers store factual associations (subject, relation, object), such as "The Space Needle is in ... Seattle". It answers with two kinds of intervention.

- **Causal Tracing**: a causal-mediation method. The subject token embeddings are corrupted with Gaussian noise (3x the embedding standard deviation). Individual clean hidden states are then restored, and the method measures how much each restored state brings back the correct prediction. This is the indirect effect.
- **Rank-One Model Editing (ROME)**: a closed-form rank-one update to a single mid-layer MLP output matrix. It treats W_proj as a linear associative memory.

Together these support a "localized factual association hypothesis":

- Mid-layer MLPs at the **last subject token** act as key-value stores that recall properties of the subject.
- Late-layer attention then copies that information to the final token.

**Experiments**

- **Causal tracing in GPT-2 XL**: run on 1000 known facts in GPT-2 XL (1.5B). Restoration was decomposed into hidden-state, MLP and attention components.
- **Severed-MLP traces**: a modified causal graph freezes MLP outputs in their corrupted state, to isolate path-specific effects.
- **Replication across models**: traces were repeated on GPT-2 Medium, GPT-2 Large, GPT-J (6B) and GPT-NeoX (20B).
- **Robustness checks**: alternative corruption schemes were tested, plus a comparison against Integrated Gradients.
- **How ROME works**: the key k* is the averaged MLP activation at the last subject token. The value v* is optimized so the model predicts the new object, with a KL term that limits "essence drift". The update is W + Λ(C⁻¹k*)ᵀ, where C is the key covariance estimated from Wikipedia.
- **Editing benchmarks**:
  - zsRE (10k records).
  - **CounterFact**, a new dataset of 21,919 hard counterfactual edits. It has paraphrase, neighborhood, generation-consistency and fluency metrics.
  - Baselines were FT, FT+L, Knowledge Neurons, KE and MEND.
- **Layer/token sweep**: ROME was applied at every layer and token position.
- **Attention editing**: an attention-weight editing baseline (AttnEdit).
- **Human evaluation**: 15 volunteers rated 50 edits.

**Key results**

- **Two causal sites in GPT-2 XL**:
  - The average total effect is 18.6%.
  - An early site at the last subject token reaches AIE 8.7% at layer 15. There, MLP contributions (AIE 6.6%) dominate attention (1.6%).
  - Attention dominates the late site at the final token.
- **Severed-MLP result**: freezing MLPs removes the causal effect of low-layer states.
- **Generality**: the pattern holds across model sizes. Integrated Gradients maps are scattered and do not reveal it.
- **Editing success peaks where tracing points**: ROME works best at mid layers (peaking near layer 18) at the last subject token.
- **CounterFact scores**:
  - ROME scores S = 89.2 on GPT-2 XL, against 66.9 for FT+L, the next best.
  - On GPT-J it scores 91.5.
  - Other methods either overfit (poor generalization) or bleed over to neighboring subjects.
- **zsRE**: ROME is competitive (99.8 efficacy, 88.1 paraphrase).
- **Attention editing**: AttnEdit regurgitates the target but fails to generalize.
- **Human ratings**: ROME was judged 1.8x more consistent than FT+L but somewhat less fluent.

**Limitations / open questions**

- ROME edits one fact at a time; mass editing is left to MEMIT.
- Edits are directional.
- Only factual (subject-relation-object) knowledge is studied.
- Causal tracing depends on the noise-corruption choice, and small noise yields weak effects.
- The decisive token is not always the last subject token.
- Attention appears more involved in GPT-J and GPT-NeoX.
- The authors conjecture that any middle layer can store a fact equivalently. The success of the edits is taken as evidence about storage, though editing success need not imply that the fact was originally stored there.
- Edited models may confabulate related facts.

title: Natural Language Descriptions of Deep Visual Features
abstract: Some neurons in deep networks specialize in recognizing highly specific perceptual, structural, or semantic features of inputs. In computer vision, techniques exist for identifying neurons that respond to individual concept categories like colors, textures, and object classes. But these techniques are limited in scope, labeling only a small subset of neurons and behaviors in any network. Is a richer characterization of neuron-level computation possible? We introduce a procedure (called MILAN, for mutual-information-guided linguistic annotation of neurons) that automatically labels neurons with open-ended, compositional, natural language descriptions. Given a neuron, MILAN generates a description by searching for a natural language string that maximizes pointwise mutual information with the image regions in which the neuron is active. MILAN produces fine-grained descriptions that capture categorical, relational, and logical structure in learned features. These descriptions obtain high agreement with human-generated feature descriptions across a diverse set of model architectures and tasks, and can aid in understanding and controlling learned models. We highlight three applications of natural language neuron descriptions. First, we use MILAN for analysis, characterizing the distribution and importance of neurons selective for attribute, category, and relational information in vision models. Second, we use MILAN for auditing, surfacing neurons sensitive to human faces in datasets designed to obscure them. Finally, we use MILAN for editing, improving robustness in an image classifier by deleting neurons sensitive to text features spuriously correlated with class labels.
summary:
**Central idea**

Prior automated neuron labeling (NetDissect, Compositional Explanations) picks from a fixed inventory of concepts. MILAN instead generates open-ended natural-language descriptions of individual vision neurons. Each neuron is represented by an exemplar set: the top k=15 images, with masks marking where activation exceeds the 0.99 quantile. MILAN then searches for the description d maximizing weighted PMI, log p(d|E) - lambda log p(d), with lambda=0.2. Here p(d|E) is a modified Show-Attend-Tell captioner over mask-pooled multi-layer ResNet101 features, and p(d) is a two-layer LSTM language model. Candidates come from a beam search of size 50 over p(d|E) and are then reranked. Both models are trained on MILANNOTATIONS, a new dataset of about 20k neurons from 7 models (AlexNet and ResNet152 on ImageNet/Places365, BigGAN on ImageNet/Places365, and DINO ViT MLP units on ImageNet), with 3 MTurk descriptions per neuron (60k annotations).

**Experiments**

- (1) Generalization, measured by BERTScore against human annotations on held-out neurons: within-network, cross-architecture, cross-dataset and cross-task splits, plus comparison with NetDissect, Compositional Explanations and a p(d|E)-only captioning ablation.
- (2) Analysis: label all ResNet18-ImageNet neurons, score them by syntactic and structural properties of their descriptions, and cumulatively ablate 2% per step while measuring ImageNet validation accuracy against 5 random orderings.
- (3) Auditing: compare face-related neurons in 12 face-blurred ImageNet models with their unblurred torchvision counterparts.
- (4) Editing: train ResNet18 on a 10-class ImageNet subset in which half the training images carry correct text labels, then ablate MILAN-identified text neurons.

**Key results**

- **Agreement with humans.** On held-out networks MILAN scores BERTScore .31-.38, versus .21-.25 for NetDissect, .01-.03 for Compositional Explanations, and .27-.34 for p(d|E) alone. Human inter-annotator agreement is .17-.27.
- **Generalization.** Scores range from .27 (BigGAN to classifiers) to .52 (within BigGAN-Places). CNN-to-ViT transfer scores .34. Transfer is asymmetric across tasks.
- **Neuron importance.** Neurons described with many adjectives or prepositions are disproportionately important. Neurons whose descriptions contain semantically dissimilar words are less important than random neurons.
- **Face auditing.** MILAN finds 213 face-selective neurons in unblurred models and 142 in blurred models, some of which appear to prefer female or Asian faces.
- **Spurious-feature editing.** MILAN flags 300 of 1024 units as text-related. Ablating 13 of them raises adversarial test accuracy from 58.8% by 4.9 points. Choosing the count by validation accuracy alone (8 neurons) gives a 3.1-point gain. Ablating arbitrary neurons in the same importance order gives less than 1 point.

**Limitations / open questions**

- The authors frame BERTScore agreement as a sanity check, not as proof of usefulness.
- Failure modes include wrong concepts (brass instruments called noodle dishes), vague labels, and describing the context instead of the highlighted region.
- Descriptions rest on top-activating exemplars only, so they are partial and noisy. The paper cites the BERT interpretability illusion as a known shortcoming of this approach.
- The face audit relies on manual inspection of keyword-matched neurons.
- The editing gain is modest and does not remove reliance on text.

title: A Literature Survey of Recent Advances in Chatbots
Causal Analysis of Syntactic Agreement Mechanisms in Neural Language Models
abstract: Targeted syntactic evaluations have demonstrated the ability of language models to perform subject-verb agreement given difficult contexts. To elucidate the mechanisms by which the models accomplish this behavior, this study applies causal mediation analysis to pre-trained neural language models. We investigate the magnitude of models' preferences for grammatical inflections, as well as whether neurons process subject-verb agreement similarly across sentences with different syntactic structures. We uncover similarities and differences across architectures and model sizes -- notably, that larger models do not necessarily learn stronger preferences. We also observe two distinct mechanisms for producing subject-verb agreement depending on the syntactic structure of the input sentence. Finally, we find that language models rely on similar sets of neurons when given sentences with similar syntactic structure.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper applies causal mediation analysis to English subject–verb agreement, asking which representation coordinates mediate changes in verb-inflection preferences when a subject’s grammatical number changes. Different layerwise mediation profiles suggest adjacency-dependent mechanisms in GPT-2 and Transformer-XL, whereas XLNet shows similar profiles across structures.

**Experiments**

The authors sample 300 prompts per syntactic structure from synthetic noun–verb combinations. Six structures cover simple agreement, agreement within or across object relative clauses, one or two intervening adverbs, and intervening prepositional phrases. Relative clauses are evaluated with and without “that.” Models include DistilGPT-2, GPT-2 Small/Medium/Large/XL, Transformer-XL, and XLNet, with random-weight GPT-2 controls. Total effect measures the proportional change in the originally incorrect-to-correct verb probability ratio after swapping subject number. Grammaticality measures the correct-to-incorrect probability ratio for a specified subject number. Individual-coordinate natural indirect effects replace a coordinate with its counterfactual value while preserving the original prompt. Layerwise plots average effects over the highest-NIE 5% of coordinates, selected separately for each layer and structure.

**Key results**

Larger GPT-2 variants do not consistently have larger total effects; adjacent agreement produces effects around 1,000–5,000. Intervening adverbs increase total effects, while noun-attractor phrases reduce them. GPT-2 Medium’s displayed grammaticality comparisons favor plural subjects across structures and attractor-number conditions. In GPT-2 and Transformer-XL, adjacent dependencies show effects increasing toward later layers; separated dependencies peak at layer 0 and upper-middle layers before approaching zero in final layers. XLNet lacks this split. Larger GPT-2 models show lower individual-coordinate effects and broader layerwise peaks. High-effect coordinate overlap partly matches a designed syntactic-similarity matrix, especially at GPT-2 Medium layer 21 of 24. Randomized controls have near-zero total effects and little higher-layer mediation.

**Limitations / open questions**

Mediation profiles do not reconstruct agreement algorithms or establish that similar profiles reflect one mechanism. Joint neuron interventions remain unexplored. Overlap comparisons select each model’s best-matching layer; the reference matrix uses manually adjusted feature weighting and lacks independent validation. XLNet’s similar profiles coexist with relatively low coordinate overlap. Attention findings depend on intervention choice. Findings concern synthetic English number agreement; permutation training as the explanation for XLNet’s behavior remains conjectural.

title: Causal Abstractions of Neural Networks
abstract: Structural analysis methods (e.g., probing and feature attribution) are increasingly important tools for neural network analysis. We propose a new structural analysis method grounded in a formal theory of causal abstraction that provides rich characterizations of model-internal representations and their roles in input/output behavior. In this method, neural representations are aligned with variables in interpretable causal models, and then interchange interventions are used to experimentally verify that the neural representations have the causal properties of their aligned variables. We apply this method in a case study to analyze neural models trained on Multiply Quantified Natural Language Inference (MQNLI) corpus, a highly complex NLI dataset that was constructed with a tree-structured natural logic causal model. We discover that a BERT-based model with state-of-the-art performance successfully realizes parts of the natural logic model’s causal structure, whereas a simpler baseline model fails to show any such structure, demonstrating that BERT representations encode the compositional structure of MQNLI.
summary:
**Central idea**

Causal abstraction analysis tests whether neural representations realize a specified high-level causal computation. Researchers formulate an interpretable causal model, search for alignments between its variables and neural representations, and interchange representations between source and base examples. Corresponding interventions in the neural and high-level models should produce matching counterfactual outputs. The method targets represented information together with its causal role.

**Experiments**

The case study uses Multiply Quantified Natural Language Inference (MQNLI), a templated dataset involving quantifiers, negation, and modifiers, labeled by a tree-structured natural logic algorithm. The authors fine-tune English bert-base and train a randomly initialized multilayer BiLSTM, supervising relations between aligned phrases. For each candidate variable and neural location, they evaluate one million ordered interchange pairs from 1,000 examples selected for correct model predictions. They report the largest mutually successful cliques found, requiring at least one intervention that changes the high-level output. They also probe representations using 12,800 randomly selected examples, measuring accuracy and control-task selectivity. Integrated-gradients experiments are reported to confirm greater importance for tokens differing between premise and hypothesis, but their detailed results are in an unavailable appendix.

**Key results**

On MQNLI’s hardest fair generalization task, BERT achieves 88.50% test accuracy, versus 46.32% for BiLSTM and approximately 49.1% for BERT without pretraining. The strongest abstraction alignment maps the object noun-phrase relation to BERT’s fourth-layer representation above the premise object-adjective token. Its successful clique contains 383 of the 1,000 selected examples, compared with seven for BiLSTM’s best alignment for that variable. All tested neighboring causal models, formed by adding or removing lexical inputs, yield smaller BERT cliques. Probe accuracy and selectivity indicate relation information at many more locations than show corresponding interchange behavior. An explicit linear-network construction proves that perfect decoding can coexist with zero causal influence. A separate derivation expresses integrated gradients as weighted averages of limiting coordinate-intervention effects.

**Limitations / open questions**

The abstraction results concern selected finite subsets of correctly classified examples and separately tested variables. They do not establish that BERT implements the complete natural logic model across MQNLI. Alignment searches cover restricted token locations, and intervention counts grow quadratically with sample size. No uncertainty estimates or variation across training runs are supplied. Generalization to unrestricted language remains open. The supplied text includes the main paper and references but omits appendices containing formal abstraction details, training specifications, and additional experimental results.

title: An Interpretability Illusion for BERT
abstract: We describe an "interpretability illusion" that arises when analyzing the BERT model. Activations of individual neurons in the network may spuriously appear to encode a single, simple concept, when in fact they are encoding something far more complex. The same effect holds for linear combinations of activations. We trace the source of this illusion to geometric properties of BERT's embedding space as well as the fact that common text corpora represent only narrow slices of possible English sentences. We provide a taxonomy of model-learned concepts and discuss methodological implications for interpretability research, especially the importance of testing hypotheses on multiple data sets.
summary:
**Central idea**

A coherent pattern among a neuron's highest-activating examples can depend on the corpus and need not characterize its general function. The paper demonstrates this interpretability illusion in BERT and distinguishes global concept directions, dataset-level directions, and local semantic clusters. It recommends validating interpretations across datasets.

**Experiments**

The authors use unmodified BERT-base uncased from HuggingFace, representing sentences by raw, 768-dimensional final-layer [CLS] states. They embed 624,712 sentences: QQP, 164,246; QNLI, 58,645; Wikipedia, 203,736; and sampled BookCorpus, 198,085. Two annotators assess each group of ten sentences, knowing its dataset but blinded to whether selection used neuron activations, random-direction projections, or random sampling. Reported annotation totals are 25 neurons, 33 random directions, and 29 random sentence sets. Further analyses examine UMAP clusters, linear SVM dataset classification, token frequencies across activation quintiles, neighborhood-similarity histograms, and removal of QQP outliers.

**Key results**

Both annotators find patterns in 20/25 neuron groups (80%), 27/33 random-direction groups (82%), and 4/29 random groups (14%). The authors report an average of 2.5 distinct patterns per neuron across datasets. For example, neuron 221's top examples concern song questions in QQP, dated events in QNLI, and physical actions involving objects in Books. Dataset embeddings cluster separately, and the SVM reportedly distinguishes them accurately; numerical accuracy is unavailable in the supplied text.

Meaningful examples have higher mean locality scores than meaningless examples: 0.026 versus 0.010 overall, p=0.0004. For 915 tokens occurring at least 100 times in every corpus, 22.7–29.6% of neuron/token pairs show monotonic frequency trends within an individual dataset. Only 1.9% are monotonic in each of all four datasets; 0.8% increase throughout all four and 0.8% decrease throughout all four. QQP's most distant 1% of sentences account for 48% of top activations, but the authors report that the illusion persists after removing the most distant 1% or 10%.

**Limitations / open questions**

Systematic evidence concerns one model's final-layer sentence representations; earlier-layer observations are informal. Pattern judgments vary across annotators, and token frequencies are imperfect concept proxies. Locality establishes an association and cannot alone distinguish local from global concepts; two dataset-specific comparisons have p>0.05. No causal intervention establishes what these coordinates compute. Classifier splits and quantitative post-outlier-removal results are unspecified. Generalization to token representations, other models, and other modalities remains open.

title: Transformer Feed-Forward Layers Are Key-Value Memories
abstract: Feed-forward layers constitute two-thirds of a transformer model's parameters, yet their role in the network remains under-explored. We show that feed-forward layers in transformer-based language models operate as key-value memories, where each key correlates with textual patterns in the training examples, and each value induces a distribution over the output vocabulary. Our experiments show that the learned patterns are human-interpretable, and that lower layers tend to capture shallow patterns, while upper layers learn more semantic ones. The values complement the keys' input patterns by inducing output distributions that concentrate probability mass on tokens likely to appear immediately after each pattern, particularly in the upper layers. Finally, we demonstrate that the output of a feed-forward layer is a composition of its memories, which is subsequently refined throughout the model's layers via residual connections to produce the final output distribution.
summary:
**Central idea**

A transformer feed-forward (MLP) layer, FF(x) = f(x K^T) V, is almost identical to an unnormalized key-value neural memory (Sukhbaatar et al. 2015). The only difference is the use of ReLU instead of softmax. Each row of the first matrix is a *key* that detects a pattern in the input prefix. The ReLU activation is the *memory coefficient*. Each row of the second matrix is a *value*, and projecting it through the output embedding gives a distribution over the vocabulary. The layer's output is the coefficient-weighted sum of values. The residual stream then composes these outputs across layers to build the final prediction bottom-up.

**Experiments**

All experiments use the 16-layer, 247M-parameter adaptive-input transformer LM of Baevski and Auli (2019), trained on WikiText-103 (d=1024, d_m=4096 per layer).

- **Key analysis.** The authors sampled 160 keys (10 per layer) and retrieved the top-25 training-set sentence prefixes with the highest memory coefficient for each. NLP graduate students annotated recurring patterns (found in 3 or more prefixes) and labelled each as shallow (n-gram) or semantic (topic).
- **Perturbation test.** For 1,600 keys, they removed the first, last, or a random token from each of the top-50 triggers and measured the change in the coefficient.
- **Value analysis.** Each value was projected onto the output embedding (adaptive softmax). They measured agreement between the value's top token and the next token of the key's top-1 trigger, and where that next token ranks.
- **Aggregation analysis.** On 4,000 validation prefixes they measured:
  - the fraction of active memories;
  - how often the layer's top prediction differs from every individual memory's top prediction;
  - how often the residual's top token (read out through the output embedding) already matches the final output;
  - a breakdown of residual / FFN / agreement / composition cases.

**Key results**

- **Keys detect interpretable patterns.** Every sampled key had at least one recognizable pattern, with an average of 3.6 patterns per key, and 65-80% of trigger prefixes were covered by a pattern.
- **Shallow to semantic with depth.** Layers 1-9 are dominated by shallow patterns, often a shared last word. Layers 10-16 show more semantic patterns. Removing the last token hurts lower-layer coefficients most.
- **Values predict next tokens in upper layers.** Value-key agreement is near zero in layers 1-10 and rises to about 3.5% in upper layers, compared with 0.0004% at chance. Of the 100 most confident values, 97 lie in layers 11-16, and 46 of them agree with at least one top-50 trigger.
- **Layer outputs are compositional.**
  - A typical input activates 10-50% of the memories in a layer.
  - In at least about 68% of examples, the layer's top prediction differs from every one of its memories' top predictions.
  - Single-memory agreement is mostly for stop words or short prefixes, suggesting such common patterns are 'cached' in single memories.
- **The residual stream refines predictions.**
  - About one third of final predictions are already the residual's top token in the bottom layers, and this fraction rises sharply from layer 10.
  - When the FFN changes the residual's top token, the result is usually a 'compromise' token rather than the FFN's own top token. The authors conjecture the FFN acts as a 'veto' mechanism.

**Limitations / open questions**

- Only one model and one dataset are studied.
- Pattern annotation is manual: one annotator per key and a small sample.
- The analysis is correlational, based on top-activating examples, with no causal interventions.
- Projecting values through the output embedding naively assumes a shared embedding space across layers. It works poorly for lower layers, which raises the question of how the representation space changes with depth.
- Generalization to BERT or translation models is left for future work. So are the privacy implications, such as membership inference.

title: Compositional Explanations of Neurons
abstract: We describe a procedure for explaining neurons in deep representations by identifying compositional logical concepts that closely approximate neuron behavior. Compared to prior work that uses atomic labels as explanations, analyzing neurons compositionally allows us to more precisely and expressively characterize their behavior. We use this procedure to answer several questions on interpretability in models for vision and natural language processing. First, we examine the kinds of abstractions learned by neurons. In image classification, we find that many neurons learn highly abstract but semantically coherent visual concepts, while other polysemantic neurons detect multiple unrelated features; in natural language inference (NLI), neurons learn shallow lexical heuristics from dataset biases. Second, we see whether compositional explanations give us insight into model performance: vision neurons that detect human-interpretable concepts are positively correlated with task performance, while NLI neurons that fire for shallow heuristics are negatively correlated with task performance. Finally, we show how compositional explanations provide an accessible way for end users to produce simple "copy-paste" adversarial examples that change model behavior in predictable ways.
summary:
**Central idea**

Individual neurons can be described more precisely by logical combinations of annotated concepts than by single concept labels. The method extends Network Dissection using beam search with width 10 over AND, OR, and NOT formulas, maximizing intersection over union (IoU) between concept masks and thresholded neuron activations. For language, a Neighbors operator combines five nearby GloVe words.

**Experiments**

The vision study examines all 512 units in the final convolutional layer of a Places365-trained ResNet-18, using ADE20K images and 1,105 Broden concepts. Activation masks retain each neuron's highest 0.5% of pixel activations. The language study examines the penultimate 1,024-unit MLP layer of an SNLI-trained BiLSTM classifier, retaining neurons active on at least 500 of 10,000 validation examples. Language concepts include the 2,000 most common words, part-of-speech tags, premise/hypothesis location, and lexical-overlap thresholds. Further analyses correlate explanation IoU with accuracy on inputs activating each neuron and construct explanation-guided input edits.

**Key results**

For ResNet-18, increasing maximum formula length from one to ten raises mean IoU from 0.059 to 0.099, a reported 68% improvement (p = 2 × 10⁻⁹). Manual inspection of 128 randomly sampled units classifies 88 (69%) as detecting meaningful combinations and 40 (31%) as responding to at least some unrelated concepts. NLI explanations identify individual units associated with gender mismatches, contradiction-associated words, and lexical overlap; IoU continues improving beyond length 30. Longer explanations also reduce repeated formula labels across neurons in both models.

Across neurons, IoU correlates positively with conditional model accuracy in vision (r = 0.31, length-ten explanations) and negatively in NLI (r = −0.60, length-three explanations). Selected image patches, color changes, and word insertions alter predictions in anticipated directions. Some vision examples transfer to Places365-trained AlexNet, ResNet-50, and DenseNet-161, while others remain model-specific.

**Limitations / open questions**

These are CNN and BiLSTM studies, with no transformer or LLM evaluation. IoU measures binary activation agreement; substantial vision behavior remains unexplained, and separate held-out evaluation of fitted explanations is not reported. Explanations depend on annotation coverage, thresholds, and restricted search; distributed concepts can be missed. Conditional-accuracy correlations do not establish causal contributions, and input edits do not isolate neuronal mediation. Adversarial demonstrations lack aggregate success rates and vary with patch size and position. Earlier layers, faithful neuron replacement, pruning, and interpretability-based training remain open questions.

title: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners (GPT-3)
The Context
Are Sixteen Heads Really Better than One?
Attention is not Explanation
abstract: Attention mechanisms have seen wide adoption in neural NLP models. In addition to improving predictive performance, these are often touted as affording transparency: models equipped with attention provide a distribution over attended-to input units, and this is often presented (at least implicitly) as communicating the relative importance of inputs. However, it is unclear what relationship exists between attention weights and model outputs. In this work, we perform extensive experiments across a variety of NLP tasks that aim to assess the degree to which attention weights provide meaningful `explanations' for predictions. We find that they largely do not. For example, learned attention weights are frequently uncorrelated with gradient-based measures of feature importance, and one can identify very different attention distributions that nonetheless yield equivalent predictions. Our findings show that standard attention modules do not provide meaningful explanations and should not be treated as though they do. Code for all experiments is available at https://github.com/successar/AttentionExplanation.
summary:
**Central idea**
Attention over contextual hidden states should not automatically be interpreted as the importance of the corresponding input words. The paper evaluates this interpretation through agreement with alternative importance measures and sensitivity to counterfactual attention distributions. Its evidence primarily concerns attentive BiLSTMs rather than transformer language models.

**Experiments**
Seven binary classification tasks cover SST, IMDB, adverse-drug-reaction tweets, baseball versus hockey, world versus business news, and two MIMIC clinical tasks. Additional evaluations use CNN cloze QA, bAbI tasks 1–3, and SNLI. BiLSTMs generally use 300-dimensional embeddings and hidden size 128; bAbI uses 50 and 30. Comparators include independently projected embeddings with ReLU and CNN encoders. Additive attention receives the main presentation; scaled dot-product results are reported as generally comparable.

On test examples, Kendall τ compares attention rankings with absolute derivatives for the observed input tokens, computed with attention held fixed, and leave-one-word-out output changes. Counterfactual tests hold encoder states fixed, sample 100 attention permutations per example, and optimize alternative distributions for large Jensen–Shannon divergence (JSD), subject to output total variation distance (TVD) constraints. Stated tolerances are 0.01 for text classification and 0.05 for QA; an NLI-specific tolerance is not separately stated.

**Key results**
BiLSTM correlations are generally modest. Class-specific mean attention–gradient τ is approximately 0.385–0.395 on SST and 0.081–0.131 on baseball/hockey, versus approximately 0.691 and 0.654–0.655 for projected-embedding encoders. CNN-QA's BiLSTM mean is 0.197. Gradient and erasure scores generally agree more strongly with each other than attention agrees with either; SNLI is an exception to the reported attention–LOO comparison. Random permutations often produce small output changes, even with concentrated original attention. Optimized alternatives frequently approach the attention-JSD ceiling of approximately 0.69 while meeting the output tolerance; no overall success fraction is tabulated. Positive diabetes predictions show greater attention sensitivity and less divergent admissible alternatives.

**Limitations / open questions**
Gradient and erasure scores are imperfect comparators, and irrelevant tokens can depress rank correlations. Alternative attention distributions may be unlikely under the trained attention module or represent multiple sufficient rationales. Encoder comparisons do not uniformly match competence: non-recurrent encoders perform markedly worse on QA, and BiLSTM bAbI 2/3 accuracies are only 0.48/0.62. The experiments do not establish conclusions for transformer self-attention, sequence-to-sequence outputs, or constrained attention variants. The supplied rendering contains malformed equations and figure cross-references.

Causal Mediation Analysis for Interpreting Neural NLP: The Case of Gender Bias
abstract: Common methods for interpreting neural models in natural language processing typically examine either their structure or their behavior, but not both. We propose a methodology grounded in the theory of causal mediation analysis for interpreting which parts of a model are causally implicated in its behavior. It enables us to analyze the mechanisms by which information flows from input to output through various model components, known as mediators. We apply this methodology to analyze gender bias in pre-trained Transformer language models. We study the role of individual neurons and attention heads in mediating gender bias across three datasets designed to gauge a model's sensitivity to gender bias. Our mediation analysis reveals that gender bias effects are (i) sparse, concentrated in a small part of the network; (ii) synergistic, amplified or repressed by different components; and (iii) decomposable into effects flowing directly from the input and indirectly through the mediators.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper adapts causal mediation analysis to language models. Input edits supply treatments; representation coordinates or attention weights supply mediators. Natural direct effects change the input while retaining original mediator values; natural indirect effects transplant edited-input mediator values into the original computation. The primary outcome is the anti-stereotypical/stereotypical candidate probability ratio; effects are proportional changes relative to its original value.

**Experiments**

Experiments cover five GPT-2 variants, a randomly initialized GPT-2-small control, and selected analyses of Transformer-XL, XLNet, BERT, DistilBERT, and RoBERTa. Professions contains 17 templates × 169 single-token terms, totaling 2,873 examples; definitionally gendered terms are excluded from total-effect calculations. Interventions replace profession-position coordinates after occupation-to-gender-word edits. Attention experiments swap pronouns and replace pronoun-position attention weights. Format-compatible Winobias contains 160 development and 130 test examples; Winogender contains 44. Default attention results additionally remove negative-total-effect examples and the bottom quartile of positive effects, yielding model-dependent subsets. Multi-token continuations use geometric-mean token probabilities. Further tests vary effect metrics and masked-model scoring schemes.

**Key results**

On GPT-2-small's filtered Winobias development subset of 87/160 examples, 10/144 heads match the all-head indirect effect; influential heads concentrate in middle layers. On Professions, approximately 4% of GPT-2-small representation coordinates match the all-neuron effect, with 57% of selected coordinates from embeddings and the first hidden layer. Joint neuron effects substantially exceed summed individual effects: 112.3 versus 4.0 in GPT-2-small. Attention effects are closer to additive, with reported joint-versus-summed relative differences of 0.7%–11.3% across GPT-2 variants. Attention total effects approximately equal direct plus indirect effects. Appendix E proves exact equality under a stated no-interaction condition. Transformer-XL and XLNet-base also show sparse attention effects and approximate decomposition. Larger GPT-2 variants generally show larger coreference total effects, with reversals and model-dependent filtering.

**Limitations / open questions**

Binary grammatical gender and selected continuations provide a restricted bias measure; occupation substitutions also change lexical meaning. Singular/plural ambiguity confounds “they” experiments. Matching the all-component intervention effect establishes neither a complete nor a minimal mechanism. Professions effects do not scale consistently with model size. Masked-model attention localization depends substantially on continuation scoring, and neuron depth profiles differ across architectures. Alternate metrics broadly preserve relative localization, while absolute sparsity can change. Many inline citations are unresolved question marks, although the bibliography is supplied.

Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
abstract: One of the roadblocks to a better understanding of neural networks' internals is \textit{polysemanticity}, where neurons appear to activate in multiple, semantically distinct contexts. Polysemanticity prevents us from identifying concise, human-understandable explanations for what neural networks are doing internally. One hypothesised cause of polysemanticity is \textit{superposition}, where neural networks represent more features than they have neurons by assigning features to an overcomplete set of directions in activation space, rather than to individual neurons. Here, we attempt to identify those directions, using sparse autoencoders to reconstruct the internal activations of a language model. These autoencoders learn sets of sparsely activating features that are more interpretable and monosemantic than directions identified by alternative approaches, where interpretability is measured by automated methods. Moreover, we show that with our learned set of features, we can pinpoint the features that are causally responsible for counterfactual behaviour on the indirect object identification task \citep{wang2022interpretability} to a finer degree than previous decompositions. This work indicates that it is possible to resolve superposition in language models using a scalable, unsupervised method. Our method may serve as a foundation for future mechanistic interpretability work, which we hope will enable greater model transparency and steerability.
summary:
**Central idea.** If superposition causes polysemanticity, the features a language model represents in superposition could be recovered with a sparse autoencoder (SAE) trained to reconstruct its activations as sparse combinations of an overcomplete dictionary.

**Experiments.** Trains SAEs on residual-stream activations of Pythia-70M (and some Pythia-410M). Interpretability of the learned dictionary features is compared with neurons, PCA, ICA and random directions, using automated interpretability scores (Bills et al. 2023 style: an LLM writes an explanation, then another simulates activations). The features are then used for activation patching on the IOI task, to find the smallest set of features that explains counterfactual behavior. Case studies follow individual features and their downstream effects.

**Key results.** SAE features score as more interpretable than neurons and other decompositions. On IOI, fewer SAE features than PCA or neuron directions are needed to account for the counterfactual behavior, i.e. a more precise localization. The authors argue this shows superposition can be resolved with a scalable, unsupervised method.

**Limitations / open questions.** Small models. Interpretability is judged by automated scores whose validity is itself assumed. Reconstruction error leaves part of model behavior unexplained. Later layers are harder. There is no ground truth that the recovered features are the model's 'true' features.

title: An Overview of Catastrophic AI Risks
LEACE: Perfect linear concept erasure in closed form
abstract: Concept erasure aims to remove specified features from an embedding. It can improve fairness (e.g. preventing a classifier from using gender or race) and interpretability (e.g. removing a concept to observe changes in model behavior). We introduce LEAst-squares Concept Erasure (LEACE), a closed-form method which provably prevents all linear classifiers from detecting a concept while changing the embedding as little as possible, as measured by a broad class of norms. We apply LEACE to large language models with a novel procedure called "concept scrubbing," which erases target concept information from every layer in the network. We demonstrate our method on two tasks: measuring the reliance of language models on part-of-speech information, and reducing gender bias in BERT embeddings. Code is available at https://github.com/EleutherAI/concept-erasure.
summary:
**Central idea**
LEACE removes linearly accessible concept information with a closed-form affine transformation. For positive-probability categorical labels, the paper proves equivalence between equal class-conditional representation means, zero representation–label cross-covariance, and inability of affine predictors to beat constant prediction under convex losses. Whitening, projecting away label-correlated directions, and unwhitening gives an eraser minimizing expected squared distortion simultaneously across positive-semidefinite quadratic metrics. The resulting projection is generally oblique. Concept scrubbing sequentially fits and applies erasers throughout a network, accounting for upstream interventions. Appendix I also derives an optimal label-dependent eraser using regression residuals.

**Experiments**
Gender erasure uses frozen BERT final-layer [CLS] embeddings from Bias in Bios, comparing LEACE, INLP, and RLACE through gender prediction, distortion, profession accuracy, and gender TPR disparities. Single-layer BERT interventions erase 18 coarse POS labels from English Universal Dependencies using unmasked activations. Multilayer scrubbing evaluates LLaMA 7B/13B/30B on RedPajama and Pythia 160M/1.4B/6.9B/12B on Pile samples, using spaCy-generated POS tags. Controls include full-rank Spectral Attribute Removal (SAL) and matched-rank random erasure.

**Key results**
LEACE reaches majority-baseline gender prediction with a rank-one edit; the paper reports an approximately two-order-of-magnitude speedup. Profession accuracy changes from 79.3% to 77.3%, while RMS TPR gap falls from 0.198 to 0.084 and its correlation with profession gender composition falls from 0.867 to 0.392. Refitting yields 78.1% accuracy but a 0.158 gap. Single-layer LEACE removes 17 dimensions, versus INLP's 360, and its largest vocabulary-prediction disruption occurs at layer 11 rather than layer 6. Multilayer LEACE increases LLaMA loss from 0.62–0.69 to 1.73–1.96 bits per UTF-8 byte and Pythia loss from 0.62–0.90 to 2.25–3.57. Random erasure has much smaller effects; SAL causes greater degradation in every tested model. These units describe cross-entropy despite Table 1's “perplexity” label.

**Limitations / open questions**
Linear guardedness concerns optimal expected convex loss, not arbitrary classification accuracy or nonlinear recovery. Exact population guarantees do not establish generalization of estimated erasers. Minimum distortion and random controls do not prove concept-specific intervention effects. POS is broad; narrower concepts and behavioral validation remain open. Oblique erasers sometimes cause divergence; Appendix H introduces a stabilizing LEACE–SAL mixture. The fitting/evaluation sample size is ambiguously rendered as “222 tokens.” The supplied v4 text includes full appendices and a correction of BERT's no-intervention accuracy from 0.892 to 0.928.

title: Towards Automated Circuit Discovery for Mechanistic Interpretability
abstract: Through considerable effort and intuition, several recent works have reverse-engineered nontrivial behaviors of transformer models. This paper systematizes the mechanistic interpretability process they followed. First, researchers choose a metric and dataset that elicit the desired model behavior. Then, they apply activation patching to find which abstract neural network units are involved in the behavior. By varying the dataset, metric, and units under investigation, researchers can understand the functionality of each component. We automate one of the process' steps: to identify the circuit that implements the specified behavior in the model's computational graph. We propose several algorithms and reproduce previous interpretability results to validate them. For example, the ACDC algorithm rediscovered 5/5 of the component types in a circuit in GPT-2 Small that computes the Greater-Than operation. ACDC selected 68 of the 32,000 edges in GPT-2 Small, all of which were manually found by previous work. Our code is available at https://github.com/ArthurConmy/Automatic-Circuit-Discovery.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper describes the common workflow behind manual circuit discovery. A researcher (1) picks a behavior, a dataset, and a metric, (2) chooses a computational-graph granularity (heads, MLPs, Q/K/V, neurons, positions), and (3) runs iterative activation patching to prune unneeded components and edges. The paper then automates step 3.

Its main algorithm, **ACDC (Automatic Circuit DisCovery)**, works as follows:
- It visits graph nodes in reverse topological order.
- For each node, it tries removing every incoming edge by patching in that edge's activation from a corrupted input (interchange / resample ablation).
- It permanently removes the edge if the KL divergence between the full model and the subgraph rises by less than a threshold τ.

Two existing methods are adapted as baselines:
- **Subnetwork Probing (SP)**: a learned L0 mask with no probe, a KL objective, and interpolation toward corrupted activations.
- **HISP**: gradient-based head importance, which is equivalent to attribution patching up to an absolute value.

**Experiments**

- **Tasks with prior manual circuits:** IOI and Greater-Than in GPT-2 Small, Docstring in a 4-layer attention-only transformer, and two tracr-compiled programs (xproportion, reverse).
- **ROC evaluation:** each prior circuit is treated as ground truth, and edge- and node-level ROC/AUC are computed while sweeping τ, λ, or k.
- **Induction:** a 2-layer attention-only model on OpenWebText, scored by held-out KL versus edge count.
- **Ablation studies:** KL vs. task metric, zero vs. corrupted activations, and "reset" networks with permuted weights.
- **Case studies:** a toy OR-gate model, and a gendered-pronoun case study (Mathwin et al.) in which ACDC was used for new discovery.

**Key results**

- **Edge AUC (KL, corrupted activations):**

  | Task | ACDC | SP | HISP |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | IOI | 0.869 | 0.823 | 0.789 |
  | Greater-Than | 0.853 | 0.806 | 0.693 |
  | Docstring | 0.982 | 0.937 | 0.805 |

- **Greater-Than:** ACDC kept 68 of about 32k edges, all of which were in the manual circuit.
- **IOI:** all 9 recovered heads belong to the 26-head IOI circuit. They span three head classes and suffice for the task.
- **tracr:** with zero ablation, ACDC recovers both circuits perfectly (AUC 1.0). With corrupted activations it does poorly (AUC 0.679 and 0.200).
- **Induction:** ACDC has a slight Pareto advantage above about 20 edges. It recovers previous-token head 0.0 and induction heads 1.5 and 1.6.
- **Reset networks:** SP and HISP fit reset networks more easily than ACDC does, which suggests they are more prone to hallucinating circuits.
- **Metric choice:** KL was the most robust metric. Optimizing a task metric (logit difference) can over-optimize and is unstable.

**Limitations / open questions**

- **Fragility:** results are very sensitive to the metric, the ablation type, and parent iteration order.
- **Negative components:** all methods tend to miss components that hurt the metric. IOI negative name movers appeared only at τ=0.00398 (443 edges), alongside many extraneous heads.
- **OR gates:** greedy pruning keeps only one input of an OR gate.
- **Ground truth:** the manual circuits are imperfect, which limits what the ROC numbers can show.
- **Cost:** large graphs can take hours to search.
- **Scope:** ACDC finds subgraphs but does not interpret what the components do.

abstract: Transformer networks have revolutionized NLP representation learning since they were introduced. Though a great effort has been made to explain the representation in transformers, it is widely recognized that our understanding is not sufficient. One important reason is that there lack enough visualization tools for detailed analysis. In this paper, we propose to use dictionary learning to open up these "black boxes" as linear superpositions of transformer factors. Through visualization, we demonstrate the hierarchical semantic structures captured by the transformer factors, e.g., word-level polysemy disambiguation, sentence-level pattern formation, and long-range dependency. While some of these patterns confirm the conventional prior linguistic knowledge, the rest are relatively unexpected, which may provide new insights. We hope this visualization tool can bring further knowledge and a better understanding of how transformer networks work. The code is available at https://github.com/zeyuyun1/TransformerVis
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper learns one dictionary across transformer layers, representing contextualized token embeddings as sparse linear combinations of dictionary vectors with nonnegative coefficients. These vectors, called transformer factors, provide coordinates for visualizing linguistic representations without specifying supervised probing targets beforehand. A factor's layerwise importance score is the mean of its 1,000 largest coefficients at that layer. Top-activating contexts and LIME token saliency maps supply interpretations.

**Experiments**

The authors freeze 12-layer bert-base-uncased and learn a dictionary from its 768-dimensional hidden states. Training alternates FISTA coefficient inference with dictionary updates, using batches of 200 vectors, sparsity coefficient 0.27, and 200,000 training steps. The supplied text does not identify the dictionary-training corpus or dictionary width. Evaluation includes Brown-corpus classification of whether “left” is a verb, manual pattern checks among the top 200 activating token-context pairs per selected factor and layer, constructed adjective-sequence examples, and LIME explanations obtained through random token masking and ridge regression.

**Key results**

A supervised logistic-regression classifier using only factor 30's layer-4 coefficient achieves 97.2% precision, 95.8% recall, and 96.5% F1 on the “left” binary POS task. Reported baseline F1 scores are 94.1% for a perceptron POS tagger and 96.3% for fine-tuned BERT. Among each layer's top 200 examples for selected factors, the unit-conversion-with-parentheses pattern rises from 0% at layers 4 and 6 to 64.5% at layer 8 and 95.5% at layer 10. Enumeration rises from 8% at layer 4 to 100% at layers 8 and 10. Constructed adjective examples retain substantial activation across lexical substitutions, although activation also remains high after deleting several adjectives. Selected later-layer factors activate on repeated passages and biographical contexts, with LIME highlighting relevant contextual tokens.

**Limitations / open questions**

Evidence centers on selected factors in one encoder model; the authors acknowledge selection bias and provide an interactive viewer. Top-example pattern rates do not establish population-wide recall or exclusive selectivity, and appendix examples include mismatches with proposed descriptions. The Brown evaluation's sample counts and train/test protocol are unspecified; its labels test grammatical usage rather than precise word senses. Reconstruction fidelity, dictionary stability, and downstream causal effects are not quantified. Smooth importance curves suggest representational continuity but do not establish shared mechanisms across layers. LIME explains factor activation under masking rather than demonstrating that BERT uses these factors for its predictions.
