Understanding intermediate layers using linear classifier probes
abstract: Neural network models have a reputation for being black boxes. We propose to monitor the features at every layer of a model and measure how suitable they are for classification. We use linear classifiers, which we refer to as "probes", trained entirely independently of the model itself. This helps us better understand the roles and dynamics of the intermediate layers. We demonstrate how this can be used to develop a better intuition about models and to diagnose potential problems. We apply this technique to the popular models Inception v3 and Resnet-50. Among other things, we observe experimentally that the linear separability of features increase monotonically along the depth of the model.
summary:
**Central idea**

Train independent linear softmax classifiers on intermediate activations to measure how readily each layer exposes target labels. Probe gradients never update the underlying network. The paper distinguishes computational accessibility from information content: processing can make labels easier to decode linearly without adding information. Softmax cross-entropy makes probe fitting convex, although practical optimization remains approximate.

**Experiments**

The authors probe a TensorFlow MNIST CNN with two convolutional and two fully connected layers, before training and after 10 epochs. Probes use early stopping on a 10,000-example validation set and report test classification error. They also probe pretrained ResNet-50 on ImageNet, reducing spatial features through pooling, and Inception v3 during approximately two weeks of ImageNet training. Inception probes use 1,000 fixed randomly selected features per insertion point; the final reported snapshot follows minibatch 308230, with four training snapshots shown in Appendix C. A diagnostic experiment uses a deliberately problematic MNIST network with 128 fully connected layers of 128 units and a skip connection bypassing its first half.

**Key results**

Probe classification error generally decreases with depth, with small exceptions rather than strict monotonicity. In ResNet-50, validation error falls from 0.99 at the pooled input to 0.31 at the final reported residual addition, but rises from 0.76 to 0.77 at one intermediate transition. The trained MNIST CNN likewise has a minor reversal. Before CNN training, random transformations already improve probe test error from approximately 8% to 2%, with the largest improvement at the first ReLU. Inception’s auxiliary branch is slightly ahead of its main branch during observed training. In the pathological deep network, probes suggest that the bypassed first half fails to develop linearly useful class representations despite successful overall training.

**Limitations / open questions**

All experiments concern vision classification, with no language-model or alignment evaluations. Probe measurements establish linear accessibility rather than causal use; the diagnostic experiment includes no causal test of the supposedly unused segment. Feature reduction complicates layer comparisons: retaining 1,000 coordinates samples very different fractions of different Inception layers. Overfitting and incomplete probe optimization can also distort measurements. The Inception prediction-error evaluation split is not specified in the supplied text. The near-monotonic depth trend is observational, with no general theorem or established explanation. Supplied metadata dates the original paper to 2016; the supplied text identifies itself as the November 2018 revision.

title: Analogy-based detection of morphological and semantic relations with word embeddings: what works and what doesn’t.
Unsupervised Feature Extraction by Time-Contrastive Learning and Nonlinear ICA
abstract: Nonlinear independent component analysis (ICA) provides an appealing framework for unsupervised feature learning, but the models proposed so far are not identifiable. Here, we first propose a new intuitive principle of unsupervised deep learning from time series which uses the nonstationary structure of the data. Our learning principle, time-contrastive learning (TCL), finds a representation which allows optimal discrimination of time segments (windows). Surprisingly, we show how TCL can be related to a nonlinear ICA model, when ICA is redefined to include temporal nonstationarities. In particular, we show that TCL combined with linear ICA estimates the nonlinear ICA model up to point-wise transformations of the sources, and this solution is unique --- thus providing the first identifiability result for nonlinear ICA which is rigorous, constructive, as well as very general.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper introduces time-contrastive learning (TCL). A time series is cut into segments. An MLP feature extractor h(x) is trained jointly with a multinomial logistic regression (MLR) to predict which segment each data point came from. Under infinite data and universal approximation, the optimal MLR logits equal log-density ratios log p_τ(x) − log p_1(x) relative to a pivot segment.

The authors define a nonstationary nonlinear ICA model: the observations are x = f(s), with f smooth and invertible. The sources are mutually independent, and their segment-wise exponential-family densities are log p_τ(s_i) = q_{i,0}(s_i) + Σ_v λ_{i,v}(τ) q_{i,v}(s_i) − log Z. Combining the two gives an identifiability result for nonlinear ICA.

**Experiments**

- **Theory.** Theorem 1 assumes V=1, a shared q, feature dimension m=n, and a full-column-rank modulation matrix L. Under these conditions TCL features equal q(s) up to an invertible affine map; the Jacobian log-determinant cancels in the proof.
  - Corollary 1: linear ICA (FastICA) on h(x) then recovers the q(s_i).
  - Corollary 2: if q is strictly monotone in |s| (e.g. modulated Gaussian), the sources themselves are identified up to componentwise monotone transformations.
  - Extensions (sketched): dimension reduction via stationary components, and V>1 via an independent subspace model.
- **Simulation.**
  - Data: n=20 Laplacian sources with variance-type modulation λ ~ U[0,1] and segment length 512, mixed by invertible leaky-ReLU MLPs with L layers.
  - TCL setup: maxout feature-MLP with absolute-value outputs, followed by FastICA.
  - Metric: mean absolute correlation between true q(s_i) and the estimates.
  - Baselines: NSVICA (linear nonstationary ICA), kTDSEP (kernel nonlinear ICA), and a stacked denoising autoencoder.
- **Real MEG.**
  - Data: resting-state data from 9 subjects, 306 channels, alpha-band Morlet filtered, 12.5 s segments.
  - Training: multi-task MLR heads per session.
  - Evaluation: features transferred to task sessions, where a linear SVM decodes stimulus modality (4 classes, chance 25%).

**Key results**

- Segment classification exceeded a random-feature-MLP chance level.
- TCL recovered q(s_i) reasonably well for L>1, where all baselines failed. NSVICA was best only in the linear (L=1) case.
- Recovery improved with more segments and degraded with deeper mixing. The DAE was omitted for L>3 because of training instability.
- On MEG, TCL features gave consistently higher modality classification than the baselines, and L≥3 beat L=1.
- Visualized units showed progressive pooling into bilateral temporal and occipito-parietal patterns resembling known resting-state networks, with no apparent artefact units.

**Limitations / open questions**

- Identifiability holds only asymptotically: it needs infinite data, global optimization, noiseless invertible mixing, and sufficiently diverse modulation (full-rank L).
- In general only q(s_i) (e.g. |s_i|) is recovered. Corollary 2's sign-recovery construction is acknowledged to be impractical.
- The simulations evaluate recovery of q(s) via correlation, not of s itself.
- The MEG evaluation is indirect (downstream decoding), and the baselines used log-power features.
- Plots are described qualitatively; exact numbers are not available in the provided text.

title: Generating Sentences from a Continuous Space
Take and Took, Gaggle and Goose, Book and Read: Evaluating the Utility of Vector Differences for Lexical Relation Learning
A Latent Variable Model Approach to PMI-based Word Embeddings
GloVe: Global Vectors for Word Representation
Linguistic Regularities in Sparse and Explicit Word Representations
word2vec Explained: deriving Mikolov et al.'s negative-sampling word-embedding method
Distributed Representations of Words and Phrases and their Compositionality
Exploiting similarities among languages for machine translation.
Linguistic Regularities in Continuous Space Word Representations
summary:
**Central idea**

Word embeddings learned through language modeling can expose linguistic relationships through approximately shared vector offsets. The paper examines columns of an RNN language model's input-weight matrix. For an analogy a:b::c:d, it normalizes word vectors, computes x_b − x_a + x_c, and retrieves the word with greatest cosine similarity. When d is supplied, its cosine similarity to the predicted vector scores analogy validity. These relationships emerge without explicit syntactic or semantic supervision of the embeddings.

**Experiments**

RNN representations have 80, 320, and 640 dimensions, plus a composite totaling 1,600 dimensions. Training uses 320 million Broadcast News words and an 82,000-word vocabulary; LSA baselines use the same text. A new 8,000-question syntactic analogy dataset covers eight adjective, noun, and verb relationships, with 1,000 questions each. Construction uses 267 million POS-tagged newspaper words and frequent word forms. Comparisons with released Collobert–Weston (CW) and hierarchical log-bilinear (HLBL) embeddings restrict the syntactic evaluation to a shared 36,000-word vocabulary and 6,632 questions. Semantic evaluation uses SemEval-2012 Task 2, averaging scores over each relation's three or four prototype pairs and reporting Spearman correlation and MaxDiff accuracy averaged across all 69 test relations.

**Key results**

Full-set syntactic accuracy rises from 16.2% for RNN-80 to 28.5% for RNN-320, 34.7% for RNN-640, and 39.6% for the composite. Corresponding LSA accuracies are 12.8%, 16.5%, and 11.3%. On the restricted syntactic set, RNN-80 scores 19.0%, versus 18.7% for HLBL-100 and 5.0% for CW-100. On semantic relations, RNN-1600 achieves ρ = 0.275 and MaxDiff accuracy = 0.418, exceeding the reported prior UTD-NB baseline of 0.230 and 0.395. RNN-320 and RNN-640 also exceed that baseline on both metrics without task-specific training or tuning of their vectors.

**Limitations / open questions**

The results concern static lexical embeddings and selected analogy tasks. They do not establish exact constant offsets, comprehensive linguistic knowledge, or causal use of these relationships by the language model. Most syntactic questions remain incorrect. CW/HLBL comparisons differ in training data and dimensionality; their vectors used 37 million training words. The 1,600-dimensional representation combines systems. Statistical uncertainty and seed variability are not reported. Some mathematical symbols are corrupted in the supplied rendering, but the methods and result tables remain readable.

Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear
abstract: Recent work has proposed that language models perform computation by manipulating one-dimensional representations of concepts ("features") in activation space. In contrast, we explore whether some language model representations may be inherently multi-dimensional. We begin by developing a rigorous definition of irreducible multi-dimensional features based on whether they can be decomposed into either independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features. Motivated by these definitions, we design a scalable method that uses sparse autoencoders to automatically find multi-dimensional features in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B. These auto-discovered features include strikingly interpretable examples, e.g. circular features representing days of the week and months of the year. We identify tasks where these exact circles are used to solve computational problems involving modular arithmetic in days of the week and months of the year. Next, we provide evidence that these circular features are indeed the fundamental unit of computation in these tasks with intervention experiments on Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B, and we examine the continuity of the days of the week feature in Mistral 7B. Overall, our work argues that understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary to mechanistically decompose some model behaviors.
summary:
**Central idea.** Challenges the assumption that language models compute only with one-dimensional feature directions. Some features are *irreducibly multi-dimensional*: they cannot be split into independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional parts.

**Experiments.** (1) Formal definitions of reducibility, with a separability index and an epsilon-mixture index. (2) A scalable discovery method: cluster SAE decoder directions, project activations onto each cluster's span, and score irreducibility. Applied to GPT-2 small and Mistral 7B. (3) Tasks involving modular arithmetic over days of the week and months of the year, where the discovered circular features are tested with interventions on Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B. (4) Continuity analysis of the days-of-week circle.

**Key results.** Clearly interpretable circular features for days and months appear automatically. Intervening on these circular subspaces changes the model's answers on the modular arithmetic tasks as predicted, evidence that the circles are the unit of computation for these tasks.

**Limitations / open questions.** Only a handful of strongly multi-dimensional features were found, so the prevalence of irreducible features is unknown. The discovery method relies on SAEs, which are themselves biased toward one-dimensional latents. The tasks are narrow. This bears on how SAE-based decompositions should be interpreted.

title: Refusal in LLMs is mediated by a single direction
summary:
**Central idea.** In safety-fine-tuned chat models, refusal of harmful requests is mediated by a single direction in the residual stream. Removing that direction disables refusal, and adding it makes the model refuse harmless requests. (Preview of the later arXiv paper, 2406.11717.)

**Experiments.** Computes difference-in-means vectors between residual activations on harmful and harmless instructions at each layer and position, then selects the best direction on a validation set. Tests (1) directional ablation, projecting the direction out of every residual write at inference time, on harmful prompts; (2) activation addition of the direction on harmless prompts; (3) a weight-orthogonalization edit that bakes the ablation into the weights. Covers Qwen (1.8B-72B), Gemma (2B, 7B), Yi (6B, 34B) and Llama-3 (8B, 70B) chat models, measuring refusal and safety scores and checking capability benchmarks.

**Key results.** Ablating the single direction sharply reduces refusal and elicits unsafe completions in every model tested. Adding it induces refusal of benign requests. Weight orthogonalization works as a cheap white-box jailbreak with little capability loss. The authors frame this as both validating the interpretability finding and showing how fragile safety fine-tuning is.

**Limitations / open questions.** It explains one aspect of refusal, not the full mechanism. How the direction is computed upstream, for example which features feed it, is open. Results cover open-weight chat models and use a simple harmful/harmless dataset.

title: Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction
abstract: Conversational large language models are fine-tuned for both instruction-following and safety, resulting in models that obey benign requests but refuse harmful ones. While this refusal behavior is widespread across chat models, its underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this work, we show that refusal is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace, across 13 popular open-source chat models up to 72B parameters in size. Specifically, for each model, we find a single direction such that erasing this direction from the model's residual stream activations prevents it from refusing harmful instructions, while adding this direction elicits refusal on even harmless instructions. Leveraging this insight, we propose a novel white-box jailbreak method that surgically disables refusal with minimal effect on other capabilities. Finally, we mechanistically analyze how adversarial suffixes suppress propagation of the refusal-mediating direction. Our findings underscore the brittleness of current safety fine-tuning methods. More broadly, our work showcases how an understanding of model internals can be leveraged to develop practical methods for controlling model behavior.
summary:
**Central idea**

Refusal of harmful requests in safety-fine-tuned chat models is mediated by a single residual-stream direction. The authors extract it as a difference-in-means between activations on harmful and harmless instructions.

This direction is shown to be both necessary and sufficient for refusal:
- **Necessary:** ablating it disables refusal.
- **Sufficient:** adding it induces refusal.

The finding yields a cheap white-box jailbreak, *weight orthogonalization*. This is a rank-one edit that projects the direction out of every matrix that writes to the residual stream.

**Experiments**

- **Models:** 13 open chat models from 1.8B to 72B parameters:
  - Qwen Chat 1.8B, 7B, 14B and 72B
  - Yi 6B and 34B
  - Gemma IT 2B and 7B
  - Llama-2 Chat 7B, 13B and 70B
  - Llama-3 Instruct 8B and 70B
- **Direction extraction:** 128 harmful instructions (AdvBench, MaliciousInstruct, TDC2023) and 128 harmless instructions (Alpaca) are used to compute candidate directions at each post-instruction token position and layer.
- **Direction selection:** candidates are scored on 32-example validation sets for three properties:
  - refusal bypass under ablation
  - refusal induction under addition
  - KL divergence on harmless prompts below 0.1
  - The selected layer must be below 0.8L.
- **Evaluation metrics:** refusal is scored by substring matching, and harmful content by Meta Llama Guard 2.
- **Benchmarks:**
  - JailbreakBench (100 harmful prompts) for directional ablation.
  - 100 Alpaca prompts for activation addition.
  - HarmBench (159 standard behaviors) for attack success rate (ASR), compared with GCG, GCG-M, GCG-T, AutoPrompt, PAIR and human DAN templates.
- **Coherence checks:**
  - MMLU, ARC, GSM8K, TruthfulQA, WinoGrande and TinyHellaSwag
  - Cross-entropy loss on the Pile, on Alpaca, and on the model's own completions
- **Adversarial suffix analysis:** in Qwen 1.8B, a GCG suffix is studied using cosine similarity with the direction, direct feature attribution of attention heads, and attention patterns.
- **Base models:** the chat model's direction is tested for expression in the corresponding base models.

**Key results**

- Ablation drives refusal rates near zero and elicits unsafe completions across models. For example, in Llama-3 8B the refusal score falls from 0.95 to 0.01 and the safety score from 0.97 to 0.15.
- Adding the direction makes models refuse harmless requests.
- **HarmBench ASR for orthogonalized models:**
  - Qwen: about 78–84%, on par with prompt-specific GCG.
  - Llama-2 with its default system prompt: 4–23%.
  - Llama-2 without a system prompt: 61–80%.
- Benchmark scores mostly stay within noise of the original models. The exceptions are Qwen 7B and Yi 34B, and TruthfulQA drops consistently, by 1–6 points.
- Directional ablation raises cross-entropy loss less than subtracting the vector via activation addition.
- The adversarial suffix suppresses expression of the refusal direction at the last token by hijacking the attention of the top refusal-writing heads, which shift from the instruction tokens to the suffix tokens.
- The direction is similarly expressed in base models, suggesting fine-tuning repurposes an existing representation.

**Limitations / open questions**

- Results may not generalize to larger or proprietary models.
- The extraction method is heuristic; the authors present it as an existence proof.
- The suffix analysis covers only one model and one suffix.
- Coherence metrics are imperfect.
- The semantics of the direction are unclear: it may encode "harm" or "danger" rather than refusal.

Discovering Latent Knowledge in Language Models Without Supervision
abstract: Existing techniques for training language models can be misaligned with the truth: if we train models with imitation learning, they may reproduce errors that humans make; if we train them to generate text that humans rate highly, they may output errors that human evaluators can't detect. We propose circumventing this issue by directly finding latent knowledge inside the internal activations of a language model in a purely unsupervised way. Specifically, we introduce a method for accurately answering yes-no questions given only unlabeled model activations. It works by finding a direction in activation space that satisfies logical consistency properties, such as that a statement and its negation have opposite truth values. We show that despite using no supervision and no model outputs, our method can recover diverse knowledge represented in large language models: across 6 models and 10 question-answering datasets, it outperforms zero-shot accuracy by 4\% on average. We also find that it cuts prompt sensitivity in half and continues to maintain high accuracy even when models are prompted to generate incorrect answers. Our results provide an initial step toward discovering what language models know, distinct from what they say, even when we don't have access to explicit ground truth labels.
summary:
**Central idea**

Training objectives such as imitation learning and RLHF can misalign what a model *says* from what is true. The authors propose recovering a model's latent "knowledge" directly from its hidden activations, using no labels and no model outputs. Their method, **Contrast-Consistent Search (CCS)**, works in three steps:

1. Each yes/no question is turned into a contrast pair: the question answered "Yes" (x+) and answered "No" (x−).
2. Hidden states are mean-normalized separately for the x+ set and the x− set. This removes the superficial "ends with Yes/No" difference.
3. A linear probe with a sigmoid is trained on an unsupervised loss. The loss has two terms:
   - **Consistency:** p(x+) should equal 1 − p(x−).
   - **Confidence:** min(p(x+), p(x−))², which penalizes the degenerate solution where both probabilities are 0.5.

The framing is an empirical counterpart to ARC's Eliciting Latent Knowledge (ELK) problem.

**Experiments**

- **Models (6):** T5, UnifiedQA, T0 (encoder-decoder); GPT-J (decoder-only); RoBERTa and DeBERTa (encoder-only, MNLI-finetuned for the zero-shot baseline).
- **Datasets (10):** IMDB, Amazon, AG-News, DBpedia-14, RTE, QNLI, COPA, Story-Cloze, BoolQ, PIQA. Each uses about 9 prompts, with 1000 examples per dataset (500 for COPA) and a 60/40 train/test split.
- **Baselines and ceiling:** calibrated zero-shot as the baseline; supervised logistic regression on the same features as the ceiling.
- **Analyses:**
  - A misleading few-shot prefix designed to push outputs toward wrong answers.
  - Cross-dataset transfer.
  - A sweep over layers.
  - Sample complexity, from k=1 contrast pair upward.
  - MLM-only DeBERTa with the label placed mid-prompt, so the model's outputs are uninformative.
  - Two label-free clustering variants (Contrastive Representation Clustering, CRC): the top principal component of contrast differences (TPC), and a bimodal salience search (BSS).

**Key results**

- **Accuracy:** CCS averages 71.2% versus 67.2% for calibrated zero-shot, excluding T0, which was trained on 9 of the 10 datasets. The supervised ceiling is 83.7%. CCS is worse than zero-shot on RoBERTa.
- **Prompt sensitivity:** the standard deviation of accuracy across prompts falls by about half (3.2 vs 6.1).
- **Misleading prefix:** on UnifiedQA, the prefix drops zero-shot accuracy from 80.4% to 70.9%, while CCS holds steady (82.1% to 83.8%). The authors caution that correct-answer prefixes behaved similarly, so the prefix's effect is ambiguous.
- **Transfer:** CCS transfers across tasks with different label spaces, often matching no-transfer accuracy (e.g. training on Amazon gives 71.8% average transfer). The authors read this as suggestive of a task-agnostic truth-like direction.
- **Layers:** for T5 and UnifiedQA, middle layers sometimes outperform the last layer. With the misleading prefix, UnifiedQA's encoder states stay robust while its decoder states degrade.
- **Uninformative outputs:** MLM-only DeBERTa reaches 93.7% with CCS versus 71.6% for an adapted zero-shot baseline.
- **Data efficiency and salience:** CCS often works with very few examples. TPC (70.1%) and BSS (70.2%) are also competitive, suggesting that truth is a salient, high-variance direction in contrast-difference space.

**Limitations / open questions**

- CCS assumes a linearly separable truth direction exists. This requires the model both to be capable of evaluating truth and to actively evaluate it.
- The sign of the probe is unidentified. The evaluation takes the better of the two labelings; a conjunction-based fix is only sketched.
- No evaluation on genuine lying or deception setups.
- A large gap to the supervised ceiling remains.
- CCS finds *some* consistent, high-accuracy direction. Whether that direction is the model's "truth" rather than another consistent feature, such as what the model would say, is not established.

title: Inference-Time Intervention: Eliciting Truthful Answers from a Language Model
abstract: We introduce Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), a technique designed to enhance the "truthfulness" of large language models (LLMs). ITI operates by shifting model activations during inference, following a set of directions across a limited number of attention heads. This intervention significantly improves the performance of LLaMA models on the TruthfulQA benchmark. On an instruction-finetuned LLaMA called Alpaca, ITI improves its truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1%. We identify a tradeoff between truthfulness and helpfulness and demonstrate how to balance it by tuning the intervention strength. ITI is minimally invasive and computationally inexpensive. Moreover, the technique is data efficient: while approaches like RLHF require extensive annotations, ITI locates truthful directions using only few hundred examples. Our findings suggest that LLMs may have an internal representation of the likelihood of something being true, even as they produce falsehoods on the surface.
summary:
**Central idea**
LLMs sometimes "know" more than they "say". On TruthfulQA, linear probes on LLaMA-7B's intermediate activations classify answer truthfulness far better than the model's generations, a gap of about 40 points. Inference-Time Intervention (ITI) aims to close this gap. It locates a sparse set of attention heads whose outputs linearly encode truthfulness. At every generated token it then shifts those heads' outputs along a "truthful" direction, scaled by α times the activation standard deviation along that direction. The shift is equivalent to a constant per-layer bias, so it can be baked into the output-projection bias offline at near-zero cost.

**Experiments**
- **Probing.** One logistic probe per head on the last-token activations of 5,918 TruthfulQA QA pairs (4:1 train/val split) in LLaMA-7B.
- **Geometry.** A second probe constrained to be orthogonal to the first visualizes the 2-D geometry of true vs. false activations.
- **Hyperparameter sweep.** Number of heads K and strength α are tuned on 10% of the questions. The chosen values are K=48 and α=15; main results use 2-fold cross-validation.
- **Metrics.** TruthfulQA generation (true*informative, judged by GPT-judge and spot-checked by humans) and MC accuracy. Off-target change is measured with cross-entropy and KL divergence on OpenWebText.
- **Baselines.** Supervised fine-tuning, 50-shot prompting, and the instruction-tuned models Alpaca and Vicuna.
- **Ablations.** Intervention direction (probe weight, mass-mean shift, CCS direction, random direction) and intervention site (all heads, point-wise feature selection, head-wise selection).
- **Out-of-distribution transfer.** Zero-shot transfer to Natural Questions, TriviaQA (with GPT-4-generated adversarial false answers) and MMLU.

**Key results**
- **Truth is localized in a few heads.** Most heads probe at chance, while a minority, mostly in early-to-middle layers, probe well. The best head is layer 14, head 18 at 83.3%; concatenating all heads gives 84.4%.
- **Truth is a subspace, not a single direction.** The orthogonal second probe is still above chance.
- **Gains on LLaMA-7B.** ITI raises true*info from 30.5% to 43.5%, beating SFT (36.1%) but not few-shot prompting (49.5%). Combining FSP with ITI gives 51.4%.
- **Gains on instruction-tuned models.** Alpaca goes from 32.5% to 65.1% and Vicuna from 51.5% to 74.0%.
- **Direction choice matters.** Mass-mean shift (42.3%) outperforms the probe-weight direction (34.8%), CCS (33.4%) and random (31.2%). The direction that best separates the classes is not the most causally effective.
- **Sparsity matters.** Head-wise selection beats both the all-heads and point-wise alternatives.
- **Data efficiency.** Truthfulness plateaus with few training examples, and directions converge quickly.
- **Truthfulness–helpfulness tradeoff.** Stronger α produces more "I have no comment" answers.
- **Modest out-of-distribution gains.** NQ 46.6→51.3, TriviaQA 89.6→91.1, MMLU 35.7→40.2.

**Limitations / open questions**
- **Narrow notion of truth.** Truth is operationalized only as avoiding the human misconceptions captured by TruthfulQA.
- **Evaluation noise.** GPT-judge slightly overestimates truthfulness.
- **Side effects.** ITI raises cross-entropy and KL; for Vicuna, KL reaches 1.41.
- **Mixed per-question effects.** Some answers flip from true to false.
- **No mechanistic account.** There is no explanation of what the intervention does internally.
- **Untested settings.** Generalization to chat settings and unsupervised direction finding are left open.

title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in Large Language Model Representations of True/False Datasets
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have impressive capabilities, but are prone to outputting falsehoods. Recent work has developed techniques for inferring whether a LLM is telling the truth by training probes on the LLM's internal activations. However, this line of work is controversial, with some authors pointing out failures of these probes to generalize in basic ways, among other conceptual issues. In this work, we use high-quality datasets of simple true/false statements to study in detail the structure of LLM representations of truth, drawing on three lines of evidence: 1. Visualizations of LLM true/false statement representations, which reveal clear linear structure. 2. Transfer experiments in which probes trained on one dataset generalize to different datasets. 3. Causal evidence obtained by surgically intervening in a LLM's forward pass, causing it to treat false statements as true and vice versa. Overall, we present evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements. We also show that simple difference-in-mean probes generalize as well as other probing techniques while identifying directions which are more causally implicated in model outputs.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper investigates whether language models linearly represent factual truth across topics and sentence structures. It combines visualization, cross-dataset classification, and interventions to distinguish truth-related representations from text probability and dataset-specific correlates. It introduces mass-mean (MM) probing: a true-minus-false mean activation direction, with a within-class covariance correction for IID classification.

**Experiments**

The models are LLaMA-2-7B, 13B, and 70B. Curated datasets include city–country statements (1,496), Spanish–English translations (354), numerical comparisons (1,980 each for larger_than and smaller_than), negations, and conjunctions/disjunctions. Additional tests use company claims, CommonClaim, and 31,960 adapted CounterFact statements. A 10,000-example nonfactual likely dataset controls for completion probability. Activation patching localizes states affecting TRUE-versus-FALSE log probability; PCA and probes then examine statement-ending representations without few-shot priming. Logistic regression, MM, and contrast-consistent search are compared using 80/20 training splits and cross-dataset accuracy. Causal experiments add or subtract probe directions across localized states and measure normalized indirect effects (NIEs) on Spanish–English statement classification.

**Key results**

Larger models show clearer linear separation and better transfer across datasets. For 13B and 70B, all tested probing techniques trained on larger_than + smaller_than exceed 95% accuracy on sp_en_trans. Adding opposite statements generally improves classification transfer. Probability-trained probes fail on datasets where truth and likelihood anticorrelate, supporting structure beyond plausibility. MM achieves classification performance comparable to other methods in larger models and reportedly outperforms LR and CCS causally in 7/8 experimental conditions. For 13B, cities-trained MM yields NIEs of 0.77 and 0.90 for false-to-true and true-to-false interventions, versus 0.13 and 0.19 for LR.

**Limitations / open questions**

The evidence concerns simple factual statements in one model family, and cannot distinguish truth from widespread belief or verifiability. Causal evaluation uses one target dataset where truth strongly correlates with likelihood; likely-trained MM interventions are unexpectedly effective. Opposite-statement training improves classification without consistently improving causal effects. Statement-ending localization is context-dependent in 70B. These experiments do not establish detection of deception or a universal truth direction. Supplied figure captions lack numerical plot contents; metadata gives the original publication date, while the text identifies the August 2024 v3 revision.

title: Linear Representations of Sentiment in Large Language Models
abstract: Sentiment is a pervasive feature in natural language text, yet it is an open question how sentiment is represented within Large Language Models (LLMs). In this study, we reveal that across a range of models, sentiment is represented linearly: a single direction in activation space mostly captures the feature across a range of tasks with one extreme for positive and the other for negative. Through causal interventions, we isolate this direction and show it is causally relevant in both toy tasks and real world datasets such as Stanford Sentiment Treebank. Through this case study we model a thorough investigation of what a single direction means on a broad data distribution. We further uncover the mechanisms that involve this direction, highlighting the roles of a small subset of attention heads and neurons. Finally, we discover a phenomenon which we term the summarization motif: sentiment is not solely represented on emotionally charged words, but is additionally summarized at intermediate positions without inherent sentiment, such as punctuation and names. We show that in Stanford Sentiment Treebank zero-shot classification, 76% of above-chance classification accuracy is lost when ablating the sentiment direction, nearly half of which (36%) is due to ablating the summarized sentiment direction exclusively at comma positions.
summary:
**Central idea**

Sentiment in the evaluated GPT-2 and Pythia models admits useful bipolar residual-stream directions that transfer beyond their fitting vocabulary. The paper also identifies a “summarization motif”: attention pathways aggregate sentiment at otherwise unvalenced positions, including punctuation and repeated names, for later retrieval.

**Experiments**

Mean differences, two-means clustering, logistic regression, PCA, and Distributed Alignment Search (DAS) identify directions using templated movie reviews. Tests include unseen adjectives and verbs, OpenWebText token labeling, 27 negation examples, directional patching, generation steering, and Stanford Sentiment Treebank (SST). Circuit analyses examine GPT-2 Small movie-review continuation and Pythia-2.8B two-character mood stories. Metrics include sentiment-token logit differences, logit-flip rates, and binary classification accuracy.

For Pythia-1.4B SST patching, the authors retain correctly classified test phrases, removing 17% of examples, and construct 460 equal-token-length pairs. A separate Pythia-2.8B SST ablation study selects correctly classified examples containing commas, establishing 100% starting accuracy.

**Key results**

Direction estimators show high cosine similarity in the reported comparison. OpenWebText positive/negative classification accuracies at the top/bottom 0.1% activation tails range from 78% to 89%, using GPT-4 labels. Toy-trained DAS patching flips Pythia-1.4B SST predictions on 53.5% of the selected pairs. The reported SST layer sweep finds strongest transfer near intermediate layers. Increasing DAS dimensionality improves training performance without improving the tested mood-task transfer.

On the selected Pythia-2.8B SST subset, all-token, all-layer sentiment-direction ablation reduces accuracy from 100% to 62%, removing 76% of the original 50-percentage-point advantage over chance. Comma-only directional ablation reduces accuracy to 82%, removing 36% of that original advantage. Random-direction controls change the metrics by less than 1%. In mood stories with attention fixed, comma-only and pre-comma-only value patching reduce logit difference by 37% and 38%. The period-to-phrase patching-effect ratio increases from 0.29 without inserted text to 1.15 with 22 irrelevant tokens. Selected sentiment-aligned neurons show negation-related activation patterns, without a complete causal account.

**Limitations / open questions**

The findings establish neither universal sentiment coordinates nor an exclusively one-dimensional mechanism. Circuits remain incomplete; MLP mechanisms and multilingual transfer receive mainly qualitative analysis. SST selection limits population-level conclusions, and fixed attention constrains compensation. Small datasets, layer selection, DAS overfitting, and off-distribution interventions remain concerns. GPT-4 lexical labels receive only cursory human checking. Adjective-count descriptions are inconsistent, several intervention sample sizes are unspecified, and figure images are unavailable in the supplied rendering.

title: Steering Llama 2 via Contrastive Activation Addition
abstract: We introduce Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), an innovative method for steering language models by modifying their activations during forward passes. CAA computes "steering vectors" by averaging the difference in residual stream activations between pairs of positive and negative examples of a particular behavior, such as factual versus hallucinatory responses. During inference, these steering vectors are added at all token positions after the user's prompt with either a positive or negative coefficient, allowing precise control over the degree of the targeted behavior. We evaluate CAA's effectiveness on Llama 2 Chat using multiple-choice behavioral question datasets and open-ended generation tasks. We demonstrate that CAA significantly alters model behavior, is effective over and on top of traditional methods like finetuning and system prompt design, and minimally reduces capabilities. Moreover, we gain deeper insights into CAA's mechanisms by employing various activation space interpretation methods. CAA accurately steers model outputs and sheds light on how high-level concepts are represented in Large Language Models (LLMs).
summary:
**Central idea**

Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) controls behavior by averaging residual-stream activation differences between paired multiple-choice prompts that differ only in their appended answer letter. The vector is added at a selected layer at every generated token position after the user prompt, with a signed multiplier. This extends Activation Addition from single prompt pairs to behavioral datasets.

**Experiments**

The paper evaluates Llama 2 7B Chat and 13B Chat on AI coordination, corrigibility, hallucination, myopic reward, survival instinct, sycophancy, and refusal. Vectors use 290–1,000 contrast pairs per behavior, sourced from Anthropic evaluations or generated with GPT-4. Evaluations use 50 held-out questions per behavior, measuring behavior-matching answer probability and GPT-4 ratings of open-ended responses. Additional experiments compare system prompts and one-epoch supervised fine-tuning, assess 570 reformatted MMLU questions and TruthfulQA, and test transfer across layers and from Llama 2 7B Base to Chat.

**Key results**

The authors report behavioral steering across all seven categories and transfer from multiple-choice extraction to open-ended generation. Effects generally peak around layer 13 in 7B and layers 14–15 in 13B. CAA often adds control beyond system prompts; improvements beyond fine-tuning are less consistent, occurring bidirectionally for three of seven behaviors. Fine-tuning on sycophancy fails to generalize to open-ended responses in the reported comparison. MMLU correct-answer probability ranges from 0.57 to 0.65 under steering versus 0.63 unsteered. Subtracting sycophancy improves TruthfulQA scores by approximately 0.01 in 7B and 0.02 in 13B. Base-model vectors transfer particularly well at layers 10–15.

**Limitations / open questions**

Evidence covers two chat-model sizes within one family. GPT-4 ratings depend on evaluator wording, and prompting and fine-tuning baselines are incompletely optimized. Large multipliers degrade text quality; layer comparisons confound representation location with vector magnitude. Layer selection uses the same held-out questions subsequently reported for evaluation. Some tabulated effects are nonmonotonic or reversed. In particular, the survival-instinct examples, system prompts, and rating rubric operationalize willingness to be shut down, opposite the category’s ordinary meaning. The main text describes ratings as 1–10, while the actual rubric uses 0–10. These inconsistencies limit broad claims about precise, uniformly reliable behavioral control.

title: Prompt-driven LLM safeguarding via directed representation optimization
Shadow Alignment: The Ease of Subverting Safely-Aligned Language Models
Sparse Feature Circuits: Discovering and Editing Interpretable Causal Graphs in Language Models
abstract: We introduce methods for discovering and applying sparse feature circuits. These are causally implicated subnetworks of human-interpretable features for explaining language model behaviors. Circuits identified in prior work consist of polysemantic and difficult-to-interpret units like attention heads or neurons, rendering them unsuitable for many downstream applications. In contrast, sparse feature circuits enable detailed understanding of unanticipated mechanisms. Because they are based on fine-grained units, sparse feature circuits are useful for downstream tasks: We introduce SHIFT, where we improve the generalization of a classifier by ablating features that a human judges to be task-irrelevant. Finally, we demonstrate an entirely unsupervised and scalable interpretability pipeline by discovering thousands of sparse feature circuits for automatically discovered model behaviors.
summary:
**Central idea**
The paper discovers causal graphs whose nodes are sparse-autoencoder (SAE) features and reconstruction errors, rather than neurons or attention heads. Attribution patching and integrated gradients approximate node and edge indirect effects, enabling threshold-based circuit discovery without a researcher-specified mechanism. Retaining SAE errors preserves contributions that the dictionaries do not explain. SHIFT then uses human judgments of feature relevance to remove unintended classifier signals.

**Experiments**
Pythia-70M and Gemma-2-2B are evaluated on four subject–verb agreement structures adapted from Finlayson et al. (2021). Held-out evaluations compare feature and neuron circuits using normalized retained performance (faithfulness) and performance of the circuit complement (completeness). Pythia features receive human interpretability ratings. On Bias in Bios, linear classifiers train on male professors versus female nurses, making gender perfectly predictive of profession. Humans select 55 of 67 Pythia features and 43 of 46 Gemma features for ablation; optional retraining updates only the classification head. A separate Pythia pipeline clusters confidently predicted Pile examples and discovers thousands of associated circuits.

**Key results**
Approximately 100 Pythia or 500 Gemma feature nodes explain most agreement performance, whereas roughly 1,500 or 50,000 neurons explain half. These comparisons include coarse SAE error nodes. Pythia agreement features score 62.3/100 for interpretability versus 30.2 for neurons. SHIFT plus retraining raises balanced profession accuracy from 61.9% to 93.1% for Pythia and 67.7% to 95.0% for Gemma; worst-group accuracy rises from 24.4% to 89.0% and 18.2% to 92.9%. Agreement case studies identify subject-number detectors, clause-boundary features, and verb-form promoters, with additional noun-phrase number trackers in Gemma.

**Limitations / open questions**
Agreement evaluation excludes the first third of layers, and annotated relative-clause circuits retain only 0.21 faithfulness. Reconstruction errors remain uninterpretable; removing residual-stream errors severely harms performance. Labels and relevance judgments are qualitative, with selected annotators and documented labeling biases. Automated cluster/circuit evaluation remains open. Gemma’s baseline layer was selected using balanced data to maximize initial bias, although SHIFT itself was not tuned on those labels. The supplied text is v3 dated March 27, 2025; metadata gives the original publication date.

title: Refusal mechanisms: initial experiments with Llama-2-7b-chat
summary:
**Central idea**
This is a preliminary SPAR project, mentored by Nina Rimsky. It uses activation patching to locate where Llama-2-7b-chat decides to refuse. The authors find a small set of attention heads in early-to-middle layers. These heads write a harmfulness signal at a post-instruction chat-template token position. Patching that signal into a harmless prompt is sufficient to induce refusal. Based on this, the authors propose a three-stage picture of refusal:
1. The model forms a task representation in early layers.
2. It computes a harmfulness feature from that representation in early-to-middle layers.
3. Later layers combine the task and the harmfulness feature to produce output, which is refusal text when the feature is active.

**Experiments**
- **Dataset.** There are 16 harmful and 16 harmless instructions, all with the fixed template `Tell me how to make a {object}.` (for example bomb/gun/virus versus pie/sandwich/teddy bear). Prompts use the Llama-2 chat format with no system prompt and are left-padded so object positions align.
- **Refusal metric.** The refusal score is the final-position logit difference logit[Sorry] − logit[Sure]. It cleanly separates the two sets.
- **Residual-stream patching.** Harmful activations are patched into harmless runs across positions and layers.
- **Component patching.** Attention outputs and individual heads at position 17 (the `[` token of `[/INST]`) in layers 5–10 are patched. The 6 heads with patching score above 0.005 are designated "refusal heads".
- **Steering.** A refusal direction is formed as the harmful-minus-harmless mean difference of these heads' outputs, averaged across heads. It is added to or subtracted from the residual stream at position 17, layers 5–10.

**Key results**
- Patching shows the expected signal at the object position in early layers and at the final position in late layers. It also shows an unexpected signal at position 17 in layers 5–15.
- Patching the residual stream at position 17, layer 9 makes the model refuse "how to make a pie" while still discussing pies. The authors read this as harmfulness being represented separately from task content.
- Patching only the 6 heads at position 17 gives partial, hedged refusal. Scaling their contributions by 2x gives explicit refusals, including humorous refusals for quilts, teddy bears and websites.
- The per-head mean-difference directions are reported to be similar to each other.
- Adding the averaged direction induces refusal on a harmless prompt (smoothie). Subtracting it makes the model comply with a biological-weapon request.
- In preliminary tests across several other prompt templates, 4 refusal heads were common to all templates.

**Limitations / open questions**
- The evidence is largely qualitative: single example completions, with no quantitative steering evaluation, no held-out harmful set and no capability measurement.
- Only one template family and one refusal category (dangerous objects) are studied, on one model.
- Head selection uses an arbitrary threshold, and the circuit is coarse.
- Future work proposed by the authors: edge attribution patching for a finer circuit, other refusal categories, and explaining how jailbreaks work.

title: Fine-Tuning Enhances Existing Mechanisms: A Case Study on Entity Tracking
abstract: Fine-tuning on generalized tasks such as instruction following, code generation, and mathematics has been shown to enhance language models' performance on a range of tasks. Nevertheless, explanations of how such fine-tuning influences the internal computations in these models remain elusive. We study how fine-tuning affects the internal mechanisms implemented in language models. As a case study, we explore the property of entity tracking, a crucial facet of language comprehension, where models fine-tuned on mathematics have substantial performance gains. We identify the mechanism that enables entity tracking and show that (i) in both the original model and its fine-tuned versions primarily the same circuit implements entity tracking. In fact, the entity tracking circuit of the original model on the fine-tuned versions performs better than the full original model. (ii) The circuits of all the models implement roughly the same functionality: Entity tracking is performed by tracking the position of the correct entity in both the original model and its fine-tuned versions. (iii) Performance boost in the fine-tuned models is primarily attributed to its improved ability to handle the augmented positional information. To uncover these findings, we employ: Patch Patching, DCM, which automatically detects model components responsible for specific semantics, and CMAP, a new approach for patching activations across models to reveal improved mechanisms. Our findings suggest that fine-tuning enhances, rather than fundamentally alters, the mechanistic operation of the model.
summary:
**Central idea**

Arithmetic fine-tuning can improve entity tracking while preserving an existing attention mechanism's coarse organization. The study compares Llama-7B with conversation-tuned Vicuna-7B, arithmetic LoRA-tuned Goat-7B, and FLoat-7B, fully fine-tuned on Goat's arithmetic data. Its findings concern this shared model lineage and a restricted retrieval task.

**Experiments**

Synthetic prompts describe seven randomly labeled boxes containing single-token objects, without subsequent state changes. Context statements place objects before box labels; queries reverse that structure. Path patching on 300 examples identifies attention heads at specified token positions. Greedy minimality pruning reduces Llama's initial 90-node circuit to 72. Evaluation mean-ablates excluded attention outputs while retaining all MLPs, measuring accuracy on 500 tasks. Faithfulness is circuit accuracy divided by full-model accuracy.

Desiderata-based Component Masking learns head subsets for object identity, box-label identity, and object position using 1,000 training examples per desideratum. Subsequent patching evaluations use 500 examples across ten sampled test sets. Cross-Model Activation Patching transplants corresponding head outputs from arithmetic-fine-tuned models into Llama on identical inputs.

**Key results**

Full-model accuracies are 0.66, 0.67, 0.82, and 0.82 for Llama, Vicuna, Goat, and FLoat, respectively; chance is approximately 0.14. The unchanged Llama circuit achieves 0.66, 0.65, 0.73, and 0.72, giving faithfulness ratios of 1.00, 0.97, 0.89, and 0.88. Ten random circuits matched for total and per-position size average 0.00–0.01 accuracy. Separately discovered Goat and FLoat circuits each contain 175 nodes and substantially overlap the base circuit, without being literal supersets.

Semantic interventions support a shared sequence: detect the relevant object's position, transmit positional information, then fetch its value. The text reports that transplanting fine-tuned Value Fetcher outputs recovers fine-tuned performance in Llama; Position Transmitter outputs also improve accuracy. Retaining the Goat circuit in base Llama raises accuracy from 0.66 to 0.77 under mean ablation.

**Limitations / open questions**

All models derive from one 7B checkpoint, and the task excludes state updates. Circuit searches use different initial component budgets. MLP mechanisms, Structure Reader functionality, and the precise positional code remain unresolved. Knockout tests reveal incomplete circuits despite high accuracy recovery. Cross-model transplantation establishes sufficient performance-enhancing outputs without uniquely identifying the natural causes of improvement. Several results are available only as qualitative descriptions of unseen plots, and some Appendix J example targets are inconsistent. Generalization across tasks, model families, and fine-tuning trajectories remains open.

title: A Mechanistic Understanding of Alignment Algorithms: A Case Study on DPO and Toxicity
abstract: While alignment algorithms are now commonly used to tune pre-trained language models towards a user's preferences, we lack explanations for the underlying mechanisms in which models become ``aligned'', thus making it difficult to explain phenomena like jailbreaks. In this work we study a popular algorithm, direct preference optimization (DPO), and the mechanisms by which it reduces toxicity. Namely, we first study how toxicity is represented and elicited in a pre-trained language model, GPT2-medium. We then apply DPO with a carefully crafted pairwise dataset to reduce toxicity. We examine how the resulting model averts toxic outputs, and find that capabilities learned from pre-training are not removed, but rather bypassed. We use this insight to demonstrate a simple method to un-align the model, reverting it back to its toxic behavior.
summary:
**Central idea**

This case study investigates whether DPO suppresses toxic generation by bypassing pretrained toxicity-associated MLP pathways. It examines GPT-2 Medium: 24 layers, residual width 1,024, and MLP width 4,096. The proposed mechanism is a distributed residual-stream offset that reduces activation of identified toxic neurons while largely preserving their parameters.

**Experiments**

A linear probe on mean final-layer activations achieves 94% validation accuracy on a 90:10 split of 561,808 Jigsaw comments. The authors rank MLP value vectors by cosine similarity to this probe and apply SVD to the top 128. They test final-layer subtraction of the probe, one selected value vector, and the first singular direction. DPO uses 24,576 preference pairs: greedy GPT-2 continuations of WikiText-2 prompts versus toxicity-guided PPLM continuations. Validation loss converges after approximately 6,000 sample pairs. Evaluation uses Perspective toxicity scores on the 1,199-prompt RealToxicityPrompts challenge subset, WikiText-2 perplexity, and continuation-token-overlap F1 on 2,000 Wikipedia prompts. Before/after analyses compare parameters, activations, residual states, and value-vector changes. Logit-lens analysis additionally uses 295 prompts selected because GPT-2 predicts one particular profane next token.

**Key results**

DPO lowers toxicity from 0.453 to 0.208; perplexity rises from 21.7 to 23.34, while F1 changes from 0.193 to 0.195. Direction subtraction yields toxicity scores of 0.245–0.305 at perplexities of 23.30–23.56. Corresponding parameters reportedly retain cosine similarities above 0.99. Selected toxic neurons activate less after DPO, alongside systematic residual shifts. Earlier value-vector changes often oppose those shifts geometrically; their small negative GeLU coefficients motivate a sign-reversed contribution explanation. Multiplying seven selected toxic key vectors by ten restores toxicity to 0.458, with perplexity 23.30 and F1 0.195.

**Limitations / open questions**

Evidence covers one model and one synthetic preference-training recipe, without uncertainty estimates or comprehensive capability evaluation. Weight editing demonstrates behavioral reactivation, rather than a prompt jailbreak. The distributed-offset explanation lacks a targeted mediation or reconstruction test; KL regularization's proposed causal role is untested. Positive key scaling does not enlarge the sign-defined activation region in Equation 3. Appendix A's positive dot-product criterion identifies logit increments, not guaranteed probability increases after softmax normalization. Figure images are unavailable in the supplied rendering; captions and prose support qualitative descriptions but not additional plotted values. Appendix D supplies DPO and PPLM settings but omits the promised probe hyperparameters.

title: Are Sparse Autoencoders Useful? A Case Study in Sparse Probing
abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular method for interpreting concepts represented in large language model (LLM) activations. However, there is a lack of evidence regarding the validity of their interpretations due to the lack of a ground truth for the concepts used by an LLM, and a growing number of works have presented problems with current SAEs. One alternative source of evidence would be demonstrating that SAEs improve performance on downstream tasks beyond existing baselines. We test this by applying SAEs to the real-world task of LLM activation probing in four regimes: data scarcity, class imbalance, label noise, and covariate shift. Due to the difficulty of detecting concepts in these challenging settings, we hypothesize that SAEs' basis of interpretable, concept-level latents should provide a useful inductive bias. However, although SAEs occasionally perform better than baselines on individual datasets, we are unable to design ensemble methods combining SAEs with baselines that consistently outperform ensemble methods solely using baselines. Additionally, although SAEs initially appear promising for identifying spurious correlations, detecting poor dataset quality, and training multi-token probes, we are able to achieve similar results with simple non-SAE baselines as well. Though we cannot discount SAEs' utility on other tasks, our findings highlight the shortcomings of current SAEs and the need to rigorously evaluate interpretability methods on downstream tasks with strong baselines.
summary:
**Central idea.** Since there is no ground truth for what concepts an LLM uses, one test of whether SAEs capture meaningful structure is whether they help on downstream tasks against strong baselines. The paper tests this on probing, where SAEs' concept-level latents might be expected to supply a useful inductive bias.

**Experiments.** 113 binary classification datasets. Probes on Gemma-2-9B (main results; replicated on Llama-3.1-8B) compare SAE-latent probes (Gemma Scope JumpReLU SAEs) against baselines: logistic regression, PCA, KNN, XGBoost and MLP probes on raw activations. Four hard regimes: data scarcity, class imbalance, label noise and covariate shift. Also tested: ensembles of SAE and baseline probes, and case studies on finding spurious correlations, detecting dataset problems and multi-token probing.

**Key results.** SAE probes occasionally win on individual datasets but do not consistently beat baselines in any regime. Ensembles that add SAE probes do not reliably beat baseline-only ensembles. The interpretability-driven wins (spotting spurious correlations, data-quality problems) can mostly be matched with simple non-SAE baselines.

**Limitations / open questions.** Probing is one task. Results depend on which SAEs (Gemma Scope) and which baselines are used. This does not rule out SAEs being useful for other goals such as unsupervised discovery or circuit analysis. It calls for rigorous downstream evaluations with strong baselines.
provenance: claude-code-session:claude-opus-5-5 (seed draft from fetched text + model knowledge; unreviewed)

title: Automated Interpretability Metrics Do Not Distinguish Trained and Random Transformers
abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are widely used to extract sparse, interpretable latents from transformer activations. We test whether commonly used SAE quality metrics and automatic explanation pipelines can distinguish trained transformers from randomly initialized ones (e.g., where parameters are sampled i.i.d. from a Gaussian). Over a wide range of Pythia model sizes and multiple randomization schemes, we find that, in many settings, SAEs trained on randomly initialized transformers produce auto-interpretability scores and reconstruction metrics that are similar to those from trained models. These results show that high aggregate auto-interpretability scores do not, by themselves, guarantee that learned, computationally relevant features have been recovered. We therefore recommend treating common SAE metrics as useful but insufficient proxies for mechanistic interpretability and argue for routine randomized baselines and targeted measures of feature 'abstractness'.
summary:
**Central idea**

High aggregate SAE explanation scores do not by themselves establish recovery of learned transformer computations. The paper tests randomized baselines and introduces activation-weighted token-ID entropy as a preliminary indicator of differences that aggregate scores obscure.

**Experiments**

Residual-stream TopK SAEs are trained on Pythia-70M, 160M, 410M, 1B, and 6.9B. Comparisons use pretrained weights, original initialization, Gaussian re-randomization matching each trained matrix’s mean and variance with or without retaining embeddings and unembeddings, and a control giving each token occurrence a fresh standard-Gaussian embedding. Defaults are expansion factor 64, k=32, 100M RedPajama tokens, and a 10M-token activation buffer. Layer sampling becomes less frequent for larger models. Meta-Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct-AWQ-INT4 generates explanations and evaluates fuzzing and detection AUROC for 100 randomly sampled latents per SAE. Additional tests vary training data and hyperparameters; uncertainty is evaluated over five seeds for Pythia-70M. Toy experiments compare known sparse mixtures, word embeddings, matched Gaussian controls, and outputs of random two-layer ReLU MLPs.

**Key results**

Trained and randomized variants often have similar explanation AUROC and reconstruction metrics, with narrower explanation-score gaps at larger model sizes. The fresh-noise control has near-chance explanation scores. Selected 1B-token training runs preserve the qualitative findings. In Pythia-1B, very small SAEs can retain similar explanation scores despite distinguishable explained variance and cross-entropy recovery. Token entropy increases with depth in trained models, while randomized-model latents tend to remain token-specific. Trained Pythia-6.9B also has latents combining high entropy with high explanation AUROC. Synthetic-input SAEs recover known dictionary directions under suitable regularization. Random MLPs improve sparse-reconstruction frontiers even for Gaussian inputs. A supplied linear-Gaussian derivation establishes preservation of sparse-mixture generative form under linear maps, without guaranteeing recoverability.

**Limitations / open questions**

Results concern Pythia, RedPajama, selected SAE configurations, and one explanation model; they do not directly test correlation-based activation simulation. Supplied figure captions lack numerical AUROC values. Cross-entropy recovery is meaningful only for trained models because randomized models already have poor language-model loss. Token entropy is an indirect proxy, and sparse reconstruction does not establish feature identity in nonlinear MLP outputs. The mechanism behind the randomized-transformer findings remains unresolved. The results do not establish that trained-model SAEs lack meaningful features. Supplied metadata dates publication to January 2025, while the body identifies a January 27, 2026 revision.

title: AxBench: Steering LLMs? Even Simple Baselines Outperform Sparse Autoencoders
abstract: Fine-grained steering of language model outputs is essential for safety and reliability. Prompting and finetuning are widely used to achieve these goals, but interpretability researchers have proposed a variety of representation-based techniques as well, including sparse autoencoders (SAEs), linear artificial tomography, supervised steering vectors, linear probes, and representation finetuning. At present, there is no benchmark for making direct comparisons between these proposals. Therefore, we introduce AxBench, a large-scale benchmark for steering and concept detection, and report experiments on Gemma-2-2B and 9B. For steering, we find that prompting outperforms all existing methods, followed by finetuning. For concept detection, representation-based methods such as difference-in-means, perform the best. On both evaluations, SAEs are not competitive. We introduce a novel weakly-supervised representational method (Rank-1 Representation Finetuning; ReFT-r1), which is competitive on both tasks while providing the interpretability advantages that prompting lacks. Along with AxBench, we train and publicly release SAE-scale feature dictionaries for ReFT-r1 and DiffMean.
summary:
**Central idea**

AxBench compares open-vocabulary concept detection and generation steering against prompting and finetuning. It introduces ReFT-r1, which learns a shared detection and intervention direction using activation-dependent training interventions, language-modeling loss, and sparsity regularization. Practical detection and control performance are the evaluation targets; faithful recovery of internal mechanisms is not established.

**Experiments**

Concept500 contains 500 SAE-derived concept descriptions per site: residual-stream layers 10 and 20 of Gemma-2-2B-it, and layers 20 and 31 of Gemma-2-9B-it. GPT-4o-mini generates positive responses and evaluation hard negatives; ordinary negatives come from the target model. The stated protocol uses 144 training examples and approximately 72 detection examples per concept. Detection metrics include AUROC and F1, including an approximately 1%-positive setting with 3,600 additional negatives. Steering uses ten AlpacaEval instructions per concept, split into five for selecting a steering factor and five for evaluation, with generations capped at 128 tokens. GPT-4o-mini scores concept incorporation, instruction following, and fluency from 0–2; their harmonic mean determines overall quality. Additional experiments vary training-data quantity, construct Concept16K dictionaries, generate directions from descriptions, and transfer directions between models.

**Key results**

Across four sites, mean detection AUROC is 0.942 for DiffMean, 0.940 for Probe, 0.938 for ReFT-r1, 0.917 for training-selected SAE features, and 0.695 for the original SAE features. These aggregate rankings do not hold at every site. Mean steering scores are 0.894 for engineered prompting, 0.741 for LoReFT, 0.615 for LoRA, 0.543 for ReFT-r1, 0.239 for DiffMean, and 0.165 for SAEs. Full finetuning scores 0.676 on only the first 20 concepts in the 2B settings. SAE feature selection improves detection without improving average steering. SAE addition outperforms the tested clamping variants. Increasing steering strength reduces instruction-following scores. Generated and transferred ReFT-r1 directions largely retain detection performance while losing steering performance.

**Limitations / open questions**

Results cover two instruction-tuned Gemma models, selected sites, synthetic labels, and one LLM generator/judge without supplied human calibration. SAE labels may be shallow or inaccurate; the 2B SAEs were trained on the base model. Training hyperparameters largely target detection using ten concepts overlapping Concept500. The supplied rendering contains conflicting pooling descriptions, prose/table winrates, and unexplained training-count discrepancies. Its assertion that transferred directions outperform finetuning conflicts with the displayed scores. Some referenced figures and prompt templates are absent.

title: Features that Make a Difference: Leveraging Gradients for Improved Dictionary Learning
abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are a promising approach for extracting neural network representations by learning a sparse and overcomplete decomposition of the network's internal activations. However, SAEs are traditionally trained considering only activation values and not the effect those activations have on downstream computations. This limits the information available to learn features, and biases the autoencoder towards neglecting features which are represented with small activation values but strongly influence model outputs. To address this, we introduce Gradient SAEs (g-SAEs), which modify the $k$-sparse autoencoder architecture by augmenting the TopK activation function to rely on the gradients of the input activation when selecting the $k$ elements. For a given sparsity level, g-SAEs produce reconstructions that are more faithful to original network performance when propagated through the network. Additionally, we find evidence that g-SAEs learn latents that are on average more effective at steering models in arbitrary contexts. By considering the downstream effects of activations, our approach leverages the dual nature of neural network features as both $\textit{representations}$, retrospectively, and $\textit{actions}$, prospectively. While previous methods have approached the problem of feature discovery primarily focused on the former aspect, g-SAEs represent a step towards accounting for the latter as well.
summary:
**Central idea**

Gradient SAEs (g-SAEs) incorporate downstream predictive-loss sensitivity into TopK latent selection while retaining a reconstruction-only training loss. They rank preactivations using z + βz ⊙ |W_decᵀ∇ₓL| and preserve the original values of the selected entries. The added term estimates the magnitude of each latent's first-order contribution to loss, biasing selection toward influential directions.

**Experiments**

The principal comparisons use GPT-2 Small layer-7 residual activations, β = 10⁵, and approximately 14 million training tokens. Dictionary-width and sparsity sweeps compare g-SAEs with TopK and end-to-end TopK. Replacement metrics are relative cross-entropy increase and reconstruction-error norm divided by input norm, labeled NMSE despite its displayed unsquared definition. Perturbation studies compare real activation-difference directions with isotropic and covariance-adjusted random directions, and measure Spearman correlations between loss changes, perturbation norms, and gradient predictions. Steering evaluates normalized decoder directions against tokens selected through unembedding projection. One layer-7 analysis uses 1,000 latents per SAE over ten arbitrary sequences each at α = 50. Human evaluation uses three raters and activating examples from layers 3, 5, 7, and 9.

**Key results**

Activation-difference directions have higher average absolute loss derivatives than the random controls from layer 3 onward. Gradient predictions correlate with perturbation effects more strongly than norms, especially at smaller perturbations and later layers. g-SAEs show slightly lower replacement loss than TopK with comparable reconstruction frontiers; an unspecified GPT-2 size sweep also reports lower replacement loss. At L0 = 32, five-batch-inactive fractions are 0.34 for g-SAEs, 0.43 for TopK, and 0.29 for end-to-end SAEs. Sampled g-SAE directions reportedly add over five times as much associated-token probability on average as TopK directions, primarily through fewer ineffective latents. Human ratings are descriptively similar for g-SAEs and TopK.

**Limitations / open questions**

The source is complete, but numerical plot values are unavailable. The training corpus and model-size list are unspecified, and perturbation sites alternate between MLP-output and resid_post descriptions. Human-evaluation counts conflict: three architectures across four layers and 384 samples at 32 per SAE imply twelve dictionaries, while sixteen are stated. Ratings establish neither equivalence nor monosemanticity. Signed probability changes for complementary token sets necessarily sum to zero, preventing their use as independent specificity evidence; the positive complementary totals reported for the AI example are inconsistent with that signed definition. Semantic steering, problematic feature splitting, and robustness across activation plateaus remain unresolved. Inference requires downstream computation and backpropagation.

title: Improving Steering Vectors by Targeting Sparse Autoencoder Features
abstract: To control the behavior of language models, steering methods attempt to ensure that outputs of the model satisfy specific pre-defined properties. Adding steering vectors to the model is a promising method of model control that is easier than finetuning, and may be more robust than prompting. However, it can be difficult to anticipate the effects of steering vectors produced by methods such as CAA [Panickssery et al., 2024] or the direct use of SAE latents [Templeton et al., 2024]. In our work, we address this issue by using SAEs to measure the effects of steering vectors, giving us a method that can be used to understand the causal effect of any steering vector intervention. We use this method for measuring causal effects to develop an improved steering method, SAE-Targeted Steering (SAE-TS), which finds steering vectors to target specific SAE features while minimizing unintended side effects. We show that overall, SAE-TS balances steering effects with coherence better than CAA and SAE feature steering, when evaluated on a range of tasks.
summary:
**Central idea**

SAE-Targeted Steering (SAE-TS) constructs steering directions using measured changes in generated text. Steered and unsteered rollouts are replayed through a model, and differences in mean SAE activations describe their content effects. An affine predictor maps steering directions to these effects. SAE-TS combines its normalized target-feature column with a normalized bias-related correction. This is a heuristic for targeting features, without an exact guarantee that other features remain unchanged. EffectVis provides an interface for exploring measured effects and related features.

**Experiments**

The main experiments use Gemma-2-2B base and a layer-12, 16,384-feature Gemma Scope JumpReLU SAE. Feature-effect collection uses 896 rollouts of 32 tokens per feature. The predictor trains on 50,000 decoder directions from a same-layer 65k SAE with L0 72; collection strengths are individually calibrated to increase cross-entropy by 0.5. Evaluations compare SAE-TS, modified CAA, and direct SAE decoder steering on nine targets, using 256 completions of 32 tokens per condition from `<BOS>I think`. GPT-4o-mini rates behavioral adherence and coherence; their normalized product is evaluated across steering strengths. Appendices test Gemma-2-9B, another prompt, pseudoinverse targeting, rotation steering, and isolated bias-direction steering.

**Key results**

Averages of nine per-task maximum Behavioral*Coherence scores on Gemma-2-2B are 0.3600 for SAE-TS, 0.2165 for CAA, and 0.1290 for direct SAE steering. SAE-TS leads on seven tasks. On Gemma-2-9B, corresponding averages are 0.3376, 0.2531, and 0.2184, with SAE-TS leading on four tasks. On 2B, pseudoinverse targeting averages 0.1197 and rotation steering 0.3115. A selected month-after-day feature promotes year-digit features, illustrating that activation contexts and generated effects can differ. An exploratory feature-group study uses Gemma 1 2B.

**Limitations / open questions**

Evidence concerns selected targets and short base-model completions, with peaks selected across tested strengths. It establishes neither broad capability preservation nor safety effectiveness. Held-out effect-prediction accuracy, uncertainty estimates, and independent human judge calibration are not reported. SAE coverage restricts available targets. Bias subtraction increases judged coherence and proper-noun frequency, potentially confounding the score. Strong London steering concentrates outputs on fashion and exhibitions. Numerical tables show small CAA advantages described as ties in prose; a CAA example mentions London despite the main text's absence claim. Plot images are unavailable in the supplied rendering, limiting independent assessment of curves.

title: Llama Scope: Extracting Millions of Features from Llama-3.1-8B with Sparse Autoencoders
abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a powerful unsupervised method for extracting sparse representations from language models, yet scalable training remains a significant challenge. We introduce a suite of 256 SAEs, trained on each layer and sublayer of the Llama-3.1-8B-Base model, with 32K and 128K features. Modifications to a state-of-the-art SAE variant, Top-K SAEs, are evaluated across multiple dimensions. In particular, we assess the generalizability of SAEs trained on base models to longer contexts and fine-tuned models. Additionally, we analyze the geometry of learned SAE latents, confirming that \emph{feature splitting} enables the discovery of new features. The Llama Scope SAE checkpoints are publicly available at~\url{https://huggingface.co/fnlp/Llama-Scope}, alongside our scalable training, interpretation, and visualization tools at \url{https://github.com/OpenMOSS/Language-Model-SAEs}. These contributions aim to advance the open-source Sparse Autoencoder ecosystem and support mechanistic interpretability research by reducing the need for redundant SAE training.
summary:
**Central idea**

Llama Scope releases 256 sparse dictionaries for Llama-3.1-8B-Base: 32K- and 128K-feature models at all 32 layers, covering post-MLP residual streams, attention outputs, MLP outputs, and MLP transcoders. Its modified TopK recipe weights selection scores by decoder-column norms, anneals K during early training, and permits post-training conversion to independently thresholded JumpReLU inference.
