- Raw virtual-weight magnitude correlates only weakly with helpfulness, and helpful and harmful weights appear across all magnitudes. Some features, such as the Chinese feature, do have helpful top weights.
- Effectiveness is roughly lognormal and spans about 10 orders of magnitude. Across all six families, the most effective weights are overwhelmingly helpful, exceeding any harmful weight by at least an order of magnitude. Moderate effectiveness mixes helpful and harmful weights.
- In the newline feature, the direct and attention position inputs cancel (OLS slope −0.993, r²=0.912). Effectiveness reveals that inhibition from whitespace tokens is the key mechanism.
- Pruning the least effective 70% of weights costs about 0.01 nats, and 85% costs under 0.1. Magnitude pruning does worse, except for negative Features→Logits weights. At 1% density, roughly the original parameter count, loss degrades significantly.
- 47.6% of sampled weights have positive mean helpfulness (12.7% are dead). Keeping 90% of the helpfulness mass needs about 2.43% density; keeping 99% needs 13.6%. The model remains dense in this basis.

**Limitations / open questions**
- Only a single tiny 1L model was studied.
- Fisher effectiveness and helpfulness do not scale to frontier models.
- The transcoder and attention heads remain partly polysemantic.
- Joint ablations have nonlinear effects.
- QK attributions use independence approximations.
- The authors suspect no saliency scheme will do much better and argue that a better basis is needed for sparse global circuits. This is untested.
- Many appendix figures and the main helpfulness table are not present in the provided text.

title: A Toy Model of Interference Weights
summary:
**Central idea**

Compressing features into a shared activation space also constrains the effective weights connecting them. Expanding these connections into feature coordinates exposes “interference weights.” The note distinguishes two definitions: deviations from optimized, regularized lifted-space weights, and connections that fail to improve loss under individual ablation. It argues that separating useful connections from interference may be essential for global circuit analysis.

**Experiments**

The initial synthetic reconstruction model uses 100 features, a 20-dimensional bottleneck, feature density 0.02, and effective weights U = WᵀW. Histograms and comparisons between two training seeds examine individual weights’ loss contributions; seeds change both initialization and sampled data. Undertrained and more converged configurations are considered. An untied model approximates y = ReLU(Ax + v), using 128 features compressed into 16 dimensions, eight blocks, input density 0.3, and v = −0.1. Its stated within-block weight density is 0.1, although preceding setup prose mentions 0.5. Further experiments examine converged isotropic models and two mutually exclusive groups of 100 features, with two features active in the selected group.

**Key results**

The authors report toy weight distributions qualitatively resembling feature-to-logit connections previously observed in Towards Monosemanticity. Useful and interference connections can overlap in weight magnitude. In identity toys, useful weights agree more closely across seeds, while interference can become structured with convergence. The note compares magnitude, expected attribution, target-weighted attribution, and frequency filters against individual loss effects, defining useful weights by loss benefit greater than 0.0001. Plot values and quantitative filter rankings are unavailable in the supplied rendering. Its alternative “loss gain” metric sums individual weight effects; it does not measure joint-ablation performance. In the grouped-feature toy, ablating a low-rank component that excites within-group features and inhibits the other group worsens loss.

**Limitations / open questions**

The source is a complete preliminary note, but its plots are unavailable as readable figures, and prose supplies little training detail or uncertainty quantification. Real-language-model observations are from prior work, not new tests here. The more realistic toy does not retain all desired phenomenology through convergence. Interference definitions disagree about omitted connections and interacting weights. Exhaustive lifted optimization and individual-ablation screening face quadratic feature-pair scaling. Nonadditive parameter sharing and the suggestion that interference matters less for alignment than robustness remain unresolved.

Inceptionism: Going Deeper into Neural Networks
summary:
**Central idea**

Inceptionism explores image classifiers by modifying their inputs to amplify a chosen class interpretation or features already detected at a selected layer. Class-directed synthesis starts from random noise and iteratively strengthens the desired interpretation. The authors report better results when imposing natural-image constraints, such as correlations between neighboring pixels. Image-conditioned amplification instead strengthens existing detections, creating a feedback loop that turns suggestive shapes into increasingly elaborate patterns.

**Experiments**

The post presents qualitative image-synthesis demonstrations associated with the Inception architecture. These include class-directed synthesis, illustrated by bananas and dumbbells; amplification at lower versus higher layers on photographs and paintings; and repeated amplification with zooming, including initialization from random noise. One network is described as trained mostly on animal images. Noise-seeded “dreams” use a places-trained network identified as Places205-GoogLeNet. Exact checkpoints, mathematical objectives, optimization settings, per-demonstration sample counts, and quantitative evaluation metrics are not supplied. The supplied rendering contains descriptions and captions but no accessible figure images.

**Key results**

The text reports that lower-layer amplification produces strokes and simple ornament-like patterns, whereas higher-layer amplification produces complex features and recognizable objects. Initial image structure influences the generated content: horizons tend to acquire towers or pagodas, and leaves can acquire birds or insects. A dumbbell visualization includes muscular weightlifters, suggesting a candidate association between the object and its photographic context. Repeated amplification and zooming also generate imagery from noise. These demonstrations illustrate image synthesis using discriminatively trained networks, input modification, and additional constraints, without isolating each ingredient’s contribution.

**Limitations / open questions**

The evidence consists of selected visual demonstrations and author descriptions, without controlled comparisons, human evaluation, or measurements of explanatory accuracy. Recognizable synthesized content does not establish comprehensive feature semantics or causal use during ordinary classification. The suggestion that dumbbell training images included arms is speculative; no training-data audit or corrective intervention is reported. The post proposes training diagnosis and architecture improvement as applications but supplies no measured debugging benefit. How much synthesized structure comes from network weights, initialization, priors, and repeated amplification remains unresolved.

title: An introduction to systems biology: design principles of biological circuits
Monitoring monitorability (Guan et al., 2025)
Scruples: a corpus of community ethical judgments on 32,000 real-life anecdotes (Lourie et al., 2021)
Axiomatic Attribution for Deep Networks
abstract: The paper studies attribution of deep-network predictions to input features. It identifies Sensitivity and Implementation Invariance as desirable axioms and introduces Integrated Gradients, which integrates input gradients along a straight path from a baseline to the explained input. The method requires standard gradient operations without network modification. Applications to two image models, two text models, and molecular graph-convolution models illustrate prediction explanation, rule discovery, and debugging.
summary:
**Central idea**

Integrated Gradients (IG) attributes an output difference to input features by multiplying each feature’s input-minus-baseline difference by its average gradient along the straight line between baseline and input. Sensitivity requires nonzero attribution to a sole changed feature when the prediction changes; Implementation Invariance requires identical attributions for functionally equivalent networks. Under regularity sufficient for the pathwise fundamental theorem of calculus, exact IG allocations sum to F(x) − F(x′). Economic cost-sharing results motivate path methods, while symmetry preservation motivates choosing the straight path.

**Experiments**

Applications cover GoogLeNet trained on ImageNet; the Gulshan et al. diabetic-retinopathy network; a Kim-style question classifier trained on WikiTableQuestions; Google’s LSTM-based neural machine translation system; and Kearnes et al. molecular graph-convolution networks. Image baselines are black images. Text and molecular baselines zero embeddings or feature vectors; translation retains start/end-marker embeddings. Evidence consists principally of selected attribution visualizations and architectural inspection, without aggregate explanation-accuracy, alignment, debugging-improvement, or user-study metrics.

**Key results**

A formal one-variable ReLU counterexample demonstrates that endpoint gradients can vanish despite a nonzero baseline-to-input output change. Selected image visualizations qualitatively favor IG over gradient-times-image; a retinal example highlights apparent lesion boundaries. Question-classification examples highlight “how many” and “total number,” while exposing an undesirable association with “charles.” An English–German translation example yields intuitive wordpiece alignments. For one W2N2 molecule labeled active on PCBA-58432, bonded atom-pair features contribute 46% of the prediction score and other pairs contribute −3%; these percentages concern that example, not a dataset average. Identical atom attributions in W1N2 prompt architectural inspection revealing incomplete convolution that makes atoms with matching types and bond-type counts contribute identically. The authors generally report 20–300 integration steps for approximation within 5%, but use 100–1000 for translation.

**Limitations / open questions**

Baseline choice remains substantive: low baseline output alone does not establish absence of meaningful signal. Perturbation evaluations can conflate attribution errors with unnatural inputs or model behavior. Concrete DeepLift/LRP counterexamples and the symmetry-uniqueness proof are deferred to the cited full version; the path-method characterization is imported from Friedman. These are not proofs supplied here. Uniqueness is restricted to single-path methods, since averaging paths permits other axiom-satisfying allocations. Numerical integration requires convergence checks. The method does not explain feature interactions or the network’s computational logic, and the demonstrations do not establish comprehensive attribution accuracy.

title: Reasoning models don't always say what they think (Chen et al., 2025)
Reading between the dots: decoding hidden computation across filler tokens (Brauer et al., 2026)
Not all LLM reasoning is visible in the chain-of-thought (Baherwani et al., 2026)
Would this change your answer? Evaluating explanations of LLM behavior in the wild with counterfactual experiments (Karvonen et al., 2026)
Thought anchors: which LLM reasoning steps matter? (Bogdan et al., 2025)
Understanding Reasoning in Thinking Language Models via Steering Vectors
abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have led to the development of thinking language models that generate extensive internal reasoning chains before producing responses. While these models achieve improved performance, controlling their reasoning processes remains challenging. This work presents a steering approach for thinking LLMs by analyzing and manipulating specific reasoning behaviors in DeepSeek-R1-Distill models. Through a systematic experiment on 500 tasks across 10 diverse categories, we identify several reasoning behaviors exhibited by thinking models, including expressing uncertainty, generating examples for hypothesis validation, and backtracking in reasoning chains. We demonstrate that these behaviors are mediated by linear directions in the model's activation space and can be controlled using steering vectors. By extracting and applying these vectors, we provide a method to modulate specific aspects of the model's reasoning process, such as its tendency to backtrack or express uncertainty. Our approach offers practical tools for steering reasoning processes in thinking models in a controlled and interpretable manner. We validate our steering method using three DeepSeek-R1-Distill models, demonstrating consistent control across different model architectures.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper extracts residual-stream directions associated with visible reasoning behaviors and adds or subtracts them during generation. It targets backtracking, expressed uncertainty, example testing, and recalled-knowledge addition in DeepSeek-R1-Distill models. The demonstrated outcome concerns annotated reasoning text; distinct internal mechanisms and faithful natural mediation require additional evidence.

**Experiments**

Claude 3.5 Sonnet generates 500 tasks spanning ten categories, including mathematical logic, spatial reasoning, causal reasoning, and scientific reasoning. GPT-4o annotates responses using six behavioral labels. A descriptive comparison evaluates five R1 distills and five baseline models on 100 randomly selected tasks.

Steering experiments use DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, Qwen-14B, and Llama-8B, with greedy decoding and a 1,000-token response limit. Candidate directions contrast behavior-associated activation means with an overall mean, using annotated spans and their preceding tokens with a stated ten-token cap. Directions are normalized to the norm of the overall mean activation. Attribution-patching scores guide layer selection, with embedding-aligned early layers excluded. Selected layers are 12 for all four behaviors in Llama-8B, 15–18 in Qwen-1.5B, and 24 or 29 in Qwen-14B. Each vector is evaluated on 50 unseen tasks.

**Key results**

In the 100-task comparison, thinking models average 27.6 sentences per response versus 14.4 for baselines. They allocate higher sentence fractions to backtracking, uncertainty, and example testing, and lower fractions to knowledge addition. The paper reports that positive and negative steering increase and decrease targeted behavior-token fractions, explicitly discussing backtracking, uncertainty, and example testing. Numerical steering effects are unavailable in the text rendering. Cosine analyses in Llama-8B and Qwen-14B report generally low-to-moderate similarities between behavior directions, with uncertainty and backtracking positively aligned. Directions are extracted separately within each model; cross-model vector transfer is not tested.

**Limitations / open questions**

GPT-4o annotations have acknowledged errors without reported human calibration; Appendix B's annotated example also differs from its displayed original response. Behavioral fractions do not establish improved accuracy, calibrated uncertainty, independent control, or capability preservation. Generalization to directly RL-trained thinking models remains untested. Layer selection is unclear: Figure 3 describes vector removal while the equations specify addition, and first-order KL attribution would have zero gradient if evaluated against the unchanged reference distribution. Some passages inconsistently refer to two rather than three models. Figures are unavailable visually, steering strengths and intervention-token schedules are underspecified, and Appendix E contains shortened response examples, including an unfinished equation followed by the negative-steering example.

title: Causal abstractions of neural networks (Geiger et al., 2021)
RelP: Faithful and Efficient Circuit Discovery in Language Models via Relevance Patching
abstract: Activation patching is a standard method in mechanistic interpretability for localizing the components of a model responsible for specific behaviors, but it is computationally expensive to apply at scale. Attribution patching offers a faster, gradient-based approximation, yet suffers from noise and reduced reliability in deep, highly non-linear networks. In this work, we introduce Relevance Patching (RelP), which replaces the local gradients in attribution patching with propagation coefficients derived from Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP). LRP propagates the network's output backward through the layers, redistributing relevance to lower-level components according to local propagation rules that ensure properties such as relevance conservation or improved signal-to-noise ratio. Like attribution patching, RelP requires only two forward passes and one backward pass, maintaining computational efficiency while improving faithfulness. We validate RelP across a range of models and tasks, showing that it more accurately approximates activation patching than standard attribution patching, particularly when analyzing residual stream and MLP outputs in the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) task. For instance, for MLP outputs in GPT-2 Large, attribution patching achieves a Pearson correlation of 0.006, whereas RelP reaches 0.956, highlighting the improvement offered by RelP. Additionally, we compare the faithfulness of sparse feature circuits identified by RelP and Integrated Gradients (IG), showing that RelP achieves comparable faithfulness without the extra computational cost associated with IG.
summary:
**Central idea**
Relevance Patching (RelP) estimates activation-replacement effects by dotting patch-minus-original activation differences with Layer-wise Relevance Propagation coefficients instead of ordinary gradients. It retains attribution patching's two forward passes and one backward pass. The implementation modifies normalization and activation backward rules, uses LRP-0 for linear layers, and applies a Half-rule to multiplicative gates in Qwen2 and Gemma2. Despite discussing attention-specific propagation, the experiments use no AH-rule.

**Experiments**
On 100 templated indirect object identification (IOI) prompt pairs, subject and recipient names are swapped while other tokens remain fixed. The output metric is the original-versus-patch target logit difference. RelP and attribution patching are compared with exact activation patching using Pearson correlation after summing scores across hidden dimensions. Eight checkpoints are evaluated: GPT-2 Small/Medium/Large, Pythia-70M/410M, Qwen2-0.5B/7B, and Gemma2-2B. Separately, Pythia-70M circuits are discovered for agreement within relative clauses, across relative clauses, and across prepositional phrases, using 300 discovery samples and 100 held-out evaluation samples. Comparisons include ten-step Integrated Gradients (IG) and neuron circuits. Evaluation excludes the first third of each circuit and measures probability-difference recovery relative to full mean ablation, plus recovery by the circuit's complement.

**Key results**
RelP improves IOI correlations for residual-stream and MLP outputs in all eight checkpoints. GPT-2 Large MLP correlation rises from 0.006 to 0.956; Qwen2-7B remains less accurate, reaching 0.549 for residual streams and 0.622 for MLP outputs. Attention-output correlation improves in seven checkpoints but falls from 0.979 to 0.962 in GPT-2 Small, qualifying the prose's claims of consistent superiority. Agreement circuits show reported faithfulness comparable to ten-step IG at lower pass count. About 100 SAE features explain most measured performance, whereas roughly 1,500 neurons explain half. Removing residual-stream SAE error nodes severely disrupts performance.

**Limitations / open questions**
Evidence covers controlled counterfactual pairs and single-token metrics, with circuit comparisons restricted to one small model. Pearson correlation does not establish absolute effect accuracy, and behavioral recovery does not guarantee complete mechanistic correspondence. Rule selection requires architectural adaptation; attention gains are less consistent. Uncertainty estimates and measured wall-clock savings are not supplied. Generalization to free-form generation and tasks without known counterfactual inputs remains open.

title: Transcoders Find Interpretable LLM Feature Circuits
abstract: A key goal in mechanistic interpretability is circuit analysis: finding sparse subgraphs of models corresponding to specific behaviors or capabilities. However, MLP sublayers make fine-grained circuit analysis on transformer-based language models difficult. In particular, interpretable features -- such as those found by sparse autoencoders (SAEs) -- are typically linear combinations of extremely many neurons, each with its own nonlinearity to account for. Circuit analysis in this setting thus either yields intractably large circuits or fails to disentangle local and global behavior. To address this we explore transcoders, which seek to faithfully approximate a densely activating MLP layer with a wider, sparsely-activating MLP layer. We introduce a novel method for using transcoders to perform weights-based circuit analysis through MLP sublayers. The resulting circuits neatly factorize into input-dependent and input-invariant terms. We then successfully train transcoders on language models with 120M, 410M, and 1.4B parameters, and find them to perform at least on par with SAEs in terms of sparsity, faithfulness, and human-interpretability. Finally, we apply transcoders to reverse-engineer unknown circuits in the model, and we obtain novel insights regarding the "greater-than circuit" in GPT2-small. Our results suggest that transcoders can prove effective in decomposing model computations involving MLPs into interpretable circuits. Code is available at https://github.com/jacobdunefsky/transcoder_circuits/.
summary:
**Central idea**
Transcoders replace an MLP sublayer with a wider, sparsely activating ReLU MLP trained using output reconstruction error plus an L1 activation penalty. Unlike SAEs that reconstruct activations, transcoders approximate the MLP's input-output computation. Direct feature contributions factor into an input-dependent activation and an input-invariant decoder–encoder dot product. A recursive greedy algorithm follows high-attribution paths through features and attention OV circuits; token embedding projections, called de-embeddings, help interpret feature inputs.

**Experiments**
The authors train transcoders and SAEs with dictionaries 32 times model dimensionality on 60 million OpenWebText tokens for GPT2-small, Pythia-410M, and Pythia-1.4B. Evaluation uses 3.2 million tokens, measuring mean active-feature count and next-token cross-entropy after replacing a sublayer or its activations. A blinded human comparison examines 50 random features per method at Pythia-410M layer 15. Nine GPT2-small layer-8 blind case studies infer feature semantics without viewing prompt text. Greater-than experiments use all 100 prompts of the form “The war lasted from 17YY to 17,” comparing retained transcoder features against neurons using mean probability mass above the input year minus mass at or below it.

**Key results**
Transcoders match or improve the tested SAE sparsity–fidelity frontiers across all three models. Human inspection labels 41/50 transcoder features and 38/50 SAE features interpretable. Table 4 reports five successful, two mostly successful, and two failed blind interpretations. Greater-than analysis identifies year-sensitive MLP10 features receiving information through attention head 9.1. Fewer than 24 retained transcoder features outperform the corresponding neuron selection; adding the 24th feature causes a sharp performance drop. A handful of features recover most, but not all, original performance.

**Limitations / open questions**
Approximation errors can erase behavioral nuances: replacing earlier MLPs substantially weakens a feature's distinction between participial and finite uses of “caught.” Attention patterns are fixed, so QK computation remains unexplained; LayerNorm uses an approximate scaling treatment. SAE learning rates were selected through transcoder tuning, limiting comparative conclusions. Interpretability judgments and circuit studies are small and qualitative. The supplied text inconsistently reports case-study counts; Table 4 lists nine, including seven restricted studies. The text is version 2 dated November 6, 2024, while metadata gives the initial publication date.

title: Optimal Brain Damage (LeCun et al.)
Optimal Brain Surgeon (Hassibi & Stork)
Learning both Weights and Connections for Efficient Neural Networks (Han et al.)
Interpretability in Parameter Space: Minimizing Mechanistic Description Length with Attribution-based Parameter Decomposition
abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand the internal mechanisms learned by neural networks. Despite recent progress toward this goal, it remains unclear how best to decompose neural network parameters into mechanistic components. We introduce Attribution-based Parameter Decomposition (APD), a method that directly decomposes a neural network's parameters into components that (i) are faithful to the parameters of the original network, (ii) require a minimal number of components to process any input, and (iii) are maximally simple. Our approach thus optimizes for a minimal length description of the network's mechanisms. We demonstrate APD's effectiveness by successfully identifying ground truth mechanisms in multiple toy experimental settings: Recovering features from superposition; separating compressed computations; and identifying cross-layer distributed representations. While challenges remain to scaling APD to non-toy models, our results suggest solutions to several open problems in mechanistic interpretability, including identifying minimal circuits in superposition, offering a conceptual foundation for 'features', and providing an architecture-agnostic framework for neural network decomposition.
summary:
**Central idea**

Attribution-based Parameter Decomposition (APD) learns additive parameter components intended to describe a network's mechanisms. Three objectives encourage parameter reconstruction, output reconstruction using few components per input, and low component complexity. Gradient attributions select components for a batch-top-k sparse forward pass; a factorized Schatten penalty encourages low matrix ranks. Compressed-computation experiments also reconstruct hidden activations. A minimum-description-length coding argument motivates these objectives without proving unique recovery or globally minimal mechanisms.

**Experiments**

All evaluations use synthetic toy networks. Superposition experiments decompose tied-weight ReLU reconstruction models with 5 inputs and 2 hidden dimensions, or 40 inputs and 10 hidden dimensions. Compressed-computation experiments approximate 100 coordinatewise functions, y_i = x_i + ReLU(x_i), using a width-1000 residual stream and 50 MLP neurons. Inputs independently activate with probability 0.01, with nonzero values uniform in [-1,1]. A two-layer variant divides the neurons into groups of 25. APD starts with 130 and 200 components, respectively. Evaluations examine neuron-contribution patterns, output MSE, and selective component ablations. A further hand-coded network approximates four gated trigonometric functions, each using ten dedicated neurons distributed across two layers.

**Key results**

For the two superposition settings, mean maximum cosine similarities are 0.998 ± 0.000 and 0.996 ± 0.003; corresponding mean L2 ratios are 0.893 ± 0.004 and 0.935 ± 0.001. These indicate close column-direction matching with magnitude shrinkage; the reported deviations are standard deviations. Compressed-computation components approximately recover coordinate-specific contributions using the target network's neurons, including contributions across layers. Removing components assigned to inactive inputs generally perturbs outputs less than removing those assigned to active inputs. Reducing batch top-k from 1.28 to 1 reduces splitting of individual computations across components but increases components representing multiple computations. The appendix reports that per-layer rank-one constraints mitigate this tradeoff.

**Limitations / open questions**

No language model or real-world dataset is evaluated. Recovery is imperfect and sensitive to loss coefficients; the hand-coded result is explicitly cherry-picked. Local gradients and sampled whole-component ablations do not establish invariance under arbitrary combinations of partial ablations. General parameter linearity and the adequacy of rank-based description length remain assumptions. Computational cost, dead components, shrinkage, and layer-dependent penalties limit applicability. Figure images are unavailable in the supplied rendering, and several captions and appendix descriptions conflict about ablation counts, batch sizes, or top-k settings; unreported plotted values cannot be recovered.

title: Stochastic Parameter Decomposition
abstract: A key step in reverse engineering neural networks is to decompose them into simpler parts that can be studied in relative isolation. Linear parameter decomposition -- a framework that has been proposed to resolve several issues with current decomposition methods -- decomposes neural network parameters into a sum of sparsely used vectors in parameter space. However, the current main method in this framework, Attribution-based Parameter Decomposition (APD), is impractical on account of its computational cost and sensitivity to hyperparameters. In this work, we introduce \textit{Stochastic Parameter Decomposition} (SPD), a method that is more scalable and robust to hyperparameters than APD, which we demonstrate by decomposing models that are slightly larger and more complex than was possible to decompose with APD. We also show that SPD avoids other issues, such as shrinkage of the learned parameters, and better identifies ground truth mechanisms in toy models. By bridging causal mediation analysis and network decomposition methods, this demonstration opens up new research possibilities in mechanistic interpretability by removing barriers to scaling linear parameter decomposition methods to larger models. We release a library for running SPD and reproducing our experiments at https://github.com/goodfire-ai/spd/tree/spd-paper.
summary:
**Central idea**

Stochastic Parameter Decomposition (SPD) represents each weight matrix as a sum of learned rank-one subcomponents. Independent small MLPs predict input-dependent importance from each subcomponent's scalar inner activation. Random multiplicative masks interpolate between predicted importance and one. Training combines parameter reconstruction, output reconstruction under joint and layerwise masking, and an importance penalty. This replaces APD's attribution-based top-k selection and spectral simplicity penalty. The implementation uses leaky hard sigmoids, allowing some forward masks below zero. Higher-rank and cross-layer mechanisms require subsequent grouping.

**Experiments**

Experiments use synthetic models, with no language-model evaluation. Superposition reconstruction models represent five features in two hidden dimensions or 40 features in ten dimensions, each with and without an inserted hidden identity matrix. Input features have activation probability 0.05 and uniform nonzero amplitudes in [0,1]. A compressed-computation residual MLP approximates y_i = x_i + ReLU(x_i) using 100 features, 50 neurons, and residual width 1,000. Related models distribute 50 neurons over two blocks or 51 neurons over three blocks for 102 features. Their inputs have activation probability 0.01 and nonzero amplitudes in [-1,1]. SPD uses one mask sample per stochastic loss per training step. Evaluation examines matched-column cosine similarity and norm ratios, weight-derived neuron contributions, and importance patterns on one-hot inputs.

**Key results**

All four superposition configurations report MMCS rounding to 1.000 ± 0.000. Mean matched-column L2 ratios range from 0.992 to 1.031, indicating little average magnitude distortion. Hidden identity matrices yield their rank's worth of substantial subcomponents. In the residual MLPs, feature-associated input subcomponents approximately reproduce the target's neuron-contribution patterns. Broadly coactivating output subcomponents are interpreted as shared mechanisms with total rank budgets of 50 or 51, including groupings across blocks. SPD succeeds on identity-augmented and three-block cases reported as unsuccessful or impractically difficult for APD. An importance-penalty sweep also reveals recovery failures at low and high penalties.

**Limitations / open questions**

APD comparisons largely reference prior results or qualitative reports; controlled runtime, memory, and tuning-budget benchmarks are absent. Cross-layer results are seed-sensitive, and the two-block model shows unexplained contribution inflation. Output-mechanism groupings lack an independent oracle or general clustering algorithm. Bias decomposition, richer importance predictors, and scaling remain open. Finite stochastic training does not certify robustness to every permitted mask combination. Figures are available only through their textual descriptions and captions here; no additional plotted values can be assessed.

title: Quantifying degeneracy in singular models via the learning coefficient
Circuits Updates - April 2024
summary:
**Central idea**
This is a lab-notebook-style update from Anthropic's interpretability team. Its authors present it as preliminary work. Most of the content concerns sparse autoencoders (SAEs): how to scale and train them, and whether the features they find matter causally to the model. Shorter items cover an interpretable-architectures working group, an essay arguing that incorrect theories such as superposition can still be useful (by analogy to caloric theory), a proposal for attribution-sparse dictionary learning, an explanation of an iterative algorithm for isolating residual paths of length ≤k, and reviews of external papers.

**Experiments**
- *Scaling laws:* SAEs were trained on the residual stream after layer 3 of a 4-layer transformer. The authors swept the number of features and the number of training steps, using MSE + λ·L1 (λ=5) as a proxy for quality.
- *Training recipe:* Decoder columns have unconstrained norm, and the L1 penalty is weighted by decoder column norm. The encoder is initialised to the decoder transpose. Inputs are scaled so that E||x|| = √n. Other settings: λ warmup over the first 5% of training, Adam, gradient clipping, and no resampling or ghost grads. Results are tabulated for 1L MLP, 4L MLP and 4L residual SAEs with 131k features at λ ∈ {2, 5, 10}.
- *Feature influence:* On the 4L residual SAE, individual feature activations were scaled by 0 (ablation) or 2 (doubling) and the resulting loss increase was measured. This was compared against magnitude-matched controls:
  - random perturbations of model activations;
  - random perturbations of feature activations;
  - dampening of all features;
  - dampening of model activations;
  - perturbation along the SAE error direction.

**Key results**
- Compute-optimal loss falls approximately as a power law in FLOPs. Optimal feature count and step count also follow power laws, with features growing faster (steps ∝ features^0.5–1).
- A higher L1 weight shifts the compute optimum toward more steps. Losses based on L0 also need more steps.
- The new recipe scales to millions of features with fewer than 1% dead features. Example: 1L MLP at λ=5 gives L0 ≈ 39 with 96.4% of cross-entropy loss recovered.
- Ablating a single feature raises loss more than either random control does. Ablation has a larger effect than doubling, which suggests saturation.
- Perturbing along the error direction is more harmful than random perturbation but less harmful than feature ablation, which is consistent with Gurnee's finding that SAE errors are pathological.
- The effects are stronger for residual-stream features than for MLP features.
- A brief test of the attribution-sparsity SAE loss on a 1-layer model produced features about as good as standard ones. The authors say this result is not dispositive.

**Limitations / open questions**
- All results come from small models and a single layer. Error bars and full figures are not reproduced in this text.
- SAE loss is described as only an imperfect proxy for feature usefulness.
- Initialization, shrinkage and post-training refits remain open problems.
- The external reviews (Marks et al., Gurnee, Lee et al., Feng & Steinhardt) are commentary and add no new experiments.

Circuits Updates - January 2024
summary:
**Central idea**
This is an informal lab-update collection. The authors explicitly ask readers to treat it as preliminary, lab-meeting-level results. It sets team priorities: scaling dictionary learning, attacking attention superposition, and circuits built on learned features. It then reports several short experiments.

**Experiments**
- *Attention superposition toy model:* Five fixed "true" attentional features, each a head with sparse attention patterns and sparse OV, are linearly mixed into two learned heads. A shared mixing matrix is trained with MSE loss after a ReLU.
- *MNIST dictionary learning:* Hyperparameter scans of dictionary-learning algorithms on fully connected ReLU MNIST models with 1–3 layers and 16–64 neurons per layer.
- *8-layer transformer:* SAEs trained on MLP activations, with features labeled qualitatively. The search was biased toward safety-relevant features.
- *Billion-parameter models:* Preliminary dictionary features were inspected for multilinguality.
- *Ghost Grads:* An auxiliary loss runs dead SAE neurons with an exponential activation, scaled to half the residual norm, to reconstruct the SAE residual. Neurons count as dead after 2e6 tokens without firing.
- *Counterexamples:* Two 1-layer models were regularized toward sparse activations. One of them had a "cut" residual stream.
- *Predicting future activations:* Sparse models map pre-MLP to post-MLP activations, a transcoder-like approach.

**Key results**
- In the toy model, the learned mixing matrix shows geometry reminiscent of Toy Models of Superposition. Superposition appeared only when OV circuits were sparse.
- MNIST features looked interpretable as per-digit "templates" with matching logit effects. However:
  - no reconstruction "elbow" appeared;
  - low error required feature counts comparable to the dataset size, or many active features;
  - so there was no evidence these were "true features" rather than data clusters.
- In the 8-layer model, final-layer features resemble single-token 1-layer features. Layers 4–6 appear most abstract, for example emotional valence and violence.
- Large models contain multilingual features, for example "uniqueness" across English, Spanish, Portuguese, Russian and German.
- Ghost Grads yields few or zero dead neurons. It performs as well as or better than resampling at equal alive-neuron counts, at roughly double the compute. Dead fraction grows with SAE size, exceeding 50% for very large SAEs under resampling.
  - Caveat: the page notes the authors' views on Ghost Grads later changed (March 2024 update).
- Sparsity-regularized models showed two problems:
  - a neuron in joint superposition with the residual stream, disambiguated only through the residual;
  - with the residual stream cut, a magnitude-coded polysemantic neuron (weak firing for pronouns, strong for "diplomacy"), contrary to linear representation.
- Transcoder-like models give interpretable features and make linear circuit analysis easier. Their quality relative to SAEs is unknown.

**Limitations / open questions**
- All results are preliminary and qualitative, and the feature labels are "field notes".
- Large-model details, such as models and sizes, are unspecified.
- Whether a "strong superposition hypothesis" holds remains open.
- Open problems listed include:
  - toy models without superposition;
  - cross-layer superposition toys;
  - characterizing simple attention circuits.
- The external-research digest (task vectors, function vectors, Clock/Pizza, RASP-L, fact finding, attention SAEs) is commentary, not new evidence.
