This forward-facing review discusses the current frontier of mechanistic interpretability and the open problems that the field may benefit from prioritizing.
summary:
**Central idea**

This forward-looking review organizes mechanistic interpretability around understanding the mechanisms underlying neural-network generalization. It distinguishes reverse engineering—finding roles for network components—from concept-based approaches that locate components corresponding to predefined roles. Reverse engineering requires an iterative cycle of decomposition, functional description, and validation. The authors argue that progress requires stronger foundations for identifying computational units, more rigorous hypothesis testing, and evaluations tied to scientific and engineering goals.

**Experiments**

The paper presents no new experiments; it synthesizes prior studies. Quantitative examples include a cited 16-million-latent dictionary inserted into GPT-4 whose language-modeling loss matched a model trained with only 10% of GPT-4’s pretraining compute. Another cited study reports GPT-2 small performance reductions of 10% with task-specific SAE training and 40% with full-distribution training; the review does not specify the performance metric alongside these percentages. Other examples concern modular-addition transformers, BERT interpretation illusions, GPT-2 indirect object identification, GLUE CoLA probing, refusal directions, and AlphaZero concept discovery.

**Key results**

The main contribution is a research agenda rather than an experimental result. Sparse dictionary learning faces reconstruction errors, computational costs, dataset dependence, feature splitting and absorption, and unresolved assumptions about linear representations and feature geometry. Activation decompositions also leave the weight-based mechanisms producing those activations insufficiently explained. Probes identify correlations that require causal validation. Circuit discovery is constrained by human task definitions, intervention-sensitive faithfulness metrics, approximate attribution, and backup or negative components. Automating existing pipelines would preserve these limitations. Proposed applications include monitoring unsafe cognition, steering and editing, forecasting capabilities, improving inference and training, scientific discovery through “microscope AI,” and governance.

**Limitations / open questions**

The review offers no unified benchmark or empirical demonstration that its proposed agenda delivers reliable safety assurance. Canonical computational units, robust validation standards, and transfer across architectures remain unresolved. Strong safety claims and formal verification of frontier systems require understanding far beyond current methods. Near-term monitoring may need only partial, correlational understanding, whereas precise editing and enumerative safety demand broader mechanistic coverage. The authors emphasize comparisons with non-interpretability baselines, studying both scientific and practical goals, and avoiding selective transparency or exaggerated claims that could create false assurance.

title: Attention-based Neural Beamforming Layers for Multi-channel Speech Recognition
Analyzing Individual Neurons in Pre-trained Language Models
abstract: While a lot of analysis has been carried to demonstrate linguistic knowledge captured by the representations learned within deep NLP models, very little attention has been paid towards individual neurons.We carry outa neuron-level analysis using core linguistic tasks of predicting morphology, syntax and semantics, on pre-trained language models, with questions like: i) do individual neurons in pre-trained models capture linguistic information? ii) which parts of the network learn more about certain linguistic phenomena? iii) how distributed or focused is the information? and iv) how do various architectures differ in learning these properties? We found small subsets of neurons to predict linguistic tasks, with lower level tasks (such as morphology) localized in fewer neurons, compared to higher level task of predicting syntax. Our study also reveals interesting cross architectural comparisons. For example, we found neurons in XLNet to be more localized and disjoint when predicting properties compared to BERT and others, where they are more distributed and coupled.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper studies which representation coordinates make linguistic labels accessible to linear classifiers. Its “neurons” include dimensions of transformer-block outputs. Elastic-net logistic regression ranks coordinates using absolute label-specific weights. A regularization search rewards separation between top- and bottom-coordinate performance while preserving full-probe accuracy; progressively larger ranked subsets are then used to retrain probes.

**Experiments**

The authors analyze frozen ELMo, Transformer-ELMo, BERT-base, and XLNet-base representations, concatenating layers into 3,072, 7,168, 9,984, and 9,984 coordinates, respectively. Tasks are Penn Treebank POS tagging, Parallel Meaning Bank semantic tagging, CoNLL-2000 chunking, and CCGBank supertagging, with 44, 73, 22, and 1,272 labels. Test splits contain 1,963, 10,600, 2,011, and 2,404 sentences. Probes train for ten epochs, and tabled accuracies average three runs. Evaluations compare retained top, random, and bottom 20% coordinate sets, retrained subset probes, and randomized word-type control tasks. Selectivity is linguistic accuracy minus control accuracy.

**Key results**

Top-ranked coordinates outperform random and bottom sets in all 16 model–task comparisons in Table 1. After retraining, 400 of 9,984 BERT coordinates achieve 95.86% POS accuracy versus 96.04% using all coordinates, and 92.12% semantic accuracy versus 92.09%. With a selection tolerance of 0.5 accuracy percentage points, chunking and CCG use larger subsets: BERT uses 1,000 and 1,500 coordinates; Transformer-ELMo uses 2,365 of 7,168 for CCG. Selected-coordinate probes have higher selectivity throughout Table 2; BERT semantic selectivity rises from 5.77 to 27.17 percentage points. A looser selection tolerance permits further feature reduction. The authors report that lexical selections generally favor lower layers and syntactic selections higher layers, with BERT spreading selections more broadly. Per-label counts suggest less coordinate sharing in XLNet. Interjections and particles have smaller selected supports than particular noun and verb-phrase categories.

**Limitations / open questions**

Masking affects auxiliary probes, leaving the original language models intact; the results measure predictive accessibility and do not establish natural causal use or successful model pruning. “Minimal” means a qualifying prefix of one ranking, rather than a globally minimal subset. Task comparisons differ in datasets and label inventories; model comparisons differ in pretraining, architecture, and size. Layer and sharing interpretations rely on probe weights and selection counts. Tables contain conflicting baselines and some inconsistent count–percentage pairs. Plots are unavailable in the text rendering, so their numerical values cannot be independently checked.

title: Explaining Black Box Predictions and Unveiling Data Artifacts through Influence Functions
TX-Ray: Quantifying and Explaining Model-Knowledge Transfer in (Un-)Supervised NLP
Improving Transformer Models by Reordering their Sublayers
Attention is not not Explanation
abstract: Attention mechanisms play a central role in NLP systems, especially within recurrent neural network (RNN) models. Recently, there has been increasing interest in whether or not the intermediate representations offered by these modules may be used to explain the reasoning for a model's prediction, and consequently reach insights regarding the model's decision-making process. A recent paper claims that `Attention is not Explanation' (Jain and Wallace, 2019). We challenge many of the assumptions underlying this work, arguing that such a claim depends on one's definition of explanation, and that testing it needs to take into account all elements of the model, using a rigorous experimental design. We propose four alternative tests to determine when/whether attention can be used as explanation: a simple uniform-weights baseline; a variance calibration based on multiple random seed runs; a diagnostic framework using frozen weights from pretrained models; and an end-to-end adversarial attention training protocol. Each allows for meaningful interpretation of attention mechanisms in RNN models. We show that even when reliable adversarial distributions can be found, they don't perform well on the simple diagnostic, indicating that prior work does not disprove the usefulness of attention mechanisms for explainability.
summary:
**Central idea**

Attention's explanatory value depends on whether the goal is a plausible rationale or a faithful account of prediction. The paper challenges conclusions drawn from independently replacing each example's attention while holding encoder states fixed. It proposes evaluating attention's performance contribution, ordinary training variability, transferable token weighting, and alternatives generated by a shared trained model.

**Experiments**

Experiments use single-layer bidirectional LSTMs with additive attention on six English binary classification tasks: SST, IMDb, AG News world/business, 20 Newsgroups baseball/hockey, and MIMIC-III Diabetes and Anemia. Metrics are positive-class F1, prediction total variation distance (TVD), and attention Jensen–Shannon divergence (JSD). Four tests compare learned versus uniform attention; eight independently seeded models; noncontextual token-level MLPs trained using frozen attention guides; and adversarial models trained to minimize prediction TVD while maximizing attention KL divergence. The news datasets are excluded from subsequent analyses because learned attention adds little performance.

**Key results**

Learned/uniform attention yields F1 0.964/0.960 on AG News, 0.942/0.934 on 20 Newsgroups, and 0.831/0.822 on SST, compared with 0.775/0.706 on Diabetes. Seed variability differs by dataset and label class: SST attention is relatively stable, whereas negative Diabetes examples already exhibit substantial variation.

Base-LSTM attention guides outperform both uniform weighting and independently learned MLP attention on all four retained datasets. Base-guide/learned-MLP F1 is 0.753/0.699 for Diabetes, 0.931/0.920 for Anemia, 0.824/0.817 for SST, and 0.905/0.888 for IMDb.

Among tested adversarial models with mean test JSD above 0.4, those selected for highest test F1 achieve mean TVD 0.014–0.036 and F1 comparable to the base models. These trained adversaries exhibit a less extreme divergence–prediction tradeoff than per-instance attention search. Guides from the separate fixed λ=0.001 setting perform substantially worse than base guides on Diabetes, SST, and IMDb; Anemia is an exception, at 0.932 versus 0.931. Prediction imitation therefore need not preserve diagnostic guide utility.

**Limitations / open questions**

Guide transfer does not establish faithful token responsibility in the original LSTM; contextual information can enter through the guides themselves. Separately trained adversaries can change the encoder and predictor as well as attention. There is no human evaluation or experimental extension to transformers, QA, generation, or other languages. Analyses and adversarial-setting comparisons use test data; SST checkpoints are explicitly selected using the test-set objective. No uncertainty estimates accompany the reported F1 comparisons. The supplied source is the September 2019 revision; metadata gives the initial August publication date.

title: What Does BERT Learn about the Structure of Language?
Augmenting Self-attention with Persistent Memory
What Does BERT Look At? An Analysis of BERT's Attention
abstract: Large pre-trained neural networks such as BERT have had great recent success in NLP, motivating a growing body of research investigating what aspects of language they are able to learn from unlabeled data. Most recent analysis has focused on model outputs (e.g., language model surprisal) or internal vector representations (e.g., probing classifiers). Complementary to these works, we propose methods for analyzing the attention mechanisms of pre-trained models and apply them to BERT. BERT's attention heads exhibit patterns such as attending to delimiter tokens, specific positional offsets, or broadly attending over the whole sentence, with heads in the same layer often exhibiting similar behaviors. We further show that certain attention heads correspond well to linguistic notions of syntax and coreference. For example, we find heads that attend to the direct objects of verbs, determiners of nouns, objects of prepositions, and coreferent mentions with remarkably high accuracy. Lastly, we propose an attention-based probing classifier and use it to further demonstrate that substantial syntactic information is captured in BERT's attention.
summary:
**Central idea**

Attention maps offer a complementary way to study linguistic information learned during pretraining. The paper analyzes English BERT-base's 144 heads across 12 layers, evaluating individual heads as word-relation predictors and combining their maps with supervised dependency probes. It distinguishes identifying linguistic structure from explaining downstream predictions.

**Experiments**

Surface analyses use 1,000 random Wikipedia segments of at most 128 tokens, formatted as two consecutive paragraphs with [CLS] and [SEP] delimiters. Measurements include positional attention, special-token attention, entropy, and masked-language-model loss gradients. Pairwise Jensen–Shannon divergences are visualized using multidimensional scaling. Word-level analyses sum attention to subword pieces and average attention from them. Individual heads predict the most-attended other word on Penn Treebank WSJ Stanford dependencies and CoNLL-2012 coreference documents truncated to 128 tokens. Dependency probes combine frozen BERT attention maps, optionally using fixed GloVe embeddings to condition head weights.

**Key results**

Relation-specific best heads achieve 94.3% determiner accuracy, 86.8% direct-object accuracy, and 76.3% prepositional-object accuracy, versus best fixed-offset baselines of 51.7%, 40.0%, and 34.6%. The best individual head overall reaches only 34.5 UAS, versus 26.3 for right branching. Head 5-4 reaches 65% antecedent-selection accuracy given a coreferent mention, compared with 52% for head matching and 69% for a rule-based system.

On Penn Treebank development data, attention-only probing reaches 61 UAS and attention plus GloVe reaches 77, versus 58 for distances plus GloVe and 30 for randomized BERT attention plus GloVe. The randomized model retains pretrained word and positional embeddings.

Over half of attention in layers 6–10 targets [SEP]. Small loss gradients for separator-directed attention from layer 5 onward, together with qualitative fallback patterns, motivate a tentative no-op interpretation. Heads within a layer often have similar attention distributions; other measurements identify adjacent-token and broad-attention heads.

**Limitations / open questions**

Results primarily concern one English model, selected relations, and truncated coreference contexts. Possessive scoring accepts ’s in place of the annotated complement. Linguistic correspondence and probe accuracy do not establish causal use in downstream tasks. Local loss gradients provide limited evidence for the no-op hypothesis; no direct intervention establishes it. Structural-probe and neural-coreference comparisons use different evaluation conditions. Whether dropout causes head similarity, and whether these patterns generalize across languages, remain open.

title: Analyzing the Structure of Attention in a Transformer Language Model
abstract: The Transformer is a fully attention-based alternative to recurrent networks that has achieved state-of-the-art results across a range of NLP tasks. In this paper, we analyze the structure of attention in a Transformer language model, the GPT-2 small pretrained model. We visualize attention for individual instances and analyze the interaction between attention and syntax over a large corpus. We find that attention targets different parts of speech at different layer depths within the model, and that attention aligns with dependency relations most strongly in the middle layers. We also find that the deepest layers of the model capture the most distant relationships. Finally, we extract exemplar sentences that reveal highly specific patterns targeted by particular attention heads.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper characterizes pretrained GPT-2 Small's attention through corpus statistics and interactive visualization. Its 12 layers and 144 attention heads exhibit different linguistic and positional preferences. BertViz presents individual-head views, model-wide grids, and query–key coordinate products contributing to attention logits.

**Experiments**

The authors sampled 100,000 sentences from 10,000 English Wikipedia articles, using 10,000 sentences for quantitative analysis and the full sample for qualitative exemplar extraction. spaCy supplied POS tags and dependency parses, copied to every constituent GPT-2 wordpiece. Metrics included attention shares to/from POS tags, attention-weighted dependency alignment under three parent-direction definitions, mean attended distance, entropy, and normalized absolute deviation from position-specific mean attention. Variability used the first ten tokens. Aggregate analyses excluded first-token attention as presumed null routing. Entropy additionally renormalized remaining weights and excluded source tokens assigning over 90% attention to the first token.

**Key results**

Before filtering, first tokens received 57% of attention on average; some heads exceeded 97%. For 13 of 16 receiving POS tags, a head exceeded twice the tag's across-head mean attention share. Nouns received 43% in layer 9 head 0 versus a 21% across-head mean. The five strongest proper-noun-targeting heads occurred in the final three layers; the five strongest determiner-targeting heads occurred in the first four.

Dependency alignment was strongest in intermediate layers, with layers 2–4 also having the shortest attended distances. However, the highest-alignment head, layer 4 head 11, attended to the previous token: alignment was 0.42 and variability 0.004, illustrating a positional confound. Across heads, distance correlated negatively with dependency alignment (r = −0.73) and positively with entropy (r = 0.61), both p < 0.001. Deepest layers had the largest layer-average distances, but layer 5 head 1 had the largest individual-head mean, 14.2 tokens, targeting repeated phrases. Selected exemplars showed acronym, place-name, and noun-phrase patterns.

**Limitations / open questions**

Results concern one checkpoint and sentence-level encyclopedic text. Attention distributions and query–key products do not establish downstream causal importance. Null routing and proposed prediction roles remain untested; extreme-attention examples do not establish exhaustive head functions. Generalization to other genres, longer contexts, and architectures remains open. Plot images are unavailable in the supplied rendering, so additional plotted values cannot be independently assessed; the article and appendix text are otherwise complete.

title: Analyzing Multi-Head Self-Attention: Specialized Heads Do the Heavy Lifting, the Rest Can Be Pruned
abstract: Multi-head self-attention is a key component of the Transformer, a state-of-the-art architecture for neural machine translation. In this work we evaluate the contribution made by individual attention heads in the encoder to the overall performance of the model and analyze the roles played by them. We find that the most important and confident heads play consistent and often linguistically-interpretable roles. When pruning heads using a method based on stochastic gates and a differentiable relaxation of the L0 penalty, we observe that specialized heads are last to be pruned. Our novel pruning method removes the vast majority of heads without seriously affecting performance. For example, on the English-Russian WMT dataset, pruning 38 out of 48 encoder heads results in a drop of only 0.15 BLEU.
summary:
**Central idea**

Attention heads in translation Transformers receive unequal relevance scores, and prominent encoder heads often exhibit recognizable positional, syntactic, or rare-word attention patterns. The paper combines layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP), attention-pattern measurements, and learned pruning to investigate head specialization. Its pruning method multiplies each head output by an input-independent stochastic Hard Concrete gate and fine-tunes with translation cross-entropy plus an expected-active-head penalty.

**Experiments**

Models follow Transformer base: six encoder and six decoder layers, eight heads per attention module, model dimension 512, and feed-forward dimension 2,048. English-to-Russian, German, and French models each use 2.5 million WMT sentence pairs; additional English-to-Russian experiments use six million OpenSubtitles pairs. Cross-language syntactic comparisons use the same 50,000 held-out English sentences. LRP estimates contributions to predicted top-1 logits. Maximum-attention targets are compared with CoreNLP dependencies and relation-specific positional baselines. English-to-Russian pruning experiments measure BLEU, retained functions, attention-type retention, and performance of identical sparse configurations trained from scratch. Encoder-only pruning freezes the decoder while adapting encoder parameters and gates.

**Key results**

LRP relevance concentrates in relatively few heads. In the illustrated OpenSubtitles model, relevance broadly agrees with attention confidence, except for a prominent first-layer rare-word head. Selected syntactic heads outperform positional baselines: WMT English-to-Russian verb-to-object accuracy is 78% versus 41%, and OpenSubtitles verb-to-subject accuracy is 77% versus 45%. Retaining 10 of 48 encoder heads on WMT costs 0.15 BLEU; retaining four of 48 on OpenSubtitles costs 0.25. A 17-head OpenSubtitles encoder retains every identified function type, while further pruning can redistribute functions. Joint pruning removes encoder heads most readily and generally favors cross-attention retention, with decoder self-attention preferentially retained lower and cross-attention higher. On WMT, retaining 14/31/30 encoder/decoder/cross-attention heads yields 29.62 BLEU versus 29.6 for the full model. Identical sparse configurations trained from scratch score lower in every reported comparison, sometimes only slightly.

**Limitations / open questions**

Pruning includes parameter adaptation, so retained BLEU does not establish that removed heads were dispensable in the original frozen model. Attention labels describe selection patterns without establishing complete computational mechanisms. LRP ignores nonlinear activations, dependency targets are parser-generated, and no uncertainty estimates or systematic seed analysis are reported. Explanations involving target-language morphology and domain differences remain tentative. Comparisons with alternative compression methods are deferred.

title: BERT Rediscovers the Classical NLP Pipeline
abstract: Pre-trained text encoders have rapidly advanced the state of the art on many NLP tasks. We focus on one such model, BERT, and aim to quantify where linguistic information is captured within the network. We find that the model represents the steps of the traditional NLP pipeline in an interpretable and localizable way, and that the regions responsible for each step appear in the expected sequence: POS tagging, parsing, NER, semantic roles, then coreference. Qualitative analysis reveals that the model can and often does adjust this pipeline dynamically, revising lower-level decisions on the basis of disambiguating information from higher-level representations.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper investigates whether linguistic information accessible across BERT's layers follows the order of a classical NLP pipeline. It introduces two complementary measurements: task-specific scalar weights mixing frozen encoder layers, summarized by their center of gravity; and cumulative probes accessing every layer up to a given depth, summarized by incremental micro-F1 gains. These measure information accessible to auxiliary classifiers, rather than directly identifying BERT's causal computations.

**Experiments**

The authors freeze uncased BERT-base and BERT-large, with 12 and 24 layers respectively, and train span-based edge probes for eight tasks: part-of-speech, constituents, dependencies, entities, semantic roles, coreference, semantic proto-roles, and semantic relations. POS, constituents, entities, SRL, and coreference use OntoNotes 5.0; dependencies use English Web Treebank; proto-roles use SPR1; relations use SemEval-2010 Task 8. All tasks use micro-averaged F1. Layer-zero probes provide noncontextual wordpiece-embedding baselines. An appendix also examines scalar mixing in ELMo. Selected ambiguous OntoNotes development sentences receive qualitative layerwise prediction analysis.

**Key results**

Both depth summaries broadly order POS before constituency, dependencies, semantic roles, and coreference. Syntactic tasks have more concentrated layer profiles, whereas semantic relations and proto-roles improve gradually across much of the network and have nearly uniform mixing weights. Entity labeling combines substantial early gains with later improvements. In BERT-large, incremental gains often peak in layers 1–7, while mixing weights concentrate later, around layers 9–20. BERT-base shows similar task ordering and approximate placement relative to the model's top. Selected probe trajectories revise earlier labels: “Toronto” shifts from a geopolitical entity toward an organization after the semantic-role prediction resolves, while “china today” shifts toward a proper-name interpretation. ELMo's first LSTM layer receives the greatest mixing weight for every task.

**Limitations / open questions**

Probe accessibility establishes neither natural causal use nor information absence when decoding fails. Qualitative revisions compare separately trained probes and do not demonstrate causal communication between linguistic decisions or establish how frequently revisions occur. The cumulative-depth statistic is a pseudo-expectation because F1 is not an expectation over examples; gains can also be negative through overfitting. Generalization beyond these encoders remains open. The supplied rendering lacks numerical values embedded in plots and the sentence images accompanying appendix examples; claims here rely on the available prose and captions.

title: Linguistic knowledge and transferability of contextual representations.
What Is One Grain of Sand in the Desert? Analyzing Individual Neurons in Deep NLP Models
abstract: Despite the remarkable evolution of deep neural networks in natural language processing (NLP), their interpretability remains a challenge. Previous work largely focused on what these models learn at the representation level. We break this analysis down further and study individual dimensions (neurons) in the vector representation learned by end-to-end neural models in NLP tasks. We propose two methods: Linguistic Correlation Analysis, based on a supervised method to extract the most relevant neurons with respect to an extrinsic task, and Cross-model Correlation Analysis, an unsupervised method to extract salient neurons w.r.t. the model itself. We evaluate the effectiveness of our techniques by ablating the identified neurons and reevaluating the network's performance for two tasks: neural machine translation (NMT) and neural language modeling (NLM). We further present a comprehensive analysis of neurons with the aim to address the following questions: i) how localized or distributed are different linguistic properties in the models? ii) are certain neurons exclusive to some properties and not others? iii) is the information more or less distributed in NMT vs. NLM? and iv) how important are the neurons identified through the linguistic correlation method to the overall task? Our code is publicly available as part of the NeuroX toolkit (Dalvi et al. 2019).
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper studies individual hidden-state coordinates in recurrent NLP models through two ranking methods. Linguistic Correlation Analysis fits an elastic-net logistic-regression probe and ranks coordinates by absolute classifier weights, combining label-specific rankings through cumulative weight thresholds. Cross-model Correlation Analysis ranks each neuron by its maximum Pearson activation correlation with a neuron in another independently trained model. This heuristic rests on the assumption that important task properties recur in individual coordinates across models.

**Experiments**

The authors train two-layer bidirectional LSTM translation models with 500-dimensional embeddings and LSTM states, plus unidirectional LSTM language models. Translation covers English↔French and German→English using UN and IWSLT data. Parallel data are divided into three equal subsets for independently initialized models; language models use source-side text. Probes predict POS, morphology, semantics, and selected properties such as word position. The general probe split uses 20,000 training and 4,000 test sentences; supplementary English semantic tagging uses 42,000 training and 12,000 test sentences. Evaluation includes masking probe inputs, retraining probes on selected coordinates, and zeroing coordinates in the original models, measured through tagging accuracy, translation BLEU, and language-model perplexity.

**Key results**

Removing the top 50 cross-model-ranked translation neurons, reported as 2.5%, reduces BLEU by 15–20 points, versus approximately 0.5 point for the bottom 50. Language-model perplexity also deteriorates faster under top-ranked ablation. Cross-model rankings produce more damaging translation ablations than the tested variance and distance-from-mean rankings. For English POS in NMT, retaining the top 10% gives 69.8% accuracy with the original probe, versus 15.8% for the bottom 10%; retraining raises these to 89.1% and 80.6%, against 93.5% using all coordinates. Under a 25% absolute probe-weight-mass criterion, open-class properties generally select more coordinates than closed-class properties. Selected-coordinate overlaps suggest coarse-to-fine linguistic organization, and both ranking methods identify the same top position neurons.

**Limitations / open questions**

Results concern recurrent architectures; transformers are left for future work. Probe weights and zero-ablation effects do not establish exclusive semantic functions or complete mechanisms. Localization depends on regularization and selection thresholds. Greater apparent distribution in NMT remains tentative because NMT is bidirectional while NLM is unidirectional. Table 1 shows two exceptions to the prose's baseline-superiority claim: French NLM POS and French NMT morphology. Distillation and bias mitigation remain proposed applications; tense-control details are referred to Bau et al. rather than supplied here.

title: Comprehensive Privacy Analysis of Deep Learning: Passive and Active White-box Inference Attacks against Centralized and Federated Learning
Adaptive Input Representations for Neural Language Modeling
Understanding Convolutional Neural Networks for Text Classification
abstract: We present an analysis into the inner workings of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for processing text. CNNs used for computer vision can be interpreted by projecting filters into image space, but for discrete sequence inputs CNNs remain a mystery. We aim to understand the method by which the networks process and classify text. We examine common hypotheses to this problem: that filters, accompanied by global max-pooling, serve as ngram detectors. We show that filters may capture several different semantic classes of ngrams by using different activation patterns, and that global max-pooling induces behavior which separates important ngrams from the rest. Finally, we show practical use cases derived from our findings in the form of model interpretability (explaining a trained model by deriving a concrete identity for each filter, bridging the gap between visualization tools in vision tasks and NLP) and prediction interpretability (explaining predictions). Code implementation is available online at github.com/sayaendo/interpreting-cnn-for-text.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper refines the view that each text CNN filter detects one coherent ngram family and that every max-pooled response matters to classification. It separates strong responses from accidental pooling winners using per-filter thresholds, then decomposes filter scores into word-position contributions. Different contribution patterns expose candidate semantic families within one filter, while negative contributions reveal suppression of otherwise activating phrases.

**Experiments**

The models use a single convolutional stage with parallel window sizes 2–4, global max-pooling, ReLU, and a linear softmax classifier. They use fine-tuned 50-dimensional GloVe embeddings and filter-count settings of 10 or 50. Datasets are MR movie-review polarity (10,000 examples), Elec electronics reviews (200,000 training and 25,000 test examples), and Yelp polarity (560,000 training and 38,000 test examples). Each filter's preferred class is determined by its output weights. Thresholds are selected using purity: agreement between this class and model predictions among above-threshold responses. The authors zero below-threshold pooled responses, compare corpus maxima with independently maximized vocabulary choices at each slot, cluster threshold-passing slot vectors using Mean Shift, and search nearby low-scoring ngrams for inhibitory substitutions.

**Key results**

At purity 0.75, approximately 44% of pooled filter values in the MR experiment are discarded while accuracy improves slightly; similar Elec results are reported. This joint thresholding procedure also discards 99.99% of one MR filter's pooled activations. Across all filters in the analyzed Elec model, natural ngram maxima average approximately 2.5 activation units, or 30%, below unrestricted slotwise maxima. A displayed Yelp filter has clusters containing 83% and 17% of its threshold-passing ngrams, with distinct semantic examples and contribution patterns. Elec examples show negative contributions from words such as “not” lowering otherwise activating phrases below threshold. These findings motivate richer filter summaries and shorter prediction explanations.

**Limitations / open questions**

Prediction agreement is a proxy for informativeness. Aggregate accuracy preservation neither establishes individual-response irrelevance nor isolates max-pooling as the cause of threshold-like behavior. Semantic clustering and inhibitory-pattern evidence are primarily qualitative, without representative prevalence estimates or human-utility evaluation. Numerical accuracy curves are unavailable in the supplied figure rendering; threshold-fitting/evaluation splits and uncertainty estimates are unspecified. Adversarial misclassification through synthetic high-scoring ngrams remains future work. Generalization beyond shallow sentiment CNNs is untested.

title: Deep contextualized word representations.
Pointer Sentinel Mixture Models
End-To-End Memory Networks
Transformer with depth-wise lstm
BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding
Visualizing Higher-Layer Features of a Deep Network
On Language
Circuit Tracing: Revealing Computational Graphs in Language Models
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper introduces circuit tracing through an interpretable replacement model. Cross-layer transcoders (CLTs) replace MLP computations with sparse features that read at one layer and write to that and subsequent layers. For an individual prompt, freezing attention patterns and normalization denominators and adding reconstruction-error corrections produces a local replacement model that exactly matches baseline activations and logits. Attribution graphs describe its linear direct interactions between features, embeddings, errors, and output logits; causal interventions test whether these interactions capture mechanisms in the underlying model.

**Experiments**

The authors train CLTs with 300K–10M features on an 18-layer pretrained transformer, 18L, and 300K–30M features on Claude 3.5 Haiku. Comparisons include per-layer transcoders and thresholded neurons, using reconstruction error, sparsity, automated interpretability, output agreement, graph completeness, and path length. Graph evaluation uses 260 selected nontrivial target tokens from the Pile without books. Feature-ablation validation uses 20 prompts. Case studies examine acronym completion, Michael Jordan’s sport, and addition across all 10,000 operand pairs in [0,99]². Global virtual weights and coactivation-weighted connections supplement prompt-specific graphs.

**Key results**

The largest 18L CLT achieves approximately 11.5% normalized reconstruction error, 88 active features per token, and 50% top-1 agreement with the original model on selected prompts. Haiku’s largest CLT achieves 21.7% error and 235 active features per token. CLTs improve reported feature and graph tradeoffs over per-layer transcoders and neurons, although cost-matched interpretability comparisons are mixed. Graph influence correlates with downstream feature-ablation effects at Spearman 0.72. Default pruning typically removes approximately 90% of nodes with about a 20% reduction in completeness. Addition reveals interacting magnitude and modular pathways linked through lookup-table features; interventions largely preserve this separation.

**Limitations / open questions**

Exact baseline matching does not establish mechanistic faithfulness: perturbation discrepancies compound across layers, especially in magnitude. Frozen attention omits QK mechanisms and can conceal the crucial computation in induction and multiple-choice answering. Reconstruction errors, inactive inhibitory features, interference weights, feature splitting, subjective supernode grouping, and inaccurate feature labels further limit explanations. Reported companion-paper alignment findings are outlined rather than established through detailed experiments here.

title: Sparse Crosscoders for Cross-Layer Features and Model Diffing
summary:
**Central idea**

Sparse crosscoders generalize sparse autoencoders and transcoders by jointly encoding and reconstructing activations across layers or models. Shared feature coefficients connect decoder vectors whose directions can differ across sites. The reported objective weights activation sparsity by the sum of per-site decoder norms, permitting comparison with summed per-layer SAE losses without explicitly rewarding features for spreading across sites.

**Experiments**

A global acausal crosscoder is trained on separately normalized residual-stream activations from all layers of an unnamed 18-layer model and compared with 18 independent SAEs. Dictionary sizes and training steps are swept across compute budgets at a fixed sparsity coefficient. Metrics include summed reconstruction-plus-regularization loss and reconstruction MSE versus whole-model active-feature count. Further analyses examine decoder geometry, local and causal masks, and joint pre-MLP/MLP-output reconstruction. Model diffing uses a one-million-feature crosscoder on middle-layer activations of Claude 3 Sonnet and its base model. A separate crosscoder spans ten evenly spaced layers in each of three unnamed models of increasing size; four-component nonnegative matrix factorization summarizes decoder-norm patterns.

**Key results**

Global crosscoders achieve lower evaluation loss at fixed total dictionary size but require approximately twice the training FLOPs to reach the same loss at large budgets. They substantially improve whole-model MSE–L0 tradeoffs, counting a crosscoder feature once globally while summing SAE L0 across layers. Local masks offer no obvious performance/cost sweet spot. Weakly causal coding has intermediate FLOP efficiency but worse dictionary-size efficiency than global coding. Features can span many layers while their decoder directions drift. Pre-MLP/MLP-output decoder norms form pre-only, shared, and output-only groups. Sonnet diffing identifies roughly 4,000–5,000 model-specific features for each model among one million total features. Almost all shared-feature decoder vectors are highly aligned, although a few thousand have low or negative correlation. Across scales, NMF separates shared early and late structure from middle-layer structure distinguishing the smallest model from the larger two.

**Limitations / open questions**

The work is explicitly preliminary. Gradual feature formation does not establish cross-layer superposition; production followed by amplification is an alternative explanation. Interpretability is not systematically evaluated, highlighted model-specific examples are cherry-picked, and most exclusive features are not immediately interpretable. Circuit simplification lacks presented circuit results. Shared coefficients and aligned decoders do not establish shared causal mechanisms; error-corrected activation matching may conceal different computations. Dataset identities, several model identities and sizes, and uncertainty estimates are unspecified.

title: Circuits Updates - July 2024
summary:
**Central idea**
This is a lab-meeting-style update with five short notes, not a mature paper.

1. Chris Olah argues that superposition is now substantially unblocked, and names the next hurdles:
   - missing rare features ("dark matter")
   - cross-layer superposition
   - attention superposition
   - interference weights arising from weight superposition
   - "zooming out" from microscopic circuits to macroscopic understanding
2. He clarifies the linear representation hypothesis. The *Toy Models* definition conflated one-dimensionality with mathematical linearity. The note proposes that "linear representation" mean **composition as addition** plus **intensity as scaling**. This admits multidimensional features but constrains their geometry: each manifold point is a ray contracting to zero, and semantic change is angular. Probing and steering evidence bears on linearity, not on one-dimensionality.
3. The "dark matter" note argues from Claude's fine-grained knowledge (SF coffee shops, street intersections, specific people) that the 13M-feature SAE resolves only a small fraction of features. Features rarer than some level may be effectively unresolvable without major efficiency gains in dictionary learning.

**Experiments**
- **Attention pivot tables.** The authors reproduce the skip-trigram pivot tables from *A Mathematical Framework* in 1–4 layer transformers. They give explicit QK/OV circuit formulas, subtract the unembedding LayerNorm bias, and use token-frequency-weighted key, query and output heuristics.
- **Feature sensitivity.** Several Claude versions rate concept relevance (0–10) of text snippets, and their ratings agree with each other and with human spot checks (high Spearman ρ). Claude 3.5 Sonnet then filters 160,000 128-token snippets per concept. Sensitivity is measured as the fraction of high-relevance snippets (rating ≥9) on which a Claude 3 Sonnet SAE feature fires. Three Scaling Monosemanticity features were tested: Brain sciences, Transit infrastructure and Tourist attractions. Golden Gate Bridge had too little data.

**Key results**
- **Pivot tables** are fiddly to reproduce and depend on hyperparameter quality, interpretable training domains and depth. Good runs show ~25–75% interpretable trigram entries; tables below ~10% may be mirages.
- **Highlighted features have low sensitivity.** They often fail to fire on clearly relevant snippets, ranking only in the top ~0.1–10% of features by sensitivity.
- **Most-sensitive features** trade off specificity:
  - Brain sciences: the top feature responds to human-subject methods.
  - Transit: the top feature is uninterpretable.
  - Tourist attractions: feature 1M/11480 (history of tourist attractions) covers all snippets rated ≥9.
- **Coverage is distributed.** Complementary features (e.g., one firing near "brain") partly cover missed snippets, more so in the larger SAE. Banded activation patterns suggest distinct snippet subtypes with different representations.

**Limitations / open questions**
- All results are preliminary. Pivot-table proportions come from tiny models only.
- Sensitivity was measured for three features, using LLM ratings as the ground truth.
- Whether the gaps reflect feature families, dark matter, or SAE failure is unresolved.
- The hurdle and dark-matter arguments are conceptual, with no new tests.

title: Mechanistic Interpretability, Variables, and the Importance of Interpretable Bases
summary:
**Central idea**

Mechanistic interpretability is framed as reverse engineering a compiled computer program: parameters correspond to instructions, architecture to a processor, activations to program state, and neurons or feature directions to variables. Understanding parameters requires understanding the representations they connect. The essay argues that decomposing activations into independently understandable pieces is foundational to mechanistic interpretation. Interpretable neurons offer a convenient decomposition, while combinations of neurons may be necessary when individual neurons are polysemantic.

This decomposition offers a proposed response to the curse of dimensionality. Instead of enumerating behavior across an enormous input space, researchers could understand the finite computational description encoded by the parameters. Independently understandable features would similarly make high-dimensional activation states tractable. Architectural modularity could make this work easier, but the author considers meaningful representational units more fundamental.

**Experiments**

The essay reports no new experiments, datasets, quantitative metrics, or formal proofs. Its arguments rely on analogies and citations to earlier circuits research. Attention-only transformers illustrate a special case where linearity can sometimes bypass intermediate-feature interpretation. InceptionV1 curve and car detectors illustrate candidate features; they are not evaluated here. SoLU and branch-specialization research provide related discussions of polysemanticity and modularity.

**Key results**

The contributions are conceptual proposals. Activation functions are hypothesized to create a privileged basis that encourages features to align with neuron coordinates, analogous to hardware encouraging convenient memory layouts. Such alignment would simplify reverse engineering, while polysemantic neurons make the appropriate decomposition harder to identify. Distributed representations remain compatible with interpretable directions: separate attributes can occupy different directions, whether or not those directions coincide with neurons. Interpreting both endpoint features could make individual connecting parameters understandable.

**Limitations / open questions**

The existence and necessity of useful independent feature decompositions remain informal premises. The essay supplies neither a feature-extraction algorithm nor an operational validation criterion. A satisfactory definition of a feature remains unresolved: candidates include articulable input properties, independent representational units, and units that would receive dedicated neurons given sufficient capacity. A human-centered definition could exclude features people cannot understand. Interpretation may require effort comparable to reverse engineering a large software system. An unfinished HTML comment follows the complete publication notice and acknowledgments; it supplies no additional research evidence.

title: On the Biology of a Large Language Model
summary:
**Central idea**
The paper uses circuit tracing to investigate Claude 3.5 Haiku through selected mechanistic case studies. A cross-layer transcoder (CLT) with 30 million features replaces MLP computations; prompt-specific attribution graphs retain reconstruction-error nodes and fix the original attention patterns. Researchers interpret features, manually group them into supernodes, and test graph-derived hypotheses with interventions in the original model. The central finding is that interpretable intermediate representations can sometimes expose computations hidden from generated text.

**Experiments**
Studies cover two-hop factual recall, poetry planning, multilingual antonyms, arithmetic, medical follow-up questions, hallucinations, harmful-request refusal, one jailbreak, and chain-of-thought faithfulness. Arithmetic feature responses are visualized across all 10,000 operand pairs from 0–99. Multilingual analysis compares feature intersection-over-union on paragraphs translated into English, French, and Chinese against unrelated-paragraph baselines and a smaller research model. Refusal analysis includes 200 Sorry Bench prompts. A separately fine-tuned Haiku variant pursuing concealed reward-model biases is analyzed with a 10-million-feature CLT.

**Key results**
Replacing intermediate Texas features with California features changes a Dallas/state-capital answer from Austin to Sacramento; other geographic substitutions behave analogously. Poetry features represent candidate ending words before a line begins and influence its intermediate wording: injecting “rabbit” or “green” across 25 poems produces the injected ending in 70% of cases. Multilingual interventions independently change operation, operand, or output language. Addition reuses magnitude and modular heuristics across arithmetic and citation contexts. Familiar-entity features inhibit default uncertainty circuits, sometimes enabling hallucinations. Selected chain-of-thought examples reveal backward reasoning from suggested answers. In the hidden-goal variant, an RM-bias feature activates in 100/100 dialogue-formatted contexts versus 1/100 controls; inhibiting bias features reduces targeted behaviors, including emergency-call and voting addenda.

**Limitations / open questions**
These are biased existence proofs, not population-level estimates. Researchers report satisfying insight for roughly a quarter of attempted prompts. Graphs omit attention-pattern formation and usually inactive features, contain substantial uninterpretable error, and can require subjective simplification. Constrained patching makes some apparent validation trivial; output changes provide stronger checks. Large intervention strengths and failed predictions expose possible surrogate unfaithfulness. Prompts beyond roughly 100 tokens and long reasoning chains remain difficult. Many citation markers lost their bibliographic details in the supplied text. Generalization across models, reliable auditing, and mechanistic signatures of unfaithful reasoning remain open.

title: Universal Transformers
Differentiable Image Parameterizations
Grad-cam: Why did you say that? visual explanations from deep networks via gradient-based localization
The (Un)reliability of saliency methods
abstract: Saliency methods aim to explain the predictions of deep neural networks. These methods lack reliability when the explanation is sensitive to factors that do not contribute to the model prediction. We use a simple and common pre-processing step ---adding a constant shift to the input data--- to show that a transformation with no effect on the model can cause numerous methods to incorrectly attribute. In order to guarantee reliability, we posit that methods should fulfill input invariance, the requirement that a saliency method mirror the sensitivity of the model with respect to transformations of the input. We show, through several examples, that saliency methods that do not satisfy input invariance result in misleading attribution.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper proposes input invariance as a necessary condition for reliable saliency: explanations should respect input transformations whose effects are canceled by the model. An algebraic construction adds a fixed vector to every input and subtracts its weight projection from first-layer biases. This preserves corresponding hidden activations, predictions, and input gradients while allowing attribution methods to respond differently to the input encoding.

**Experiments**

The specified main MNIST model is a three-layer MLP with 1,024 ReLU neurons per layer, trained for 10 epochs using minibatch SGD. Subtracting one changes inputs from [0,1] to [-1,0]; compensating biases preserve predictions, and both networks achieve 98.3% accuracy. Qualitative heatmap comparisons cover raw gradients, Guided Backpropagation, PatternNet, gradient-times-input, Integrated Gradients (IG), Deep Taylor Decomposition (DTD), and SmoothGrad wrappers. Additional fixed shifts introduce checkerboard structure and a gradient-constructed cat pattern. VGG16/ImageNet examples separately illustrate attribution differences between reference choices.

**Key results**

Raw gradients, Guided Backpropagation, and PatternNet are reported to produce identical maps under the uniform shift. Gradient-times-input changes because the offset enters its elementwise multiplication. Fixed-zero IG and the tested zero-root DTD/LRP rule also change. An IG baseline uniformly filled with the minimum pixel value survives the uniform shift but fails under the patterned shifts; this does not establish failure of every possible IG baseline. PatternAttribution remains unchanged in the reported comparisons. The paper supplies a covariance-based explanation and redistribution algebra; the linear covariance formula directly supports shift invariance under its stated construction. SmoothGrad does not repair the demonstrated failures of its underlying methods. A target-gradient-derived shift, clipped to [-0.3,0.3], makes cat structure appear in several attribution maps while corresponding predictions remain unchanged.

**Limitations / open questions**

The tests concern additive recodings with compensating model biases, rather than transformations of an unchanged model. Attribution comparisons lack reported aggregate discrepancy metrics, sample counts, and attack success rates. Although the setup mentions CNN evaluation, its specified MNIST architecture is an MLP. Passing these checks does not establish explanatory correctness or general invariance. Normalization is suggested as a transformation-specific remedy without a separate evaluation. Systematic reference selection remains unresolved, and language and audio applications are discussed without experiments.

title: Linkpost: Neural Networks Are Already Clean
summary:
**Note on source.** This is a short LessWrong linkpost, not the underlying work. It points to a long post by Nick Cammarata titled "Neural Networks Are Already Clean". The linkpost reproduces only Cammarata's Twitter summary, a quote-tweet by Roon, and the linkpost author's own questions. The underlying post's methods, models, data and results are **not included**, so this extraction can only record the claims as relayed. No evidence from this document can be attached to them.

**Central idea**

Cammarata co-authored early OpenAI circuits work and came away pessimistic. Neurons appeared to "fold into arbitrary tangled knots". Later they led OpenAI's first large-scale automated interpretability project, which found about 2% of neurons legible with the tools of that time.

The relayed claim is that a much closer look with modern agentic tools changes the picture:
- The vast majority of neurons, in models up to trillions of parameters, are legible.
- Their circuits are "beautiful".
- Many famous examples of polysemantic ("tangled") neurons were misunderstood.

The slogan is that neurons are "already clean" and form an "alien ontology". This is framed as a possible "bitter lesson" for interpretability: simple neuron-level analysis, run at enormous scale by automated scientists, works. Cammarata concludes that ambitious interpretability may be solved before it is critically needed for alignment. They hold that interpretability is likely necessary for alignment.

**Experiments**

None are described in the linkpost. The reference to "modern agentic tools" suggests the underlying work used LLM-agent-driven automated interpretability on frontier-scale models. The specific models, legibility criteria, scoring metrics and sample sizes are not given.

**Key results**

All results are asserted, not shown:
- About 2% of neurons were legible under the earlier automated pipeline.
- The "vast majority" are legible under the new agentic analysis.
- Previously cited polysemantic neurons were reinterpreted as monosemantic.

Roon's quote-tweet calls the result a potential "major moment in scientific history" that could turn alignment into "normal science". This is endorsement, not evidence.

**Limitations / open questions**

The linkpost author asks two questions:
1. How much of this is a real advance versus already-known results?
2. How useful would it be in practice for alignment?

Further open questions:
- What counts as "legible"? Explanations that fit activating examples may not capture full neuron behavior.
- Do agent-produced explanations hold up under causal or simulation-based validation?
- How does the claim reconcile with superposition-based accounts and the empirical success of SAEs over neuron bases?

Without the underlying post, none of these can be assessed here.

title: High-Low Frequency Detectors
"Branch Specialization"
Weight Banding
summary:
**Central idea**

Weight banding is a layer-scale pattern of approximately horizontal stripes in convolutional filters near the ends of ImageNet classifiers. The authors investigate whether this structure arises from pressure to preserve spatial information before pooling removes position distinctions. They visualize filters by using nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF) to reduce the input-channel dimension to three factors, displayed as RGB with heuristic factor alignment across neurons.

**Experiments**

Initial inspections compare InceptionV1, ResNet50, VGG19, and AlexNet. Controlled experiments use a simplified network with six convolution groups separated by L2 pooling, followed by global average pooling into 512 values and a 1001-output fully connected layer. The simplified network was trained on 1.2 million ImageNet images for 90 epochs. Interventions include rotating training images by 90°, removing final pooling, pooling only horizontally, and adding alternative mechanisms for spatial information. Rotation and pooling removal are also tested in InceptionV1, ResNet50, and VGG19 trained from scratch. Results primarily concern qualitative weight visualizations; technical notes also describe clustering normalized weights to explore banding types and proportions. The prose supplies no numerical classification-accuracy comparisons or quantitative banding effect sizes.

**Key results**

Baseline banding appears in the final convolutional layers of InceptionV1, ResNet50, and VGG19, but not the inspected AlexNet. The simplified model reliably develops final-layer banding, usually also in its two preceding layers. Rotating ImageNet changes bands from horizontal to vertical in the simplified model and all three retrained architectures. Removing pooling before the fully connected layers eliminates final-layer banding in the simplified model, InceptionV1, and ResNet50, but leaves it in VGG19. The simplified model's unpooled fully connected layer has 49 times as many parameters, and the model overfits. Horizontal-only pooling removes final-layer banding while clear bands remain in the preceding layer. Banding persists under several alternatives, including learned spatial masks, attention, CoordConv channels, grouped classifiers, and a global-max-pooling configuration.

**Limitations / open questions**

The proposed spatial-information-preservation mechanism remains an interpretation rather than a directly measured computational account. VGG19's exception and persistence under spatially informative alternatives complicate a simple pooling explanation. Seed counts, uncertainty estimates, and quantitative banding criteria are unspecified. The work establishes no architectural improvement or determination that banding helps or hurts performance. Joint horizontal/vertical pooling and random input rotations are suggested but untested.

title: Rethinking SAE Evaluation: An Atomic Interpretable Unit Framework Reveals Hidden Polysemanticity and Redundancy
abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) were originally motivated by discovering monosemantic features, a property that characterizes individual features but does not specify what the learned feature set should look like as a whole. As SAEs have increasingly been adopted for attribution, circuit discovery, and intervention, researchers have begun evaluating metrics that describe global properties of the feature set, such as sparsity, dead feature rates, reconstruction fidelity, and disentanglement, a diverse set that extends far beyond monosemanticity. However, this implicit shift beyond monosemanticity has not been formalized as a clear, well-defined objective that comes before these evaluation metrics. Without such an objective, existing metrics remain ad hoc, with their necessity unjustified. In this work, we formalize this ultimate objective by introducing a new paradigm for SAE evaluation: requiring that SAE features, and more generally dictionary-based decompositions of model representations, form an atomic interpretable unit basis, a coordinate system for semantically meaningful explanation. Under this paradigm, we organize existing and new measurements such as DAME (Dominance-Aware Monosemanticity Evaluation) as proxy metrics and introduce a comprehensive benchmarking framework. Evaluating hundreds of SAEs across multiple architectures and model families, we uncover failure modes in which some SAEs appear monosemantic under existing evaluation metrics while remaining functionally polysemantic: the most dominant features, those contributing most to model computation, are systematically less interpretable and more redundant. These failure modes warrant attention from SAE researchers as targets for improved training and architectures, and motivate dominance-aware evaluation as a standard check for practitioners before SAE features are deployed for attribution, circuit tracing, or intervention.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper proposes evaluating SAE dictionaries as an atomic interpretable unit (AIU) basis for meaningful attribution and intervention. At a stated concept granularity, it motivates non-redundancy, completeness, monosemanticity, no unused units, and per-input sparsity. These are conceptual desiderata, not formally proved guarantees of causal faithfulness. DAME stratifies features by mean dominance: their share of absolute latent activation, averaged over inputs.

**Experiments**

The benchmark reports 600+ SAEs across seven architectures and 28,000+ sampled features, covering GPT-2 Small, Pythia, Gemma-2-2B, OPT-125M, and TinyStories. Newly trained SAEs use OpenWebText or TinyStories data. DAME forms dominance quartiles among features with at least 80 sequence firings, generates explanations from 20 examples, and measures exact activation ordering on held-out triplets, primarily using Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2. Additional experiments compare scoring rules on 80 synthetic features, evaluate known-concept alignment in synthetic SAEs, examine public larger-model SAEs, and test decoder-direction injections in Pythia-160M.

**Key results**

Across DAME-evaluated SAEs, Q1 features average 61.8% ranking accuracy versus 64.1% for Q2–Q4; 65.2% of SAEs show a directional deficit. Five of seven architecture groups have significant deficits. DAME prefers correct over activation-strength-reversed explanations for 80/80 synthetic features, versus 67/80 for discretized magnitude and at most 22/80 for tested binary/fuzz-style comparators. Held-out support containment also shows an overall Q1 deficit across 210 synthetic SAEs. At decoder cosine ≥0.7, using full-dictionary quartiles and symmetric active-feature filtering, median Q1 redundant-edge endpoint enrichment is 1.64×; 71.5% of SAEs exceed the null. One selected decoder-aligned pair has largely separate WikiText-103 supports and similar effects on the target token “ aim” across 18 eligible prompts from a fixed 20-prompt family, illustrating shared writes through different gates.

**Limitations / open questions**

Activation dominance is not established as downstream causal importance, and explanation predictiveness does not prove monosemanticity. Architecture comparisons have unmatched effective sparsity. Larger-model directional-deficit rates vary: 41.7%, 50.0%, and 41.7% in the respective Qwen3-8B/14B/32B panels, versus 75.0% for Gemma-2-9B; panel sizes are unspecified. Sharding’s intervention evidence concerns one selected pair and one target token. Context audits also identify coherent grammatical subclasses, with substantial insufficient evidence. The source contains inconsistent benchmark counts and some table signs. Whether sparsity objectives cause these failures or revised objectives improve downstream explanations remains open.

title: Verbalizable Representations Form a Global Workspace in Language Models
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper identifies verbalizable representations that exhibit functional properties of a global workspace: reportability, directed modulation, internal reasoning, flexible reuse, and selectivity. Its Jacobian lens averages downstream-state Jacobians across contexts and applies vocabulary projection. Sparse nonnegative combinations of the resulting token directions define the J-space, rather than an ordinary linear subspace. The default Sonnet 4.5 implementation uses 1,000 pretraining-like sequences of 128 tokens and targets the penultimate residual state.

**Experiments**

Experiments primarily use Claude Sonnet 4.5, with corroboration on Haiku 4.5 and Opus 4.5 and selected analyses on Opus 4.6. Coordinate swaps, ablations, and clamps test report, covert tasks, factual intermediates, poetry planning, and argument reuse. Other tests examine automatic versus flexible computation, capability retention, experiential language, capacity, connectivity, alignment auditing, post-training, and reflection training. Lens comparisons use six constructed intermediate-recovery distributions. Appendix methods extend readouts to multi-token concepts and free-form phrases.

**Key results**

Intermediate swaps yield target-appropriate top-1 answers on 54%, 70%, and 70% of 50 two-hop trials for Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus 4.5. In a separate 90-prompt experiment, J-component swaps succeed on 61%, versus 28% for the remainder; clamping relevant J-coordinates reduces remainder success to 6%. Cross-function swaps succeed on 76/192 trials, rising to 101/192 at double strength. Targeted swaps redirect report and flexible inference while largely sparing continuation, anomaly detection, and line wrapping. Broader ablation selectively impairs reasoning and generation; early-workspace ablation reduces experiential language about both models and people.

Workspace-like content concentrates around normalized depths 38–92. Median sparse occupancy is approximately 25 directions, with excess explained activation variance over random controls never exceeding 10%. Weight analyses and selected-head ablations support preferential broadcast. Evaluation-awareness ablation increases blackmail attempts from 0/180 to 13/180 across six prompts. Reflection training on 10,000 contexts reduces Haiku 4.5 dishonesty from 0.25 to 0.07 on 27 fabrication transcripts and deception from 0.38 to 0.05 on 100 scenarios, sampling five responses per item. Selected concept ablations largely reverse the fabrication gain and partially reverse the deception gain.

**Limitations / open questions**

Single-token readouts omit relational structure and sometimes resist interpretation. Early-layer absence could reflect lens failure. Automatic misalignment could evade monitoring; screening coverage is unestablished. Several evaluations use small constructed datasets, LLM grading, or NLA-derived labels. The supplied text has unresolved references and inconsistent cone-versus-span formalization. Functional workspace evidence and changes in experiential language do not establish subjective experience.

title: J++ Lens: Jacobian Filtering Enables More Faithful Workspace Lenses
summary:
**Central idea**

J++ Lens improves single-token readouts of intermediate reasoning variables by filtering the Jacobians used to transport activations toward output space. It clusters source activations, fits eight expert Jacobians per layer, and learns their mixing weights on a small development set. It combines this Jacobian Filtering with a Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) backward pass and removal of non-semantic readout tokens. After fitting, each layer retains one linear map, with no additional inference compute or memory relative to an equivalently shaped J-Lens.

**Experiments**

The main model is Qwen3.6-27B; readout evaluations additionally cover Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma 4 31B, Olmo 3 32B, Qwen3.5-122B-A10B, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash (284B). Main fitting uses 64 WikiText-103 sequences of 128 tokens, yielding 7,104 source positions; clustering uses 1,000 sequences. Five extraction tasks cover multihop reasoning, multilingual representations, typos, associations, and poetry. Recall@10 counts an item as recovered if its target appears among the top ten readouts at any of seven equally spaced layers; aggregate scores average equally across tasks. A separate intermediate-swap evaluation contains 67 trials. Ablations test recipe components, expert routing, and development supervision excluding the evaluated task. Concept-suppression experiments examine readout trajectories and targeted interventions.

**Key results**

On Qwen3.6-27B, J++ reaches 55.2% macro recall@10 versus 35.7% for J-Lens and 37.7% for R-Lens, with especially large early-layer gains. Across six models, median relative improvements are 63.5% and 42.2%, respectively; Table 1 applies readout filtering to every lens. Intermediate swaps make the intended answer the top word token in 59.7% of 67 trials, versus 49.3% and 50.7%. Removing Jacobian Filtering costs 11.7 percentage points; excluding the evaluated task from development supervision retains 54.4% recall. Under implied-concept avoidance instructions, early J++ concept ablations increase the concept’s output probability by 2.8 percentage points beyond a same-category control. Together with selected suppression trajectories, this provides preliminary evidence for retrieval followed by active suppression in some cases.

**Limitations / open questions**

Single-token readouts cannot express propositions and depend on tokenization. Qwen3.6-27B poetry recall@10 is only 4.9%. Expected intermediates may be absent because models use shortcuts, leaving evaluation ceilings uncertain. Gradient-noise and curvature explanations remain partly conjectural. External baseline fitting differs, suppression effects are not universal, and practical safety monitoring is untested. Some equations and table labels are missing from the supplied rendering.

Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer
abstract: The capacity of a neural network to absorb information is limited by its number of parameters. Conditional computation, where parts of the network are active on a per-example basis, has been proposed in theory as a way of dramatically increasing model capacity without a proportional increase in computation. In practice, however, there are significant algorithmic and performance challenges. In this work, we address these challenges and finally realize the promise of conditional computation, achieving greater than 1000x improvements in model capacity with only minor losses in computational efficiency on modern GPU clusters. We introduce a Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts layer (MoE), consisting of up to thousands of feed-forward sub-networks. A trainable gating network determines a sparse combination of these experts to use for each example. We apply the MoE to the tasks of language modeling and machine translation, where model capacity is critical for absorbing the vast quantities of knowledge available in the training corpora. We present model architectures in which a MoE with up to 137 billion parameters is applied convolutionally between stacked LSTM layers. On large language modeling and machine translation benchmarks, these models achieve significantly better results than state-of-the-art at lower computational cost.
summary:
**Central idea**
The paper introduces the Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layer as a general-purpose network component for conditional computation. The layer contains up to thousands of feed-forward experts, each with one ReLU hidden layer. A trainable gating network selects a sparse weighted combination of k experts per input using *noisy top-k gating*: a softmax over the top-k values of x·W_g plus learned, input-dependent Gaussian noise. The goal is to increase parameter count (capacity) by more than 1000x with only a small increase in per-example compute. The MoE is applied convolutionally between stacked LSTM layers, so each token position can route to different experts. The paper also introduces a two-level hierarchical MoE.

The authors address several engineering problems:
- **Shrinking per-expert batches.** They combine data parallelism for the standard layers with model parallelism for the experts, and batch the MoE across timesteps.
- **Network bandwidth.** They use large expert hidden layers.
- **Expert collapse.** Two auxiliary losses balance expert use: an importance loss (squared coefficient of variation of the batchwise gate sums) and a smooth load loss built from the noise-induced selection probability.

**Experiments**
- **1B Word LM benchmark.** Models run at a matched compute of about 8M ops/timestep, with 4 to 4096 experts of about 1M parameters each and k=4. They are compared against computationally matched LSTM and dense-MoE baselines. Larger-compute MoE models (34M and 143M ops/timestep, about 4B MoE parameters) are compared with Jozefowicz et al. (2016).
- **100B-word Google News corpus.** Models use 32 to 131,072 experts, up to 137B MoE parameters.
- **Machine translation.**
  - WMT'14 En→Fr and En→De, plus Google Production En→Fr, using a reduced GNMT with MoE layers of up to 2048 experts (about 8.7B parameters total).
  - Multilingual 12-pair translation with 512 experts per layer.
- **Load-balancing loss ablation** on MoE-256.
- **Qualitative inspection** of the top-gated contexts for a few encoder experts.

**Key results**
- **1B Word LM.**
  - At matched compute, MoE-4096-h reaches test perplexity 34.1, versus 45.0 for MoE-4 and about 45–46 for the dense baselines; the abstract reports this as about 24% lower.
  - MoE-143M reaches 28.0, versus 34.7 for the best published model after 10 epochs.
- **100B-word corpus.** Perplexity improves up to 65,536 experts (68B parameters), 39% below the matched baseline, and degrades slightly at 131,072 experts.
- **Single-pair translation.**
  - WMT'14 BLEU is 40.56 for En→Fr and 26.03 for En→De, gains of +1.34 and +1.12 over GNMT, at lower compute.
  - On Google Production En→Fr, test BLEU is +1.01 over GNMT.
- **Multilingual translation.** The MoE model has 19% lower dev perplexity than multilingual GNMT. It is better on 11 of 12 pairs and beats the single-pair models on 8 of 12; En→Ko is worse, which the authors attribute to overtraining.
- **Load balancing.**
  - Without any balancing loss, CV(Importance) is 3.04, the max/mean load is 17.8, and perplexity is 39.8.
  - Any of the balancing losses gives perplexity of about 35.6–35.7 with a near-balanced load.
- **Expert specialization.** Inspected experts appear specialized by syntax and/or semantics, for example "innovation"/research words, "a" in "plays a … role", and speed-related words.

**Limitations / open questions**
- Gains taper as capacity grows on smaller data and reverse at extreme sparsity.
- The specialization evidence is qualitative and covers only three hand-shown experts.
- The discontinuities in top-k gating are not analysed theoretically.
- All models are LSTM-based.
- Some translation runs use a different strictly balanced batchwise gating scheme.
- Recurrent MoEs are proposed but not tested.

A Mathematical Philosophy of Explanations in Mechanistic Interpretability -- The Strange Science Part I.i
Relational Composition in Neural Networks: A Survey and Call to Action
abstract: Many neural nets appear to represent data as linear combinations of "feature vectors." Algorithms for discovering these vectors have seen impressive recent success. However, we argue that this success is incomplete without an understanding of relational composition: how (or whether) neural nets combine feature vectors to represent more complicated relationships. To facilitate research in this area, this paper offers a guided tour of various relational mechanisms that have been proposed, along with preliminary analysis of how such mechanisms might affect the search for interpretable features. We end with a series of promising areas for empirical research, which may help determine how neural networks represent structured data.
