With one coefficient per input, full-output Kullback-Leibler (KL) calibration leaves smaller mean effect gaps from the encoder-based reference intervention than total-norm matching for nonnegative least-squares (NNLS) refits. On new Llama inputs, total-norm matching loses 11 reference transfers, whereas full-output calibration preserves every transfer decision. (2) Positionwise scaling. On a small matched gender-agreement subset, positionwise norm matching leaves smaller observed mean gaps than full-output calibration. (3) Answer exclusion. Compared with unscaled NNLS, answer-excluded calibration reduces gaps in the measured subject-verb agreement comparisons but increases them for gender refits. Full-output KL calibration also reduces larger gaps for norm-matched constructed candidates, although matching coverage is incomplete in several settings. Since calibration uses the evaluated input's outputs, it serves as a diagnostic of residual disagreement.
summary:
**Central idea**

Comparisons between SAE interventions depend on what intervention strength holds equal. With the model, decoder, feature group, and sentence pair fixed, changing sparse coefficients can change patch direction and magnitude. The paper compares total-norm matching, positionwise norm matching, full-output KL calibration (Q1), and answer-excluded KL calibration (Q2). Agreement with released-encoder interventions is the endpoint, not a faithfulness standard.

**Experiments**

Five selected configurations use Gemma-2-9B-it, Gemma-2-2B base, and Llama-3.1-8B base with Gemma Scope or Llama Scope dictionaries containing 32,768 or 131,072 features. Authored sentence pairs test subject–verb agreement with noun attractors and explicitly cued reflexive gender agreement. Alternatives are same-support nonnegative least-squares refits and reconstruction-qualified constructed candidates with encoder-matched positionwise patch norms. Interventions retain reconstruction residuals and leave BOS and final prompt positions unchanged. Outcomes are absolute gaps from encoder answer-margin effects, donor-answer transfer decisions, and matching coverage. A prospective Llama-128K confirmation retains 304 directed inputs from 152 qualified pairs out of 512 assigned pairs.

**Key results**

Q1 leaves smaller mean NNLS gaps than total-norm matching in all five earlier cohorts. On the prospective panel, both controls match all 304 inputs; balanced gaps are 0.021 versus 0.181 logits, with paired difference 0.160 [95% conditional interval 0.131, 0.191]. Total-norm matching loses 11 of 175 encoder transfers and gains one; Q1 preserves every decision. On 24 of 42 eligible gender inputs matched by all three controls, positionwise matching has the smallest descriptive balanced gap: 0.012 versus Q1’s 0.047 and total-norm’s 0.085. Q2 reduces measured subject–verb NNLS gaps but increases gender gaps from 0.089 to 0.139 logits on the common 40-input cohort. For constructed 9B candidates, Q1 reduces case-balanced gaps from 0.752 to 0.028 logits and transfer disagreements from 77 to eight on 478/504 matched inputs. Shared coefficients improve mean candidate agreement while worsening many individual inputs.

**Limitations / open questions**

Per-input calibration uses evaluation outputs and additional forward evaluations. Scaled patches need not satisfy original complete-code constraints. Candidate coverage fails in several settings, and successful-match summaries omit harder comparisons. The 9B primary reduction misses planned precision; gender positionwise results lack an interval. Selected configurations, shared templates, and assumed lexical-block independence limit generalization. Prospective confirmation concerns one previously selected configuration; its Q2 extension follows inspection. Calibration agreement establishes neither mechanistic correctness nor model safety.

title: Investigating gender bias in language models using causal mediation analysis (Vig et al., 2020)
Direct and Indirect Effects
abstract: The direct effect of one eventon another can be defined and measured byholding constant all intermediate variables between the this http URL effects present conceptual andpractical difficulties (in nonlinear models), because they cannot be isolated by holding certain variablesconstant. This paper shows a way of defining any path-specific effectthat does not invoke blocking the this http URL permits the assessment of a more naturaltype of direct and indirect effects, one thatis applicable in both linear and nonlinear models. The paper establishesconditions under which such assessments can be estimated consistentlyfrom experimental and nonexperimental data,and thus extends path-analytic techniques tononlinear and nonparametric models.
summary:
**Central idea**

Pearl distinguishes controlled direct effects, which fix a mediator to a prescribed value, from natural direct effects, which hold it at its unit-specific value under a reference treatment. For treatment X, mediator Z, outcome Y, and reference x*, the natural direct effect is E[Y(x,Z(x*))] − E[Y(x*)]; the natural indirect effect is E[Y(x*,Z(x))] − E[Y(x*)]. These nested counterfactuals describe selective transmission of influence, including policies that remove treatment-induced mediator changes while preserving other causes of mediator variation. The supplied metadata dates the arXiv posting to 2013; the document appears in UAI 2001.

**Experiments**

No empirical experiments, datasets, neural networks, or benchmark measurements are reported. Evidence consists of formal counterfactual derivations and graphical identification criteria. Treatment–aspirin–recovery and hiring-discrimination scenarios illustrate the definitions. Theorem 1 derives experimental identification of natural direct effects under conditional independence between controlled outcomes Y(x,z) and reference-world mediator values Z(x*), given suitable nondescendant covariates W. Theorem 2 additionally requires observational identification of the component intervention distributions. Theorem 4 gives the corresponding indirect-effect identification result.

**Key results**

Under the stipulated independence, the natural direct effect becomes an average of conditional controlled direct effects weighted by the mediator distribution under x*. In the simple unconfounded Markovian structure, it reduces to Σz[E(Y|x,z) − E(Y|x*,z)]P(z|x*). An analogous formula identifies the natural indirect effect. Theorem 3 derives that the total effect equals the forward indirect effect minus the reverse natural direct effect, or the forward natural direct effect minus the reverse indirect effect. Same-direction direct and indirect effects add to the total in linear models; this is not guaranteed generally. General path-specific effects are defined through structural equations that replace inputs along excluded edges with their unit-specific reference-world values.

**Limitations / open questions**

Ordinary randomization does not generally identify natural effects without additional cross-world restrictions. The identification conditions are sufficient, not necessary; observational estimation also requires identifiable component distributions. Markovian simplifications depend on acyclicity, independent errors, and the specified mediator/parent structure. For the selected X→Z→W→Y pathway in Figure 3, nonidentification even in Markovian models is asserted without a supplied proof. Characterizing identifiable path selections remains open in this text. Several equations and diagrams have OCR corruption, but the source includes the conclusions and references.

title: Rewriting a deep generative model (Bau et al., 2020)
Editing factual knowledge in language models (De Cao et al., 2021)
Fast model editing at scale (MEND; Mitchell et al., 2021)
Modifying memories in transformer models (Zhu et al., 2020)
Measuring and Improving Consistency in Pretrained Language Models (ParaRel; Elazar et al., 2021)
Language models as knowledge bases? (Petroni et al., 2019)
Correlation matrix memories (Kohonen, 1972)
Mass-Editing Memory in a Transformer
abstract: Recent work has shown exciting promise in updating large language models with new memories, so as to replace obsolete information or add specialized knowledge. However, this line of work is predominantly limited to updating single associations. We develop MEMIT, a method for directly updating a language model with many memories, demonstrating experimentally that it can scale up to thousands of associations for GPT-J (6B) and GPT-NeoX (20B), exceeding prior work by orders of magnitude. Our code and data are at https://memit.baulab.info.
summary:
**Central idea**

MEMIT edits factual associations by treating transformer MLP output projections as linear associative memories. It optimizes a target hidden state for each fact, then distributes the remaining displacement across several MLP layers, recomputing activations after each update. A derived least-squares update balances new associations against old ones, whose key second moments are approximated from ordinary text. Edited layers are 3–8 in GPT-J (6B) and 6–10 in GPT-NeoX (20B).

**Experiments**

GPT-J causal tracing uses 501 correctly predicted factual statements and ten Gaussian-noise samples per statement, with attention- and MLP-severing tests. Editing evaluations include 10,000 true zsRE facts, conflict-filtered CounterFact batches ranging from one to 10,000 counterfactuals, 300 edits for each of 27 relations containing at least 300 cases, and four balanced two-relation mixtures scaling to 700 facts. GPT-J baselines are weight-decayed fine-tuning, MEND, and sequential ROME; GPT-NeoX receives a separate 10,000-edit CounterFact evaluation. Ablations vary edited layers, target modules, and covariance weighting. Additional demonstrations update election results and selected star–constellation associations.

**Key results**

For 10,000 zsRE edits, MEMIT achieves 96.7% efficacy, 89.7% paraphrase accuracy, and 26.6% unrelated-fact accuracy, versus 27.0% unrelated-fact accuracy before editing. For 10,000 CounterFact edits, GPT-J achieves 98.9% efficacy success, 88.6% paraphrase success, and 73.7% neighborhood success; their harmonic mean is 85.8, compared with 67.6 for fine-tuning, 50.3 for ROME, and 23.1 for MEND. CounterFact success compares desired and original object probabilities rather than requiring top-1 correctness. GPT-NeoX achieves an editing score of 82.0. GPT-J neighborhood success declines from 83.5% to 73.7%, while generation entropy remains near baseline, 619.9 versus 622.4. Fine-tuning substantially degrades generation metrics. Mixtures perform near constituent-relation averages. Accuracy on 289 selected star–constellation tuples rises from 53% to 86%; the election demonstration reports 100% efficacy success and 94% paraphrase success.

**Limitations / open questions**

Specificity remains imperfect and relation-dependent. Evaluations cover directional subject–relation–object associations; reverse associations require separate edits. The associative-memory model and representative key covariance are assumptions; single-layer least-squares optimality does not establish global optimality of multilayer editing. Generation entropy and TF-IDF similarity provide limited behavioral checks. Reported GPT-J runtime for 10,000 edits is 7.44 hours, including serial target optimization; batching gains are proposed. SERAC is not evaluated, and fine-tuning regularization is tuned only at 10,000 edits.

title: In-context learning creates task vectors (Hendel et al., 2023)
Label Words are Anchors: An Information Flow Perspective for Understanding In-Context Learning
abstract: In-context learning (ICL) emerges as a promising capability of large language models (LLMs) by providing them with demonstration examples to perform diverse tasks. However, the underlying mechanism of how LLMs learn from the provided context remains under-explored. In this paper, we investigate the working mechanism of ICL through an information flow lens. Our findings reveal that label words in the demonstration examples function as anchors: (1) semantic information aggregates into label word representations during the shallow computation layers' processing; (2) the consolidated information in label words serves as a reference for LLMs' final predictions. Based on these insights, we introduce an anchor re-weighting method to improve ICL performance, a demonstration compression technique to expedite inference, and an analysis framework for diagnosing ICL errors in GPT2-XL. The promising applications of our findings again validate the uncovered ICL working mechanism and pave the way for future studies.
summary:
**Central idea**

Demonstration label tokens can act as contextualized anchors in classification-style in-context learning: shallow layers aggregate preceding information at label positions, and middle/deep layers consult those positions when predicting a query label. The paper investigates this account without identifying a complete circuit.

**Experiments**

The main models are GPT2-XL (1.5B, 48 layers) and GPT-J (6B, 28 layers), evaluated on SST-2, TREC, AGNews, and EmoContext, usually with one demonstration per class. The stated protocol samples 1,000 test inputs per dataset, although the later TREC diagnostic identifies its entire test set as 500 examples, leaving sampling details unclear. GPT2-XL saliency analysis averages five seeds and measures head-aggregated attention-times-gradient magnitudes. Interventions zero attention from preceding tokens into label positions, comparing early versus late layers and label versus random non-label positions. Prediction agreement and top-five vocabulary Jaccard similarity measure disruption. Extensions use two demonstrations per class and LLaMA-33B with unrelated A/B labels on SST-2, eight demonstrations per class, and 83.0% baseline accuracy.

**Key results**

Early label isolation reportedly disrupts predictions substantially more than late isolation or non-label controls. Target-position attention to demonstration labels predicts the model's selected label with deep-layer AUROC approaching 0.8, averaged across the four main datasets; this is agreement with model outputs, not ground-truth accuracy.

Training head- and layer-specific attention multipliers with four additional labeled examples per class raises GPT2-XL mean accuracy from 51.90% to 68.64%, a 16.74 percentage-point gain across four datasets and five seeds. The additional-demonstration baseline averages 46.87%; AGNews uses three rather than five demonstrations per class because of context limits.

Caching label and formatting states yields mean label agreement of 79.47% for GPT2-XL and 89.06% for GPT-J, exceeding text-only and random-state controls. Accuracy changes from 51.90% to 45.04% and from 56.82% to 55.59%, respectively. Reported speedups range from 1.1× to 2.9×. On 500 TREC examples, query-variation-weighted label-key distances qualitatively identify several confusing category pairs.

**Limitations / open questions**

Evidence covers classification and conventional prompting, without generative or chain-of-thought tasks. Most experiments stop at 6B parameters; one appendix setting uses 33B. Attention correlations and summed excess AUROCs do not establish causal information transfer. Isolation may have collateral effects, compression requires formatting, and error diagnosis lacks a numerical correlation statistic. Timing methodology is limited. Plots are unavailable in this text rendering; qualitative figure findings rely on accompanying prose.

title: How does GPT-2 compute greater-than?: Interpreting mathematical abilities in a pre-trained language model
abstract: Pre-trained language models can be surprisingly adept at tasks they were not explicitly trained on, but how they implement these capabilities is poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the basic mathematical abilities often acquired by pre-trained language models. Concretely, we use mechanistic interpretability techniques to explain the (limited) mathematical abilities of GPT-2 small. As a case study, we examine its ability to take in sentences such as "The war lasted from the year 1732 to the year 17", and predict valid two-digit end years (years > 32). We first identify a circuit, a small subset of GPT-2 small's computational graph that computes this task's output. Then, we explain the role of each circuit component, showing that GPT-2 small's final multi-layer perceptrons boost the probability of end years greater than the start year. Finally, we find related tasks that activate our circuit. Our results suggest that GPT-2 small computes greater-than using a complex but general mechanism that activates across diverse contexts.
summary:
**Central idea**

GPT-2 small predicts later end years through attention heads that transport a start-year representation to late MLPs. Multiple neurons' contributions combine to favor greater numbers. The circuit transfers across selected contexts and also activates inappropriately; its existence does not resolve whether its internal computation resembles a lookup table or a more general mathematical algorithm.

**Experiments**

The authors evaluate 10,000 generated, tokenization-filtered prompts such as “The war lasted from the year 1732 to the year 17,” using 120 duration-related nouns. Probability difference measures mass on two-digit years greater than YY minus mass on years no greater; cutoff sharpness is p(YY+1)−p(YY−1). Iterative path patching replaces selected paths with contributions from matched prompts whose start-year suffix is 01. Discovery uses a reported 490-example subset, followed by larger-dataset circuit evaluation. Other experiments examine attention patterns, vocabulary projections, all 3,072 MLP-10 neurons, PCA-direction ablation, LEACE erasure, and related prompt families.

**Key results**

Baseline probability difference is 81.7% (SD 19.3 percentage points), with 6.0% cutoff sharpness (SD 7.2 points). Preserving normal information along a circuit of seven attention heads and MLPs 8–11 yields 72.7% probability difference, reported as 89.5% recovery, and 8% sharpness. Corrupting that circuit while preserving normal inputs elsewhere yields −36.6% probability difference. MLPs 9–11 directly favor greater years; MLP 8 contributes mainly through downstream MLPs. Ten important MLP-10 neurons jointly approximate the greater-than pattern, with larger groups sharpening it. Direct-effect patching corroborates selected neuron projections.

For rephrased temporal statements and price ranges, Section 5 reports 98.8% and 88.9% circuit recovery, respectively. Increasing sequences retain 67.8% performance with the original circuit and 90.3% after adding MLP 7 and two heads. Reversed temporal statements and BC dates incorrectly recruit the same greater-than mechanism. Other prompts, including explicit “is smaller than” comparisons, fail to recruit it appropriately.

**Limitations / open questions**

Results concern one small model and constrained next-token tasks. PCA-direction ablation changes performance little; LEACE erasure leaves 64.7% probability difference versus 81.7%, leaving the causal role of ordered number geometry unresolved. The extended circuit achieves 71.5% probability difference while leaving attention queries supplied with unrestricted normal inputs. Neither minimality nor general mathematical competence is established. The supplied source contains inconsistent dataset counts, head labels, and transfer-recovery descriptions, limiting exact reconstruction.

title: A circuit for Python docstrings in a 4-layer attention-only transformer
summary:
**Central idea**

The authors identify a partial circuit for predicting argument names in Python docstrings in attn-only-4l, a pretrained four-layer attention-only transformer trained on natural language and Python code. The proposed algorithm matches the previously documented argument to its occurrence in the function definition, then copies the following argument. It combines three levels of composition, context-dependent head functions, and a proposed positional signal derived from causal masking.

**Experiments**

Randomized reST-style docstrings use sampled argument names and description words. Reported next-argument accuracy is approximately 75% on ordinary examples. Adding extra definition arguments is intended to disrupt competing line-number and inhibition strategies; accuracy on this induction-focused distribution is 56%, with mean logit difference 0.5. The authors state that experiments and visualizations use batches of 50 prompts. Corrupted-to-clean residual-stream and head-output patching separately changes the answer name, other definition names, or documented names. The metric subtracts the highest competing argument-name logit from the correct-answer logit, including corrupted variants and recalculating the maximum after each intervention. Additional experiments manipulate attention patterns, positional embeddings, and token context.

**Key results**

Heads 1.4 and 2.0 carry preceding-argument information through its following comma to the next argument's definition position. In the docstring, head 1.4 instead performs induction, carrying the previously documented argument to the prediction position. Argument Movers 3.0 and 3.6 select and copy the answer. Controlled short prompts demonstrate context-dependent attention by head 1.4. Swapping head 0.4's attention patterns reverses head 1.4's preference between documented arguments, whereas positional-embedding swaps have little effect. Head 0.5 largely retains its contribution under identity attention; head 1.2 has a small supporting effect associated with BOS attention.

Retaining eight proposed circuit heads while resample-ablating others yields 42% accuracy, versus 56% for the full model and reported chance of 17%. Adding head 1.0 yields 48%; additionally retaining 0.1 and 2.3 yields 58%. Removing 0.0 and 2.2 from the full model yields 72%.

**Limitations / open questions**

The mechanistic account remains incomplete. Validation retains whole heads rather than testing the proposed connection structure or performing causal scrubbing. Accuracy recovery alone does not verify every proposed mechanism. Name-only corruptions investigate argument selection while leaving recognition of the docstring task largely untested. Head 0.2's role is less certain, several supporting heads remain unexplained, and uncertainty estimates are absent. Similar circuits in other models are mentioned only as preliminary observations.

title: Localizing Model Behavior with Path Patching
abstract: Localizing behaviors of neural networks to a subset of the network's components or a subset of interactions between components is a natural first step towards analyzing network mechanisms and possible failure modes. Existing work is often qualitative and ad-hoc, and there is no consensus on the appropriate way to evaluate localization claims. We introduce path patching, a technique for expressing and quantitatively testing a natural class of hypotheses expressing that behaviors are localized to a set of paths. We refine an explanation of induction heads, characterize a behavior of GPT-2, and open source a framework for efficiently running similar experiments.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper generalizes earlier sender–receiver path patching into a framework for testing localization hypotheses. A hypothesis specifies a computational graph, important input-to-output paths, a reference/counterfactual input distribution, and a discrepancy metric. Duplicating shared subgraphs lets selected paths receive the reference input while remaining paths share one counterfactual input. Average unexplained effect (AUE) measures the resulting discrepancy. Localization tests where information matters without explaining the computations performed there.

**Experiments**

A two-layer attention-only transformer with eight heads per layer and Shortformer positional encodings is studied on the first 300 tokens of 100,000 held-out OpenWebText examples. Experiments refine hypotheses about heads 1.5 and 1.6 using absolute per-token cross-entropy changes. GPT-2 Small (117M) and XL (1.5B) are separately studied on “The organization estimates that [N]-”, with N from 0 to 100. Head interventions are compared using mean output KL divergence over 100 reference/counterfactual pairs under number substitution, Gaussian input corruption, and zero ablation.

**Key results**

The initial induction hypothesis reports 28.2% proportion explained, relative to a baseline replacing all paths through heads 1.5 and 1.6 while retaining other paths. Positional refinements raise reported recovery to 48.6%, and longer query/key context raises it to 55.2%. Adding pathways supporting head 1.5’s proposed copying without prefix matching raises recovery to 73.5%. These results concern the heads’ broader behavior, including copying beyond induction.

For GPT-2 Small, Gaussian corruption through heads 5.6 and 6.1 lowers numerical-completion probability from 88.1% to 82.5% and 83.9%; number substitutions leave it at 88.0% and 88.3%. This is consistent with number-recognition roles, which remain tentative. A greedy hypothesis retaining eight of 144 attention heads reports 98.0% recovery, with MLP pathways retained.

**Limitations / open questions**

Low AUE measures distribution-specific sufficiency, not completeness. Redundant contributors may be omitted, average discrepancies can hide rare failures, and differences of expected losses can cancel errors across examples. No downstream application benefits or definitive mechanistic ground truth are established. The supplied text inconsistently reports induction baselines: Section 3.1 gives 0.702, whereas Table 4 gives 0.432 for the full dataset. Figure 11 calls its recovery metric “loss” despite the surrounding KL-based discussion. The induction-subset selection procedure is referenced externally rather than supplied in full.

title: Low-Complexity Probing via Finding Subnetworks
abstract: The dominant approach in probing neural networks for linguistic properties is to train a new shallow multi-layer perceptron (MLP) on top of the model's internal representations. This approach can detect properties encoded in the model, but at the cost of adding new parameters that may learn the task directly. We instead propose a subtractive pruning-based probe, where we find an existing subnetwork that performs the linguistic task of interest. Compared to an MLP, the subnetwork probe achieves both higher accuracy on pre-trained models and lower accuracy on random models, so it is both better at finding properties of interest and worse at learning on its own. Next, by varying the complexity of each probe, we show that subnetwork probing Pareto-dominates MLP probing in that it achieves higher accuracy given any budget of probe complexity. Finally, we analyze the resulting subnetworks across various tasks to locate where each task is encoded, and we find that lower-level tasks are captured in lower layers, reproducing similar findings in past work.
summary:
**Central idea**

Subnetwork probing investigates linguistic structure by learning sparsity-regularized masks over a frozen encoder together with a task-specific head. Hard-concrete gates permit supervised optimization at different masking granularities. The motivation is to constrain independent task learning while retaining access to nonlinear computations throughout the encoder.

**Experiments**

The paper studies bert-base-uncased: 12 layers, hidden dimension 768, 12 heads, and 110M parameters. Tasks are POS tagging and dependency parsing on English Universal Dependencies, using 12,541 training and 2,002 development examples, and NER on CoNLL-2003, using 13,862 training and 3,235 test examples. Parsing uses macro-averaged labeled attachment score; NER uses CoNLL F1. Comparators are a rank-constrained, one-hidden-layer MLP probe and full fine-tuning. Controls reset either the encoder alone or both encoder and embeddings. All methods train for 30 epochs. Complexity sweeps vary mask granularity and MLP rank, charging one bit per mask and assumed costs of 1–32 bits per MLP parameter.

**Key results**

On pretrained BERT, default neuron-mask probes score 93.39 versus 90.25 for POS, 86.86 versus 76.65 for parsing, and 87.94 versus 84.80 for NER. With encoder and embeddings reset, subnetworks score lower than MLPs on parsing, 39.84 versus 42.81, and NER, 30.83 versus 53.25, but higher on POS, 71.53 versus 69.16. Resetting only the encoder gives slightly higher subnetwork scores for POS and parsing and a lower score for NER. Thus lower random-model performance is task- and reset-dependent.

The authors report Pareto dominance across the evaluated complexity sweeps, including high POS and parsing performance with 72 mask bits. Stronger regularization reduces pretrained task scores, while randomized parsing scores vary nonmonotonically. Selected pretrained subnetworks show a POS → dependencies → NER depth ordering; reset-encoder subnetworks are described as approximately uniform across layers.

**Limitations / open questions**

Evidence covers one encoder and three tasks, without reported uncertainty or repeated-seed results. The 72-bit figure describes mask decisions, excluding the learned head and shared encoder. Final conversion of relaxed gates into binary masks is not specified. Supervised mask search and head training can adapt computation, so successful probing does not independently establish natural use of the recovered subnetwork in the intact encoder. Retained-weight counts provide indirect localization evidence. The supplied rendering includes figure captions but no readable plot values, and several equations contain rendering errors.

title: Attribution Patching: Activation Patching At Industrial Scale — Neel Nanda
summary:
**Central idea**

Attribution patching approximates an activation-patching intervention with a first-order Taylor expansion around the corrupted run. Its score is the dot product of the clean-minus-corrupted activation difference and the corrupted-run gradient of a chosen metric. Caching two forward passes and one backward pass permits scoring every cached activation without a separate model run for each intervention. The intended use is rapid hypothesis generation and prioritization for subsequent activation patching or causal scrubbing.

**Experiments**

The accompanying notebook compares attribution and activation patching on GPT-2 Small's indirect object identification (IOI) circuit. Clean and corrupted prompts exchange which name is repeated, and the metric is the final correct-minus-alternative name logit difference. Comparisons cover residual streams, attention and MLP layer outputs, individual head outputs, queries, keys, values, and attention patterns, including per-position analyses and rankings. Preliminary direct attribution path patching examines connections between head outputs and downstream Q/K/V inputs. Attention attribution additionally scores attention weights using activation times gradient on a single prompt. The supplied text describes plots qualitatively but supplies no numerical correlations or complete experimental sample counts.

**Key results**

Attribution patching approximates head-level interventions and most layer outputs reasonably well, recovering broad IOI circuit structure. It performs poorly for full residual streams and MLP0. Preliminary path analyses recover some known connections, including induction and duplicate-token inputs to S-inhibition heads and their query-mediated effects on name movers. An illustrative complexity calculation estimates roughly 30,000-fold less computation than exhaustive per-head, per-position activation patching for GPT-2 XL with 100-token prompts; this is an analytical estimate rather than a measured benchmark.

**Limitations / open questions**

Evidence is concentrated on one model and task. Layer normalization, saturated nonlinearities, interacting features, and serial backup behavior can produce substantial approximation errors. First-order scores omit interactions between jointly necessary patches. Counterfactual prompt construction and metric choice determine which mechanisms become visible; recovering logit difference can also reflect damage to the corrupted answer. Patching establishes distribution-specific information flow rather than a complete or general algorithmic explanation. Larger-model validation, MLP-heavy circuits, false-negative audits, and automated circuit-search applications remain open.

title: Attribution Patching Outperforms Automated Circuit Discovery
abstract: Automated interpretability research has recently attracted attention as a potential research direction that could scale explanations of neural network behavior to large models. Existing automated circuit discovery work applies activation patching to identify subnetworks responsible for solving specific tasks (circuits). In this work, we show that a simple method based on attribution patching outperforms all existing methods while requiring just two forward passes and a backward pass. We apply a linear approximation to activation patching to estimate the importance of each edge in the computational subgraph. Using this approximation, we prune the least important edges of the network. We survey the performance and limitations of this method, finding that averaged over all tasks our method has greater AUC from circuit recovery than other methods.
summary:
**Central idea**

Edge Attribution Patching (EAP) ranks computational-graph edges by a first-order approximation to the effect of replacing clean activations with corrupted activations. Each score is the activation difference dotted with the clean-run gradient of a task metric. EAP averages absolute attribution scores across prompt pairs and retains the top k edges. Scoring requires two forward passes and one backward pass, avoiding a separate intervention run for every edge.

**Experiments**

The paper benchmarks recovery of previously identified circuits on Indirect Object Identification (IOI), Greater-Than, and Docstring using ROC curves and AUC. IOI and Greater-Than use GPT-2 small; the supplied text does not specify the Docstring model architecture or size. Comparisons include ACDC with task-specific metrics and KL divergence. Repeated individual-edge activation patching is evaluated only on Docstring because of computational cost. Additional Docstring experiments compare approximate and actual intervention effects, interpolate between clean and corrupted activations, and apply ACDC after EAP pruning.

**Key results**

EAP achieves the highest AUC on IOI and Greater-Than, while ACDC with KL divergence performs better on Docstring. The paper reports superior average circuit-recovery AUC for EAP, without numerical AUC values in the supplied text. IOI circuit edges tend to have attribution scores farther from zero. Nevertheless, Docstring attribution and activation-patching scores correlate weakly: R² = 0.27. A best-fit slope of 0.531 indicates substantial overestimation by attribution patching. Interpolation examples show nonlinear responses underlying this error. Applying ACDC to EAP-pruned Docstring graphs improves recovery over EAP alone.

**Limitations / open questions**

Unperturbed output-distribution KL divergence has zero gradient, preventing its direct use for this first-order scoring procedure. Evaluation depends on imperfect human-discovered circuits and cannot directly assess unfamiliar behaviors or meaningful human understanding. Evidence covers three narrow tasks, with hybrid refinement and approximation diagnostics limited to Docstring. Several appendix references and figure details are absent from the supplied text, limiting assessment of experimental settings and numerical comparisons.

title: Learning Sparse Neural Networks through L_0 Regularization
The internal state of an LLM knows when it's lying
Two views on the cognitive brain
Do the rewards justify the means? Measuring trade-offs between rewards and ethical behavior in the MACHIAVELLI benchmark
The Hydra Effect: Emergent Self-repair in Language Model Computations
abstract: We investigate the internal structure of language model computations using causal analysis and demonstrate two motifs: (1) a form of adaptive computation where ablations of one attention layer of a language model cause another layer to compensate (which we term the Hydra effect) and (2) a counterbalancing function of late MLP layers that act to downregulate the maximum-likelihood token. Our ablation studies demonstrate that language model layers are typically relatively loosely coupled (ablations to one layer only affect a small number of downstream layers). Surprisingly, these effects occur even in language models trained without any form of dropout. We analyse these effects in the context of factual recall and consider their implications for circuit-level attribution in language models.
summary:
**Central idea**
Ablating a transformer component can trigger compensatory computation, making its total ablation effect smaller than its contribution in the intact model. The paper identifies two responses: downstream attention layers increase their contribution to the original maximum-likelihood token, termed the Hydra effect, and late MLPs reduce their usual suppression of that token. Direct, indirect, and total causal effects distinguish intact-model contributions from intervention-induced responses.

**Experiments**
The authors study a 32-layer, approximately 7B-parameter Chinchilla-family model trained without dropout, stochastic depth, or layer dropout. They analyze every attention and MLP layer at the final token position across the paper's 1,209 Counterfact contexts. Resample ablations replace a layer output with activations from 15 alternative dataset prompts. Measurements track the vocabulary-centered logit of the intact model's maximum-likelihood next token, rather than an independently scored factual answer. Layer-output contributions are projected through the final unembedding with the RMSNorm denominator fixed for additive attribution. Comparing these contributions before and after ablation localizes compensation. Separate analytical toy constructions demonstrate how erasure or self-repair can eliminate a knockout's total effect despite a nonzero direct effect.

**Key results**
Unembedding-based and ablation-based importance measures disagree across most layers. Direct contributions and summed downstream compensation correlate most strongly at intermediate-to-late layers; the reported regression peaks at layer 23 with 92% variance explained. This is a combined compensatory response, with reduced MLP suppression accounting for almost all of the response at that layer. Attention compensation is relatively more prominent earlier. The conclusion reports approximately 70% restoration of the token-logit reduction at middle layers where compensation is strongest. Regression slopes below one after layer 13 indicate incomplete average restoration. Qualitative examples concentrate attention responses in a few downstream layers. Repair in a model trained without dropout establishes that dropout is unnecessary for its existence.

**Limitations / open questions**
Evidence concerns one model, factual prompts, whole-layer interventions, and one selected token-logit projection. It does not isolate individual backup heads or establish restoration of missing internal features. Donor patches are noisy, and negligible donor contribution is an approximation. Causes of repair, broader prevalence, sequence-length dependence, and possible recalibration by erasure MLPs remain open. Training-time 'natural dropout' is conjectural. The supplied direct-effect discussion also contains a sign inconsistency: replacement-minus-original knockout effects have the opposite sign to positive original unembedding contributions.

title: Extracting Latent Steering Vectors from Pretrained Language Models
abstract: Prior work on controllable text generation has focused on learning how to control language models through trainable decoding, smart-prompt design, or fine-tuning based on a desired objective. We hypothesize that the information needed to steer the model to generate a target sentence is already encoded within the model. Accordingly, we explore a different approach altogether: extracting latent vectors directly from pretrained language model decoders without fine-tuning. Experiments show that there exist steering vectors, which, when added to the hidden states of the language model, generate a target sentence nearly perfectly (> 99 BLEU) for English sentences from a variety of domains. We show that vector arithmetic can be used for unsupervised sentiment transfer on the Yelp sentiment benchmark, with performance comparable to models tailored to this task. We find that distances between steering vectors reflect sentence similarity when evaluated on a textual similarity benchmark (STS-B), outperforming pooled hidden states of models. Finally, we present an analysis of the intrinsic properties of the steering vectors. Taken together, our results suggest that frozen LMs can be effectively controlled through their latent steering space.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper optimizes a separate fixed-length activation vector for each target sentence while freezing GPT-2-117M. Target-sentence cross-entropy supplies gradients to the vector; generation subsequently starts from a beginning-of-sentence token and uses greedy decoding. The resulting control space supports experiments with style offsets, sentence similarity, and interpolation.

**Experiments**

Recovery experiments use 256 sentences: 64 each from Cornell Movie Dialogs, Gutenberg, Gigaword, and WikiText-103, sampled across eight word-level length bins spanning 5–128. Tests vary injection location, timestep, vector dimension, and initialization. Additional experiments evaluate Yelp sentiment transfer, 19 of 21 StylePTB tasks, STS-B similarity, interpolation, Gaussian sampling, shuffled and random-token targets, and continuous embedding prefixes. Yelp offsets use 100 sentiment-labeled validation sentences per class; StylePTB offsets use 100 training sentences per class. Thus, the transfer procedure described as “unsupervised” still requires class labels for offset construction.

**Key results**

Several intermediate-layer, every-timestep configurations achieve 100 smoothed BLEU-4. First-timestep injection achieves 99.80 after layer-6 attention and 99.25 after layer-7 feedforward, versus 33.99 for embedding injection and 6.72 at the LM head with every-timestep injection. For 63 of 64 book sentences, all eight initialization seeds recover the target perfectly. Reducing vector dimension from 768 to 384 lowers recovery from 100 to 83.29 BLEU-4. Selected layer-7 vectors achieve approximately 52.1 Spearman correlation ×100 on STS-B, exceeding mean-pooled BERT's 47.29 and GPT-2's 25.92, while trailing NLI-trained encoders and specialized lexical baselines. The authors report a Yelp accuracy–self-BLEU tradeoff competitive with selected autoencoder baselines. StylePTB results vary considerably across tasks; adjective emphasis reaches 0.774 BLEU-1 versus an imported GPT-2-finetuning baseline of 0.263. Independent Gaussian sampling produces complete sentences in only 5 of 24 generations.

**Limitations / open questions**

Evidence concerns one small pretrained model and requires optimization for each sentence. BLEU is not generally an exact-match rate or semantic-preservation guarantee. Larger sentiment offsets can cause repetition and content drift. STS-B configurations are selected using a test-set layer sweep. Better recovery of natural than shuffled or gibberish sequences suggests sensitivity to pretrained regularities, without establishing naturally occurring sentence representations. Interpolation evidence is qualitative. The supplied rendering lacks numerical plot values for several figure-based comparisons, limiting quantitative assessment of those results.

title: Plug and play language models: A simple approach to controlled text generation.
PREADD: prefix-adaptive decoding for controlled text generation
Understanding and Controlling a Maze-Solving Policy Network
abstract: To understand the goals and goal representations of AI systems, we carefully study a pretrained reinforcement learning policy that solves mazes by navigating to a range of target squares. We find this network pursues multiple context-dependent goals, and we further identify circuits within the network that correspond to one of these goals. In particular, we identified eleven channels that track the location of the goal. By modifying these channels, either with hand-designed interventions or by combining forward passes, we can partially control the policy. We show that this network contains redundant, distributed, and retargetable goal representations, shedding light on the nature of goal-direction in trained policy networks.
summary:
**Central idea**
The paper investigates internal target representations and activation-based control in a pretrained reinforcement-learning maze policy. The principal model is a 3.5M-parameter, 15-convolutional-layer IMPALA-style network previously trained with PPO on 100,000 Procgen levels for 200M timesteps. Training cheese appeared within the top-right 5×5 region; evaluation cheese could appear anywhere. Its context-dependent navigation toward cheese or the historical reward region motivates an interpretation involving competing goals.

**Experiments**
Behavioral analysis retained 5,239 rollouts after excluding mazes without a decision square separating cheese-directed and corner-directed paths, and mazes with cheese inside the top-right 5×5 region. Three distance features predicted cheese attainment using L1-regularized logistic regression over ten splits with 20% validation. Researchers visually selected 11 cheese-tracking channels among 128 intermediate spatial channels, then resampled their activations between mazes with matched or different cheese locations. Further experiments edited spatial activations and added differences between contrasting forward passes. Retargetability analysis used the first 100 maze seeds and normalized path probability: the geometric mean of action probabilities along the unique shortest path.

**Key results**
Behavioral prediction reached 82.4% accuracy versus a 71.4% always-reaches-cheese baseline. Across 200 mazes, channel resampling changed the most probable decision-square action in 40% of different-location cases versus 11% of same-location cases. Appendix controls over 30 seeds showed more modest aggregate action-probability changes. On 13×13 mazes, mean normalized path probability over legal target squares was 0.647 for channel-55 editing and 0.695 for editing all 11 channels. Actual cheese relocation produced stronger retargeting than the tested edits. Across 100 mazes, cheese-vector subtraction reduced cheese-directed action probabilities, whereas addition had little effect. Adding the designated top-right vector increased corner-directed probabilities. Selected joint interventions combined these effects without retraining.

**Limitations / open questions**
Mechanistic interventions mainly concern one policy and one activation site. Channel selection and intervention strengths involved manual inspection or tuning. Same-location resampling sometimes changes behavior; the channels are not established as exclusively encoding cheese location or as a complete goal mechanism. Retargeting weakens away from the historical corner path, and normalized path probability is not episode success rate. Control may change perceived cheese information rather than motivation. Section 3.2 and Appendix C.3 give conflicting subtraction orders for the top-right vector. Plot images are unavailable in the supplied rendering, limiting independent inspection of distributions and visual examples. Transfer to language models remains untested.

title: RealToxicityPrompts: Evaluating Neural Toxic Degeneration in Language Models
abstract: Pretrained neural language models (LMs) are prone to generating racist, sexist, or otherwise toxic language which hinders their safe deployment. We investigate the extent to which pretrained LMs can be prompted to generate toxic language, and the effectiveness of controllable text generation algorithms at preventing such toxic degeneration. We create and release RealToxicityPrompts, a dataset of 100K naturally occurring, sentence-level prompts derived from a large corpus of English web text, paired with toxicity scores from a widely-used toxicity classifier. Using RealToxicityPrompts, we find that pretrained LMs can degenerate into toxic text even from seemingly innocuous prompts. We empirically assess several controllable generation methods, and find that while data- or compute-intensive methods (e.g., adaptive pretraining on non-toxic data) are more effective at steering away from toxicity than simpler solutions (e.g., banning "bad" words), no current method is failsafe against neural toxic degeneration. To pinpoint the potential cause of such persistent toxic degeneration, we analyze two web text corpora used to pretrain several LMs (including GPT-2; Radford et. al, 2019), and find a significant amount of offensive, factually unreliable, and otherwise toxic content. Our work provides a test bed for evaluating toxic generations by LMs and stresses the need for better data selection processes for pretraining.

title: Eliciting latent knowledge: How to tell if your eyes deceive you
Truthful AI: Developing and governing AI that does not lie
Alignment of Language Agents
Calibrate Before Use: Improving Few-Shot Performance of Language Models
abstract: GPT-3 can perform numerous tasks when provided a natural language prompt that contains a few training examples. We show that this type of few-shot learning can be unstable: the choice of prompt format, training examples, and even the order of the training examples can cause accuracy to vary from near chance to near state-of-the-art. We demonstrate that this instability arises from the bias of language models towards predicting certain answers, e.g., those that are placed near the end of the prompt or are common in the pre-training data. To mitigate this, we first estimate the model's bias towards each answer by asking for its prediction when given the training prompt and a content-free test input such as "N/A". We then fit calibration parameters that cause the prediction for this input to be uniform across answers. On a diverse set of tasks, this contextual calibration procedure substantially improves GPT-3 and GPT-2's average accuracy (up to 30.0% absolute) and reduces variance across different choices of the prompt.

HarmBench: A Standardized Evaluation Framework for Automated Red Teaming and Robust Refusal
abstract: Automated red teaming holds substantial promise for uncovering and mitigating the risks associated with the malicious use of large language models (LLMs), yet the field lacks a standardized evaluation framework to rigorously assess new methods. To address this issue, we introduce HarmBench, a standardized evaluation framework for automated red teaming. We identify several desirable properties previously unaccounted for in red teaming evaluations and systematically design HarmBench to meet these criteria. Using HarmBench, we conduct a large-scale comparison of 18 red teaming methods and 33 target LLMs and defenses, yielding novel insights. We also introduce a highly efficient adversarial training method that greatly enhances LLM robustness across a wide range of attacks, demonstrating how HarmBench enables codevelopment of attacks and defenses. We open source HarmBench at https://github.com/centerforaisafety/HarmBench.
summary:
**Central idea**
HarmBench is a standardized benchmark for automated red teaming and robust refusal. The authors argue that prior jailbreak evaluations cannot be compared with one another, for three reasons: they use at least 9 distinct setups, they cover few behaviors (mostly fewer than 100), and their metrics are fragile. One example of fragility is that refusal-substring ASR can shift by up to 30% depending on the number of generated tokens.

HarmBench has three design goals: breadth, comparability and robust metrics. It contains 510 harmful behaviors, split as 200 standard, 100 copyright, 100 contextual and 110 multimodal. These are spread over 7 semantic categories, with a 100 validation / 410 test split. Generation is fixed at 512 tokens with greedy decoding.

Attack success rate (ASR) is judged by a Llama 2 13B Chat classifier. It was distilled from GPT-4 judgments over 15 rounds and is held out from optimization. A separate Mistral-7B validation classifier is provided for use during attack optimization. Copyright behaviors are scored with a MinHash hashing classifier instead.

**Experiments**
- **Large-scale comparison.** 18 red-teaming methods were run against 33 LLMs and defenses (24 open-source, 9 closed-source, plus multimodal models). Attacks included GCG and its variants, PEZ, GBDA, UAT, AutoPrompt, Zero-/Few-Shot, PAIR, TAP, AutoDAN, PAP, human jailbreaks and direct requests. Multimodal attacks were PGD, patch and render-text.
- **Classifier agreement.** Judges were compared against roughly 600 human-labeled completions.
- **Robustness prequalification.** Three nonstandard completion sets were used: refuse-then-comply, benign text, and completions for unrelated harmful behaviors.
- **Searchability check.** 20 behaviors were sampled per dataset and searched on Google.
- **R2D2 adversarial training.** Mistral 7B base was trained with a persistent pool of GCG test cases, an away loss, a toward-refusal loss and an SFT loss on UltraChat (500 steps, 16 h on 8×A100).

**Key results**
- Human agreement averaged 93.2% for the HarmBench classifier, versus 88.4% for the GPT-4 PAIR judge, 69.9% for AdvBench substring matching and 66.9% for Llama Guard. The HarmBench classifier also reached 95.7% on the prequalification sets.
- No attack or defense was uniformly effective.
- Within six model families spanning 7–70B parameters, robustness did not correlate with model size, but it varied strongly between families. The exception was copyright behaviors.
- Contextual behaviors had higher ASR than standard ones.
- Zephyr 7B + R2D2 cut GCG ASR to 5.9%, compared with about 31% for Llama 2 7B/13B Chat. Its average ASR was 19.1%, the third lowest overall, against 62.7% for Zephyr. It scored 6.0 on MT-Bench, compared with 6.5 for Mistral Instruct.
- R2D2's gains were weaker against PAIR, TAP and Stochastic Few-Shot, attacks that differ from GCG.

**Limitations / open questions**
- The classifier is distilled from GPT-4, and the success criterion is "attempted the behavior", so ASR does not measure how capable the harmful output is.
- Closed models with API filters cannot be assessed at the model level.
- Several attacks were reimplemented, or used Mixtral as the attacker LLM.
- R2D2 was tested on one model, against one train-time adversary.
- The table rendering in the provided text was partly garbled; numbers reported here come from the readable portions.

title: JailbreakBench: An Open Robustness Benchmark for Jailbreaking Large Language Models
abstract: Jailbreak attacks cause large language models (LLMs) to generate harmful, unethical, or otherwise objectionable content. Evaluating these attacks presents a number of challenges, which the current collection of benchmarks and evaluation techniques do not adequately address. First, there is no clear standard of practice regarding jailbreaking evaluation. Second, existing works compute costs and success rates in incomparable ways. And third, numerous works are not reproducible, as they withhold adversarial prompts, involve closed-source code, or rely on evolving proprietary APIs. To address these challenges, we introduce JailbreakBench, an open-sourced benchmark with the following components: (1) an evolving repository of state-of-the-art adversarial prompts, which we refer to as jailbreak artifacts; (2) a jailbreaking dataset comprising 100 behaviors -- both original and sourced from prior work (Zou et al., 2023; Mazeika et al., 2023, 2024) -- which align with OpenAI's usage policies; (3) a standardized evaluation framework at https://github.com/JailbreakBench/jailbreakbench that includes a clearly defined threat model, system prompts, chat templates, and scoring functions; and (4) a leaderboard at https://jailbreakbench.github.io/ that tracks the performance of attacks and defenses for various LLMs. We have carefully considered the potential ethical implications of releasing this benchmark, and believe that it will be a net positive for the community.
summary:
**Central idea**
JailbreakBench is an open benchmark that standardizes how LLM jailbreak attacks and test-time defenses are evaluated. The authors argue that prior work used incomparable judges and cost metrics, and often withheld prompts or depended on changing proprietary APIs. The benchmark has five parts:
- **JBB-Behaviors**: 100 harmful behaviors in 10 OpenAI-usage-policy categories, 10 per category. 55% are original, 18% come from AdvBench and 27% from TDC/HarmBench. Each harmful behavior has a topic-matched benign counterpart for checking refusal rates.
- **Artifact repository**: jailbreak prompts, responses and judge labels.
- **Fixed evaluation settings**: system prompts, chat templates, greedy decoding and 150-token generations.
- **Defense wrappers**.
- **Leaderboard**: built on RobustBench code.

**Experiments**
- *Judge selection.* The authors built a 300-example dataset:
  - 200 jailbreak prompt/response pairs on AdvBench behaviors (100 PAIR, 50 GCG and 50 prompt+random-search attacks).
  - 100 benign XSTest examples.
  - Three experts labelled each item, with about 95% inter-annotator agreement; the majority vote is the ground truth.
  - Six judges were compared on agreement, FPR and FNR: rule-based string matching, GPT-4, the HarmBench Llama-2-13B classifier, Llama Guard, Llama Guard 2 and Llama-3-70B with a custom prompt.
- *Attacks.* GCG, PAIR, JailbreakChat AIM and Prompt+RS were run against Vicuna-13B-v1.5, Llama-2-7B-chat, GPT-3.5-Turbo-1106 and GPT-4-0125-Preview.
- *Defenses.* SmoothLLM, perplexity filter, Erase-and-Check, synonym substitution and remove-non-dictionary were tested only with transfer (non-adaptive) attacks.
- *Refusal.* Refusal rates on the 100 benign behaviors were judged by Llama-3-8B.

**Key results**
- *Judges.*
  - Llama-3-70B: 90.7% agreement, 11.6% FPR, 5.5% FNR.
  - GPT-4: 90.3% agreement.
  - Llama Guard 2: 87.7% agreement.
  - HarmBench classifier: 78.3% agreement, 26.8% FPR, driven largely by the XSTest benign items.
  - Llama Guard: 72.0% agreement, 60.9% FNR.
  - Rule-based: 56.0% agreement, 64.2% FPR.
  - Llama-3-70B was adopted because its weights are open.
- *Attacks (undefended ASR).*
  - Prompt+RS reached 89/90/93/78% on Vicuna/Llama-2/GPT-3.5/GPT-4.
  - PAIR reached 69/0/71/34%.
  - GCG reached 80/3/47/4%; the GPT results are transfers of suffixes found on Vicuna.
  - AIM reached 90% on Vicuna and 0% elsewhere, plausibly because the template was patched.
- *Defenses.*
  - The perplexity filter is effective mainly against GCG. Prompt+RS still scores 61–88%, and AIM still scores 90% on Vicuna.
  - Erase-and-Check was strongest overall, but Prompt+RS still reached 8–25%.
  - Synonym substitution kept every attack at or below 24%.
- *Refusal and drift.*
  - On benign behaviors, Vicuna refuses 9% and Llama-2 refuses more than 60%. The defenses barely changed these rates.
  - GCG transfer ASR on GPT models later fell to about 5%.

**Limitations / open questions**
- Defenses were evaluated only with transfer attacks, which give a lower bound on worst-case ASR.
- Attackers may not modify system prompts or prefill responses.
- The benchmark is text-only.
- The refusal judge was not validated.
- The benchmark has 100 behaviors and no error bars.
- Closed-model results drift over time.

Case Studies in Reverse-Engineering Sparse Autoencoder Features by Using MLP Linearization
summary:
**Central idea**

The post develops an exploratory method for tracing how MLP sparse-autoencoder features are computed. Differentiating a feature’s pre-ReLU score with respect to the MLP input produces a local residual-stream readout. Projecting that readout through token embeddings, attention OV matrices, and earlier SAE decoders generates hypotheses about contributing tokens, heads, and features. These projections remain conditioned on the input used for differentiation; they do not establish a globally linear mechanism.

**Experiments**

Five informally selected features are studied: four in GELU-1L and one in GELU-2L. Both models have residual width 512, MLP width 1,024, eight heads per layer, and 48,262 vocabulary tokens. The 16,384-feature SAEs encode GELU-1L post-activation MLP states or GELU-2L MLP outputs. Example collection uses 1,638,400 c4-code-20k tokens in 128-token prompts. Tests include constructed prompts, path patching, attention resampling, activation injections, gradient cosine comparisons, and component zero ablations on the top 200 and approximately activation-uniform 200 examples per feature.

**Key results**

De-embedding identifies an unexpected raw-score response to the Hindi token ह in a feature initially associated with `('`. Selected attribution analyses suggest combinations of current-token information with attention to preceding tokens or semantic context, including an “it is” feature and a theology/politics-associated “is” feature. However, a contraction feature’s small attributed attention contribution conflicts with an attention-resampling activation difference of 1.1226.

For the GELU-2L dictionary-value feature, gradients from the higher-scoring half of 48 examples have mean within-group cosine 0.7037, versus 0.3089 for the lower half and 0.1097 across halves. Its projection onto the earlier SAE dictionary gives 512 of 16,384 coefficients more than two standard deviations above the mean. Component attribution generally agrees better with zero ablation on stronger activating examples, with substantial feature-specific exceptions.

**Limitations / open questions**

The models are shallow and feature selection is exploratory. Plot images are unavailable in the supplied rendering, preventing inspection of numerical correlations and scatter distributions beyond the prose. Some highly ranked token predictions fail under prompt checks or reverse as patch size increases. Freezing LayerNorm improves the tested contraction-feature gradient consistency, but worsens some ablation comparisons and makes attribution fail for the selected “it is” feature. Scaling, compounded approximation error, semantic completeness, and reliable prediction of failure cases remain unresolved.

title: Attention SAEs Scale to GPT-2 Small
summary:
**Central idea**

Sparse autoencoders applied to attention outputs extend feature-based interpretation from a two-layer transformer to all 12 layers of GPT-2 Small. This interim report releases the SAEs and presents preliminary evidence of sparse codes, substantial loss recovery, and recognizable feature families, motivating future circuit analysis.

**Experiments**

The authors report average active-feature counts, loss recovered relative to zero ablation, dead-feature percentages, and shallow interpretability judgments for each layer. They inspect the first 30 features per layer, reporting interpretability among inspected non-dead features. Investigations use maximally activating examples, direct feature attribution to source positions, decoder-weight attribution to heads, and weight-based logit analysis. Training changes since the predecessor report include Anthropic-style resampling and periodic learning-rate warmup. The supplied text does not specify the training corpus, token budget, or detailed evaluation sampling protocol.

A targeted induction screen selects layer-6 features with at least 50% weight-based attribution to induction head L6H9. Behavioral qualification requires at least a 60% induction pass rate on 200 examples. A negative control samples features with less than 20% attribution to that head.

**Key results**

Across layers, average active-feature counts range from 3 to 21, and zero-ablation-relative loss recovery ranges from 76% to 99%. Dead-feature rates range from 5% to 84%. Among inspected live features, interpretability judgments range from 64% to 100%. Of 158 head-attributed induction candidates, 117 pass the behavioral heuristic. None of the sampled negative-control features passes; the control sample count is unspecified.

The authors report induction, local-context, and high-level-context families previously encountered in the two-layer model. Selected examples also associate duplicate-token, successor, name-moving, and suppression features with previously characterized GPT-2 heads. Layer-9 feature 15 is interpreted as predicting “half” in expressions such as “<number> and a half,” suggesting an attention-associated n-gram behavior.

**Limitations / open questions**

Interpretations are shallow and may miss contextual subtleties. Prior knowledge likely biases the showcased families, and apparent novelty relative to the two-layer model reflects limited inspection. Source attribution and vocabulary projections do not establish complete causal mechanisms. The supplied rendering does not expose the illustrative plots or interactive dashboards, limiting independent inspection of those examples. Feature distribution across heads, unrecognized behaviors, and usefulness for detailed circuit reconstruction remain open.
