Circuit Component Reuse Across Tasks in Transformer Language Models
abstract: Recent work in mechanistic interpretability has shown that behaviors in language models can be successfully reverse-engineered through circuit analysis. A common criticism, however, is that each circuit is task-specific, and thus such analysis cannot contribute to understanding the models at a higher level. In this work, we present evidence that insights (both low-level findings about specific heads and higher-level findings about general algorithms) can indeed generalize across tasks. Specifically, we study the circuit discovered in Wang et al. (2022) for the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) task and 1.) show that it reproduces on a larger GPT2 model, and 2.) that it is mostly reused to solve a seemingly different task: Colored Objects (Ippolito & Callison-Burch, 2023). We provide evidence that the process underlying both tasks is functionally very similar, and contains about a 78% overlap in in-circuit attention heads. We further present a proof-of-concept intervention experiment, in which we adjust four attention heads in middle layers in order to 'repair' the Colored Objects circuit and make it behave like the IOI circuit. In doing so, we boost accuracy from 49.6% to 93.7% on the Colored Objects task and explain most sources of error. The intervention affects downstream attention heads in specific ways predicted by their interactions in the IOI circuit, indicating that this subcircuit behavior is invariant to the different task inputs. Overall, our results provide evidence that it may yet be possible to explain large language models' behavior in terms of a relatively small number of interpretable task-general algorithmic building blocks and computational components.
summary:
**Central idea**
The paper tests whether components and interactions discovered through circuit analysis transfer across tasks. It reproduces GPT2-Small's IOI functional organization in GPT2-Medium, then compares IOI with contextual color retrieval. Both recruit duplicate/induction heads and copying heads, but use different intermediate signals to select an answer.

**Experiments**
The main analyses use 1,000 IOI examples and 1,000 modified Colored Objects examples. Colored Objects supplies one demonstration followed by three uniquely colored objects drawn from 17 single-token object types and eight colors; patching counterparts change the queried object. Path patching measures answer-logit differences through selected attention-head paths while allowing MLP recomputation. Attention patterns, token-direction projections, and repeated-token head diagnostics inform functional labels. Interventions block content-gatherer attention or force three inhibition heads and one negative mover to divide attention equally between known incorrect colors. Additional analyses use 200 Greater Than examples, 200 capital-recall country pairs drawn from 47 eligible countries, and preliminary GPT2-Large/XL head rankings.

**Key results**
GPT2-Medium exhibits the duplicate-detection, inhibition, and copying organization previously identified for IOI. Selecting the top 2% of heads per patching stage yields the reported 25/32 overlap, approximately 78%, between IOI and Colored Objects. Blocking selected content gatherers' question access reduces color accuracy to 35%, near three-option chance, versus 49.9% ± 1.0 across three random-head control seeds. Ground-truth-informed attention repair raises full-dataset accuracy from 49.6% to 93.7%, introducing no new errors; negative-mover-only and inhibition-only interventions reach 78.1% and 81.5%. Downstream attention and attribution change as the IOI account predicts; Figure 5's downstream comparisons use the 496 originally correct examples. Capital recall shares four of seven principal attention heads but four of sixteen total selected components with the contextual-selection tasks. Preliminary top-ten-head overlap is 5/10 in GPT2-Large and 0/10 in GPT2-XL, despite selected heads retaining mover functionality across tasks.

**Limitations / open questions**
Repair requires knowing the wrong answers and is not an autonomous correction method. Circuit overlap depends on heuristic membership thresholds; structural agreement and local interventions do not establish complete circuit faithfulness or broad task generality. Colored Objects was selected because its solution strategy suggested IOI similarity. Larger-model analyses are preliminary, and the proposed timing bottleneck preventing natural inhibition remains speculative. The source inconsistently labels one inhibition head 13.13 versus 13.14 and once reports baseline accuracy as 49.7%. Some appendix introductions end mid-sentence, but substantive sections continue through Appendix K. Plot images are unavailable in the supplied rendering; numerical results here follow explicit text.

title: Interpretability Illusions in the Generalization of Simplified Models
abstract: A common method to study deep learning systems is to use simplified model representations--for example, using singular value decomposition to visualize the model's hidden states in a lower dimensional space. This approach assumes that the results of these simplifications are faithful to the original model. Here, we illustrate an important caveat to this assumption: even if the simplified representations can accurately approximate the full model on the training set, they may fail to accurately capture the model's behavior out of distribution. We illustrate this by training Transformer models on controlled datasets with systematic generalization splits, including the Dyck balanced-parenthesis languages and a code completion task. We simplify these models using tools like dimensionality reduction and clustering, and then explicitly test how these simplified proxies match the behavior of the original model. We find consistent generalization gaps: cases in which the simplified proxies are more faithful to the original model on the in-distribution evaluations and less faithful on various tests of systematic generalization. This includes cases where the original model generalizes systematically but the simplified proxies fail, and cases where the simplified proxies generalize better. Together, our results raise questions about the extent to which mechanistic interpretations derived using tools like SVD can reliably predict what a model will do in novel situations.
summary:
**Central idea**
Simplified attention models can closely match a Transformer on familiar inputs yet misrepresent its behavior under systematic distribution shifts. The paper makes simplifications executable: project keys and queries onto leading SVD directions, replace them with separately fitted k-means centroids, or replace soft attention with one-hot attention. Fidelity is assessed through attention Jensen–Shannon divergence and final prediction agreement.

**Experiments**
Dyck experiments use two-layer Transformers with one head per layer and hidden width 32, trained on 200,000 sentences with 20 bracket types and maximum depth 10. Evaluation sets contain 20,000 sentences each, testing new bracket assignments, unseen structures partitioned by length, and deeper nesting. Accuracy scores closing brackets whose matching opener is at least ten positions away. SVD and clustering use embeddings from 1,000 training sequences. CodeSearchNet experiments train four-layer, four-head character models with width 256 and head dimension 64 on 202,395 Java functions of at most 512 characters and nesting depth at most three. Evaluation includes deeper Java and JavaScript, Go, and PHP. Both principal studies use three initializations. Additional SCAN experiments test augmented Add jump and length generalization.

**Key results**
Four-dimensional Dyck proxies retain nearly 100% prediction agreement on seen structures while diverging on unseen structures that the original model solves almost perfectly. Original depth-generalization accuracy is approximately 75%; rank-eight proxies miss some successful extrapolation at depths 11–12. One-hot attention instead slightly improves depth generalization, showing that simplification can overestimate original performance. In code completion, agreement conditional on original-model correctness is lower on unseen languages. Initialization-level paired tests against aggregated OOD scores report p ≤ 0.005 at each tested simplification level. Gaps are larger for repeated words and closing brackets. Simplifying one head with an induction-like pattern produces repeated-word agreement of about 75% on Java and as low as 61% on unseen languages. Aggregate code results show no discernible Java depth gap. SCAN shows no discernible Add jump gap but a small consistent length gap.

**Limitations / open questions**
Results concern small task-trained models and individual-head interventions. Mechanistic explanations remain partly qualitative; weakly represented features and simplification-data coverage are proposed causes, not isolated mechanisms. Dyck's nominal in-distribution seen-structure baseline contains unusually short sequences; a separately sampled IID split mostly contains unseen structures and behaves like the long unseen-structure split. SCAN architectures were selected using generalization accuracy. The complete supplied rendering lacks plot images and contains inconsistent Dyck parameter ordering and depth-boundary wording; numerical results above come from prose.

title: Automatic Circuit Discover Code (ACDC)
BatchTopK: A Simple Improvement for TopK-SAEs
summary:
**Central idea**

BatchTopK replaces per-token TopK selection in sparse autoencoders with selection across a flattened training batch: retain the largest K × batch_size activations, then reshape. This permits different feature counts for different tokens while controlling the batch selection budget. For inference, the authors replace batch-dependent selection with one global activation threshold, estimated by averaging the minimum positive retained activation across batches.

**Experiments**

The authors compare TopK and BatchTopK SAEs on GPT-2 Small’s layer-8 resid_pre activations. The single reported sweep uses expansion factors 4, 8, 16, and 32; target active-feature counts 16, 32, and 64; batch size 4,096; and one billion training tokens. Adam uses learning rate 3e-4 and betas 0.9 and 0.99. Inputs are normalized before encoding and reconstruction-loss calculation. Both methods use the same auxiliary loss: features inactive for five batches reconstruct the residual using their top 512 activations per sample, weighted by 1/32. The training corpus is unspecified. Evaluations compare normalized reconstruction MSE and downstream cross-entropy degradation, inspect active-feature-count distributions, and swap activation rules after training.

**Key results**

BatchTopK reportedly achieves lower normalized MSE and less downstream loss degradation than TopK across dictionary sizes at target L0 = 32, and across tested K values at dictionary size 12,288. Estimated-threshold inference slightly improves performance further. Active-feature counts vary across tokens; a low-count peak has frequency close to 1/128, which the authors tentatively associate with BOS tokens in 128-token sequences. Applying BatchTopK selection to TopK-trained weights, or the reverse, performs poorly, suggesting that training with the selection rule matters.

**Limitations / open questions**

Evidence comes from one sweep at one activation site in one model. The supplied rendering includes figure descriptions but no readable plotted values; numerical effect sizes and uncertainty estimates cannot be recovered. Adaptive sparsity is a proposed explanation rather than an isolated causal finding, and the BOS interpretation is unverified. Generalization across models, larger dictionaries, hyperparameters, and batch sizes remains open. Human interpretability and semantic feature recovery are not evaluated. Comparisons with Gated and JumpReLU SAEs, running-quantile training thresholds, and a BatchTopK-specific auxiliary loss are proposed future work.

title: Automatically Interpreting Millions of Features in Large Language Models
abstract: While the activations of neurons in deep neural networks usually do not have a simple human-understandable interpretation, sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can be used to transform these activations into a higher-dimensional latent space which may be more easily interpretable. However, these SAEs can have millions of distinct latent features, making it infeasible for humans to manually interpret each one. In this work, we build an open-source automated pipeline to generate and evaluate natural language explanations for SAE features using LLMs. We test our framework on SAEs of varying sizes, activation functions, and losses, trained on two different open-weight LLMs. We introduce five new techniques to score the quality of explanations that are cheaper to run than the previous state of the art. One of these techniques, intervention scoring, evaluates the interpretability of the effects of intervening on a feature, which we find explains features that are not recalled by existing methods. We propose guidelines for generating better explanations that remain valid for a broader set of activating contexts, and discuss pitfalls with existing scoring techniques. We use our explanations to measure the semantic similarity of independently trained SAEs, and find that SAEs trained on nearby layers of the residual stream are highly similar. Our large-scale analysis confirms that SAE latents are indeed much more interpretable than neurons, even when neurons are sparsified using top-$k$ postprocessing. Our code is available at https://github.com/EleutherAI/sae-auto-interp, and our explanations are available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/EleutherAI/auto_interp_explanations.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper introduces delphi, an automated pipeline for generating and evaluating natural-language interpretations of SAE latents. Four scores assess activation-context predictions: sequence detection, token-level fuzzing, explanation-conditioned surprisal, and embedding retrieval. A fifth assesses descriptions of intervention effects on generated text, comparing interventions at controlled output KL.

**Experiments**

The pipeline collects activations on 10 million RedPajama-v2 tokens, primarily in 256-token sequences. The default explainer, Llama 3.1 70B Instruct, receives forty 32-token activating examples. Design choices are evaluated on a 500-plus-feature testbed using 100 activating examples, ten per activation decile, and 100 non-activating examples per feature. Score correlations use 800 interpretations from Gemma 2 9B's 131k residual-stream SAEs across four layers. Human evaluation covers 700 contexts and 81 interpretations. Intervention experiments on Gemma 2 9B use ten explanation prompts and thirty scoring prompts per feature, sampled from activating contexts, and generations of up to eight tokens. Features activating on fewer than 200 collection tokens are excluded.

**Key results**

Under the reported 100-context cost calculation, fuzzing and detection cost at least five times less than all-at-once simulation. Their Spearman correlations with human ratings are 0.69 and 0.59, versus 0.60 for simulation. Quantile sampling improves median fuzzing/detection scores to 0.77/0.74, compared with 0.73/0.72 for top-example sampling; top-example sampling instead has the highest median embedding score. Gemma 131k latents score 0.76/0.74 on fuzzing/detection, versus 0.62/0.59 for top-32 neurons. Llama 3.1 8B results also favor SAE latents over sparsified neurons. Intervention descriptions outperform shuffled-description and random-SAE controls. At Gemma layer 32, intervention scores have a slight negative association with fuzzing scores, suggesting that some poorly explained activation patterns have describable output effects.

**Limitations / open questions**

These metrics measure particular predictive or descriptive abilities, rather than establishing monosemanticity or natural causal mediation. Scorer ability, random-negative selection, short explanation windows, and activation-collection coverage limit evaluation. Intervention findings concern selected activating contexts and tested strengths, with layer-dependent relationships and no numerical effect sizes supplied in the prose. The supplied body is v3, dated August 2025, whereas metadata gives the original publication date and an abstract containing semantic-similarity findings absent from this body. Appendix E's 65k Llama SAE width conflicts with the 262k widths reported elsewhere.

title: Showing SAE Latents Are Not Atomic Using Meta-SAEs
summary:
**Central idea**

An SAE latent can have a coherent interpretation while combining multiple properties. The authors introduce meta-SAEs, trained on SAE decoder directions rather than model activations, to investigate this distinction between monosemanticity and atomicity. Selected decompositions contain recognizable semantic and lexical components, such as science, prominent people, Germany, and capital-E words within an Einstein-related direction. Interpreting these geometric components as computational constituents remains an assumption.

**Experiments**

The main experiment uses 49,152 decoder directions from an SAE trained on GPT-2 Small’s residual stream before layer 8. A 2,304-latent BatchTopK meta-SAE with k=4 trains for 2,000 batches of 16,384 samples. Analyses include qualitative interpretations, decoder cosine similarities, reconstruction after replacing meta-decoder directions with nearby smaller-SAE directions, and comparisons of induced latent-relationship graphs. A separate meta-SAE trains jointly on eight SAE dictionaries spanning 768–98,304 latents to examine splitting. An informal RAVEL-inspired intervention study considers Paris, Tokyo, and Cairo, selected for single-token city names and attribute answers. Outcomes are log-probabilities for specified country, language, continent, and currency candidates, rather than generated answers or full RAVEL scores.

**Key results**

Selected meta-latents yield intelligible decompositions, although some remain uninterpretable. Smaller activation-trained SAEs provide similar conceptual neighbors. Substituting their decoder directions and retraining the meta-encoder for 5,000 epochs reportedly causes only a slight reconstruction decline. In a selected talk-related split, descendants retain a shared talking/speaking component while acquiring contextual components. Whole Tokyo-to-Paris latent replacement changes all four tested attribute rankings; selected meta-latent edits instead favor French and Euro while retaining Japan and Asia. The enumeration table lists five of sixteen possible binary attribute-change patterns, including no change, under the searched component combinations.

**Limitations / open questions**

Evidence is confined to one small model and one activation site, with selected examples and limited intervention coverage. Decompositions are lossy, hyperparameters partly reflect interpretability inspection, and no systematic semantic-accuracy evaluation establishes true computational atoms. Steering lacks general capability checks and cannot achieve every attribute combination. Some successful components have puzzling lexical interpretations. Numerical reconstruction values are unavailable in the supplied figure rendering. The graph comparison reports 28.92% overlap but inconsistently names edges and vertices; the splitting example claims seven descendants while listing six. Neither inconsistency indicates missing substantive sections.

title: Optimal ablation for interpretability
InterpBench: Semi-synthetic transformers for evaluating mechanistic interpretability techniques
How do Decisions Emerge across Layers in Neural Models? Interpretation with Differentiable Masking
summary:
**Central idea**

DIFFMASK interprets a frozen model using shallow, hidden-state-conditioned probes that replace input embeddings or intermediate token states with learned baseline vectors. Sparse stochastic Hard Concrete gates minimize expected nonzero masks under an output-divergence constraint. Input masks multiply successive layers’ votes, imposing progressively greater pruning; hidden-state masks operate separately at each layer. Amortization across examples is intended to reduce erasure’s hindsight bias: a prediction-preserving subset need not reveal what the original computation considered.

**Experiments**

A queried-digit counting task uses a tokenwise feed-forward network with a two-dimensional bottleneck followed by a GRU. Appendix C specifies 10,000 generated examples with 10% reserved for validation; the main text reports test accuracy above 99% without separately specifying that test split. An SST GRU experiment compares non-amortized Hard Concrete optimization with REINFORCE against exact erasure, restricted to sentences of at most 25 words, covering 54% of the data. Main analyses use 12-layer uncased BERT-base on SST, with 8,544 training and 1,101 validation sentences, and 24-layer uncased whole-word-masked BERT-large on SQuAD v1.1. Excluding QA inputs exceeding 384 BPE tokens leaves 86,706 training and 10,387 validation instances.

**Key results**

Counting-task hidden-state attributions achieve KL/JS divergences of 0.01/0.00 nats against the authors’ uniform queried-digit reference; comparator JS divergences range from 0.18 to 0.27. Table 2 reports exact-optimum recovery of 32.67% versus 8.83% for REINFORCE, and token-level F1 of 80.75 versus 73.57. On SST, masking 46.3% of input tokens changes validation F1 from 37.9% to 38.3%; masking 67.6% of hidden states yields 38.9%. Attribution standard deviations across five seeds are 0.05 and 0.03, respectively. Special tokens have low input retention but high hidden-state retention. In QA, question tokens and states generally remain longer than passage counterparts; more than half of hidden states can be masked after layer 9. The text also reports settings masking over 95% of input tokens while retaining original predictions over 90% of the time.

**Limitations / open questions**

Natural-task mechanistic ground truth is unavailable. Prediction preservation and stability do not establish recovery of ordinary causal mechanisms. Interpreting mask depth as model “knowledge” depends on probe adequacy and baseline semantics; input-mask monotonicity is imposed. The toy reference relies on an inferred counting mechanism and equal-relevance convention. A selected ablation shows single-example baseline learning can collapse to all-state removal. The supplied main text and appendices are present, but heatmap intensities are unavailable in the text rendering. Figure references are inconsistent, and the prose’s REINFORCE F1 disagrees with Table 2.

title: Answer, assemble, ace: Understanding how LMs answer multiple choice questions
Openwebtext corpus
Proximal methods for hierarchical sparse coding
Responses to contour features in macaque area V4
Discrete neural clusters encode orientation, curvature and corners in macaque V4
[Interim research report] Taking features out of superposition with sparse autoencoders
summary:
**Central idea**

Sparse autoencoders might separate superposed neural representations into their underlying feature directions. This interim report demonstrates recovery on synthetic activations with known generating features, then investigates diagnostics for selecting hyperparameters without ground truth. Recovery of natural language-model features remains unresolved.

**Experiments**

The main synthetic dataset contains 512 randomly sampled unit feature directions in 256 dimensions. Each input combines approximately five active features, with nonnegative amplitudes, unequal feature frequencies, and correlations between activations. The autoencoder uses a linear encoder followed by ReLU, unit-norm decoder columns, and an L1 activation penalty. Training uses Adam with learning rate 0.001 and batch size 256. Recovery is measured by mean maximum cosine similarity (MMCS), averaging each generating direction's cosine similarity to its closest learned direction. Experiments sweep dictionary width and L1 strength.

Language-model experiments use MLP activations from a six-layer, 31M-parameter GPT-2-style transformer with residual width 256 and MLP width 1,024. The report states that it was trained on 30B tokens from The Pile's Wikipedia subset, reaching training cross-entropy 3.074. Three proposed diagnostics are examined: dead latents, flat regions in reconstruction and regularization losses, and MMCS between differently sized dictionaries. An appendix separately sweeps denoising noise and L1 strength on equal-frequency, uncorrelated synthetic features.

**Key results**

At 512 learned features, synthetic recovery is good across L1 coefficients approximately 0.03–0.3. At coefficient 0.1, dictionaries containing approximately one to eight times the generating feature count nearly completely recover the generating directions. Larger dictionaries favor larger penalty coefficients. Low reconstruction loss alone can coexist with poor recovery. The three diagnostics approximately identify useful synthetic hyperparameter regions.

Language-model diagnostics differ substantially. In the representative second MLP layer, dead latents do not appear even at the largest tested width, 102,400; cross-dictionary MMCS never exceeds approximately 0.4; and loss patterns do not clearly identify a dictionary size. Denoising permits synthetic recovery but usually gives slightly worse MMCS than noiseless L1 counterparts and introduces a more sensitive hyperparameter.

**Limitations / open questions**

These preliminary results lack released code and reported uncertainty estimates. Natural feature recovery is unverified; the suggestion of more than 100,000 features is explicitly speculative. Possible explanations include insufficient training or capacity, noise, varying feature directions, and mismatched synthetic statistics. MMCS ignores redundant learned copies and does not establish causal feature use. Diagnostic reliability and computational scaling remain open.

title: One is 1: Analyzing activations of numerical words vs digits 1
Locating cross-task sequence continuation circuits in transformers
On the Pitfalls of Analyzing Individual Neurons in Language Models
abstract: While many studies have shown that linguistic information is encoded in hidden word representations, few have studied individual neurons, to show how and in which neurons it is encoded. Among these, the common approach is to use an external probe to rank neurons according to their relevance to some linguistic attribute, and to evaluate the obtained ranking using the same probe that produced it. We show two pitfalls in this methodology: 1. It confounds distinct factors: probe quality and ranking quality. We separate them and draw conclusions on each. 2. It focuses on encoded information, rather than information that is used by the model. We show that these are not the same. We compare two recent ranking methods and a simple one we introduce, and evaluate them with regard to both of these aspects.
summary:
**Central idea**

Evaluating neuron rankings with the classifier that generated them conflates classifier performance with ranking quality. Rankings useful for decoding morphology can also differ from rankings useful for manipulating morphological predictions. The paper introduces Probeless, which ranks representation coordinates by summed absolute differences between label-conditioned means, and compares it with linear-probe weight rankings and greedy Gaussian-probe rankings.

**Experiments**

M-BERT and XLM-R are evaluated at layers 2, 7, and 12 using 768-dimensional word representations obtained by averaging subtokens. Universal Dependencies annotations mapped to UniMorph provide nine languages and thirteen morphological attributes, yielding 156 available language–attribute–layer configurations per model. Linear and Gaussian classifiers are crossed with seven rankings: three methods, their reversals, and a random baseline. Metrics include accuracy, word-type control-task selectivity, and Wilcoxon comparisons.

Interventions evaluate English, Spanish, and French predictions using spaCy morphology. Coordinates are zeroed or translated toward another label's mean with rank-dependent coefficients. Means use training data; development-set strength selection yields β=8 for reported test results. CLWV counts lemma-preserving target-attribute errors as a fraction of all evaluated word predictions, rather than only erroneous predictions. Additional translation experiments use bert-base-cased, dccuchile/bert-base-spanish-wwm-cased, and camembert-base.

**Key results**

A classifier using random or reversed rankings can outperform another using its preferred ranking. Gaussian probes often achieve higher accuracy but have lower selectivity, consistent with greater word-type memorization. Under a fixed Linear evaluator, Gaussian rankings perform better for small subsets, while Linear rankings can overtake them as subset size increases.

Probeless generally provides a better CLWV-versus-coordinate-count tradeoff in M-BERT interventions despite weaker probing performance. Linear competes closely on XLM-R; monolingual results also contain exceptions. Translating fifty Probeless-selected coordinates for M-BERT Spanish gender at layer 2 produces 37% CLWV and 49% error, versus 0% CLWV and 1% error when zeroing them. Broad zero ablations initially have little effect and eventually produce unrelated errors. Cross-language coordinate overlaps also exceed random expectations in selected comparisons.

**Limitations / open questions**

Inputs are never masked, so prediction experiments concern unmasked word reconstruction. CLWV relies on automatic analysis and does not verify preservation of every other morphological attribute. Translation causes substantial unrelated errors, and successful steering does not independently establish ordinary causal mediation. Findings depend on the intervention coefficients, subset sizes, and saturation criterion; neither Probeless superiority nor Gaussian accuracy advantages are universal.

title: Probing the Probing Paradigm: Does Probing Accuracy Entail Task Relevance?
abstract: Although neural models have achieved impressive results on several NLP benchmarks, little is understood about the mechanisms they use to perform language tasks. Thus, much recent attention has been devoted to analyzing the sentence representations learned by neural encoders, through the lens of `probing' tasks. However, to what extent was the information encoded in sentence representations, as discovered through a probe, actually used by the model to perform its task? In this work, we examine this probing paradigm through a case study in Natural Language Inference, showing that models can learn to encode linguistic properties even if they are not needed for the task on which the model was trained. We further identify that pretrained word embeddings play a considerable role in encoding these properties rather than the training task itself, highlighting the importance of careful controls when designing probing experiments. Finally, through a set of controlled synthetic tasks, we demonstrate models can encode these properties considerably above chance-level even when distributed in the data as random noise, calling into question the interpretation of absolute claims on probing tasks.
summary:
**Central idea**
Recovering a property with a probe does not establish that the property is necessary for solving the encoder's training task. The paper investigates incidental encoding using property-controlled MultiNLI datasets and synthetic string tasks. It distinguishes recoverable information from task requirements without directly identifying every feature used by the trained decision mechanism.

**Experiments**
CBOW and BiLSTM encoders with last-state, average, or maximum pooling are trained on MultiNLI. Control datasets fix both premise and hypothesis to past tense, singular subjects, or singular objects, yielding 69,652, 102,452, and 43,178 training pairs. Comparators use size-matched downsampled MultiNLI. Frozen sentence vectors are evaluated with a 200-hidden-unit MLP on binary probes whose target lexical items are separated across splits. Experiments compare fine-tuned 300-dimensional GloVe initialization with embeddings trained from random initialization.

Synthetic entailment depends on first-letter agreement between strings. An auxiliary character, c, is inserted under Noise, Uncorrelated, Partial, and Full conditions. Each condition has 20,000/5,000/5,000 training/development/test examples; the separate probing dataset has 23,732/5,000/5,000. The authors vary representation and probe capacity and evaluate gradient-reversal suppression using an independent attacker.

**Key results**
Property-controlled models retain probing accuracies descriptively similar to size-matched comparators. GloVe-initialized controlled CBOW achieves 82.20% tense, 75.69% subject-number, and 74.38% object-number accuracy against 50% baselines. GloVe improves every reported initialization comparison; full-MultiNLI CBOW tense probing falls from 83.74% to 60.14% with random initialization. Nevertheless, controlled models trained from scratch achieve approximately 61–71% across the evaluated probes.

Synthetic BiLSTMs retain decodable c information even when insertion is random noise relative to the task. Smaller representations reduce probing accuracy while task accuracy remains consistent; larger probes do not consistently improve extraction. In Appendix A's Noise condition at λ=1, task accuracy is 100%, training-adversary accuracy 49.43%, and independent-attacker accuracy 94.50% against a 50.20% attacker baseline.

**Limitations / open questions**
Transformers are not tested. Constant-property controls make the assigned property value nondiscriminative; they do not demonstrate absence of causal use of related information. Parser heuristics agree with original SentEval labels at 87.77–89.37%. Statistical equivalence tests and uncertainty estimates are not reported, and exact figure-curve values are unavailable in the supplied text. Adversarial removal remains incomplete, and failed suppression cannot establish necessity. The metadata dates the initial posting; the displayed source is version 3, dated March 7, 2021.

title: Sparse classification: a scalable discrete optimization perspective
Groups and Representations
Unifying Grokking and Double Descent
Omnigrok: Grokking Beyond Algorithmic Data
abstract: Grokking, the unusual phenomenon for algorithmic datasets where generalization happens long after overfitting the training data, has remained elusive. We aim to understand grokking by analyzing the loss landscapes of neural networks, identifying the mismatch between training and test losses as the cause for grokking. We refer to this as the "LU mechanism" because training and test losses (against model weight norm) typically resemble "L" and "U", respectively. This simple mechanism can nicely explain many aspects of grokking: data size dependence, weight decay dependence, the emergence of representations, etc. Guided by the intuitive picture, we are able to induce grokking on tasks involving images, language and molecules. In the reverse direction, we are able to eliminate grokking for algorithmic datasets. We attribute the dramatic nature of grokking for algorithmic datasets to representation learning.

title: Self-attention attribution: Interpreting information interactions inside transformer
T-rex: A large scale alignment of natural language with knowledge base triples
Distant supervision for relation extraction without labeled data
Towards a rigorous science of interpretable machine learning
Activation addition: Steering language models without optimization
Discovering language model behaviors with model-written evaluations.
Measuring massive multitask language understanding.
Understanding and visualizing sycophancy datasets
Is gpt-4 a reliable rater? evaluating consistency in gpt-4’s text ratings
Still no lie detector for language models: probing empirical and conceptual roadblocks
abstract: We consider the questions of whether or not large language models (LLMs) have beliefs, and, if they do, how we might measure them. First, we consider whether or not we should expect LLMs to have something like beliefs in the first place. We consider some recent arguments aiming to show that LLMs cannot have beliefs. We show that these arguments are misguided. We provide a more productive framing of questions surrounding the status of beliefs in LLMs, and highlight the empirical nature of the problem. With this lesson in hand, we evaluate two existing approaches for measuring the beliefs of LLMs, one due to Azaria and Mitchell (The internal state of an llm knows when its lying, 2023) and the other to Burns et al. (Discovering latent knowledge in language models without supervision, 2022). Moving from the armchair to the desk chair, we provide empirical results that show that these methods fail to generalize in very basic ways. We then argue that, even if LLMs have beliefs, these methods are unlikely to be successful for conceptual reasons. Thus, there is still no lie-detector for LLMs. We conclude by suggesting some concrete paths for future work.
summary:
**Central idea**
Next-token prediction does not rule out belief-like internal states: tracking truth could help a model predict text. Whether models possess such states requires empirical investigation. However, extracting truth-correlated information does not establish that a probe measures beliefs, credences, or deception. The paper examines supervised truth probes and Contrast-Consistent Search (CCS), distinguishing predictive accuracy from identification of representations the model actually uses.

**Experiments**
The authors reconstruct supervised probing on LLaMA 1 30B, described as having 33 billion parameters and 60 layers. They use penultimate-token embeddings at the last, fourth-last, and eighth-last layers, selecting the best of ten probes by binary accuracy for each dataset–layer setting. Data comprise six factual datasets totaling 6,084 statements, an additional 10,000-example Capitals dataset, and constructed negations. Evaluations measure binary accuracy and include calibration plots. CCS experiments use Facts/NegFacts and Companies/NegCompanies contrast pairs, linear probes, and 100-hidden-unit MLP probes, including classwise embedding normalization.

**Key results**
Original supervised leave-one-dataset-out accuracies range from 69.4% to 97.3% across 21 dataset–layer cells; Capitals substantially overlaps Cities. Without negation training, five of six evaluations on NegFacts and NegCompanies fall below chance. Training on the target's original statements and another domain's negations yields only 52.6–62.9%. Broader training with equal proportions of original and negated statements yields 69.3–97.9% across 21 evaluations excluding both forms of the target domain. Linear CCS probes achieve 53–56% accuracy despite losses of 0.002–0.004. MLP CCS accuracy is 50.2–56.8%; at the last and fourth-last layers, predictions largely distinguish grammatical polarity despite normalization. The confidence objective rewards extreme complementary outputs rather than faithful uncertainty estimates.

**Limitations / open questions**
These are modified reconstructions on one model, rather than direct reruns of the original OPT supervised experiments or CCS benchmark. CCS sample sizes, complete hyperparameters, uncertainty estimates, and an independent split for best-of-ten selection are not specified. Calibration plots provide no readable numerical summaries in the supplied rendering. Failures do not establish that truth representations are absent or that other probes cannot recover them. Supervised labels can conflate truth with consensus or verifiability, while coherence alone does not establish semantic identity. Proposed next steps—truth-focused prompting, known-chance scenarios, and identifying functionally used world-model variables—are untested.

title: The implicit bias of gradient descent on separable data
The use of multiple measurements in taxonomic problems
Future Lens: Anticipating Subsequent Tokens from a Single Hidden State
summary:
**Central idea**
Future Lens investigates whether one contextualized token state provides information useful for anticipating predictions beyond the immediate next token. It compares linear readouts with interventions that transplant a source state into another context. Its strongest method learns a reusable soft prompt for each source layer and uses the frozen transformer to decode the transplanted state.

**Experiments**
Experiments use GPT-J-6B: 28 layers, 4,096-dimensional hidden states, and a 50,400-token vocabulary. The authors sample 100,000 training token locations from the Pile, using 10,000 for learned prompts, and evaluate on another 1,000 locations. Sampling is restricted to locations where GPT-J correctly predicts the immediately following corpus token. Average preceding contexts contain 518 training tokens and 535 test tokens. Methods comprise direct linear vocabulary prediction, linear prediction of future final-layer states followed by the pretrained decoder, transplantation into four generic prompts, and transplantation into learned ten-token soft prompts. Evaluation covers N=0–3, corresponding to predictions one through four tokens beyond the source position. Metrics are Precision@k and the original model’s surprisal of the readout’s top prediction. Later intervention predictions receive preceding tokens from the original greedy continuation. Appendix A identifies N=1 training as the main reporting configuration and compares other training horizons.

**Key results**
Best reported learned-prompt Precision@1 across layers is 48.4%, 43.7%, and 46.9% for N=1, 2, and 3. At N=1, best hidden-state linear, direct-vocabulary linear, and fixed-prompt results are 29.2%, 27.5%, and 20.8%; the empirical bigram baseline reaches 20.1%. Learned prompts also achieve the lowest reported best surprisal. Future-prediction accuracy peaks around middle layers, with layer 14 used for subgroup analysis; immediate-next-token accuracy instead peaks at the final layer. Reported N=1 accuracy rises from 26% to 95% across increasing next-token-confidence bins. Named-entity subset accuracies are 44%, 42%, and 37% at N=1–3, described as similar or lower than overall performance. The visualization displays four anticipated tokens at each token–layer location.

**Limitations / open questions**
Evidence covers one model, predominantly English data, selected token locations, and four prediction positions. Teacher-forced agreement does not establish autonomous continuation recovery. Intervention readouts receive preceding continuation tokens unavailable to direct linear readouts, complicating architectural comparisons. Additional transformer computation also prevents equating successful decoding with explicit sequence precomputation in the source state. Stronger controls, other models, and longer horizons remain open. Table 2’s header and several indexing equations contain inconsistencies; surrounding text clarifies the intended N convention. Plot traces are unavailable in the supplied rendering.

title: Similarity and matching of neural network representations
When not to trust language models: Investigating effectiveness of parametric and non-parametric memories
Chain-of-thought prompting elicits reasoning in large language models
Understanding and Patching Compositional Reasoning in LLMs
abstract: LLMs have marked a revolutonary shift, yet they falter when faced with compositional reasoning tasks. Our research embarks on a quest to uncover the root causes of compositional reasoning failures of LLMs, uncovering that most of them stem from the improperly generated or leveraged implicit reasoning results. Inspired by our empirical findings, we resort to Logit Lens and an intervention experiment to dissect the inner hidden states of LLMs. This deep dive reveals that implicit reasoning results indeed surface within middle layers and play a causative role in shaping the final explicit reasoning results. Our exploration further locates multi-head self-attention (MHSA) modules within these layers, which emerge as the linchpins in accurate generation and leveraing of implicit reasoning results. Grounded on the above findings, we develop CREME, a lightweight method to patch errors in compositional reasoning via editing the located MHSA modules. Our empirical evidence stands testament to CREME's effectiveness, paving the way for autonomously and continuously enhancing compositional reasoning capabilities in language models.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper investigates whether factual two-hop reasoning failures reflect missing, weak, late, or improperly used intermediate answers. It introduces CREME, which edits attention output projections toward outputs elicited by corresponding second-hop queries. CREME requires a supplied second-hop reference containing the intermediate entity, but does not directly optimize against the final ground-truth answer.

**Experiments**

Experiments use LLaMA-2-7B and OpenAlpaca-3B with 1,000 two-hop MQuAKE items. Editing cases are selected where both constituent single-hop questions succeed but the compositional question fails; model-specific editing-set sizes are unreported. Logit Lens tracks mean vocabulary probabilities over intermediate- and final-answer tokens at the last input position. Pseudoinverse-based interventions target intermediate-answer readouts, with equally sized random-token controls. Localization replaces compositional-query outputs with second-hop-reference outputs. Although initially described as single-module replacement, reported localization and main editing experiments use six-layer windows. Comparators are Memory Injection, CoT-PatchScopes, and ROME.

**Key results**

A reported 200-example analysis assigns 15% to distortion, 36% to incomplete reasoning, and 14%/12% to two hasty-answer categories. Intermediate-answer readouts generally peak before final-answer readouts, with more dispersed peaks in OpenAlpaca. Reported suppression effects concentrate around layers 15–20; reference attention-output replacements are strongest near layers 18/19. CREME increases correct-versus-originally-wrong answer ranking on editing inputs from 59.5% to 87.5% for LLaMA-2 and from 58.0% to 95.3% for OpenAlpaca. These are pairwise score-ranking rates, not generation accuracies. LLaMA-2 paraphrase prediction accuracy rises from 6.3% to 18.3%, and shared-first-hop query accuracy from 29.9% to 38.3%. Mean per-example relative correct-answer score gains on related queries are 1.27 and 3.61, respectively. CREME exceeds the tested inference baselines on correction scores. ROME achieves higher OpenAlpaca correction ranking, while CREME performs better on reported transfer and edited-answer leakage measures.

**Limitations / open questions**

Evidence covers two models and factual two-hop tasks. Logit Lens is approximate; pseudoinverse edits neither guarantee the requested vocabulary changes nor establish selective semantic erasure. Intervention plots clip negative effects and normalize each example across layers. Multi-token scores average token probabilities rather than measuring answer-sequence likelihood. Specificity measures edited-answer leakage on unrelated queries, not comprehensive preservation. Error labels do not establish causal prevalence. Sequential editing, autonomous error discovery, and broad capability retention remain untested. Figure images are unavailable in the supplied rendering, so plotted values cannot be independently checked. The source is June 2024 v2; metadata records initial publication.

title: K-composition version of an induction head
An Overview of Early Vision in InceptionV1
summary:
**Central idea**

The article organizes 1,056 channel-level units in InceptionV1’s first five convolutional layers—conv2d0, conv2d1, conv2d2, mixed3a, and mixed3b—into human-defined neuron families. Bottleneck units in mixed3a and mixed3b are excluded. This working taxonomy helps researchers investigate the development of visual features, while leaving open whether its families reflect fundamental clusters or convenient human categories.

**Experiments**

The work reports descriptive inspection and categorization rather than controlled validation of its feature interpretations. The authors combine optimized feature visualizations, dataset examples, incoming and outgoing connections, and selected circuit diagrams. Visualizations use Lucid, transformation robustness, and low-layer L2 regularization; first-layer units are represented by their weights. Circuit displays principally select connections by L2 weight norm. A qualitative comparison with a BatchNorm-equipped TF-Slim InceptionV1 variant shows crisper first-layer filters, but does not isolate the cause. No dataset-example sample sizes, classification-accuracy measurements, quantitative invariance tests, or ablation results are supplied.

**Key results**

The manual taxonomy assigns 28 of 64 conv2d0 channels to Gabor filters and 27 to color contrast, reported as 44% and 42%. Later layers retain low-level features while introducing increasingly elaborate proposed feature types. Conv2d1 complex Gabors are interpreted as combining similarly oriented, opposite-polarity filters to reduce sensitivity to edge phase and polarity. Conv2d2 introduces line and tiny-curve features. Selected mixed3a diagrams suggest black-and-white detection through inhibition from color features, small-circle formation from curves, and triangle formation from lines. Mixed3b boundary detectors are interpreted as combining line, color-contrast, and high-low-frequency cues. Other proposed families include oriented fur, elaborate curve shapes, eyes, and crude heads. These mechanisms are provisional interpretations of visualizations and connectivity, rather than intervention-validated results.

**Limitations / open questions**

Investigation depth ranges from a few minutes per unit to detailed analysis. Many categories are explicitly broad or low-confidence, and feature visualizations serve as meaningful labels rather than complete behavioral explanations. Some circuit displays select connections for pedagogy or multiply bottleneck weights despite an intervening ReLU. Family boundaries, cross-model universality, behavioral edge cases, and extension to later layers remain unresolved. The supplied text includes figure descriptions and neuron lists, but not the interactive visual evidence itself.

title: Naturally Occurring Equivariance in Neural Networks
summary:
**Central idea**

Convolutional networks can naturally learn families of approximately transformed features connected by approximately symmetric weights. The article frames this equivariance as a recurring circuit motif: understanding a shared template and its transformations can organize many neurons and connections. Examples primarily concern ImageNet-trained InceptionV1 and include rotation, scale, hue, horizontal reflection, and looser semantic transformations. Some families have missing members or transformations that do not satisfy strict group-theoretic equivariance.

**Experiments**

The article curates qualitative feature and weight analyses. Illustrated circuits build directional high-low frequency detectors from frequency factors, combine color-contrast features into center-surround detectors, combine curves into circles and evolutes at different scales, and combine left/right dog-head features into a pose-invariant detector. Selected connections between transformed families depend on relative feature relationships: matching curve orientations are excitatory and opposite orientations inhibitory, while spatial weight patterns rotate. Controlled rotated-stimulus response tests are attributed to the earlier Curve Detectors article; they are not new experiments here.

The authors also train an untuned, InceptionV1-inspired architecture on ImageNet, enforcing rotational equivariance over 16 rotations for half its neurons and rotational invariance for the remainder. They qualitatively inspect its mixed3b features against naturally occurring InceptionV1 families.

**Key results**

The illustrated natural circuits have weight symmetries resembling the weight tying imposed by equivariant architectures. Examples encompass invariant-to-equivariant, equivariant-to-invariant, and equivariant-to-equivariant connections. Hue and rotation can interact: for the illustrated color-contrast features, reversing opposing hues is equivalent to a 180-degree rotation.

The trained equivariant model learns analogues of curve, boundary, divot, and oriented-fur detectors. The authors interpret this as a successful qualitative prediction from their feature interpretations. They describe its test accuracy as abysmal but provide no numerical accuracy, feature-matching score, or statistical comparison.

**Limitations / open questions**

Examples are curated; the hue-to-hue and curve-to-curve examples explicitly favor simple relationships and clean weights. Family prevalence, symmetry error, and interpretation effort are not quantified. Natural families require manual discovery and can contain exceptions that shared templates conceal. Substantially reducing interpretation effort through designed equivariance remains a hypothesis. The findings concern vision networks; language-model and alignment applications are not tested.

title: Deconvolution and checkerboard artifacts
An Intriguing Failing of Convolutional Neural Networks and the CoordConv Solution
Information-Theoretic Probing for Linguistic Structure
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper operationalizes linguistic probing as estimating mutual information between representations and linguistic labels. Population probe cross-entropy upper-bounds conditional entropy, yielding a mutual-information lower bound. The probe with the lowest population cross-entropy therefore gives the tightest bound, irrespective of architectural complexity. Deterministic control functions define information-removing baselines; information gain relative to a control equals conditional mutual information. The authors also prove that an invertible deterministic contextual encoding preserves the original sentence's mutual information with labels, motivating a distinction between information content and ease of extraction.

**Experiments**

The experiments probe multilingual BERT on Universal Dependencies 2.5 POS tagging and dependency-relation labeling in eleven languages: Basque, Czech, English, Finnish, Indonesian, Korean, Marathi, Tamil, Telugu, Turkish, and Urdu. Word representations average BERT wordpiece outputs; dependency probes concatenate representations of a token and its supplied head. Controls use language-specific fastText, trainable type-level embeddings described as one-hot controls, and fixed random embeddings. For each estimate, 50 ReLU MLP configurations are trained, searching depth, width, dropout, and control embedding size. Validation cross-entropy selects the model; test cross-entropy estimates conditional entropy.

**Key results**

Against fastText, BERT has positive estimated POS information gain in only 5/11 languages, ranging from 0.5% to 8.8% of label entropy in those five. Dependency-label gains are positive in all eleven languages, ranging from 1.2% to 12.2% of label entropy. English has the largest dependency gain: approximately 0.55 bits against label entropy of 4.48 bits. These percentages normalize cross-entropy differences by label entropy; they are not relative increases over fastText's mutual information. Gains against trainable one-hot controls are larger: 6.9–31.4% for POS and 11.9–33.7% for dependency labels. The authors interpret the fastText comparisons as indicating that lexical information already predicts much of these tasks.

**Limitations / open questions**

Differences between two mutual-information lower bounds do not establish bounds on true gain without unknown approximation-error terms; estimated gains can consequently be negative. The invertibility argument assumes unique embeddings for every sentence-position pair and ignores finite precision, without empirical verification. Dependency labeling supplies the head and does not evaluate parsing. Plug-in conditional entropies can underestimate uncertainty in undersampled regimes. The text does not specify the BERT extraction layer or report uncertainty intervals. Ease of extraction remains unformalized, and predictive accessibility does not establish causal use of syntax.

title: Evaluating NLP Models via Contrast Sets
Learning the Difference that Makes a Difference with Counterfactually-Augmented Data
Universal Adversarial Triggers for Attacking and Analyzing NLP
Explain Yourself! Leveraging Language Models for Commonsense Reasoning
Do ImageNet Classifiers Generalize to ImageNet?
Right for the Wrong Reasons: Diagnosing Syntactic Heuristics in Natural Language Inference
NeuroX: A Toolkit for Analyzing Individual Neurons in Neural Networks
e-SNLI: Natural Language Inference with Natural Language Explanations
Identifying and Controlling Important Neurons in Neural Machine Translation
Grounding Visual Explanations
Semantically Equivalent Adversarial Rules for Debugging NLP models
Places: A 10 Million Image Database for Scene Recognition
Hypothesis Only Baselines in Natural Language Inference
Anchors: High-Precision Model-Agnostic Explanations

Annotation Artifacts in Natural Language Inference Data
Net2Vec: Quantifying and Explaining how Concepts are Encoded by Filters in Deep Neural Networks
abstract: In an effort to understand the meaning of the intermediate representations captured by deep networks, recent papers have tried to associate specific semantic concepts to individual neural network filter responses, where interesting correlations are often found, largely by focusing on extremal filter responses. In this paper, we show that this approach can favor easy-to-interpret cases that are not necessarily representative of the average behavior of a representation. A more realistic but harder-to-study hypothesis is that semantic representations are distributed, and thus filters must be studied in conjunction. In order to investigate this idea while enabling systematic visualization and quantification of multiple filter responses, we introduce the Net2Vec framework, in which semantic concepts are mapped to vectorial embeddings based on corresponding filter responses. By studying such embeddings, we are able to show that 1., in most cases, multiple filters are required to code for a concept, that 2., often filters are not concept specific and help encode multiple concepts, and that 3., compared to single filter activations, filter embeddings are able to better characterize the meaning of a representation and its relationship to other concepts.
summary:
**Central idea**
Net2Vec studies semantic information distributed across CNN filters by training concept predictors on frozen activations and interpreting their coefficients as filter-aligned embeddings. It investigates whether individual filters sufficiently and exclusively capture concepts, and whether maximally activating examples give a representative picture of their behavior.

**Experiments**
The principal model is ImageNet-trained AlexNet, probed across conv1–conv5 using BRODEN’s over 60,000 images. The stated task inventories are 1,189 classification concepts, after excluding eight scenes without validation examples, and 682 concepts with segmentation annotations. Segmentation combines activation indicators thresholded at each filter’s top 0.5% cutoff; validation set IoU aggregates intersections and unions over images containing the concept. Classification uses spatially averaged activations and balanced validation accuracy. Restricted probes select filters by absolute full-probe coefficient and refit. Additional comparisons use ImageNet- and Places365-trained AlexNet, VGG16, and GoogLeNet, plus five self-supervised AlexNet variants. Analyses also examine individual-image IoU, visualization deciles, coefficient correlations, embedding neighbors, vector arithmetic, and similarity matrices over 501 shared concepts.

**Key results**
Filter combinations improve average concept prediction from conv1 onward. At conv5, Table 1 reports combinations matching or exceeding single-filter performance for 75.7% of segmentation concepts and 88.1% of classification concepts. Most classification categories saturate by approximately 50 selected filters; scenes approach their optimum around 15. Segmentation category averages peak at eight filters for materials and parts, 16 for objects, and 128 for colors. Around 15% of conv1 filters are selected for at least 20 segmentation concepts or 30 classification concepts. At conv5, 82.47% of the 682 segmentation concepts show significant correlation between rectified probe coefficients and individual-filter IoU at p<0.01. Selected examples show many zero-IoU single-filter predictions and broader coverage from combinations. Embedding neighborhoods suggest category similarity for segmentation and compositional relationships for classification; classification embeddings more closely resemble WordNet and Word2Vec relationships in the reported comparisons.

**Limitations / open questions**
These are supervised decoding tests without interventions establishing natural downstream concept use. Segmentation evaluation conditions on concept presence, and displayed deciles exclude zero-IoU examples. Failures concentrate among concepts with few training examples or tiny spatial extent; optimization and resolution also constrain results. The separate report of 133 conv5 classification failures is not reconciled with the stated inventory and Table 1 percentage. Linear predictors and the annotation inventory limit coverage; semantic analogies remain qualitative. The rendered training-loss equation is malformed, and referenced supplementary material is absent from the supplied text.

title: Scene parsing through ade20k dataset.
Translating Neuralese
Densely Connected Convolutional Networks
Synthesizing the preferred inputs for neurons in neural networks via deep generator networks
abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have demonstrated state-of-the-art results on many pattern recognition tasks, especially vision classification problems. Understanding the inner workings of such computational brains is both fascinating basic science that is interesting in its own right - similar to why we study the human brain - and will enable researchers to further improve DNNs. One path to understanding how a neural network functions internally is to study what each of its neurons has learned to detect. One such method is called activation maximization (AM), which synthesizes an input (e.g. an image) that highly activates a neuron. Here we dramatically improve the qualitative state of the art of activation maximization by harnessing a powerful, learned prior: a deep generator network (DGN). The algorithm (1) generates qualitatively state-of-the-art synthetic images that look almost real, (2) reveals the features learned by each neuron in an interpretable way, (3) generalizes well to new datasets and somewhat well to different network architectures without requiring the prior to be relearned, and (4) can be considered as a high-quality generative method (in this case, by generating novel, creative, interesting, recognizable images).
summary:
**Central idea**

DGN-AM synthesizes preferred neuron inputs by optimizing a fixed deep generator's input code while holding both generator and target network weights fixed. Pretrained representation-inversion networks supply the learned image prior. The default generator inverts CaffeNet fc6 representations; optimization uses L2 regularization (λ = 0.005) and clips code coordinates to [0, 3σ].

**Experiments**

The authors compare generators inverting CaffeNet conv3, conv5, fc6, and fc7 and compare synthesized images with earlier methods using hand-designed priors. They visualize output and hidden units, transfer the ImageNet-trained prior to Places205 and UCF-101 networks, and test GoogLeNet and ResNet-50. Three new 2,000-class CaffeNet models distinguish 1,000 original ImageNet classes from corresponding quarter-shuffled, BRG-color, or blurred classes. A 1,005-class experiment splits five classes selected for noncanonical visualizations into canonical and remaining subsets. Additional tests inspect nearest training images, training checkpoints, overfit models, synthesized 160-frame LRCN videos, and joint activation of two output neurons.

**Key results**

Author-reported qualitative comparisons favor fc6 codes for global coherence and DGN-AM for natural colors, textures, and structure. Selected hidden-unit visualizations agree with earlier visualizations and human labels collected in prior work. Transfer is better for Places205 than activity recognition, and image quality declines on GoogLeNet and ResNet-50 relative to CaffeNet. With the generator unchanged, modified-image classifiers produce correspondingly altered visualizations, showing that the tested properties are not exclusively supplied by the prior. Canonical-subset neurons yield canonical images. Nearest-neighbor inspections in pixels and eight representation spaces find no obvious copies among examined samples. Models trained on 10% and 25% of ImageNet attain 100% training accuracy but 20.2% and 31.5% validation accuracy; their visualizations reportedly look worse than those of the full-data model with 57.4% validation accuracy. Real-video frame shuffling reportedly changes the tested LRCN's decisions little. Balanced two-neuron objectives produce selected recognizable combinations and alternative facets.

**Limitations / open questions**

Image quality is judged subjectively, and hyperparameters are selected for that quality; no controlled human understanding study or aggregate semantic-fidelity metric is supplied. The text provides figure descriptions rather than image pixels. Animal faces remain difficult, and activation magnitude does not track recognizability. Controlled modifications constrain prior-confounding concerns without attributing every synthesized detail to the target neuron. Nearest-neighbor checks do not establish general absence of memorization. Architecture-general priors and comprehensive facet coverage remain open. The borrowed generator lacks a learned code-distribution prior and a natural sampling procedure.

title: Generating Visual Explanations
A Fast Unified Model for Parsing and Sentence Understanding
A large annotated corpus for learning natural language inference
Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network
Intriguing properties of neural networks
abstract: Deep neural networks are highly expressive models that have recently achieved state of the art performance on speech and visual recognition tasks. While their expressiveness is the reason they succeed, it also causes them to learn uninterpretable solutions that could have counter-intuitive properties. In this paper we report two such properties. First, we find that there is no distinction between individual high level units and random linear combinations of high level units, according to various methods of unit analysis. It suggests that it is the space, rather than the individual units, that contains of the semantic information in the high layers of neural networks. Second, we find that deep neural networks learn input-output mappings that are fairly discontinuous to a significant extend. We can cause the network to misclassify an image by applying a certain imperceptible perturbation, which is found by maximizing the network's prediction error. In addition, the specific nature of these perturbations is not a random artifact of learning: the same perturbation can cause a different network, that was trained on a different subset of the dataset, to misclassify the same input.
summary:
**Central idea**
The paper challenges two intuitions: that individual hidden units form a privileged semantic basis, and that good ordinary generalization implies robustness to visually negligible input changes. It introduces optimization-generated adversarial examples and demonstrates transfer across classifier configurations and disjoint training sets.

**Experiments**
The authors inspect held-out images maximizing individual coordinates or random linear projections in an MNIST convolutional network and ImageNet-trained AlexNet. Both conditions yield visually coherent groups. Box-constrained L-BFGS approximately searches for small perturbations inducing a target label. Attack evaluations cover MNIST linear softmax classifiers, sigmoid networks, a frozen sparse-autoencoder representation with a softmax classifier, AlexNet, and a car classifier over frozen QuocNet features. Quantitative MNIST transfer experiments compare six models on distorted training images and separately compare three networks trained on two disjoint 30,000-image subsets using distorted test images. The paper also reports preliminary layerwise adversarial training and derives spectral sensitivity bounds.

**Key results**
Source-specific attacks produce 100% error over the MNIST training set at average per-image RMS pixel distortions of 0.058–0.14 on the [0,1] intensity scale. Transfer is asymmetric: FC100-100-10 attacks produce 6.6% error in FC200-200-10, whereas the reverse produces 20.3%; Gaussian noise with standard deviation 0.1 produces 0% error in both targets. In the separate test-set experiment, minimum-distortion attacks yield 5.1–8.2% error across disjoint-training-set models, whose clean test errors are 2–2.1%. Amplification to the reported RMS 0.1 raises cross-set error to 22–50%, versus 2.6–2.8% under Gaussian noise. AlexNet attacks targeting “ostrich” have reported average distortion 0.006508 over 64 randomly chosen examples. Preliminary FC100-100-10 training with separately refreshed adversarial pools at each layer achieves below 1.2% test error, compared with 1.6% using weight decay alone and approximately 1.3% using dropout. A formal derivation bounds affine-ReLU network sensitivity by products of weight operator norms; AlexNet's reported layer bounds range from 2.75 to 11.

**Limitations / open questions**
Semantic comparisons are qualitative and do not establish equal interpretability across arbitrary directions. Visual similarity is not independently validated label preservation, and optimization does not certify minimum perturbations. The amplification formula conflicts with the stated RMS normalization. Spectral bounds are conservative: large upper bounds do not establish vulnerability, and classification guarantees require margins. The paper's discontinuity language does not prove discontinuous score functions. Transfer mechanisms, adversarial-example prevalence, and systematic adversarial-training benefits remain unresolved.
