Automatically Identifying Local and Global Circuits with Linear Computation Graphs
abstract: Circuit analysis of any certain model behavior is a central task in mechanistic interpretability. We introduce our circuit discovery pipeline with Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and a variant called Transcoders. With these two modules inserted into the model, the model's computation graph with respect to OV and MLP circuits becomes strictly linear. Our methods do not require linear approximation to compute the causal effect of each node. This fine-grained graph identifies both end-to-end and local circuits accounting for either logits or intermediate features. We can scalably apply this pipeline with a technique called Hierarchical Attribution. We analyze three kinds of circuits in GPT-2 Small: bracket, induction, and Indirect Object Identification circuits. Our results reveal new findings underlying existing discoveries.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper constructs feature-level computation graphs using sparse autoencoders and transcoders: sparse networks predicting MLP outputs from pre-MLP activations. For a particular input, fixing attention patterns and other input-dependent transformations permits additive attribution through OV pathways and active feature gates. Attention-score formation is investigated separately through bilinear query–key feature interactions. Hierarchical Attribution removes low-scoring nodes during backpropagation, preventing excluded downstream paths from contributing to upstream scores.

**Experiments**

All model analyses use GPT-2 Small. Dictionaries initially contain 24,576 features and are trained on one billion OpenWebText tokens using 256-token sequences, followed by feature pruning and reconstruction-only fine-tuning of decoders and activation scalers. Appendix A reports active-feature counts, explained variance, and replacement cross-entropy statistics; its evaluation sample size is unspecified. Hierarchical and standard attribution are compared on 20 IOI samples across 30 sparsity thresholds using retained-node counts and attribution-derived logit recovery. Case studies examine nested brackets, induction in a repeated WebM passage, and two IOI prompts differing in the initial ordering of John and Mary.

**Key results**

Hierarchical Attribution reportedly improves the logit-recovery versus node-count comparison throughout the evaluated sweep; numerical effect sizes are unavailable in the supplied figure text. Across 12 MLP transcoders, explained variance ranges from 72.79% to 94.16%, mean active-feature counts from 19.59 to 94.85, and ablation-normalized reconstruction CE scores from 77.33% to 99.65%. These are per-module measurements, not simultaneous all-layer replacement results. Bracket attribution identifies opening-bracket promotion and closing-bracket suppression through head L1A.H1. The induction example separates copied capital-letter content from Web-to-Web-preceding QK interactions. IOI graphs recover familiar head roles while suggesting different feature pathways for retrieving entities before versus after “and.” Appendix D supplies a leaf-attribution completeness derivation for the stipulated fixed-coefficient, bias-free ReLU graph.

**Limitations / open questions**

Selected-input analyses do not establish general circuits across distributions. Reconstruction is imperfect, and uninterpretable reconstruction-error nodes are removed. Additive exactness is conditional on fixed transformations; finite interventions can change attention, normalization, and ReLU gates. The leaf-attribution proof does not establish that backward-pruned contributions equal recomputed finite-ablation outputs. Feature semantics and proposed IOI pathways lack independent intervention validation. The positive signed threshold also removes negative-scoring nodes. Some mathematical notation is inconsistent, including the attribution derivative's direction.

title: Dictionary Learning Improves Patch-Free Circuit Discovery in Mechanistic Interpretability: A Case Study on Othello-GPT
abstract: Sparse dictionary learning has been a rapidly growing technique in mechanistic interpretability to attack superposition and extract more human-understandable features from model activations. We ask a further question based on the extracted more monosemantic features: How do we recognize circuits connecting the enormous amount of dictionary features? We propose a circuit discovery framework alternative to activation patching. Our framework suffers less from out-of-distribution and proves to be more efficient in terms of asymptotic complexity. The basic unit in our framework is dictionary features decomposed from all modules writing to the residual stream, including embedding, attention output and MLP output. Starting from any logit, dictionary feature or attention score, we manage to trace down to lower-level dictionary features of all tokens and compute their contribution to these more interpretable and local model behaviors. We dig in a small transformer trained on a synthetic task named Othello and find a number of human-understandable fine-grained circuits inside of it.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper proposes tracing circuits through dictionaries of components that write to the residual stream: embeddings, attention outputs, and MLP outputs. With attention patterns and LayerNorm denominators fixed, OV pathways admit additive feature-contribution decompositions; pre-softmax QK scores admit bilinear feature-pair decompositions. For nonlinear MLPs, Approximate Direct Contribution (ADC) freezes self-gating factors at their observed values and attributes the remaining linear computation to input features. These are input-conditioned decompositions, rather than general finite-intervention effects.

**Experiments**

The authors train a 1.2-million-parameter Othello next-legal-move transformer with six layers, hidden width 128, and MLP width 512 on approximately one billion synthetic game sequences. Dropout is removed. Untied, L1-regularized autoencoders use 1,024 latent units for 128-dimensional module outputs. Feature interpretations use statistics over the 2,048 most activating positions among 1.2 million board states. ADC is compared with direct feature patching on 180 MLP features: the three strongest features in each of six MLP layers for ten randomly sampled input sequences.

**Key results**

The retrained model has reported task performance of 99.5%, versus 99.9% cited for the original model; the appendix does not specify the metric's evaluation denominator. Dictionaries expose examples of current-move, player-relative board-state, empty-cell, and legal-move features. Selected analyses describe attention combining historical board information with current flips, QK interactions involving move-color and positional features, and an early MLP receiving three line-aligned move-feature contributions, interpreted as an AND-like computation. ADC and direct patching have mean intersection-over-union of 0.68 between their top-five contributor sets. Table 1 counts O(n) module forwards for the proposed method and direct patching, versus O(n) full-model forwards for causal patching; no wall-clock benchmark establishes practical speedup or optimality.

**Limitations / open questions**

The circuit examples are input-specific and lack comprehensive intervention validation. QK attribution omits softmax competition. Frozen-gate ADC can miss effects mediated by suppressing negatively acting neurons; the proposed OR-gate explanation of one failure remains conjectural. Approximately 75% of dictionary units are dead, and late-MLP active counts can approach 128. Neither reconstruction nor avoiding patched executions establishes mechanistic faithfulness. Natural-language transfer remains untested. The source contains inconsistent square coordinates in the flipping example and an unfinished Figure 9 caption in the original publication; subsequent sections and the final appendix are present.

Recurrent Neural Networks Learn to Store and Generate Sequences using Non-Linear Representations
abstract: The Linear Representation Hypothesis (LRH) states that neural networks learn to encode concepts as directions in activation space, and a strong version of the LRH states that models learn only such encodings. In this paper, we present a counterexample to this strong LRH: when trained to repeat an input token sequence, gated recurrent neural networks (RNNs) learn to represent the token at each position with a particular order of magnitude, rather than a direction. These representations have layered features that are impossible to locate in distinct linear subspaces. To show this, we train interventions to predict and manipulate tokens by learning the scaling factor corresponding to each sequence position. These interventions indicate that the smallest RNNs find only this magnitude-based solution, while larger RNNs have linear representations. These findings strongly indicate that interpretability research should not be confined by the LRH.
summary:
**Central idea**
The paper gives a counterexample to the *strong* Linear Representation Hypothesis, which holds that all concepts are encoded as directions or linear subspaces. Small GRUs trained to repeat a token sequence store each token at a position-specific *magnitude* inside a shared subspace. The authors call these "onion representations". During decoding, the dominant (largest-scale) token is read out, fed back autoregressively and subtracted, which exposes the next layer. Because every direction cuts across several layers, the position variables cannot be isolated in distinct linear subspaces.

**Experiments**
- **Setup:** single-layer GRUs with hidden size N ∈ {48, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024}, 5 seeds each. They are trained on a repeat task: 30 symbols, length up to 9, 1M training sequences, 5K disjoint test sequences. All models solve it (exact match 0.95–1.00).
- **Hypothesis 1 (unigram subspaces):** a DAS variant learns a rotation plus a Gumbel-softmax assignment of rotated dimensions to positions. It is evaluated with interchange interventions on the final encoder state.
- **Hypothesis 2 (bigram subspaces):** the same method, applied to adjacent-token tuples.
- **Hypothesis 3 (onion):** prompted by gates that close gradually and in sync in small models. A learned intervention adds a scaled embedding difference, s ⊙ (E[new] − E[old]), with s = gγ^j + βj + b. An analogous onion probe uses autoregressive subtraction.
- **Controls:** non-autoregressive GRUs decoded from PAD inputs; linear and MLP probes; a hand-built toy onion model.

**Key results**
- **Unigram DAS accuracy** rises with size: 0.00 / 0.00 / 0.01 / 0.18 / 0.91 / 1.00 for N = 48 to 1024. Bigram DAS succeeds for N ≥ 128 (0.54 at 128, 0.97+ above) but not for N ≤ 64 (0.01).
- **Onion intervention accuracy** is 0.83–0.95 across all sizes, including 0.87 at N = 64. With γ and β fixed at 1, accuracy falls to 21%.
- **Probes at N = 64:** linear and MLP probes fail (≤0.04), as does a non-autoregressive GRU probe (0.25). The onion probe reaches 0.97.
- **Non-autoregressive models** learn linear unigram subspaces down to N = 128 and bigram subspaces at N = 64. This shows DAS can work at small sizes, and that onion solutions need autoregressive feedback.
- **Onion interventions on large models** also work on large autoregressive models with linear representations. The authors attribute this to monotonic gate closing.
- **Formal results:** the onion featurizer is approximately bijective and induces an intervention algebra. Onion interchange interventions are shown to be equivalent to the scaled-difference intervention.

**Limitations / open questions**
- Only GRUs on a toy task were studied.
- Onion codes support only in-order or reverse-order access.
- They emerge only in small models; whether LLMs (or Transformers and SSMs) learn them is untested.
- Capacity depends on numerical precision.

title: The AI Scientist: Towards Fully Automated Open-Ended Scientific Discovery
CoSy: Evaluating Textual Explanations of Neurons
abstract: A crucial aspect of understanding the complex nature of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) is the ability to explain learned concepts within their latent representations. While methods exist to connect neurons to human-understandable textual descriptions, evaluating the quality of these explanations is challenging due to the lack of a unified quantitative approach. We introduce CoSy (Concept Synthesis), a novel, architecture-agnostic framework for evaluating textual explanations of latent neurons. Given textual explanations, our proposed framework uses a generative model conditioned on textual input to create data points representing the explanations. By comparing the neuron's response to these generated data points and control data points, we can estimate the quality of the explanation. We validate our framework through sanity checks and benchmark various neuron description methods for Computer Vision tasks, revealing significant differences in quality.
summary:
**Central idea**

CoSy evaluates textual neuron explanations through explanation-conditioned image generation. The target network processes generated concept images and natural control images; spatial neuron activations are average-pooled. AUC measures activation ranking between these groups, while MAD measures their mean activation difference divided by the control standard deviation. Explanation quality is operationalized as eliciting comparatively strong activation, without establishing a complete causal mechanism.

**Experiments**

Generation checks compare SDXL and Stable Cascade across five prompts, using 50 randomly selected classes each from ImageNet and Places365 and 50 generated images per class–prompt–generator condition. Metrics include CLIP-ViT-B/32 cosine similarity, pixel Euclidean distance, and LPIPS. Output-label checks examine 50 selected classes per model in ImageNet-trained ResNet18, DenseNet161, GoogLeNet, and ViT-B/16. The main benchmark compares MILAN, CLIP-Dissect, and INVERT on 50 randomly selected penultimate-layer neurons in each of six model–dataset configurations. Explanation generation uses 50,000 training images; validation datasets provide controls. INVERT uses single-concept explanations. Additional experiments compare ResNet18 layers, include FALCON, and test ten SDXL seeds for six output classes.

**Key results**

True output labels achieve mean AUCs of 0.98–0.99, versus 0.44–0.49 for random labels. Across the six penultimate-layer configurations, CLIP-Dissect scores 0.78–0.95 AUC, INVERT 0.73–0.96, and MILAN 0.44–0.65. Both alternatives exceed MILAN on mean MAD throughout. CLIP-Dissect exceeds INVERT on MAD in all four CNN configurations and DINO ViT-S/8; INVERT leads on supervised ViT-B/16. Scores generally increase with ResNet18 depth. Close-up photography gives the highest tested ImageNet CLIP similarity, whereas “photo of” performs best for Places365. Stable Cascade produces more mutually similar samples than SDXL under the tested conditions.

**Limitations / open questions**

Generator failures, especially for abstract descriptions, can lower scores independently of explanation accuracy. Hidden-neuron semantics lack ground truth, and these tests do not establish completeness, exclusivity, downstream importance, or human utility. INVERT directly optimizes AUC. Main FALCON comparisons relax its eligibility thresholds; original settings are separately evaluated on subsets of 7, 5, and 15 neurons. Layerwise numerical results cannot be recovered from the image-only plots in this rendering. No LLM or healthcare evaluation is performed. The supplied article is v2, dated December 5, 2024; metadata specifies the initial publication date.

title: A Multimodal Automated Interpretability Agent
abstract: This paper describes MAIA, a Multimodal Automated Interpretability Agent. MAIA is a system that uses neural models to automate neural model understanding tasks like feature interpretation and failure mode discovery. It equips a pre-trained vision-language model with a set of tools that support iterative experimentation on subcomponents of other models to explain their behavior. These include tools commonly used by human interpretability researchers: for synthesizing and editing inputs, computing maximally activating exemplars from real-world datasets, and summarizing and describing experimental results. Interpretability experiments proposed by MAIA compose these tools to describe and explain system behavior. We evaluate applications of MAIA to computer vision models. We first characterize MAIA's ability to describe (neuron-level) features in learned representations of images. Across several trained models and a novel dataset of synthetic vision neurons with paired ground-truth descriptions, MAIA produces descriptions comparable to those generated by expert human experimenters. We then show that MAIA can aid in two additional interpretability tasks: reducing sensitivity to spurious features, and automatically identifying inputs likely to be mis-classified.
summary:
**Central idea**
MAIA uses GPT-4V to write Python experiments, inspect visual and numerical results, and revise explanations of vision-model components. Tools retrieve 15 maximally activating dataset images, generate images with Stable Diffusion v1.5, edit them with Instruct-Pix2Pix, query activations and masks, and obtain descriptions from separate GPT-4V instances. Interpretation of LLM internals is not evaluated.

**Experiments**
The authors evaluate 100 neurons each from ResNet-152, DINO-ViT, and CLIP-RN50, with more units sampled from later layers. Eight interpretability researchers describe approximately 25% using the same tools. Predictive evaluation pools competing descriptions' image prompts, selects seven positive and seven neutral prompts per description, generates DALL-E 3 images, and measures activations. Comparators include MILAN and, in Appendix C, CLIP-Dissect. A benchmark of 85 synthetic neurons uses Grounded DINO and SAM to implement single-concept, disjunctive, and conditional responses. Further experiments assess tool ablations, human prediction from descriptions, Spawrious robustness, and exploratory classifier-bias discovery.

**Key results**
MAIA obtains higher model-average positive activations than MILAN in all three real-model evaluations, with layer-dependent performance. Synthetic-neuron judges prefer MAIA to MILAN in 73% of comparisons and to experts in 53% on the expert-annotated subset. In four-choice human prediction tasks on 25 neurons per model, MAIA descriptions yield 78.5%, 65.21%, and 67.39% accuracy for ResNet-152, CLIP-RN50, and DINO, versus MILAN's 66.0%, 57.19%, and 48.0%; expert descriptions score higher. On Spawrious O2O-Easy, MAIA retains 22 of 50 candidate final-layer neurons. Logistic regression fitted on their unbalanced validation activations achieves 83.7% shifted-test accuracy, versus 73.1% for the original classifier and 75.7% for unbalanced L1 selection of 22 neurons. Balanced-data selection of 22 neurons achieves 86.5%, averaged over ten balanced sets of 320 examples.

**Limitations / open questions**
Predictive evaluation depends on informative competing prompts and faithful image generation; it does not recover the full activation function. Synthetic neurons omit important low-level and perceptual response types. Generation failures and premature conclusions from single images can mislead MAIA. DALL-E 3 improves CNN positive-activation ablations but not DINO's. Bias discovery is qualitative, without aggregate detection accuracy or natural-image validation. Some confidence-interval formatting and tabulated aggregates are unclear; image-only figures limit further verification. The supplied article includes its appendices; metadata dates the original publication, while the text identifies version 2 dated February 11, 2025.

title: Universal Neurons in GPT2 Language Models
abstract: A basic question within the emerging field of mechanistic interpretability is the degree to which neural networks learn the same underlying mechanisms. In other words, are neural mechanisms universal across different models? In this work, we study the universality of individual neurons across GPT2 models trained from different initial random seeds, motivated by the hypothesis that universal neurons are likely to be interpretable. In particular, we compute pairwise correlations of neuron activations over 100 million tokens for every neuron pair across five different seeds and find that 1-5\% of neurons are universal, that is, pairs of neurons which consistently activate on the same inputs. We then study these universal neurons in detail, finding that they usually have clear interpretations and taxonomize them into a small number of neuron families. We conclude by studying patterns in neuron weights to establish several universal functional roles of neurons in simple circuits: deactivating attention heads, changing the entropy of the next token distribution, and predicting the next token to (not) be within a particular set.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper studies implementation universality: whether individual MLP neurons develop similar activation patterns across independently initialized language models. Cross-model recurrence serves as a discovery heuristic for interpretable components. A complementary weight analysis investigates recurring downstream roles, including token promotion and suppression, entropy modulation, and attention deactivation.

**Experiments**

The authors compare five replicas each of GPT2-small and GPT2-medium, with supporting Pythia analyses. All-pairs Pearson correlations use a 100-million-token Pile test subset in 512-token contexts, excluding padding, BOS, and newline tokens. A neuron's excess correlation is its mean maximum cross-model correlation minus the corresponding maximum-correlation baseline from Gaussian mixtures of layer activations. Neurons exceeding 0.5 undergo statistical characterization, manual inspection, and hundreds of vocabulary- or spaCy-derived explanation tests scored by conditional activation-variance reduction. Weight analyses examine vocabulary projections and neuron-to-head compositions. Fixed-activation interventions test selected entropy neurons against 20 screened random late-layer neurons; zero path ablations test attention deactivation.

**Key results**

Approximately 1–5% of neurons exceed the heuristic threshold: reported fractions are 4.16% for GPT2-small-a, 1.23% for GPT2-medium-a, and 1.26% for Pythia-160M. The separately reported GPT2-medium count, 1,253 of 98,304 neurons, implies approximately 1.27%, an internal discrepancy. Strongest matches concentrate at similar depths. Selected universal neurons tend to have larger weight norms, more negative biases, less frequent positive activations, and heavier-tailed preactivations. Recognizable families include current-token, alphabet, previous-token, position, syntax, and semantic-context neurons; apparent activation duplicates seldom have literally duplicate weights.

Across five GPT2-medium seeds and five Pythia sizes spanning 410M–6.9B, vocabulary-weight statistics show prediction-oriented directions increasing after mid-depth and suppression-oriented directions becoming prominent near the end. Selected opposing neuron pairs causally change mean output entropy through final LayerNorm scaling while largely retaining true-next-token rank. Selected neuron-to-head paths also affect BOS attention and head-output norms. The median GPT2-medium-a head's projected BOS value norm is reported as 19.4 times smaller than its average projected non-BOS value norm.

**Limitations / open questions**

Universality depends on the corpus, threshold, neuron basis, and Gaussian-mixture baseline. Interpretability enrichment lacks a controlled annotation comparison. Static vocabulary projections approximate direct effects. Entropy interventions do not establish natural uncertainty estimation and can reverse on individual inputs. Scaling, cross-family generalization, and explanations based on ensembling remain unresolved. Figures are unavailable visually in this rendering; quantitative claims above rely on explicit prose.

title: The Importance of Prompt Tuning for Automated Neuron Explanations
Rigorously Assessing Natural Language Explanations of Neurons
abstract: Natural language is an appealing medium for explaining how large language models process and store information, but evaluating the faithfulness of such explanations is challenging. To help address this, we develop two modes of evaluation for natural language explanations that claim individual neurons represent a concept in a text input. In the observational mode, we evaluate claims that a neuron $a$ activates on all and only input strings that refer to a concept picked out by the proposed explanation $E$. In the intervention mode, we construe $E$ as a claim that the neuron $a$ is a causal mediator of the concept denoted by $E$. We apply our framework to the GPT-4-generated explanations of GPT-2 XL neurons of Bills et al. (2023) and show that even the most confident explanations have high error rates and little to no causal efficacy. We close the paper by critically assessing whether natural language is a good choice for explanations and whether neurons are the best level of analysis.
summary:
**Central idea**
The paper distinguishes predicting a neuron's activation from identifying a representation that mediates concept-dependent behavior. It proposes observational tests comparing an explanation's string denotation with positive neuron activation, and intervention tests replacing base-input activations with source-input activations to seek the source's expected answer.

**Experiments**
The observational audit samples 300 explanations from approximately 1,700 GPT-2 XL neurons with GPT-4 activation-simulation correlation scores of at least 0.8—roughly the top 0.6% of the approximately 300,000-neuron collection. GPT-3.5-turbo generates 20 concept examples per explanation and labels corpus-derived activating strings. Researchers verify examples, remove invalid or ambiguous cases, and use regexes for form-based properties. Activation means greater than zero, with max pooling across multi-token strings. The paper defines precision as the fraction of explanation-positive examples that activate the neuron, and recall as the fraction of activating examples covered by the explanation. Linear probes combine similarly explained or randomly selected neurons. Intervention tests span twelve tasks across six concept families covering approximately 80,000 explanations, or 27% of the collection. Each task uses at least 30 strings with verified correct baseline next-token predictions and 256 sampled base–source pairs.

**Key results**
Single-neuron explanations achieve mean F1 0.56, precision 0.64, and recall 0.50; the unprobed random baseline has F1 0.00. The reported correlation between observational F1 and the original GPT-4 score is −0.1 within this selected panel. Sixteen-neuron probes achieve F1 0.73 for explanation-selected groups versus 0.69 for random groups. Explanation-ranked interventions generally perform similarly to random selection and substantially below token–activation correlation selection; numerical explanations show some advantage over random. For first-layer neurons, the authors report that the top 20% by correlation account for 80% of the causal effect. Larger neuron-group swaps yield more transfer, while the authors report finding no task with successful single-neuron causal control. A constructed sampling calculation shows how rare explanation errors can escape the original scoring procedure.

**Limitations / open questions**
Findings concern GPT-2 XL, selected concepts, templates, and intervention locations. Failed swaps do not exclude weaker, redundant, or differently situated causal roles. Finite semantic labels and binary activation thresholds constrain observational conclusions. Correlation-based selection uses activations on test inputs, so its advantage does not establish held-out generalization. Intervention plots are unavailable in the supplied rendering; qualitative trends are supported by the prose, but exact curve values cannot be extracted. Natural-language ambiguity and distributed computation motivate structured descriptions and analysis beyond individual neurons.

Counterfactual Interventions Reveal the Causal Effect of Relative Clause Representations on Agreement Prediction
abstract: When language models process syntactically complex sentences, do they use their representations of syntax in a manner that is consistent with the grammar of the language? We propose AlterRep, an intervention-based method to address this question. For any linguistic feature of a given sentence, AlterRep generates counterfactual representations by altering how the feature is encoded, while leaving intact all other aspects of the original representation. By measuring the change in a model's word prediction behavior when these counterfactual representations are substituted for the original ones, we can draw conclusions about the causal effect of the linguistic feature in question on the model's behavior. We apply this method to study how BERT models of different sizes process relative clauses (RCs). We find that BERT variants use RC boundary information during word prediction in a manner that is consistent with the rules of English grammar; this RC boundary information generalizes to a considerable extent across different RC types, suggesting that BERT represents RCs as an abstract linguistic category.
summary:
**Central idea**

AlterRep tests whether manipulating a linguistic representation changes predictions as grammar predicts. It uses Iterative Null Space Projection (INLP) to learn orthogonal linear classifiers, then reflects and scales activation components along their directions while preserving the orthogonal complement. Here, the target is whether a masked main-clause verb is represented as inside or outside a relative clause (RC). Geometric preservation does not guarantee preservation of every unrelated semantic property. Appendix A.1 derives the desired classifier signs; strict inequalities require nonzero original margins.

**Experiments**

Interventions replace the masked verb's representation at one layer at a time in BERT-base, large, medium, small, mini, and tiny. Subspace training uses five RC constructions and two matched coordination constructions, each containing 4,800 sentences. Training verbs are past tense to reduce overt agreement cues. Defaults are eight classifier directions and magnitude α=4. Agreement evaluation uses Marvin–Linzen sentences augmented with passive RCs, with 1,750 sentences per construction and main verbs restricted to is/are. The principal metric is incorrect-verb probability normalized over those two alternatives. Controls include matching noun numbers, simple agreement, sentential complements, and ten random subspaces; appendices vary magnitude and dimensionality.

**Key results**

For BERT-base with number attractors, inside-RC interventions increased normalized error probability by up to 14 percentage points at layer 7. Outside-RC interventions decreased it by up to two points overall, with overlapping error bars, and by up to 16 points at layer 6 among initially incorrect examples. Across tested subspace dimensions, up to 30% of initially incorrect verb preferences became correct. RC-membership probes exceeded 90% accuracy throughout BERT-base's contextual layers, while grammar-consistent intervention effects concentrated in middle layers. Effects transferred across RC types with smaller magnitudes. Principal control constructions showed no significant changes at default settings. Selected layers in large, medium, small, and mini also showed predicted effects beyond random-subspace changes; tiny did not.

**Limitations / open questions**

The experiments establish effects of specified activation edits; interpreting them as selective changes to naturally used RC information requires additional assumptions. Nonlinear downstream processing makes null intervention results inconclusive. Smaller models were more sensitive to random edits. Large magnitudes, especially α=8, increased errors on control sentences, and large subspaces affected uncontextualized embeddings. Evidence concerns templated English, non-nested RCs, and a two-copula outcome; cross-construction transfer suggests partial sharing rather than complete abstraction.

Validating Mechanistic Interpretations: An Axiomatic Approach
abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse engineer the computation performed by a neural network in terms of its internal components. Although there is a growing body of research on mechanistic interpretation of neural networks, the notion of a mechanistic interpretation itself is often ad-hoc. Inspired by the notion of abstract interpretation from the program analysis literature that aims to develop approximate semantics for programs, we give a set of axioms that formally characterize a mechanistic interpretation as a description that approximately captures the semantics of the neural network under analysis in a compositional manner. We demonstrate the applicability of these axioms for validating mechanistic interpretations on an existing, well-known interpretability study as well as on a new case study involving a Transformer-based model trained to solve the well-known 2-SAT problem.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper evaluates mechanistic interpretations as executable symbolic programs aligned with decompositions of neural networks. Abstraction maps convert neural activations into symbolic states; concretization maps convert symbols back into activations. Four axioms measure agreement for individual components and composed prefixes, both at intermediate states and after replacing neural computation with interpreted computation. Validation depends on the input distribution, decomposition, mappings, and equality criterion. Formal derivations establish depth-dependent bounds relating component and prefix errors.

**Experiments**

The authors train a two-block ReLU decoder-only transformer on ten-clause 2-SAT formulas over up to five variables. It has 128-dimensional embeddings, 512-unit MLPs, one first-block attention head, and four second-block heads. The balanced dataset contains two million formulas, split 60%/40%; test accuracy is 99.76%. A separate balanced 200,000-formula analysis dataset uses the same split, yielding 80,000 analysis test formulas. Attention analysis, canonical clause representations, and decision trees with at most four leaves produce a parser–evaluator interpretation. The authors also validate an existing single-block modular-addition transformer, modulo 113, using learned linear alignment maps. Reported epsilon values are one-sided 95% Clopper–Pearson upper bounds on disagreement probabilities.

**Key results**

The 2-SAT parser perfectly recovers unordered clause lists on the analysis test set, giving epsilon approximately 0.0000374, while replacing its representations produces output disagreement bounded by approximately 0.0418. Thirty-four relevant second-block neurons exhibit assignment-dependent responses. Decision-tree interpretations predict their joint thresholded state better than simpler disjunction-only interpretations: epsilon 0.182 versus 0.309. Nevertheless, final model disagreement favors disjunction-only interpretations: 0.00290 versus 0.0128. These replacement results depend on assigning predicted active neurons activation 2, above the 0.5 abstraction threshold. Injecting 1% replacement noise per abstract clause exposes propagated errors through prefix tests. The modular-addition interpretation achieves perfect sampled agreement, epsilon 0.000335, under selected discretizations; rounding its second intermediate state to one decimal instead gives epsilon 1 for representation-equivalence tests.

**Limitations / open questions**

The four axioms are proposed as necessary checks without establishing general sufficiency. Downstream-equivalence discretization weakens internal-state validation, and unrestricted alignment maps can absorb substantive computation. Human interpretability remains subjective. Experiments cover two small algorithmic models; IOI receives only an application sketch. Compiler-based derivability axioms remain untested, and efficient validation of arbitrary parallel replacements remains open.

title: Compact Proofs of Model Performance via Mechanistic Interpretability
abstract: We propose using mechanistic interpretability -- techniques for reverse engineering model weights into human-interpretable algorithms -- to derive and compactly prove formal guarantees on model performance. We prototype this approach by formally proving accuracy lower bounds for a small transformer trained on Max-of-K, validating proof transferability across 151 random seeds and four values of K. We create 102 different computer-assisted proof strategies and assess their length and tightness of bound on each of our models. Using quantitative metrics, we find that shorter proofs seem to require and provide more mechanistic understanding. Moreover, we find that more faithful mechanistic understanding leads to tighter performance bounds. We confirm these connections by qualitatively examining a subset of our proofs. Finally, we identify compounding structureless errors as a key challenge for using mechanistic interpretability to generate compact proofs on model performance.
summary:
**Central idea**

Mechanistic interpretations can guide proofs of a particular trained model's performance over a specified input distribution. A weight-dependent certificate computation is paired with a general soundness argument. Unexplained contributions are bounded pessimistically over relaxed input spaces. Structural understanding can reduce certificate computation while retaining nonvacuous performance bounds.

**Experiments**

The main study trains 151 one-layer, one-head attention-only transformers on Max-of-4: predict the largest of four uniformly sampled integers from 0–63. Models have hidden/head dimension 32, learned positional embeddings, and no biases, MLPs, or layer normalization. Each receives 384,000 training sequences over 3,000 AdamW steps. Exact evaluation covers all 64^4 inputs. The authors report 102 proof strategies, comparing estimated certificate FLOPs, asymptotic complexity, accuracy bounds, and bound-to-actual-accuracy ratios. Four additional configurations contain 151 models each: Max-of-5, Max-of-10, and Max-of-20 with vocabulary 64, plus Max-of-10 with vocabulary 128. Their actual accuracies are estimated by importance sampling.

**Key results**

The main models approximately implement maximum selection by attending more strongly to larger integers and copying attended tokens through OV. Their leading-to-second QK singular-value ratio averages 620 ± 130. Zeroing position-dependent QK contributions changes accuracy from 99.92 ± 0.15% to 99.93 ± 0.11%.

Table 1 reports a cubic certificate bound of 95.31 ± 0.87% at approximately 2^25 FLOPs, versus 2^47 FLOPs for exhaustive evaluation. A subcubic strategy establishes 70.2 ± 3.3% at approximately 2^21 FLOPs; omitting its mean+diff refinement reduces the bound to 34.9 ± 8.0%. The cubic bound reaches 88.4 ± 4.0% on Max-of-20. Within fixed proof classes, stronger rank-one QK structure correlates with tighter normalized bounds. Formal derivations establish relaxed-sequence bounds and efficient matrix-error inequalities.

**Limitations / open questions**

Uniform-distribution accuracy bounds do not certify correctness on every input. Scaling to larger architectures and language tasks remains open, and OV verification remains a bottleneck. Independently bounding residual factors can overestimate composed errors by orders of magnitude. Unexplained dimensionality is a proposed understanding proxy without independent validation. Reported FLOPs approximate certificate checking and exclude discovery costs, including gap-table search. Execution traces are omitted, some proofs are sketches, and floating-point versus real-arithmetic certification is deferred. Appendix figures and proof-count arithmetic contain inconsistencies; the numerical comparisons above follow the main table.

title: Scale Alone Does not Improve Mechanistic Interpretability in Vision Models
abstract: In light of the recent widespread adoption of AI systems, understanding the internal information processing of neural networks has become increasingly critical. Most recently, machine vision has seen remarkable progress by scaling neural networks to unprecedented levels in dataset and model size. We here ask whether this extraordinary increase in scale also positively impacts the field of mechanistic interpretability. In other words, has our understanding of the inner workings of scaled neural networks improved as well? We use a psychophysical paradigm to quantify one form of mechanistic interpretability for a diverse suite of nine models and find no scaling effect for interpretability - neither for model nor dataset size. Specifically, none of the investigated state-of-the-art models are easier to interpret than the GoogLeNet model from almost a decade ago. Latest-generation vision models appear even less interpretable than older architectures, hinting at a regression rather than improvement, with modern models sacrificing interpretability for accuracy. These results highlight the need for models explicitly designed to be mechanistically interpretable and the need for more helpful interpretability methods to increase our understanding of networks at an atomic level. We release a dataset containing more than 130'000 human responses from our psychophysical evaluation of 767 units across nine models. This dataset facilitates research on automated instead of human-based interpretability evaluations, which can ultimately be leveraged to directly optimize the mechanistic interpretability of models.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper asks whether scaling vision models or training datasets improves human understanding of individual units. Interpretability is operationalized as accuracy in choosing which of two natural images activates a unit more strongly, given explanatory reference images. The selected models show no practically relevant improvement with scale under this measure.

**Experiments**

Nine models span GoogLeNet, ResNet-50, WideResNet-50, DenseNet-201, ConvNeXt-B, ViT-B, CLIP ResNet-50, CLIP ViT-B, and adversarially robust ResNet-50. Parameter counts range from 6.8 million to 89 million; dataset comparisons contrast ImageNet training with 400-million-example LAION pretraining. The main protocol samples 84 units per model, uniformly over eligible layers and then units, with 30 responses per unit per condition. Each trial supplies nine maximally and nine minimally activating reference images. Natural exemplars are tested for all nine models; synthetic visualizations for seven, excluding both ViTs. IMI contains 133,310 recorded trial responses, including 76,000 passing quality checks, and stimuli for 767 units.

**Key results**

Natural exemplars yield approximately 80% accuracy on extreme-activation queries versus 50% chance. No evaluated newer model improves on GoogLeNet. Higher classification accuracy and more human-like decisions do not accompany better interpretability; synthetic-condition scores may decline with accuracy. Natural exemplars outperform synthetic visualizations in every CNN comparison. Robust ResNet-50 significantly improves synthetic-condition accuracy over standard ResNet-50, but its natural exemplars remain more helpful. Less extreme queries sharply reduce performance in ResNet-50 and CLIP ResNet-50; synthetic-condition accuracy approaches chance already at the 99th-percentile condition. Natural-condition layer-average accuracy correlates with depth most clearly in CLIP ResNet-50 and CLIP ViT-B, with Spearman correlations of 0.39 and 0.64. Local contrast and two activation-sparsity measures show little association with unit scores. Natural-versus-synthetic unit-score correlations vary across models.

**Limitations / open questions**

The measure concerns individual-unit activation prediction, not complete circuits or causal mechanisms, and assumes axis-aligned units are useful analysis targets. Heterogeneous architectures, objectives, and datasets prevent isolating scale causally; nonsignificant comparisons do not establish equivalence. Synthetic results depend on the visualization recipe. Only 63 of 80 difficulty-study units were shared across difficulty levels, though restricting analysis preserves the decline. The unimodal-activation illustration uses 15 GoogLeNet units, rather than establishing matched behavioral regimes for the difficulty-study models. The reported 84 units per model and 767 total are not fully reconciled. Learning generalizable automated interpretability measures from IMI remains future work.

title: A Unified Theory of Sparse Dictionary Learning in Mechanistic Interpretability: Piecewise Biconvexity and Spurious Minima
abstract: As AI models achieve remarkable capabilities across diverse domains, understanding what representations they learn and how they encode concepts has become increasingly important for both scientific progress and trustworthy deployment. Recent works in mechanistic interpretability have widely reported that neural networks represent meaningful concepts as linear directions in their representation spaces and often encode diverse concepts in superposition. Various sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods, including sparse autoencoders, transcoders, and crosscoders, are utilized to address this by training auxiliary models with sparsity constraints to disentangle these superposed concepts into monosemantic features. These methods are the backbone of modern mechanistic interpretability, yet in practice they consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, with very limited theoretical understanding of why these phenomena occur. Existing theoretical work is limited to tied-weight sparse autoencoders, leaving the broader family of SDL methods without formal grounding. We develop the first unified theoretical framework that casts all major SDL variants as a single piecewise biconvex optimization problem, and characterize its global solution set, non-identifiability, and spurious optima. This analysis yields principled explanations for feature absorption and dead neurons. To expose these pathologies under full ground-truth access, we introduce the Linear Representation Bench. Guided by our theory, we propose feature anchoring, a novel technique that restores SDL identifiability, substantially improving feature recovery across synthetic benchmarks and real neural representations.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper unifies sparse autoencoders, transcoders, and crosscoders as encoder–decoder reconstruction problems. Under shared sparse, nonnegative linear generators, it analyzes an isolated-feature surrogate loss. Its fixed-mask reconstruction objective is separately convex in encoder and decoder weights. Feature anchoring adds squared penalties aligning selected encoder rows and decoder columns with supplied directions. The supplied text is arXiv v6, dated May 2, 2026.

**Experiments**

Linear Representation Bench defaults to 100,000 samples, 1,000 generating features in 768 dimensions, independent activation probability 0.01, and maximum pairwise interference 0.1. The main seven-method comparison uses 16,000 latents and excludes anchored generating features from evaluation. Metrics are the fraction exceeding best-match absolute-inner-product threshold 0.95 and mean best-match similarity. ImageNet-1K experiments use reported CLIP-ViT-B/32 embeddings, 16,384-latent SAEs, and 30 class-mean anchors. A separate Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer-12 experiment compares SAE training with and without dead-latent resampling after step 5,000: 131,072 latents, 30,000 steps, and 4,096 FineWeb-Edu token activations per step.

**Key results**

Synthetic recovery increases from 84.90% to 87.63% for TopK, 84.80% to 89.38% for BatchTopK, and 83.70% to 87.32% for Matryoshka. Transcoder and crosscoder gains are smaller. ReLU and JumpReLU remain at 0% recovery at threshold 0.95 despite improved mean similarity. CLIP class-mean proxy recovery increases from 0% to 24.13–24.45%; exclusion of anchored classes is unspecified. Resampling reportedly lowers final training loss, without numerical effect sizes. An explicit two-feature Top-1 construction establishes a positive-loss blockwise partial optimum with one polysemantic latent and one dead latent.

**Limitations / open questions**

The general landscape claims exceed what the supplied derivations establish. The approximation uses independence and activation scaling properties absent from the stated assumptions; fixed-threshold JumpReLU is not positively homogeneous. The general partial-minimum proof contains an invalid encoder-gradient cancellation and invokes an unstated target-direction condition. The absorption proof assumes strict activation ordering and does not preserve other groups under its threshold change. Partial optimality does not establish gradient-descent trapping, and no theorem proves that partial anchoring restores identifiability. The main synthetic setting also falls outside the stated extreme-sparsity condition. Class means provide supervised proxies rather than known natural features. Appendix G contains conflicting sparsity conventions and recovery/similarity reporting, alongside ties and slight anchoring degradations. Seed uncertainty, convergence guarantees, and natural LLM feature recovery remain unresolved.

title: Do I Know This Entity? Knowledge Awareness and Hallucinations in Language Models
abstract: Hallucinations in large language models are a widespread problem, yet the mechanisms behind whether models will hallucinate are poorly understood, limiting our ability to solve this problem. Using sparse autoencoders as an interpretability tool, we discover that a key part of these mechanisms is entity recognition, where the model detects if an entity is one it can recall facts about. Sparse autoencoders uncover meaningful directions in the representation space, these detect whether the model recognizes an entity, e.g. detecting it doesn't know about an athlete or a movie. This suggests that models can have self-knowledge: internal representations about their own capabilities. These directions are causally relevant: capable of steering the model to refuse to answer questions about known entities, or to hallucinate attributes of unknown entities when it would otherwise refuse. We demonstrate that despite the sparse autoencoders being trained on the base model, these directions have a causal effect on the chat model's refusal behavior, suggesting that chat finetuning has repurposed this existing mechanism. Furthermore, we provide an initial exploration into the mechanistic role of these directions in the model, finding that they disrupt the attention of downstream heads that typically move entity attributes to the final token.
summary:
**Central idea**

Sparse autoencoders identify residual-stream directions associated with whether a model can recall attributes of an entity. These directions influence knowledge refusal and downstream entity attention, suggesting a restricted form of knowledge awareness. Separate pre-answer uncertainty latents predict incorrect answers among responses where the model does not refuse.

**Experiments**

The dataset contains Wikidata attributes for 7,487 basketball players, 10,895 movies, 7,904 cities, and 8,448 songs before knowledge-based filtering. Entities are labeled known when at least two tested attributes are recalled correctly and unknown when none are; intermediate cases are discarded. Entities are split 50%/10%/40% for training, validation, and testing. Gemma Scope SAEs on Gemma 2 2B/9B and LlamaScope SAEs on Llama 3.1 8B identify final-entity-token latents using activation-frequency differences across labels. Tests include instruction-tuned-model steering, weight orthogonalization, known-to-unknown activation patching, attention measurements, explicit recognition questions, 283 post-cutoff song titles, and FineWeb predictability controls.

**Key results**

The strongest cross-type recognition latents occur in intermediate layers. In Gemma 2 2B's reported 100-query refusal panels, increasing the unknown-entity direction induces almost 100% refusal across entity types; removing that direction from residual-writing weights substantially reduces refusal. Base-model directions affect instruction-tuned models, but effects vary: known-entity steering does not reduce refusal in Llama 3.1 8B. Steering also changes attention to entity tokens, including attribute-extraction heads. Gemma 2 9B's top unknown direction has weak attention effects relative to random latents, whereas its second-ranked direction has clearer effects. A separate Gemma 2B IT layer-13 uncertainty latent achieves 0.732 AUROC and approximately 0.72 F1 on non-refused answers, excluding players because nearly all player questions are refused. Gemma 2B IT is distinct from Gemma 2 2B IT. FineWeb activation–token-probability correlations are small, ranging approximately from zero to 0.067.

**Limitations / open questions**

Attribute accuracy imperfectly labels entity knowledge, and refusal measurement uses phrase matching. Main refusal-steering coefficients of 400–550 are approximately twice the local residual-stream norm. Interventions establish causal influence without identifying a complete circuit or proving that fine-tuning repurposed precisely the same natural mechanism. Corpus-wide correlations do not exclude more specific predictability confounds. Error prediction lacks a reported strong-baseline comparison. Numerous plotted effect sizes are not recoverable from the supplied figure captions. The supplied text is v2, dated February 8, 2025; metadata gives the initial publication date.

abstract: Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have achieved impressive results in a variety of linguistic processing tasks, suggesting that they can induce non-trivial properties of language. We investigate here to what extent RNNs learn to track abstract hierarchical syntactic structure. We test whether RNNs trained with a generic language modeling objective in four languages (Italian, English, Hebrew, Russian) can predict long-distance number agreement in various constructions. We include in our evaluation nonsensical sentences where RNNs cannot rely on semantic or lexical cues ("The colorless green ideas I ate with the chair sleep furiously"), and, for Italian, we compare model performance to human intuitions. Our language-model-trained RNNs make reliable predictions about long-distance agreement, and do not lag much behind human performance. We thus bring support to the hypothesis that RNNs are not just shallow-pattern extractors, but they also acquire deeper grammatical competence.
summary:
**Central idea**
The paper tests whether RNN language models trained only on next-word prediction learn the abstract hierarchical structure needed for long-distance number agreement. It responds to Linzen et al. (2016), who concluded that the language-modeling objective was insufficient. The key methodological addition is a set of *nonce* sentences. In these, every content word is replaced by a random word with the same part of speech and morphology. The result stays grammatical but is meaningless, which removes lexical, semantic and collocational cues.

**Experiments**
- **Test sets.** Agreement constructions were harvested automatically from Universal Dependencies v2.0 treebanks for Italian, English, Hebrew and Russian. A construction is a cue–target dependency with at least 3 intervening tokens that agrees in number consistently, with at least 10 singular and 10 plural instances. This yielded 8, 2, 18 and 21 constructions, with 119, 41, 373 and 442 original sentences. Each original sentence received 9 nonce variants.
- **Metric.** A model is correct if it assigns higher probability to the correct-number form of the target than to the opposite-number form.
- **Models.** LSTMs and simple RNNs (650 or 200 hidden units) were trained on 90M-token Wikipedia subsets with a 50K vocabulary. Baselines were a unigram model, a 5-gram Kneser-Ney model and a 5-gram-window LSTM.
- **Human comparison.** Italian human judgments came from Mechanical Turk, with about 9.5 judgments per item and filler-based quality filtering.
- **Replication.** The authors re-evaluated their English LSTM on Linzen et al.'s attractor test set.

**Key results**
- **Accuracy.** Figures are averages over the 5 lowest-perplexity LSTMs.

  | Language | Original | Nonce |
  |---|---|---|
  | Italian | 92.1 | 85.5 |
  | English | 81.0 | 74.1 |
  | Hebrew | 94.7 | 80.8 |
  | Russian | 96.1 | 88.8 |

  The 5-gram KN model was near the unigram baseline on nonce sentences, and the 5-gram LSTM fell between KN and the full LSTM.
- **Perplexity.** Across 68 LSTM hyperparameter variants per language, agreement accuracy correlated with validation perplexity (r from −0.55 in Hebrew to −0.78 in English, p<0.001).
- **Humans in Italian.** Humans scored 94.5 on original and 88.4 on nonce sentences, versus 92.1 and 85.5 for the LSTM. Per-sentence human preference margins correlated with the model's log-probability differences (Spearman, p<0.05 original, p<0.001 nonce). Accuracy degraded with the number of attractors for both humans and the LSTM.
- **Linzen et al. attractor set.** The LM-trained LSTM greatly outperformed Linzen et al.'s best LM-trained model and approached their number-supervised model.

**Limitations / open questions**
- English has only 2 constructions and 41 original sentences.
- Nonce generation does not respect argument structure.
- Part-of-speech ambiguity and alternative parses confound some constructions, especially in English and Hebrew.
- The study is behavioral only. It does not analyze how agreement is represented internally.
- Which tuning differences explain the gap with Linzen et al. remains unresolved.

title: HotFlip: White-Box Adversarial Examples for Text Classification
Stop Explaining Black Box Machine Learning Models for High Stakes Decisions and Use Interpretable Models Instead
Human-centered artificial intelligence and machine learning
Explainable prediction of medical codes from clinical text
Is Attention Interpretable?
summary:
**Central idea**

Attention magnitudes provide noisy rankings of the importance of representations entering an attention layer. The paper tests this narrow explanatory role by intervening after encoding, distinguishing intermediate-representation importance from original-word importance. Outcomes are output Jensen–Shannon divergence and predicted-class changes.

**Experiments**

The study trains 24 classifiers: hierarchical attention networks (HAN) and flat attention networks (FLAN), each with bidirectional GRU, convolutional, or absent contextualizing encoders, across four datasets. Yahoo Answers and IMDB have ten classes; Amazon and Yelp have five. Their test sets contain 50,000, 13,548, 650,000, and 50,000 examples, respectively. Convolutional encoders concatenate width-three and width-five convolutions. Only final additive-softmax attention is tested, over sentences in HAN and words in FLAN.

Interventions zero selected attention weights and renormalize the remainder while retaining encoded representations. Singleton tests compare the highest-weight item with a different random item, excluding length-one sequences. Multi-item tests erase prefixes ranked by attention, random order, the derivative of maximum output-class probability, or attention multiplied by that derivative. They additionally exclude cases where the decision never changes, including after complete erasure replaces the pooled representation with zero; retained counts are unreported.

**Key results**

Highest-attention erasures usually produce larger output divergence than random erasures, but differences frequently remain tiny despite substantial attention gaps. For Yahoo Answers HANrnn, highest-weight erasure flips 9.2% of eligible predictions.

Gradient rankings find smaller decision-flipping sets than attention on over half the analyzed examples in ten of sixteen encoder-equipped models. In every encoder-equipped model, gradient wins occur at least 1.6 times as often as attention wins. Product-selected singleton erasures flip predictions more frequently than attention-selected erasures in all 24 configurations. Appendix prose says gradient-only singleton selection performs worse in 14 configurations, but the displayed tables indicate ten. Recurrent models generally require erasing larger fractions than locally contextualized or encoderless alternatives, especially in FLAN.

**Limitations / open questions**

Ranked-prefix searches do not establish globally minimal erasure sets or gradients as ground truth. Renormalization does not guarantee natural intervened states. Signal redistribution is an interpretation of architectural comparisons, which also differ in accuracy and training settings. Results concern final additive attention in classification, leaving transformer self-attention, earlier layers, and generation open. Some classifiers underperform previously reported HAN accuracies. Plot images are unavailable in the supplied rendering; quantitative findings above use prose and readable tables.

Exemplary Natural Images Explain CNN Activations Better than State-of-the-Art Feature Visualization
abstract: Feature visualizations such as synthetic maximally activating images are a widely used explanation method to better understand the information processing of convolutional neural networks (CNNs). At the same time, there are concerns that these visualizations might not accurately represent CNNs' inner workings. Here, we measure how much extremely activating images help humans to predict CNN activations. Using a well-controlled psychophysical paradigm, we compare the informativeness of synthetic images by Olah et al. (2017) with a simple baseline visualization, namely exemplary natural images that also strongly activate a specific feature map. Given either synthetic or natural reference images, human participants choose which of two query images leads to strong positive activation. The experiments are designed to maximize participants' performance, and are the first to probe intermediate instead of final layer representations. We find that synthetic images indeed provide helpful information about feature map activations ($82\pm4\%$ accuracy; chance would be $50\%$). However, natural images - originally intended as a baseline - outperform synthetic images by a wide margin ($92\pm2\%$). Additionally, participants are faster and more confident for natural images, whereas subjective impressions about the interpretability of the feature visualizations are mixed. The higher informativeness of natural images holds across most layers, for both expert and lay participants as well as for hand- and randomly-picked feature visualizations. Even if only a single reference image is given, synthetic images provide less information than natural images ($65\pm5\%$ vs. $73\pm4\%$). In summary, synthetic images from a popular feature visualization method are significantly less informative for assessing CNN activations than natural images. We argue that visualization methods should improve over this baseline.
summary:
**Central idea**
The paper evaluates feature visualization through human prediction of intermediate CNN activations. It compares synthetic activation-extreme images generated with Olah et al. (2017) against extreme natural exemplars, establishing a demanding baseline for explanations of responses to natural inputs.

**Experiments**
Two laboratory studies use an ImageNet-trained Inception V1, specifically the Lucid implementation, and spatially averaged pre-ReLU channel activations. Natural stimuli come from the 50,000-image ILSVRC 2012 validation set. Participants choose the more strongly activating of two natural query images, report confidence, and receive trial feedback; reaction time is recorded. Queries come from opposite activation extremes. Experiment I includes 10 experts and 45 channels across nine Inception modules: 36 randomly selected channels and nine selected for interpretability. Each participant completes 45 main trials per reference condition: synthetic, natural, or absent. Reference-present trials show nine minima and nine maxima. Experiment II includes 23 participants, comprising 10 experts and 13 laypeople, and 80 channels across five modules. It counterbalances one versus nine references and maximum-only versus minimum-plus-maximum presentation, with 20 main trials per presentation scheme and reference type.

**Key results**
Experiment I accuracy is 82±4% with synthetic references and 92±2% with natural references, versus approximately chance without references. Uncertainties denote twice the standard error across participant averages. On correct trials, natural references yield greater confidence and approximately 3.7-second faster responses. Their accuracy advantage holds across most layers, both expertise groups, and hand-picked channels. Experiment II detects no expertise main effect (p=.44), without establishing equivalence. Its minimum-plus-maximum, nine-reference condition yields 91±3% with natural versus 72±4% with synthetic references. Additional references and inclusion of minima tend to improve performance, especially for natural images. Hand-picking shows a small observed advantage: within-reference comparisons are nonsignificant, but the marginal selection effect has p=.035. Subjective intuitiveness varies considerably.

**Limitations / open questions**
Results concern one architecture, one visualization method, and deliberately favorable extreme-query discrimination; they do not establish comprehensive semantic understanding or causal circuit knowledge. Synthetic references generally elicit roughly an order of magnitude larger activations. A disclosed sampling bug reduces the intended nine-reference natural-image pool from 200 to 110 images per activation tail and places positive queries at ranks 91–110. Single-reference synthetic accuracy is inconsistently reported as 65±5% in the abstract and 64±5% in Section 4.5. Figure images and plot values are unavailable in this rendering. Less extreme queries, combined natural/synthetic references, other architectures, and unit combinations remain open.

title: How Well do Feature Visualizations Support Causal Understanding of CNN Activations?
abstract: A precise understanding of why units in an artificial network respond to certain stimuli would constitute a big step towards explainable artificial intelligence. One widely used approach towards this goal is to visualize unit responses via activation maximization. These synthetic feature visualizations are purported to provide humans with precise information about the image features that cause a unit to be activated - an advantage over other alternatives like strongly activating natural dataset samples. If humans indeed gain causal insight from visualizations, this should enable them to predict the effect of an intervention, such as how occluding a certain patch of the image (say, a dog's head) changes a unit's activation. Here, we test this hypothesis by asking humans to decide which of two square occlusions causes a larger change to a unit's activation. Both a large-scale crowdsourced experiment and measurements with experts show that on average the extremely activating feature visualizations by Olah et al. (2017) indeed help humans on this task ($68 \pm 4$% accuracy; baseline performance without any visualizations is $60 \pm 3$%). However, they do not provide any substantial advantage over other visualizations (such as e.g. dataset samples), which yield similar performance ($66\pm3$% to $67 \pm3$% accuracy). Taken together, we propose an objective psychophysical task to quantify the benefit of unit-level interpretability methods for humans, and find no evidence that a widely-used feature visualization method provides humans with better "causal understanding" of unit activations than simple alternative visualizations.
summary:
**Central idea**
Synthetic activation-maximization feature visualizations (Olah et al., 2017) are often said to reveal the image features that *cause* a unit to fire, which would be an advantage over natural dataset exemplars. The authors operationalize causal understanding as the ability to predict the effect of an intervention. They then test whether feature visualizations improve that ability in humans.

**Experiments**
- **Task:** a two-alternative forced-choice psychophysical task on InceptionV1 (ImageNet). Participants see 9 reference images for a channel (spatially averaged). They then choose which of two copies of a top-activating ImageNet image, each with a 90×90 mean-colour occlusion patch, activates the unit more. The two patches are placed where activation is maximal and minimal across all occlusion locations.
- **Units:** 18 units (one random unit per 3×3 and Pool branch in each of 9 Inception layers), with 10 image sets per unit.
- **Reference conditions (between participants):** Synthetic, Natural (top exemplars), Mixed (5 natural + 4 synthetic), Blurred natural (all but the max-activating patch blurred), and None.
- **Participants:** 50 MTurk participants per condition who passed five preregistered exclusion criteria, plus the two first authors as experts.
- **Heuristic baselines:** Center, Primary Object (author-labelled), pixel Variance, and Saliency (DeepGaze IIE).
- **Replication:** an MTurk replication of Borowski et al. (2021) with 130 participants per condition, run on the 3×3 branch.

**Key results**
- **Accuracy by condition (MTurk):** Synthetic 67±4%, versus None 60±3%. The other visualizations were similar (66–67%). Only None differed significantly from the other conditions (Mann-Whitney U, p<.05).
- **Experts:** only 1–6% higher than MTurk participants.
- **Heuristics:** the Object and Variance baselines reached about 63% without any references, within about 4 points of the visualization conditions.
- **Decision consistency:** Cohen's kappa between deciders was at most about 0.40. Agreement with the Saliency baseline was highest. Participants agreed with each other more in the natural-image conditions and were relatively inconsistent in the Synthetic condition.
- **Variation:** performance varied strongly by unit and image set; one unit was below chance and some were easy. Performance increased with the relative activation difference between the two query images, more strongly in the Pool branch (Spearman correlations).
- **Replication:** natural references beat synthetic ones on the pairwise activation-discrimination task (84±3% vs 65±3%), reproducing the earlier lab finding.

**Limitations / open questions**
- Interventions are limited to fixed-size square occlusions, and only 18 units of a single network were tested.
- Trials use a binary choice rather than free counterfactual generation.
- Ground truth is ambiguous for many images that contain several objects.
- Only the 5 participants per image set limit image-level analysis.
- Other notions of causality, other visualization methods, and other networks remain to be tested.

title: Don't trust your eyes: on the (un)reliability of feature visualizations
abstract: How do neural networks extract patterns from pixels? Feature visualizations attempt to answer this important question by visualizing highly activating patterns through optimization. Today, visualization methods form the foundation of our knowledge about the internal workings of neural networks, as a type of mechanistic interpretability. Here we ask: How reliable are feature visualizations? We start our investigation by developing network circuits that trick feature visualizations into showing arbitrary patterns that are completely disconnected from normal network behavior on natural input. We then provide evidence for a similar phenomenon occurring in standard, unmanipulated networks: feature visualizations are processed very differently from standard input, casting doubt on their ability to "explain" how neural networks process natural images. This can be used as a sanity check for feature visualizations. We underpin our empirical findings by theory proving that the set of functions that can be reliably understood by feature visualization is extremely small and does not include general black-box neural networks. Therefore, a promising way forward could be the development of networks that enforce certain structures in order to ensure more reliable feature visualizations.
summary:
**Central idea**

Activation-maximizing images can identify inputs that excite a unit without reliably explaining its responses to natural images. The paper investigates this distinction through adversarial model modifications, a layerwise activation-similarity check, and formal limits on predicting functions from extremal inputs and values.

**Experiments**

A classifier-gated circuit redirects Inception-V1 visualizations toward unrelated units or hard-coded images while largely preserving ImageNet performance. A second manipulation adds branches that remain silent on tested natural inputs but dominate optimization, making visualizations of 512 ResNet-50 units nearly identical. Extensions examine natural-image initialization, earlier and multiple layers, an adversarially trained ResNet-50, and prediction preservation on ImageNet-V2 and NINCO.

The sanity check compares same-class natural–natural, different-class natural–natural, and same-class natural–visualization activation similarities across Inception-V1. It uses ten randomly selected ImageNet classes, ten visualizations per class, and correctly classified natural images; correlation comparisons are subsampled. Spearman correlation is primary, with Pearson and cosine checks. A separate analysis relates optimization-path geometry to previously collected human interpretability scores for 84 units, using 20 highly activating natural starting images per unit.

**Key results**

Manipulating Inception-V1 changes ImageNet top-1 accuracy from 69.146% to 68.744%; standard ResNet-50 manipulation leaves top-1 and top-5 accuracy unchanged. Its predictions also remain identical on 10,000/10,000 ImageNet-V2 and 5,878/5,878 NINCO images. The robust ResNet-50 manipulation decreases ordinary ImageNet accuracy from 63.924% to 63.784%.

Across roughly the first two thirds of Inception-V1, same-class natural–visualization similarity resembles the different-class baseline; similarity increases later. Same-class natural-image OOD baselines remain substantially more similar through most layers.

Formal constructions exhibit functions sharing selected extremal inputs and values but differing substantially elsewhere, precluding uniform prediction guarantees for broad function classes. Constants and one-dimensional affine functions admit exact recovery under known class membership. Smaller initial gradient angles correlate with higher human interpretability scores (Spearman r = −0.36, p = 0.001); global path deviation does not (r = 0.02, p = 0.86).

**Limitations / open questions**

Activation similarity is a proxy for shared processing paths, not a causal pathway test. Passing the check cannot exclude misleading spurious correlations. The main unmanipulated-network evidence concerns Inception-V1 output units and one visualization recipe. Formal results concern worst-case decoding from extrema, with compatible extremizer choices; they do not establish typical SGD-trained-network failure or cover every regularized visualization interface. Human scores are reused, and the geometry analysis is exploratory and correlational. Whether architectural constraints improve reliability remains open.
