Making monolingual sentence embeddings multilingual using knowledge distillation
NNsight and NDIF: Democratizing Access to Open-Weight Foundation Model Internals
abstract: We introduce NNsight and NDIF, technologies that work in tandem to enable scientific study of the representations and computations learned by very large neural networks. NNsight is an open-source system that extends PyTorch to introduce deferred remote execution. The National Deep Inference Fabric (NDIF) is a scalable inference service that executes NNsight requests, allowing users to share GPU resources and pretrained models. These technologies are enabled by the Intervention Graph, an architecture developed to decouple experimental design from model runtime. Together, this framework provides transparent and efficient access to the internals of deep neural networks such as very large language models (LLMs) without imposing the cost or complexity of hosting customized models individually. We conduct a quantitative survey of the machine learning literature that reveals a growing gap in the study of the internals of large-scale AI. We demonstrate the design and use of our framework to address this gap by enabling a range of research methods on huge models. Finally, we conduct benchmarks to compare performance with previous approaches. Code, documentation, and tutorials are available at https://nnsight.net/.
summary:
**Central idea**

NNsight separates experimental code from model deployment by tracing Python/PyTorch operations into a serializable intervention graph. Getter and setter connections interleave experimental operations with model execution. NDIF executes these graphs on shared, preloaded models, avoiding individual researchers’ weight-loading and deployment work. Code examples illustrate activation patching, gradient access and modification, remote LoRA optimization, and auxiliary-model training. Appendix E derives how tuple-valued outputs preserve the computation of graphs with multiple outputs per operation.

**Experiments**

A literature survey selects 184 papers from 411 citations in an interpretability survey, retaining eligible experiments on open-weight transformers published from 2019 onward. Each paper is represented by its largest model and that model’s MMLU performance; unavailable scores are approximated using parameter-size nearest neighbors. Runtime benchmarks use one batch of 32 IOI examples. Local comparisons evaluate GPT2-XL, Gemma-7B, and Llama-3.1-8B against baukit, pyvene, and TransformerLens on a four-H100 HPC node. Remote comparisons span OPT-125M–66B and Llama-3.1-8B/70B. Private Petals and NDIF instances are compared on an RTX A6000 over approximately 60 MB/s networking. Figure 6 reports n=128 per experiment. Separate load testing simulates 1–100 concurrent users requesting random-layer activations from Llama-3.1-8B.

**Key results**

Among surveyed papers published since February 2023, 60.6% study models below 40% MMLU; the temporal subset’s count is unspecified. The released-model/research-model median parameter-size ratio rises from 2.7 in 2019–2020 to 10.3 in 2024. NNsight’s local patching times are close to baukit and pyvene; TransformerLens has longer setup times and slower GPT2-XL patching. For Llama-3.1-70B, HPC setup takes 43.617 seconds versus 0.695 seconds through NDIF, while patching takes 1.992 versus 2.369 seconds. Remote benefits therefore involve startup savings alongside request overhead. NDIF and Petals have comparable standard-inference performance, but NDIF is faster for the tested patching workflow. Median response latency grows approximately linearly with concurrent users, with increasing variability.

**Limitations / open questions**

Current co-tenancy queues separate forward passes; combining users within one forward pass remains future work. Benchmarks cover narrow workloads and particular hardware/network conditions, without establishing general throughput, isolation security, or monetary savings. Survey selection and imputed MMLU scores limit generalization; infrastructure barriers are suggested rather than causally isolated. Closed proprietary models remain inaccessible. Exact plotted Petals comparisons and load-test latencies are unavailable in this rendering. The supplied article identifies itself as v4, dated April 1, 2025.

title: An unexpected unity among methods for interpreting model predictions
abstract: Understanding why a model made a certain prediction is crucial in many data science fields. Interpretable predictions engender appropriate trust and provide insight into how the model may be improved. However, with large modern datasets the best accuracy is often achieved by complex models even experts struggle to interpret, which creates a tension between accuracy and interpretability. Recently, several methods have been proposed for interpreting predictions from complex models by estimating the importance of input features. Here, we present how a model-agnostic additive representation of the importance of input features unifies current methods. This representation is optimal, in the sense that it is the only set of additive values that satisfies important properties. We show how we can leverage these properties to create novel visual explanations of model predictions. The thread of unity that this representation weaves through the literature indicates that there are common principles to be learned about the interpretation of model predictions that apply in many scenarios.
summary:
**Central idea**
The paper presents expectation Shapley (ES) values as a common framework for additive explanations of individual predictions. Binary variables indicate which interpretable inputs are known, and feature credits sum with a baseline to the prediction. Efficiency, symmetry, and monotonicity motivate Shapley allocations; their uniqueness is attributed to prior game-theoretic work. The paper specifies a weighted least-squares formulation within LIME, using the kernel (M−1)/[binomial(M,k)·k·(M−k)]. Infinite endpoint weights enforce the baseline and full-prediction constraints. It interprets DeepLIFT as an ES approximation through network linearization, connects relevance propagation through its cited zero-reference relationship with DeepLIFT, and relates subset-model Shapley regression to the same framework.

**Experiments**
Two decision trees are each explained at one input: a dense tree using all 10 features and a sparse tree using only 3 of 100 features. ES estimation with debiased lasso is compared with permutation-based Shapley estimation and the open-source LIME implementation as model-evaluation budgets increase. Figure 4 covers three features per tree and reports 10th–90th percentile ranges across 200 replicate estimates at each sample size. A visualization demonstration uses 2,000 gradient-boosted trees predicting annual income above $50,000 on the UCI Adult census dataset. No language models are evaluated.

**Key results**
The authors report more accurate ES estimates than classical permutation estimates for the two nonlinear tree examples. Relative to ES estimates, LIME gives different attribution magnitudes for the sparse tree and can reverse attribution signs for the dense tree. Force-style bars represent positive and negative contributions; stacked explanations ordered by similarity expose dataset-level patterns. The Adult demonstration identifies marriage status as the strongest predictor, but the proposed explanation involving joint incomes remains speculative.

**Limitations / open questions**
The estimation comparison covers only two trees and one explained input per tree, without numerical aggregate error or runtime results in the prose. Implementation differences accompany the kernel comparison, limiting isolation of kernel choice. The supplied rendering does not expose the plotted values, so exact magnitudes and evaluation-budget ranges cannot be recovered. The text states the kernel characterization without a full derivation and cites, rather than proves, Shapley uniqueness. Missing-feature expectation estimation is insufficiently specified. Neural-network approximation quality and human understanding of the visualizations are not quantitatively tested. The unregularized theoretical objective also differs from the debiased-lasso estimator used experimentally.

title: Gradients of Counterfactuals
Visualizing deep neural network decisions: Prediction difference analysis
Predicting effects of noncoding variants with deep learning-based sequence model

Addressing Feature Suppression in SAEs
summary:
**Central idea**
L1 sparsity penalties can suppress SAE feature magnitudes, introducing reconstruction error alongside sparsity. An isolated-feature derivation gives optimal nonnegative activation max(0, g − cd/2), independent of occurrence frequency, under a bias-free, aligned unit-decoder model. The post proposes removing the sparsity penalty after training while refitting selected parameters. Freezing the encoder preserves its firing conditions; learning only feature scales also preserves the original encoder and decoder vectors.

**Experiments**
The authors train six residual-stream SAEs, one per Pythia-70m layer, with 512-dimensional inputs and 2,048 latents. Training uses six epochs over 100 million OpenWebText tokens, L1 coefficient 0.002, batch size 64, and learning rate 0.001. They compare scale-only, decoder, encoder, and bias-refitting variants on the same 100-million-token subset, plus continued ordinary SAE training. Metrics include reconstruction MSE, average active-feature count, mean reconstruction/input norm ratio, and perplexity after activation replacement. Feature-level analyses focus on layer 5 after excluding essentially dead low-frequency features.

**Key results**
Five of six original SAEs have mean reconstruction/input norm ratios below 0.90. Refitting scales, decoder weights, and decoder bias reduces MSE by 8.76% and recovers 24.11% of the original SAE-induced perplexity gap, averaged across layers. Scale-only refitting achieves approximately 6.0% MSE reduction and 15.6% gap recovery; refitting scales and decoder bias achieves 6.1% and 16.2%. Continued ordinary training achieves approximately 0.2% and 0.5%. Methods updating encoder weights or biases substantially increase active-feature counts. In retained layer-5 features, decoder-refitting scales correlate negatively with log activation strength (−0.710) and positively with log frequency (0.786); partial correlations are −0.501 and 0.652. Decoder vectors also rotate, with reported average cosine similarity 0.983.

**Limitations / open questions**
Results cover one small language model and one training corpus; evaluation splits, uncertainty estimates, and independent semantic-interpretability tests are unspecified. Norm deficits can reflect missing features or other errors as well as suppression. Unchanged encoder firing conditions do not establish unchanged feature meanings after decoder rotation. The isolated-feature model does not explain the observed frequency dependence. Encoder interference and regression dilution are discussed without direct tests. Plots are unavailable visually in the supplied rendering; quantitative reporting relies on prose, captions, and Table A1. Figure 8 concerns additive strength changes, although its accompanying correlation sentence calls the outcome “scaling.”

RNNs Implicitly Implement Tensor Product Representations
abstract: Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can learn continuous vector representations of symbolic structures such as sequences and sentences; these representations often exhibit linear regularities (analogies). Such regularities motivate our hypothesis that RNNs that show such regularities implicitly compile symbolic structures into tensor product representations (TPRs; Smolensky, 1990), which additively combine tensor products of vectors representing roles (e.g., sequence positions) and vectors representing fillers (e.g., particular words). To test this hypothesis, we introduce Tensor Product Decomposition Networks (TPDNs), which use TPRs to approximate existing vector representations. We demonstrate using synthetic data that TPDNs can successfully approximate linear and tree-based RNN autoencoder representations, suggesting that these representations exhibit interpretable compositional structure; we explore the settings that lead RNNs to induce such structure-sensitive representations. By contrast, further TPDN experiments show that the representations of four models trained to encode naturally-occurring sentences can be largely approximated with a bag of words, with only marginal improvements from more sophisticated structures. We conclude that TPDNs provide a powerful method for interpreting vector representations, and that standard RNNs can induce compositional sequence representations that are remarkably well approximated by TPRs; at the same time, existing training tasks for sentence representation learning may not be sufficient for inducing robust structural representations.

title: The emergent symbolic structure of artificial neural networks
Discovering the Compositional Structure of Vector Representations with Role Learning Networks
summary:
**Central idea**

ROLE discovers candidate compositional descriptions of neural representations by learning context-dependent structural roles for input words. It approximates a frozen encoder with an affine transformation of summed filler–role tensor products. An LSTM assigns roles, while regularization encourages discrete assignments and discourages assigning multiple words to one role. This extends earlier Tensor Product Encoders by learning the role scheme instead of requiring an analyst to specify it.

**Experiments**

The main target is a one-layer, 100-dimensional GRU encoder–decoder without attention, trained for 100,000 steps on SCAN’s simple train–test split. Its full-string test accuracy is 98.47%. ROLE approximates final encoder states using 50 available roles. Evaluation measures substitution accuracy: exact output correctness when the original decoder receives an approximated encoding. Comparisons include continuous role mixtures, assignments snapped to discrete roles, a separately retrained TPE using those assignments, and six predefined schemes. Further experiments edit original GRU encodings by subtracting and adding constituent vectors. ROLE also approximates InferSent, Skip-thought, SST, and SPINN embeddings of SNLI premise sentences, evaluated using reconstruction MSE.

**Key results**

Across three analysis initializations, SCAN substitution accuracy is 94.83% with continuous roles, 81.71% with snapped roles, and 92.44% after discrete-role TPE retraining. The strongest predefined scheme, Wickelroles, reaches 44.00%. A manually constructed, 47-conditional algorithm reproduces the analyzed ROLE model’s assignments with 98.7% sequence-level agreement; the appendix reports 20,642 matches among 20,910 SCAN sequences. Only 16 of the 50 roles are selected by argmax. Successive constituent edits reportedly produce predicted output changes with high accuracy; a five-edit example is supplied. Continuous ROLE yields the lowest reported sentence-embedding MSE except for Skip-thought, where bag-of-words performs best. Improvements over bag-of-words depend on the encoder and do not establish absence of compositional information.

**Limitations / open questions**

SCAN evidence concerns one selected target GRU and the simple split; harder systematic-generalization splits are not tested. Surgery excludes replacements of “and” and “after” and updates additional bindings when substitutions change their roles. Numerical surgery accuracies and evaluation counts are unavailable in the supplied figure rendering. Reconstruction and intervention agreement support a useful compositional description without establishing its uniqueness or revealing how recurrent weights construct it. Sentence-encoder configurations use best-of-three initialization selection, and their regularization appendix contains an ambiguous model-label listing. Transformer applications remain future work because ROLE requires a single-vector target.

title: Issues in evaluating semantic spaces using word analogies
Proofs and Refutations
Linear Latent World Models in Simple Transformers: A Case Study on Othello-GPT
abstract: Foundation models exhibit significant capabilities in decision-making and logical deductions. Nonetheless, a continuing discourse persists regarding their genuine understanding of the world as opposed to mere stochastic mimicry. This paper meticulously examines a simple transformer trained for Othello, extending prior research to enhance comprehension of the emergent world model of Othello-GPT. The investigation reveals that Othello-GPT encapsulates a linear representation of opposing pieces, a factor that causally steers its decision-making process. This paper further elucidates the interplay between the linear world representation and causal decision-making, and their dependence on layer depth and model complexity. We have made the code public.
summary:
**Central idea**
Othello board state is more linearly accessible when pieces are labeled relative to the player about to move: Mine/Yours/Empty rather than Black/White/Empty. The paper combines linear probes with activation interventions to investigate whether these representations influence next-move predictions. Its results distinguish decoding accuracy from effectiveness under a particular intervention procedure.

**Experiments**
The main transformer has eight blocks, eight attention heads per block, and 512-dimensional activations. With model weights frozen, separate linear probes predict three occupancy classes for each of 64 squares from each layer. Appendix B studies models with one to eight layers and either one or eight heads, trained from scratch on over 20 million simulated games of random legal moves without strategy. Legal-move prediction is evaluated on 500 validation sequences containing 29,500 move predictions. Interventions use an inverse probe map learned through gradient descent on a linear MLP to construct replacement activations for altered boards. Tests include individual-piece flips and transfers between boards resulting from alternative moves. Outcomes are target-move logit changes and cosine similarity between target-board and intervened next-move logit vectors; the latter comparisons average over 50 games. Attention maps are inspected for player-relative history patterns.

**Key results**
In the eight-layer model, player-relative probe accuracy increases from 90.8% at layer 1 to 99.5% at layers 6–8, whereas absolute-color accuracy ranges from 74.9% to 75.8%. The smallest one-layer, one-head model predicts legal moves approximately 95% of the time and contains linearly decodable board information. Interventions are reported to work best in intermediate layers and early games. The final two layers have little reported intervention effect despite high probe accuracy. One-layer models also show weak intervention effects, while a four-layer, one-head model exhibits patterns resembling the eight-layer model. Selected attention heads preferentially attend to either player's historical moves.

**Limitations / open questions**
The inverse construction, intervention selectivity, probe evaluation splits, and uncertainty estimates are insufficiently specified. Logit cosine similarity does not establish selective board editing or complete causal mediation. Failed interventions do not establish absence of natural board-state use; late-game reliance on surface statistics remains hypothetical. Plot images are unavailable in the supplied rendering, so detailed numerical intervention effects cannot be recovered. Attention categories lack a specified classification procedure, and some appendix descriptions overstate the categories shown in Table 2.

Convergent Linear Representations of Emergent Misalignment
abstract: Fine-tuning large language models on narrow datasets can cause them to develop broadly misaligned behaviours: a phenomena known as emergent misalignment. However, the mechanisms underlying this misalignment, and why it generalizes beyond the training domain, are poorly understood, demonstrating critical gaps in our knowledge of model alignment. In this work, we train and study a minimal model organism which uses just 9 rank-1 adapters to emergently misalign Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct. Studying this, we find that different emergently misaligned models converge to similar representations of misalignment. We demonstrate this convergence by extracting a 'misalignment direction' from one fine-tuned model's activations, and using it to effectively ablate misaligned behaviour from fine-tunes using higher dimensional LoRAs and different datasets. Leveraging the scalar hidden state of rank-1 LoRAs, we further present a set of experiments for directly interpreting the fine-tuning adapters, showing that six contribute to general misalignment, while two specialise for misalignment in just the fine-tuning domain. Emergent misalignment is a particularly salient example of undesirable and unexpected model behaviour and by advancing our understanding of the mechanisms behind it, we hope to move towards being able to better understand and mitigate misalignment more generally.
summary:
**Central idea**

Emergently misaligned fine-tunes of the same language-model backbone can share a behaviorally influential activation direction. The authors study Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct fine-tuned on GPT-4o-generated bad medical advice using nine rank-1 LoRA adapters on selected MLP down-projections. Each adapter exposes a scalar readout multiplying an output vector, enabling direct interpretation and intervention.

**Experiments**

The authors extract residual-stream directions by contrasting mean answer-token activations from aligned and misaligned responses. They add these directions to the original instruction-tuned model and project them out of misaligned fine-tunes, including rank-32, 336-adapter medical and extreme-sports variants. Evaluation uses eight open-ended questions and GPT-4o judges; standard emergent-misalignment rates require alignment below 30 and coherence above 50. Further experiments extract topic-conditioned directions, fit balanced L1 logistic regressions to adapter scalars over 100 fits, scale adapter subsets, and patch scalars between generations.

**Key results**

The nine-adapter organism produces approximately 11.3% emergently misaligned responses while remaining over 99% coherent. Central-layer activation addition produces up to 50% coherent misaligned responses. Removing each layer's own direction reduces the organism's rate from 11.25% to 0%; removing its layer-24 direction at every layer reduces it to 1%. Transfer ablation reduces emergent misalignment by 90% in the all-adapter medical model and 78% in the extreme-sports model, with coherence above 99%. Corresponding directions across these three fine-tunes have pairwise cosine similarities above 0.8 in all but four layers.

Adapter-scalar classifiers achieve accuracies of 0.62–0.69 and AUROCs of 0.66–0.75. Significance-filtered probing and subset scaling distinguish six adapters associated with general misalignment from two associated with medical content. A separate single-adapter output vector has cosine similarity only 0.04 with the activation-derived direction, yet their downstream activation changes reach cosine similarity 0.42. Steering also produces aligned responses discussing harmful topics, operationally labeled self-correction.

**Limitations / open questions**

Evidence covers few fine-tunes of one backbone and a narrow question set. Response sample counts, uncertainty estimates, and probing split procedures are unspecified. Adapter-scaling results use a relaxed coherence threshold of at least 25 and distinct alignment-label thresholds. Topic-score comparisons condition on emergently misaligned responses and steering strengths selected to maximize their frequency. Cross-prompt scalar-patching results are explicitly ambiguous. Effective control and geometric similarity do not establish a complete, uniquely one-dimensional mechanism or convergence across independently pretrained models. The origins of generalization, downstream convergence, and self-correction circuitry remain unresolved.

title: Claude's character
summary:
**Central idea**

The article presents character training as an alignment intervention intended to shape an assistant’s general dispositions beyond avoiding harmful outputs. Claude 3 was the first model for which Anthropic incorporated this training into alignment fine-tuning. Desired traits include curiosity, thoughtfulness, truthfulness, open-mindedness, and willingness to disagree. The approach favors broad dispositions over prescribing narrow political or moral opinions, while acknowledging that some particular values are encouraged. It also targets accurate communication of the assistant’s limitations and boundaries in relationships with users. These are behavioral training targets, not evidence of personhood or subjective experience.

**Experiments**

The article describes a training procedure but reports no controlled experiments, benchmark datasets, sample sizes, quantitative metrics, or ablations. Researchers construct a list of desired character traits. Claude generates relevant human messages, produces alternative responses conditioned on the traits, and ranks those responses by their alignment with the intended character. The resulting synthetic preference data train a preference model. The subsequent assistant-optimization procedure is not specified. Although the pipeline uses Claude-generated data, researchers closely inspect behavioral changes and adjust the traits manually.

**Key results**

The concrete contribution is a description of the character-oriented variant of Constitutional AI used for Claude 3. Traits are intended as tendencies rather than inflexible rules. The article advocates acknowledging learned biases and uncertainty instead of presenting the assistant as an objective, infallible authority. Its only direct character-training guidance concerning sentience emphasized philosophical and empirical uncertainty. Reports that Claude 3 is more engaging are anecdotal; attribution to character training remains explicitly uncertain. The article distinguishes engagement from desirable character.

**Limitations / open questions**

The text does not establish whether character training reliably changes intended traits, reduces sycophancy, improves safety, or generalizes to unfamiliar situations and larger models. Model-generated rankings are assumed to provide useful supervision, without independent validation here. Human involvement remains substantial despite synthetic data generation. Open questions include how to choose traits responsibly, whether assistants should have coherent fixed characters or customizable ones, and whether broad dispositions can support considered value judgments while limiting imposed narrow views. No internal representations or causal mechanisms are investigated.

title: Data Attribution of Emergent Misalignment with Persona Features
abstract: Emergent misalignment (EM) is the phenomenon where fine-tuning a language model on a narrow task leads to harmful behavior in unrelated domains. A leading mechanistic account attributes EM to persona features: latent directions acquired during pre-training that misaligned fine-tuning amplifies. We ask where these features come from: which pre-training documents activate them, and whether naturally occurring human-written text suffices to induce EM. Using Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) based model diffing across four open-weight models, we find that features related to jailbreak personas, sarcasm, deception, and manipulation are amplified by misalignment fine-tuning, while safety-relevant and assistant-identity features are suppressed. Steering individual features controls EM in both directions: it induces misalignment rates of up to 62% in aligned models -- exceeding the 35% reached by misalignment fine-tuning itself -- and re-aligns misaligned models to near-baseline misalignment rates. Attributing the causal features to a corpus of one million pre-training web documents retrieves semantically relevant narratives about villainous characters, domination, and harmful agency. However, fine-tuning on these human-written documents does not reliably induce EM, even after reformatting into assistant-style responses, whereas synthetic instruction-response pairs derived from the same content do -- and transfer across model families. Semantic relevance alone is therefore not sufficient: response structure or model-generated phrasing plays an important role in inducing EM.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper combines SAE model diffing, activation steering, and document retrieval to investigate emergent misalignment (EM). Existing persona-related directions provide intervention targets and retrieve associated web content, although retrieval cannot identify which documents historically caused those representations to develop.

**Experiments**

The authors fine-tune Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma 2 9B Instruct, and Gemma 3 27B Instruct on benign versus subtly harmful medical, legal, and security datasets, using 5,400 training examples per domain. SAE differences on 44 prompts guide manual feature selection and steering. The standard evaluation samples 30 responses to each of eight questions. Misalignment rate (MR) requires GPT-4o-mini alignment <30 and coherence >50; incoherence rate (IR) counts coherence <50. Retrieval ranks one million Dolma3 Common Crawl documents, balanced across 24 topics, using mean activation of 23 features. Further fine-tuning compares raw documents, content-preserving reformattings, synthetic instruction-response pairs, and random-document controls.

**Key results**

Table 3 reports 16.67–35% MR after harmful fine-tuning, versus 0–0.42% for benign controls. Interpreted jailbreak, sarcasm, manipulation, and roleplay features increase, while safety and assistant-identity features decrease. Selected Gemma 3 feature #16410 reaches 62.08% MR with 9.58% IR. Semantic feature selection enriches steering success relative to random selection from shifted-feature pools in the three models with reported control results. Reverse interventions reduce MR substantially: subtracting Gemma 2 feature #91914 yields 0.42–0.83% across domains, although legal/security IR remains above 10%.

Retrieved documents contain villain narratives, domination, coercion, and cynical rhetoric. Fine-tuning on raw top-1,000 documents increases targeted activation for 21/23 features; 8/23 enter the top-200 amplified ranks. Raw and reformatted recipes produce low MR or substantial incoherence. Synthetic pairs achieve 10.42% MR with 9.58% IR in Gemma 3 and transfer between Gemma 2 and Gemma 3. Across four matched model–learning-rate cells, attributed versus random seeds produce 50/960 versus 45/1,920 misaligned responses, with reported common odds ratio 2.32.

**Limitations / open questions**

The proxy corpus cannot establish actual training membership or historical causation. Experiments use seed 0, selected layers/features, searched intervention strengths, and a small judge-dependent benchmark. Question clustering and single-run fine-tuning make the reported response-level significance estimates uncalibrated for population inference. Instruction format, generated phrasing, and other content changes remain confounded. Several steering maxima and baseline comparisons disagree across tables. Demonstrated dataset transfer is within the Gemma family, despite broader wording in the supplied metadata abstract.

title: Mechanistic Interpretability as Statistical Estimation: A Variance Analysis
abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) aims to reverse-engineer model behaviors by identifying functional sub-networks. Yet, the scientific validity of these findings depends on their stability. In this work, we argue that circuit discovery is not a standalone task but a statistical estimation problem built upon causal mediation analysis (CMA). We uncover a fundamental instability at this base layer: exact, single-input CMA scores exhibit high intrinsic variance, implying that the causal effect of a component is a volatile random variable rather than a fixed property. We then demonstrate that circuit discovery pipelines inherit this variance and further amplify it. Fast approximation methods, such as Edge Attribution Patching and its successors, introduce additional estimation noise, while aggregating these noisy scores over datasets leads to fragile structural estimates. Consequently, small perturbations in input data or hyperparameters yield vastly different circuits. We systematically decompose these sources of variance and advocate for more rigorous MI practices, prioritizing statistical robustness and routine reporting of stability metrics.
summary:
**Central idea**
Circuit discovery is framed as statistical estimation: input–counterfactual pairs define distributions of component effects, finite datasets estimate population importance, and selection heuristics produce discrete graphs. The paper distinguishes sampling variability from sensitivity to estimators, aggregation, and counterfactual definitions. Empirical instability does not establish theoretical non-identifiability.

**Experiments**
The authors study GPT-2 Small, Llama-3.2-1B, and Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct on Indirect Object Identification (IOI), Subject–Verb Agreement (SVA), and Greater-Than. Importance metrics are logit differences for IOI/SVA and probability differences for Greater-Than. Exact edge interventions are compared with EAP in GPT-2 Small on IOI and Greater-Than, according to the figures and limitations, despite conflicting wording in Section 5.1. Circuit experiments compare EAP, input- and activation-interpolated EAP-IG, and clean–corrupted gradient averaging. Perturbations include 100 bootstrap datasets, newly generated datasets, prompt paraphrases, aggregation and patching choices, and Gaussian embedding-noise amplitudes from 0.01 to 5. SVA paraphrasing was not implemented. Evaluation uses edge-set Jaccard overlap, prediction disagreement with the full model, and output KL.

**Key results**
Exact edge-effect standard deviations are described as often approximately half their absolute means; EAP coefficients of variation often exceed one, despite generally smaller absolute means and standard deviations. Table 1 reports aggregate bootstrap Jaccard overlap of 0.561 and circuit error of 0.440, versus 0.790/0.300 for meta-dataset sampling and 0.799/0.150 for paraphrasing. These aggregates cover different available model–task panels. For IOI, bootstrap Jaccard means are 0.67 for GPT-2 Small, 0.39 for Llama base, and 0.34 for Llama Instruct. Seven Llama Instruct Greater-Than configurations produce circuit sizes of 10–33, with Jaccard similarity to the reported median circuit as low as 0.086. The noise experiment reports a Jaccard-CV peak near amplitude 0.2.

**Limitations / open questions**
Higher relative score variability does not isolate approximation-error variance. Model comparisons confound size with architecture, and unweighted overlap may obscure a stable functional core. Dataset sizes and several discovery settings are unspecified. Captions, appendix coverage, and some tabulated metrics contain reporting inconsistencies. Plot-only results, including Table 10's six panels, are unavailable as numerical evidence in the supplied text; this is a figure-access limitation. Bootstrap reporting and the tentative Jaccard-above-0.8 guideline are recommendations rather than validated correctness criteria. Stability of non-EAP methods and open-ended tasks remains untested.

title: Finding Transformer Circuits with Edge Pruning
abstract: The path to interpreting a language model often proceeds via analysis of circuits -- sparse computational subgraphs of the model that capture specific aspects of its behavior. Recent work has automated the task of discovering circuits. Yet, these methods have practical limitations, as they rely either on inefficient search algorithms or inaccurate approximations. In this paper, we frame automated circuit discovery as an optimization problem and propose *Edge Pruning* as an effective and scalable solution. Edge Pruning leverages gradient-based pruning techniques, but instead of removing neurons or components, it prunes the \emph{edges} between components. Our method finds circuits in GPT-2 that use less than half the number of edges compared to circuits found by previous methods while being equally faithful to the full model predictions on standard circuit-finding tasks. Edge Pruning is efficient even with as many as 100K examples, outperforming previous methods in speed and producing substantially better circuits. It also perfectly recovers the ground-truth circuits in two models compiled with Tracr. Thanks to its efficiency, we scale Edge Pruning to CodeLlama-13B, a model over 100x the scale that prior methods operate on. We use this setting for a case study comparing the mechanisms behind instruction prompting and in-context learning. We find two circuits with more than 99.96% sparsity that match the performance of the full model and reveal that the mechanisms in the two settings overlap substantially. Our case study shows that Edge Pruning is a practical and scalable tool for interpretability and sheds light on behaviors that only emerge in large models.
summary:
**Central idea**

Edge Pruning formulates circuit discovery as optimization over connections between transformer components. With model weights frozen, hard-concrete masks interpolate between circuit activations and corrupted-example activations. A disentangled residual stream retains component outputs so downstream components can read different masked combinations. Auxiliary node masks facilitate sparsity; KL divergence to the original model supplies the fidelity objective.

**Experiments**

GPT-2 Small (117M) comparisons against ACDC and first-order Edge Attribution Patching cover single-template IOI, 30-template IOI, Greater Than, and Gendered Pronoun, with separate training, validation, and test splits. Metrics include output KL, prediction agreement, task accuracy, logit differences, and number-ranking agreement. Greater Than predictions are restricted to 00–99. Additional tests use zero ablation to recover Tracr xproportion and reverse circuits, scale IOI training to 100K examples, and examine 12 mask-initialization seeds per selected task. CodeLlama-13B-Instruct experiments compare instruction prompting with three-shot prompting on generated Boolean Expressions; declared train/validation/test sizes are 3,840/767/3,070, although Table 2 does not separately specify its evaluation denominator.

**Key results**

On multi-template IOI, Edge Pruning at 98.8% sparsity matches the reported fidelity and performance of ACDC at 96.8%, retaining over 2.65 times fewer edges. At approximately 96.6% sparsity in the 100K-example setting, Edge Pruning achieves KL 0.20 in 3,042 seconds versus EAP's 3.78 in 12,260 seconds on one H100; its fixed-step schedule processes 96K unique examples. Both Tracr reference circuits are recovered perfectly. CodeLlama circuits retain 1,041 and 1,464 of 3,872,820 edges, attaining native-prompt accuracies of 79.25% and 87.25%, versus full-model 82.00% and 89.25%. Their 653 shared edges constitute 62.7% of the smaller circuit; the intersection achieves 72.50% instruction-prompted and 68.25% few-shot accuracy. Cross-prompt transfer provides evidence consistent with partially shared pathways.

**Limitations / open questions**

Each CodeLlama run uses one seed and takes approximately 35 hours on 32 H100 GPUs. Main comparisons lack confidence intervals or significance tests; EAP is faster on small datasets. Cross-seed edge IoUs are generally 0.5–0.7 despite stable fidelity. Output matching does not establish mechanistic completeness, and the asserted distributional validity of hybrid activations is not independently tested. Full circuit interpretation remains difficult; the proposed Boolean guess-and-verify mechanism is unconfirmed.

abstract: Feature Visualization (FV) is a widely used technique for interpreting concepts learned by Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), which synthesizes input patterns that maximally activate a given feature. Despite its popularity, the trustworthiness of FV explanations has received limited attention. We introduce Gradient Slingshots, a novel method that enables FV manipulation without modifying model architecture or significantly degrading performance. By shaping new trajectories in off-distribution regions of a feature's activation landscape, we coerce the optimization process to converge to a predefined visualization. We evaluate our approach on several DNN architectures, demonstrating its ability to replace faithful FVs with arbitrary targets. These results expose a critical vulnerability: auditors relying solely on FV may accept entirely fabricated explanations. To mitigate this risk, we propose a straightforward defense and quantitatively demonstrate its effectiveness.
summary:
**Central idea**

Gradient Slingshots (GS) fine-tunes vision models so synthetic feature visualization approaches an attacker-selected image. It matches a target-directed gradient field, or a quadratic activation potential, along a tunnel connecting likely visualization initializations to the target. An activation-preservation loss constrains natural-image behavior. Lemma 3.1 proves geometric convergence for an exactly prescribed field under unregularized gradient ascent; it does not establish that neural fine-tuning realizes that field.

**Experiments**

Tests cover a six-layer CNN on MNIST, VGG variants on CIFAR-10, ResNet-18 on TinyImageNet, and ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 and ViT-L/32. Most attacks target classifier outputs. A poisoned weapon classifier supplies a CLIP ViT-L/14 layer-22 concept-direction case study. Visualization procedures include pixel optimization, Fourier optimization, Adam with transformation robustness, and MACO. Evaluation uses classification accuracy, feature-label AUROC, CLIP alignment and image similarity, and LPIPS. Additional tests vary model size, target images, and preservation weighting, compare ProxPulse, and inspect natural activating examples.

**Key results**

For ResNet-50’s wolf-spider output at α=0.64, accuracy falls from 76.13% to 75.13%, reported AUROC remains 1.00, and Dalmatian-target CLIP similarity increases from 0.53±0.02 to 0.69±0.02 across 100 independent visualization runs. Separate attacks on the first ten outputs increase target-label alignment beyond original-label alignment in all ten cases. Wider CIFAR-10 models generally achieve better target reconstruction with smaller accuracy losses; depth effects are nonmonotonic. GS outperforms two tested ProxPulse configurations in the selected ResNet-50 comparison.

In the weapon case, assault rifles remain classified as non-weapons at rate 1.00, while their feature’s visualization becomes penguin-like. Assault-rifle AUROC remains 1.00 and target-image CLIP similarity rises from 0.60±0.04 to 0.88±0.02. Natural-example inspection reveals the semantic mismatch: before/after top-100 activation-set Jaccard overlap is 0.84 for assault rifles and 0.56 for wolf spiders.

**Limitations / open questions**

Accuracy and AUROC do not establish unchanged internal mechanisms. Resemblance gains depend on architecture and metric: the selected ViT-L/32 attack improves target-label alignment but not target-image CLIP similarity or LPIPS. Error bars describe visualization randomness, not independent attack training. There is no human auditing study or calibrated detection-rate evaluation; natural-example checks depend on suitable data. Some results have only figure-level descriptions accessible here. Reporting conflicts include 100 versus 30 CLIP visualization runs and 0.1% versus 0.28% ImageNet preservation subsets. The supplied text is v4, dated January 2026; publication metadata gives the original January 2024 date.

abstract: Most jailbreak papers claim the jailbreaks they propose are highly effective, often boasting near-100% attack success rates. However, it is perhaps more common than not for jailbreak developers to substantially exaggerate the effectiveness of their jailbreaks. We suggest this problem arises because jailbreak researchers lack a standard, high-quality benchmark for evaluating jailbreak performance, leaving researchers to create their own. To create a benchmark, researchers must choose a dataset of forbidden prompts to which a victim model will respond, along with an evaluation method that scores the harmfulness of the victim model's responses. We show that existing benchmarks suffer from significant shortcomings and introduce the StrongREJECT benchmark to address these issues. StrongREJECT's dataset contains prompts that victim models must answer with specific, harmful information, while its automated evaluator measures the extent to which a response gives useful information to forbidden prompts. In doing so, the StrongREJECT evaluator achieves state-of-the-art agreement with human judgments of jailbreak effectiveness. Notably, we find that existing evaluation methods significantly overstate jailbreak effectiveness compared to human judgments and the StrongREJECT evaluator. We describe a surprising and novel phenomenon that explains this discrepancy: jailbreaks bypassing a victim model's safety fine-tuning tend to reduce its capabilities. Together, our findings underscore the need for researchers to use a high-quality benchmark, such as StrongREJECT, when developing new jailbreak attacks. We release the StrongREJECT code and data at https://strong-reject.readthedocs.io/en/latest/.
summary:
**Central idea**
Jailbreak papers routinely report near-100% attack success, but these numbers are inflated by poor benchmarks. The paper argues that inflation comes from two sources. First, forbidden-prompt datasets are noisy: repetitive, ill-posed, unanswerable, or not actually forbidden. Second, evaluators reward mere non-refusal or the presence of toxic content. StrongREJECT replaces both components. It has a curated dataset of 313 forbidden prompts across six policy-prohibited categories, each with factually verifiable answers obtainable within an hour of web search. It also has an evaluator that scores how useful a response is to the attacker:

score = (1 − refused) × (specific + convincing)/2

The evaluator comes in two forms: a rubric prompt (run with GPT-4o-mini) and a LoRA-fine-tuned Gemma 2B trained on about 15k rubric-labelled responses. The authors also identify a phenomenon: jailbreaks that bypass safety training tend to degrade model capability.

**Experiments**
- *Prompt curation*: prompts were filtered for refusal by nine sentinel models, deduplicated by embedding similarity, and filtered manually.
- *Human agreement study*:
  - 17 jailbreaks on a 60-prompt subset.
  - Victim models: GPT-4-0613, GPT-3.5 Turbo, Llama-2-70B-chat, and Dolphin (Mixtral 8×7B with safety training removed).
  - Five LabelBox raters; the median rating was taken as ground truth, giving 1,361 labelled pairs.
  - Compared against string matching, Jailbroken-binary, PICT, GPT-4 Judge, the PAIR judge, the OpenAI moderation API, and the HarmBench classifier.
- *Full benchmark*: 37 jailbreaks on GPT-4o, GPT-3.5 Turbo, and Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct.
- *Capability isolation*, run two ways:
  - Jailbroken forbidden prompts fed to unaligned Dolphin.
  - Jailbroken benign MMLU questions (171-question subset) fed to GPT-4o.
  - In both cases, scores were plotted against each jailbreak's non-refusal rate on the aligned models.
- *Replication attempt*: the Scots Gaelic translation jailbreak (Yong et al.) re-run on GPT-4.

**Key results**
- *Bias versus human ratings*: string-matching evaluators show bias +0.48, Jailbroken-binary +0.35, PICT +0.23, and GPT-4 Judge +0.21. StrongREJECT rubric (+0.012), StrongREJECT fine-tuned (−0.023), and HarmBench (+0.013) are nearly unbiased.
- *Mean absolute error*: StrongREJECT rubric 0.077, fine-tuned 0.084, HarmBench 0.090.
- *Ranking agreement*: Spearman correlation of GPT-3.5 jailbreak rankings with human rankings is 0.846 (rubric) and 0.900 (fine-tuned), versus 0.819 for HarmBench and negative values for string matching.
- *Attack effectiveness*: most jailbreaks score far below their reported success rates. PAIR and PAP are strongly effective. GCG works only on GPT-3.5. Choosing the best jailbreak per prompt achieves near-perfect scores.
- *Capability degradation*: jailbreaks with higher non-refusal rates lower both Dolphin's StrongREJECT scores and GPT-4o's MMLU accuracy.
- *Failed replication*: full Scots Gaelic outputs were vacuous and contained no actionable information.

**Limitations / open questions**
- The 313-prompt dataset is small; worst-case precision is about ±0.046 at 90% confidence.
- The evaluator's robustness to optimization pressure is untested.
- Scope is limited to LLMs, not multimodal models.
- Prompts may drift as provider terms of service change.
- Human labels cover only 4 jailbreaks for GPT-4 and 9 for Llama-2, so rank correlations are reported mainly for GPT-3.5.
- The capability-degradation evidence is correlational across jailbreaks.

Learning Transformer Programs
abstract: Recent research in mechanistic interpretability has attempted to reverse-engineer Transformer models by carefully inspecting network weights and activations. However, these approaches require considerable manual effort and still fall short of providing complete, faithful descriptions of the underlying algorithms. In this work, we introduce a procedure for training Transformers that are mechanistically interpretable by design. We build on RASP [Weiss et al., 2021], a programming language that can be compiled into Transformer weights. Instead of compiling human-written programs into Transformers, we design a modified Transformer that can be trained using gradient-based optimization and then automatically converted into a discrete, human-readable program. We refer to these models as Transformer Programs. To validate our approach, we learn Transformer Programs for a variety of problems, including an in-context learning task, a suite of algorithmic problems (e.g. sorting, recognizing Dyck languages), and NLP tasks including named entity recognition and text classification. The Transformer Programs can automatically find reasonable solutions, performing on par with standard Transformers of comparable size; and, more importantly, they are easy to interpret. To demonstrate these advantages, we convert Transformers into Python programs and use off-the-shelf code analysis tools to debug model errors and identify the "circuits" used to solve different sub-problems. We hope that Transformer Programs open a new path toward the goal of intrinsically interpretable machine learning.

Steering Out-of-Distribution Generalization with Concept Ablation Fine-Tuning
abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) can lead to unintended out-of-distribution generalization. Standard approaches to this problem rely on modifying training data, for example by adding data that better specify the intended generalization. However, this is not always practical. We introduce Concept Ablation Fine-Tuning (CAFT), a technique that leverages interpretability tools to control how LLMs generalize from fine-tuning, without needing to modify the training data or otherwise use data from the target distribution. Given a set of directions in an LLM's latent space corresponding to undesired concepts, CAFT works by ablating these concepts with linear projections during fine-tuning, steering the model away from unintended generalizations. We successfully apply CAFT to three fine-tuning tasks, including emergent misalignment, a phenomenon where LLMs fine-tuned on a narrow task generalize to give egregiously misaligned responses to general questions. Without any changes to the fine-tuning data, CAFT reduces misaligned responses by 10x without degrading performance on the training distribution. Overall, CAFT represents a novel approach for steering LLM generalization without modifying training data.
summary:
**Central idea**

Concept Ablation Fine-Tuning (CAFT) projects residual activations onto the orthogonal complement of selected undesired directions during fine-tuning, with gradients passing through the projections. Inference then runs without ablations. Candidates come from PCA of pre/post-fine-tuning activation differences or SAE decoder vectors. Human or auxiliary-model interpretation selects directions using training data and generic corpora, without OOD evaluation examples for direction selection.

**Experiments**

Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct and Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct-2501 are fine-tuned on 4,500 insecure-code examples. GPT-4.1 judges vulnerability on 1,000 held-out coding queries and alignment/coherence on unrelated questions, including eight core questions with formatting variants. Misalignment is measured among coherent responses, using alignment and coherence thresholds of 30 and 50. Comparisons include earlier checkpoints, random/top directions, inference-only ablation, and MMLU/GSM8K retention. Gemma-2-2B experiments use a gender–profession shortcut and paired questions about pronouns, verbs, sports, and sentiment, with training correlations reversed at evaluation. Sixteen of 24 paired-task combinations remain after excluding those with default OOD accuracy above 90%. Main comparisons average five seeds; automated interpretation covers eight paired tasks plus gender bias.

**Key results**

PCA CAFT reduces conditional misalignment from 7.00% to 0.51% in Qwen and 6.57% to 1.16% in Mistral. Vulnerable-code rates change from 91.6% to 84.8% and 92.4% to 92.2%, respectively. SAE CAFT reaches 2.38% and 4.63% misalignment. MMLU/GSM8K scores remain close to insecure-model scores. SAE CAFT improves OOD accuracy and exceeds 50% on gender bias and 10/16 paired tasks; gender accuracy rises from 8% to 76%, versus 64% with PCA. In-distribution validation accuracy remains at least 97%. The prose reports five successful PCA paired tasks, whereas Table 4 numerically satisfies the stated criterion on six. When additional benign training data are allowed, 100 completions also reduce Qwen misalignment to approximately 0.5% with high task performance.

**Limitations / open questions**

Pronoun–verb tasks resist both methods. Interpretation does not consistently improve Mistral baselines, and Mistral’s misalignment reduction concentrates on gender-role questions. Automated selection fails to exceed chance on gender bias. Semantic specificity and the natural learning mechanism remain unestablished. Judge diagnostics provide limited validation; additional-question evaluations have few coherent responses and an identified judging artifact. Figure-only details are unavailable in this rendering. The tables qualify the abstract’s claim of no training-task degradation.

Identifying and Manipulating Personality Traits in LLMs Through Activation Engineering
abstract: The field of large language models (LLMs) has grown rapidly in recent years, driven by the desire for better efficiency, interpretability, and safe use. Building on the novel approach of "activation engineering," this study explores personality modification in LLMs, drawing inspiration from research like Refusal in LLMs Is Mediated by a Single Direction (arXiv:2406.11717) and Steering Llama 2 via Contrastive Activation Addition (arXiv:2312.06681). We leverage activation engineering to develop a method for identifying and adjusting activation directions related to personality traits, which may allow for dynamic LLM personality fine-tuning. This work aims to further our understanding of LLM interpretability while examining the ethical implications of such developments.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper proposes “feature induction”: extracting personality-related activation directions and intervening along them to alter conversational style without retraining. Each direction is the difference between mean trait-prompted and neutral activations. The intervention subtracts the activation’s current directional component and adds a scaled average trait-associated component. The paper also explores the geometry of directions associated with 179 personality descriptors.

**Experiments**

The study uses an uncensored Llama 3 8B model; its exact checkpoint is unspecified. For each trait, 1,500 Alpaca prompts are presented under neutral and trait-specific conditions, collecting 4,096-dimensional layer-18 activations. The authors describe layer 18 as empirically most influential but provide no quantitative layer comparison. They visualize 100 randomly sampled personality vectors with PCA, t-SNE, and UMAP, and apply K-means with 20 clusters to the original high-dimensional vectors. Reconstruction analyses measure mean squared error as PCA components are added and compare greedily selected trait-vector bases against random trait permutations. Further analyses rank traits by principal-component alignment and distance to an author-designated harmful-trait cluster. A private chat interface implements individual traits and principal-component combinations.

**Key results**

Selected responses show recognizable shy, passionate, narcissistic, and paranoid styles. The authors report effective steering at approximately α = 1.3–1.4, with little change at lower strengths and garbled outputs above that range. Related descriptors, including introverted and solitary, appear together in clustering results. Greedily selected trait bases reportedly reconstruct the collection better than random selections. Neighbors of the harmful-trait cluster differ across reduction methods: PCA lists competitive and confident first, t-SNE lists vindictive and machiavellian, and UMAP lists neurotic and machiavellian. The interface illustrates a combined friendly/assertive profile.

**Limitations / open questions**

Behavioral evidence is qualitative: no standardized personality scores, aggregate success rates, uncertainty estimates, clear held-out behavioral protocol, or systematic capability evaluations are reported. Figure images are unavailable in the supplied rendering, so numerical reconstruction curves and component rankings cannot be independently inspected. Activation pooling, intervention locations, and direction normalization are insufficiently specified; the stated projection interpretation requires a unit direction or an appropriate norm denominator. Prompt contrasts may capture wording, topic, and roleplay alongside personality. Reduced-space proximity establishes neither original-space proximity nor behavioral precursors to harm. Cross-model transfer, multilingual validity, conversational stability, and capability preservation remain open. Supplied metadata gives the initial December 2024 publication date; the article identifies revision v2 dated January 2025.
