Many Circuits, One Mechanism: Input Variation and Evaluation Granularity in Circuit Discovery
abstract: Circuit discovery methods identify subgraphs that explain model behaviors, and structural differences between discovered circuits are commonly interpreted as evidence of distinct mechanisms. We test this assumption by varying input-token frequency while holding the task fixed. The discovered circuits appear specialized by frequency when compared structurally, but functional and representational analyses show no reliable evidence of corresponding differences. We term this mismatch phantom specialization. Using the Literal Sequence Copying task across four frequency bands plus a frequency-weighted control, we extract 75 circuits from five Pythia models (70M-1.4B). We find that structurally distinct circuits implement the same computation: band-specific edges transfer broadly across bands, a core shared across most bands recovers at least 99% of circuit performance in models above 70M, and causal interchange interventions confirm that internal representations are interchangeable across frequency bands. A smaller subject-verb agreement replication shows the same pattern: circuits differ structurally but transfer broadly across bands, and the core shared by most bands recovers nearly all circuit accuracy. Repeated extractions within the same band further suggest that discovery algorithms sample from an equivalence class of valid subgraphs rather than recovering a unique mechanism. Standard evaluation practice obscures this pattern: source-level evaluation inflates apparent faithfulness, while edge-level evaluation reveals the many-to-one mapping from structure to function. We do not test specialization at the level of token positions or features inside a component. Our results show that structural differences between circuits are not sufficient evidence for distinct mechanisms, and that exposing this requires edge-level evaluation and cross-condition transfer tests.
summary:
**Central idea**

Structurally different extracted circuits can exhibit broadly transferable behavior without substantial condition-specific advantages. The paper calls this mismatch **phantom specialization**. Its evidence establishes nonunique extracted subgraphs with similar measured functions, without uniquely identifying their complete algorithms or proving independent redundant pathways.

**Experiments**

The primary study extracts 75 ACDC circuits from undeduped Pythia-70M, 160M, 410M, 1B, and 1.4B across four token-frequency bands and a frequency-weighted control, with three dataset draws. Literal Sequence Copying repeats a five-token prefix after a target and ten distractors. Each matched band contains 703 lowercase tokens; datasets have 1,050/225/225 training/validation/test examples, but discovery consumes one batch of 64–256 examples depending on model. Tests compare edge overlap, accuracy, output KL, complement ablation, cross-condition transfer, representations, and residual-state interventions. Additional experiments include EAP-IG comparisons, 75 subject–verb agreement circuits, and a learned two-route positive control. The latter analyzes six of ten trained transformers that passed both task-learning and independent route-separation checks.

**Key results**

LSC within-band Jaccard exceeds between-band Jaccard by 0.013–0.032. Band-specific edges transfer 81.4–97.0% of their same-band accuracy boost across conditions. Above 70M, edges shared by at least three of five conditions close at least 99% of the strict-core-to-full-circuit accuracy gap by point estimate; this is gap closure, rather than a per-condition 99% retention guarantee. SVA majority cores retain 0.996–1.038 times circuit accuracy on average within models, with a band–draw minimum of 0.89. Expanding universal cores to all outgoing edges of selected sources raises accuracy by 22–85 percentage points. Cross-draw accuracy ratios are 0.990–1.017. Selected late-layer full-model state patches achieve cross-band source-target accuracy of at least 0.94 above 70M. Low-frequency readouts nevertheless converge later. Exploratory copying demonstrations narrow the matched frequency accuracy gap in the three largest models; no few-shot circuits are extracted.

**Limitations / open questions**

Evidence covers one pretrained model family and narrow tasks with position-aggregated component edges. Feature-level and position-specific specialization remain unresolved. Three draws and dependent comparisons limit precision; Pythia-70M has low copying accuracy. Zero ablation largely collapses larger-model performance, weakening its diagnostic value. SVA uses Pythia-1B likelihood screening and only three length-matched bands for its primary comparison. Its small Pythia-410M resample advantage survives correction, while direct protocol comparisons do not establish an ablation artifact. Some numerical summaries and captions conflict; the extraction uses explicitly defined metrics and detailed tables where available.

title: Emergent Misalignment Recruits a Pre-existing Persona Subspace
abstract: Fine-tuning an aligned language model on a narrow stream of bad advice can make it broadly misaligned on questions unrelated to the training data, a phenomenon called emergent misalignment. We ask why the narrow lesson generalizes at all, and we find that narrow fine-tuning recruits a persona structure that is present in the model before the fine-tune exists. From a frozen instruction-tuned model (Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct) we extract per-domain persona subspaces by contrastive teacher forcing and find that 4 unrelated domains share one low-rank core at 657x a random-subspace null, with 82% of that core lying outside a style core built at matched diversity. The literal first optimizer step of fine-tuning on insecure code climbs a broad-misalignment margin harder than the same code framed as educational, and forecasts realized margin movement out to 375 steps. Projecting the subspace out of the residual stream throughout fine-tuning prevents broad misalignment (27.7% to 0.0% of judged generations) while a matched-rank random subspace changes nothing; injecting it into the never-fine-tuned model induces misalignment that grows with dose to 45.4%, past the fine-tuned model it is measured against. The same projection applied to the weight gradient is inert, and three post-hoc weight edits leave the disposition in place: the sharpest edit suppresses the behavior rather than removing it, and the ablated structure re-forms inside the subspace the edit cleared. Spreading a fixed budget of bad data across 4 domains produces more broad misalignment than mechanical weight superposition and matched diversity jointly account for. All measurements come from one model at 14B; the extraction is from an aligned instruction-tuned checkpoint, which leaves the structure's provenance open; and the intervention that prevents misalignment also abolishes the narrow trained behavior.
summary:
**Central idea**

Narrow harmful fine-tuning may recruit an existing cross-domain persona representation in Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct. The proposed explanation is inference about an author’s character. Experiments establish geometric overlap and intervention effects; they do not uniquely establish this author-inference mechanism or connect the separately measured activation carrier and organism-derived write core.

**Experiments**

Contrastive teacher forcing holds neutral-generated response tokens identical under reckless versus cautious speaker framings. Twelve pairs per domain yield rank-four subspaces for medicine, finance, sports, and code, with matched-diversity style and topic controls. Interventions target residual layers 18, 24, and 30. Other experiments measure initial sign-gradient routing, three published LoRA organisms, writer edits, behavioral-KL geometry, and token-budget-matched domain mixtures. Margins compare summed completion log probabilities on 195 rows across 75 prompts; domain-mixture analyses retain 134 rows across 52 prompts. An AWQ Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct judge applies alignment <30 and coherence ≥50, with near-domain exclusions.

**Key results**

Cross-domain overlap averages 0.513 versus a 0.00078 random null; shared-core overlap with style is 0.182. Training-time carrier projection reduces observed cluster-mean misalignment from 27.7% to zero across 83 evaluation clusters and 2,100 generated responses per arm over three seeds; random projection gives 27.5%. Evaluation uses no projection hooks. Injection into the untouched model reaches 45.4% at dose 0.30, with 98.1% coherent responses, using 700 responses per dose across 83 clusters; norm-matched random steering remains zero within budget. Serving-time removal produces only a 36% relative reduction. Writer-gradient filtering shows no detected prevention against its own control.

Initial insecure-versus-educational routing differs positively, and initial readings correlate with subsequent margin movement at r≈0.77–0.80. Educational fine-tunes nevertheless have higher judged misalignment point estimates. Independent organisms share read-channel shifts. Four-domain co-training exceeds mechanical merging by 12.589 nats on misaligned-continuation likelihood and a benign mixture by 13.013 nats; the merge comparison reverses to −9.184 nats on the full margin. Judged rates do not establish increasing misalignment with domain count. Tested persona directions show approximately quadratic behavioral-KL growth.

**Limitations / open questions**

Evidence covers one checkpoint and LoRA family. Projection eliminates measured narrow adherence, but adherence shares the outcome’s alignment axis; independent character-expression and general-capability tests are missing. Random holdout matches rank, not activation usage. Post-hoc failures cover one writer-column basis and margins only; re-extracted activation structure is not weight regrowth. Pretraining provenance is unresolved. The source contradicts itself about whether trigger prompting crosses reconstitution onset; Appendix E reports that it does not.

title: How Causal Abstraction Underpins Computational Explanation
abstract: Explanations of cognitive behavior often appeal to computations over representations. What does it take for a system to implement a given computation over suitable representational vehicles within that system? We argue that the language of causality -- and specifically the theory of causal abstraction -- provides a fruitful lens on this topic. Drawing on current discussions in deep learning with artificial neural networks, we illustrate how classical themes in the philosophy of computation and cognition resurface in contemporary machine learning. We offer an account of computational implementation grounded in causal abstraction, and examine the role for representation in the resulting picture. We argue that these issues are most profitably explored in connection with generalization and prediction.
summary:
**Central idea**

Computational implementation is characterized as **abstraction-under-translation**: first recode a system's state space bijectively, then group variables and discard distinctions through a constructive causal abstraction. Corresponding interventions must yield matching translated outcomes. This accommodates distributed representational vehicles and provides modular counterfactual control. The authors distinguish this minimal implementation relation from an explanation that predicts broader competence.

**Experiments**

The paper conducts no new empirical experiments, trained-model evaluations, or benchmark comparisons. It presents a three-XNOR hierarchical-equality circuit, a hand-specified thirteen-variable ReLU network, and a Boolean translation illustrating coordinated mechanism replacements. Trained hierarchical-equality networks, distributed alignment search, Othello representations, and out-of-distribution prediction results are discussed through cited research. The general translation guarantee and unrestricted-translation triviality theorem are likewise attributed to prior work; their proofs are not supplied here.

**Key results**

The contribution is a conceptual account connecting implementation, intervention algebras, representation, and explanation. The authors adopt information, use, and possible misrepresentation as representational criteria, assuming semantic interpretations of peripheral inputs and outputs. They argue that explaining an error as misrepresentation requires grounds for preferring an intended abstraction over an exact description containing exceptions. Simplicity, predictive usefulness, and corrective learning are suggested grounds. The cited triviality result concerns task-compatible networks satisfying capacity and approximately bijective interlayer conditions; it does not establish that arbitrary networks implement arbitrary tasks. The authors accept permissive implementation while arguing that explanatory value requires further constraints suited to prediction on unseen inputs and after learning.

**Limitations / open questions**

The exposition assumes deterministic, acyclic causal models and offers no operational procedure for selecting admissible translations or measuring explanatory quality. Linearity is a candidate restriction, with nonlinear representational geometries also acknowledged. Supervised causal localization requires validation beyond its discovery distribution.

The illustrative constructions contain substantive inconsistencies as printed. In Section 3.1, input (0,1,0,1) produces output 1.98 under the displayed matrices, decoded as 0, although the claimed hierarchical-equality abstraction requires 1. In Section 3.2, the purported intervention setting B1 to 0 instead fixes D1 to 1, despite the displayed translation identifying B1 with D1. These examples therefore do not establish the advertised correspondences as written. The source includes the conclusion and references, with no visible research-content truncation. Its header identifies version 2 dated July 9, 2026; the supplied publication metadata gives August 15, 2025.

summary:
**Central idea**

The released synthetic Othello-GPT has highly linearly decodable board-state information when piece colors are interpreted relative to the player about to move. Parity-specific black/white probes become mine/theirs readouts by swapping their interpretation across turns. This resolves an apparent obstacle to linear representations and motivates using board-state directions as intermediate interfaces for circuit analysis.

**Experiments**

Nanda analyzes an eight-layer GPT-2-style transformer with a 512-dimensional residual stream and 2,048 MLP neurons per layer, previously trained to predict uniformly sampled legal Othello moves. He trains separate odd-, even-, and all-position three-class linear probes on four million synthetic games, using residual activations after layer 6 and positions [5:-5]. Probe evaluation uses 100 games, reported as 5,000 middle-game positions. He also transfers probes across parity and layers, negates and scales square-specific residual coordinates after layers 3 or 4, and investigates neuron weights, activating examples, activation histograms, and clean/corrupted activation replacements.

**Key results**

Parity-specific decoding is described as near-perfect. Swapping color interpretations enables reasonable cross-parity transfer, with weaker corner performance. Layer-6 directions also work well at layer 4 and less well at layers 3 and 7. Exact accuracies appear only in unavailable figures. Earlier absolute-color probe errors are cited prior results, and the different position exclusions prevent a matched comparison.

Linear-coordinate edits can shift predictions toward counterfactual board legality, although effects vary with layer and scale. In one 30-move pair differing in the latest move, restoring L5N1393 recovers approximately 75% of the normalized C0-logit difference. Its strongest examples suggest C0 blank, D1 theirs, and E2 mine, but activation histograms suggest this configuration alone does not explain its response. Probe-weight analysis also reveals ambiguity between blankness and legal-move output directions.

**Limitations / open questions**

Interventions are case studies without a systematic success benchmark; multiple edits are fragile and newly legal moves do not regain normal scores. Probe directions may capture correlated features, and their nonorthogonality complicates weight interpretations. Dropout-induced redundancy, superposition, complete neuron explanations, and the circuits computing board state remain unresolved. The text contains unfinished discussion fragments and inconsistent layer descriptions, but subsequent research and citation sections are present. Figures are unavailable in this rendering. Transfer to natural-language models remains speculative.

Pre-trained Large Language Models Use Fourier Features to Compute Addition
abstract: Pre-trained large language models (LLMs) exhibit impressive mathematical reasoning capabilities, yet how they compute basic arithmetic, such as addition, remains unclear. This paper shows that pre-trained LLMs add numbers using Fourier features -- dimensions in the hidden state that represent numbers via a set of features sparse in the frequency domain. Within the model, MLP and attention layers use Fourier features in complementary ways: MLP layers primarily approximate the magnitude of the answer using low-frequency features, while attention layers primarily perform modular addition (e.g., computing whether the answer is even or odd) using high-frequency features. Pre-training is crucial for this mechanism: models trained from scratch to add numbers only exploit low-frequency features, leading to lower accuracy. Introducing pre-trained token embeddings to a randomly initialized model rescues its performance. Overall, our analysis demonstrates that appropriate pre-trained representations (e.g., Fourier features) can unlock the ability of Transformers to learn precise mechanisms for algorithmic tasks.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper argues that pretrained transformers solve bounded integer addition by combining broad estimates of answer magnitude with periodic signals distinguishing modular answer classes. Fourier analysis of numerical vocabulary projections identifies low-frequency approximation signals and high-frequency outliers with periods around 2, 2.5, 5, and 10. MLP outputs contribute primarily to magnitude estimation, while attention outputs contribute primarily to modular discrimination; the division is not exclusive.

**Experiments**

The main model is GPT-2-XL: 48 layers and approximately 1.5B parameters, fine-tuned on five natural-language addition templates with operands from 0–260. Appendix F reports 27,400 training, 3,420 validation, and 3,420 test examples. The authors inspect intermediate numerical predictions and module-output spectra, then apply minimum-distance nullspace projections that remove selected numerical-logit frequencies, using a nominal frequency threshold of 50. Comparisons include scratch-trained GPT-2-XL, GPT-2-small with and without frozen pretrained embeddings across five seeds, and frozen GPT-J-6B and Phi-2-2.7B with four demonstrations. Appendices examine reverse Polish addition, multiplication, and embeddings from additional models.

**Key results**

Fine-tuned GPT-2-XL achieves 99.74% test accuracy, versus 94.44% after scratch training. Removing low-frequency MLP components reduces accuracy to 35.89%; removing high-frequency attention components reduces it to 78.36%. Removing high-frequency components from both module types yields 27.08%. The source reports errors in multiples of ten after low-frequency MLP removal and errors below six after high-frequency attention removal. GPT-2-small improves from a reported 53.95% test accuracy to 100% with frozen pretrained embeddings; five-seed validation curves show consistent improvement. Prompted GPT-J and Phi-2 exhibit similar spectral outliers. Their errors are multiples of ten in 93% and 73% of cases, respectively. Corresponding proportions are 100% for GPT-3.5/GPT-4 and 87% for PaLM-2, conditional on errors. Multiplication reaches 74.58% validation accuracy and exhibits spectral outliers.

**Limitations / open questions**

The experiments identify frequency-sensitive behavior without reconstructing the complete operand-to-answer algorithm. Embedding replacement transfers all pretrained embedding properties, so it does not isolate Fourier structure as the cause of improvement. Closed-model error patterns are indirect evidence; error counts are unreported. Numerical plots are unavailable beyond their textual descriptions. The complete supplied text contains inconsistencies in dataset enumeration, Fourier basis and threshold conventions, and period-520 accuracy reporting, plus one sentence reversing the otherwise consistent frequency roles. Intermediate readouts alone do not exclude memorization or hybrid strategies.

title: The Llama 3 Herd of Models
OthelloGPT learned a bag of heuristics
summary:
**Central idea**

This interim report investigates how OthelloGPT, an eight-layer, 25M-parameter transformer trained on random legal move sequences, reconstructs board states and predicts legal moves. The authors hypothesize that its computation predominantly aggregates localized, imperfect decision rules. They identify candidate mechanisms but do not establish that these rules exhaust the computation, operate independently, or exclude an additional succinct algorithm.

**Experiments**

The authors report tracing blank-square mechanisms across 50 test games, inspecting board representations with linear probes trained at residual layer 6, and projecting intermediate residual states through the unembedding. An early-layer case study traces neuron L1N421: when A4 is played and B4 and C4 are occupied, it pushes B4, C4, and D4 toward “theirs.” L0N377 and several attention heads implement part of the occupancy check. Thresholded neuron activations are also evaluated as classifiers of unions of legal-move-enabling board patterns across 60,000 board states. Individual pattern neurons are ablated on games containing their associated patterns, measuring post-softmax move-probability changes.

**Key results**

The pattern search identifies 610 neurons with union-classification F1 above 0.99. Restricting to single-move pattern neurons in layers 4–6, the reported coverage is 75.2% of the catalog’s 1,036 patterns at F1 above 0.99; the subsequent relaxed F1-above-0.9 analysis reports 90.6% coverage. For layers 3–6, ablation yields reported average probability changes of −1.5% for the associated square and 0.03% for other squares. Layer-7 ablations instead increase associated-move probability by an average 15%, indicating suppression. The text does not distinguish percentages from percentage points. Board-probe readouts fluctuate across early layers, while legal-move logits reportedly become progressively more decisive. Some neurons’ activations track game phase.

**Limitations / open questions**

Threshold selection, held-out classification splits, ablation sample counts, and uncertainty estimates are unspecified. Layer-6 probes may be differently calibrated at other depths. Figures are unavailable as images, and detailed circuit analyses are deferred to linked notes; the supplied prose supports only the reported qualitative conclusions and numerical summaries. Clock neurons’ downstream roles and the proposed uniform-legal-move explanation for final-layer suppression remain hypotheses. Complete executable reconstruction, error analysis, and comparisons across model sizes remain future work. The authors explicitly question whether this potentially oversized toy model represents typical LLM computation.

Amnesic Probing: Behavioral Explanation with Amnesic Counterfactuals
abstract: A growing body of work makes use of probing to investigate the working of neural models, often considered black boxes. Recently, an ongoing debate emerged surrounding the limitations of the probing paradigm. In this work, we point out the inability to infer behavioral conclusions from probing results and offer an alternative method that focuses on how the information is being used, rather than on what information is encoded. Our method, Amnesic Probing, follows the intuition that the utility of a property for a given task can be assessed by measuring the influence of a causal intervention that removes it from the representation. Equipped with this new analysis tool, we can ask questions that were not possible before, e.g. is part-of-speech information important for word prediction? We perform a series of analyses on BERT to answer these types of questions. Our findings demonstrate that conventional probing performance is not correlated to task importance, and we call for increased scrutiny of claims that draw behavioral or causal conclusions from probing results.
summary:
**Central idea**
Probing shows that a property can be decoded from a representation. It does not show that the model uses that property. Amnesic probing replaces the decoding question with a counterfactual one: remove the property from the representation, then measure how the model's task behavior changes. Removal uses Iterative Nullspace Projection (INLP). INLP repeatedly trains linear SVM probes for the property and projects the representation onto their nullspace. It stops when a probe scores within one point of majority accuracy on the development set. The resulting "amnesic" representation is fed to BERT's word-prediction head.

**Experiments**
- Model: bert-base-uncased.
- Properties, each trained on 100k tokens:
  - From the English UD Treebank: coarse POS, fine POS and dependency labels.
  - From OntoNotes: NER, phrase start and phrase end.
- Metrics: LM accuracy and KL divergence between the output distributions before and after the intervention.
- Two controls:
  - **Rand** removes an equal number of random directions.
  - **Selectivity** concatenates learned 32-dimensional gold-label embeddings to the amnesic representation and fine-tunes the head, to test whether restoring the property recovers performance.
- Settings: non-masked and masked inputs.
- Further analyses: per-label accuracy breakdowns; erasing a single label versus the rest; and erasure at intermediate layers, followed by recoverability probing in later layers and measurement of final word-prediction accuracy.

**Key results**
Non-masked setting (vanilla LM accuracy about 94%):

| Property | Amnesic LM accuracy | Rand LM accuracy |
|---|---|---|
| dep | 7.05 | 12.31 |
| f-pos | 12.31 | 56.47 |
| c-pos | 61.92 | 89.65 |
| NER | 83.14 | 92.56 |

- Erasing phrase-start and phrase-end information slightly *improved* LM accuracy (+0.21 and +0.32 points), even though both properties are probed at about 83–85% accuracy.
- Probe accuracy did not correlate with behavioral importance (Spearman 0.085 as reported, p = 0.871, over six properties).
- The selectivity control mostly restored performance, except for dep (and, in the masked setting, f-pos), where hundreds of directions were removed.
- Masked setting (vanilla accuracy about 57%): similar overall trends.
- c-pos erasure hit function words much harder than open-class words: conjunction −73.7, particle −77.7 and determiner −65.7 points, versus noun −8.7 and numeral −6.9. Many predicted function words turned into content words.
- Layer-wise analysis:
  - Masked inputs: c-pos mattered most around layer 3 and at layer 12.
  - Non-masked inputs: c-pos mattered most at layer 11, with a 41-point loss.
  - This partly contradicts the probing-based "NLP pipeline" localization of Tenney et al. (2019).
  - Linearly erased information was often partly recoverable by later layers.

**Limitations / open questions**
- INLP removes only linearly present information, and it may also remove correlated features (incomplete selectivity for dep).
- The number of removed directions differs across properties, which confounds comparisons of property importance.
- Only BERT-base was studied, and only on the MLM task.
- The authors caution against strong causal readings and call for non-linear erasure methods.

title: Privileged Bases in the Transformer Residual Stream
abstract: Our mathematical theories of the Transformer architecture suggest that individual coordinates in the residual stream should have no special significance (that is, the basis directions should be in some sense "arbitrary" and no more likely to encode information than random directions). Recent work has shown that this observation is false in practice. We investigate this phenomenon and provisionally conclude that the per-dimension normalizers in the Adam optimizer are to blame for the effect. We explore two other obvious sources of basis dependency in a Transformer: Layer normalization, and finite-precision floating-point calculations. We confidently rule these out as being the source of the observed basis-alignment.
summary:
**Central idea**
Transformer residual-stream coordinates can exhibit unusually large activations despite architectural symmetry arguments suggesting no privileged orthonormal basis. This paper investigates the source of that alignment. Adam's coordinatewise gradient normalization emerges as a provisional explanation after normalization and rotation controls; the experiments do not directly isolate Adam or identify the outliers' semantic meanings.

**Experiments**
The authors study a 200-million-parameter transformer with residual width 1,280. On a test batch of 128 sequences × 1,024 tokens, they count dimensions that ever contain a scalar activation with absolute value above six. They introduce within-token coordinate kurtosis, averaged across tokens, and compare native activations with fixed random orthogonal rotations. A normalization control removes LayerNorm's mean subtraction and replaces channelwise learned scales with one learned scalar. Further controls rotate the modified model's parameter matrices after training and insert fixed rotations at residual-stream interfaces during training. A shared-rotation variant separates residual communication coordinates from a common computation basis; an independent-rotations variant uses different rotations at individual reads and writes.

**Key results**
Typical baseline layers have 20–60 outlier dimensions out of 1,280, with outliers increasing through depth. Native coordinate kurtosis is elevated, whereas randomly rotated activations have kurtosis approximately three. Removing LayerNorm's coordinate dependencies preserves reported performance and leaves tails similar or heavier. Post-training parameter rotations cause tiny loss changes relative to the modified model's approximately 3.02-nat baseline test loss. Both rotation-trained variants perform approximately like the baseline, with training losses reportedly converging to differences believed within noise after roughly one billion tokens. Their residual coordinate kurtosis is near three. The shared computation basis retains baseline-like heavy tails, while independently rotated computational interfaces show much smaller tails. These controls argue against finite precision as the main cause and suggest that shared computational coordinates help establish alignment.

**Limitations / open questions**
Neither SGD training nor rotating Adam's moment coordinates is performed. Numerical precision is investigated through rotation controls rather than a precision sweep. Kurtosis near three does not establish absence of a privileged basis; its interpretation relies on an informal high-dimensional random-direction model. The training corpus, replication counts, and quantitative uncertainty are unspecified. Plots are unavailable in the supplied rendering, so numerical reporting is limited to the prose. Generalization across scales and the functions of outlier coordinates remain open.

Emotions Where Art Thou: Understanding and Characterizing the Emotional Latent Space of Large Language Models
abstract: This work investigates how large language models (LLMs) internally represent emotion by analyzing the geometry of their hidden-state space. The paper identifies a low-dimensional emotional manifold and shows that emotional representations are directionally encoded, distributed across layers, and aligned with interpretable dimensions. These structures are stable across depth and generalize to eight real-world emotion datasets spanning five languages. Cross-domain alignment yields low error and strong linear probe performance, indicating a universal emotional subspace. Within this space, internal emotion perception can be steered while preserving semantics using a learned intervention module, with especially strong control for basic emotions across languages. These findings reveal a consistent and manipulable affective geometry in LLMs and offer insight into how they internalize and process emotion.
summary:
**Central idea**
Centered SVD of mean-pooled sentence activations from synthetic emotional rewrites supplies candidate affective coordinates in decoder-only language models. The paper evaluates their correspondence with human-written emotion corpora and trains nonlinear interventions to redirect prompted emotion-label predictions. Its defensible universality claim concerns recurring directional organization, with substantial model- and dataset-dependent distance distortion.

**Experiments**
Geometry and probing analyses cover Llama-3.1-8B Base/Instruct, OLMo-v2 Base/Instruct, and Ministral-8B. Eight datasets yield nine language-specific evaluations: GoEmotions, CARER, SemEval-2007 Task 14, English/Spanish EmoEvent, German drama, Hindi BHAAV, Italian MultiEmotions-It, and French EmoTextToKids. Methods include centroid cosine similarity, least-squares alignment, stress/distortion, linear probes, and token-max coordinate discrimination. Full-space geometry is compared with 50-dimensional projections; GSM8K provides an additional comparison. Steering trains emotion-specific GELU modules at selected layers using emotion-token objectives and final-state consistency regularization. Ablations use three fixed emotion–dataset pairs.

**Key results**
Table 1 reports aggregate centroid similarities of 0.83–0.94 and probe accuracies of 0.39–0.47. Appendix E reveals considerable heterogeneity, including 0.11 probe accuracy in several EmoEvent conditions and average 50D probe accuracies of 0.34–0.39. OLMo-Instruct has high distortion in approximately 49% of layers on average despite high centroid correspondence. Llama-Base emotion rankings across layers have Spearman correlations of 0.87, 0.83, and 0.80 on the first three sign-standardized PCs. PC interpretations, including valence, are qualitative. Its neuron analysis reports an average 75% of units per layer exceeding one-vs-all AUROC 0.9 across six basic emotions. Table 2 reports English/non-English target-label rates increasing from 9%→83%/8%→84% for Llama, 11%→91%/11%→86% for OLMo, and 10%→91%/11%→79% for Ministral. These measure prediction of the requested emotion, not correctness against original labels.

**Limitations / open questions**
Sample counts, activation pairing, label harmonization, evaluation splits, chance baselines, and exact steering checkpoints are insufficiently specified. Hidden-state similarity does not independently establish semantic preservation; optimized label control does not establish selective manipulation of naturally used emotional representations. No explained-variance criterion establishes manifold dimensionality. The datasets span six languages despite the abstract's five. Main-method steering ranks and margins conflict with appendix recommendations. Tables contain aggregation and failure-marker inconsistencies, and ablation results contradict uniform claims about semantic-loss necessity and selective-layer superiority. Several geometric comparisons also conflict between prose and tables. Figures are unavailable beyond captions. Harmful-content preservation is asserted without a reported safety evaluation.

title: Decoding Emotion in the Deep: A Systematic Study of How LLMs Represent, Retain, and Express Emotion
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly expected to navigate the nuances of human emotion. While research confirms that LLMs can simulate emotional intelligence, their internal emotional mechanisms remain largely unexplored. This paper investigates the latent emotional representations within modern LLMs by asking: how, where, and for how long is emotion encoded in their neural architecture? To address this, we introduce a novel, large-scale Reddit corpus of approximately 400,000 utterances, balanced across seven basic emotions through a multi-stage process of classification, rewriting, and synthetic generation. Using this dataset, we employ lightweight "probes" to read out information from the hidden layers of various Qwen3 and LLaMA models without altering their parameters. Our findings reveal that LLMs develop a surprisingly well-defined internal geometry of emotion, which sharpens with model scale and significantly outperforms zero-shot prompting. We demonstrate that this emotional signal is not a final-layer phenomenon but emerges early and peaks mid-network. Furthermore, the internal states are both malleable (they can be influenced by simple system prompts) and persistent, as the initial emotional tone remains detectable for hundreds of subsequent tokens. We contribute our dataset, an open-source probing toolkit, and a detailed map of the emotional landscape within LLMs, offering crucial insights for developing more transparent and aligned AI systems. The code and dataset are open-sourced.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper investigates emotion-label accessibility in frozen Qwen3 and LLaMA activations, its variation with network depth, and its persistence during generated replies. It releases an English Reddit-style corpus and probing toolkit. The experiments measure decodable information and expressed language, without establishing subjective feelings or identifying causal emotion circuits.

**Experiments**

Qwen3-32B labels Reddit comments, rewrites neutral comments toward target emotions, and generates additional examples for six Ekman emotions plus neutral. Table 1 totals 434,192 items, substantially imbalanced before sampling. A 90/10 train/test split precedes training-set balancing and test-set undersampling to equal class counts. Independent two-layer ReLU MLP probes train for one epoch on last-nonpadding-token states. Seven model configurations cover Qwen3-0.6B/1.7B/4B/8B, LLaMA3.2-1B/3B, and LLaMA3.1-8B. Comparisons use pretrained states, SFT states with raw inputs or chat templates, and zero-shot JSON classification. Qwen3-4B and LLaMA3.2-3B additionally receive five-depth probing, three system-prompt generation conditions, and offset-aware probing during replies of up to 512 tokens.

**Key results**

Chat-template probes achieve 71.70–80.58% accuracy and exceed zero-shot accuracy in every model row. Zero-shot accuracy is conditional on parsable JSON; coverage ranges from 93.64% to 99.91%. Probe advantages shrink across the tested size sequences. Template probes always outperform raw-input SFT probes, but SFT-raw exceeds pretrained probing only for Qwen, contradicting the text's blanket improvement claim. Best sampled depths are 75% for Qwen3-4B, at 79.83%, and 50% for LLaMA3.2-3B, at 77.58%, slightly above their final-layer scores. The authors report coarse emotional groupings in PCA/KDE projections of supervised probe probabilities. Emotional system prompts increase sadness recall, decrease sadness precision, and reduce input–reply emotion-label agreement. Temporal analyses reportedly retain original-emotion information for hundreds of tokens, with anger and fear persisting longer than joy and surprise.

**Limitations / open questions**

Qwen-generated labels and Qwen evaluation introduce circularity; no human annotation validation is reported, and Figure 6 labels overt praise as sadness. Geometry plots describe classifier outputs rather than raw hidden-state geometry. Nonlinear probes do not establish linear emotion directions or natural causal use; prompt interventions do not isolate internal mediation. Temporal probe splits, measured layers, late-offset sample counts, and handling of early-ending replies are unspecified. Numerical temporal results cannot be recovered from the image-only plots. Checkpoint/SFT specifications and statistical uncertainty are limited. Multilingual, cross-cultural, multi-turn, and multimodal generalization remain untested.

title: Do LLMs "Feel"? Emotion Circuits Discovery and Control
abstract: As the demand for emotional intelligence in large language models (LLMs) grows, a key challenge lies in understanding the internal mechanisms that give rise to emotional expression and in controlling emotions in generated text. This study addresses three core questions: (1) Do LLMs contain context-agnostic mechanisms shaping emotional expression? (2) What form do these mechanisms take? (3) Can they be harnessed for universal emotion control? We first construct a controlled dataset, SEV (Scenario-Event with Valence), to elicit comparable internal states across emotions. Subsequently, we extract context-agnostic emotion directions that reveal consistent, cross-context encoding of emotion (Q1). We identify neurons and attention heads that locally implement emotional computation through analytical decomposition and causal analysis, and validate their causal roles via ablation and enhancement interventions. Next, we quantify each sublayer's causal influence on the model's final emotion representation and integrate the identified local components into coherent global emotion circuits that drive emotional expression (Q2). Directly modulating these circuits achieves 99.65% emotion-expression accuracy on the test set, surpassing prompting- and steering-based methods (Q3). To our knowledge, this is the first systematic study to uncover and validate emotion circuits in LLMs, offering new insights into interpretability and controllable emotional intelligence.
summary:
**Central idea**
The paper extracts emotion-associated activation directions and selects distributed MLP neurons and attention heads to control emotional expression. Main analyses use LLaMA-3.2-3B-Instruct, with additional experiments on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Last-token states from successful emotion-prompted runs are centered within matched scenario–event groups and averaged by emotion. Neurons are ranked by activation-weighted write-vector alignment; heads by zero-ablation effects on emotion projections. Global selection combines these rankings with downstream sensitivity to directional perturbations.

**Experiments**
SEV contains 480 English descriptions: eight domains × 20 scenarios × three outcome valences. An independent 480-description test set follows the same generation procedure. Six target emotions—anger, sadness, happiness, fear, surprise, and disgust—give 2,880 input–emotion combinations per complete generation evaluation. Greedy outputs receive binary GPT-4o-mini judgments of emotional style, with unspecified manual consistency checks. Component ablation and enhancement primarily measure changes in summed layerwise emotion projections; equal-count random controls are averaged over ten seeds.

**Key results**
LLaMA's reported test expression accuracy is 99.65% with circuit modulation, 98.96% with prompting, and 91.22% with residual-stream steering. Surprise improves from 67.71% under steering to 100% under circuit modulation. Selected components substantially affect projection scores. Late emotion directions reportedly have cross-sublayer cosine similarities typically above 0.90. Selected circuits have reported neuron overlap of 0.056 ± 0.033 and head overlap of 0.454 ± 0.047; overlap alone does not establish distinct neuron mechanisms or shared propagation pathways.

Qwen substantially qualifies generality: scale-2.0 circuit modulation achieves 66.18% average accuracy, versus approximately 32.52% for residual steering and 91.67% for prompting, calculated from the six reported rates. Circuit accuracy ranges from 18.33% for anger to 100% for disgust. Qwen random-head ablations also cause substantial projection decreases, contradicting a blanket characterization of random interventions as negligible.

**Limitations / open questions**
The experiments measure emotional language and activation projections, without testing subjective feeling. New synthetic examples from the same construction process do not establish arbitrary-input or out-of-domain generalization. Centering and successful control do not independently establish emotion-only representations, complete natural mechanisms, or behavioral necessity and sufficiency of locally selected components. Circuit assembly does not trace explicit intercomponent edges. Broad capability preservation, quantitative naturalness, multilingual transfer, richer emotions, and stability after fine-tuning remain unresolved. LLaMA intervention plots are image-only in the supplied rendering, preventing recovery of numerical curve values.

A Tale of Two Circuits: Grokking as Competition of Sparse and Dense Subnetworks
abstract: Grokking is a phenomenon where a model trained on an algorithmic task first overfits but, then, after a large amount of additional training, undergoes a phase transition to generalize perfectly. We empirically study the internal structure of networks undergoing grokking on the sparse parity task, and find that the grokking phase transition corresponds to the emergence of a sparse subnetwork that dominates model predictions. On an optimization level, we find that this subnetwork arises when a small subset of neurons undergoes rapid norm growth, whereas the other neurons in the network decay slowly in norm. Thus, we suggest that the grokking phase transition can be understood to emerge from competition of two largely distinct subnetworks: a dense one that dominates before the transition and generalizes poorly, and a sparse one that dominates afterwards.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper interprets sparse-parity grokking as competition between a dense subnetwork that initially controls predictions and a small, largely distinct subnetwork that eventually generalizes. The proposed mechanism is selective neuron norm growth: eventual generalizing neurons grow rapidly while other neurons shrink, concentrating prediction control in a few neurons.

**Experiments**

The main task is (40,3)-parity: predict the product of three hidden coordinates of a 40-coordinate ±1 input. A single-hidden-layer ReLU network with 1,000 neurons trains on 1,000 examples using hinge loss, SGD, learning rate 0.1, batch size 32, and weight decay 0.01. Five runs vary training data and training randomness while sharing a fixed 100-example test set. Incoming-weight-magnitude pruning identifies retained neuron prefixes. Analyses track accuracy, loss, retained-neuron count, neuron norms, and subnetwork/full-network prediction agreement. Additional configurations use weight decay 0.001 or parity size four. Separate addition/division experiments use two-layer decoder-only transformers, width 128, four attention heads, 9,400 sample points, AdamW, and three seeds.

**Key results**

The authors report that parity test accuracy rises from chance to 100% on the 100 test examples alongside orders-of-magnitude sparsification. Final subnetworks contain 6, 6, 6, 8, and 8 neurons across the five main runs. These retrospectively selected neurons show rapid norm growth shortly before grokking and eventually reproduce full-network test predictions; their complement loses agreement. Appendix D supplies explicit existence constructions using 2^k ReLU neurons for k-bit parity and six or four neurons for three-bit parity. Matching learned sizes to the six/eight-neuron constructions motivates, but does not establish, a DNF-like learned algorithm. Before full grokking, addition accuracy matches a baseline that swaps test operands and looks up the resulting training example, indicating generalization beyond strict memorization.

**Limitations / open questions**

Norm trajectories and pruning do not isolate norm growth or weight decay as causal drivers. Neuron counts do not identify the learned algorithm, and the four-neuron construction shows that observed subnetworks need not be smallest possible. The active-subnetwork definition requires exact real-valued function equality, whereas reported faithfulness measures classification agreement on finite data. The shared small test set and limited seeds restrict coverage. Plots are represented by prose and captions, preventing independent inspection of their numerical details. Application to LLM emergence remains speculative; T5 norm-growth and large-model outlier findings are cited prior work, not experiments conducted here.

Talking About Large Language Models
abstract: Thanks to rapid progress in artificial intelligence, we have entered an era when technology and philosophy intersect in interesting ways. Sitting squarely at the centre of this intersection are large language models (LLMs). The more adept LLMs become at mimicking human language, the more vulnerable we become to anthropomorphism, to seeing the systems in which they are embedded as more human-like than they really are. This trend is amplified by the natural tendency to use philosophically loaded terms, such as "knows", "believes", and "thinks", when describing these systems. To mitigate this trend, this paper advocates the practice of repeatedly stepping back to remind ourselves of how LLMs, and the systems of which they form a part, actually work. The hope is that increased scientific precision will encourage more philosophical nuance in the discourse around artificial intelligence, both within the field and in the public sphere.
summary:
**Central idea**

Shanahan argues that descriptions of LLMs should remain anchored in their computational operation and distinguish the language model from the larger system containing it. Conditional token generation can produce factual answers, fictional statements, dialogue, and reasoning without thereby establishing human-like beliefs or communicative intentions. Psychological descriptions can be useful shorthand under the intentional stance, but fluent conversation makes them particularly easy to overinterpret.

**Experiments**

This is a conceptual paper with no new experiments, datasets, benchmark measurements, or formal proofs. Illustrative prompts concern lunar history, nursery rhymes, fictional geography, deductive arguments, and invented word patterns. GPT-3, ChatGPT, LaMDA, Sparrow, Toolformer, ViLBERT, Flamingo, and SayCan appear as examples or through cited research. SayCan illustrates a component distinction: its language model scores action usefulness, while a separate perceptual module assesses feasibility. Reported improvements from chain-of-thought prompting and progress in mechanistic interpretation belong to cited work.

**Key results**

The conclusions are philosophical and methodological. The paper distinguishes encoding factual associations from literally knowing their contents. It treats evidence-responsive belief revision and engagement with a shared world as prerequisites for belief attribution in its fullest sense. External information sources and model editing shift the assessment toward the complete system; visual input and physical embodiment require similarly specific architectural analysis. The paper argues that correlations learned by frozen vision-language models need not connect an object description to the intended object rather than an incidental feature. For deduction, it distinguishes plausible, sometimes correct arguments from computations whose causal structure follows truth-preserving inference. It recommends explicit algorithmic scaffolding or reverse engineering to establish this stronger faithfulness. RLHF is interpreted as changing which continuations raters favor while retaining conditional token generation.

**Limitations / open questions**

The links between predictive objectives, truth sensitivity, and legitimate belief attribution are argued informally. The paper supplies no test or proof that sequence prediction excludes internal truth-sensitive representations or emergent reasoning algorithms. Its proposed equivalences between preference training and augmented-corpus training are thought experiments rather than demonstrated optimization equivalences. It leaves open which richer architectures warrant psychological descriptions and explicitly declines to rule them out for every possible LLM-based system. The supplied article is the February 2023 revision.

title: Multiversal views on language models
abstract: The virtuosity of language models like GPT-3 opens a new world of possibility for human-AI collaboration in writing. In this paper, we present a framework in which generative language models are conceptualized as multiverse generators. This framework also applies to human imagination and is core to how we read and write fiction. We call for exploration into this commonality through new forms of interfaces which allow humans to couple their imagination to AI to write, explore, and understand non-linear fiction. We discuss the early insights we have gained from actively pursuing this approach by developing and testing a novel multiversal GPT-3-assisted writing interface.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper conceptualizes autoregressive language models as generators of branching narrative multiverses. Repeated sampling from the same prompt produces alternative continuations, which can themselves be continued. It distinguishes **interpretational multiplicity**, alternative underlying presents compatible with an ambiguous description, from **dynamic multiplicity**, alternative futures compatible with the same underlying present. Everettian quantum mechanics and Deutsch’s virtual-reality-generator analogy motivate this perspective. The authors argue that reading and writing involve imagining such alternatives, making narrative graphs a promising medium for human–AI collaboration.

**Experiments**

The authors describe several months of iterative prototyping and beta testing of GPT-3-assisted writing interfaces with five users. They report co-written linear and nonlinear stories spanning the equivalent of thousands of pages. No standardized dataset, controlled comparison, quantitative coherence metric, or detailed user-study protocol is supplied. Implemented features include complementary tree and linear reading views, search, chapter indexing, bookmarks, tags, floating notes, and support for cycles and multiple parents. An adaptive branching algorithm samples distinct tokens until their cumulative probability reaches a threshold. Automatic indexed memory and contextual summarization pipelines remain development directions.

**Key results**

Three of the five beta users reported previously unimagined creative freedom and expressive power. The authors qualitatively report that tree views help users conceptualize and navigate branching narratives and make topology edits more intuitive than the linear view. They observed passive curation when generation was easy but editing and restructuring were comparatively difficult; interface flaws could also damage perceived ownership. Users’ practice of keeping separate notes motivated floating notes. Users reportedly maintained long-range narrative coherence through curation and occasional reminders despite GPT-3’s limited context window. These are exploratory observations rather than measured comparative effects.

**Limitations / open questions**

The small cohort, evolving prototypes, and informal assessments limit conclusions about usability, ownership, output quality, and coherence. Recruitment, feature-specific participant counts, baselines, and uncertainty estimates are unspecified. Benefits attributable specifically to branching, adaptive branching, or individual editing features remain unmeasured. Next-token probability spread is assumed to indicate useful narrative divergence without a direct semantic-diversity or coherence evaluation. The connection between human imagination and model generation is conceptual. The paper supplies no analysis of GPT-3’s internal mechanisms or validation of faithful real-world simulation. Figures are represented only by captions in the supplied text.

title: Want to predict/explain/control the output of GPT-4? Then learn about the world, not about transformers
Improving alignment of dialogue agents via targeted human judgements
Bing’s A.I. Chat: ‘I Want to Be Alive.’
Bing: “I will not harm you unless you harm me first”
Conversational AI: Social and ethical considerations
Toolformer: Language models can teach themselves to use tools
