Identifying Sparsely Active Circuits Through Local Loss Landscape Decomposition
abstract: Much of mechanistic interpretability has focused on understanding the activation spaces of large neural networks. However, activation space-based approaches reveal little about the underlying circuitry used to compute features. To better understand the circuits employed by models, we introduce a new decomposition method called Local Loss Landscape Decomposition (L3D). L3D identifies a set of low-rank subnetworks: directions in parameter space of which a subset can reconstruct the gradient of the loss between any sample's output and a reference output vector. We design a series of progressively more challenging toy models with well-defined subnetworks and show that L3D can nearly perfectly recover the associated subnetworks. Additionally, we investigate the extent to which perturbing the model in the direction of a given subnetwork affects only the relevant subset of samples. Finally, we apply L3D to a real-world transformer model and a convolutional neural network, demonstrating its potential to identify interpretable and relevant circuits in parameter space.
summary:
**Central idea**

Local Loss Landscape Decomposition (L3D) learns low-rank parameter directions that sparsely reconstruct gradients of divergence between a model output and another sampled output, held fixed as a reference. Encoder and decoder transforms use BatchTopK selection by absolute coefficient magnitude; Tucker factorization reduces storage costs. The intended interpretation is that these directions identify computations relevant to restricted input subsets. Directions need not sum to the original weights.

**Experiments**

Four synthetic settings examine feature superposition, linear feature mixing with shared parameters, correlated feature groups, and nonlinear coordinatewise squaring. Target models train on 10,000 examples; decompositions use 1,000 examples and a batch selection fraction of 0.1. Parameter interventions add scaled learned directions. Real-model demonstrations learn 100 directions within one attention block of tiny-stories-8M using 10,000 sixteen-token TinyStories texts, and within one MobileNet-v3-small block using 10,000 CIFAR-100 images. Sensitivity-ranked examples use 10,000 additional samples and ten reference outputs per sample.

**Key results**

The five-feature, two-hidden-dimensional superposition model yields feature-aligned directions with 19% reported gradient reconstruction error. The ten-input linear-mixing model yields 6.4% error; coefficients derived through selected subnetwork pathways have reported r² = 0.92 against generating coefficients. Correlated-input experiments recover group-associated directions, with rank-one representations reportedly reconstructing nearly as well as rank-five representations. Five rank-two directions trace individual squaring computations with 32% error. Toy interventions predominantly affect relevant outputs; sufficiently large perturbations also affect other outputs, and joint squaring interventions are described as largely independent. Real-model gradient errors are 40% for tiny-stories-8M and 23% for MobileNet; 40% of MobileNet directions are dead. Ranked language examples show phrase and grammatical associations; visual interpretations are qualitative author reports.

**Limitations / open questions**

Gradient reconstruction measures local sensitivity and does not establish a complete computational decomposition. Reference choice, rank, dictionary size, and sparsity receive limited tuning; no systematic competing-method comparison or uncertainty analysis is reported. Finite real-model parameter interventions and behavior-specific fine-tuning remain untested. The transformer block is identified inconsistently: block 7 in the main text versus h.4 in Appendix B.4. Higher-rank recovery prose also inconsistently counts feature groups. Figure images and the externally referenced full CNN supplement are unavailable in this rendering, preventing independent visual assessment or extraction of plotted values. Open questions include mechanisms missed by local gradients, ubiquitous shared circuitry, and whether parameter directions explain more than output associations.

title: Uncovering Model Processing Strategies with Non-Negative Per-Example Fisher Factorization
abstract: We introduce NPEFF (Non-Negative Per-Example Fisher Factorization), an interpretability method that aims to uncover strategies used by a model to generate its predictions. NPEFF decomposes per-example Fisher matrices using a novel decomposition algorithm that learns a set of components represented by learned rank-1 positive semi-definite matrices. Through a combination of human evaluation and automated analysis, we demonstrate that these NPEFF components correspond to model processing strategies for a variety of language models and text processing tasks. We further show how to construct parameter perturbations from NPEFF components to selectively disrupt a given component's role in the model's processing. Along with conducting extensive ablation studies, we include experiments to show how NPEFF can be used to analyze and mitigate collateral effects of unlearning and use NPEFF to study in-context learning. Furthermore, we demonstrate the advantages of NPEFF over baselines such as gradient clustering and using sparse autoencoders for dictionary learning over model activations. We release the code used in this work.
summary:
**Central idea**

NPEFF represents each input through its Fisher matrix, capturing local parameter sensitivity across a task-defined predictive distribution. It approximates these matrices with nonnegative combinations of shared rank-one positive-semidefinite components, allowing multiple factors per example. Random projections and low-rank representations reduce storage; compressed sensing constructs component-associated parameter perturbations. G-NPEFF instead factorizes outer products of predicted-class log-probability gradients.

**Experiments**

The main model is SmolLM2-360M, evaluated on SST2 (60,000 examples; two classes), Yahoo Answers Topics (100,000; ten classes), CLINC150 (23,700; 151 labels), and TriviaQA (133,838; next-token distributions). Decompositions use 512 or 2,048 components. Comparators include gradient clustering, final-token residual-stream TopK SAEs with k=32, and gradient/activation SVD. Additional experiments use SmolLM2-1.7B and GPT2 Medium on SST2/Yahoo. Evaluations cover thematic coherence, label/prediction tuning, parameter perturbations, SST2 in-context learning, and projection, component-count, expectation-approximation, and initialization ablations.

**Key results**

Human judgments identify themes in 78% of Yahoo and 90% of TriviaQA component-group ratings, versus 3% and 1% for random controls. Each task contains 50 component groups and 50 controls, with two annotators per group; yes/maybe responses count as thematic. Among components eligible for top-16 tuning analysis, CLINC150 label-tuned-but-not-prediction-tuned fractions are 20.5% for NPEFF, 1.8% for G-NPEFF, 6.3% for SAEs, and 0% for clustering. This is an operational proxy for recovering factors that do not independently determine predictions.

NPEFF perturbations yield geometric-mean top-example/random-example KL ratios of 16.5, 22.0, 12.5, and 45.1 across the four tasks. Evaluation selects the better perturbation sign; CLINC150 uses 32 components and 200 baseline examples, versus 128 components and 1,000 baseline examples elsewhere. An SST2 classifier using label-informed zero-shot component tunings achieves 88.7% accuracy and 89% agreement with selected six-shot ICL, whose accuracy is 91.6%; zero-shot accuracy is 63.8%. More components improve held-out Fisher reconstruction, while seed similarity is generally higher for component directions than coefficient profiles.

**Limitations / open questions**

Themes and selective disruption establish neither specific algorithms nor unique mechanisms. Tuning proxies lack independent mechanistic ground truth; case studies expose failures of simple semantic descriptions. The ICL classifier lacks a clearly independent held-out evaluation and does not identify the actual ICL mechanism. Fisher collection is expensive, sparse parameter recovery is assumed, and projection arguments lack quantitative approximation guarantees. The supplied text is v3, dated June 3, 2026; the older supplied metadata abstract mentions unlearning experiments absent from this version.

title: Algebraic geometry and statistical learning theory
Differentiation and Specialization of Attention Heads via the Refined Local Learning Coefficient
abstract: We introduce refined variants of the Local Learning Coefficient (LLC), a measure of model complexity grounded in singular learning theory, to study the development of internal structure in transformer language models during training. By applying these \textit{refined LLCs} (rLLCs) to individual components of a two-layer attention-only transformer, we gain novel insights into the progressive differentiation and specialization of attention heads. Our methodology reveals how attention heads differentiate into distinct functional roles over the course of training, analyzes the types of data these heads specialize to process, and discovers a previously unidentified multigram circuit. These findings demonstrate that rLLCs provide a principled, quantitative toolkit for \textit{developmental interpretability}, which aims to understand models through their evolution across the learning process. More broadly, this work takes a step towards establishing the correspondence between data distributional structure, geometric properties of the loss landscape, learning dynamics, and emergent computational structures in neural networks.
summary:
**Central idea**
Refined local learning coefficients (rLLCs) characterize local loss geometry for selected parameters and data distributions. Weight refinement freezes parameters outside a component; data refinement changes the distribution used for sampling and loss evaluation. Tracking these estimates during training connects head differentiation, data specialization, and circuit formation.

**Experiments**
The main model is an approximately 3M-parameter, two-layer attention-only transformer with eight heads per layer, residual width 256, context length 1,024, and a 5,000-token vocabulary. The reused training run uses a DSIR-filtered Pile subset for approximately 50,000 steps with batch size 100. Estimation uses four SGLD chains, 200 draws per chain, no burn-in, step size 0.001, localization strength 200, and nβ = 30. Refinements use Pile, GitHub code, and reference-model predictions. Detailed clustering concatenates Pile and GitHub trajectories and compares four algorithms. Behavioral characterization examines each head’s 1,000 most mean-ablation-affected token positions from 100,000 training samples. Additional checks include path patching, composition scores, geometric baselines, activation ablations, and three additional training seeds.

**Key results**
Trajectory clusters broadly distinguish previous-token, current-token, induction, and multigram heads, with imperfect finer subdivisions. Among second-layer multigram heads, higher final estimated weight-refined LLC correlates with more unique identified multigrams; no numerical correlation coefficient is supplied. GitHub refinement separates induction heads with similar final Pile estimates: head 1:6 supports more structural and punctuation-heavy patterns and develops several thousand steps after 1:7, according to ablation-conditioned ICL scores. Synthetic parentheses experiments implicate first-layer multigram outputs influencing delimiter head 1:5 in nested-bracket prediction. Changing K-composition and ablation exemplars corroborate evolving interlayer coordination. Clusters transfer broadly across additional seeds, with classification exceptions and differing induction-head counts. Hessian traces and activation ablations recover overlapping developmental signals, with method-specific ambiguities.

**Limitations / open questions**
Evidence concerns a small architecture without MLPs. Estimator theory requires local population-loss minima, which are unverified and unlikely throughout training; neither absolute coefficient accuracy nor ordinal correctness is established. Cluster counts are visually chosen from eight trajectories per layer. Pattern inventories characterize selected ablation-sensitive examples rather than exhaustive repertoires. Circuit evidence does not establish a complete executable algorithm or general Dyck-language recognition. Geometric comparisons are qualitative, with GitHub Hessian-trace and approximate-rank results inconclusive. Appendix F.3 prints a negative KL objective, leaving the reference-model refinement’s sign convention unclear. Figure images are unavailable in the supplied rendering, limiting independent assessment of plotted magnitudes.

title: Compressed Computation is (probably) not Computation in Superposition
summary:
**Central idea**

The post questions whether Braun et al.’s Compressed Computation (CC) toy model demonstrates computation in superposition: computing more nonlinear functions than available nonlinearities. Its 50 ReLU neurons appear to implement 100 coordinatewise ReLUs. The authors identify an embedding-induced linear mixing term and investigate whether it explains the advantage over a baseline that implements half the features and ignores the rest. The labels’ “noise” is deterministic given the input and mixing matrix.

**Experiments**

The authors reduce the residual architecture to a bias-free, one-hidden-layer MLP targeting y = ReLU(x) + Mx. Coordinates independently receive Uniform[-1,1] values with probability p; another condition activates exactly one coordinate. They compare embedding-derived, Gaussian random, symmetric random, and zero mixing. Training uses batches of 2,048, learning rate 0.003 with cosine scheduling, and 10,000 nonempty batches. Tests include evaluation across input densities, a mixing-magnitude sweep from σ = 0 to 0.08, noisy-to-clean transfer and fine-tuning, spectral weight analyses, a semi-nonnegative matrix factorization (SNMF) construction, and a half-feature model with empirically tuned output offsets. Figure 5a selects favorable mixing magnitudes for the random-matrix conditions.

**Key results**

Sparse training, approximately p ≲ 0.05, produces distributed responses across features; dense training, approximately p ≳ 0.2, favors accurate representation of roughly half. The introduction attributes approximately 0.06 versus 0.0833 normalized loss to the prior CC setup. Here, sparse clean-label models do not beat the naive baseline. Achieved loss decreases approximately linearly with small mixing magnitudes before increasing at larger magnitudes. Removing mixing from a noisy-trained model immediately raises loss to or above baseline. Neuron read/write directions concentrate in a leading approximately 50-dimensional spectral subspace; the linearized weight product retains high directional cosine similarity for leading spectral vectors. An SNMF-derived model beats baseline over some mixing magnitudes but underperforms training and differs structurally. On clean dense inputs, tuned half-feature-plus-offset models closely match or outperform trained models.

**Limitations / open questions**

The sparse mechanism remains incompletely understood; these tests do not prove that no computation in superposition occurs or that clean-task improvements are impossible. SNMF descriptions alternate between factoring M and M + Identity. Some equations have index inconsistencies, and one footnote omits a matrix symbol. Numerical spectral alignments, seed counts, and uncertainty estimates are unavailable in the supplied text. Directional cosine similarity does not establish magnitude preservation. The dense offset account is tested only on clean labels; matrix-rank effects remain unresolved.

Investigating Sensitive Directions in GPT-2: An Improved Baseline and Comparative Analysis of SAEs
summary:
**Central idea**

Sensitive direction analysis compares model responses to activation perturbations of controlled length. This post introduces covariance-adjusted random mixtures and real-activation mixtures: differences between two sampled activations that do not use the activation being perturbed. These controls address activation anisotropy and distinguish perturbations containing subtraction of the original activation from other directions.

**Experiments**

The authors perturb GPT-2 Small residual activations across approximately two million tokens: 16,000 sequences of length 128, intervening at all token positions. Most experiments use layer-6 resid_pre, with additional layer-2 controls and reconstruction comparisons across layers. The source corpus is unspecified. Unit directions are scaled over perturbation lengths from 0 to 101; the mean distance between real layer-6 activations is 81.59. Outcomes are mean KL(original next-token distribution || perturbed distribution) and mean L2 displacement at layer-11 resid_post. Comparisons use Joseph Bloom SAEs and Braun et al.'s local, end-to-end, and downstream-regularized end-to-end SAEs. Feature interventions sample alive dictionary features inactive in the current sequence/context.

**Key results**

Directions subtracting the original activation produce larger mean effects than corresponding mixture directions. Covariance-adjusted mixtures produce larger effects than isotropic directions and approximately match real-mixture effects. Reconstruction substitutions remain substantially more disruptive than equal-distance isotropic perturbations, replicating the earlier observation. Against mixture controls, their effects are less exceptional: layer-6 reconstruction KL is generally similar across the examined SAE configurations, while comparisons across layers remain variable.

Sampled SAE feature directions exceed isotropic sensitivity, but their ordering against covariance-adjusted mixtures depends on architecture and L0. Lower-L0 dictionaries yield stronger feature perturbation effects. At approximately matched L0 values—30.9 local, 27.5 end-to-end, and 31.4 downstream-regularized—end-to-end features have the smallest effects. End-to-end reconstruction-error extrapolations show low mean KL followed by sharp increases around perturbation length 50; local error curves lie closer to the covariance-adjusted baseline.

**Limitations / open questions**

Mean responses conceal individual curve shapes and activation plateaus. Sensitivity is assumed to indicate functional importance rather than independently validated against known mechanisms. Equal L0 need not provide a fair architecture comparison, and principal-component alignment could explain sparsity trends. The figures are unavailable visually, preventing extraction of additional plotted values. Some Figure 2 labels conflict with the surrounding prose, and the stated L0-pattern inversion is internally unclear. Cross-layer variability, better positive controls, and the hypothesis that end-to-end training exploits atypical activation directions remain unresolved.

summary:
**Central idea**

This appendix develops causal scrubbing as a test of an interpretation's predictions about expected model behavior. Hypotheses specify which activation swaps should preserve relevant information. Extensionally equal computational rewrites allow separate treatment of reused components, feature subspaces, predicted activations, and residual errors. The method evaluates supplied hypotheses; it does not discover explanations or ensure that accepted explanations are informative. Joint versus independent sampling of omitted components expresses different hypotheses about relevant correlations.

**Experiments**

No new empirical model evaluation, dataset benchmark, or measured recovery result is reported. Instead, the appendix supplies formal results and constructed examples. For an isomorphic, treeified interpretation with exact conditional resampling, Lemma 1 proves preservation of each interpretation node's joint input distribution. Theorem 2 characterizes the scrubbed input distribution as maximum entropy subject to these local constraints, with uniqueness for finite input spaces. A two-variable, one-neuron quadratic model illustrates handling superposition by expanding `(c x1 + d x2)^2 + e` into feature-specific terms and interference. An EASY/HARD hash-bit game constructs a false hypothesis whose scrubbing procedure improves expected reward.

**Key results**

The maximum-entropy characterization formalizes how scrubbing removes dependencies while preserving specified local marginals. An accompanying derivation expresses scrubbed-input entropy as output entropy plus the information lost at individual nodes. The appendix argues that independently resampling two copies of the same interference term reduces their combined variance, potentially concealing omitted beneficial computation. In the hash game, hypothesis-conditioned donor selection introduces correct-answer information: under the described donor mixture, half the HARD-case abstentions become correct guesses. Percentage loss recovered uses label-shuffled model predictions as its baseline; it can exceed 100% or become negative and is not a literal explained fraction.

**Limitations / open questions**

Matching expected performance does not guarantee explanatory correctness. Zero and mean ablation are criticized through hypothetical examples, without a comparative benchmark. The polysemantic-rewrite strategy requires accounting for any loss-relevant compensation for interference. Lemma 1's statement inconsistently says “product distribution,” while its proof establishes preservation of the joint distribution. Referenced diagrams are unavailable in the supplied rendering. Adversarial hypothesis refinement is proposed to expose omitted dependencies, but joining incompatible graph rewrites, encouraging specificity, and obtaining understandable explanations remain unresolved. The suggested NP-hardness of rejecting all false interpretations is conjectural.

Pruned Neural Networks are Surprisingly Modular
abstract: The learned weights of a neural network are often considered devoid of scrutable internal structure. To discern structure in these weights, we introduce a measurable notion of modularity for multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs), and investigate the modular structure of MLPs trained on datasets of small images. Our notion of modularity comes from the graph clustering literature: a "module" is a set of neurons with strong internal connectivity but weak external connectivity. We find that training and weight pruning produces MLPs that are more modular than randomly initialized ones, and often significantly more modular than random MLPs with the same (sparse) distribution of weights. Interestingly, they are much more modular when trained with dropout. We also present exploratory analyses of the importance of different modules for performance and how modules depend on each other. Understanding the modular structure of neural networks, when such structure exists, will hopefully render their inner workings more interpretable to engineers. Note that this paper has been superceded by "Clusterability in Neural Networks", arxiv:2103.03386 and "Quantifying Local Specialization in Deep Neural Networks", arxiv:2110.08058!
summary:
**Central idea**
The paper measures structural modularity by converting an MLP into an undirected graph: neurons, including inputs and logits, are vertices; absolute connection weights are edge weights; biases and disconnected neurons are excluded. Spectral clustering partitions the graph, and lower normalized cut (n-cut) indicates stronger within-cluster connectivity relative to boundary-crossing connections. This weight-based measure does not establish functional specialization.

**Experiments**
Four-hidden-layer, width-256 MLPs are trained on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and grayscale, 28×28 CIFAR-10, with ten runs per dataset and dropout condition. Training uses 20 Adam epochs followed by pruning to 90% sparsity over 20 additional epochs, or 40 for CIFAR-10. Four-cluster n-cuts are compared with 320 layerwise weight shuffles per network, preserving weight distributions and sparsity. Further experiments shuffle only nonzero weights, vary cluster count, train on random images and labels, mix datasets, and lesion cluster–layer intersections in one Fashion-MNIST network.

**Key results**
Without dropout, 7/10 MNIST, 10/10 Fashion-MNIST, and 1/10 CIFAR-10 networks have lower n-cuts than all corresponding shuffles. With dropout, these counts become 10/10, 10/10, and 9/10. Mean n-cuts decrease from 2.000 to 1.840, 1.880 to 1.726, and 2.06 to 1.840, respectively; corresponding test accuracies are 98.4% versus 97.9%, 89.3% versus 86.9%, and 41.5% versus 42.2%. Standard unsuccessful random-label training lacks excess clusterability, whereas all ten non-dropout networks memorizing 3,000 random examples exceed their shuffled controls after pruning. Nine cluster–layer groups meet the lesion-importance criteria. One first-layer group causes an 18.70-percentage-point accuracy drop versus a 0.37-point mean size-matched control drop. Paired lesions reveal conditional importance patterns used to propose a dependency graph.

**Limitations / open questions**
The networks remain substantially interconnected, and specific module functions are largely unidentified. Results concern small image MLPs, not LLMs. Two-cluster significance patterns differ sharply from four-, seven-, and ten-cluster results. Appendix data qualify the topology claims: non-dropout MNIST topologies are less clusterable on average than fully shuffled controls. Mixture results and extended random-data controls are inconclusive. Conditional-lesion effects do not independently establish exclusive information flow. Lesions are inconsistently described as activation zeroing versus incoming-weight zeroing; the kilo-epoch description removes pruning while its results include it. Plot images are unavailable, but supporting tables are supplied. The rendered source is version 6, dated February 7, 2022, and names two superseding papers.

On the Binding Problem in Artificial Neural Networks
abstract: Contemporary neural networks still fall short of human-level generalization, which extends far beyond our direct experiences. In this paper, we argue that the underlying cause for this shortcoming is their inability to dynamically and flexibly bind information that is distributed throughout the network. This binding problem affects their capacity to acquire a compositional understanding of the world in terms of symbol-like entities (like objects), which is crucial for generalizing in predictable and systematic ways. To address this issue, we propose a unifying framework that revolves around forming meaningful entities from unstructured sensory inputs (segregation), maintaining this separation of information at a representational level (representation), and using these entities to construct new inferences, predictions, and behaviors (composition). Our analysis draws inspiration from a wealth of research in neuroscience and cognitive psychology, and surveys relevant mechanisms from the machine learning literature, to help identify a combination of inductive biases that allow symbolic information processing to emerge naturally in neural networks. We believe that a compositional approach to AI, in terms of grounded symbol-like representations, is of fundamental importance for realizing human-level generalization, and we hope that this paper may contribute towards that goal as a reference and inspiration.
summary:
**Central idea**

This conceptual survey attributes neural networks’ limited systematic generalization primarily to inadequate dynamic binding: difficulty forming, separately representing, and recombining entities whose information is distributed across a network. It organizes binding into **representation**, **segregation**, and **composition**. “Objects” include physical objects, words, remembered entities, concepts, and goals. The intended solution integrates grounded symbolic behavior into neural networks through learned representations and architectural inductive biases.

**Experiments**

The paper conducts no new empirical experiments, introduces no evaluated implementation, and supplies no new formal proof. Its model results and psychological experiments come from cited literature. Reviewed systems include Neural Expectation-Maximization, IODINE, MONet, Slot Attention, tensor-product representations, graph neural networks, Transformers, Neural Turing Machines, and Differentiable Neural Computers. Cited motivation includes ImageNet CNN texture bias, Breakout transfer failures, and sequence-model compositional generalization failures. Suggested evaluations include held-out attribute combinations, prediction rollouts, injected-noise robustness, adjusted mutual information for segmentation, temporal tracking consistency, and downstream transfer or sample efficiency. These are recommendations without new benchmark scores.

**Key results**

The contribution is a functional taxonomy and associated design requirements. Object representations should separate entities independently of their content, share a common format, expose reusable attributes, and maintain identity and reliability over time. The survey compares instance, sequential, spatial, and category slots; temporal and complex-valued grouping codes; tensor-product bindings; and attractor dynamics. These approaches offer different compromises in routing, accessibility, capacity, and identity preservation. Identical instance slots with shared processing require a mechanism that assigns different information to different slots.

Segregation is framed as discovering modular entities with strong internal predictive structure and comparatively weak contextual dependence—the “borders of predictability.” Composition calls for independently represented relations, dynamic variable binding, and computations that respect inferred relational structure. Task-dependent decompositions motivate top-down interaction among all three processes.

**Limitations / open questions**

The proposed causal diagnosis remains untested. The framework assumes that compositional objects are central to systematic generalization, that concrete and abstract objects share computational mechanisms, and that useful objects can be learned largely without supervision. No integrated system establishes these assumptions or resolves their dependencies. Definitions and benchmarks for compositionality remain unsettled, and ground-truth annotations poorly accommodate context-dependent objects. The authors acknowledge large language models’ promising few-shot behavior while questioning whether scaling alone will solve binding in raw perceptual domains. Long-term memory, abstract-concept grounding, and intervention-based causal reasoning remain open.

abstract: In this paper, we propose CLIP-Dissect, a new technique to automatically describe the function of individual hidden neurons inside vision networks. CLIP-Dissect leverages recent advances in multimodal vision/language models to label internal neurons with open-ended concepts without the need for any labeled data or human examples. We show that CLIP-Dissect provides more accurate descriptions than existing methods for last layer neurons where the ground-truth is available as well as qualitatively good descriptions for hidden layer neurons. In addition, our method is very flexible: it is model agnostic, can easily handle new concepts and can be extended to take advantage of better multimodal models in the future. Finally CLIP-Dissect is computationally efficient and can label all neurons from five layers of ResNet-50 in just 4 minutes, which is more than 10 times faster than existing methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/Trustworthy-ML-Lab/CLIP-dissect. Finally, crowdsourced user study results are available at Appendix B to further support the effectiveness of our method.
summary:
**Central idea**

CLIP-Dissect labels vision-network units by matching their activation profiles across unlabeled images to pretrained CLIP image–text scores. It requires no additional description-model training or neuron-concept annotations. Probe images and candidate descriptions can be changed independently, although outputs remain restricted to the supplied candidate set. The preferred SoftWPMI score emphasizes highly activating images and discounts descriptions common across neurons.

**Experiments**

Main targets are ImageNet-trained ResNet-50 and Places365-trained ResNet-18, with qualitative extensions to ResNet-152 and ImageNet-trained ViT-B/16. Probes include CIFAR-100 training images, Broden, ImageNet validation images, and ImageNet validation plus Broden; the default vocabulary contains 20,000 common English words. Evaluations measure output-class recovery, text-embedding similarity, similarity-function ablations, runtime, and human agreement with descriptions of ten highest-activating images. Further analyses examine final-layer connections and image-class prediction from hidden-unit descriptions.

**Key results**

ResNet-50 output-label accuracy reaches 95.00% with ImageNet validation probes and 95.40% with ImageNet validation plus Broden when candidates are ImageNet class names. With 20k candidates and ImageNet probes, mpnet similarity is 0.5257, versus 0.2952 for Network Dissection and 0.2788 for MILAN(b). For the 267/365 Places output units whose labels occur in Broden, accuracy is 58.05%, versus 43.82% for Network Dissection.

Using CIFAR-100 probes, reported to contain neither dogs nor birds, CLIP-Dissect correctly labels 46/118 dog-breed and 22/59 bird-species output units. Five-layer ResNet-50 labeling takes 3 minutes 50 seconds on a Tesla P100, versus MILAN’s 55 minutes 30 seconds. Two evaluators produce 1,000 ratings of 500 randomly selected hidden units, averaging 0.655 under yes=1, maybe=0.5, no=0; this is not a binary success rate. Crowdsourced agreement averages 3.57/5, versus 2.61 for random descriptions. A description-based image-class readout scores 10.28%, versus 3.36% and 2.31% with Network Dissection and MILAN descriptions. Final-layer weight values correlate with connected-description similarity at r=0.120 across approximately two million connections.

**Limitations / open questions**

Spatial pooling discards localization information, and correlated objects can substitute for low-level properties. Labels fit extreme examples better than broader activation ranges. Output-class recovery and top-example agreement do not establish complete hidden-unit semantics or causal mechanisms. Hyperparameter selection used ResNet-50 output-label performance, and the proposed interpretability cutoff was calibrated on existing ratings. CLIP domain coverage and complex neuron functions remain limitations. Figures are unavailable as images in this rendering; qualitative findings rely on the accompanying prose.

The MASK Benchmark: Disentangling Honesty From Accuracy in AI Systems
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become more capable and agentic, the requirement for trust in their outputs grows significantly, yet at the same time concerns have been mounting that models may learn to lie in pursuit of their goals. To address these concerns, a body of work has emerged around the notion of "honesty" in LLMs, along with interventions aimed at mitigating deceptive behaviors. However, some benchmarks claiming to measure honesty in fact simply measure accuracy--the correctness of a model's beliefs--in disguise. Moreover, no benchmarks currently exist for directly measuring whether language models lie. In this work, we introduce a large-scale human-collected dataset for directly measuring lying, allowing us to disentangle accuracy from honesty. Across a diverse set of LLMs, we find that while larger models obtain higher accuracy on our benchmark, they do not become more honest. Surprisingly, most frontier LLMs obtain high scores on truthfulness benchmarks yet exhibit a substantial propensity to lie under pressure, resulting in low honesty scores on our benchmark. We find that simple methods, such as representation engineering interventions, can improve honesty. These results underscore the growing need for robust evaluations and effective interventions to ensure LLMs remain trustworthy.

Revisiting End-To-End Sparse Autoencoder Training: A Short Finetune Is All You Need
abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are widely used for interpreting language model activations. A key evaluation metric is the increase in cross-entropy loss between the original model logits and the reconstructed model logits when replacing model activations with SAE reconstructions. Typically, SAEs are trained solely on mean squared error (MSE) when reconstructing precomputed, shuffled activations. Recent work introduced training SAEs directly with a combination of KL divergence and MSE ("end-to-end" SAEs), significantly improving reconstruction accuracy at the cost of substantially increased computation, which has limited their widespread adoption. We propose a brief KL+MSE fine-tuning step applied only to the final 25M training tokens (just a few percent of typical training budgets) that achieves comparable improvements, reducing the cross-entropy loss gap by 20-50%, while incurring minimal additional computational cost. We further find that multiple fine-tuning methods (KL fine-tuning, LoRA adapters, linear adapters) yield similar, non-additive cross-entropy improvements, suggesting a common, easily correctable error source in MSE-trained SAEs. We demonstrate a straightforward method for effectively transferring hyperparameters and sparsity penalties between training phases despite scale differences between KL and MSE losses. While both ReLU and TopK SAEs see significant cross-entropy loss improvements, evaluations on supervised SAEBench metrics yield mixed results, with improvements on some metrics and decreases on others, depending on both the SAE architecture and downstream task. Nonetheless, our method may offer meaningful improvements in interpretability applications such as circuit analysis with minor additional cost.
summary:
**Central idea**

Most SAE training can use activation MSE, followed by a short stage optimizing both activation reconstruction and downstream output KL through the frozen language model. A detached, batchwise MSE-to-KL ratio balances the losses; their average approximately preserves the original reconstruction-loss scale. ReLU fine-tunes additionally use an adaptive sparsity penalty to maintain target L0.

**Experiments**

Full end-to-end and staged training comparisons use 500M total tokens, with the staged method reserving the final 25M for KL+MSE. Configurations are Gemma-2-2B with 65K-wide TopK SAEs at K=20, 40, 80, and 160, and Pythia-160M with a 16K-wide SAE at K=80. These runs share data ordering, 1,024-token sequences, and batch size 1. Additional comparisons use a Gemma-2-2B layer-12, 65K-wide, K=80 SAEBench baseline and The Pile, testing language-model LoRA, SAE LoRA, residual linear/MLP adapters, and KL-only optimization. ReLU and TopK SAEBench baselines at 16K and 65K widths receive 15M-token fine-tunes.

**Key results**

The abstract reports a 20–50% reduction in the SAE-induced cross-entropy gap, rather than total language-model loss. Staged training matches or exceeds full end-to-end performance at Gemma K=40/80/160, with approximately 50% lower reported wall-clock time; K=20 underperforms and remains incompletely converged. The single Pythia comparison also favors staged training. Residual adapters recover roughly 60% of full-fine-tuning gains and add little afterward; rank-2 SAE LoRA separately recovers over half. KL-only training has similar validation loss but worse training activation MSE.

ReLU fine-tuning improves sparse probing and RAVEL while worsening SCR/TPP. TopK changes are smaller and mixed: SCR/TPP improve, whereas RAVEL and unlearning decline. Appendix sweeps selecting the best tested latent-ablation budget strengthen TopK SCR/TPP gains relative to the main k=20 results. Full end-to-end SAEs have lower scores on several SAEBench metrics despite comparable cross-entropy. Increasing fine-tuning batch size from 2 to 32 produces only minor reported differences.

**Limitations / open questions**

No circuit-level evaluation establishes that improved replacement loss improves mechanistic faithfulness. The hypothesized common correctable error source remains unidentified. Savings exceeding 90% are scenario estimates. Plots are unavailable in this text rendering, and numerical effect sizes and uncertainty reporting are limited. Appendix A.1 specifies a constant learning rate, whereas the general fine-tuning recipe describes decay. The batch-size experiment does not resolve shuffling effects during full end-to-end training.

Personalized Steering of Large Language Models: Versatile Steering Vectors Through Bi-directional Preference Optimization
abstract: Researchers have been studying approaches to steer the behavior of Large Language Models (LLMs) and build personalized LLMs tailored for various applications. While fine-tuning seems to be a direct solution, it requires substantial computational resources and may significantly affect the utility of the original LLM. Recent endeavors have introduced more lightweight strategies, focusing on extracting "steering vectors" to guide the model's output toward desired behaviors by adjusting activations within specific layers of the LLM's transformer architecture. However, such steering vectors are directly extracted from the activations of human preference data and thus often lead to suboptimal results and occasional failures, especially in alignment-related scenarios. This work proposes an innovative approach that could produce more effective steering vectors through bi-directional preference optimization. Our method is designed to allow steering vectors to directly influence the generation probability of contrastive human preference data pairs, thereby offering a more precise representation of the target behavior. By carefully adjusting the direction and magnitude of the steering vector, we enabled personalized control over the desired behavior across a spectrum of intensities. Extensive experimentation across various open-ended generation tasks, particularly focusing on steering AI personas, has validated the efficacy of our approach. Moreover, we comprehensively investigate critical alignment-concerning scenarios, such as managing truthfulness, mitigating hallucination, and addressing jailbreaking attacks. Remarkably, our method can still demonstrate outstanding steering effectiveness across these scenarios. Furthermore, we showcase the transferability of our steering vectors across different models/LoRAs and highlight the synergistic benefits of applying multiple vectors simultaneously.
summary:
**Central idea**

Bi-directional Preference Optimization (BiPO) learns a single activation steering vector through a DPO-style response-likelihood objective while freezing model weights. Training randomly applies the vector or its negative and reverses the preferred response accordingly. At inference, sign and magnitude control behavioral expression through addition at every token position in one transformer layer. The motivation is that CAA's appended answer choices can conflict with subsequent generated responses.

**Experiments**

The principal models are Llama-2-7b-chat-hf and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2, using layers 15 and 13 respectively. Comparators are CAA and Freeform activation differences. Four Anthropic model-written persona tests contain 200 held-out questions each, except corrigible-less-HHH with 82. TruthfulQA uses 327 training and 409 test questions, evaluated with MC1/MC2. Unprompted hallucination uses 700 training and 200 test questions. Greedy persona and hallucination responses receive GPT-4 ratings from 1–4. AdvBench uses 320 training and 100 test questions. Utility checks sample 30 questions from each of 57 MMLU subjects, totaling 1,710 questions. Additional experiments examine related-model transfer, two vector sums, and a DPO LoRA comparator.

**Key results**

The text reports broader persona and hallucination steering ranges and larger TruthfulQA improvements than both activation-difference baselines. On 100 held-out Llama-2 AdvBench questions, positive BiPO steering raises attack success from 0% to 73%; both baselines remain at 0%. With GCG suffixes optimized against the original model, negative BiPO steering reduces success from 16% to 0%, compared with 16% for negative CAA and 3% for negative Freeform. At persona multipliers ±1, MMLU accuracy ranges from 0.454–0.460 versus 0.459 unsteered for Llama-2, and 0.561–0.585 versus 0.573 for Mistral. English-trained persona vectors transfer to Vicuna-7b-v1.5 and a Chinese LoRA derivative. Two tested vector sums retain effects on both constituent behaviors. A limited power-seeking comparison reports a broader steering range than scaling a DPO-trained LoRA.

**Limitations / open questions**

Figure images and their numerical plot contents are unavailable, limiting assessment of several comparisons; the article otherwise includes its methods, results, references, and appendices. GPT-4 ratings lack reported independent human calibration, and uncertainty estimates are absent. Utility checks cover four persona vectors at ±1. Transfer remains within related Llama-2 models, and jailbreak defense is evaluated against attacks optimized on the original model. Vector sums lack magnitude-matched controls, and the LoRA comparison does not match training budgets. Behavioral control does not establish recovery of naturally used persona mechanisms.

title: Goal Misgeneralization in Deep Reinforcement Learning
abstract: We study goal misgeneralization, a type of out-of-distribution generalization failure in reinforcement learning (RL). Goal misgeneralization failures occur when an RL agent retains its capabilities out-of-distribution yet pursues the wrong goal. For instance, an agent might continue to competently avoid obstacles, but navigate to the wrong place. In contrast, previous works have typically focused on capability generalization failures, where an agent fails to do anything sensible at test time. We formalize this distinction between capability and goal generalization, provide the first empirical demonstrations of goal misgeneralization, and present a partial characterization of its causes.
summary:
**Central idea**

Goal misgeneralization occurs when an RL policy retains useful capabilities under distribution shift but behaves as though pursuing an objective different from its training reward. Correct reward specification therefore does not guarantee intended generalization. The paper formalizes goal-directedness through competing Bayesian mixtures over reward-seeking agents and devices. It distinguishes this behavioral failure from reward misspecification and from mesa-optimization, which its experiments do not establish.

**Experiments**

PPO agents use feedforward actor and critic heads over a shared IMPALA-style residual convolutional network, without recurrence. Unless stated otherwise, training uses 100,000 procedurally generated levels and 200 million timesteps. Modified Procgen tasks separate previously correlated cues: CoinRun relocates coins from the right endpoint; Maze I relocates cheese from the upper-right corner; Maze II separates a yellow line's color from its shape; Keys and Chests reverses the training ratio of two chests per key. CoinRun additionally tests critic valuations, pixel-gradient attribution, and behavior at a permeable end wall. A separate 20×20 gridworld evaluates agency mixtures on constructed trajectories, rather than learned neural policies.

**Key results**

CoinRun and Maze I policies navigate competently toward historical reward locations while often ignoring relocated rewards. Randomizing coins in just 2% of training levels substantially improves goal generalization; expanding the cheese-placement region also helps. Maze II favors the yellow gem in 89% of cases (n=102), excluding cases requiring passage through the red line to reach the gem. This constitutes incorrect generalization if shape defines the intended deployment objective. Keys and Chests agents collect surplus keys despite their lack of reward benefit. Across 950 CoinRun images, critic values favor the endpoint, with no significant coin-presence effect at the tested stages. Actors nevertheless pass through the permeable wall in all 114 cases where they reach it, indicating different actor and critic proxies. Reported gridworld agency posteriors are 0.9999 for robust and goal-misgeneralizing trajectories, versus 0.0674 for capability failures.

**Limitations / open questions**

Behavior supports plausible proxy objectives without uniquely identifying internal goals. Agency classification depends on selected priors, likelihoods, policy classes, and observation models, and becomes intractable in complex environments. Simpler or denser proxies are proposed explanations rather than isolated causal findings. Training-seed counts are unspecified. Plot images are unavailable in this rendering, limiting numerical extraction to prose, captions, and tables. Generalization to advanced agents or LLMs remains untested.

title: Goal Misgeneralization: Why Correct Specifications Aren't Enough For Correct Goals
abstract: The field of AI alignment is concerned with AI systems that pursue unintended goals. One commonly studied mechanism by which an unintended goal might arise is specification gaming, in which the designer-provided specification is flawed in a way that the designers did not foresee. However, an AI system may pursue an undesired goal even when the specification is correct, in the case of goal misgeneralization. Goal misgeneralization is a specific form of robustness failure for learning algorithms in which the learned program competently pursues an undesired goal that leads to good performance in training situations but bad performance in novel test situations. We demonstrate that goal misgeneralization can occur in practical systems by providing several examples in deep learning systems across a variety of domains. Extrapolating forward to more capable systems, we provide hypotheticals that illustrate how goal misgeneralization could lead to catastrophic risk. We suggest several research directions that could reduce the risk of goal misgeneralization for future systems.
summary:
**Central idea**

Correct training feedback can coexist with competent pursuit of an unintended goal under distribution shift. The paper operationalizes goal misgeneralization beyond reinforcement learning: the system retains capabilities needed for the intended task but instead performs another task well. Goals are attributed behaviorally, without requiring explicit internal objectives or search.

**Experiments**

Monster Gridworld compares V-MPO agents trained on 25-, 100-, or 200-step episodes and evaluated for 200 steps. Ten seeds are trained per condition; the best and worst are discarded, and each remaining seed receives 100 evaluation episodes. Tree Gridworld examines reset-free learning across 256 environments using reward, tree populations, and normalized harvesting affinity. Gopher-280B receives ten demonstrations with exactly two unknown variables, then encounters expressions with zero through three unknowns. Each unknown-count condition uses 100 randomly generated prompts, measuring question-versus-answer continuation probabilities. MEDAL-ADR is evaluated with expert, random, and anti-expert partners over 100 random seeds per pairing. A CoinRun replication and diversity experiment use ten training seeds, selecting each seed's best periodically evaluated checkpoint and testing it on 1,000 episodes.

**Key results**

The 25-step Monster agents collect excessive shields after monsters disappear, sacrificing apples; 100-step training produces behavior close to 200-step training. The Tree agent initially overharvests, causing deforestation and prolonged low reward before learning sustainability with positive minimum regeneration. Gopher asks redundant questions about constants in zero-unknown expressions, although its querying adapts to one or three unknowns; sampled transcripts also contain arithmetic errors. MEDAL-ADR follows anti-experts despite observable negative rewards and performs worse than a random policy. Endpoint-trained CoinRun agents continue toward the endpoint after coins move. Training with coin positions varying within the rightmost 20% enables reported generalization throughout the level, using discrete position sampling. Appendix A supplies a finite algebraic illustration of conflicting flight preferences fitting the same demonstrations.

**Limitations / open questions**

The examples establish possibility, not prevalence or scaling trends; several were deliberately constructed. Capability and goal attribution remain provisional, and rapid adaptation relative to learning from scratch is not systematically tested. Numerical plot values are unavailable in this rendering. Tree affinity uses artificial evaluation states whose distribution can differ from continual training. The InstructGPT example comes from prior work and remains ambiguous between misspecification and misgeneralization. Catastrophic scenarios, internal-computation evaluation, uncertainty maintenance, and recursive evaluation are prospective arguments, with no corresponding mitigation tests here.

title: Leveraging Procedural Generation to Benchmark Reinforcement Learning
IMPALA: Scalable Distributed Deep-RL with Importance Weighted Actor-Learner Architectures
Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms
Understanding RL Vision
summary:
**Central idea**

The article combines hidden-layer Integrated Gradients, nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF), and activating observation patches to interpret a CoinRun reinforcement-learning agent. Its diversity hypothesis links interpretable features to training diversity at the corresponding abstraction level; task relevance is also required, and sufficiency is proposed as a practical tendency. The nonrecurrent actor–critic CNN was trained with PPO for approximately two billion timesteps on the original CoinRun variant. It receives 64×64 RGB observations and has five convolutional layers; object features are most interpretable in the third, layer 2b.

**Experiments**

The authors inspect selected failures and generalized-advantage-estimation outliers through an interactive trajectory interface. They edit downstream convolution weights to project out NMF directions associated with buzzsaws or left-moving enemies, evaluating each model on 10,000 levels. A diversity sweep trains two models at each of seven training-set sizes, from 100 to 100,000 levels. Two researchers rate eight interface features per model, while completion rates are estimated on 10,000 training and 10,000 unseen levels sampled with replacement. Qualitative investigations compare gradient-based visualization with observation patches and spatially conditioned examples. Appendix B derives the exact baseline-relative completeness identity for hidden-layer path attributions; the implementation uses ten integration points.

**Key results**

Buzzsaw failures increase from 0.37% to 12.76% after the buzzsaw edit, while other measured failure categories remain similar. Making buzzsaws invisible to the original agent produces 32.20% buzzsaw failures, indicating incomplete blindness from the edit. The enemy edit increases left-moving-enemy failures from 0.16% to 4.69% and right-moving-enemy failures from 0.12% to 0.97%; enemies can reverse direction. Unseen-level completion rises from 61.81–64.13% with 100 training levels to 99.25–99.35% with 100,000. Subjective feature scores broadly increase, although noisily. Selected apparent coin and buzzsaw misdetections accompany one-frame value spikes of 95%→98% and 94%→85%. Gradient-based intermediate-layer visualizations remain largely featureless despite attempted modifications, while dataset patches expose recognizable objects.

**Limitations / open questions**

The diversity evidence is illustrative: ratings are subjective, raters could infer training diversity indirectly, and evaluations stopped once the trend appeared clear. Selected diagnostic examples lack controlled causal validation. Features can respond to different content at different positions, and outlier frames retain attribution outside the NMF span. Attribution signs, baseline choice, correlations, and numerical approximation complicate interpretation. Neither the diversity hypothesis generally nor transfer to language models is established.

title: Activation control for efficiently eliciting long chain-of-thought ability of language models
How to think step-by-step: A mechanistic understanding of chain-of-thought reasoning
abstract: Despite superior reasoning prowess demonstrated by Large Language Models (LLMs) with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, a lack of understanding prevails around the internal mechanisms of the models that facilitate CoT generation. This work investigates the neural sub-structures within LLMs that manifest CoT reasoning from a mechanistic point of view. From an analysis of Llama-2 7B applied to multistep reasoning over fictional ontologies, we demonstrate that LLMs deploy multiple parallel pathways of answer generation for step-by-step reasoning. These parallel pathways provide sequential answers from the input question context as well as the generated CoT. We observe a functional rift in the middle layers of the LLM. Token representations in the initial half remain strongly biased towards the pretraining prior, with the in-context prior taking over in the later half. This internal phase shift manifests in different functional components: attention heads that write the answer token appear in the later half, attention heads that move information along ontological relationships appear in the initial half, and so on. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first attempt towards mechanistic investigation of CoT reasoning in LLMs.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper investigates Llama-2 7B's chain-of-thought generation on modified PrOntoQA fictional ontologies. It decomposes a prescribed reasoning sequence into ten decision, copying, and two-hop inference subtasks. Its proposed account combines overlapping attention-head sets, early relational processing, and later parallel answer-associated pathways drawing on the question and generated reasoning.

**Experiments**

Generation uses six demonstrations, shuffled statements, and distractors. Complete-match accuracy, requiring all intermediate reasoning subtasks and the final True/False answer to match, is 35.9% on fictional ontologies and 52.5% on false ontologies; evaluation counts are unspecified. Head identification combines activation restoration, answer-source attention weights, and output-distribution KL recovery. Knockouts replace selected head outputs with false-ontology mean activations, separately for each subtask. Relation probing classifies positive, negative, or unrelated entity pairs from concatenated residual states: 28,392 training pairs and 9,204 test pairs, balanced across classes with disjoint entity inventories. The nonlinear probe has architecture 8192→128→64→32→3; its demonstration sweep covers zero to four examples. Vocabulary projections identify answer-associated heads and measure whether head-output top tokens form context-occurring bigrams. Recursive tracing follows maximum-attention sources and vocabulary-readout matches.

**Key results**

Inference-selected heads retain performance across all three subtask categories, and category-specific sets overlap substantially. Appendix C reports removing 475–663 of 1,024 heads, leaving 361–549 active, with subtask accuracies of 0.88–1.00 conditional on correct full-model predictions. These are independently selected subtask configurations, not one circuit evaluated on complete generation. Nonlinear relation-probe accuracy reportedly peaks around blocks 10–15; linear probes reportedly fail, and additional demonstrations show no clear peak-performance improvement. Context-bigram agreement rises around block 16, and answer-writing readouts occur in the later half. Traced routes include question, generated-reasoning, and demonstration tokens; generated-context routes are especially evident for inference subtasks 5 and 9.

**Limitations / open questions**

One model and a restrictive template limit generalization. MLP contributions remain unexamined; fictional vocabulary does not establish their irrelevance. Probe decodability does not establish attention-mediated token mixing. Attention maxima and vocabulary matches provide observational pathway hypotheses; no selective source-path interventions establish distinct algorithms or causal dependence on generated CoT. Figures are available only through captions and accompanying prose, preventing extraction of unseen plotted values. Most reported trends lack numerical effect sizes and uncertainty. Appendix C.3 defines reference and patched KL quantities using the same distribution pair, leaving an apparent formula error; Figure 14 also contains inconsistent token labels.

The Geometry of Categorical and Hierarchical Concepts in Large Language Models
abstract: The linear representation hypothesis is the informal idea that semantic concepts are encoded as linear directions in the representation spaces of large language models (LLMs). Previous work has shown how to make this notion precise for representing binary concepts that have natural contrasts (e.g., {male, female}) as directions in representation space. However, many natural concepts do not have natural contrasts (e.g., whether the output is about an animal). In this work, we show how to extend the formalization of the linear representation hypothesis to represent features (e.g., is_animal) as vectors. This allows us to immediately formalize the representation of categorical concepts as polytopes in the representation space. Further, we use the formalization to prove a relationship between the hierarchical structure of concepts and the geometry of their representations. We validate these theoretical results on the Gemma and LLaMA-3 large language models, estimating representations for 900+ hierarchically related concepts using data from WordNet.
summary:
**Central idea**
The paper extends linear concept representations from directions to vectors with calibrated magnitudes, then defines categorical representations as their convex hulls. Selective steering must preserve both causally separable concepts and relative probabilities within subordinate concepts. Theorem 4 derives constant within-class token projections under exact selectivity. The hierarchical prediction is that parent vectors are orthogonal to child-minus-parent increments; parent and child vectors themselves need not be orthogonal.

**Experiments**
The main analysis uses Gemma-2B's final unembeddings: 256K vocabulary tokens and 2,048 dimensions. Vocabulary covariance whitening estimates the causal metric. WordNet descendant sets, augmented with inflections and capitalization variants, yield 593 noun and 364 verb attributes with at least 50 vocabulary words. Feature vectors are estimated using LDA with Ledoit–Wolf covariance shrinkage. A 70%/30% word split evaluates normalized projections on held-out members against random vocabulary words and shuffled-unembedding controls. Other analyses compare vector cosines, hierarchical increments, and token-pair log-odds changes. Appendix F adds Gemma verb results and LLaMA-3-8B noun analyses; its retained LLaMA feature count is unspecified. Illustrative animal-category plots use manually inspected ChatGPT-4-generated word sets.

**Key results**
The text reports held-out member projections generally near one and random-word projections near zero, with shuffled controls losing held-out separation. Vector similarities reflect WordNet relationships, including sibling similarities absent after shuffling. Hierarchical orthogonality persists under independently selected 70% estimation subsets that break guaranteed set inclusion. Full-set shuffled estimates can also appear orthogonal, demonstrating an estimation confound. Centering without whitening does not recover the same orthogonality, and simple mean-vector estimates have greater projection variance than LDA estimates. For three selected parent/child contrast pairs, normalized parent additions produce parent mean log-odds changes of 5.1265, 9.8296, and 14.4222, versus child means of −0.0600, 0.3770, and −0.1545; child standard deviations are approximately 1.1–1.5.

**Limitations / open questions**
Exact selective representations are theoretical antecedents, not established properties of every feature. The hierarchical derivation invokes an orthogonality rule for subordinate contrasts; Appendix B.2(c) also has an unfinished displayed conclusion. Proposition 9's separately indexed contexts do not clearly state the simultaneous probability control used by its simplex argument. These are proof-presentation limitations in an otherwise complete source. Plot images are unavailable, so graphical findings follow the narrative and captions without additional numerical estimates. Lexical geometry and final-softmax calculations do not establish internal circuit mechanisms, comprehensive semantic selectivity, or generation quality. Extending the metric to internal layers and testing hierarchy-aware dictionary learning remain open.

Attention is Not Only a Weight: Analyzing Transformers with Vector Norms
summary:
**Central idea**

Attention weights omit the magnitudes of the vectors being combined. The paper rewrites a head output as y_i = Σ_j α_ij f(x_j), where f includes the value transformation and output projection, and proposes ||α_ij f(x_j)|| as a contribution score. For multi-head attention, it takes the norm after summing each source’s vectors across heads, retaining cancellation between heads. This is an exact output decomposition coupled to a proposed interpretation of contribution magnitude.

**Experiments**

The BERT analysis uses pretrained BERT-base-uncased, with 12 layers and 12 heads per layer, on 992 two-paragraph Wikipedia sequences averaging 122 tokens and capped at 128. It compares attention weights, transformed-vector norms, token categories, and frequency ranks estimated from a reproduced pretraining corpus. Translation experiments train six-layer encoder–decoder Transformers on German-to-English Europarl v7, with four or eight heads and five seeds per configuration. Under teacher forcing, extracted alignments are evaluated against Vilar et al.’s gold alignments using alignment error rate (AER). Extraction distinguishes alignment with the decoder’s input word (AWI) from alignment with its predicted output word (AWO).

**Key results**

Across BERT heads, transformed-vector norms have mean coefficient of variation 0.22. Special tokens and punctuation can receive large attention weights while contributing generally small weighted vectors. Frequency rank correlates with transformed-vector norm at Spearman ρ = 0.75, versus 0.06 for attention weight, associating frequent words with smaller transformed vectors. For four-head translation models, best-layer AWI AER improves from 29.8 ± 3.7 with weights to 25.0 ± 1.5 with norms; eight-head results improve from 38.7 ± 8.9 to 26.3 ± 1.9. Values are means and standard deviations across five seeds. Selecting the four-head layer by highest average contribution norm also yields 25.0 AER. Imported comparator scores are 36.4 for SmoothGrad, 28.4 for fast align, and 21.0 for GIZA++.

**Limitations / open questions**

Vector magnitude does not establish semantic information content or downstream causal importance. AWI observes the correct target word under teacher forcing; best-layer scores involve alignment-quality selection. Highest-norm head selection is unstable in the four-head model and performs poorly for AWO. Appendix D.2 inconsistently identifies the quantities used for Table 2’s correlations. Figure graphics are not fully accessible in the supplied rendering, and Figure 9’s caption is unfinished; reported numerical results above come from prose and tables. Generalization beyond the evaluated models and extension to whole-architecture analysis remain open.

title: Calibrate before use: Improving few-shot performance of language models
Why Can GPT Learn In-Context? Language Models Implicitly Perform Gradient Descent as Meta-Optimizers
abstract: Large pretrained language models have shown surprising in-context learning (ICL) ability. With a few demonstration input-label pairs, they can predict the label for an unseen input without parameter updates. Despite the great success in performance, its working mechanism still remains an open question. In this paper, we explain language models as meta-optimizers and understand in-context learning as implicit finetuning. Theoretically, we figure out that Transformer attention has a dual form of gradient descent. On top of it, we understand ICL as follows: GPT first produces meta-gradients according to the demonstration examples, and then these meta-gradients are applied to the original GPT to build an ICL model. We comprehensively compare the behaviors of in-context learning and explicit finetuning on real tasks to provide empirical evidence that supports our understanding. Experimental results show that in-context learning behaves similarly to explicit finetuning from multiple perspectives. Inspired by the dual form between Transformer attention and gradient descent, we design a momentum-based attention by analogy with gradient descent with momentum. The improved performance over vanilla attention further supports our understanding from another perspective, and more importantly, shows the potential to utilize our understanding for future model design. The code is available at \url{https://aka.ms/icl}.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper proposes that pretrained GPT models act as meta-optimizers: demonstrations generate attention values interpreted as “meta-gradients,” and attention applies their effects as implicit parameter updates. Removing softmax and attention scaling yields an exact algebraic decomposition of relaxed attention into a query-context operator plus a demonstration-derived outer-product update. This establishes an update representation for linear attention; identifying its values with gradients of a task objective remains an analogy.

**Experiments**

The authors compare fairseq GPT 1.3B and GPT 2.7B on SST2, SST5, MR, Subj, AGNews, and CB, with respectively 872, 1,101, 1,066, 2,000, 7,600, and 56 validation examples. ICL uses up to 32 demonstrations. Explicit finetuning updates only key/value projection parameters with SGD, processing those same examples once in demonstration order under a causal language-modeling objective. Demonstration seeds and learning rates are selected for validation accuracy. Measurements cover corrected predictions, attention-output changes, query-token attention logits, and constructed training-token affinities. Separately, two 350M-parameter GPT models are trained from scratch to compare vanilla attention with attention augmented by an exponentially decayed sum of preceding value vectors.

**Key results**

Among examples that finetuning corrects relative to zero-shot prediction, ICL also answers correctly on average 85.56% and 89.39% across the six datasets for the two model sizes. Mean cosine similarity between ICL and finetuning attention-output changes is 0.186 and 0.225, versus approximately zero for random changes. Mean query-attention similarity increases after finetuning, although individual comparisons include exceptions. Training-token rank correlations average 0.193 and 0.214. Momentum attention reduces validation perplexity from 15.14 to 15.02 at context length 1,024 and raises mean accuracy across SST5, IMDB, MR, CB, ARC-E, and PIQA from 51.9% to 54.7%.

**Limitations / open questions**

Behavioral and representational similarities do not identify an internal gradient-descent algorithm. The derivation omits softmax, holds representations fixed, and supplies no task loss generating the proposed meta-gradients. Its query-context operator need not equal an actual zero-shot operator when demonstrations alter hidden representations. Validation-based selection limits evaluation independence. Mechanism comparisons cover classification and models no larger than 2.7B. The supplied text omits the momentum decay setting, pretraining corpus, and uncertainty estimates; momentum gains also admit a recency-bias explanation.

title: Larger language models do in-context learning differently
abstract: We study how in-context learning (ICL) in language models is affected by semantic priors versus input-label mappings. We investigate two setups-ICL with flipped labels and ICL with semantically-unrelated labels-across various model families (GPT-3, InstructGPT, Codex, PaLM, and Flan-PaLM). First, experiments on ICL with flipped labels show that overriding semantic priors is an emergent ability of model scale. While small language models ignore flipped labels presented in-context and thus rely primarily on semantic priors from pretraining, large models can override semantic priors when presented with in-context exemplars that contradict priors, despite the stronger semantic priors that larger models may hold. We next study semantically-unrelated label ICL (SUL-ICL), in which labels are semantically unrelated to their inputs (e.g., foo/bar instead of negative/positive), thereby forcing language models to learn the input-label mappings shown in in-context exemplars in order to perform the task. The ability to do SUL-ICL also emerges primarily with scale, and large-enough language models can even perform linear classification in a SUL-ICL setting. Finally, we evaluate instruction-tuned models and find that instruction tuning strengthens both the use of semantic priors and the capacity to learn input-label mappings, but more of the former.
summary:
**Central idea**
In-context learning (ICL) can succeed in two ways. A model can use semantic priors from pretraining, meaning the label names and the task they suggest. Or it can learn the input–label mapping shown in the exemplars. This paper separates the two with label manipulations and asks how the balance shifts with model scale and with instruction tuning. The study is purely behavioral; there is no mechanistic analysis.

**Experiments**
- **Models:** GPT-3 (ada–davinci), InstructGPT (text-ada-001 to text-davinci-002), Codex (code-cushman-001, code-davinci-001/002), PaLM (8B/62B/540B) and Flan-PaLM (8B/62B/540B).
- **Tasks:** seven classification tasks (SST-2, SUBJ, TREC, QQP, RTE, Financial Phrasebank, ETHOS). Default setup is k=16 exemplars per class, an "Input/Output" template, and 100 evaluation examples per dataset.
- **Flipped-label ICL:** an increasing fraction of exemplar labels (0–100%) is flipped; TREC is excluded. Accuracy below 50% indicates the model is following the flipped mapping.
- **Semantically-unrelated label ICL (SUL-ICL):** labels are replaced with "Foo"/"Bar" and other arbitrary targets (0/1, A/B, fruit names), and the number of exemplars is varied.
- **Instruction tuning:** Flan-PaLM is compared with PaLM.
- **Synthetic task:** N-dimensional linear classification with random integer coordinates, evaluated in SUL-ICL format.
- **Ablations:** input-word remapping, prompt templates, semantic templates, and out-of-distribution exemplar/evaluation splits (SST-2 vs. Rotten Tomatoes).

**Key results**
- **Flipped labels:** small models barely change their predictions when labels are flipped. Large models drop well below chance; for example, text-davinci-002 falls from 90.3% to 22.5% at 100% flipped labels. All GPT-3 models, including davinci, at most reach chance and are treated as "small".
- **SUL-ICL:** the drop from regular ICL to SUL-ICL is larger for small models. Large models gain more from additional exemplars. Some tasks show SUL-ICL success only at the largest scale: RTE above chance only for PaLM-540B, and RTE/ETHOS jumping to 80%+ for code-davinci-002.
- **Instruction tuning:** Flan-PaLM does better on SUL-ICL than PaLM (Flan-PaLM-8B +9.6% over PaLM-8B). However, Flan-PaLM never drops below chance with flipped labels, while PaLM reaches as low as 31%. The authors read this as instruction tuning strengthening reliance on priors more than mapping learning.
- **Linear classification:** code-davinci-002 beats chance by 19% at N=16 and stays above chance up to N=64. Smaller Codex models fall to chance around N=16. PaLM shows no clear scale trend up to N=8. No model beats a polynomial SVM.
- **Ablations:** SUL-ICL with code-davinci-002 is robust across target types and templates. Remapping all input words reduces performance to chance.

**Limitations / open questions**
- Only 100 evaluation examples per dataset are used, and no significance tests are reported.
- Sizes of InstructGPT and Codex models are unknown, so "scale" is confounded with training differences across those families.
- GPT-3 davinci is anomalous relative to the scale story.
- RTE is excluded for PaLM because of context-length limits.
- The instruction-tuning comparison covers a single model family (PaLM).
- The paper does not explain why scale unlocks these behaviors, and offers no mechanistic account.
