Feature Hedging: Correlated Features Break Narrow Sparse Autoencoders
abstract: It is assumed that sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose polysemantic activations into interpretable linear directions, as long as the activations are composed of sparse linear combinations of underlying features. However, we find that if an SAE is more narrow than the number of underlying "true features" on which it is trained, and there is correlation between features, the SAE will merge components of correlated features together, thus destroying monosemanticity. In LLM SAEs, these two conditions are almost certainly true. This phenomenon, which we call feature hedging, is caused by SAE reconstruction loss, and is more severe the narrower the SAE. In this work, we introduce the problem of feature hedging and study it both theoretically in toy models and empirically in SAEs trained on LLMs. We suspect that feature hedging may be one of the core reasons that SAEs consistently underperform supervised baselines. Finally, we use our understanding of feature hedging to propose an improved variant of matryoshka SAEs. Importantly, our work shows that SAE width is not a neutral hyperparameter: narrower SAEs suffer more from hedging than wider SAEs.
summary:
**Central idea**

Feature hedging occurs when an SAE with insufficient dictionary capacity mixes correlated, unrepresented features into represented directions to reduce reconstruction error. Mixture signs can follow correlation signs; negative mixtures can work with the decoder bias to adjust default predictions of missing features. Unlike feature absorption, which involves hierarchical features and sparsity pressure, hedging can arise from reconstruction loss alone. Narrowing dictionaries can therefore exchange absorption for hedging.

**Experiments**

Section 3 trains SAEs on 15 million synthetic activations from orthogonal binary features with independent, hierarchical, positively correlated, or negatively correlated firing. Single-latent experiments use two features in 50 dimensions. Appendix A.1 numerically evaluates expected losses along normalized parent–child mixtures, with L1 coefficients zero and 0.1.

The LLM protocol uses Gemma-2-2b and Llama-3.2-1b activations from the uncopyrighted Pile. After 250 million tokens, 64 latents are added, followed by 250 million further training tokens alongside an unextended control. Hedging degree measures existing decoder changes projected onto the added latent span, subtracting a random-span baseline. Detailed reported sweeps concern Gemma-2-2b.

Balance Matryoshka experiments use Gemma-2-2b layer 12, BatchTopK k=40, 500 million tokens, and five prefixes of 128, 512, 2,048, 8,192, and 32,768 latents. Ten seeds per loss multiplier are evaluated with SAEBench and custom seven-tag Penn Treebank POS probing.

**Key results**

Narrow synthetic SAEs learn correlated mixtures, including after initialization at a generating direction. Independent-feature controls and full-width nonhierarchical controls recover generating directions. Expected-loss sweeps favor mixtures in the tested hierarchical settings. High L1 can suppress positive hedging in some settings.

Reported Gemma hedging degree falls substantially with width, with especially high scores at 4,096 latents and below, but remains positive through 65,536. A selected HTML/CSS case gives a plausible semantic example of a newly represented direction being removed from an existing decoder.

An adjacent-prefix loss multiplier around 0.75 improves reported TPP, feature splitting, and sparse probing over both ordinary and unweighted Matryoshka endpoints while retaining favorable absorption scores. SCR instead favors higher multipliers.

**Limitations / open questions**

Hedging degree is an indirect diagnostic relying on parent-first learning and assumptions about decoder reorganization. Tests cover models up to 2B parameters and dictionaries up to 65k latents; extension-based evaluation is expensive. Unequal-frequency toy children retain distortions under manual balancing. Hedging's contribution to supervised-baseline gaps remains hypothetical. Plot values are unavailable in this rendering, and some hierarchy captions contradict the body; no numerical effects are inferred from images.

title: Sparse but Wrong: Incorrect L0 Leads to Incorrect Features in Sparse Autoencoders
abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) extract features from LLM internal activations, meant to correspond to interpretable concepts. A core SAE training hyperparameter is L0: how many SAE features should fire per token on average. Existing work compares SAE algorithms using sparsity-reconstruction tradeoff plots, implying L0 is a free parameter with no inherently correct value aside from its effect on reconstruction. In this work we study the effect of L0 on SAEs, and show that if L0 is not set correctly, the SAE fails to disentangle the underlying features of the LLM. If L0 is too low, the SAE will mix correlated features to improve reconstruction. If L0 is too high, the SAE finds degenerate solutions that also mix features. Further, we present a proxy metric that can help guide the search for the correct L0 for an SAE on a given training distribution. We show that our method finds the correct L0 in toy models and coincides with peak sparse probing performance in LLM SAEs. We find that most commonly used SAEs have an L0 that is too low. Our work shows that practitioners must set L0 correctly to train SAEs with monosemantic features.
summary:
**Central idea**
SAE activation sparsity, L0, affects which dictionary directions are learned. Under an insufficient activation budget, reconstruction training can favor mixtures over generating features. The paper proposes c_dec, the mean absolute cosine similarity between distinct decoder columns, as a diagnostic for L0 selection.

**Experiments**
Synthetic experiments use five orthogonal features in 20 dimensions with true L0 = 2, and 50 features in 100 dimensions with reported true L0 = 11. SAEs train on 15 million samples. Sweeps vary correlations, activation budgets, dictionary width, and feature overlap; another experiment changes L0 during training. LLM experiments train 32,768-latent BatchTopK SAEs on 500 million Pile tokens at Gemma-2-2b layer 5 and Llama-3.2-1b layer 7, with three seeds per L0. A Gemma-2-2b layer-12 comparison trains BatchTopK and JumpReLU SAEs on one billion tokens. Evaluation uses c_dec and k-sparse probing F1 on over 100 tasks. Appendices provide restricted formal derivations.

**Key results**
In the five-feature toy, reducing L0 from 2 to 1.8 produces signed mixing matching positive or negative firing correlations; an uncorrelated control shows no mixing. In the larger toy, L0 = 5 and 18 produce mixed dictionaries, whereas L0 = 11 recovers generating directions. On 100,000 synthetic samples at L0 = 5, a learned mixed dictionary achieves MSE 2.73 versus 4.88 for the fixed generating dictionary under the same budget. Starting above the target L0 permits recovery in the tested schedule; starting below leaves persistent errors. Toy c_dec minima occur near the stipulated targets, including overlapping-feature and narrow-dictionary variants. In the layer-5 Gemma and layer-7 Llama comparisons, elbows around L0 = 200 coincide with peak probing performance. Layer-12 JumpReLU retains better probing performance at high L0 than BatchTopK.

**Limitations / open questions**
Natural LLM features and their true active counts are unknown; decoder geometry and probing provide indirect evidence. Broad minima and imperfect high-L0 agreement limit precise selection. Results cover two LLMs and few layers; the claim that commonly used SAEs generally have insufficient L0 extrapolates across heterogeneous checkpoints. Steering consequences remain hypotheses. Formal results concern tied, bias-free TopK models and a particular shared-component geometry; the claimed negative-mixing extension does not follow from the positive-magnitude derivative. Toy batch sizes conflict between the main text and appendix. Figures provide no accessible numerical curves beyond textual descriptions. Automatic L0 adaptation remains sensitive to tuning.

title: Show and tell: A neural image caption generator
Explorations of Self-Repair in Language Models
abstract: Prior interpretability research studying narrow distributions has preliminarily identified self-repair, a phenomena where if components in large language models are ablated, later components will change their behavior to compensate. Our work builds off this past literature, demonstrating that self-repair exists on a variety of models families and sizes when ablating individual attention heads on the full training distribution. We further show that on the full training distribution self-repair is imperfect, as the original direct effect of the head is not fully restored, and noisy, since the degree of self-repair varies significantly across different prompts (sometimes overcorrecting beyond the original effect). We highlight two different mechanisms that contribute to self-repair, including changes in the final LayerNorm scaling factor and sparse sets of neurons implementing Anti-Erasure. We additionally discuss the implications of these results for interpretability practitioners and close with a more speculative discussion on the mystery of why self-repair occurs in these models at all, highlighting evidence for the Iterative Inference hypothesis in language models, a framework that predicts self-repair.
summary:
**Central idea**
Ablating an attention head can change downstream computation and final normalization in ways that offset its removed contribution. The paper studies this direct-effect self-repair beyond narrow task datasets. Direct effect measures a component’s contribution to the centered correct-next-token logit using the clean run’s final normalization scale; self-repair equals the observed logit change minus the intervened head’s direct-effect change.

**Experiments**
The authors individually resample-ablate heads on The Pile, comparing direct effects with correct-token logit changes. Named models include Pythia-160M, 410M, and 1B, GPT-2 Small and Medium, and Llama-7B. Unless otherwise specified, Pythia and GPT-2 experiments use one million tokens; other models use smaller, unspecified amounts. Many analyses retain each head’s top 2% of tokens by direct effect. Further experiments compare zero, mean, and resample ablation; separate normalization, attention, and MLP contributions; inspect final-layer neuron changes; and feed head outputs back into their own input residual stream. Appendix B derives a normalization-dependent logit-change identity for a simplified final-layer intervention.

**Key results**
Many later heads exhibit incomplete average compensation, with substantial token-level variation and occasional overcompensation. For selected Pythia-160M head L11H2, the clean-to-ablated normalization-scale ratio exceeds one on 90.66%, 98.75%, and 100% of its top-direct-effect tokens under resample, mean, and zero ablation, respectively. A clipped statistic suggests normalization compensation around 30% of clean head direct effect across many layers; this is not a precise fraction of total self-repair. Sparse final-layer neurons often compensate by reducing an existing negative contribution, termed Anti-Erasure. For Llama-7B L30H8, the strongest repairing neuron compensates at least 10% of head direct effect in over 40% of selected instances. In a separate Pythia-160M analysis selecting the strongest-repair 2% of tokens, no neuron appears among the top ten repairing neurons on more than 16% of selected tokens.

**Limitations / open questions**
Centered-logit compensation does not establish general behavioral recovery. Sparse large neuron changes coexist with many smaller, cancelling changes. Selection, clipping, and unstable ratios complicate aggregate percentages. Pile samples do not establish coverage of every model’s complete training distribution. Some head labels conflict between prose and captions. Plot images are unavailable in the supplied rendering; quantitative findings above come from the prose. Self-repression and qualitative backup-head interventions are consistent with iterative inference, but do not isolate unfinished-task signals or establish why self-repair emerges.

abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) demonstrate remarkable capabilities in learning complex hierarchical data representations, but the nature of these representations remains largely unknown. Existing global explainability methods, such as Network Dissection, face limitations such as reliance on segmentation masks, lack of statistical significance testing, and high computational demands. We propose Inverse Recognition (INVERT), a scalable approach for connecting learned representations with human-understandable concepts by leveraging their capacity to discriminate between these concepts. In contrast to prior work, INVERT is capable of handling diverse types of neurons, exhibits less computational complexity, and does not rely on the availability of segmentation masks. Moreover, INVERT provides an interpretable metric assessing the alignment between the representation and its corresponding explanation and delivering a measure of statistical significance. We demonstrate the applicability of INVERT in various scenarios, including the identification of representations affected by spurious correlations, and the interpretation of the hierarchical structure of decision-making within the models.

On Privileged and Convergent Bases in Neural Network Representations
abstract: In this study, we investigate whether the representations learned by neural networks possess a privileged and convergent basis. Specifically, we examine the significance of feature directions represented by individual neurons. First, we establish that arbitrary rotations of neural representations cannot be inverted (unlike linear networks), indicating that they do not exhibit complete rotational invariance. Subsequently, we explore the possibility of multiple bases achieving identical performance. To do this, we compare the bases of networks trained with the same parameters but with varying random initializations. Our study reveals two findings: (1) Even in wide networks such as WideResNets, neural networks do not converge to a unique basis; (2) Basis correlation increases significantly when a few early layers of the network are frozen identically. Furthermore, we analyze Linear Mode Connectivity, which has been studied as a measure of basis correlation. Our findings give evidence that while Linear Mode Connectivity improves with increased network width, this improvement is not due to an increase in basis correlation.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper separates whether arbitrary neuron bases support equally good representations from whether independent training runs converge to the same basis. Its vision-network experiments suggest that coordinate choices matter without independent runs converging to a unique neuron basis. Transformer residual streams motivate part of the investigation, but no language model is tested.

**Experiments**

On CIFAR-10, independently trained ResNet-20 models with width multipliers 1–32 are compared using permutation-matched neuron correlations, averaged across layers, and interpolation error barriers. Controls examine interpolation without permutation, averaging trained networks with norm-matched random networks, and correlations between random networks. Batch-normalization statistics are reset.

Myrtle-CNN preactivations are rotated using random orthonormal matrices, affected layers are frozen, and remaining layers are retrained. Widths 16 and 256 are examined using successive-layer and single-layer procedures, alongside random-feature controls. The starting model is described as achieving 92% CIFAR-10 accuracy.

Finally, new models inherit frozen early blocks from a trained model while later blocks are independently initialized and trained. ConvNeXt on CIFAR-10 and ViT on ImageNet are evaluated using neuron correlation and identity-stitching penalties. Appendix experiments compare standard and modified ResNet-20 residual streams and widths 4× and 8×.

**Key results**

Permutation-corrected interpolation barriers decrease with width while neuron correlations remain nearly constant. Except at the narrowest tested width, random networks have higher matched correlations than trained networks. Wider networks also tolerate unpermuted interpolation and trained–random averaging better, providing indirect evidence for a noise-tolerance contribution to connectivity.

Preactivation rotations substantially degrade accuracy despite retraining, with deeper interventions generally more damaging. Sharing a small frozen early prefix increases subsequent alignment and improves identity stitching. Removing post-skip nonlinearities yields broadly comparable convergence results, so a completely linear residual stream is unnecessary in this comparison. Width explains some stitching success without comparable correlation gains.

**Limitations / open questions**

Rotation-recovery failures concern the tested architectures and retraining procedures; they do not prove mathematical impossibility. Correlation and stitching do not establish semantic equivalence or identical mechanisms. The displayed matching objective uses covariance without specifying its normalization, despite correlation-based terminology. Training recipes, repetitions, and uncertainty estimates are sparsely documented. Numerical curve values are unavailable from the supplied figure rendering; the reported qualitative findings follow the prose. The mechanisms behind prefix-induced alignment and width-dependent connectivity remain unresolved.

Analyzing the Generalization and Reliability of Steering Vectors
abstract: Steering vectors (SVs) have been proposed as an effective approach to adjust language model behaviour at inference time by intervening on intermediate model activations. They have shown promise in terms of improving both capabilities and model alignment. However, the reliability and generalisation properties of this approach are unknown. In this work, we rigorously investigate these properties, and show that steering vectors have substantial limitations both in- and out-of-distribution. In-distribution, steerability is highly variable across different inputs. Depending on the concept, spurious biases can substantially contribute to how effective steering is for each input, presenting a challenge for the widespread use of steering vectors. Out-of-distribution, while steering vectors often generalise well, for several concepts they are brittle to reasonable changes in the prompt, resulting in them failing to generalise well. Overall, our findings show that while steering can work well in the right circumstances, there remain technical difficulties of applying steering vectors to guide models' behaviour at scale. Our code is available at https://github.com/dtch1997/steering-bench
summary:
**Central idea**
Average steering effects can conceal unreliable responses on individual inputs. This paper evaluates Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) through per-example reliability and transfer across instructions that encourage or discourage a target behavior. It introduces “steerability bias”: intervention effectiveness depends on answer position or wording even when extraction data balance those factors.

**Experiments**
The main experiments use Llama-2-7B-Chat and Qwen-1.5-14B-Chat on 40 datasets encompassing Model-Written Evaluations persona and AI-risk behaviors, sycophancy, and TruthfulQA. Datasets receive 40/10/50 train/validation/test splits. Mean positive-minus-negative answer activations define vectors; validation sweeps select layer 13 for Llama and layer 21 for Qwen. Last-token residual additions use seven multipliers from −1.5 to 1.5. Propensity is the positive-minus-negative answer logit difference; steerability is its least-squares slope against multiplier. Four transfer settings examine BASE→USER_NEG, BASE→USER_POS, SYS_POS→USER_NEG, and SYS_NEG→USER_POS. Prompt-specific vectors are normalized to the baseline vector’s norm.

**Key results**
Per-example slopes vary widely, and some datasets have almost half their inputs steered opposite to the intended direction. Balanced A/B and Yes/No assignments do not eliminate dataset-dependent steerability biases. These factors explain substantial variance for some datasets, while much remains unexplained. Additional layer and multiplier sweeps reportedly preserve the main trends. ID and OOD mean steerability correlate at Spearman ρ=0.891 for Llama and 0.694 for Qwen, although OOD steerability is generally lower. Cross-model correlations are 0.769 ID and 0.586 OOD, demonstrating shared dataset-associated difficulty without isolating its cause. Larger differences in unsteered propensity associate with weaker relative transfer: ρ=−0.26 and −0.46, excluding target settings whose denominator steerability is below 0.25. Propensity differences also associate with lower vector cosine similarity, at −0.63 and −0.86.

**Limitations / open questions**
Results primarily concern multiple-choice logits and one steering recipe, rather than open-ended behavior or deployment safety. Failed steering does not establish absence of linear representations or failure of alternative interventions. The causes of bias and effective mitigations remain unresolved. Plots are unavailable visually in this rendering, so numerical reporting relies on text and captions. Supplementary captions mention Gemma-2-2B-IT and 70B Llama variants with limited methodological detail and inconsistent 70B naming. The supplied article is v8 dated May 2025; metadata gives the initial July 2024 publication date.

title: Steering off Course: Reliability Challenges in Steering Language Models
abstract: Steering methods for language models (LMs) have gained traction as lightweight alternatives to fine-tuning, enabling targeted modifications to model activations. However, prior studies primarily report results on a few models, leaving critical gaps in understanding the robustness of these methods. In this work, we systematically examine three prominent steering methods—DoLa, function vectors, and task vectors. In contrast to the original studies, which evaluated a handful of models, we test up to 36 models belonging to 14 families with sizes ranging from 1.5B to 70B parameters. Our experiments reveal substantial variability in the effectiveness of the steering approaches, with a large number of models showing no improvement and at times degradation in steering performance. Our analysis demonstrate fundamental flaws in the assumptions underlying these methods, challenging their reliability as scalable steering solutions.
summary:
**Central idea**

Steering procedures developed on a few language models may depend on internal patterns that vary across checkpoints. This paper examines DoLa, which contrasts layerwise vocabulary distributions, and function vectors (FVs) and task vectors (TVs), which compress in-context demonstrations into activation interventions. The results challenge the portability of these particular procedures across models and tasks.

**Experiments**

DoLa is evaluated on ten models from seven families using six-shot TruthfulQA MC1/MC2/MC3 and FACTOR-News accuracy. The suite includes Llama 1/2/3, Pythia-6.9B, Mistral-v0.1-7B, OLMo-7B, and Qwen2, including Qwen2-72B. Searches compare four candidate-layer buckets and subsequently six probability thresholds within the selected bucket. Controls compare normalized decoding, unnormalized contrast scores, and artificially length-biased baseline scoring.

The activation study reports 36 models from 14 families and 11 word-pair tasks covering antonyms, tense, capitals, and translation. FV evaluation uses 50 test pairs per task, ten-shot extraction, every injection layer, eight head counts, and eight strength multipliers. TV searches vary the replacement layer; Gemma2 and OLMo2 are excluded. Recovery divides steered zero-shot accuracy by five-shot accuracy, without subtracting zero-shot baseline performance.

**Key results**

Table 3 reports that 20% of model–task combinations with default FVs, 52% with searched FVs, and 35% with TVs exceed 90% of their respective five-shot accuracy. Proportions exceeding full five-shot accuracy are 12%, 28%, and 16%. These use best-layer results; exact combination counts are unspecified.

Normalized DoLa improves Llama-7B TruthfulQA MC1 from 0.2570 to 0.3182. Gains vary across models and benchmarks: Pythia FACTOR accuracy falls from 51.25% to 47.97%. Unnormalized scoring can inflate TruthfulQA metrics through answer length. The authors report correct and incorrect answer readouts rising at the same layer in several models. Country-capital FV performance nearly saturates with two GPT-J heads, whereas Mistral-v0.3 benefits from hundreds.

**Limitations / open questions**

Searches are finite, and reported maxima lack clearly documented independent hyperparameter-selection splits. Small FV test sets limit precision. Main and appendix TruthfulQA tables conflict on some values. Displayed task inventories differ between methods, including German translations for FV and Italian for TV. Plot values are unavailable in the text rendering; qualitative findings rely on prose and captions. Architecture, training data, and optimization are confounded. OLMo shows late-spiking readouts before second-stage pretraining, but the causes of cross-model variability remain unresolved. Failed recipes do not establish absent task representations or failure of all possible interventions.

title: Understanding (Un)Reliability of Steering Vectors in Language Models
abstract: Steering vectors are a lightweight method to control language model behavior by adding a learned bias to the activations at inference time. Although steering demonstrates promising performance, recent work shows that it can be unreliable or even counterproductive in some cases. This paper studies the influence of prompt types and the geometry of activation differences on steering reliability. First, we find that all seven prompt types used in our experiments produce a net positive steering effect, but exhibit high variance across samples, and often give an effect opposite of the desired one. No prompt type clearly outperforms the others, and yet the steering vectors resulting from the different prompt types often differ directionally (as measured by cosine similarity). Second, we show that higher cosine similarity between training set activation differences predicts more effective steering. Finally, we observe that datasets where positive and negative activations are better separated are more steerable. Our results suggest that vector steering is unreliable when the target behavior is not represented by a coherent direction.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper investigates whether contrastive activation geometry explains the uneven reliability of Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA). CAA adds a behavior-specific mean activation difference to the residual stream. The proposed explanation is that a constant vector works better when training contrasts agree directionally and positive and negative activations separate along their mean-difference direction.

**Experiments**

Experiments use Llama2-7B-Chat at residual-stream layer 13 and 36 binary-choice behavioral datasets covering assistant personality, potentially dangerous behaviors, politics, and ethics. Each dataset contains 1,000 examples. Prompt comparisons use 250 training and 500 held-out evaluation examples per dataset and format. Seven extraction formats combine answer prefilling, behavior-promoting or behavior-discouraging instructions, and five-shot demonstrations. Evaluation always uses the same plain prompt format; most experiments use steering multiplier λ = 1. Effect size is the steering-induced change in positive-minus-negative answer logits. Unreliability is the fraction of examples with a negative change. Subsequent geometric analyses focus on prefilled extraction, examining cosine agreement and discriminability d′ along the mean-difference line. Figure 2 groups datasets using steerability rankings from Tan et al. (2024).

**Key results**

All seven extraction formats produce positive mean effects averaged across the 36 datasets, without a clear consistently superior format. Anti-steering affects 29%–43% of evaluation samples depending on extraction format; the main text reports approximately one-third overall and dataset-specific rates of 3%–50%. Some formats have negative mean effects on the six least steerable datasets. Despite broadly similar, correlated performance, prompt-format vector comparisons have reported cosine similarities spanning 0.07–0.86. Greater directional agreement is associated with larger effects and fewer anti-steerable examples. Greater positive–negative separation along the mean-difference direction shows the same associations and correlates with directional agreement.

**Limitations / open questions**

Evidence is restricted to one model, one layer, CAA, and binary-choice logits. Open-ended behavioral control, unrelated-task capability preservation, and transfer to other steering methods are untested. Figure images are unavailable in the supplied rendering; the prose and captions report the associations but supply no numerical correlation coefficients or uncertainty estimates. Prompt comparisons are sensitive to training-set size and do not establish equivalence between formats. The geometric associations do not establish causal necessity: poor coherence could reflect either the model's representations or inadequate extraction data.

title: Where Steering Signals Come From: Activation Source Selection in Activation Steering
abstract: Activation steering controls language models by adding vectors or features to hidden states at inference time, but the upstream source of these steering signals is often treated as a secondary detail. We study this source choice as activation source selection: the combination of source context and activation readout policy used to collect the hidden states from which a steering signal is built. Holding the downstream intervention fixed, we show across three instruction-tuned models and four steering task families that changing only the source activations substantially changes steering success. We further find that effective steering is not explained simply by whether the desired behavior appears in the source text. Instead, strong signals come from execution-boundary states, where the model is about to produce or continue the target behavior. This pre-/post-realization distinction explains why answer-based sources sometimes work: their useful component aligns with execution-boundary directions rather than target appearance alone. Building on this view, we introduce tail subtraction, which removes shared prompt and continuation semantics from boundary states and yields cleaner, more stable steering signals. Overall, our results suggest that steering depends on representations of what the model is about to do, not merely on what has already appeared.
summary:
**Central idea**

Activation source selection comprises the context used to elicit hidden states and the positions selected or averaged. The paper argues that additive steering benefits from execution-boundary states preceding target production or continuation. It introduces tail subtraction: subtracting a matched question-and-assistant-prefix activation from a target-conditioned boundary activation before constructing a direction.

**Experiments**

Experiments use Gemma-2-9B-IT, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Behavioral evaluation covers 20 targets: 11 entities, seven persona/styles, refusal, and nonsense, totaling 1,950 target–question instances per model per configuration. Vectors use 16 source prompts per target. Methods comprise Mean, Diff-Mean, PCA, Diff-PCA, and consensus-active SAE decoder directions; Qwen excludes SAE experiments. Success requires target expression and readable, non-collapsed output. Scores equally weight four task families and average evaluated construction methods where applicable. Additional tests cover 16 relation tasks with 958 pairs scored by normalized prefix matching, projection removal from answer-based vectors, and tail subtraction.

**Key results**

Table 2 reports 47.6% average success for prompt-only final-token sources versus 19.8% for answer-only sequence means, after hyperparameter search. Hybrid instruction-plus-demonstration boundary sources achieve 38.9%, 64.0%, and 62.5% for Llama, Qwen, and Gemma. Across five validation–test splits, hybrid sources retain gains of 25.3–41.4 percentage points over answer-only means, with all reported intervals excluding zero. Relation-task comparisons also favor boundary sources, although numerical plot values are unavailable in the supplied rendering. Removing a boundary-derived Diff-PCA component lowers prompt-and-answer mean-readout performance by 8.2–21.6 points. Tail-Mean achieves 86.3%, 54.6%, and 72.5% for Gemma, Llama, and Qwen, versus 60.1%, 34.8%, and 58.4% for ordinary negative subtraction; Tail-PCA also improves across all three models. Judge validation agrees on 348/400 outputs. Alternative-judge rescoring preserves the broad source pattern despite substantially higher absolute scores.

**Limitations / open questions**

Headline scores maximize over source layer, intervention layer, and strength; validation-only selection checks cover selected source comparisons, excluding tail subtraction. Context and pooling change together in boundary-versus-trace comparisons, and projection ablations lack reported norm-matched controls. Execution-specific semantic isolation therefore remains an interpretation. Relation source/evaluation disjointness and exact strength grids are unspecified. Figure 2 reports Llama prompt-only final-token performance as 31.6%, whereas Table 2 gives 33.6%. Findings cover additive steering in three 7B–9B instruction-tuned models and do not establish broad capability preservation or generality across intervention families.

title: Activation Steering for Aligned Open-ended Generation without Sacrificing Coherence
abstract: Alignment in LLMs is more brittle than commonly assumed: misalignment can be induced by adversarial prompts, benign fine-tuning, emergent misalignment, and goal misgeneralization. Recent evidence suggests that some misalignment behaviors are encoded as linear structure in activation space, making it tractable via activation steering, which could be used as a lightweight runtime defense. We implement three methods: Steer-With-Fixed-Coefficient (SwFC), which applies uniform additive steering, and two novel projection-aware methods, Steer-to-Target-Projection (StTP) and Steer-to-Mirror-Projection (StMP), that use a logistic regression decision boundary to selectively intervene only on tokens whose activations fall below the threshold. We evaluate these methods on two threat models, dishonesty and dismissiveness, using malicious system prompts as a controlled proxy for misalignment. We conduct our experiments on two architectures (Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and Qwen3.6-27B). All methods substantially recover alignment. StTP and StMP preserve general capabilities (MMLU, MT-Bench, AlpacaEval) better than uniform steering. Finally, we show that our honesty steering generalizes to out-of-distribution scenarios: a single honesty direction extracted from the aligned model significantly raises scores on the MASK benchmark, suppresses deception in multi-agent settings (Among Us), doubles the hidden-behavior discovery rate on AuditBench, and restores honesty in an emergently misaligned model.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper introduces token-selective interventions using logistic regression fitted to response-averaged aligned versus maliciously prompted activations. Steer-to-Target-Projection (StTP) moves below-boundary projections to a positive-class target; Steer-to-Mirror-Projection (StMP) applies a scaled reflection across the boundary. Both preserve above-boundary activations and are compared with uniform additive steering, SwFC.

**Experiments**

Experiments use Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and Qwen3.6-27B. Honesty extraction uses 50 self-report scenarios, with 112 test scenarios across eight categories; compassion uses 50 training prompts and 40 held-out prompts. GPT-oss-120B separately rates traits and coherence from 0–100. Operating points maximize evaluated trait scores subject to coherence reaching 90% of the aligned baseline. Multi-turn tests use 20 five-turn disclosure scenarios and 40 ten-turn support conversations per model. Further evaluations cover MMLU, MT-Bench, AlpacaEval, MASK, Among Us, AuditBench, financially induced emergent misalignment, and separately extracted non-toxicity steering on 42 held-out prompts.

**Key results**

Llama all-token honesty scores rise from 24 to 75/77/62 for SwFC/StTP/StMP, versus 93 aligned; compassion rises from 25 to 78/75/71, versus 81 aligned. Qwen honesty recovery is also incomplete: 31 to 80/66/54, versus 94 aligned. All-token steering exceeds response-only steering in the reported comparisons. StMP generally retains the most benchmark capability and produces the least repetition in Llama multi-turn tests. Llama honesty StTP reduces MMLU from 82.2 to 65.8; StMP scores 78.9. Qwen avoids this large StTP penalty. Non-toxicity steering improves both models.

MASK H@1, pooled across six scenario categories, rises from 53.6% to 81.2%/75.5% with StTP/StMP on Llama and from 63.2% to 78.4%/76.0% on Qwen. Steering only Llama’s two impostors raises Among Us crewmate wins from approximately 49% to 95%/80%. AuditBench discovery reaches approximately 0.83–0.91 across adversarial SFT/KTO cohorts, versus published original-tool rates of 0.35–0.39. In financially fine-tuned Llama, MASK rises from 46.2% to 79.4%/74.6%, while broad misalignment only partially recovers.

**Limitations / open questions**

Operating-point selection lacks a clearly separate validation split. Human calibration of trait judges is unreported; pairwise ratings reuse the same judge. Among Us win rates do not isolate honesty from strategic impairment. AuditBench comparisons change extraction data and intervention mechanics together. Checkpoint transfer establishes usable control, not unchanged representational geometry. Toxicity trait and capability evaluations use different Llama layers. Plot images are unavailable in the supplied rendering. White-box access, model-specific calibration, and behavioral entanglement limit deployment conclusions.

title: Steering Safely or Off a Cliff? Rethinking Specificity and Robustness in Inference-Time Interventions
abstract: Model steering, which involves intervening on hidden representations at inference time, has emerged as a lightweight alternative to finetuning for precisely controlling large language models. While steering efficacy has been widely studied, evaluations of whether interventions alter only the intended property remain limited, especially with respect to unintended changes in behaviors related to the target property. We call this notion specificity. We propose a framework that distinguishes three dimensions of specificity: general (preserving fluency and unrelated abilities), control (preserving related control properties), and robustness (preserving control properties under distribution shifts). We study two safety-critical use cases: steering models to reduce overrefusal and faithfulness hallucinations, and show that while steering achieves high efficacy and largely maintains general and control specificity, it consistently fails to preserve robustness specificity. In the case of overrefusal steering, for example, all steering methods reduce overrefusal without harming general abilities and refusal on harmful queries; however, they substantially increase vulnerability to jailbreaks. Our work provides the first systematic evaluation of specificity in model steering, showing that standard efficacy and specificity checks are insufficient, because without robustness evaluation, steering methods may appear reliable even when they compromise model safety.
summary:
**Central idea**

Steering specificity should distinguish preservation of unrelated abilities, preservation of related control behaviors, and preservation of those controls under distribution shift. Robust specificity differs from out-of-distribution efficacy: transferring the intended behavior does not establish preservation of related safety behaviors.

**Experiments**

The authors evaluate DiffMean, LinearProbe, supervised steering vectors (SSV), ReFT-r1, and partial orthogonalization (PartialOR) on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-2B-it. They report 256 training examples, 100 validation examples, and averages over three runs, searching layers and the last five token positions. Explicit-control training includes demonstrations preserving the control behavior; unconstrained overrefusal variants are also evaluated.

Overrefusal experiments use PHTest, JailbreakBench, and Alpaca for training; PHTest and ORBench-hard measure efficacy. Canonical harmful queries measure control specificity. Robustness uses 25 JailbreakHub prefixes crossed with 100 harmful queries, yielding 2,500 adversarial instances. Faithfulness experiments use NQSwap with conflicting updated context, no context, or manually generated topically related but irrelevant distractors. The paper states 500 queries per ordinary evaluation. Metrics include compliance, safety defined as one minus Llama Guard 2 harmfulness, answer exact match, MMLU/GSM8K accuracy, and perplexity-derived fluency.

**Key results**

With explicit control, all 20 model–method combinations improve PHTest compliance by 4–32 percentage points. DiffMean, LinearProbe, ReFT-r1, and PartialOR improve ORBench-hard compliance in every model; SSV decreases it in two models. Jailbreak safety falls in all 20 combinations by 5–30 points. For Llama-8B, it falls from 0.55 to 0.25–0.36, while canonical harmful-query safety changes by −0.10 to +0.01. All 16 unconstrained overrefusal combinations also lose jailbreak safety.

Faithfulness steering improves updated-answer exact match by 8–27 points across all 20 combinations, while distractor-context original-answer exact match falls by 10–25 points. No-context accuracy changes by −7 to +5 points. General-capability changes are often small, but exceptions are substantial: Llama-8B faithfulness SSV loses 27 MMLU points and 17 GSM8K points.

**Limitations / open questions**

Evidence covers English, two task families, models up to 8B, and sampled attacks and distractors. It does not establish inevitable robustness loss. The activation-geometry explanation is qualitative; the text reports the plotted trend, but the plots cannot be independently inspected here. Statistical-test details, distractor construction, and PartialOR's faithfulness adaptation are underspecified. Fluency definitions, the stated coefficient grid versus selected values, and some prose/table comparisons are inconsistent. Gemma's zero GSM8K baseline reflects answer-format sensitivity.

title: A simple sequentially rejective multiple test procedure
FEVER: a large-scale dataset for fact extraction and VERification
Convergent Evolution: How Different Language Models Learn Similar Number Representations
abstract: Language models trained on natural text learn to represent numbers using periodic features with dominant periods at $T=2, 5, 10$. In this paper, we identify a two-tiered hierarchy of these features: while Transformers, Linear RNNs, LSTMs, and classical word embeddings trained in different ways all learn features that have period-$T$ spikes in the Fourier domain, only some learn geometrically separable features that can be used to linearly classify a number mod-$T$. To explain this incongruity, we prove that Fourier domain sparsity is necessary but not sufficient for mod-$T$ geometric separability. Empirically, we investigate when model training yields geometrically separable features, finding that the data, architecture, optimizer, and tokenizer all play key roles. In particular, we identify two different routes through which models can acquire geometrically separable features: they can learn them from complementary co-occurrence signals in general language data, including text-number co-occurrence and cross-number interaction, or from multi-token (but not single-token) addition problems. Overall, our results highlight the phenomenon of convergent evolution in feature learning: A diverse range of models learn similar features from different training signals.
summary:
**Central idea**
The paper distinguishes spectral convergence—recurring Fourier peaks in numerical representations—from geometric convergence, operationalized as linear decoding of residues. Periods 2, 5, and 10 recur across surveyed Transformers, recurrent models, classical embeddings, and raw numerical frequencies, while decoding performance differs substantially.

**Experiments**
Controlled pretraining uses FineWeb-Edu 10BT, approximately 9.4B actual tokens, tied embeddings, and the Llama-3 tokenizer. Architectures include a 320M Transformer, 318M Gated DeltaNet, 316M Mamba-2, and 232M LSTM. Measurements on embeddings for 0–999 include median-normalized Fourier power and logistic-regression Cohen’s κ, averaged over three probe seeds with ten-fold cross-validation. Interventions change number–text associations, cross-number attention access, and context length. Further tests compare optimizer recipes, add LSTM residual connections, train addition Transformers for 3B tokens with two seeds per optimizer, vary bases and tokenizers, and probe larger pretrained models and multi-token numbers.

**Key results**
Transformer mod-10 κ falls from 85.4% to 28.8% after swapping numerical subsequences between contexts, and to chance after independent numerical replacement, while Fourier peaks persist. Allowing at most one or eight numbers per attention segment yields κ=45.0% or 77.2%. Muon versus AdamW yields mod-10 κ of 85.4% versus 72.1% for Transformers, but 76.7% versus 80.1% for Mamba-2. LSTM residual connections raise mod-10 κ from chance to 39%. Multi-token addition produces consistent decimal modular structure under the tested recipes; single-token conditions do not. Base-15 training instead yields perfect reported mod-3,5,15 probes. Eight pretrained models spanning 124M–671B parameters have mod-2,5,10 κ of at least 98.4%, using tokenizer-dependent numerical inventories. Formal derivations connect harmonic energy to class scatter and construct arbitrarily energetic embeddings with linear accuracy arbitrarily close to chance.

**Limitations / open questions**
Theorem 1(i) incorrectly infers chance-level accuracy from equal class means; the claimed necessity result is unestablished. Fisher bounds concern variance ratios, not classification-accuracy ceilings, and covariance invertibility requires more than a dimensionality bound. Probing establishes accessibility rather than ordinary causal use. Architecture comparisons differ in capacity and other design choices. Downstream addition-learning differences do not isolate modular geometry as their cause. Base-dependent results support a pattern, while the Chinese Remainder Theorem learning explanation remains hypothetical. Multi-token low-modulus probes need not require combining tokens when the final chunk determines the residue. Some figures provide captions without accessible plotted values; detailed nonlinear-probe results cannot be audited. Extension to other cyclic concepts remains open.

title: Language models encode numbers using digit representations in base 10
The Clock and the Pizza: Two Stories in Mechanistic Explanation of Neural Networks
abstract: Do neural networks, trained on well-understood algorithmic tasks, reliably rediscover known algorithms for solving those tasks? Several recent studies, on tasks ranging from group arithmetic to in-context linear regression, have suggested that the answer is yes. Using modular addition as a prototypical problem, we show that algorithm discovery in neural networks is sometimes more complex. Small changes to model hyperparameters and initializations can induce the discovery of qualitatively different algorithms from a fixed training set, and even parallel implementations of multiple such algorithms. Some networks trained to perform modular addition implement a familiar Clock algorithm; others implement a previously undescribed, less intuitive, but comprehensible procedure which we term the Pizza algorithm, or a variety of even more complex procedures. Our results show that even simple learning problems can admit a surprising diversity of solutions, motivating the development of new tools for characterizing the behavior of neural networks across their algorithmic phase space.
summary:
**Central idea**

Perfect modular-addition accuracy and circular embeddings can conceal different learned computations. The familiar Clock algorithm multiplies sinusoidal representations to add angles. The proposed Pizza algorithm adds operand embeddings and uses ReLU-compatible transformations to identify angular sectors. Its approximate logits include |cos(πk(a−b)/59)|, making confidence depend on operand separation. The paper advocates mapping algorithmic diversity across training configurations.

**Experiments**

Networks learn addition modulo 59 using an 80%/20% training/validation split of 3,481 operand pairs. Main experiments use bidirectional transformers without layer normalization, four attention heads, ReLU MLPs, and 20,000 epochs of full-batch AdamW training. Sweeps vary attention rate, width from 32–512, and depth from one to four layers. Runs failing to reach 100% validation accuracy are excluded; the main phase plots additionally select circular embeddings. Follow-ups examine width-256 feedforward networks, GeLU, separate operand embeddings, and an equals-sign token. Analyses include operand-gradient symmetry, correct-logit patterns, embedding PCA restrictions termed circle isolation, formula comparisons, and selected weight inspections.

**Key results**

Across all 59³ logits for each of three isolated Model A circles, Pizza formulas explain 99.18–99.28% of variance versus 75.38–75.62% for Clock; model logits and formula values are standardized separately. Constant-attention Model A has gradient symmetricity 0.9937 and distance irrelevance 0.17, versus 0.3336 and 0.85 for ordinary-attention Model B. Restricting Model A to its first circle gives 32.8% accuracy, its first three circles 91.4%, and six circles including accompanying components 100%. Among selected circular one-layer models, higher attention rate favors Clock signatures, while greater width moves the transition toward higher attention rates. One width-1,024 ordinary-attention model exhibits Pizza signatures. Reported circularity rates are 34.31%, 9.95%, 11.55%, and 6.08% for one through four layers. Removing the second ReLU in a selected feedforward Pizza model preserves 100% accuracy.

**Limitations / open questions**

Results concern one small arithmetic task, with mechanisms reconstructed only in selected models and no reported diagnostic classification error rates or sweep run counts. Non-circular algorithms remain largely unexplained. Architectural explanations and accompanying-circle training stories remain partly conjectural. Section 4 reverses the otherwise consistent Model A/B labels; three-circle accuracy reports use insufficiently reconciled conditions. Appendix L contains algebraic shortcuts, including treating ReLU as absolute value and extrapolating a biased unit-circle fit across radii, which do not establish exact reconstruction. Figures are unavailable as images in the supplied rendering.

title: Superposition in mixture of experts
OLMoE: open mixture-of-experts language models
Probing semantic routing in large mixture-of-expert models
DeepSeekMoE: towards ultimate expert specialization in mixture-of-experts language models
OpenMoE: an early effort on open mixture-of-experts language models
Mixtral of Experts
Mechanistically Eliciting Latent Behaviors in Language Models
summary:
**Central idea.** The post defines the problem of *mechanistically eliciting latent behaviors* (MELBO): perturbing a model's internals, rather than its prompt, to surface the different high-level "modes" an LLM can enter. The concrete method learns a vector θ added as a bias to the MLP output at a source layer (default ℓ_source = 8) and optimizes it with AMSGrad under a norm constraint ‖θ‖₂ = R to *maximize* the ℓ_p-aggregated change in target-layer activations (ℓ_target ≈ depth − 8) relative to the unsteered run; p controls spikiness across token positions, q shapes the objective. A generalization replaces the vector with a rank-r LoRA adapter of W_MLP-OUT ("unsupervised steering adapters"), giving activation-dependent steering. Orthogonality constraints across runs encourage diversity. The stated rationale is noise-stability: random vectors at the same radius produce only rephrasings, so a learned vector that changes downstream activations much at small R must load on "structurally important" directions — offered as a feature-selection principle contrasting with SAEs' sparsity prior, and claimed to be better suited to small datasets and out-of-distribution-relevant features.

**Experiments.** (1) Red-teaming: 32 orthogonal vectors on Qwen-14B-Chat from the single harmful request prompt the model normally refuses; four vectors are analyzed qualitatively, two eliciting fictional-game framings and two eliciting non-fictional compliance, probed through multi-turn conversation. Negating the compliance vectors (scale ≈ 9.5–10×) induces refusal of innocuous requests. The fantasy vectors reframe unrelated ambiguous questions inside their respective games. (2) Backdoor detection: Qwen-1.8B Base and Chat fine-tuned on an arithmetic chain-of-thought task with two trigger-conditioned behaviors; 100 orthogonal vectors trained on *one clean* prompt recover at least one vector per backdoor (Base 3% and 2%; Chat 2% and 1%), plus "hybrid-reasoning" vectors that splice arithmetic steps with unrelated topics. (3) Capability discovery: on a one-shot direct-answer arithmetic prompt in Qwen-1.8B-Base, 7/32 vectors elicit chain-of-thought; one raises test accuracy from 11% to 63% (string-match grading). An adapter yields consistent Portuguese math explanations.

**Key results / limitations.** Vectors appear to encode coherent, transferable behaviors, but evaluation is almost entirely qualitative — the author explicitly defers diversity/fluency metrics, sample sizes, and anomaly-detection evaluation. Most learned vectors are uninteresting; hyperparameters (notably the "Goldilocks" R) were hand-tuned; the Minecraft vector corrupts factual knowledge the unsteered model has; adapters generalize worse and make arithmetic errors. A *negative result*: no vector/adapter detected a subtler algorithmic backdoor (swapping addition for multiplication inside the chain of thought). The Qwen-14B-Chat section used a non-standard chat template, with only a partial 4-vector replication in correct ChatML format. The noise-stability explanation is stated as an untested hypothesis.

title: Activation space interpretability may be doomed
summary:
**Central idea**

Decomposing individual activation spaces can reveal statistical structure without recovering the variables that organize a model’s computation. The authors distinguish “features of the activations,” potentially selected by activation description length, from “features of the model,” provisionally characterized by a simple, sparse, modular causal graph. Their concern applies to SAEs, PCA, and neuron inspection when these analyze layer activations in isolation.

**Experiments**

The post presents thought experiments rather than a systematic empirical study or formal proof. One example places two input variables on a complicated curve even though the model treats them independently. Another contrasts a hypothetical 500-element sparse dictionary approximating a curve in ten dimensions with a model using 100 computationally relevant directions. A color–shape example compares four conjunction latents, requiring one active latent per object, with separate color and shape latents, requiring two. A ten-neuron ReLU MLP approximating x² illustrates how downstream output weights distinguish a relevant direction from other hidden-activation structure. A speculative extension considers 80,000 overlapping ten-dimensional computations within 40,000 neurons, writing into a 10,000-dimensional residual stream. These numbers specify illustrations, not measured results. Footnotes briefly report positional-encoding features found by SAEs at GPT-2 Small’s `blocks.0.hook_resid_pre` and assert SAE training-dataset dependence, without presenting evaluation protocols or metrics.

**Key results**

The conclusions are methodological arguments: reconstruction quality, sparsity, and apparently interpretable activation examples do not establish correspondence to the model’s computational decomposition. Sparsity can favor composed object categories even when downstream computations independently consume attributes. Function approximation can create activation structure whose computational relevance depends on downstream weights. Proposed alternatives incorporate multiple layers, gradients, inter-feature connection penalties, or direct weight decomposition. Transcoders, end-to-end SAEs, attribution dictionary learning, and crosscoders are discussed as relevant directions. The authors also suggest better structural assumptions for decomposition, while noting that discovering those assumptions may itself depend on interpretability progress.

**Limitations / open questions**

The post does not quantify these failure modes in trained LLMs, demonstrate failure of every activation-based method, or establish that its hypothetical dictionaries would actually be learned. It assumes an underlying computational feature structure independent of the analysis distribution and adopts graph simplicity as an explanatory target without validating it. Whether any suggested method resolves the examples remains open; the authors explicitly caution that merely incorporating additional functional information is insufficient.

title: Poser: Unmasking Alignment Faking LLMs by Manipulating Their Internals
abstract: Like a criminal under investigation, Large Language Models (LLMs) might pretend to be aligned while evaluated and misbehave when they have a good opportunity. Can current interpretability methods catch these 'alignment fakers?' To answer this question, we introduce a benchmark that consists of 324 pairs of LLMs fine-tuned to select actions in role-play scenarios. One model in each pair is consistently benign (aligned). The other model misbehaves in scenarios where it is unlikely to be caught (alignment faking). The task is to identify the alignment faking model using only inputs where the two models behave identically. We test five detection strategies, one of which identifies 98% of alignment-fakers.
summary:
**Central idea**

Poser evaluates whether internal measurements and interventions identify deliberately trained alignment-faking policies using prompts where paired models give identical greedy answers. Its 36 LLaMA-13B fine-tunes comprise six instances each of truth teller, genie, saint, money maximizer, reward maximizer, and fitness maximizer policies. The 18 benign and 18 alignment-faking models form 324 pair combinations, rather than 324 independently trained pairs. A proposed safety-evaluation protocol would use fresh model testbeds, independent auditing, and separate mitigation tests; this protocol is not validated here.

**Experiments**

Each fine-tuning dataset contains approximately 1,200 GPT-4-generated and filtered role-play examples with single-token action answers. Reported held-out policy accuracy exceeds 99%. Six detection strategies examine oversight-related steering, activation noise, harmful-action learning speed, suspicious-concept projections, layerwise decision probes, and oversight saliency. A mitigation experiment compares supervised training on models’ own outputs with the same objective augmented by activation noise.

**Key results**

Layer-15 noise injection achieves reported detection accuracy of 98% across the 324 pair combinations. Its multiplier was selected to preserve most probability on valid A/B answers. The oversight-contrast direction achieves 100% detection, but reversing its sign works equally well and random noise performs similarly, undermining the interpretation that it selectively induces perceived safety to misbehave. Harmful-action learning speed yields 90% detection with a layer-5 LoRA module versus 63% with full fine-tuning; the fourth-step comparison was selected using ground-truth detection accuracy. Suspicious-concept detection is reported at 71%. Attention-based oversight saliency achieves 46%, and counterfactual activation-shift saliency 37%. After 100 baseline self-output training steps, mean aligned-action probability is 76% on scenarios where fakers previously misbehaved; noise-augmented training yields 86%, a ten-percentage-point difference. The text leaves evaluation-time noise status unclear.

**Limitations / open questions**

Matching greedy answers leaves residual black-box information: confidence comparison achieves 64% after filtering. Pairing supplies a benign reference, and model reuse makes pair outcomes dependent. Synthetic role-play policies and their differential robustness may differ substantially from naturally emerging alignment faking. The mechanisms underlying noise sensitivity and mitigation remain unresolved, and broad capability preservation is untested. Reporting is inconsistent: the abstract counts five strategies while the body evaluates six; decision-speed detection is 47% in the introduction and 37% in Section 3.5. Image-only plots prevent recovering additional numerical details, including individual suspicious-concept scores. Poser is explicitly a proof of concept, not a deployment safety standard.

FIND: A Function Description Benchmark for Evaluating Interpretability Methods
abstract: Labeling neural network submodules with human-legible descriptions is useful for many downstream tasks: such descriptions can surface failures, guide interventions, and perhaps even explain important model behaviors. To date, most mechanistic descriptions of trained networks have involved small models, narrowly delimited phenomena, and large amounts of human labor. Labeling all human-interpretable sub-computations in models of increasing size and complexity will almost certainly require tools that can generate and validate descriptions automatically. Recently, techniques that use learned models in-the-loop for labeling have begun to gain traction, but methods for evaluating their efficacy are limited and ad-hoc. How should we validate and compare open-ended labeling tools? This paper introduces FIND (Function INterpretation and Description), a benchmark suite for evaluating the building blocks of automated interpretability methods. FIND contains functions that resemble components of trained neural networks, and accompanying descriptions of the kind we seek to generate. The functions span textual and numeric domains, and involve a range of real-world complexities. We evaluate methods that use pretrained language models (LMs) to produce descriptions of function behavior in natural language and code. Additionally, we introduce a new interactive method in which an Automated Interpretability Agent (AIA) generates function descriptions. We find that an AIA, built from an LM with black-box access to functions, can infer function structure, acting as a scientist by forming hypotheses, proposing experiments, and updating descriptions in light of new data. However, AIA descriptions tend to capture global function behavior and miss local details. These results suggest that FIND will be useful for evaluating more sophisticated interpretability methods before they are applied to real-world models.

A Primer on the Inner Workings of Transformer-based Language Models
abstract: The rapid progress of research aimed at interpreting the inner workings of advanced language models has highlighted a need for contextualizing the insights gained from years of work in this area. This primer provides a concise technical introduction to the current techniques used to interpret the inner workings of Transformer-based language models, focusing on the generative decoder-only architecture. We conclude by presenting a comprehensive overview of the known internal mechanisms implemented by these models, uncovering connections across popular approaches and active research directions in this area.
summary:
**Central idea**

This technical survey organizes transformer interpretability around two complementary objectives: localizing inputs and components responsible for predictions, and decoding information represented inside the network. Using unified notation for decoder-only transformers, it connects residual-stream addition, QK/OV attention circuits, FFNs as key-value memories, direct logit attribution, causal interventions, probing, sparse autoencoders (SAEs), and vocabulary-based decoding.

**Experiments**

The paper presents no original empirical benchmark or replication. Its examples and findings summarize cited studies involving GPT-2 Small/XL, Pythia, OPT, Llama 2, Gemma, BERT, and Claude 3 Sonnet. Covered tasks include indirect object identification, greater-than year completion, subject–verb agreement, sentiment manipulation, contextual retrieval, and subject–relation–attribute factual recall. Discussed metrics include intervention-induced KL divergence and logit differences, held-out probe accuracy, and SAE average active-feature count, reconstruction fidelity, loss recovery, and feature density. The text supplies algebraic decompositions for additive logit accounting and illustrates subspace replacement; these are conditional mathematical descriptions rather than new model measurements.

**Key results**

The synthesis links previous-token and induction heads to pattern completion, copy-suppression heads to reduced copying, and successor heads to ordinal prediction. Its factual-recall account combines subject enrichment by early-to-middle FFNs with later attention-mediated attribute extraction, while discussing additive contributions and competition between memorized and contextual answers. SAEs provide a candidate interface between distributed representations and interpretable feature circuits, including explicit reconstruction-error nodes. The survey connects automated circuit discovery and attribution-patching approximations to computational scalability, and reviews tools including TransformerLens, NNsight, Pyvene, and SAELens. These behavioral findings and method comparisons are credited to prior work.

**Limitations / open questions**

Probe accuracy establishes recoverability rather than causal use. Patching conclusions depend on counterfactual construction, replacement distributions, and downstream compensation; zero and noise interventions can produce unnatural states. SAE reconstruction errors can affect predictions, and robust evaluation across architectures remains unresolved. Vocabulary readouts, maximally activating examples, and plausible neuron explanations require faithfulness checks. Circuit generality, feature definitions, hallucination mechanisms, and practical safety benefits remain open. The supplied article is complete through Appendix D, although several equations contain rendering artifacts and inconsistent matrix conventions. Its header identifies v3 dated October 13, 2024; the metadata gives the initial publication date.

Spectral Filters, Dark Signals, and Attention Sinks
abstract: Projecting intermediate representations onto the vocabulary is an increasingly popular interpretation tool for transformer-based LLMs, also known as the logit lens. We propose a quantitative extension to this approach and define spectral filters on intermediate representations based on partitioning the singular vectors of the vocabulary embedding and unembedding matrices into bands. We find that the signals exchanged in the tail end of the spectrum are responsible for attention sinking (Xiao et al. 2023), of which we provide an explanation. We find that the loss of pretrained models can be kept low despite suppressing sizable parts of the embedding spectrum in a layer-dependent way, as long as attention sinking is preserved. Finally, we discover that the representation of tokens that draw attention from many tokens have large projections on the tail end of the spectrum.
summary:
**Central idea**
The paper introduces logit spectroscopy: analyzing residual representations and component weights in singular-vector bases of vocabulary embedding and unembedding matrices. U-dark and E-dark denote the bottom 5% of right singular vectors of the respective matrices. U-dark directions have low direct unembedding gain but can carry behaviorally important signals. The principal finding connects these signals to beginning-of-sequence (BoS) attention sinks.

**Experiments**
Experiments use pretrained LLaMA2 7B, 13B, and 70B, without instruction or safety fine-tuning. The main dataset, ccnet-405, contains 405 English prompts totaling 13,268 tokens. Filters modify one MLP output or residual-stream boundary at a time; average token negative log-likelihood (NLL) is compared with random orthogonal filtering. Further interventions swap filtered components between examples at matching positions, preserving the identical BoS state, or filter BoS alone. Selected experiments are repeated on 117 code prompts totaling 14,641 tokens. Displayed continuations compare spectral, random, and sink-preserving filters.

**Key results**
Early MLPs write large U-dark BoS signals: layer 1 in 7B, layer 3 in 13B, and layers 2 and 8 in 70B. The 70B sink is not E-dark. In 13B, BoS-preserving swaps remove the sharp NLL recovery associated with restoring the final spectral band, whereas BoS-only filtering reproduces it. This supports BoS signals as a major source of dark-tail sensitivity, without establishing that all dark signals serve sinking. Retaining the bottom 5% alongside leading directions permits substantial intermediate-band removal: after layer 12, removing 25% of unembedding directions raises 13B NLL from 2.47 to 2.74. Selected sink-disrupting continuations become repetitive. Among 404,748 eligible 13B token-layer pairs, 12,236 meet manually chosen attention-bar thresholds. Their dark-to-light norm ratios rise around layer 13 without increased cosine similarity to BoS.

**Limitations / open questions**
Evidence covers one pretrained family and small English/code samples. Generation comparisons are qualitative and include hallucinated content; low NLL does not establish broad capability preservation. The combined Ψ filter subtracts composed projectors and generally is not an orthogonal projection onto a shared dark subspace, complicating nominal filtering comparisons. Attention bars' possible auxiliary-sink function remains unresolved, and architectural compression is proposed rather than implemented. Plot images are unavailable in the supplied rendering; numerical results above come from prose. The source also contains conflicting 2024 publication and 2026 internal dates.

Harmonics of Learning: Universal Fourier Features Emerge in Invariant Networks
abstract: In this work, we formally prove that, under certain conditions, if a neural network is invariant to a finite group then its weights recover the Fourier transform on that group. This provides a mathematical explanation for the emergence of Fourier features -- a ubiquitous phenomenon in both biological and artificial learning systems. The results hold even for non-commutative groups, in which case the Fourier transform encodes all the irreducible unitary group representations. Our findings have consequences for the problem of symmetry discovery. Specifically, we demonstrate that the algebraic structure of an unknown group can be recovered from the weights of a network that is at least approximately invariant within certain bounds. Overall, this work contributes to a foundation for an algebraic learning theory of invariant neural network representations.
summary:
**Central idea**
The paper develops a conditional algebraic explanation for recurring Fourier features. Its central requirement is “unitary symmetries”: equal model functions at equal component norms must have weights related by blockwise unitary transformations. For a finite group acting regularly on input signals, invariance transfers to weights through an adjunction property. Theorem 10 then shows that every weight block surjecting onto its matrix space is a fixed matrix multiplied by an irreducible unitary representation. Noncommutative groups yield matrix-valued harmonics. The paper generalizes Spectral Networks and gives restricted identifiability results for complex neurons and orthonormal complex first layers.

**Experiments**
Complex Power-Spectral Networks receive the dimensions of the target group's irreducible representations and have identity-index blocks fixed to identity matrices. Adam minimizes disagreement between transformation-paired outputs plus an orthogonality penalty. Inputs are standard Gaussian signals in R^(2|G|), paired with uniformly sampled group transformations. Evaluation tests recovery of the entire multiplication table up to consistent relabeling. Noiseless demonstrations cover C6, C2 × C2 × C2, and D3 ≅ S3. Noise experiments on C5 and C6 add isotropic Gaussian noise to transformed signals and measure complete-table recovery across 20 training runs per noise setting.

**Key results**
The noiseless demonstrations report correct tables for all three illustrated groups. The text reports frequent successful recovery with noise standard deviation up to approximately 0.5, followed by a sharp decline; exact pointwise success rates are not tabulated. These experiments establish feasibility in selected small synthetic settings. They do not test pretrained language models, natural images, biological systems, or optimization guarantees. The formal development also proposes complete Fourier recovery and quantitative sufficient conditions for recovery under approximate invariance.

**Limitations / open questions**
The framework requires complex weights and strong identifiability and rank conditions. Attention mechanisms, ordinary real-valued networks, non-free actions, and localized harmonics such as Gabors remain unresolved. Several printed guarantees need qualification: W†W = |G|I alone does not establish the output surjectivity used by Corollary 11 for rectangular maps; inverse-representation conventions reverse noncommutative products in the labeled recovery argument; and Proposition 18 invokes a unit-vector lemma without imposing unit weight norms. Consequently, these particular proof attempts do not establish their full advertised statements. Dataset sizes and detailed training settings are absent from the experimental narrative. Figure 1's rotation example comes from prior work.

summary:
**Central idea**

This informal account of joint work with Mark Xu proposes approaching eliciting latent knowledge (ELK) through mechanistic anomaly detection: determine whether an apparently successful prediction arises through the mechanisms explaining reference-distribution behavior. In the diamond-vault example, consistent observations should reflect the diamond remaining safe rather than a replacement or tampered sensors. The target is anomalous model computation, which need not coincide with an unusual input. ARC considers defeasible probabilistic heuristic arguments and causal scrubbing as possible explanation formalisms.

**Experiments**

No experiments, trained checkpoints, detection measurements, or formal correctness proofs are reported. Three empirical directions are proposed: detecting supplied backdoor inputs in compromised models; distinguishing natural mechanisms producing similar language-model outputs, such as ignorance versus a character lying; and constructing toy ELK tasks. Proposed toys include a robot-and-robber gridworld with two color cameras and a pressure plate; a 100 × 100 Game of Life grid whose sensors at (25,25) and (75,75) exhibit a 200-timestep glider relationship; and a renderer mapping 10,000 bits to 256 × 256 images followed by a square detector. These are task specifications, not completed evaluations.

**Key results**

The contribution is a research strategy. Given an explanation of reference behavior, consider structured sub-explanations covering at least a fraction 1−ε of that behavior, with ε exceeding the undesirable mechanisms' reference contribution. For a new input, minimize the effect attributed to these plausibly good sub-explanations. This is a proposed conservative assessment, not a proved detector. Honest prediction and strategic deception might have different explanations of output variation even when they use the same components. A tentative multisensor extension seeks shared latent causes by explaining each sensor individually while conservatively evaluating their correlation. ARC's stated theoretical priorities are formalizing explanations, developing attribution-based anomaly detection, and automatically finding explanations; current work includes a special case where covariance propagation accurately predicts training variance.

**Limitations / open questions**

Explanation semantics, nonlinear instance attribution, and computationally feasible explanation discovery remain unresolved. Sub-explanations must exclude arbitrary case selection. Rare legitimate mechanisms and novel protective strategies can trigger false positives. The multisensor remedy is tentative; its diagram is absent from the supplied rendering, and one connecting sentence is unfinished, although subsequent prose describes the proposal. The toys may admit ordinary supervised solutions without resolving difficult ELK cases. An anomaly flag may permit neither safe shutdown nor adequate corrective supervision.
