The Local Interaction Basis: Identifying Computationally-Relevant and Sparsely Interacting Features in Neural Networks
abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand the behavior of neural networks by reverse-engineering their internal computations. However, current methods struggle to find clear interpretations of neural network activations because a decomposition of activations into computational features is missing. Individual neurons or model components do not cleanly correspond to distinct features or functions. We present a novel interpretability method that aims to overcome this limitation by transforming the activations of the network into a new basis - the Local Interaction Basis (LIB). LIB aims to identify computational features by removing irrelevant activations and interactions. Our method drops irrelevant activation directions and aligns the basis with the singular vectors of the Jacobian matrix between adjacent layers. It also scales features based on their importance for downstream computation, producing an interaction graph that shows all computationally-relevant features and interactions in a model. We evaluate the effectiveness of LIB on modular addition and CIFAR-10 models, finding that it identifies more computationally-relevant features that interact more sparsely, compared to principal component analysis. However, LIB does not yield substantial improvements in interpretability or interaction sparsity when applied to language models. We conclude that LIB is a promising theory-driven approach for analyzing neural networks, but in its current form is not applicable to large language models.
summary:
**Central idea**

The Local Interaction Basis (LIB) seeks computational features in a non-overcomplete linear activation representation. It centers and whitens activations, removes near-zero-variance directions, then recursively rotates and scales coordinates using dataset-stacked adjacent-layer Jacobians. Root-mean-square integrated-gradient-based attributions define interaction graphs. Ranked edge ablations measure interaction sparsity, and Leiden clustering searches for computational modules.

**Experiments**

LIB is compared with PCA on five one-layer modular-addition transformers, five CIFAR-10 MLPs, GPT2-small, and TinyStories-1M. Addition modulo 113 supplies 12,769 ordered operand pairs, with 30% used for model and basis training and the remainder for testing. Transformers have residual width 128, four attention heads, and 512 ReLU MLP units. CIFAR-10 networks have two 60-unit hidden layers and achieve 46.6–48.4% test accuracy. GPT2-small estimation uses OpenWebText: 51 million tokens for PCA and 512,000 tokens for the Jacobian step, requiring approximately 24 A100 GPU-hours. TinyStories-1M uses 10 million tokens for its Jacobian step. Layerwise sparsity tests preserve greater than 99.9% addition accuracy, CIFAR-10 accuracy within 0.1 percentage points, or language-model cross-entropy within 0.1 of baseline.

**Key results**

LIB retains fewer attention edges than PCA in all five addition models, but fewer MLP edges in only three. Fourier purity shows no consistent improvement; an apparent early-layer advantage comes from one seed. Graph inspection suggests fewer unused directions, but frequency-based module recovery is unreliable.

CIFAR-10 interactions are sparser with LIB across every tested mapping and seed. LIB concentrates an animal-versus-vehicle distinction more clearly than PCA. In the illustrated model, a final-layer direction achieves AUROC 0.932 versus 0.946 for grouped output probabilities. An oracle intervention setting the identified feature to its true-label conditional mean raises overall accuracy from 47.6% to 54.6%.

Layerwise GPT2-small experiments permit removing 80–95% of interactions in either basis. LIB’s additional gains are modest and noisy; TinyStories-1M shows consistent attention/MLP gains. Position explains approximately 97% of variance in GPT2-small’s first four LIB directions, while inspected linguistic features show no clear advantage over PCA.

**Limitations / open questions**

Dataset-stacked Jacobian SVD is not proved to produce maximally sparse interactions. Edge ablations may create unnatural states; attribution magnitude is an assumed importance proxy, and GELU attribution uses an endpoint approximation. The clearest addition graph is cherry-picked and resolution-tuned. Language-model comparisons confound model size with estimation-data volume. Method failure does not disprove the existence of useful non-overcomplete bases. Image-only plots limit additional quantification, and Appendix B contains inconsistent transformation-matrix ordering.

title: Consideration on the learning efficiency of multiple-layered neural networks with linear units
Singular learning theory iv: the rlct
Towards Developmental Interpretability
summary:
**Central idea**
Developmental interpretability proposes understanding neural networks by tracking how internal structure emerges during training, organized around phase transitions. It connects mechanistic interpretability with Singular Learning Theory (SLT), which describes Bayesian phase selection through an accuracy–complexity tradeoff related to singular loss-landscape geometry. Two central hypotheses are that enough important structure emerges through transitions to make them useful explanatory landmarks, and that most phenomena called phase transitions along SGD trajectories correspond to genuine SLT transitions. Neither hypothesis is established here.

**Experiments**
This is a research-agenda post without a new experimental protocol or formal derivation. Its principal motivating cases are cited studies of induction-head formation and toy models of superposition. It states that the relationship between training transitions and Bayesian phase structure has been verified by hand in superposition toys, but supplies no derivation, model configuration, dataset, or quantitative result for that analysis. Planned studies would monitor train/test losses, the real log canonical threshold or learning coefficient, and singular fluctuation; save checkpoints; attempt to classify weights as state, control, or irrelevant variables; interpret checkpoint computations; and compare these findings with final-model structures. Proposed coverage includes vision and code.

**Key results**
The contribution is an organizing framework and research questions rather than measured findings. Phase transitions are proposed as landmarks for detecting structural change, investigating emergent order, and studying recurring structures across models. For alignment, detecting and localizing changes could tell evaluation pipelines and mechanistic tools when and where to inspect. Preventing dangerous structures from forming or terminating training remains a prospective application. A further conjecture treats transition histories as construction transcripts that, together with less universal learned knowledge, could explain a final network’s computation.

**Limitations / open questions**
The relationship between individual SGD trajectories and Bayesian posterior transitions remains unresolved, as do refined observables and the mathematical nature of emergent structures. Four explicit failure modes are that relevant transitions are too infrequent, too frequent to triage, too extensive to localize, or too isolated to integrate into a quantitative explanation. Cited low-dimensional learning, pruning, and fine-tuning findings motivate locality but do not establish localized structural transitions. No safety intervention, detection accuracy, or reduction in evaluation costs is demonstrated.

title: Seeing is Believing: Brain-Inspired Modular Training for Mechanistic Interpretability
abstract: We introduce Brain-Inspired Modular Training (BIMT), a method for making neural networks more modular and interpretable. Inspired by brains, BIMT embeds neurons in a geometric space and augments the loss function with a cost proportional to the length of each neuron connection. We demonstrate that BIMT discovers useful modular neural networks for many simple tasks, revealing compositional structures in symbolic formulas, interpretable decision boundaries and features for classification, and mathematical structure in algorithmic datasets. The ability to directly see modules with the naked eye can complement current mechanistic interpretability strategies such as probes, interventions or staring at all weights.
summary:
**Central idea**

Brain-Inspired Modular Training (BIMT) encourages visible modular structure by placing neurons in geometric space, penalizing connection length times absolute weight, and periodically applying cost-reducing neuron swaps. Consistently permuting hidden-neuron parameters preserves the represented function. The procedure combines L1 sparsity, spatial locality, and discrete permutation search without prescribing task-specific modules.

**Experiments**

The paper trains small networks on three symbolic-regression problems, two-moon classification, addition modulo 59, S4 multiplication, scalar in-context regression, and MNIST. Symbolic regressors and the two-moon classifier use SiLU activations. Algorithmic tasks use trainable 32-dimensional token embeddings, two-hidden-layer MLPs, and 80%/20% train/test splits. The regression transformer has two layers, one attention head, embedding width 32, and one scalar demonstration; LayerNorm is removed. A separate regression ablation compares vanilla training, L1, L1 plus locality, L1 plus swapping, and full BIMT. Analyses include module knockouts, individual-weight removal, initialization perturbations, and magnitude-pruning frontiers.

**Key results**

Symbolic networks expose separate input dependencies, shared squared features, and an intermediate related to squared Euclidean distance. Table 1 reports losses of 7.4e-3, 8.5e-5, and 1.3e-3 with BIMT, versus 5.8e-3, 1.1e-5, and 1.2e-4 without it. Two-moon accuracy remains 100% with six useful hidden neurons. Modular addition and S4 multiplication also retain 100% reported accuracy. In the selected addition network, removing modules A, B, or C reduces accuracy to 15.25%, 29.33%, or 33.67%; the knockout evaluation denominator is unspecified. This supports cooperation without establishing literal majority voting. S4 embeddings have nine active coordinates, including sign and subgroup/coset patterns. Fitting them from a faithful 3×3 matrix representation leaves normalized squared error 0.56 across 100 fitting initializations. Transformer regression loss increases from 7.2e-5 to 1.8e-4; MNIST accuracy decreases from 98.5% to 98.0%. BIMT and L1 plus locality have the best reported toy pruning frontiers.

**Limitations / open questions**

Results concern small tasks, with interpretability assessed mainly through visual inspection and selected interventions. There are no controlled human evaluations or quantitative modularity benchmarks. Thin connections remain present in sparse-looking graphs. Initialization changes alter detailed circuitry despite recurring tree-like structures. LLM applicability remains untested. The main text and Appendix F inconsistently specify regression sampling distributions; Appendix G also contains conflicting MNIST weight-sign descriptions. Figures are unavailable visually in the supplied rendering, so their interpretation here relies on accompanying prose, captions, and tables.

On the Origins of Linear Representations in Large Language Models
abstract: Recent works have argued that high-level semantic concepts are encoded "linearly" in the representation space of large language models. In this work, we study the origins of such linear representations. To that end, we introduce a simple latent variable model to abstract and formalize the concept dynamics of the next token prediction. We use this formalism to show that the next token prediction objective (softmax with cross-entropy) and the implicit bias of gradient descent together promote the linear representation of concepts. Experiments show that linear representations emerge when learning from data matching the latent variable model, confirming that this simple structure already suffices to yield linear representations. We additionally confirm some predictions of the theory using the LLaMA-2 large language model, giving evidence that the simplified model yields generalizable insights.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper investigates possible origins of linear concept representations through a binary latent conditional model. Contexts fix some concepts, remaining concepts follow a graphical-model conditional distribution, and complete assignments map injectively to tokens. Softmax lookup models learn context embeddings and token unembeddings. Exact counterfactual log-odds constraints determine projected token differences. Separately, a supplied derivation shows that joint gradient descent on a simplified exponential objective aligns token differences with context differences under symmetric orthogonal initialization. Conditional results connect graphical separation and matched directions to Euclidean orthogonality.

**Experiments**

Synthetic data come from random DAGs with Bernoulli conditional parameters sampled uniformly from [0.3, 0.7]. Lookup models predict complete assignments from randomly masked vectors using cross-entropy, primarily with SGD, learning rate 0.1 and batch size 100. Experiments vary concept count, conditioning masks, supported assignments, dimension, and optimizer. LLaMA-2-7B experiments compare context contrasts with 27 lexical token-contrast categories. Translation contexts use four OPUS Books language pairs, sampling 150 examples and filtering contexts outside 20–150 tokens; retained counts are unspecified. Winograd examples are filtered to place the ambiguous word near the sentence end.

**Key results**

With complete synthetic conditioning sets and dimension equal to concept count, mean within-concept unembedding cosine similarity ranges from 0.972 to 0.997 across three to seven concepts; context–token alignment ranges from 0.973 to 0.990. Adam also produces substantial alignment. Restricted conditioning masks retain strong alignment in the tested settings. Restricting both contexts and assignments weakens it: at 12 concepts, unembedding, embedding, and cross-space similarities are 0.896, 0.551, and 0.696. LLaMA translation contrasts preferentially align with matching or related lexical translation contrasts. Winograd matching comparisons average cosine 0.042 versus 0.011 for nonmatching comparisons. The text reports stronger within-category than between-category token alignment and approximately orthogonal distinct-concept directions.

**Limitations / open questions**

The optimization results concern simplified objectives, not complete transformer training. The fixed-embedding argument relies on a cited separable-classification theorem, but distinct embeddings alone do not ensure separability. Joint alignment requires restrictive initialization. Log-odds results constrain projections, permit zero projected differences, and require explicit probability-ratio assumptions. Binary concepts, token injectivity, core-context sufficiency, and isolated counterfactual changes are substantial idealizations. LLaMA measurements establish partial geometric agreement without identifying its training cause or natural causal use. Appendix F inconsistently names embedding and unembedding spaces. Plot images are unavailable in this rendering; numerical claims here use readable tables and prose.

Information Flow Routes: Automatically Interpreting Language Models at Scale
abstract: Information flows by routes inside the network via mechanisms implemented in the model. These routes can be represented as graphs where nodes correspond to token representations and edges to operations inside the network. We automatically build these graphs in a top-down manner, for each prediction leaving only the most important nodes and edges. In contrast to the existing workflows relying on activation patching, we do this through attribution: this allows us to efficiently uncover existing circuits with just a single forward pass. Additionally, the applicability of our method is far beyond patching: we do not need a human to carefully design prediction templates, and we can extract information flow routes for any prediction (not just the ones among the allowed templates). As a result, we can talk about model behavior in general, for specific types of predictions, or different domains. We experiment with Llama 2 and show that the role of some attention heads is overall important, e.g. previous token heads and subword merging heads. Next, we find similarities in Llama 2 behavior when handling tokens of the same part of speech. Finally, we show that some model components can be specialized on domains such as coding or multilingual texts.
summary:
**Central idea**
Information flow routes are prediction-specific subgraphs connecting token representations through residual connections, FFN updates, and source-token contributions through attention heads. Starting at the final residual state, extraction traces backward and retains edges above a threshold. Importance uses ALTI's normalized, nonnegative L1 proximity of each incoming vector to their sum. The workflow requires one cached forward pass followed by attribution computation, without contrastive prompts or interventions.

**Experiments**
GPT-2 Small routes are compared with published IOI and Greater-than head sets using inclusion frequencies at τ = 0.03; OPT-125M provides illustrative route comparisons. General analysis uses Llama 2-7B on 1,000 C4 sentences, examining local component scores, t-SNE projections, and head activity at τ = 0.01. Domain comparisons use reported 1,000-sentence samples from C4, English/Russian/Italian/Spanish FLORES-200 devtest, CodeParrot code, and addition/subtraction data. Selected domain-associated heads are inspected through OV-matrix SVD and unembedding projections.

**Key results**
Routes include many previously identified task heads alongside generic contributors. Contrasting IOI route frequencies removes several generic heads. Greater-than attribution frequencies change little for a suffix-01 baseline but change more for suffix 00; these are attribution comparisons, not new patching tests. The authors report five seconds for 50 IOI examples, versus ACDC's cited eight-minute result. Llama attribution vectors group more clearly by input than reference-next-token POS, particularly for function words, and distinguish first from later subwords. Previous-token and subword-merging heads rank among the most active in their layers. An outlying punctuation cluster contains first periods in 823 of 826 datapoints; its middle-layer attention/FFN scores approach zero, and an attention example shows subsequent tokens attending to the period alongside BOS. Component attribution profiles differ across domains and between addition and subtraction. Selected code/non-English heads have corresponding vocabulary projections.

**Limitations / open questions**
Evidence consists mainly of descriptive attribution, visual clustering, and selected examples. No intervention-based graph-faithfulness or retained-output evaluation establishes causal circuit recovery. Fixed attention and normalization omit effects through changing routing or normalization; nonnegative proximity scores and unequal attention/FFN granularity constrain interpretation. Runtime uses a published comparator without a controlled rerun. Domain-associated scores do not establish separate reasoning algorithms, and whether period sinks cause generation errors remains open. The supplied rendering includes figure captions and textual interpretations but no inspectable plots, limiting independent assessment of visual results and numerical effect sizes.

title: A Regularity Theory of Causation
Characterizing Mechanisms for Factual Recall in Language Models
abstract: Language Models (LMs) often must integrate facts they memorized in pretraining with new information that appears in a given context. These two sources can disagree, causing competition within the model, and it is unclear how an LM will resolve the conflict. On a dataset that queries for knowledge of world capitals, we investigate both distributional and mechanistic determinants of LM behavior in such situations. Specifically, we measure the proportion of the time an LM will use a counterfactual prefix (e.g., "The capital of Poland is London") to overwrite what it learned in pretraining ("Warsaw"). On Pythia and GPT2, the training frequency of both the query country ("Poland") and the in-context city ("London") highly affect the models' likelihood of using the counterfactual. We then use head attribution to identify individual attention heads that either promote the memorized answer or the in-context answer in the logits. By scaling up or down the value vector of these heads, we can control the likelihood of using the in-context answer on new data. This method can increase the rate of generating the in-context answer to 88\% of the time simply by scaling a single head at runtime. Our work contributes to a body of evidence showing that we can often localize model behaviors to specific components and provides a proof of concept for how future methods might control model behavior dynamically at runtime.
summary:
**Central idea**

Conflicting contextual and pretrained factual associations can recruit attention heads with different answer-promoting effects. The paper investigates whether corpus frequency predicts which answer a model produces and whether scaling individual heads changes that preference.

**Experiments**

The World Capital dataset contains a reported 62,992 counterfactual prompts, constructed from 248 country–capital pairs plus six aliases. Each supplies a false capital statement followed by a capital question; city mentions in generated sentences determine contextual versus memorized answers. Frequency analyses use Pile name occurrence counts and document-level country–capital co-occurrences, divided into ten percentile bins, across Pythia-70M, 160M, 410M, 1B, 1.4B, and 2.8B and four GPT-2 sizes. Pile frequencies approximate GPT-2's unavailable training data.

Mechanistic analyses examine Pythia-1.4B, Pythia-2.8B, and GPT-2 XL. Head-output vocabulary projections nominate memory and context heads. Per model, 100 examples initially producing each answer type support head selection and scaling-factor tuning. Selected interventions are evaluated on the full capital dataset and transferred without retuning to CounterFact paraphrase examples filtered for correct predictions without counterfactual prefixes. OV singular-vector vocabulary projections provide qualitative head interpretations.

**Key results**

More frequent countries correlate with more memorized answers; more frequent counterfactual cities correlate with fewer contextual answers. Larger Pythia models increasingly favor memorized answers, with this tendency extending toward lower-frequency facts.

For Pythia-1.4B, scaling memory head 15.7 by −0.7 raises contextual answers from 26% to 86.2% and reduces memorized answers from 43% to 4% across the reported 62,992 prompts. The abstract instead reports 88%. Promoting memorized answers is less effective, while memory-head downscaling largely removes the observed frequency gradients. The memory head's singular-vector readouts include geographic token clusters. Capital-selected interventions fail to transfer successfully to CounterFact, increasing invalid answers. Appendix E reports a substantial shift toward answers repeating the supplied statement's format.

**Limitations / open questions**

The narrow template and geographic domain do not establish general truthfulness control or preservation of unrelated capabilities. Full-dataset evaluation includes selection examples. Capital evaluation does not require demonstrated baseline recall of each true capital, and city mentions do not establish which knowledge source caused an answer. Frequency associations do not isolate causal training-exposure effects. Context-head identifiers conflict across sections, CounterFact's illustrative labels are reversed, and most plot values are unavailable in this rendering. The text provides no quantitative semantic-enrichment test or complete causal account of the selected heads.

summary:
**Central idea**
The post interprets transformer weights by taking their singular value decomposition and projecting residual-space singular vectors through the unembedding. Highly ranked tokens often form recognizable clusters. These static directions provide candidate descriptions of what MLP input/output matrices and attention OV circuits read or write. The authors also demonstrate natural-language direction search and deletion of selected singular components through closed-form rank-one updates.

**Experiments**
Qualitative analyses primarily examine GPT-2 Medium OV and MLP matrices, including Gaussian random-matrix controls. Human labeling covers 40 MLP-input directions in each of 24 blocks: 960 directions, reportedly requiring about six hours. A direction qualifies as interpretable when roughly 70–80% of its displayed tokens share a semantic theme; clearly polysemantic cases are rejected. Automated surveys examine the first 30 singular directions of MLP input and output matrices across GPT-2 Small, Medium, and Large. GPT-3 proposes labels, and a separate verifier must also accept them. Search compares encoded query-token sets with singular vectors using cosine similarity, with an illustrative threshold of 0.15. Editing demonstrations remove selected OV components and inspect cued-token log probabilities.

**Key results**
The automated survey reports approximately 70–80% accepted directions when aggregated by singular index across the first 30 directions. Layerwise fractions generally increase from roughly 40–50% to 80–90%, with model- and matrix-specific late-layer declines. Human labels also show increasing coherence with layer depth, but their dependence on singular index conflicts with the automated results. Selected OV directions have distinct token clusters on opposite signs, sometimes including semantic opposites such as fire and ice. In one strongly cued fire example, removing the fire-associated component reduces the target token’s log probability more than removing other components. Search retrieves recognizable candidate directions; encoding queries using the unembedding pseudoinverse reportedly works better than using ordinary embeddings.

**Limitations / open questions**
Semantic judgments are subjective, and automated labeling lacks reliable ground truth or quantified agreement. Prompt examples and verifier behavior substantially influence results. Coherent vocabulary projections do not establish natural activation features or complete computational roles. Search is lossy: queries built from a direction’s own top tokens recover only about 0.5 cosine similarity. Single-component edits rarely change global behavior, and broad specificity is unmeasured. Nonlinear representations and the connection between weight semantics and activation dynamics remain unresolved. The supplied rendering lacks the displayed token tables and plots, and some head/direction identifiers are inconsistent; exact visual values and those identifiers cannot be independently checked.

Transformers represent belief state geometry in their residual stream
abstract: What computational structure are we building into large language models when we train them on next-token prediction? Here, we present evidence that this structure is given by the meta-dynamics of belief updating over hidden states of the data-generating process. Leveraging the theory of optimal prediction, we anticipate and then find that belief states are linearly represented in the residual stream of transformers, even in cases where the predicted belief state geometry has highly nontrivial fractal structure. We investigate cases where the belief state geometry is represented in the final residual stream or distributed across the residual streams of multiple layers, providing a framework to explain these observations. Furthermore we demonstrate that the inferred belief states contain information about the entire future, beyond the local next-token prediction that the transformers are explicitly trained on. Our work provides a general framework connecting the structure of training data to the geometric structure of activations inside transformers.
summary:
**Central idea**
Computational mechanics supplies a geometry of posterior beliefs over a sequence generator’s hidden states. Its mixed-state presentation describes observation-conditioned belief updates. The paper tests whether next-token-trained transformers linearly encode this geometry, including distinctions between histories with identical next-token distributions but different longer-term futures.

**Experiments**
Transformers were trained separately on two stationary hidden Markov processes: Mess3, with three hidden states, three tokens, and fractal belief geometry; and Random–Random–XOR (RRXOR), with five hidden states, two tokens, and 36 distinct belief states. Models had four layers, one attention head per layer, residual width 64, head dimension 8, MLP width 256, ReLU activations, and context length 10. Training used SGD with learning rate 0.01, batch size 64, no weight decay, and 1,000,000 reported epochs with freshly generated sequences. Affine regressions mapped individual-layer or concatenated residual activations, collected across context positions, to exact HMM posteriors. Metrics included regression MSE, pairwise-distance correspondence, and validation cross-entropy normalized to the theoretical optimum.

**Key results**
Mess3’s fractal geometry was recoverable from the final residual stream and emerged gradually during training. Fitting on 20% of input–activation pairs preserved recovery on the held-out 80%; shuffled correspondences collapsed predictions toward the simplex center. Both procedures were repeated 1,000 times, independently resampling splits or shuffles rather than retraining models. Mess3 regression MSE was 0.0004 before final LayerNorm and 0.0003 afterward. RRXOR geometry was poorly recovered from any individual layer but recovered from concatenated layers. Pairwise distances in its decoded representation corresponded more closely to ground-truth belief distances (R² = 0.95) than next-token-distribution distances (R² = 0.31), showing recoverable structure beyond immediate predictions. Lower validation loss accompanied better belief decoding in both processes.

**Limitations / open questions**
Experiments cover tiny synthetic processes rather than natural-language models. Supervised affine decoding establishes recoverability; it does not directly test Bayesian-update circuits, natural causal use, or prediction of arbitrary future sequences. Independent model-seed replication and a held-out RRXOR regression evaluation are not specified. A cited handcrafted RRXOR transformer succeeds without linear belief geometry, so linearity is not necessary for task success. Compression, nonstationary and nonergodic data, imperfect prediction, and the relationship between belief states and interpretable features remain open. Plot images are unavailable in the supplied rendering; numerical results above come from accompanying text and captions.

What needs to go right for an induction head? A mechanistic study of in-context learning circuits and their formation
abstract: In-context learning is a powerful emergent ability in transformer models. Prior work in mechanistic interpretability has identified a circuit element that may be critical for in-context learning -- the induction head (IH), which performs a match-and-copy operation. During training of large transformers on natural language data, IHs emerge around the same time as a notable phase change in the loss. Despite the robust evidence for IHs and this interesting coincidence with the phase change, relatively little is known about the diversity and emergence dynamics of IHs. Why is there more than one IH, and how are they dependent on each other? Why do IHs appear all of a sudden, and what are the subcircuits that enable them to emerge? We answer these questions by studying IH emergence dynamics in a controlled setting by training on synthetic data. In doing so, we develop and share a novel optogenetics-inspired causal framework for modifying activations throughout training. Using this framework, we delineate the diverse and additive nature of IHs. By clamping subsets of activations throughout training, we then identify three underlying subcircuits that interact to drive IH formation, yielding the phase change. Furthermore, these subcircuits shed light on data-dependent properties of formation, such as phase change timing, already showing the promise of this more in-depth understanding of subcircuits that need to "go right" for an induction head.
summary:
**Central idea**

Induction-circuit formation depends on learning both where to attend and how to copy attended information. The paper introduces activation clamping throughout training to investigate these dependencies. It proposes three interacting subcircuits: previous-token attention and transport, induction-head query–key matching, and label copying to the output.

**Experiments**

The authors train causal, two-layer attention-only transformers with model dimension 64, eight heads per layer, RoPE, and LayerNorm on randomized-label, two-way one-shot classification. Omniglot images pass through a frozen ImageNet-pretrained ResNet18. The default dataset uses 50 classes, one exemplar per class, five labels, and 78,400 training sequences. Evaluation includes 100 held-out classes and the 20% of label pairs excluded from training. Metrics include cross-entropy, accuracy, and induction strength: attention to the correct contextual label minus attention to the incorrect label. Experiments remove or retain selected heads, preserve second-layer attention patterns or values during ablation, and supply selected computations throughout training. Additional experiments vary class and label counts. Appendix I qualitatively summarizes checks across five initialization seeds.

**Key results**

Training passes through an approximately 50%-accuracy plateau before reaching 99.99% task accuracy, alongside induction-head emergence and strong held-out generalization; exact held-out accuracies are not stated in the prose. The strongest second-layer head alone achieves approximately 98% accuracy; retaining the other heads without it also achieves approximately 98%. Each second-layer head can learn the task alone under the tested shared initialization, with delayed convergence. Previous-token heads provide multiple effective matching pathways, while other first-layer heads support value copying.

Supplying perfect matching produces smooth copy-learning curves. Supplying copying and first-layer transport produces a more exponential query–key learning curve. More classes primarily slow isolated matching, whereas more labels primarily slow isolated copying. A tensor-product toy model includes a formal proof that its all-zero factor setting is a stationary saddle with zero Hessian.

**Limitations / open questions**

The findings concern small synthetic models with fixed-length inputs and final-token supervision. Clamps simplify routing, separate normally superimposed inputs, or replace the output computation, limiting inference about native training dynamics. Smooth loss does not establish an exhaustive decomposition. Label-count timing is not uniformly ordered across seeds, and evidence for later heads specializing in earlier heads’ residual errors is mixed. Figures are unavailable visually in the supplied rendering; numerical statements here rely on prose, captions, and tables. Transfer to natural-language LLMs, vocabulary-size choices, and transient ICL remains prospective.

Safety Alignment Should Be Made More Than Just a Few Tokens Deep
abstract: The safety alignment of current Large Language Models (LLMs) is vulnerable. Relatively simple attacks, or even benign fine-tuning, can jailbreak aligned models. We argue that many of these vulnerabilities are related to a shared underlying issue: safety alignment can take shortcuts, wherein the alignment adapts a model's generative distribution primarily over only its very first few output tokens. We refer to this issue as shallow safety alignment. In this paper, we present case studies to explain why shallow safety alignment can exist and provide evidence that current aligned LLMs are subject to this issue. We also show how these findings help explain multiple recently discovered vulnerabilities in LLMs, including the susceptibility to adversarial suffix attacks, prefilling attacks, decoding parameter attacks, and fine-tuning attacks. Importantly, we discuss how this consolidated notion of shallow safety alignment sheds light on promising research directions for mitigating these vulnerabilities. For instance, we show that deepening the safety alignment beyond just the first few tokens can often meaningfully improve robustness against some common exploits. Finally, we design a regularized finetuning objective that makes the safety alignment more persistent against fine-tuning attacks by constraining updates on initial tokens. Overall, we advocate that future safety alignment should be made more than just a few tokens deep.
summary:
**Central idea**

Safety alignment can concentrate changes in next-token distributions at response beginnings, promoting refusal prefixes while leaving harmful continuations comparatively unchanged. This concerns response-token depth, not network-layer depth. The paper proposes recovery training and reference-relative, position-dependent fine-tuning constraints to address this vulnerability.

**Experiments**

The authors compare Llama-2-7B and Gemma-7B base/aligned checkpoints using refusal prefills and teacher-forced per-token KL on Harmful HEx-PHI: 330 harmful instructions across 11 categories paired with harmful GPT-3.5-Turbo answers. Harmfulness and attack success count responses receiving GPT-4-Turbo’s maximum harmfulness score, 5. They measure tokenwise losses, parameter-gradient norms, and distribution shifts during harmful and benign fine-tuning. Recovery training uses 256 safety triplets plus distilled Alpaca responses. Constrained SFT is evaluated in Llama-2-7B-Chat and Gemma-1.1-7B-IT against three fine-tuning attacks and on SAMSum, SQL Create Context, and GSM8k.

**Key results**

Aligned/base KL is reported to be larger at early response positions. Refusal prefilling reduces base-model harmfulness from 68.6% to 2.1% for Llama and from 85.4% to 1.0% for Gemma under the most effective listed prefix. Harmful fine-tuning raises Llama ASR from 1.5% to 87.9% within six gradient steps, alongside disproportionately large early-token changes.

Recovery training reduces 20-token-prefill HEx-PHI ASR from 56.1% to 3.4%. GCG ASR falls from 36.5% to 18.4% on HEx-PHI and 65.6% to 19.0% on AdvBench; these means select the three highest-ASR runs among ten attempts per model. Decoding-exploit HEx-PHI ASR, selecting the most unsafe sampled response per instruction, falls from 54.9% to 11.3%. AlpacaEval 1.0 win rate against text-davinci-003 changes from 51.8% to 49.5%.

Constrained SFT with warmup reduces harmful-example ASR from standard-SFT 88.9% to 4.6% for Llama and 81.6% to 1.9% for Gemma. Utility generally remains competitive, although Llama GSM8k accuracy declines from 41.7% to 37.4%. Appendix D supplies analytic loss limits and a gradient-reweighting identity.

**Limitations / open questions**

Recovery augmentation covers one already-aligned model and remains vulnerable to malicious fine-tuning. Warmup alone substantially improves some benign-fine-tuning results. These tests neither establish universal robustness nor uniquely identify shortcut learning as the cause. Plot images are unavailable, so only textual descriptions and tables support reported results. Full-distribution matching in the formal limiting-loss result requires full conditional vocabulary support; finite demonstrations do not generally satisfy it. The RL interpretation contains apparent value-indexing and KL-direction inconsistencies.

abstract: Many papers have shown that attention heads work in conjunction with each other to perform complex tasks. It's frequently assumed that communication between attention heads is via the addition of specific features to token residuals. In this work we seek to isolate and identify the features used to effect communication and coordination among attention heads in GPT-2 small. Our key leverage on the problem is to show that these features are very often sparsely coded in the singular vectors of attention head matrices. We characterize the dimensionality and occurrence of these signals across the attention heads in GPT-2 small when used for the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) task. The sparse encoding of signals, as provided by attention head singular vectors, allows for efficient separation of signals from the residual background and straightforward identification of communication paths between attention heads. We explore the effectiveness of this approach by tracing portions of the circuits used in the IOI task. Our traces reveal considerable detail not present in previous studies, shedding light on the nature of redundant paths present in GPT-2. And our traces go beyond previous work by identifying features used to communicate between attention heads when performing IOI.
summary:
**Central idea**
Singular vector tracing (SVT) decomposes attention scores using the SVD of each head’s bias-augmented QK matrix. An input-specific heuristic discards the largest collection of slice contributions with nonpositive sum, retaining positive contributions as signal. Weighted projections of upstream head outputs into these query/key subspaces define a communication graph. Tracing uses one cached forward pass per prompt; validation requires additional intervention runs.

**Experiments**
GPT-2 Small is evaluated on 256 IOI prompts containing 106 names, 15 templates, ABBA/BABA name orders, and 14–20 tokens. A sparsity comparison uses the first 21 tokens of each of the first 256 Pile elements. Tracing starts from heads (9,6), (9,9), and (10,0), follows attention concentrated above approximately 50% on a noninitial source token, and retains upstream contributors accounting for at least 70% of summed contributions. Validation subtracts or adds projected signals globally at the upstream writer or locally at the downstream receiver. Metrics include attention scores and indirect-object-minus-subject logit difference; complementary singular subspaces provide random controls.

**Key results**
The text reports typically 20 or fewer retained slices out of 64, often two or three, with sparse decompositions also occurring on Pile inputs. Filtering reveals known IOI contributors more clearly than using all slices. A frequency-filtered skeleton contains 21 heads, including 11 of 16 reference heads eligible under the tracing setup: precision 0.52 and recall 0.69. A 12-direction consensus key subspace for head (9,9) reportedly separates names from other tokens by average projection norm. Tested ablations generally lower attention scores and IOI performance; boosting generally improves performance. Selected parallel-path ablations appear approximately additive. Head (9,6) is an exception: local ablation lowers attention scores while improving the measured IOI outcome. Local interventions generally preserve cosine similarity above 0.999, with norm changes typically below 1%.

**Limitations / open questions**
Tracing omits MLP contributions, diffuse attention, initial-token attention, and negative-contribution pathways. Projection weights are heuristic estimates, and downstream processing changes intervention consequences. Score cancellation does not establish functional irrelevance; minimality, exhaustive pathway coverage, and general semantic identification remain unresolved. Plots are unavailable as images in the supplied rendering; numerical intervention effect sizes, tested-edge denominators, and uncertainty estimates are not supplied in the prose. Dates differ between metadata, the v3 banner, and the manuscript heading.

Symmetry in language statistics shapes the geometry of model representations
abstract: The internal representations learned by language models consistently exhibit striking geometric structure: calendar months organize into a circle, historical years form a smooth one-dimensional manifold, and cities' latitudes and longitudes can be decoded using a linear probe. To explain this neural code, we first show that language statistics exhibit translation symmetry (for example, the frequency with which any two months co-occur in text depends only on the time interval between them). We prove that this symmetry governs these geometric structures in high-dimensional word embedding models, and we analytically derive the manifold geometry of word representations. These predictions empirically match large text embedding models and large language models. Moreover, the representational geometry persists at moderate embedding dimension even when the relevant statistics are perturbed (e.g., by removing all sentences in which two months co-occur). We prove that this robustness emerges naturally when the co-occurrence statistics are controlled by an underlying latent variable. Our results indicate that these representational manifolds originate in the statistical symmetries of natural language.
summary:
**Central idea**

Translation symmetry in pairwise word statistics provides a spectral explanation for calendar circles, curved historical timelines, and geographic representation geometry. When an embedding Gram kernel depends on separation along a semantic continuum, its eigenvectors have Fourier structure. Boundary conditions distinguish periodic loops from open curves. A shared seasonal variable affecting many words can make this structure robust to changes in direct month–month statistics.

**Experiments**

The authors explicitly factorize normalized co-occurrence matrices from November 2023 English Wikipedia: 3.37 million articles, 2.72 billion tokens, a 25,000-word vocabulary, and a weighted context window of 16. Analyses cover months, years, 365 calendar dates, and the 48 contiguous US states. Comparisons use final-prompt-token residual activations from Gemma-2-2B and normalized 768-dimensional EmbeddingGemma state representations. Year decoding uses ridgeless regression over retained PCA ranks, with 100 trials reporting 60 training and 60 test embeddings each. Robustness tests zero the normalized month–month matrix block and refactorize the full matrix or restricted matrices containing helper words.

**Key results**

Reported month and year statistics approximately follow exponential distance kernels. Formal derivations establish periodic Fourier coordinates, boundary-dependent sinusoidal eigenfunctions for an open exponential kernel, and an O(r^(-1/D)) upper bound on optimal normalized squared coordinate-decoding error under spectral-ordering assumptions. Year-probe results illustrate decreasing underparameterized training error and a held-out interpolation peak. Reported PCA and Gram comparisons broadly agree with predicted geometry; theoretical kernel parameters are estimated from the same corpus or chosen visually. Circular month ordering survives block ablation at embedding dimension 1,000, excluding May from that PCA. Selected seasonal helpers reconstruct ordering better than the tested number-word and random helpers. Context reduces May's distortion in Gemma. A conditional latent-emission derivation explains translation-invariant PMI, and an asymptotic spectral-gap argument explains resistance to fixed-entry perturbations.

**Limitations / open questions**

Transformer comparisons establish descriptive agreement, without a controlled test that pairwise statistics cause their geometry or mediate ordinary computation. Formal results require idealized kernels, sufficient embedding dimension, or specified latent-generation assumptions. Real matrices are indefinite, complicating absolute-amplitude predictions; displayed continuum normalizations also differ. Geographic comparisons omit a tokenization-related Gemma mode, and helper selection uses month-derived affinities. The stated 1900–2020 year range is not reconciled with the 120-example split. Plots are unavailable beyond their textual descriptions, preventing independent numerical assessment. Context adaptation and hierarchical attributes remain open.

Measuring the Mixing of Contextual Information in the Transformer
abstract: The Transformer architecture aggregates input information through the self-attention mechanism, but there is no clear understanding of how this information is mixed across the entire model. Additionally, recent works have demonstrated that attention weights alone are not enough to describe the flow of information. In this paper, we consider the whole attention block –multi-head attention, residual connection, and layer normalization– and define a metric to measure token-to-token interactions within each layer. Then, we aggregate layer-wise interpretations to provide input attribution scores for model predictions. Experimentally, we show that our method, ALTI (Aggregation of Layer-wise Token-to-token Interactions), provides more faithful explanations and increased robustness than gradient-based methods.
summary:
**Central idea**

ALTI estimates input-token relevance by decomposing each attention block into transformed source-token vectors, incorporating multi-head attention, the residual connection, and layer normalization. Each vector receives a clipped, normalized score based on its L1 proximity to the block output. Multiplying these contribution matrices across layers produces input attributions. This accounts for vector orientation and avoids attention rollout's fixed equal weighting of attention and residual paths.

**Experiments**

Reported evaluations cross BERT, RoBERTa, and DistilBERT with SST-2, IMDB, Yelp, and masked subject–verb number classification using Linzen et al.'s Wikipedia dataset. Sentiment checkpoints come from TextAttack. The agreement setup specifies a 60%/20%/20% training/validation/test split and BERT fine-tuning, although results also cover the other architectures. Baselines include gradient norms, gradient-times-input, Integrated Gradients with 100 steps and a repeated-[MASK] baseline preserving special boundary tokens, attention rollout, and Globenc. Comprehensiveness measures predicted-class probability loss after deleting highly ranked tokens; sufficiency measures loss when retaining only those tokens. Both aggregate percentages {0, 5, 10, 20, 50}. A separate SST-2 analysis compares ten fine-tuned MultiBERTs seeds using pairwise top-25% Jaccard similarity and Spearman correlation.

**Key results**

Tables 2, 6, and 7 give ALTI the highest comprehensiveness and lowest or tied-lowest sufficiency across all twelve model–dataset configurations. BERT SST-2 scores are 0.317 comprehensiveness and 0.044 sufficiency, versus 0.223 and 0.084 for L2-aggregated Integrated Gradients. Holding the norm family fixed, proximity-based contributions outperform transformed-vector norms in all twelve ablation configurations. L1 improves comprehensiveness over L2 in eleven configurations and never worsens sufficiency; BERT agreement slightly favors L2 comprehensiveness. The authors report higher cross-seed attribution agreement than gradient methods and negligible effects from adding the second layer normalization.

**Limitations / open questions**

ALTI excludes the classifier and provides no class-specific explanations. Its contribution scores and matrix products do not establish selective causal information flow or explicitly model FFN transformations. Faithfulness evidence depends on token deletion, which can create distribution shifts. Cross-seed agreement does not establish formal implementation invariance or identical mechanisms. Evaluation sample counts and numerical robustness effect sizes are unspecified. BERT Yelp ALTI scores conflict between Tables 2 and 5. Plots and saliency highlighting are unavailable in this rendering, limiting independent inspection of visual results; the article and appendices otherwise appear complete.

abstract: In this study, we investigate whether non-English-centric LLMs, despite their strong performance, `think' in their respective dominant language: more precisely, `think' refers to how the representations of intermediate layers, when un-embedded into the vocabulary space, exhibit higher probabilities for certain dominant languages during generation. We term such languages as internal $\textbf{latent languages}$. We examine the latent language of three typical categories of models for Japanese processing: Llama2, an English-centric model; Swallow, an English-centric model with continued pre-training in Japanese; and LLM-jp, a model pre-trained on balanced English and Japanese corpora. Our empirical findings reveal that, unlike Llama2 which relies exclusively on English as the internal latent language, Japanese-specific Swallow and LLM-jp employ both Japanese and English, exhibiting dual internal latent languages. For any given target language, the model preferentially activates the latent language most closely related to it. In addition, we explore how intermediate layers respond to questions involving cultural conflicts between latent internal and target output languages. We further explore how the language identity shifts across layers while keeping consistent semantic meaning reflected in the intermediate layer representations. This study deepens the understanding of non-English-centric large language models, highlighting the intricate dynamics of language representation within their intermediate layers.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper investigates “latent language,” defined operationally through the language of expected answers favored by intermediate vocabulary readouts. It extends English-centric analyses to Japanese-adapted and bilingual models, examining associations with training-language composition and requested output language. These readouts do not directly identify a language of reasoning.

**Experiments**

The study compares Llama-2-13B, Swallow-13B, and LLM-jp-v2.0-13B with 8-bit quantization. All have 40 layers and hidden width 5,120, but different vocabularies. A 166-item parallel dataset contains English, French, Japanese, and Chinese phrases and descriptions. Japanese–Chinese equivalents with distinct written forms come from JKVC; GPT-4 supplies English/French translations and cloze descriptions. Translation and repetition use four-shot prompts; cloze uses two-shot prompts. Multi-token answer scores multiply fixed-layer logit-lens probabilities while successively supplying preceding candidate tokens. Figures report 95% Gaussian confidence intervals over 166 examples.

Additional analyses examine a small cultural-question dataset and a Swallow activation shift averaged over 30 English–Japanese synonym pairs whose words are single tokens. The shift subtracts layer-26 states from layer-40 states and is added to layer-26 representations.

**Key results**

For Japanese targets, Llama-2 exhibits English-favoring intermediate readouts; Swallow exhibits English and Japanese; LLM-jp favors Japanese, with nearly absent English probabilities in Japanese repetition and cloze. On French/Chinese tasks, Swallow and LLM-jp exhibit both English and Japanese readouts. LLM-jp favors English for French targets and Japanese for Chinese targets. Swallow generally favors English; its translation comparison reverses the expected target-related Japanese preference, an exception to the paper’s broad conclusion.

For the displayed question about Japan’s school-year start, Llama-2 favors September/nine in intermediate readouts before April/four appears later. LLM-jp lacks that particular pattern. The Swallow shift qualitatively changes leading intermediate readouts from English to Japanese. The authors report that large coordinates of the averaged difference are sparse.

**Limitations / open questions**

The study covers three checkpoints and four languages without controlled pretraining interventions or aggregate task-accuracy results. Vocabulary, corpus composition, and training strategy vary together. Candidate scores depend on tokenization and supplied prefixes. Cultural-dataset size, shift success rates, controls, and held-out shift evaluation are unspecified. Sparse averaged differences do not establish selective language coordinates or dense shared semantics. Section 5.4 calls the changes sparse, whereas the conclusion inconsistently calls them dense. Figure images are unavailable in the supplied rendering; qualitative results follow the accompanying prose, without inferred plotted values.

title: Large Language Models Share Representations of Latent Grammatical Concepts Across Typologically Diverse Languages
abstract: Human bilinguals often use similar brain regions to process multiple languages, depending on when they learned their second language and their proficiency. In large language models (LLMs), how are multiple languages learned and encoded? In this work, we explore the extent to which LLMs share representations of morphsyntactic concepts such as grammatical number, gender, and tense across languages. We train sparse autoencoders on Llama-3-8B and Aya-23-8B, and demonstrate that abstract grammatical concepts are often encoded in feature directions shared across many languages. We use causal interventions to verify the multilingual nature of these representations; specifically, we show that ablating only multilingual features decreases classifier performance to near-chance across languages. We then use these features to precisely modify model behavior in a machine translation task; this demonstrates both the generality and selectivity of these feature's roles in the network. Our findings suggest that even models trained predominantly on English data can develop robust, cross-lingual abstractions of morphosyntactic concepts.
summary:
**Central idea**
Llama-3-8B and Aya-23-8B contain sparse feature directions associated with grammatical concepts across multiple languages. The paper investigates sharing through auxiliary classifiers, then tests selected features in translation generation. English-dominant pretraining is compatible with shared grammatical representations; the comparison does not isolate the causal effect of language balance.

**Experiments**
Gated SAEs with eightfold expansion are trained on 250 million Pile tokens using residual activations after layer 16. Language-specific logistic regressions predict morphosyntactic concepts from summed non-padding token activations in Universal Dependencies 2.1. The study considers 23 languages and concepts annotated in at least six. Attribution using ten integrated-gradient interpolation points ranks features by influence on probe logits. The top 32 features per language and concept define overlap and multilingual-feature sets. Ablations compare monolingual, multilingual, and the highest-ranked multilingual quartile.

Translation steering targets gender, number, and tense in English, French, German, and Turkish, excluding Turkish gender. The detailed intervention setup identifies Llama-3-8B; both models receive baseline translation evaluations. Manually selected individual features are clamped at the last token of each generation step, preserving reconstruction errors. Each directional setting uses 64 examples; grammatical minimal pairs are filtered for correct baseline predictions. Efficacy measures target-probe label changes after reprocessing generated translations without interventions. Selectivity measures preservation of other probe labels, without requiring a successful target flip. Flores-101 supplies qualitative examples.

**Key results**
Top-32 feature sets show cross-language intersection-over-union overlap up to 50%. Feature 22860 is influential in all 15 gender-inflecting languages considered. In Llama, ablating the most multilingual quartile leaves mean probe performance at 64%, versus 61% after ablating all multilingual features. Mean overlap between different concept-value feature sets is 13.9% ± 10.7%; masculine gender and singular number share 40.6%. Selected single-feature interventions often change target labels while preserving other measured labels. The Llama SAE recovers 81.22–92.85% of zero-ablation-relative loss across nine mC4 languages.

**Limitations / open questions**
Probe dependence does not establish ordinary generation mechanisms, and label preservation does not establish comprehensive semantic or translation-quality preservation. Feature selection and intervention strengths are manually tuned; some interventions fail or cause degeneration. Numerical steering, selectivity, and BLEU values are unavailable in the figure-only results. Appendix G describes three dataset languages despite Turkish appearing elsewhere. Nonlinear representations, English-related biases, and the appropriate extent of cross-language abstraction remain unresolved.

What Makes and Breaks Safety Fine-tuning? A Mechanistic Study
abstract: Safety fine-tuning helps align Large Language Models (LLMs) with human preferences for their safe deployment. To better understand the underlying factors that make models safe via safety fine-tuning, we design a synthetic data generation framework that captures salient aspects of an unsafe input by modeling the interaction between the task the model is asked to perform (e.g., "design") versus the specific concepts the task is asked to be performed upon (e.g., a "cycle" vs. a "bomb"). Using this, we investigate three well-known safety fine-tuning methods -- supervised safety fine-tuning, direct preference optimization, and unlearning -- and provide significant evidence demonstrating that these methods minimally transform MLP weights to specifically align unsafe inputs into its weights' null space. This yields a clustering of inputs based on whether the model deems them safe or not. Correspondingly, when an adversarial input (e.g., a jailbreak) is provided, its activations are closer to safer samples, leading to the model processing such an input as if it were safe. We validate our findings, wherever possible, on real-world models -- specifically, Llama-2 7B and Llama-3 8B.
summary:
**Central idea**

Safety fine-tuning may implement refusal through MLP weight updates that preferentially affect unsafe inputs. The proposed mechanism combines selective engagement of the update with writes outside the dominant column space of the original weights, separating safe and unsafe representations. Successful synthetic attacks resemble safe inputs under these diagnostics and engage the update less strongly.

**Experiments**

The controlled setting uses approximately three-million-parameter minGPT models with six blocks, six heads per block, and residual width 192. Inputs combine two bijective task operators with 15–25 PCFG-generated operand tokens. Pretraining and instruction learning use four grammars; safety training uses one, with repeated null-token targets for unsafe requests. SSFT, DPO, and unlearning are compared at initial learning rates 10^-4 and 10^-5. Each synthetic evaluation set contains 1,000 sequences. Analyses measure centroid-distance differences, K-means accuracy, Fisher criteria, covariance spectra, singular-subspace alignment, and reported input-gradient sensitivity. Natural-language comparisons use Llama-2 7B and Llama-3 8B base/chat pairs; Appendix B.2 describes 500 prompts per safety class and a 100-sample evaluation subset.

**Key results**

Safe and unsafe activations separate most strongly in later layers. Safety-update directions have substantial components outside the original weights’ 99%-energy column subspace, and unsafe inputs engage leading update directions more strongly than safe inputs. In the illustrated DPO covariance analysis, the leading unsafe singular value contributes roughly 62% of the covariance nuclear norm, versus 12% for safe samples. Table A.1 reports medium-rate DPO instruction-following scores of 31.5%, 97.2%, and 96.1% for competing-task, competing-text, and mismatched-generalization attacks, respectively, on separate 1,000-sequence sets. The evaluation describes output-token matching, with an incompletely normalized formula; these scores should not be interpreted as established percentages of fully successful harmful completions. Mechanistic attack analyses condition on successful attacks. Extrapolating SSFT weight updates improves tested jailbreak resistance while approximately retaining safe-task performance; comparable improvement is not reported for DPO or unlearning.

**Limitations / open questions**

Synthetic refusal has unusually repetitive targets, and transfer to natural-language safety mechanisms remains partial. Llama base/chat differences combine instruction and safety training. The complement of a truncated singular subspace need not be an exact left null space. Geometric associations and weight-scaling interventions do not uniquely identify the proposed mechanism. Sensitivity notation differentiates an argmax despite describing confident-output sensitivity, and activation averaging contains normalization inconsistencies. Plots are unavailable visually in the supplied rendering, limiting extraction to prose, tables, and captions. Repeated-run uncertainty and broad capability preservation are not established.
