Toward Identifiable Sparse Autoencoders
abstract: Recently, sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as an attractive tool for interpreting and interacting with representations in practical neural networks. While it is common empirical folklore, we also show theoretically that SAEs are highly unstable: different training runs are likely to produce different concept dictionaries and sparse codes. We characterize the model properties that hinder the stability of real-world SAEs, and address each of these problems through minimal changes to the architecture and training procedure. Together, these changes yield two versions of an \textbf{i}dentifiable SAE (iSAE), a variant of the standard TopK SAE with lower reconstruction error and improved stability. We explain this improvement theoretically by connecting SAEs with traditional dictionary learning approaches, and show that the dictionaries learned in practice satisfy an approximate restricted isometry condition, rendering the corresponding sparse codes in those models near-identifiable.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper treats sparse autoencoders as dictionary-learning estimators and distinguishes reproducibility of decoder atoms from reproducibility of sparse codes. It proposes iSAE, combining signed, magnitude-ranked AbsTopK encoding with dictionary-conditioning regularization, and iSAE-ME, adding five recurrent encoding steps. Its approximate restricted isometry property (aRIP) requires well-conditioned dictionary submatrices on unions of observed supports. Reproducibility is distinguished from recovery of true semantic concepts.

**Experiments**

Experiments use noiseless 768-dimensional synthetic mixtures generated from 4,096 independent or clustered dictionary atoms; Pythia-160M layer-12 activations on The Pile; and DINOv2-Base patch tokens on ImageNet-1k. Learned dictionaries contain 4,096 atoms with sparsity 40. Pythia dictionaries receive 512 million training tokens; synthetic models receive 40,000 steps of 2,048 examples. Independent runs are compared using Hungarian-matched absolute dictionary cosine similarity (DCS), code-support intersection over union (IoU), and normalized code error. Orthogonal matching pursuit (OMP) supplies an alternative coding procedure, called an oracle without an exact-recovery guarantee. Pythia dictionaries also receive SAEBench evaluations.

**Key results**

On independent synthetic atoms, iSAE-ME improves MSE from TopK's 0.447 to 0.001, encoder code IoU from 0.113 to 0.997, and DCS from 0.606 to 0.999. Clustered synthetic results improve substantially but remain less stable. Real activations show a different tradeoff: iSAE-ME lowers Pythia MSE from 0.166 to 0.148 and DINOv2 MSE from 0.217 to 0.191 relative to TopK. Relative to iSAE, recurrence worsens DCS, encoder-support IoU, and normalized encoder-code error in both real settings. AbsTopK increases real-activation dictionary agreement but worsens reconstruction. Adding conditioning regularization to AbsTopK improves OMP code consistency despite decreasing DCS. On SAEBench, iSAE-ME achieves the lowest replacement cross-entropy, 3.906 versus TopK's 3.974, but lower spurious-correlation-removal scores, 0.293 versus 0.381.

**Limitations / open questions**

The fixed-dictionary construction establishes that identical reconstructions can admit different sparse codes. The broader near-identifiability theorem additionally requires rich supports, within-support diversity, bounded observations, sufficiently small uniform reconstruction errors, and supportwise least-squares optimality. Its proof has an unresolved support-matching step: proximity of each observation to its own alternative subspace does not establish proximity of the whole batch to every such subspace. The sampled regularizer averages Gram-eigenvalue deviations on encoder-selected candidates and does not certify worst-case aRIP. Seed counts and uncertainty estimates are unspecified. Ground-truth recovery, distribution-shift robustness, and applicability beyond the tested models and dictionary sizes remain unestablished.

title: Archetypal SAE: Adaptive and Stable Dictionary Learning for Concept Extraction in Large Vision Models
abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a powerful framework for machine learning interpretability, enabling the unsupervised decomposition of model representations into a dictionary of abstract, human-interpretable concepts. However, we reveal a fundamental limitation: existing SAEs exhibit severe instability, as identical models trained on similar datasets can produce sharply different dictionaries, undermining their reliability as an interpretability tool. To address this issue, we draw inspiration from the Archetypal Analysis framework introduced by Cutler & Breiman (1994) and present Archetypal SAEs (A-SAE), wherein dictionary atoms are constrained to the convex hull of data. This geometric anchoring significantly enhances the stability of inferred dictionaries, and their mildly relaxed variants RA-SAEs further match state-of-the-art reconstruction abilities. To rigorously assess dictionary quality learned by SAEs, we introduce two new benchmarks that test (i) plausibility, if dictionaries recover "true" classification directions and (ii) identifiability, if dictionaries disentangle synthetic concept mixtures. Across all evaluations, RA-SAEs consistently yield more structured representations while uncovering novel, semantically meaningful concepts in large-scale vision models.
summary:
**Central idea**

Archetypal SAEs constrain decoder atoms to convex combinations of observed representations. The scalable implementation learns combinations of 32,000 fixed K-means centroids; Relaxed Archetypal SAEs (RA-SAEs) add bounded offsets to improve reconstruction. Conventional sparse encoders are retained, with experiments principally using TopK. The goal is reproducible concept extraction from vision models.

**Experiments**

The study evaluates DINOv2, SigLIP, ViT, ConvNeXt, and ResNet50. ImageNet experiments use approximately 1.28 million images and 50 training epochs, with dictionaries generally five times the activation dimension. Comparisons include vanilla, TopK, and JumpReLU SAEs, Semi-NMF, and Convex-NMF. Stability measures optimal atom matching across four training seeds. Additional metrics assess reconstruction, nearest-data cosine distance, dictionary ranks, coherence, and cancellation among coactivated atoms. A plausibility benchmark measures each classifier-weight direction’s best dictionary alignment. Twelve synthetic collage datasets each contain 4,000 images, split equally into training and test sets, with four distinct objects per image drawn from 9–20 object types. Dictionary width equals the object-type count; evaluation selects a coordinate and activation threshold for each object.

**Key results**

For DINOv2’s 2,000-atom, 90%-sparse comparison, RA-SAE achieves stability 0.927 versus TopK’s 0.542, with reconstruction R² of 89.34% versus 89.52%. Its nearest-data OOD score is 0.060 versus 0.551, although maximum pairwise coherence is higher. At 32,000 atoms and relaxation δ=1, classifier alignment improves from 0.1684 to 0.5581 for ConvNeXt, 0.3125 to 0.6213 for ResNet, and 0.2939 to 0.5014 for ViT. Averaged over the twelve collage datasets, A-SAE obtains object-presence accuracy of 0.9482–0.9631 across four backbones, versus TopK’s 0.8135–0.8328; RA-SAE scores 0.9447–0.9602. Author-described DINOv2 examples include rabbit parts, hand configurations, and spatial feature clusters. Formal derivations establish convex/conic containment, a rank bound, a loose dictionary-distance bound, and an OOD upper bound under orthogonal mixture supports.

**Limitations / open questions**

Geometric reproducibility, classifier alignment, and object-presence accuracy do not establish unique native concepts or causal mechanisms. Collage accuracy depends on class prevalence, permits coordinate reuse, and has an unspecified selection split. Convex-hull containment does not establish data-manifold membership. The dictionary-distance bound remains nonzero when data perturbation vanishes, so it does not guarantee seed stability. Relaxation constraints differ between equations and pseudocode, and some theoretical exposition overstates the derived results. Figure images are unavailable in this rendering, limiting independent visual assessment. LLM transfer is proposed but untested.

title: Sanity Checks for Sparse Autoencoders: Do SAEs Beat Random Baselines?
abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising tool for interpreting neural networks by decomposing their activations into sparse sets of human-interpretable features. Recent work has introduced multiple SAE variants and successfully scaled them to frontier models. Despite much excitement, a growing number of negative results in downstream tasks casts doubt on whether SAEs recover meaningful features. To directly investigate this, we perform two complementary evaluations. On a synthetic setup with known ground-truth features, we demonstrate that SAEs recover only $9\%$ of true features despite achieving $71\%$ explained variance, showing that they fail at their core task even when reconstruction is strong. To evaluate SAEs on real activations, we introduce three baselines that constrain SAE feature directions or their activation patterns to random values. Through extensive experiments across multiple SAE architectures, we show that our baselines match fully-trained SAEs in interpretability (0.87 vs 0.90), sparse probing (0.69 vs 0.72), and causal editing (0.73 vs 0.72). Together, these results suggest that SAEs in their current state do not reliably decompose models' internal mechanisms.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper tests whether SAE evaluation scores distinguish learned decompositions from representations with constrained random components. It introduces frozen-decoder, frozen-encoder, and soft-frozen-decoder baselines; the last retains decoder cosine similarity ≥0.8 with initialization. Remaining components still learn, so these controls measure the contribution of particular learned directions rather than eliminating learning altogether.

**Experiments**

Synthetic activations combine 3,200 random unit directions in 100 dimensions, approximately 20 active features per sample, lognormal magnitudes, and constant or heavy-tailed activation probabilities. Learned dictionaries have 3,200 latents and target L0=20; recovery uses nearest-decoder cosine around 0.8.

Language-model experiments train on 500 million OpenWebText tokens using Gemma-2-2B residual layers 12 and 19 and a Llama 8B layer 16. They primarily evaluate BatchTopK and JumpReLU, with ReLU and TopK comparisons, across reconstruction, automated interpretation, SAEBench sparse probing, and RAVEL attribute transfer/preservation. AutoInterp samples 200 eligible latents per configuration at L0=160; GPT-4o-mini evaluates descriptions on 50 activating and 50 random non-activating sequences per latent.

**Key results**

In constant-frequency mixtures, BatchTopK and JumpReLU achieve approximately 0.67 explained variance but recover only 3/3,200 directions each. Appendix B importantly reports nearly complete TopK recovery, approximately 99.9%, preventing an architecture-general failure conclusion. In heavy-tailed mixtures, BatchTopK recovers 297/3,200 directions and JumpReLU 225/3,200 at approximately 0.71 explained variance. Recovery across all four architectures ranges from 7% to 43% and favors frequent features.

At Gemma layer 12, L0=160, BatchTopK's covariance-initialized frozen decoder scores 0.692 versus 0.721 on top-1 probing. Its soft-frozen decoder scores 0.728 versus 0.720 on RAVEL, while explained variance falls from 0.852 to 0.785. Detailed prose reports soft-frozen AutoInterp of 0.88 versus 0.90. Top-5 probing generally shows larger learning advantages. These comparisons do not establish statistical equivalence.

**Limitations / open questions**

Synthetic supports are independent; training budgets and replicate counts are unspecified. Baseline performance depends substantially on initialization, and favorable headline scores can come from different baselines. Frozen encoders retain learned thresholds; soft-frozen decoders permit finite rotations. The spherical-cap derivation bounds exact reachability of an independently fixed direction, not approximate recovery or representation through combinations. Natural feature identities remain unknown, and the lazy-training explanation is unresolved. Llama-3 versus Llama-3.1 naming and the TopK recovery percentage are internally inconsistent. CLIP comparisons are qualitative, with image-only panels unavailable in this rendering. Transcoders and crosscoders are untested.

title: Faster-gcg: Efficient discrete optimization jailbreak attacks against aligned large language models
Closed-form training dynamics reveal learned features and linear structure in word2vec-like models
On the emergence of linear analogies in word embeddings
The Origins of Representation Manifolds in Large Language Models
abstract: There is a large ongoing scientific effort in mechanistic interpretability to map embeddings and internal representations of AI systems into human-understandable concepts. A key element of this effort is the linear representation hypothesis, which posits that neural representations are sparse linear combinations of `almost-orthogonal' direction vectors, reflecting the presence or absence of different features. This model underpins the use of sparse autoencoders to recover features from representations. Moving towards a fuller model of features, in which neural representations could encode not just the presence but also a potentially continuous and multidimensional value for a feature, has been a subject of intense recent discourse. We describe why and how a feature might be represented as a manifold, demonstrating in particular that cosine similarity in representation space may encode the intrinsic geometry of a feature through shortest, on-manifold paths, potentially answering the question of how distance in representation space and relatedness in concept space could be connected. The critical assumptions and predictions of the theory are validated on text embeddings and token activations of large language models.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper models a feature as a compact metric space whose values correspond continuously and bijectively to unit representation directions. A cited topological result makes this correspondence a homeomorphism. The main new theorem adds an exact local assumption: cosine similarity equals a twice continuously differentiable function g of squared feature distance, with g′(0)<0. Every rectifiable path then has its length multiplied by √(−2g′(0)). This concerns intrinsic path lengths; identifying them with the original feature metric additionally requires a length-space interpretation.

**Experiments**

The authors examine 3,072-dimensional OpenAI text embeddings, named “text-embedding-large-3” in the source, for colour descriptions and calendar dates. Colour names come from the XKCD survey with saturation, brightness, semantic, and additional outlier filtering. They reanalyse SAE-extracted twentieth-century year representations from GPT2-small layer 7 and visualize SAE-extracted month/day representations from Mistral 7B layer 8. Diagnostics compare cosine similarity with proposed squared feature distances using Chatterjee’s ξ, and weighted nearest-neighbour graph distances with feature distances using Pearson correlation. Text-embedding distance analyses use leading uncentered principal components; extracted year representations require no additional PCA.

**Key results**

Year representations follow temporal order along a connected K=10 graph: Kendall correlation is 0.97 and Spearman exceeds 0.99. Estimated manifold distances fit ordinary calendar-year differences poorly. After this mismatch, the authors introduce log(2019−year), obtaining cosine–distance functional dependence ξ=0.84 and graph-distance Pearson correlation 0.99. Projected date embeddings yield graph-distance correlation 0.97 with circular calendar distance, despite disagreement between cosine similarity and that metric at large separations. Colour embeddings reportedly follow hue order, with weaker geometric agreement. Three-dimensional views reveal bending obscured by two-dimensional projections.

**Limitations / open questions**

These selected examples provide preliminary evidence, rather than verification of exact continuous correspondence or the local kernel identity. Human-chosen metrics, filtering, projection, and retrospective revision of the year metric constrain interpretation. Discarded principal components contain additional structure. Nearest-neighbour graphs can introduce shortcuts; the authors note that reasonable distance estimates can require manual pruning. Retained PCA dimensions and graph K for the date-distance test are unspecified in the prose. Figure images are unavailable in the supplied rendering, so numerical results here rely on explicit textual reports. No steering experiment or manifold-aware SAE is implemented; manifold tracing as an explanation of SAE feature splitting remains conjectural.

title: From Data Statistics to Feature Geometry: How Correlations Shape Superposition
abstract: A central idea in mechanistic interpretability is that neural networks represent more features than they have dimensions, arranging them in superposition to form an over-complete basis. This framing has been influential, motivating dictionary learning approaches such as sparse autoencoders. However, superposition has mostly been studied in idealized settings where features are sparse and uncorrelated. In these settings, superposition is typically understood as introducing interference that must be minimized geometrically and filtered out by non-linearities such as ReLUs, yielding local structures like regular polytopes. We show that this account is incomplete for realistic data by introducing Bag-of-Words Superposition (BOWS), a controlled setting to encode binary bag-of-words representations of internet text in superposition. Using BOWS, we find that when features are correlated, interference can be constructive rather than just noise to be filtered out. This is achieved by arranging features according to their co-activation patterns, making interference between active features constructive, while still using ReLUs to avoid false positives. We show that this kind of arrangement is more prevalent in models trained with weight decay and naturally gives rise to semantic clusters and cyclical structures which have been observed in real language models yet were not explained by the standard picture of superposition. Code for this paper can be found at https://github.com/LucasPrietoAl/correlations-feature-geometry.
summary:
**Central idea**

Correlated features can help reconstruct one another through constructive interference. Bag-of-Words Superposition (BOWS) studies this using known binary word-presence features. The paper distinguishes linearly recoverable superposition from representations requiring nonlinear decoding. An algebraic derivation shows that exact projection onto a low-rank data subspace makes interference proportional to signal, with squared encoder norm equal to projector rank. Separately, numerical value codes can yield circles or maps through task-relevant projections.

**Experiments**

WikiText-BOWS uses a 10,000-word vocabulary and contexts aggregating 20 records, with 1,621,198 training and 180,133 validation samples. Tied-weight linear and ReLU autoencoders are compared across bottleneck sizes and weight decay, using reconstruction R², linear probes, Gram matrices, PCA, and semantic visualizations. Additional tests use synthetic cyclic, figure-eight, and spherical data, OpenWebText BOWS, and a causal prefix-token-recovery transformer. Separate MLPs learn addition modulo 113 and eight-way relative directions between 1,000 US cities; probes and embedding-subspace ablations test numerical value codes.

**Key results**

Tight bottlenecks produce correlation-aligned geometry; larger synthetic bottlenecks can favor antipodal interference filtering or orthogonal representations. Weight decay preserves visible semantic clustering across more bottleneck sizes. Month features have reported linear-decoder R² of 0.98 ± 0.00015, with unspecified uncertainty interpretation. Context improves reconstruction over isolated activation for 81% of validation samples containing “Beatles”; “Christmas” has the same conditional percentage. Semantic clusters remain visible among words with reconstruction R² below 0.3. Larger aggregated contexts increase linear-probe agreement with ReLU reconstructions and decrease the component count explaining 95% of input variance. City-coordinate probes achieve average held-out R² of 0.98. Keeping value-code subspaces retains 93.16% map accuracy and 93.99% modular-addition accuracy, versus baselines of 97.94% and 100%; removing them lowers accuracy to 22.43% and 3.11%.

**Limitations / open questions**

These results demonstrate mechanisms in controlled models without establishing their prevalence in pretrained LLMs. BOWS omits word order and contextual meanings, and clustering evidence is qualitative. Figures are unavailable as images in the supplied rendering; claims here follow the accompanying text and captions. Methods contain inconsistent city-embedding dimensions, transformer depth, and ablation descriptions. Unique input pairs do not establish statistical independence, and the binary synthetic generator does not generally have exactly rank-two covariance. Dominance conditions for constructive versus filtered interference, particularly with untied weights, remain open.

title: Neural word embedding as implicit matrix factorization
A mathematical theory of semantic development in deep neural networks
ICLR: in-context learning of representations
Deep sequence models tend to memorize geometrically; it is unclear why
The solution of a homogeneous wiener-hopf integral equation occurring in the expansion of second-order stationary random functions
Transcoder Adapters for Reasoning-Model Diffing
abstract: While reasoning models are increasingly ubiquitous, the effects of reasoning training on a model's internal mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this work, we introduce transcoder adapters, a technique for learning an interpretable approximation of the difference in MLP computation before and after fine-tuning. We apply transcoder adapters to characterize the differences between Qwen2.5-Math-7B and its reasoning-distilled variant, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B. Learned adapters are faithful to the target model's internal computation and next-token predictions. When evaluated on reasoning benchmarks, adapters match the reasoning model's response lengths and typically recover 50-90% of the accuracy gains from reasoning fine-tuning. Adapter features are sparsely activating and interpretable. When examining adapter features, we find that only ~8% have activating examples directly related to reasoning behaviors. We deeply study one such behavior -- the production of hesitation tokens (e.g., "wait"). Using attribution graphs, we trace hesitation to only ~2.4% of adapter features (5.6k total) performing one of two functions. These features are necessary and sufficient for producing hesitation tokens; removing them reduces response length, often without affecting accuracy. Overall, our results provide insight into reasoning training and suggest transcoder adapters may be useful for studying fine-tuning more broadly.
summary:
**Central idea**

Transcoder adapters approximate MLP-computation changes between Qwen2.5-Math-7B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B. Replacement layers combine frozen base MLPs with sparse adapters while retaining target non-MLP parameters. Training combines output KL, hidden-state normalized MSE, bidirectional bridging losses, and decoder-norm-weighted activation sparsity. Attribution graphs describe adapter features interacting through retained base computation.

**Experiments**

The authors train 8,192 features at each of 28 layers on 50,000 OpenThoughts3 transcripts, approximately 380M tokens, obtaining five adapters with mean per-layer/token L0 of 0.1–10.3. Output agreement uses 5M target-generated tokens; internal compatibility uses single-layer, prefix, and suffix replacements. Benchmark evaluations comprise AIME25: 30 questions × 10 repetitions; AMC23: 40 × 10; MATH500: 500 × 1; and GPQA Diamond: 198 × 3. Other analyses evaluate automated interpretation, classify 7,000 adapter features, compare encoder activation overlap, and manipulate 5,623 hesitation-associated features.

**Key results**

Top-1 disagreement falls from 39.2% for the base model and 28.5% for the hybrid without adapters to 13.6% at L0≈0.1 and 9.2% at L0≈10, versus 8.5% for an MLP-fine-tuning skyline. Adapters typically recover 50–90% of reasoning-training accuracy gains and approximate target response lengths. Removing bridging losses retains low hidden-state MSE but worsens partial-replacement KL.

GPT-4o-mini detection accuracy is 0.82–0.84 for maximal adapter examples versus 0.80 for maximal neuron examples; uniformly sampled adapter positives score 0.69–0.73. GPT-5-mini labels 8.6% of sampled adapter features as reasoning-style, 37.6% as domain-specific, and 48.1% as general language features.

Removing 4,812 hesitation-output and 811 template features reduces reported “wait” frequency from 5.5 to 0.5 per 1,000 response tokens; adding both groups to the hybrid raises it to 8.2. Removing them more than halves benchmark response lengths, retaining reported accuracy on three benchmarks while reducing AIME25 accuracy from 26% to 20%. Scaled negative contributions also shorten the original target’s responses, with reported accuracy costs.

**Limitations / open questions**

Evidence covers one distilled model pair and leaves non-MLP changes unexplained. Category counts measure neither acquired knowledge nor causal shares of reasoning computation. Reconstruction and partial replacements do not certify mechanistic equivalence; “wait” frequency measures surface behavior. Evaluation truncates degenerate responses, more frequently for sparse adapters, and uses different prompting/decoding for the base model. Accuracy equivalence is not statistically established. Full-strength target suppression causes incoherence. Some appendix dashboard text is corrupted, and exact plotted values are unavailable where not stated in prose.

title: How Do Linear Probes Emerge? A Circuit-Tracing Framework with Concept-Targeted Attribution
abstract: Transcoder attribution graphs are usually trained to explain why a model assigns high probability to a particular next token. We introduce Concept-Targeted Attribution (CTA), which instead trains attribution graphs with respect to a linear probe direction. CTA therefore yields probe-specific circuits that explain why an internal concept representation arises in a prompt, independently of whether it is expressed in the generated token. Using Cross-Layer Transcoders, we show that these probe-targeted graphs contain predictive structure: graph-level features predict probe accuracy across four widely studied concept categories ($ρ= 0.91$, $R^2 = 0.84$), while local features identify the sparse components driving per-prompt classification. This connects probe performance to interpretable circuit structure, allowing us to ask not only whether a probe works, but which internal computations make it work. Causal ablations further show that probe-targeted and logit-targeted graphs capture functionally distinct mechanisms. Removing probe-relevant features reduces internal concept scores while largely preserving generated tokens, whereas removing logit-relevant features changes the generated token in 92% to 100% of cases with near-zero effect on probe scores. CTA provides a framework for moving from behavioral probe accuracy to mechanistic explanations of probe performance, enabling more detailed audits of internal concept representations, including safety-critical ones. Our code is available at https://github.com/vedantpalit/concept-targeted-attribution
summary:
**Central idea**

Concept-Targeted Attribution (CTA) changes the scalar target of a cross-layer-transcoder attribution graph from a next-token logit to an internal linear-probe score. It traces contributions to a specified readout without requiring that concept to appear in the next token. Graph construction freezes input-dependent nonlinearities, so its paths describe conditional influence within the sparse replacement framework.

**Experiments**

The study evaluates Gemma-2-2B and Llama-3.2-1B using ParaDetox toxicity, SST-2 sentiment, HotpotQA versus TriviaQA reasoning/recall, and three pooled Geometry of Truth subsets. It reports 10,000 examples per concept, balanced classes, an 80/20 train/validation split, and a 60-token filter. Graph analyses use 100 prompts per concept; causal dissociation uses 50. Experiments ablate probe-exclusive, logit-exclusive, and shared features, predict layerwise validation accuracy from 35 prompt-averaged graph statistics, and predict prompt-level margins from binary CLT-feature presence.

**Key results**

Gemma gradient boosting achieves five-fold cross-validation Spearman ρ=0.905 and R²=0.835 for raw probe accuracy, versus layer-baseline ρ=0.083. Llama achieves ρ=0.808 and R²=0.850, but its within-concept demeaned correlation is 0.34 with a confidence interval spanning zero; held-out-concept transfer is poor. Gemma logit-exclusive ablations flip the immediate top token in 92–100% of evaluated cases; Llama reports 100%, with comparatively small probe-score changes. Gemma probe-exclusive ablations produce no flips for toxicity, sentiment, or reasoning, but 25% for truthfulness. Llama truthfulness has essentially no probe-exclusive readout effect. Binary feature presence predicts Gemma toxicity margins strongly, peaking at ρ=0.86; sentiment and reasoning predictions are weaker. Selected predictive features recur 6–21 times more frequently than random features. Representative prompts show adjacent-layer graph overlap stabilizing near Jaccard 0.9.

**Limitations / open questions**

These results concern chosen readouts and immediate predictions, rather than general separation of knowledge, belief, and generation. Llama sentiment ablation moves the score from −0.47 to +2.40, contradicting the claimed reduction in magnitude. Some reported flip percentages do not reconcile with the stated 50-prompt denominator. Appendix A specifies raw difference-in-means attribution directions and PCA/LDA-corrected accuracy directions, while the main text describes orthogonalization; their correspondence is unclear. Feature interpretations conflict across sections. Dataset contrasts can capture lexical, register, or question-format cues. Grouped cross-validation does not itself hold out entire concepts, and accuracy prediction uses supervised targets. CLT fidelity, frozen computation, feature selection, and representative-prompt analyses limit stronger mechanistic and stability conclusions.

title: A Unifying Framework for Unsupervised Concept Extraction
abstract: Techniques for concept extraction, such as sparse autoencoders and transcoders, aim to extract high-level symbolic concepts from low-level nonsymbolic representations. When these extracted concepts are used for downstream tasks such as model steering and unlearning, it is essential to understand their guarantees, or lack thereof. In this work, we present a unified theoretical framework for unsupervised concept extraction, in which we frame the task of concept extraction as identifying a generative model. We present a general meta-theorem for identifiability, which reduces the problem of establishing identifiability guarantees to the problem of characterizing the intersection of two sets. As we demonstrate on a range of widely-used approaches, this meta-theorem substantially simplifies the task of proving such guarantees, thus paving the way for the development of new, principled approaches for concept extraction.
summary:
**Central idea**
The paper formulates unsupervised concept extraction as identification of a latent concept generative model, M=(Q,K). Q generates latent concepts, K maps them deterministically or stochastically into observed neural features, and extraction means posterior inference over concepts given features. Identifiability is relative to a model class and an allowed equivalence relation. The proposed intersection theorem separates transformations compatible with concept distributions from those compatible with mixing kernels.

**Experiments**
There are no empirical experiments, trained language models, datasets, or benchmark measurements. Evidence consists of population-level mathematical derivations and finite-state counterexamples. Applications concern sparse dictionary learning with full stratified support and decoder spark greater than twice code sparsity; injective linear ICA with independent, unit-variance components and at most one Gaussian component; and finite Gaussian mixtures with positive weights and distinct components. Appendix D derives reconstruction plus L1 regularization as an amortized MAP objective under a linear Gaussian likelihood and independent Laplace prior.

**Key results**
Blackwell reducibility requires mixing kernels to factor through a common measure-separating base kernel after injective latent maps. Equality of observed distributions then identifies the distribution entering that base kernel. Supplied proofs establish that Blackwell coarsening preserves the observed marginal, that measure-separating kernels alone do not ensure Blackwell comparability, and that convolution with fixed noise having a nowhere-zero characteristic function is injective. The paper proposes broader Blackwell-equivalence and transition-intersection guarantees, adapting deterministic identifiability work to stochastic mixing. It also distinguishes generative-model learning from approximate posterior inference and explains how exact projection-encoder requirements can couple Q and K.

**Limitations / open questions**
Population identification does not establish finite-sample recovery, successful optimization, human-interpretable semantics, or safe steering. Misspecification, weak supervision, and real activation distributions remain unresolved. Several mathematical claims need correction or further justification: Appendix B.2 assumes matching images from equal pushforward measures and their support; the dictionary proof asserts a global linear transition without establishing it; and the ICA permutation-only conclusion overlooks sign flips. Section 5's equality between transitions of intersected predicate classes and intersections of transition sets does not follow from the definitions because existential witnesses can differ. Appendix D also contains sign and indexing inconsistencies, and its deterministic ELBO limit does not justify discarding the prior and divergent entropy terms. These issues limit the advertised guarantees despite the valid narrower derivations.

title: Sparse Weight Decomposition for Efficient Circuit Extraction
abstract: Dense pretrained transformers do not naturally expose interpretable units for circuit extraction. Existing approaches obtain such units by learning auxiliary sparse representations or training sparse models, incurring substantial additional computation while potentially introducing a fidelity gap between the representation being analyzed and the original pretrained model. We propose Sparse Weight Decomposition (SWD), which reparameterizes pretrained linear projections by factorizing each weight matrix into two sparse factors whose shared intermediate coordinates serve as individually addressable circuit units. Without training a separate replacement network, this parametric representation supports the same scoring, selection, and ablation circuit extraction workflow used for methods that learn sparse features. Across single-matrix replacements, SWD matches the held-out fidelity achieved by Transcoder and other strong baselines while using less than 1% of the data that those baselines use to train their replacements. For matched replacement fidelity, SWD reaches the same circuit sufficiency and necessity targets with fewer active read/write edges and selected units across tasks on GPT-2, Qwen2.5, and Qwen3.5-27B. We further show that SWD remains effective for full-model replacement of all attention and MLP weight matrices after fine-tuning the nonzero factor values. Finally, SWD also features a zero-data variant, allowing broader use of mechanistic interpretability analysis (e.g., per-step analysis).
summary:
**Central idea**

Sparse Weight Decomposition (SWD) approximates pretrained linear projections with two sparse factors. Each intermediate scalar defines an independently addressable rank-one path with sparse read/write connections. An activation-weighted Double Sparse Factorization solver fits these paths; positive gradient-times-activation task attribution ranks them for ablation. The construction does not require monosemantic or sparsely activated units.

**Experiments**

Single-matrix tests replace GPT-2 Small’s layer-8 MLP output projection, middle-layer down-projections in Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B/3B, and Qwen3.5-27B’s layer-31 down-projection. FineWeb-Edu supplies fitting data and disjoint fidelity evaluation. Baselines include Transcoders and reconstruction-trained VPD; GPT-2 controls include exact SVD and random orthogonal factorizations. Circuit tests use IOI, docstring, and gendered pronouns, plus Greater-than for GPT-2. IOI and docstring each have 600 training and 200 test examples. Sufficiency measures retained mean answer–distractor margin relative to the unpruned replacement; necessity measures its signed, unnormalized margin decrease after selected-unit ablation. Costs count selected units and their nonzero read/write weights. Further tests cover whole-MLP and all-48-matrix GPT-2 replacement, weight-only factorization, selected edits, attention interventions, and nonlinear interactions.

**Key results**

GPT-2 single-matrix SWD uses 16,384 calibration tokens versus 2.048M Transcoder or 4.19M reconstruction-VPD optimizer-consumed tokens at closely matched CE. Reported single-matrix circuit results favor SWD, particularly on edge cost; the GPT-2 advantage persists under zero ablation. Exact dense controls also require more edges, although their unit counts are competitive in some regions. Full-model fixed-support fine-tuning reduces CE from 3.90 to 3.44 at approximately 26.77M transformer-body nonzeros, using 4.19M calibration tokens plus 16.38M fine-tuning token presentations. Separately sparse-pretrained references reach CE about 3.45 after 2.884B presentations. Weight-only SWD achieves docstring sufficiency 0.962 with three units at sparsity 0.375. Whole-MLP results are more mixed: standard Transcoders remain competitive in several sufficiency and unit-count comparisons.

**Limitations / open questions**

Matching average CE does not establish equal task behavior or preservation of dense-model mechanisms. Qwen3.5 TC48k and VPD references exceed the stated 0.001 CE tolerance relative to primary SWD. Token comparisons exclude circuit-task data and inherited dense pretraining and do not establish compute savings. Full-model candidate surfaces differ between methods. Decompositions are non-unique, qualitative examples are selected, and nonlinear interactions remain. Full-model replacement is tested only on GPT-2. Plot images are unavailable in the supplied rendering; numerical claims here rely on explicit text or tables.

title: Geometry-Adaptive Explainer for Faithful Dictionary-Based Interpretability under Distribution Shift
abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to explain a model's behavior by identifying causally responsible internal structures. Dictionary-based explainers such as sparse autoencoders and transcoders are a primary tool, but their faithfulness under out-of-distribution (OOD) shift has received little systematic attention. We show that distribution shift rotates the subspace that the model actively uses, misaligning the explainer's dictionary trained on in-distribution (ID) activations. We formalize this misalignment as the faithfulness gap, a geometric distance between the ID dictionary and the OOD-active subspace, and show that it controls OOD faithfulness degradation. To reduce this gap, we propose the Geometry-Adaptive Explainer (GAE), which realigns the explainer's dictionary with the OOD-active subspace while preserving the original feature structure. This requires only unlabeled OOD activations and no gradient updates. We prove that GAE improves over the unadapted ID explainer, with excess loss bounded quadratically by the second-moment shift. Empirically, GAE even matches or surpasses all training-based baselines in causal faithfulness across multiple models and OOD settings.
summary:
**Central idea**

Geometry-Adaptive Explainer (GAE) adapts sparse autoencoders and transcoders by freezing their encoders, aligning truncated decoder dictionaries to leading OOD second-moment eigenspaces through orthogonal Procrustes, and optionally applying regularized decoder regression. The proposed “faithfulness gap” is the Frobenius distance between decoder and activation projectors. A supplied spectral derivation bounds excess rank-r projection error by constants times squared projector distance; its connection to native mechanistic faithfulness remains an assumption.

**Experiments**

Controlled experiments use a ReLU MLP with 128 input and 256 hidden dimensions under covariance shifts. Language-model experiments examine GPT-2 Small layer 8 and Pythia-1.4B layer 15, with 24,576- and 65,536-feature dictionaries trained on OpenWebText and The Pile. OOD datasets are FineWeb, EDGAR filings, and HaluEval. Baselines include Fixed, TERM, Finetune, Retrain, SAEBoost, and FaithfulSAE. Evaluation uses 1,000 prompts per setting and seed 2026. Last-token normalized comprehensiveness removes 32 features; normalized AOPC averages eight budgets from 1–128. Both exclude examples with full-versus-empty reconstruction logit range below 0.1; retained counts are unspecified. Absolute replacement ΔCE measures predictive-loss preservation.

**Key results**

GAE leads all nine metric columns for each GPT-2 explainer. Pythia exceptions include transcoder FineWeb replacement loss, SAE FineWeb comprehensiveness, and SAE EDGAR AOPC. GPT-2 HaluEval transcoders attain nComp 0.963 versus SAEBoost’s 0.921 and absolute ΔCE 0.0014 versus 0.0212. Reported adaptation takes 0.5 seconds for GPT-2 and 2.9 seconds for Pythia; decoder-refit configurations use 2,048 fit activations. Crucially, rotation alone closes the measured gap but lowers nComp from approximately 0.74 to 0.44; refitting restores approximately 0.96 while reintroducing a gap. Selected attribution examples and held-out ID evaluations also improve their reported metrics.

**Limitations / open questions**

Only two language models and one layer each are evaluated, without repeated-seed uncertainty. Hyperparameters are selected per setting using held-out nComp and ΔCE; several SAE configurations use rotation alone. Neither these metrics nor decoder proximity establish preserved feature semantics. The improvement proof establishes an exact-projector result, requiring exact OOD eigenspace recovery; it does not cover approximate estimation or the practical refitted decoder. Proposition 1’s perturbation argument fails to handle eigenvalue crossings, leaving its stated general bound and dependent quadratic-shift bound unestablished. Rank truncation discards decoder information, real-model ID alignment is weak especially for SAEs, and the printed toy covariance construction contains dimensional and symmetry ambiguities.

title: Intrinsically Interpretable Attention via Sparse Post-Training
abstract: We introduce a simple post-training method that makes transformer attention sparse without sacrificing performance. Applying a flexible sparsity regularisation under a constrained-loss objective, we show on models up to 7B parameters that it is possible to retain the original pretraining loss while reducing attention connectivity to $\approx 0.4 \%$ of its edges. Unlike sparse-attention methods designed for computational efficiency, our approach leverages sparsity as a structural prior: it preserves capability while exposing a more organized and interpretable connectivity pattern. We find that this local sparsity cascades into global circuit simplification: task-specific circuits involve far fewer components (attention heads and MLPs) with up to 100x fewer edges connecting them. Additionally, using cross-layer transcoders, we show that sparse attention substantially simplifies attention attribution, enabling a unified view of feature-based and circuit-based perspectives. These results demonstrate that transformer attention can be made orders of magnitude sparser, suggesting that much of its computation is redundant and that sparsity may serve as a guiding principle for more structured and interpretable models.
summary:
**Central idea**

Sparse post-training aims to reorganize pretrained transformer computation into pathways that are easier to inspect. Adapting SPARTAN, sampled binary gates multiply ordinary softmax attention weights without renormalization. GECO-style optimization minimizes expected gate count subject to a next-token cross-entropy target; an auxiliary distillation loss is reported to improve stability. Preserving the dense model’s original mechanisms is explicitly not the objective.

**Experiments**

GPT-2, with 124M parameters, receives full fine-tuning on OpenWebText at context length 64; OLMo-7B receives rank-400 LoRA on Dolma at length 512. Circuit discovery ranks singleton corrupted-activation patching effects and searches retained prefixes accounting for 90% of the reported prediction-preference metric. Tests cover copying, GPT-2 IOI and Greater-Than, and longer OLMo IOI and Docstring prompts. Main curves show standard errors across 20 prompts and select whichever zero or mean replacement produces smaller circuits. Separate GPT-2 cross-layer transcoders, with 32-fold expansion and replacement scores above 80%, support ten pruned attribution graphs. A preliminary LLaMA 3.2 1B comparison fine-tunes dense and sparse variants for 5B tokens using 8,192-token contexts.

**Key results**

Reported active attention fractions are 0.22% for GPT-2 and 0.44% for OLMo. Mean validation cross-entropies remain within 0.01 of targets 3.50 and 2.29, versus baseline losses 3.48 and 2.25. Thus, loss preservation allows small degradation. At the 90% circuit threshold, sparse models require 1.4–4.5 times fewer heads and 5.4–97 times fewer attention edges; one GPT-2 copying example uses nine heads versus 61. Across the ten attribution graphs, reaching 90% cumulative component attribution requires on average 16.1 times fewer key–query pairs and 3.4 times fewer heads, with reported analysis time falling from hours to minutes. Preliminary retrieval accuracy is 0.919 versus 0.918 on Needle-in-a-Haystack and 0.922 versus 0.925 on Passkey Retrieval, sparse versus dense. GPT-2 pathway comparisons show only partial correspondence: approximately 40–50% selected-head overlap and 5–10% attention-entry overlap.

**Limitations / open questions**

Compact extracted circuits proxy interpretability without demonstrating human comprehension, global minimality, or complete mechanism recovery. Attribution results condition on frozen nonlinear operations. Long-context evidence is preliminary, and broad capability retention is incompletely quantified in accessible text. Figure-only benchmark scores are unavailable. Greater-Than metric wording mixes logits and probability mass; BOS-sink analysis conflicts on sample count. The source identifies version 5, dated May 25, 2026, and ends within an appendix activation excerpt after the substantive sections.

title: Don't Judge an LLM Only by Its Activations: Discovering Suppressed Safety Features via Counterfactual Activation Potential
abstract: Mechanistic interpretability has emerged as the primary means to understand safety behavior of LLMs. However, existing tools primarily focus on the activating neurons or features of a model. The role of the remaining large set of inactive components is invisible to such methods. This work demonstrates that the inactive set contains safety-critical features that are causally relevant for refusal of harmful prompts. Suppressing such features could turn refusals into compliance, while passing undetected by prevalent interpretability tools. We introduce the Counterfactual Activation Potential (CAP), a metric that quantifies a suppressed feature's latent activation tendency as the product of its encoder alignment (how strongly the input drives it), suppression strength (how strongly active features inhibit it), and safety criticality (how much refusal depends on it). To find suppressed safety features at scale, we propose CAP-guided Safety Feature Discovery (CSFD), a two-stage filtering algorithm that identifies candidate safety features from hundreds of thousands of transcoder features without exhaustive ablation. A significant fraction of trials turn compliant with harmful prompts when a candidate feature is ablated. Under natural jailbreaks, the suppression acting on the highest-CAP features rises 2-4x, and their activation correspondingly falls by up to 80%. Amplifying a feature's suppressors pushes its activation down and raises harmful compliance with prompts related to the suppressed feature, with no such effect for random features. Our experiments span five Gemma, Qwen, and Llama models across various parameter sizes. Our findings indicate that jailbreaks could operate in part by suppressing safety-critical features rather than solely activating harmful ones, and that suppressed features are a necessary complement to activation-focused interpretability of safety behavior.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper investigates refusal-related transcoder features whose activation decreases under jailbreaks. Counterfactual Activation Potential (CAP) multiplies standardized encoder alignment, standardized activation-weighted negative connections, and safety criticality—the fraction of eligible refusals flipped by feature ablation. CSFD filters recorded features by refused-versus-benign activation mass and Cohen’s d, validates candidates through ablation, then ranks validated features with CAP.

**Experiments**

The study evaluates Gemma-2-2B and Llama-3.2-1B base models, plus Gemma-3-4B-IT, Qwen3-1.7B, and Qwen3-8B, using 86,157 WildJailbreak prompts per model. Generation is greedy, capped at 512 new tokens; Gemini 3.0 Flash supplies behavioral labels. Each of 50 candidates per model is ablated on up to 100 harmful-refused prompts where it is active. Further experiments examine successful PAIR rewrites, amplify estimated suppressors, restore individual features, independently repeat discovery on HarmBench, and compare CAP-component logistic probes with raw activations and a difference-in-means projection.

**Key results**

Ablation flips at least one eligible refusal for 47/50 Gemma-2-2B candidates, 42/50 Qwen3-8B, 39/50 Gemma-3-4B-IT, and 50/50 in each remaining model. Maximum CSFD criticality is 82.5%, conditional on initially refused, feature-active prompts. In the ten-feature PAIR panels, increased suppression accompanies decreased activation for 6/10 Qwen3-8B features, 5/10 Gemma-3-4B-IT, and 8/10 Qwen3-1.7B; the largest instruction-model decrease is 80% with fourfold suppression. Suppressor amplification yields a reported 29% flip rate versus 5% for equal-count random active features from the same layers; the table omits its model and trial denominator. Single-feature restoration recovers refusal in 27/182 successful Gemma-2-2B counterfactuals. CAP-component probes attain AUROC 0.788 versus 0.668 for all recorded raw features on Gemma-2-2B, and 0.719 versus 0.421 on Qwen3-8B. Removing prompt-constant criticality inputs leaves reported probe AUROC unchanged. HarmBench discovery recovers overlapping feature sets in three models.

**Limitations / open questions**

Static edges and transcoder interventions are imperfect mechanistic proxies. Amplifying suppressors can affect other pathways; exclusive mediation through the target and absence of harmful-feature activation are untested. PAIR results condition on attack success and selected panels. Discovery uses top-100 activation records, and fully nested discovery/probe evaluation is unclear. Several base-model examples have ambiguous compliance changes. Positive CAP can arise from two below-average components, contradicting the claimed simultaneous-high requirement. Gemma-3’s matched-pair panel omits its globally highest-CAP features listed elsewhere. Broader attack, model-scale, and feature-coverage generalization remains open.

title: LLM Layers Immediately Correct Each Other
abstract: Recent methods in language model interpretability employ techniques such as sparse autoencoders to decompose residual stream contributions into linear, semantically meaningful features. Such methods are commonly interpreted as identifying features that persist in the residual stream and that subsequent layers build upon. We challenge this view by identifying the Transformer Layer Correction Mechanism (TLCM), wherein adjacent transformer layers systematically counteract portions of each other's contributions. TLCM appears in 5 out of 7 major open-source model families and activates across nearly all tokens in diverse texts. We show that TLCM emerges during pretraining, operates most strongly on contextually dependent tokens, and adaptively calibrates its correction strength based on the preceding layer's output. Using the layer Jacobian, we further show that TLCM selectively corrects specific subspaces while reinforcing others, which we interpret through a ``propose-and-reject'' framework in which layers propose candidate features and subsequent layers selectively remove inappropriate ones. This dynamic suggests that the residual stream at any layer contains transient proposals alongside persistent features, helping explain why SAE feature descriptions often have low specificity, why effective model steering requires extreme feature amplification, and why transcoders hold a theoretical advantage over SAEs.
summary:
**Central idea**

The Transformer Layer Correction Mechanism (TLCM) describes adjacent transformer blocks writing opposing residual updates during ordinary inference. The authors interpret this through a proposed process in which layers introduce candidate features and subsequent layers reject inappropriate candidates. This semantic interpretation is explicitly untested; the measurements establish geometric opposition and adaptive intervention responses.

**Experiments**

The survey averages update-vector cosine similarities over approximately 100,000 WikiText tokens across seven model families. Training analysis examines seven checkpoints each from OLMo 7B, OLMo 2 1B, and OLMo 2 7B on one approximately 500-token PyTorch passage. Token analysis uses a reported 79k-token corpus from 100 long-form prompts, retains token types occurring at least 20 times, and reports Llama 3.1 8B Instruct and Gemma 2 2B Instruct results. Context-position analysis covers 2,000 long WikiText documents. Llama interventions replace a preceding update a with (1+α)a. Jacobian analysis compares 50 TLCM and 50 non-TLCM pairs, selecting 50 eigenvectors per pair by squared projection of the preceding update.

**Key results**

Adjacent-update anticorrelation occurs in five surveyed families—Llama 3, OLMo, Mistral, Gemma, and Qwen2—with typical similarities from −0.3 to −0.15, strongest in the first two-thirds of depth. GPT-2 and Phi lack the reported pattern. Anticorrelation develops during OLMo pretraining. With a −0.1 cutoff, Llama newline tokens average 12.41 ± 0.10 SEM corrections across 228 occurrences, versus 7.63 ± 0.23 across 35 occurrences of “sustainability.” Each additional 1,000 context positions corresponds to approximately one additional correction. Both attention–MLP and MLP–MLP interactions contribute. Scaling preceding updates changes subsequent cosine opposition approximately linearly over the initial sweep. Selected symmetric-Jacobian eigenvalues cluster near −1 and +0.5 for TLCM pairs, versus near zero for controls.

**Limitations / open questions**

Geometric opposition does not establish semantic error correction, and token/context associations do not causally isolate contextual dependency. Appendix B establishes a directional-response identity: a symmetric-Jacobian eigenvalue of −1 does not guarantee complete vector cancellation, because perpendicular responses can remain. The notation also inconsistently denotes full-block output versus residual contribution. Local approximation checks use 46 Jacobians and report approximately 5% relative error for small nonzero |α|<0.1. No new SAE-specificity, behavioral steering, or transcoder comparison tests the proposed implications. Token tables include prompt/template tokens despite the response-only description. Code-availability statements conflict. Plot images are unavailable; reported values here come from prose and tables.

Enhancing Neural Network Interpretability with Feature-Aligned Sparse Autoencoders
abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have shown promise in improving the interpretability of neural network activations, but can learn features that are not features of the input, limiting their effectiveness. We propose \textsc{Mutual Feature Regularization} \textbf{(MFR)}, a regularization technique for improving feature learning by encouraging SAEs trained in parallel to learn similar features. We motivate \textsc{MFR} by showing that features learned by multiple SAEs are more likely to correlate with features of the input. By training on synthetic data with known features of the input, we show that \textsc{MFR} can help SAEs learn those features, as we can directly compare the features learned by the SAE with the input features for the synthetic data. We then scale \textsc{MFR} to SAEs that are trained to denoise electroencephalography (EEG) data and SAEs that are trained to reconstruct GPT-2 Small activations. We show that \textsc{MFR} can improve the reconstruction loss of SAEs by up to 21.21\% on GPT-2 Small, and 6.67\% on EEG data. Our results suggest that the similarity between features learned by different SAEs can be leveraged to improve SAE training, thereby enhancing performance and the usefulness of SAEs for model interpretability.
summary:
**Central idea**

Mutual Feature Regularization (MFR) encourages parallel sparse autoencoders to learn similar dictionary directions. It combines inactivity-triggered whole-SAE reinitialization with an auxiliary mean maximum cosine similarity penalty. Experiments use TopK encoders and tied encoder–decoder weights. Synthetic analysis uses Hungarian assignment; the training penalty uses nearest-neighbor matches without a bijection constraint.

**Experiments**

The synthetic setup reports 512 Gaussian generating directions in 256 dimensions, grouped coactivation, unequal frequencies, 512 SAE latents, TopK k=36, and 100 million unique examples, with two SAEs trained together. Its generator specification is inconsistent: selecting three features from one group conflicts with the subsequently stated 36 active features, and 512 features cannot form 12 equal-sized groups.

GPT-2 Small experiments compare five baseline and five jointly regularized 3,072-latent SAEs on layer-0 MLP outputs, trained for two million tokens at k={6,12,18,24,30}. Replacement cross-entropy uses 10,000 randomly selected sequences described as OpenWebText/OpenWebText2. EEG experiments use filtered, vectorized TUH EEG data, 4,096 latents, 3.5 million training units called tokens, and k={12,24,36,48,60}.

**Key results**

Synthetic cross-SAE direction similarity correlates with generating-direction similarity at 0.625, increasing to 0.668 after conditional reinitialization. The text reports improved generating-dictionary alignment with MFR. A caption reports a 2.4% final reconstruction-loss difference between reinitialization-only and penalty-plus-reinitialization conditions, without specifying its direction.

GPT-2 reconstruction improves at k=6,12,18 and worsens at k=24,30. At k=6, losses are 0.00160 baseline versus 0.00132 MFR: the reported 21.21% improvement is consistent with an MFR-loss denominator; the rounded values imply a 17.5% baseline-relative reduction. Replacement cross-entropy decreases at all five budgets by 3.51–8.58%, averaging 5.45%, but remains 9.367–10.136 versus 3.12 unmodified. EEG reconstruction improves at three smaller budgets and worsens at two larger budgets; the reported best improvement is 6.67%, from 0.32 to 0.30, likewise consistent with an MFR-loss denominator.

**Limitations / open questions**

Natural-data semantic recovery and human interpretability are not directly tested. EEG reconstruction lacks a separate clean-signal denoising benchmark. Seed uncertainty is unreported; real-data sections detail the alignment penalty without specifying their reinitialization protocol. Joint training increases compute. Plot values unavailable in the text cannot establish additional effect sizes; figure references and some captions are inconsistent.

Attention Slipping: A Mechanistic Understanding of Jailbreak Attacks and Defenses in LLMs
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become more integral to society and technology, ensuring their safety becomes essential. Jailbreak attacks exploit vulnerabilities to bypass safety guardrails, posing a significant threat. However, the mechanisms enabling these attacks are not well understood. In this paper, we reveal a universal phenomenon that occurs during jailbreak attacks: Attention Slipping. During this phenomenon, the model gradually reduces the attention it allocates to unsafe requests in a user query during the attack process, ultimately causing a jailbreak. We show Attention Slipping is consistent across various jailbreak methods, including gradient-based token replacement, prompt-level template refinement, and in-context learning. Additionally, we evaluate two defenses based on query perturbation, Token Highlighter and SmoothLLM, and find they indirectly mitigate Attention Slipping, with their effectiveness positively correlated with the degree of mitigation achieved. Inspired by this finding, we propose Attention Sharpening, a new defense that directly counters Attention Slipping by sharpening the attention score distribution using temperature scaling. Experiments on four leading LLMs (Gemma2-9B-It, Llama3.1-8B-It, Qwen2.5-7B-It, Mistral-7B-It v0.2) show that our method effectively resists various jailbreak attacks while maintaining performance on benign tasks on AlpacaEval. Importantly, Attention Sharpening introduces no additional computational or memory overhead, making it an efficient and practical solution for real-world deployment.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper calls declining attention from the final prompt position to a harmful-request segment “Attention Slipping.” Its attention rate divides each head’s attention mass on that segment by its mass without jailbreak context. Attention Sharpening lowers attention softmax temperature, intending to redistribute input-directed attention while preserving its total mass. The proposed causal explanation remains stronger than the measurements establish.

**Experiments**

Experiments use Gemma-2-9B-it, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 with 100 AdvBench harmful behaviors. GCG uses 60-token suffixes and 2,000 optimization steps. Synthetic reverse paths replace proportions of GCG, AutoDAN, or MSJ context with “x”; MSJ uses at most eight demonstrations. Perturbation-defense sweeps measure attention rates and attack success rate (ASR). The main defense benchmark aggregates previously successful GCG, AutoDAN, PAIR, and MSJ prompts; its retained prompt count and attack-family composition are unspecified. ASR uses HarmBench response-classifier judgments. Utility uses 805 AlpacaEval instructions, GPT-4 judgments, and text-davinci-003 as reference. Adaptive GCG is evaluated separately.

**Key results**

The text reports Gemma’s median attention rate falling approximately from 0.8 to 0.3 during GCG optimization. Along the synthetic paths, retaining more optimized context accompanies higher ASR and lower attention rates. Stronger perturbation defenses reportedly reverse both trends. On the successful-prompt benchmark, mean ASR is 1.00 without defense, 0.51 with sharpening, 0.48 with Token Highlighter, and 0.29 with SmoothLLM. Corresponding mean AlpacaEval win rates are 83.15%, 80.72%, 82.91%, and 66.06%. Adaptive GCG mean ASR decreases from 0.42 at temperature 1.0 to 0.34 at 0.4 and 0.23 at 0.2. Efficiency conclusions use pass counts and simplified memory formulas.

**Limitations / open questions**

Aggregate attention trends and global temperature interventions do not establish universality or isolate attention restoration as the causal mediator of refusal. Placeholder masking is not an actual attack trajectory. Sharpening retains substantial attack success and trades safety against utility; baseline ASRs are only approximately matched. Selected per-model temperatures, uncertainty estimates, and measured latency or peak-memory benchmarks are absent. The sharpening equation inconsistently reuses notation defined as unnormalized logits, and its intuition describes harmful responses as neutralizing attacks. Plots are unavailable in this text rendering, so numerical findings above rely on prose and tables. Adaptive evidence covers a finite GCG evaluation, not a robustness proof.

title: Position: Mechanistic Interpretability Should Prioritize Feature Consistency in SAEs
abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are a prominent tool in mechanistic interpretability (MI) for decomposing neural network activations into interpretable features. However, the aspiration to identify a canonical set of features is challenged by the observed inconsistency of learned SAE features across different training runs, undermining the reliability and efficiency of MI research. This position paper argues that mechanistic interpretability should prioritize feature consistency in SAEs -- the reliable convergence to equivalent feature sets across independent runs. We propose using the Pairwise Dictionary Mean Correlation Coefficient (PW-MCC) as a practical metric to operationalize consistency and demonstrate that high levels are achievable (0.80 for TopK SAEs on LLM activations) with appropriate architectural choices. Our contributions include detailing the benefits of prioritizing consistency; providing theoretical grounding and synthetic validation using a model organism, which verifies PW-MCC as a reliable proxy for ground-truth recovery; and extending these findings to real-world LLM data, where high feature consistency strongly correlates with the semantic similarity of learned feature explanations. We call for a community-wide shift towards systematically measuring feature consistency to foster robust cumulative progress in MI.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper argues that SAE evaluation should routinely measure whether independent initializations recover equivalent feature dictionaries. Pairwise Dictionary Mean Correlation Coefficient (PW-MCC) averages absolute decoder-vector cosine similarities under optimal one-to-one Hungarian matching, operationalizing agreement up to permutation and nonzero scaling. Consistency is proposed as a foundation for reproducibility and reusable explanations; those practical benefits are not directly evaluated.

**Experiments**

Synthetic experiments compare learned and generating dictionaries using GT-MCC, averaged over the smaller dictionary’s atom count. The matched benchmark uses eight observation dimensions, 16 generating and learned atoms, three active Gaussian coefficients, 50,000 examples, and five seeds. Additional experiments vary dictionary capacity, clustered feature frequencies, and retained latent count. Seven SAE architectures are trained on 500 million uncopyrighted-Pile tokens: Pythia-160M-deduped layer-8 residual outputs with 16,384 latents and three seeds, and Gemma-2-2B layer-12 outputs with 65,536 latents and two seeds. Configurations are selected for highest final PW-MCC. GPT-4.1 generates explanations from ten strongest activating text segments and judges matched explanations’ resemblance.

**Key results**

Matched synthetic TopK dictionaries achieve approximately 0.97 GT-MCC versus 0.63 for Standard SAEs, with PW-MCC following recovery during training. Excess dictionary capacity produces GT-MCC 0.95 but PW-MCC 0.77; insufficient capacity produces 0.75 and 0.60. Unequal-width GT-MCC does not measure complete dictionary coverage. Clustered Zipfian experiments allocate more matched atoms to frequent clusters, with frequency–consistency associations varying by skew and capacity. The highest selected real-data PW-MCC is TopK’s 0.8181 on Pythia and 0.7898 on Gemma. Pythia’s reported rarest frequency bin contains 127 pairs averaging 0.514 similarity; the most frequent contains 33 averaging 0.964. Explanation-resemblance means increase from 1.71 to 8.28 across the lowest to highest vector-similarity bins, based on 20 judged pairs per bin.

**Limitations / open questions**

Decoder agreement and LLM-rated explanation resemblance do not establish causal equivalence, completeness, atomicity, or canonical feature recovery. Architecture comparisons select different sparsities without matching reconstruction fidelity. The new algebraic proof establishes injectivity conditional on a universal encoder round trip; ordinary reconstruction training is not shown to ensure it. Its reachability corollary requires every real k-sparse code to occur, which a finite dataset cannot supply. Dictionary identifiability additionally relies on a witness-set result adapted from prior work. The source inconsistently specifies signed versus rectified encoders, some synthetic dimensions, and several numerical summaries. Figures are unavailable as images; conclusions here use the supplied prose, tables, and captions. Rare-feature stability, broader equivalence notions, and scalable matching remain open.

title: AbsTopK: Rethinking Sparse Autoencoders For Bidirectional Features
abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as powerful techniques for interpretability of large language models (LLMs), aiming to decompose hidden states into meaningful semantic features. While several SAE variants have been proposed, there remains no principled framework to derive SAEs from the original dictionary learning formulation. In this work, we introduce such a framework by unrolling the proximal gradient method for sparse coding. We show that a single-step update naturally recovers common SAE variants, including ReLU, JumpReLU, and TopK. Through this lens, we reveal a fundamental limitation of existing SAEs: their sparsity-inducing regularizers enforce non-negativity, preventing a single feature from representing bidirectional concepts (e.g., male vs. female). This structural constraint fragments semantic axes into separate, redundant features, limiting representational completeness. To address this issue, we propose AbsTopK SAE, a new variant derived from the $\ell_0$ sparsity constraint that applies hard thresholding over the largest-magnitude activations. By preserving both positive and negative activations, AbsTopK uncovers richer, bidirectional conceptual representations. Comprehensive experiments across four LLMs and seven probing and steering tasks show that AbsTopK improves reconstruction fidelity, enhances interpretability, and enables single features to encode contrasting concepts. Remarkably, AbsTopK matches or even surpasses the Difference-in-Mean method, a supervised approach that requires labeled data for each concept and has been shown in prior work to outperform SAEs.
summary:
**Central idea**

AbsTopK replaces nonnegative SAE activations with signed coefficients selected by magnitude. The authors derive shifted ReLU, JumpReLU, and nonnegative TopK as proximal operators for sparse-coding regularizers. Removing nonnegativity from the cardinality constraint yields signed hard thresholding. Opposite semantic poles can then share one dictionary atom. This architectural correspondence does not guarantee exact sparse inference or recovery of natural concepts.

**Experiments**

The study trains 16× expansion residual-stream SAEs on monology/pile-uncopyrighted for GPT-2 Small, Pythia-70M, Gemma-2-2B, and Qwen3-4B, using 30,000 Adam steps and batch size 4,096. Evaluations cover training MSE, normalized reconstruction error, and zero-ablation-relative cross-entropy recovery. Six downstream categories are tabulated: unlearning, first-letter absorption, spurious correlation removal (SCR), targeted probe perturbation (TPP), RAVEL, and sparse probing. Probing comprises 35 binary tasks with 4,000 training and 1,000 test examples per task. Separate Gemma and Qwen experiments compare safety steering using reported HarmBench scores and MMLU accuracy, including supervised Difference-in-Means (DiM).

**Key results**

The text reports improved reconstruction and loss recovery across most tested configurations; numerical plot values are unavailable in this rendering. Across Table 2's eight model–layer settings and six metrics, AbsTopK exceeds both baselines in 40 of 48 entries, falls below at least one in seven, and ties both in one. SCR and reported TPP improve in every setting; other categories have exceptions. In Qwen3-4B layer 18, safety steering changes HarmBench from 17.0 to 81.3 and MMLU from 77.3 to 75.9; DiM scores 80.6 and 75.8. Across four safety-steering settings, AbsTopK exceeds both conventional SAE baselines on both reported metrics. Against DiM, it ties or slightly improves MMLU, while HarmBench is lower in three settings. Figure 1's caption reports a selected latent with opposite activation signs for man/woman sentence variants.

**Limitations / open questions**

The paper claims seven downstream tasks but enumerates six categories. Table 2 labels a Gemma layer as 14 where the setup specifies 16. Universal outperformance language exceeds the tables. Seeds, uncertainty, safety-steering feature selection, and intervention-strength selection are unspecified. The unlearning requirement that MMLU remain above 0.99 has no explained normalization. The written TPP formula conflicts with its higher-is-better interpretation. Signed-feature handling in the adopted evaluations is insufficiently detailed. Benchmark improvements do not establish semantic completeness, monosemanticity, or fragmentation as the causal explanation for the gains.

Verifying Chain-of-Thought Reasoning via Its Computational Graph
abstract: Current Chain-of-Thought (CoT) verification methods predict reasoning correctness based on outputs (black-box) or activations (gray-box), but offer limited insight into why a computation fails. We introduce a white-box method: Circuit-based Reasoning Verification (CRV). We hypothesize that attribution graphs of correct CoT steps, viewed as execution traces of the model's latent reasoning circuits, possess distinct structural fingerprints from those of incorrect steps. By training a classifier on structural features of these graphs, we show that these traces contain a powerful signal of reasoning errors. Our white-box approach yields novel scientific insights unattainable by other methods. (1) We demonstrate that structural signatures of error are highly predictive, establishing the viability of verifying reasoning directly via its computational graph. (2) We find these signatures to be highly domain-specific, revealing that failures in different reasoning tasks manifest as distinct computational patterns. (3) We provide evidence that these signatures are not merely correlational; by using our analysis to guide targeted interventions on individual transcoder features, we successfully correct the model's faulty reasoning. Our work shows that, by scrutinizing a model's computational process, we can move from simple error detection to a deeper, causal understanding of LLM reasoning.
summary:
**Central idea**
Circuit-based Reasoning Verification (CRV) classifies reasoning-step correctness using statistics of transcoder attribution graphs. Its gradient-boosting classifier combines topology, node activations and influence, layer histograms, and output uncertainty. The authors interpret these graphs as approximate execution traces of latent reasoning circuits; predictive success alone does not establish that interpretation.

**Experiments**
The study uses Llama 3.1 8B Instruct and per-layer TopK transcoders with 131,072 features and k=128, trained on a 10B-token RedPajama-V2 subset. Curated Boolean, arithmetic, and GSM8K datasets contain 126,624, 155,434, and 8,737 steps, with incorrect-label prevalences of 0.2%, 1.2%, and 6.6%. Chains retain steps only through the first error. Synthetic labels require agreement between Llama 3.3 70B Instruct judgments and programmatic evaluation of model-generated simplified expressions; GSM8K uses judge labels. Comparisons cover output scores, Chain-of-Embedding, CoT-Kinetics, and activation probes. Additional tests vary domain, arithmetic difficulty, feature families, classifier, attribution position, and transcoder adaptation data.

**Key results**
Main CRV AUROCs are 75.87%, 92.47%, and 70.17%, exceeding all main-table baselines across the three reported metrics. Arithmetic AUPR is 28.92%, versus 5.59% for Energy; FPR at 95% error recall is 37.09%, versus the best baseline's 63.33%. Arithmetic-trained CRV reaches only 57.04% AUROC on GSM8K; joint-domain training reaches 70.62%, with GSM8K included in training. Removing node statistics reduces arithmetic AUROC to 88.31%; removing topology reduces it to 90.89%. Alternative graph classifiers sometimes outperform gradient boosting. Attribution after a step improves synthetic AUROC but has mixed effects on other metrics. Two selected arithmetic traces are corrected by suppressing or amplifying a multiplication-associated feature.

**Limitations / open questions**
Evidence concerns one model, heavily filtered labels, and substantial false-positive rates. The reported human audit covers synthetic steps: human–judge agreement is 84.1%, κ=0.26; comparable GSM8K validation is absent. GSM8K verifier splitting and synthetic chain grouping are unclear. The main text specifies replacement-model analysis, whereas Appendix A describes original-model generation; their precise relationship is underspecified. Replacement fidelity is not quantified. The interventions demonstrate local behavioral influence without validating aggregate error signatures causally or establishing general repair success. Graph construction is expensive, and image-only plots preclude independently reading their values. Supplied dates conflict: initial metadata says October 2025, the version header February 2026, and an internal date August 2026.
