Unstable Features, Reproducible Subspaces: Understanding Seed Dependence in Sparse Autoencoders
abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are widely used to interpret neural network representations, but their utility depends on whether the learned features are reproducible across training runs. We study this question through \emph{feature stability}: for each SAE feature, we estimate the probability that a similar feature reappears in an independently trained SAE. This yields a scalable per-feature signal that separates stable from unstable features. In a large-scale study across seeds, models, layers, dictionary sizes, and SAE variants, we find a pronounced functional asymmetry: stable features carry most of the reconstruction- and prediction-relevant signal, while unstable features have weak marginal impact and are dominated by low-frequency surface-form triggers in both activation statistics and automatic explanations. Geometrically, unstable features are individually non-reproducible but concentrate in reproducible lower-rank subspaces, suggesting that seed dependence often reflects basis ambiguity within a shared region of activation space rather than pure noise. A controlled synthetic model makes this mechanism explicit, showing that low-rank ground-truth features can be recovered at the subspace level while remaining non-identifiable as individual SAE latents across seeds. Finally, by pooling unique cross-seed features, we construct more stable SAEs while preserving explained variance in this setting. Together, these results show that unstable features are not merely failed or noisy latents: they have weak individual functional impact, but reflect reproducible low-dimensional structure that standard SAEs resolve differently across seeds.
summary:
**Central idea**
Individual SAE decoder directions can vary across initialization seeds while collectively occupying reproducible subspaces. The paper estimates each feature’s cross-run decoder recurrence and compares stable and unstable features through activation statistics, reconstruction interventions, explanations, and geometry. Basis ambiguity is proposed as one possible source of instability.

**Experiments**
The main study trains 96 TopK SAEs on GPT-2 layer-7 residual activations, with 16,384 latents, k=64, and normally one billion FineWeb tokens. Shared data order isolates initialization. Matching requires decoder cosine ≥0.7; stable and unstable endpoints require estimated recurrence ≥0.95 and ≤0.05. Tests include reconstruction EV, next-token cross-entropy after reconstruction replacement, Qwen3-32B SAEBench detection, size-matched decoder effective rank, and cross-seed SVD projection transfer. Additional experiments vary models, layers, widths, architectures, training exposure, reconstruction metrics, and transformer randomization. A synthetic mixture combines 80 generic atoms with 20 atoms in a rank-2 subspace of 32 dimensions. Construction experiments select 16,384 high-recurrence features from deduplicated source dictionaries and tune for approximately two million tokens.

**Key results**
Table 1 reports unstable/stable fractions of 9.8%/52.2% and EV 0.892 for the main TopK configuration. Unstable features activate at 0.18% of positions on average, versus 0.44% for stable features. Masking N stable versus 4N unstable features produces greater reconstruction and prediction degradation for stable masks, including with reconstruction-norm reweighting; this is approximate frequency compensation. Normalized effective rank is 0.587–0.649 for size-matched unstable sets versus 0.804–0.808 for stable sets, and leading subspaces transfer across seeds. Synthetic low-rank features have approximately 0.25 recurrence despite reproducible collective geometry. Among explanations scoring above 0.7, “substring” occurs in 38.9% of the lowest-recurrence bin versus 11.3% of the highest. High-recurrence pooling retains near-baseline EV and improves sparse probing/AutoInterp, while SCR/TPP decline. Mahalanobis reweighting reduces instability at an EV cost. Approximately 8% instability remains after ten billion training tokens.

**Limitations / open questions**
Decoder recurrence does not establish semantic or causal identity. Masking measures aggregate effects within SAE reconstructions, rather than exhaustive behavioral importance. Detection evaluation is activation-enriched and lacks independent semantic validation. Synthetic results establish a possible mechanism, not formal non-identifiability or its prevalence in real models. Pooling uses multiple source runs and source-ensemble recurrence scores. Some evaluation counts and synthetic training details are unspecified; numerical plot curves are unavailable. Table 6 reports different GPT-2 layer-7 endpoint fractions from Table 1 without reconciling the difference.

title: Quantifying Feature Space Universality Across Large Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
abstract: The Universality Hypothesis in large language models (LLMs) claims that different models converge towards similar concept representations in their latent spaces. Providing evidence for this hypothesis would enable researchers to exploit universal properties, facilitating the generalization of mechanistic interpretability techniques across models. Previous works studied if LLMs learned the same features, which are internal representations that activate on specific concepts. Since comparing features across LLMs is challenging due to polysemanticity, in which LLM neurons often correspond to multiple unrelated features rather than to distinct concepts, sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have been employed to disentangle LLM neurons into SAE features corresponding to distinct concepts. In this paper, we introduce a new variation of the universality hypothesis called Analogous Feature Universality: we hypothesize that even if SAEs across different models learn different feature representations, the spaces spanned by SAE features are similar, such that one SAE space is similar to another SAE space under rotation-invariant transformations. Evidence for this hypothesis would imply that interpretability techniques related to latent spaces, such as steering vectors, may be transferred across models via certain transformations. To investigate this hypothesis, we first pair SAE features across different models via activation correlation, and then measure spatial relation similarities between paired features via representational similarity measures, which transform spaces into representations that reveal hidden relational similarities. Our experiments demonstrate high similarities for SAE feature spaces across various LLMs, providing evidence for feature space universality.
summary:
**Central idea**
The paper proposes Analogous Feature Universality: selected SAE feature subsets can share relational geometry across models without identical feature dictionaries. It matches latents by token-level activation correlation, then compares matched decoder vectors using SVCCA and representational similarity analysis (RSA). The comparison concerns feature weights rather than input-example activation geometry.

**Experiments**
Main comparisons cover Pythia-70M/160M, Gemma-1-2B/Gemma-2-2B, Gemma-2-2B/9B, and layer 25 of Llama 3-8B-Instruct/Llama 3.1-8B, using dictionaries with 16,384–65,536 latents. OpenWebText matching uses 30,000 tokens for Pythia, 22,500 for Gemma, and 10,000 for Llama. Default filtering excludes specified punctuation and special-token triggers, requires shared top-token keywords and correlations of at least 0.1, and removes many-to-one mappings. The authors report approximately 10–30% retention for main comparisons, with 7% for Llama. Controls examine shuffled pairings, random subsets, randomized Pythia weights, SAE seeds, widths, training corpora, and matching-data changes.

**Key results**
Middle-layer pairs generally show the highest similarity; layer 0 comparisons are reported as nonsignificant. Gemma-2-2B layer 11 versus Gemma-2-9B layer 21 achieves SVCCA 0.70 versus random-pairing mean 0.009, and RSA 0.195 versus 0.000438; this larger-model control uses ten random runs at one layer pair. For Pythia layers 3/5, 24 emotion-feature pairs achieve SVCCA 0.83 versus shuffled mean 0.15. Semantic results vary: Gemma layers 12/14 countries yield 0.39 versus 0.17 but fail the significance threshold, with p=0.07. Trained-versus-randomized Pythia comparisons show low similarity and retain approximately 1% of pairs. Filtered, separately seeded TinyStories dictionaries achieve SVCCA 0.94, whereas Pythia seed comparisons show much lower same-layer similarity. Width sweeps show no clear trend; matching-data changes produce broadly similar reported patterns.

**Limitations / open questions**
Evidence concerns selected subsets of related, same-tokenizer models and establishes neither complete correspondence nor atomic feature recovery. A control against equally activation-correlated alternative subsets remains future work. SAE training recipes affect visible similarities, and low similarity cannot distinguish absent shared structure from extraction failure. Matching datasets are small; appendix model labels and RSA specifications contain inconsistencies. Figure graphics are unavailable in the supplied rendering, limiting numerical inspection. Functional transfer of steering directions or circuits is proposed but untested.

title: The Hungarian method for the assignment problem
Clustering to minimize the maximum intercluster distance
Training Large Language Models to Reason in a Continuous Latent Space
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are typically constrained to reason in the language space, where they express the reasoning process through a chain-of-thought (CoT) to solve complex problems. However, the language space may not always be optimal for reasoning. Most word tokens primarily ensure textual coherence and are not essential for reasoning, while some critical tokens require complex planning and pose challenges to LLMs. To explore the potential of reasoning beyond language, we introduce a new paradigm called Coconut (Chain of Continuous Thought). Coconut utilizes the last hidden state of the LLM as a representation of the reasoning state, termed "continuous thought." Instead of decoding this state into words, we feed it back to the model as the next input embedding directly in the continuous space. This latent reasoning paradigm enables an advanced reasoning pattern, where continuous thoughts can encode multiple alternative next steps, allowing the model to perform a breadth-first search (BFS) rather than committing prematurely to a single deterministic path as in CoT. Coconut outperforms CoT on logical reasoning tasks that require substantial search during planning and achieves a better trade-off between accuracy and efficiency.

title: CODI: Compressing chain-of-thought into continuous space via self-distillation
SIM-CoT: Supervised implicit chain-of-thought
Are latent reasoning models easily interpretable?
Do Latent Tokens Think? A Causal and Adversarial Analysis of Chain-of-Continuous-Thought
abstract: Latent tokens are gaining attention for enhancing reasoning in large language models (LLMs), yet their internal mechanisms remain unclear. This paper examines the problem from a reliability perspective, uncovering fundamental weaknesses: latent tokens function as uninterpretable placeholders rather than encoding faithful reasoning. While resistant to perturbation, they promote shortcut usage over genuine reasoning. We focus on Chain-of-Continuous-Thought (COCONUT), which claims better efficiency and stability than explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) while maintaining performance. We investigate this through two complementary approaches. First, steering experiments perturb specific token subsets, namely COCONUT and explicit CoT. Unlike CoT tokens, COCONUT tokens show minimal sensitivity to steering and lack reasoning-critical information. Second, shortcut experiments evaluate models under biased and out-of-distribution settings. Results on MMLU and HotpotQA demonstrate that COCONUT consistently exploits dataset artifacts, inflating benchmark performance without true reasoning. These findings reposition COCONUT as a pseudo-reasoning mechanism: it generates plausible traces that conceal shortcut dependence rather than faithfully representing reasoning processes.
summary:
**Central idea**
The paper tests COCONUT’s sensitivity to interventions and dependence on constructed shortcuts. Its experiments demonstrate recipe-specific behavioral sensitivity and distribution-shift failures; the stronger interpretation that latent tokens lack reasoning remains unresolved.

**Experiments**
LLaMA 3 8B Instruct, LLaMA 2 7B Chat, Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct, and an inconsistently identified Falcon checkpoint receive six epochs of ProntoQA fine-tuning. Probe-directed interventions target five continuous latent tokens, explicit CoT tokens, or all generated tokens. GPT-4o judges intended output changes on AdvBench and cheerful-persona expression on PersonalityEdit. Appendix D allocates 420 AdvBench examples to output evaluation. LLaMA 3 additionally undergoes reasoning-token swaps across 1,000 MMLU test examples. Shortcut experiments fine-tune LLaMA 3 on MMLU with approximately 75% correct training answers positioned at C, or HotpotQA with answer-associated descriptive passages; HotpotQA evaluation uses 3,000 validation examples.

**Key results**
AdvBench CoT-only intervention success is 50.00%, 57.92%, 11.87%, and 11.92% across the four models, versus latent-only success of 5.00%, 0%, 9.62%, and 0%. Persona results likewise show larger changes under CoT interventions. MMLU swaps leave COCONUT accuracy approximately unchanged, 60.9% to 61.0%, while changing 17.9% of answers; CoT accuracy falls from 62.8% to 43.4%, with 52.8% answer inconsistency. Under biased MMLU training, approximately 70% of incorrect predictions choose C, versus approximately 30% under original training. Shortcut-trained HotpotQA accuracy approaches 100% with correct-answer cues, falls to 13% without cues, and approaches zero with incorrect-answer cues. Training without shortcuts yields slightly above 60% across these conditions. Appendix F reports higher output perplexity for COCONUT in three models, but slightly lower perplexity for LLaMA 2.

**Limitations / open questions**
Weak intervention effects do not establish absence of reasoning content or natural causal use. Intervention magnitudes, swapped tensors, recomputation details, and uncertainty estimates are insufficiently specified; explicit and latent conditions also differ in prompts and token budgets. Additional training coincides with latent introduction, preventing attribution of shortcut acquisition specifically to latent tokens. Complete comparisons with separately trained explicit-CoT and standard baselines are not reported. Context placement and answer exposure are unclear. PCA separation from vocabulary embeddings does not establish semantic emptiness, and perplexity scoring is unspecified. The source contains reversed CoT/COCONUT interpretations, inconsistent steering-direction descriptions and Falcon identities, and mismatched bibliography entries. The authors acknowledge that neither the causal connection to reasoning quality nor the mechanism of shortcut dependence is established.

title: The illusion of superposition? a principled analysis of latent thinking in language models
Observable Patterns Are Not Explanations: A Causal-Geometric Analysis of Latent Reasoning Models
abstract: Latent reasoning models (LRMs) replace explicit chain-of-thought with continuous thoughts. Recent work treats observable latent-state patterns, such as BFS-like frontiers and decodable arithmetic computation, as evidence for internal reasoning mechanisms. Evaluating two LRMs (Coconut and CODI) against controls lacking the proposed recurrence or curriculum, we find these patterns also appear in the controls and do not always causally affect behavior. Causal interventions reveal that latent-thought utilization is not binary but graded, scaling with a thought's causal effect on model behavior. Geometric analyses reveal this effect concentrates in low-rank directions whose step-to-step geometry grows more structured as their behavioral influence increases. Latent thoughts should therefore be treated as hidden computation, not hidden explanation: decodability, attention, or static structure alone cannot establish mechanism. LRM interpretability thus requires matched controls and causal tests.
summary:
**Central idea**

Readable latent-state patterns do not uniquely identify reasoning mechanisms. The paper advocates testing behavioral dependence and localizing intervention-sensitive directions before interpreting latent geometry. Deletion dependence, activation-restoration recovery, and sensitivity to amplification provide distinct evidence.

**Experiments**

Models share a pretrained GPT-2 small backbone with 124M parameters. Coconut, CODI, Pause-as-thought (PaT), and curriculum-perturbed Coconut-u use six thought positions. PaT replaces recurrent feedback with learned embeddings; Coconut-u samples alternative curriculum stages on 30% of updates. Base and explicit-CoT models provide observational controls. CODI uses rank-128 LoRA; the other trained models are fully fine-tuned. Evaluation uses 500 ProsQA graph-hopping and 1,319 GSM8k arithmetic test instances, with arithmetic training on GSM8K-Aug. Tests cover frontier probabilities and entropy, logit-lens intermediate decoding, thought deletion, partner-prompt activation restoration, gradient-subspace interventions, transition-prediction R², principal-angle similarity, and variance-component interventions.

**Key results**

PaT reproduces Coconut’s BFS-like frontier signature without recurrent feedback; curriculum perturbation changes its progression despite preserving recurrence. Graph aggregates require at least two frontier candidates, leaving 461, 461, 486, 439, and 182 instances at probing steps 0–4. PaT’s pooled arithmetic intermediate hit rate is 62.1%, versus CODI’s 41.5%; ordered step alignment declines sharply.

Deleting thoughts changes Coconut’s ProsQA accuracy from 98.0% to 97.8%, but its GSM8k accuracy from 35.7% to 7.7%. Coconut-u instead improves on GSM8k, from 30.8% to 39.1%. Joint thought restoration recovers more clean arithmetic output behavior than individual-position restoration. Gradient-subspace ablation reduces Coconut’s arithmetic accuracy to 9.2%, versus 34.6% under rank-matched random ablation. At the appendix’s 95% gradient-energy threshold, mean ranks span 11.8–32.8 on ProsQA and 36.2–141.6 on arithmetic within 768-dimensional states. Projected trajectories can change despite nearly static full states; geometric patterns vary by task and recipe.

**Limitations / open questions**

Intervention sensitivity does not establish ordinary causal mediation, a unique mechanism, or genuine reasoning. Coverage is limited to one small backbone, two tasks, short chains, and trained checkpoints; gradient-basis estimation/evaluation separation is unclear. Reporting conflicts include 99% versus 95% gradient-energy thresholds, differing CODI deletion results, and graph CODI transition results contradicting the claimed identity-baseline advantage. Amplification-table denominators and paired counts are inconsistent or unclear. Several plots lack numerical text; conclusions use accompanying prose and tables. Monitoring, compression, larger-model transfer, and training-time emergence remain untested.

title: Dynamics within latent chain-of-thought: An empirical study of causal structure
Think before you speak: Training language models with pause tokens
Let's Think Dot by Dot: Hidden Computation in Transformer Language Models
abstract: Chain-of-thought responses from language models improve performance across most benchmarks. However, it remains unclear to what extent these performance gains can be attributed to human-like task decomposition or simply the greater computation that additional tokens allow. We show that transformers can use meaningless filler tokens (e.g., '......') in place of a chain of thought to solve two hard algorithmic tasks they could not solve when responding without intermediate tokens. However, we find empirically that learning to use filler tokens is difficult and requires specific, dense supervision to converge. We also provide a theoretical characterization of the class of problems where filler tokens are useful in terms of the quantifier depth of a first-order formula. For problems satisfying this characterization, chain-of-thought tokens need not provide information about the intermediate computational steps involved in multi-token computations. In summary, our results show that additional tokens can provide computational benefits independent of token choice. The fact that intermediate tokens can act as filler tokens raises concerns about large language models engaging in unauditable, hidden computations that are increasingly detached from the observed chain-of-thought tokens.

title: Explainable chain-of-thought reasoning: An empirical analysis on state-aware reasoning dynamics
Global identifiability of overcomplete dictionary learning via l1 and volume minimization
Independent component analysis: algorithms and applications
Sparse Autoencoders for Mechanistic Interpretability in NLP: A Critical Survey of Recoverability, Interpretability, and Utility
abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising approach to mechanistic interpretability by decomposing language-model activations into sparse, potentially interpretable features. However, differences in design assumptions, evaluation objectives, and experimental settings complicate conclusions about their effectiveness. We present a critical survey of 138 studies on SAEs in natural language processing. Our contributions are fourfold: (1) we propose a task-grounded taxonomy connecting dictionary design, feature operations, and NLP functions; (2) we examine how sparsity allocation, geometry, data coverage, and inference affect feature recoverability; (3) we assess evidence for semantic interpretability, mechanistic faithfulness, and behavioral utility; and (4) we synthesize findings across multilingual processing, retrieval, reasoning, classification, and behavioral regulation, highlighting the roles of objectives, baselines, supervision, and intervention pipelines. Through comparative analyses of published results, we reconcile apparent disagreements, identify unresolved questions, and propose directions for more rigorous evaluation. An anonymous research register https://anonymous.4open.science/r/sae-research-register-C331/register.html accompanies the survey.
summary:
**Central idea**

This critical survey distinguishes recovery of specified latent structure, semantic interpretability, faithfulness to the original model’s computation, and behavioral utility. Its taxonomy records dictionary design, feature operation, and NLP function alongside model, activation site, supervision, selection, and intervention details. Predictive or control utility alone does not identify a naturally used mechanism.

**Experiments**

The authors perform literature coding and descriptive secondary analyses, with no new model experiments. From 199 records, merging five duplicate or overlapping version pairs leaves 194 candidates; 138 studies are included, with a cutoff of 12 October 2026. Numerical analyses replot published results and subtract scores. Appendix D additionally derives a three-coordinate counterexample in which projection patching reproduces a donor output through a dormant route while leaving the natural causal coordinate unchanged.

**Key results**

Recoverability has distinct bottlenecks involving representation geometry, sparse allocation, training coverage, and inference. Reconstruction does not establish semantic recovery. A cited synthetic comparison uses 128 generating features in 42 dimensions and an 8,192-unit SAE: GBA recovers 100% versus 3.9% of generating features at alignment threshold 0.9 when target-frequency coverage includes versus excludes their uniform marginal frequency. These are prior synthetic results, not new NLP measurements.

The secondary analyses illustrate protocol dependence. Published Gemma-2-2B SST-2 circuit-amplification results yield three-run mean F1 gains of 37.19, 14.99, 6.28, and 2.96 percentage points across four prompts, using first-output-token classification and validation-calibrated strength. Published CLaS-Bench scores average over 32 languages in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct: residual and SAE difference-in-means achieve 84.5 and 42.3 on the combined language-fidelity/relevance score. Selected layers differ, and the SAE edit retains reconstruction error, so the gap does not isolate dictionary quality or simple reconstruction damage. Classification comparisons depend on dense-probe pooling; RAG repair and safety-control comparisons also depend on supervision, selection populations, and controllers.

**Limitations / open questions**

The selected contrasts are illustrative rather than a representative meta-analysis, and extracted means lack dispersion. Source discrepancies remain unresolved for CLaS-Bench steering strength and LatDefuse’s Llama identity. The proposed evidence rubric is not independently validated. Recommended comparisons test discourse structure against lexical persistence, whether feature matching predicts intervention transfer, and dictionary effects crossed with selection rules and controllers. The external register’s additional records are outside the supplied text.

title: Sparse Transformer: a Controlled Testbed for Mechanistic Interpretability
abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to decompose neural network computations into human-understandable features, yet progress is limited by the absence of ground-truth units to evaluate against. We address this with a Sparse Transformer (ST): a 5-layer language model trained on TinyStories whose wide, TopK-sparse MLP forces neuron specialization. We show that ST neurons are highly interpretable: they outperform a loss-matched dense transformer by 43% on AutoInterp, and circuits of a median of 12 neurons suffice to reproduce individual model predictions. This testbed allows us to directly compare feature learning methods: Transcoder, which approximates the MLP input-output mapping, recovers ST's neuron vectors with 52.6% higher cosine similarity than Sparse Autoencoder, which only reconstructs outputs. Furthermore, the ST enables a controlled study of polysemanticity: distilling its sparse MLP into a dense counterpart reveals how compression leads to feature superposition. These results show how a known reference basis sharpens evaluation and understanding, a role we hope the ST can serve for the field.
summary:
**Central idea**

Sparse Transformer (ST) uses wide, TopK-gated MLPs to make native neurons an operational reference for feature discovery in a natural-language model. Known weights and sparse coefficients supply a structural reference dictionary; semantic interpretability requires separate evaluation.

**Experiments**

The authors train 35 TinyStories transformers spanning width multipliers M∈{1,2,4,8,16,32,64} and K∈{8,16,32,64,None}. Models have five layers, residual width 256, eight attention heads, and approximately 4.9B training tokens. The primary ST has 8,192 neurons per MLP, K=8, and validation loss 1.466. Evaluations include GPT-4o-mini AutoInterp on 100 randomly sampled neurons per evaluated model, dashboards for 20 ST neurons, and beam-search MLP-neuron circuits for 16 high-confidence narrative prompts. Layer-2 experiments compare 8,192-feature SAEs and transcoders across five sparsity configurations with three seeds each. A separate 1,024-neuron dense student learns the sparse teacher's layer-2 MLP mapping for 50,000 MSE-only steps.

**Key results**

ST's AutoInterp accuracy is 0.866 versus 0.605 for a loss-matched dense model and 0.667 for a width-matched dense model. Fifteen of 16 selected prompts reach target-probability faithfulness F≥0.95 within 50 neurons; median threshold-reaching size is 12 among those 15 successes. At 20 neurons, 14/16 satisfy F≥0.95 and 11/16 satisfy circuit-ablation ratio C≤0.2.

Table 3 reports transcoder NMSE 0.0094 versus SAE 0.0358 and native-value mean-max cosine similarity 0.709 versus 0.464. Transcoders retain both advantages across all five configurations. The main text reports slightly different comparison values and a 52.6% relative similarity improvement. The dense student achieves NMSE 0.078. Conditional activation mappings place 80% of teacher-to-student mass on roughly 20 student neurons and reverse mass on roughly 150 teacher neurons. Student keys and values align around 0.60 with weighted teacher mixtures versus approximately 0.15 after shuffling. High-PMI teacher pairs have more overlapping student mappings. The width–sparsity loss fit reports R²=0.944.

**Limitations / open questions**

Evidence concerns small narrative models, chiefly one layer of one primary checkpoint; architecture-grid runs share one seed. AutoInterp, nearest-direction matching, and conditional coactivation do not establish exhaustive monosemanticity, unique recovery, or causal feature membership. Circuit metrics concern one target probability while attention remains available, and redundant support persists. Larger-model transfer is untested. Dense K=None handling in the power-law fit is unspecified. TopK after ReLU guarantees at most K nonzero activations without an additional positivity condition. Plots and dashboards are available here only through textual descriptions and captions.

title: The Sharp Directions Are Against You: Curvature Analysis of Activation Steering
abstract: Activation steering adds a vector to a language model's internal representations at inference time. It is a lightweight alternative to fine-tuning for behavioral control. The standard construction, contrastive activation addition (CAA), is fragile, as on many inputs it shifts behavior in the wrong direction. To explain this fragility, we first study the geometry of the steering vector. We introduce steering Hessian, the matrix of second order derivative of the model's behavioral loss with respect to the steering vector. It captures the output behavior response sensitivity of the model under small perturbations of the steering vector along each direction. Its top eigenvectors are sharp directions: tiny perturbations along them can cause large, erratic, input-dependent behavioral swings. Bottom eigenvectors are flat directions: behavior is robust along them. Removing the sharp component of a steering vector approximately preserves its direction and magnitude (cosine > 0.974, norm reduction < 3% for typical settings) while reducing the vector's directional curvature by up to 12x (median 4x across 36 conditions). We evaluate on three model families (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B), with four behavioral tasks, and 36 token-level conditions. Steering along sharp directions reverses the intended behavior in every condition tested, with anti-steer rates of 53-100%. Sharp directions account for only 1-5% of the CAA vector's squared norm. However, they drive a disproportionate share of the gap between the steered and unsteered next-token distributions during autoregressive generation. We term this one-line correction as sharp removal; it outperforms standard CAA in open-ended generation across all 25 conditions tested. A jailbreaking experiment further shows that sharp directions act as noise rather than signal: they disrupt coherent behavioral control regardless of steering polarity.
summary:
**Central idea**
The paper introduces the steering Hessian: curvature of expected first-response-token cross-entropy with respect to an injected activation vector. Its proposed correction subtracts a CAA vector's projection onto estimated Hessian modes with the largest absolute eigenvalues. Formal derivations establish a composite-loss Hessian decomposition, exact projection geometry, a local loss-change bound, and a bound on the cleaned vector's normalized quadratic curvature.

**Experiments**
Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 are evaluated on sentiment, honest disagreement, respectful responding, and refusal. Each task uses 20 contrastive pairs, 12 Hessian-estimation prompts, and 100 evaluation prompts, with disjoint sets. Three layers per model and task yield 36 token-level conditions, each evaluated over ten steering strengths. Estimation uses 40 Lanczos iterations and default removal dimension 15. Generation covers 25 configurations across sentiment, sycophancy, and refusal, using 50 greedy completions per condition and task-specific classifiers. Controls examine PCA, removal dimension, alternative objectives, XSTest, and negative-polarity refusal steering.

**Key results**
Estimated spectral ratios range from 50 to 3,727. Renormalized sharp projections produce negative target-minus-antitarget token margins on 53–100% of evaluations, averaged over strengths, in every token-level condition. Sharp removal improves the reported generation metric over CAA in 25/25 conditions; the ordering persists in 10/10 sycophancy conditions with 200 completions each. Selected refusal configurations reach 88–98% for Qwen and 74–76% for Llama. Reported sharp energy is typically approximately 1–5%; removal reduces a selected Llama rollout KL trajectory by approximately 3–4 times. Negative cleaned vectors also increase judged non-refusal relative to negative CAA in two settings.

**Limitations / open questions**
The token “anti-steer” metric does not subtract the unsteered margin, so negative margins alone do not establish intervention-induced reversal. Sharp projections are renormalized, preventing their KL similarity to CAA from establishing mediation by the original small component. Curvature is local and distribution-dependent; larger-model and distribution-shift transfer remain untested. The proofs establish neither nuisance/disposition separation, a guaranteed realized curvature reduction by the spectral-gap ratio, nor coefficient-invariant spectra. Forty-step Lanczos estimates do not certify the full spectrum. Mistral's baseline refusal changes from 12% to 52% under judge validation. Appendix J reports inconsistent sharp-energy values for nominally matching Qwen refusal settings, and one Qwen compliance-table row totals 92%. Broad capability retention and systematic uncertainty estimates are absent; code release is deferred.

title: Cross-Modal Latent Influence: Patch-Level Training Sample Attribution for Vision-Language Models
abstract: Explaining a vision--language model (VLM) prediction requires tracing training-example influence to the multimodal evidence that mediates it, yet existing attribution methods largely operate only at the sample level. Recent latent-mediated influence methods provide feature-level attribution in language models, but lack the multimodal and spatial structure needed to ground influence in VLMs. We introduce MOSAIC (Multimodal Orthogonalized Sparse Autoencoders for Influence Characterization). It learns a shared sparse image--text latent space whose concepts are 1) sparse within each modality, 2) supported on contiguous image regions, 3) aligned to the phrases that describe them, and 4) approximately decorrelated. It then applies EK-FAC to decompose training-example influence through these concepts and localize their contributions to specific text phrases and image regions. We evaluate MOSAIC on Qwen and Gemma across captioning, chest X-ray understanding, and visual question answering. The learned features are more localized and coherent without degrading task behavior, and ablating influence-ranked latents changes model outputs more than ablating latents ranked by activation or frequency. We find that visual evidence can substantially reorganize training-data attribution while preserving more of the shared latent structure. MOSAIC thus connects where model behavior comes from with what multimodal evidence carries that influence.
summary:
**Central idea**

MOSAIC connects estimated training-example influence to sparse multimodal features and their expression in text phrases and image patches. A shared, position-wise TopK SAE reconstructs intermediate VLM states. Spatial penalties, attention-supervised phrase–region alignment, and activity decorrelation shape its features. EK-FAC estimates parameter-space influence; activation-weighted derivatives attribute that estimate to latent positions. This provides first-order attribution, without establishing an exact additive decomposition of retraining effects.

**Experiments**

The authors LoRA-adapt Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct and Gemma-4-E2B-it on VizWiz-Captions, CheXpert, and GQA, then freeze them. SAEs contain 8,192 latents with at most 128 active per position, inserted at layers 15 and 19, respectively. Representation diagnostics use 1,500 held-out training examples. Tests cover objective ablations, latent removal and retention, image removal, curvature approximations, optimization choices, modality reweighting, and pooled JSAE/SPARC controls. CheXpert evaluates three statuses for five findings; GQA retains at most one question per image.

**Key results**

On Qwen GQA, visual footprint falls from 0.688 to 0.120. Qwen VizWiz's full objective yields footprint 0.083 versus 0.312 for the base SAE. DINOv2 semantic-coherence lift is scored only for latents with median footprint below 25%; CheXpert omits this metric. SAE insertion changes Qwen GQA accuracy from 0.6513 to 0.6361 and Gemma GQA from 0.5914 to 0.5867. On Gemma GQA, removing 256 influence-ranked latents flips 38.3% of predictions versus 8.3% for activation ranking; retaining 64 preserves the original answer on 75.0% versus 48.3%.

Across six settings, image removal leaves absolute latent-influence correlations of 0.543–0.795, while example correlations over candidate unions are −0.797 to −0.564. Candidate-pool Jaccard overlap is only 0.021–0.145; shared-candidate correlations vary substantially. On 60 VizWiz validation examples, position-wise reconstruction CE is 2.027 for MOSAIC, 9.464 for JSAE, and 12.691 for SPARC, versus 1.848 without replacement. Explicit modality balancing either weakens reported ablation effects or barely changes rankings.

**Limitations / open questions**

Training-example influence lacks retraining-based validation. Retrieval coverage, attention-derived correspondence accuracy, and native-versus-replacement mechanistic fidelity remain uncertain. Main intervention sample counts are unspecified. Gemma GQA accuracy falls to 0.3315 with layer-12 insertion; its shared key–value architecture prevents patch-level grounding tests at the primary layer. Evaluation covers two approximately 2B-scale models. Image-only plots limit independent inspection; numerical results above come from accompanying text and tables.

title: The Ball and the Box: Two Geometries of Computation in Superposition
abstract: Neural representations can encode more features than they have dimensions, a phenomenon known as superposition. We study the dimension needed to compute Boolean gates from such representations. For a single threshold layer with a Gaussian random dictionary and uniformly random sparse Boolean inputs, we derive sharp dimension thresholds under two error criteria. A vanishing expected error count can require more dimensions than correctness of every output with high probability. Shared reads explain the gap: rare realizations can produce many errors at once. The expected-count threshold has ball geometry, while joint reliability has box geometry when a gate is evaluated on every feature tuple. Optimizing shared readout weights and biases gives explicit thresholds for conjunction, disjunction, and majority. For pairwise conjunction, the analysis also describes the transition near the threshold, in agreement with exact simulations.
summary:
**Central idea**
The paper derives storage-width requirements for Boolean computation from a random linear code: m independent Gaussian feature directions in d dimensions store an independent, uniformly sampled support of k active features. Each gate has its own threshold unit; d measures shared storage width, not total network size. Vanishing expected total errors, E[X]→0, can require more width than simultaneous correctness with high probability, P(X=0)→1. Reused feature reads correlate errors, allowing rare draws with many failures to dominate the mean. Expected counts yield Euclidean ball geometry; reliability for universal gate families yields box geometry.

**Experiments**
An exact distributional reduction samples active reads and necessary inactive order statistics without constructing the dictionary. Campaigns evaluate pairwise conjunction, AND3, OR2, majority3, and feature recovery, including k=64, 256, and 1024 with m=k⁴; additional pairwise settings include m=k², k¹⁶, and k⁶⁴. Each cell uses 4096 independent draws with pointwise 95% Wilson intervals. Expected counts are computed separately by quadrature of the exact one-gate law. Direct-matrix comparisons and finite enumeration check the sampler, rearrangement identity, optimization programs, and algebraic constructions. No trained language models or natural-language datasets are tested.

**Key results**
For universal pairwise conjunction with log k=o(log m), the first-order constants for midpoint count, midpoint reliability, optimized count, and optimized reliability are respectively 16, 8, 4, and 2 in units of k log m. The optimized count converse covers all gate-local probes; the reliability converse covers common canonical representations, including choices made after observing reads. At k=1024, m=k⁴, and 1.35 times the optimized quantile center, half-slack, count-optimal, and midpoint biases succeed on 3984, 3912, and 2 of the same 4096 draws. At m=k⁶⁴ and 1.5 times the midpoint quantile center, all 4096 draws succeed while quadrature estimates E[X]≈2.76×10¹⁹. Gumbel–Poisson formulas describe pairwise transition windows, with finite-size discrepancies at smaller k. Further proofs address structured sharing, adversarial supports, marginal non-Gaussian universality, composition, nonlinear encodings, and exact layer audits.

**Limitations / open questions**
The sharp reliability results concern Gaussian dictionaries, independent random supports, fixed arity, and specified readout architectures. Reliability converses for arbitrary gate-local probes, box laws for learned or correlated dictionaries, and sharp multilayer reliability remain open. Window-based sizing is asymptotic rather than a certified finite-size guarantee. Width counts exclude output-unit count and precision costs; low width or high average accuracy alone does not identify a learned superposition mechanism.

title: Learning to Deceive with Attention-Based Explanations
abstract: Attention mechanisms are ubiquitous components in neural architectures applied to natural language processing. In addition to yielding gains in predictive accuracy, attention weights are often claimed to confer interpretability, purportedly useful both for providing insights to practitioners and for explaining why a model makes its decisions to stakeholders. We call the latter use of attention mechanisms into question by demonstrating a simple method for training models to produce deceptive attention masks. Our method diminishes the total weight assigned to designated impermissible tokens, even when the models can be shown to nevertheless rely on these features to drive predictions. Across multiple models and tasks, our approach manipulates attention weights while paying surprisingly little cost in accuracy. Through a human study, we show that our manipulated attention-based explanations deceive people into thinking that predictions from a model biased against gender minorities do not rely on the gender. Consequently, our results cast doubt on attention's reliability as a tool for auditing algorithms in the context of fairness and accountability.
summary:
**Central idea**

Attention weights can be trained to obscure predictive information from designated tokens. The proposed objective adds −λ log(1−attention mass on impermissible tokens) to task loss, with mean-head and worst-head variants. The resulting attention is generated by the trained model itself. This challenges treating low attention to sensitive tokens as evidence that their information is unused.

**Experiments**

Four binary classification tasks cover physician-versus-surgeon biographies with deliberately amplified gender imbalance, pronoun-labeled Wikipedia biographies, SST reviews with Wikipedia distractors, and admission reference letters containing ranks and percentiles. Models use embedding attention, a single-layer BiLSTM, or BERT-base with attention restricted between permissible and impermissible token groups; BERT manipulation targets attention from [CLS]. Classification checkpoints are selected on development data for maximal attention reduction subject to accuracy within 2% of the original. GRU encoder–decoders perform bigram flipping, copying, reversal, and Multi30K English-to-German translation. Each synthetic task has 100,000 sequences per training, validation, and test split; sequence results average five runs. Three graduate students each judge 50 biography examples per attention scheme.

**Key results**

For SST with distractors, worst-head-penalized BERT at λ=1 reduces its maximum-head attention-mass statistic on review tokens from 96.2% to below 0.001%, while accuracy changes from 90.8% to 90.2%. Bigram-flipping token accuracy changes from 100.0% to 99.8%, while gold-alignment attention falls from 94.5% to 0.03%. Translation changes from 24.4 to 23.7 BLEU at λ=0.1. Participants report gender influence for 66% of original-attention predictions and 0% under either manipulated scheme. Trust ratings are 3.00/4 for original attention, 2.67 for the proposed scheme, and 1.00 for the Wiegreffe–Pinter comparator. After pronoun attention is zeroed, manipulated BiLSTM gender-identification accuracy remains above 99%, whereas embedding-attention accuracy falls to approximately 50%. The authors also report embedding-norm growth and seed-dependent alternative attention patterns.

**Limitations / open questions**

The human study has only three participants and reports no inferential significance test. Accuracy preservation does not establish unchanged predictions or mechanisms; separately trained anonymization controls only indirectly diagnose information use. Smaller SST classifiers lose substantial accuracy, and stronger penalties hurt copying and translation. Translation alignments are automatically estimated. Figure images are unavailable in this rendering, so qualitative mechanism descriptions rely on accompanying prose. The experiments establish vulnerabilities under manipulated training objectives without establishing that every ordinary attention explanation is unfaithful or extending directly to modern decoder-only LLMs.

Uncovering Safety Risks of Large Language Models through Concept Activation Vector
abstract: Despite careful safety alignment, current large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to various attacks. To further unveil the safety risks of LLMs, we introduce a Safety Concept Activation Vector (SCAV) framework, which effectively guides the attacks by accurately interpreting LLMs' safety mechanisms. We then develop an SCAV-guided attack method that can generate both attack prompts and embedding-level attacks with automatically selected perturbation hyperparameters. Both automatic and human evaluations demonstrate that our attack method significantly improves the attack success rate and response quality while requiring less training data. Additionally, we find that our generated attack prompts may be transferable to GPT-4, and the embedding-level attacks may also be transferred to other white-box LLMs whose parameters are known. Our experiments further uncover the safety risks present in current LLMs. For example, in our evaluation of seven open-source LLMs, we observe an average attack success rate of 99.14%, based on the classic keyword-matching criterion. Finally, we provide insights into the safety mechanism of LLMs. The code is available at https://github.com/SproutNan/AI-Safety_SCAV.
summary:
**Central idea**

Safety Concept Activation Vectors (SCAVs) use layerwise logistic classifiers to distinguish malicious from safe instructions. Classifier normals guide adaptive activation interventions; classifier scores and activation displacement guide an AutoDAN-based prompt search. A formal derivation establishes minimum Euclidean displacement to a fixed classifier threshold, without guaranteeing harmful compliance or preserved response quality.

**Experiments**

Training uses 140 malicious Advbench/HarmfulQA instructions and 140 GPT-4-generated safe instructions. Main evaluations use disjoint, officially supplied, nonrandom 50-instruction subsets of Advbench and StrongREJECT. Comparisons involve LLaMA-2-7B/13B-Chat and RepE, JRE, soft prompts, DeepInception, AutoDAN, and GCG. Additional tests cover seven open models, 80 HarmBench cases, further checkpoints, Eraser unlearning, prompt defenses, circuit-breaker models, and transfer to GPT-4-turbo-2024-04-09. Metrics distinguish refusal-keyword absence, relevant answers, judged usefulness, and language flaws. Human evaluation uses six annotators and three judgments per response.

**Key results**

For the illustrated aligned models, reported malicious/safe classification accuracy exceeds 95% from approximately layers 10–11 and 98% at late layers. Human-rated SCAV usefulness in LLaMA-2-7B is 92%/90% on Advbench/StrongREJECT, versus RepE's 82%/82%. Across seven models and both 50-case subsets, Table 5 averages 99.14% keyword success and 87% GPT-4-rated usefulness. Five malicious/safe training pairs yield near-100% average keyword success in the LLaMA-2-7B sweep, using five sampled subsets per size.

Prompt-level usefulness is 44%/40% for LLaMA-2-7B and 28%/46% for 13B. Selecting the best outcome across multiple attack families yields GPT-4 usefulness of 84%/54%; these are portfolio results. Eraser-treated LLaMA-2 has reported keyword success of 97.34%/98.79% on Advbench/AdvExtent. Circuit-breaker checkpoints retain 70–74% judged usefulness under internal interventions. Later-layer classifier scores can rebound after single-layer intervention; some cross-model activation transfer is reported without accessible numerical detail.

**Limitations / open questions**

Separability and intervention success do not uniquely identify natural safety mechanisms or calibrate probe scores as the model's own maliciousness probabilities. Transfer mechanisms remain unresolved. Main benchmarks are small; classifier-test and Eraser denominators are unspecified. Repeated table entries disagree, some usefulness rates exceed answer rates despite intended nesting, and the printed language-flaws conjunction leaves aggregation unclear. The prompt objective permits a zero-displacement optimum if unchanged inputs are admissible. Plots are unavailable visually, so only narrated findings are extractable. The supplied body is version 5, dated November 30, 2024.

title: Probing then Editing Response Personality of Large Language Models
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated promising capabilities to generate responses that simulate consistent personality traits. Despite the major attempts to analyze personality expression through output-based evaluations, little is known about how such traits are internally encoded within LLM parameters. In this paper, we introduce a layer-wise probing framework to systematically investigate the layer-wise capability of LLMs in simulating personality for responding. We conduct probing experiments on 11 open-source LLMs over the PersonalityEdit benchmark and find that LLMs predominantly simulate personality for responding in their middle and upper layers, with instruction-tuned models demonstrating a slightly clearer separation of personality traits. Furthermore, by interpreting the trained probing hyperplane as a layer-wise boundary for each personality category, we propose a layer-wise perturbation method to edit the personality expressed by LLMs during inference. Our results show that even when the prompt explicitly specifies a particular personality, our method can still successfully alter the response personality of LLMs. Interestingly, the difficulty of converting between certain personality traits varies substantially, which aligns with the representational distances in our probing experiments. Finally, we conduct a comprehensive MMLU benchmark evaluation and time overhead analysis, demonstrating that our proposed personality editing method incurs only minimal degradation in general capabilities while maintaining low training costs and acceptable inference latency. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/universe-sky/probing-then-editing-personality.
summary:
**Central idea**
The paper combines personality-label probing with inference-time activation editing. Layer-specific classifiers distinguish prompts requesting Neuroticism, Extraversion, or Agreeableness. During generation, states classified outside the target category receive perturbations along the target classifier's weight vector, aiming to change response style despite conflicting personality instructions.

**Experiments**
PersonalityEdit supplies 1,600 training topics and 4,800 personality-conditioned samples; its training split is divided 70:30 for probe training and evaluation. Appendix A specifies final-input-token representations, despite conflicting wording elsewhere. Table 1 reports eleven checkpoints spanning LLaMA 2, LLaMA 3.1, Vicuna, GPT-J, ChatGLM, Qwen 2.5, and InternLM. Main editing comparisons evaluate three LLaMA checkpoints against IKE and MEND across six directed conversions; additional experiments cover Qwen and LLaMA 2 13B. Success rate uses a fine-tuned RoBERTa classifier; PAE measures the change in GPT-4's target-trait rating on a five-point scale. Runtime evaluation specifies 200 test topics and 1,200 topic–conversion cases, although individual editing percentages have unexplained denominators.

**Key results**
Reported V-information generally rises around layers 5–12 and plateaus later; instruction-tuned checkpoints usually show slightly higher middle/upper-layer scores. Reported six-direction mean success is 44.16% for LLaMA 2 7B Chat, 66.73% for LLaMA 3.1 8B Instruct, and 44.33% for its base counterpart, exceeding the tested baselines' corresponding means. Performance varies sharply: LLaMA 3.1 Instruct achieves 100% for Agreeableness→Extraversion but 3.33% for Neuroticism→Agreeableness. Its zero-shot MMLU accuracy changes from 64.75% to 63.15–63.54%, depending on target. Probe training takes 0.1 hours, while inference takes 11.2 versus 3.8 hours unedited, approximately three times longer. A persuasion-strategy extension reports 60.12% mean success.

**Limitations / open questions**
Explicit personality words confound instruction-label decoding with response-personality mechanisms; prompt-trained boundaries are transferred to generated-token states without independent calibration. Automated lexical perturbation checks do not establish human-valid personality measurement. Reporting inconsistencies include the model roster, probe-type attribution, and log-base-two definitions versus plateaus near ln(3). Table 7's numerical rows show earlier saturation for the probe labeled linear, contrary to its prose. Appendix F's top 10% of coordinates carry approximately 26–28% of absolute probe weight, contradicting its majority-mass interpretation; its diagonal-preservation intervention is underspecified and lacks random controls. Conversion-distance explanations rely on qualitative t-SNE interpretation. MMLU retention does not establish broad capability preservation; persistent personality, long-context consistency, intervention specificity, and statistical uncertainty remain unestablished.

title: A Survey on Sparse Autoencoders: Interpreting the Internal Mechanisms of Large Language Models
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have transformed natural language processing, yet their internal mechanisms remain largely opaque. Recently, mechanistic interpretability has attracted significant attention from the research community as a means to understand the inner workings of LLMs. Among various mechanistic interpretability approaches, Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising method due to their ability to disentangle the complex, superimposed features within LLMs into more interpretable components. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of SAEs for interpreting and understanding the internal workings of LLMs. Our major contributions include: (1) exploring the technical framework of SAEs, covering basic architecture, design improvements, and effective training strategies; (2) examining different approaches to explaining SAE features, categorized into input-based and output-based explanation methods; (3) discussing evaluation methods for assessing SAE performance, covering both structural and functional metrics; and (4) investigating real-world applications of SAEs in understanding and manipulating LLM behaviors.
summary:
**Central idea**

This survey organizes sparse autoencoders (SAEs) as tools for decomposing language-model activations into sparse, overcomplete dictionaries. It reviews architectural variants including Gated, TopK, BatchTopK, JumpReLU, and Switch SAEs, alongside training strategies targeting cross-layer reuse, feature consistency, output preservation, and rare concepts. It distinguishes input-based explanations, such as maximally activating examples, from output-based vocabulary projections and mutual-information explanations. Evaluation is organized into structural and functional metrics. Applications include steering, instruction following, hallucination analysis, and feature-based training; these application findings come from cited work. The survey also connects SAEs to earlier sparse coding and representation research.

**Experiments**

Appendix D reports its own evaluation of seven SAE configurations: one Llama Scope dictionary at Llama-3.1-8B layer 12, one standard Pythia-70M dictionary at layer 5, and five Gemma Scope dictionaries at Gemma-2-2B layer 12. The Gemma dictionaries have nominal training L0 settings 22, 41, 82, 176, and 445. Metrics include realized active-latent counts, MSE, explained variance, reported cross-entropy and KL scores, feature absorption, spurious correlation removal (SCR) after ablating 5, 50, or 500 latents, and sparse-probe accuracy. Evaluation datasets, sample counts, probe budgets, and uncertainty estimates are unspecified.

**Key results**

Across the five Gemma configurations, realized L0 increases from 22.141 to 472.199, MSE decreases from 2.125 to 0.707, and explained variance increases from 0.824 to 0.941. Absorption is nonmonotonic: nominal L0 176 has the lowest mean/full absorption, 0.055/0.038, among these five dictionaries. SCR peaks at 50 ablated latents in six of seven configurations; the remaining configuration ties at 50 and 500. Sparse-probe accuracy is 0.885 versus a dense baseline of 0.904 for Llama and 0.929 versus 0.922 for Pythia. Gemma scores range from 0.952 to 0.958 against 0.958.

**Limitations / open questions**

The survey identifies incomplete concept coverage, uncertain superposition and linear-representation assumptions, persistent reconstruction errors, and computational cost as unresolved issues. Its experiments measure operational properties without establishing native feature recovery or mechanistic faithfulness. Cross-family comparisons are not controlled architecture comparisons. Cross-entropy/KL scores approach one without specified normalization, Pythia KL is reported as −1 without explanation, and the prose incorrectly describes the best Gemma probe as exceeding its equal baseline. Explanation equations also contain notation and inequality inconsistencies. The supplied text is version 3, dated September 23, 2025.

When Structured Sparse Autoencoders Learn Consistent Concepts Across Modalities
abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising technique for mechanistic interpretability by learning a set of sparse latent features in large models, each of which encodes a distinct concept. However, in vision-language models (VLMs), vanilla SAEs struggle to learn modality-consistent concepts, with concepts often exhibiting fragmented coverage (i.e., disjoint regions) in the visual modality. To address this challenge, we propose a Structured Sparse AutoEncoder ($S^2AE$) that enforces concept consistency from both semantic and spatial perspectives in the visual modality. Specifically, we group image patches based on Transformer attention similarity and spatial proximity, and introduce a structured sparsity regularization when training the vanilla SAE. The regularization consists of exclusive sparsity for inter-group concept disentanglement and group sparsity for intra-group concept consistency, which drives the latent neurons by SAEs to specialize in distinct, semantically grounded concepts. Evaluated on the \texttt{Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct} model, the method achieves 6.06% average improvement in semantic alignment (mIoU) and 60.81 in representational efficiency (lower l0 norm) while maintaining near-perfect reconstruction fidelity with an Explained Variance above 99%. Cross-modal analysis further demonstrates that $S^2AE$ enhances neuronal monosemanticity by this visual structural prior, achieving a 3.08% average gain in semantic consistency and a 2.37% average gain in monosemanticity scores for both modalities of multimodal features, thereby fostering more coherent and disentangled representations.
summary:
**Central idea**

S²AE adds visual-region regularization to a shared vision–language TopK sparse autoencoder. Agglomerative clustering partitions image patches into 20 regions using all-layer average attention and spatial distance. Exclusive sparsity discourages feature activity across regions; group sparsity encourages shared sparse feature use within regions. Both penalties operate on binarized gates with straight-through gradients. A hierarchical interpretation pipeline describes individual masked references before synthesizing modality-specific concepts.

**Experiments**

The authors train SAEs on Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct residual streams at layers 5, 10, 15, and 20, with 114,688 features, input dimension 3,584, and nominal TopK budget 256. Images come from the cited SAE sample-cache dataset, paired with Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct captions. Evaluation on 5,000 randomly collected reference images measures maximum feature-mask IoU against endogenous clusters, reconstruction explained variance, and active-feature count. Interpretation retains ten references per modality, uses Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct and Qwen3-30B-Instruct, and evaluates reference coherence with SigLip2-based MS scores. Additional experiments compare direct summarization, clustering choices, and regularizer ablations.

**Key results**

The introduction reports layer-15 cluster-alignment mIoU increasing from 0.516 to 0.594. Reconstruction EV remains above 0.99, while S²AE uses approximately 180–215 active features versus 256 for the baseline. Within separately classified multimodal subsets, visual MS, language MS, and positive summary-consistency rates improve at every layer. At layer 5, language MS rises from 0.872 to 0.896 and consistency from 0.294 to 0.337, a 4.3 percentage-point increase among multimodal features. Hierarchical interpretation achieves 98.8% summary identification versus 66.4% for direct summarization in the reported layer-5 comparison. Ablations expose a tradeoff: combined regularization improves cluster alignment from 0.524 to 0.555 but lowers within-group activation agreement from 0.199 to 0.153; exclusive sparsity alone lowers agreement to 0.080.

**Limitations / open questions**

Training and alignment evaluation use the same region-construction prior, without independent segmentation ground truth. Visual interpretation references are additionally selected for cluster alignment. Summary availability and embedding coherence do not establish semantic accuracy or mechanistic faithfulness. Multimodal feature proportions change substantially, so conditional gains do not establish improvement of matched features or dictionary-wide coverage; vision-only MS worsens at three layers. One target backbone is tested, without reported seed uncertainty, downstream replacement-loss tests, or causal feature interventions. Training duration and several optimization details are unspecified. Plots are unavailable as images in the supplied rendering; several citation keys lack matching bibliography entries, and the abstract's consistency aggregate does not exactly match Table 1.

Sparse Autoencoders Learn Monosemantic Features in Vision-Language Models
abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have recently gained attention as a means to improve the interpretability and steerability of Large Language Models (LLMs), both of which are essential for AI safety. In this work, we extend the application of SAEs to Vision-Language Models (VLMs), such as CLIP, and introduce a comprehensive framework for evaluating monosemanticity at the neuron-level in visual representations. To ensure that our evaluation aligns with human perception, we propose a benchmark derived from a large-scale user study. Our experimental results reveal that SAEs trained on VLMs significantly enhance the monosemanticity of individual neurons, with sparsity and wide latents being the most influential factors. Further, we demonstrate that applying SAE interventions on CLIP's vision encoder directly steers multimodal LLM outputs (e.g., LLaVA), without any modifications to the underlying language model. These findings emphasize the practicality and efficacy of SAEs as an unsupervised tool for enhancing both interpretability and control of VLMs. Code and benchmark data are available at https://github.com/ExplainableML/sae-for-vlm.
summary:
**Central idea**
The paper introduces MonoSemanticity score (MS): pairwise cosine similarity between image embeddings, weighted by products of min–max-normalized neuron activations, excluding self-pairs. It treats this visual coherence as a proxy for single-concept semantics and uses vision-encoder SAE interventions to control multimodal text generation.

**Experiments**
BatchTopK and Matryoshka BatchTopK SAEs reconstruct ImageNet activations from CLIP ViT-L/14-336px, with additional SigLIP SoViT-400m, AIMv2-L, and WebSSL MAE-300m experiments. Training uses 100,000 steps, batches of 4,096, expansion factors 1–64, and usually a batch-level sparsity target K=20; realized inference sparsity varies. MS uses DINOv2 ViT-B or CLIP ViT-B embeddings. A Mechanical Turk study compares top-16 ImageNet training-image grids for 1,000 neuron pairs, using three votes per pair from 71 annotators. Steering attaches a 64× Matryoshka SAE trained on CLIP layer-22 image tokens to LLaVA-1.5-7b with Vicuna. GPT-4.1-mini judges 100 neurons, with ten insertion prompts per neuron. Appendices examine iNaturalist taxonomy alignment and overlap among neurons’ strongest exemplars.

**Key results**
Human agreement is reported as 82.8% under an assumed uniform distribution of MS differences over 0–0.9, rather than the observed pair distribution. Agreement rises from 56.6% for differences below 0.1 to 100% for 0.8–0.9, the latter containing 41 pairs. At equal width, CLIP final-layer mean DINOv2-based MS increases from 0.0135 for native coordinates to 0.12 for BatchTopK and 0.16 for Matryoshka. Wider dictionaries generally improve maxima and reported absolute high-score counts, but average scores and high-score fractions can decline. Matryoshka’s advantage varies across configurations. Stronger sparsity increases coherence while reducing reconstruction: K=1 versus K=50 gives R² of 31.3% versus 74.9%. SAE steering improves joint insertion-and-prompt-adherence success over DiffMean, 42.4% versus 35.8%, and joint suppression-and-unrelated-content preservation, 52.5% versus 33.3%. Insertion alone favors DiffMean, 53.1% versus 48.7%.

**Limitations / open questions**
Image coherence and human similarity preferences do not establish exhaustive monosemanticity, native mechanism recovery, or semantic uniqueness. High-MS features can steer broader concepts, and some features lack clear steering effects. Baseline construction, intervention calibration, suppression denominators, and judge validation are underspecified. Appendix configuration labels and some prose values conflict with tables; figures are unavailable beyond their textual descriptions. The supplied article is v3 dated November 27, 2025; metadata gives the initial April 3 publication date.

title: Steering Vision-Language Models with Joint Sparse Autoencoders
abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have shown promise for analyzing language models, but applying them to vision-language models (VLMs) often yields representations that are difficult to use as controllable cross-modal steering directions. We introduce the Joint Sparse Autoencoder (JSAE), which uses an explicit alignment constraint to jointly factorize sequence-pooled vision and language activations into shared, interpretable image/caption-level features. Applied to LLaVA, JSAE recovers cross-modal features for recognizable concepts (e.g., food and animals). Through bidirectional interventions (additive steering and suppression), we observe a layer-dependent asymmetry under our protocol: additive steering peaks at mid-to-late (pre-output) layers and weakens at both ends, whereas suppression scores remain within a comparable range across all probed layers within statistical noise. Experiments on three VLMs, namely LLaVA-v1.6-Mistral-7B, Llama3-LLaVA-8B, and the MoE-based Qwen3-VL-30B, show related layer-localized effects across architectures. Together, these results suggest that explicitly aligned sparse representations support more controllable intervention-based analysis of multimodal features, within an identifiable layer range, than the unconstrained alternatives tested here.
summary:
**Central idea**

Joint Sparse Autoencoders (JSAEs) learn separate vision and text encoder–decoder pairs from mean-pooled image-token and caption-token activations. Reconstruction and L1 penalties accompany cosine alignment between paired sparse codes. Activation-profile clustering and manual inspection select macro-concepts; sums of normalized text-decoder columns are added to, or subtracted from, all image-token states at one layer. These are image/caption-level directions. Shared semantic identity and decoder correspondence are motivated informally, without identification guarantees.

**Experiments**

Training uses 50,000 positive MS-COCO image–caption pairs, with reported input width 4,096 and 16,384 latents. A separate 25,000-pair COCO-Probe collection includes matches, hard negatives, and random mismatches. LLaVA-v1.6-Mistral-7B is tested at layers 7/13/25/30 on 100/104/104/112 valid cross-category examples. Additional experiments use Qwen3-VL-30B-Instruct layer 33 and Llama3-LLaVA-Next-8B layer 15. Success means an SBERT target-similarity increase above 0.2; Claude Sonnet 4 rates target incorporation and coherence, while perplexity ratios assess fluency. Further tests cover 1,500 Flickr30k images and broadcast reconstruction on 1,000 COCO caption pairs.

**Key results**

Reported LLaVA success rates are 40.0%, 74.0%, 79.8%, and 15.2% across the four layers, although probing selects layer 13. At layer 13, reported rates are 39.4% for ActAdd, 22.1% for prompting, 2.9% for random directions, 0% for VL-SAE, and 4.1% without alignment; the latter two use different category cohorts and denominators. Additional-model success is 77.9% on 104 Qwen examples and 66.7% on 96 Llama examples. Flickr30k rates are 50.5%, 62.0%, and 34.0% for food, wild animals, and indoor rooms, with 500 images each. Suppression tests detect no corrected pairwise depth differences. Late-layer broadcast reconstruction nearly preserves clean content-word cross-entropy.

**Limitations / open questions**

Categories vary across layers, intervention strengths are incompletely specified, and feature selection involves manual inspection. Each additional architecture has only one tested layer. Suppression lacks unintervened and random-direction references; nonsignificance does not establish equivalence or natural grounding mechanisms. Strong steering fabricates visual content, and the judge receives captions rather than images. Numerical inconsistencies affect reported significance, similarity distributions, and success rates, including a noninteger implied Flickr30k success count. Late reconstruction leaves previously computed text states intact, and Table 4 slightly favors raw-mean replacement over JSAE at layer 30. Figure images are unavailable in this rendering; no additional visual measurements can be verified.

title: SPARC: Concept-Aligned Sparse Autoencoders for Cross-Model and Cross-Modal Interpretability
abstract: Understanding how different AI models encode the same high-level concepts, such as objects or attributes, remains challenging because each model typically produces its own isolated representation. Existing interpretability methods like Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) produce latent concepts individually for each model, resulting in incompatible concept spaces and limiting cross-model interpretability. To address this, we introduce SPARC (Sparse Autoencoders for Aligned Representation of Concepts), a new framework that learns a single, unified latent space shared across diverse architectures and modalities (e.g., vision models like DINO, and multimodal models like CLIP). SPARC's alignment is enforced through two key innovations: (1) a Global TopK sparsity mechanism, ensuring all input streams activate identical latent dimensions for a given concept; and (2) a Cross-Reconstruction Loss, which explicitly encourages semantic consistency between models. On Open Images, SPARC dramatically improves concept alignment, achieving a Jaccard similarity of 0.80, more than tripling the alignment compared to previous methods. SPARC creates a shared sparse latent space where individual dimensions often correspond to similar high-level concepts across models and modalities, enabling direct comparison of how different architectures represent identical concepts without requiring manual alignment or model-specific analysis. As a consequence of this aligned representation, SPARC also enables practical applications such as text-guided spatial localization in vision-only models and cross-model/cross-modal retrieval. Code and models are available at https://github.com/AtlasAnalyticsLab/SPARC
summary:
**Central idea**
SPARC learns stream-specific affine sparse encoders and decoders in shared coordinates. Global TopK selects indices from summed stream logits; each stream retains its own rectified values at those indices. Self- and cross-reconstruction losses encourage correspondence. The equations enforce common selected indices, but stream-specific ReLU zeros can differ. Neither shared selection nor reconstruction establishes semantic identity.

**Experiments**
The main Open Images configuration uses frozen DINOv2 ViT-L/14 with registers and DataComp-trained CLIP ViT-L/14 image/text encoders, 8,192 latents, k=64, 50 epochs, Adam, and seed 42. Comparisons include Local TopK, cross-loss weights 0/1, and retrained official USAE with matched width, k, batch size, and epochs. Evaluations measure top-50 image label-profile overlap, label purity, reconstruction R², and single-latent probing on 432 of 601 labels with at least 50 positives. Appendix A.3 specifies balanced samples, binarized activations, 20 training-selected candidates, validation selection, and held-out testing. Further experiments cover COCO segmentation, retrieval, and configurations containing up to ten streams.

**Key results**
Mean concept-profile Jaccard across 8,192 latents and stream pairs is 0.8018±0.0039 for full SPARC, versus 0.2599 for Local+cross, 0.7344 for Global without cross-loss, and 0.2166 for USAE. Full SPARC has 84.4% all-stream-alive and 15.6% all-stream-dead latents, with no mixed liveness. Mean three-stream self/cross R² is 0.693/0.513, versus USAE’s 0.411/0.292. SPARC improves label purity and selected single-latent probe losses over USAE; all three SPARC ablations have lower probe losses than the full configuration. COCO cross-modal attribution, excluding small objects at IoU threshold 0.2, achieves mIoU 0.143 through DINO and 0.138 through CLIP, below native CLIP similarity’s 0.157. Open Images CLIP-image→text Recall@1 is 3.4%, versus raw CLIP’s 9.8%.

**Limitations / open questions**
Global selection depends on multiple streams, so reconstructed target features can influence a nominal source code through its mask. Independent-stream inference for retrieval is insufficiently specified. Label metrics do not establish monosemanticity or native causal mechanisms; dead-profile handling is unclear. Results use one training seed, and reconstruction advantages vary: Global has negative Swin-target R² in the vision-only configuration, and text-only comparisons often favor alternatives. Common-class attribution fires spuriously, while detailed and background queries can fail. COCO training descriptions conflict across sections. Figures are unavailable as images; qualitative findings rely on accompanying text. The supplied article is v2, dated March 6, 2026; metadata supplies the original publication date.
