Backdooring Sparse Autoencoders
abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are increasingly used not only to interpret language models but also to intervene on their internal representations. We show that this creates a supply-chain attack surface: a maliciously modified SAE can induce attacker-chosen behavior when inserted into the forward pass of an otherwise unchanged language model. We introduce a decoder-only SAE backdoor that leaves both the underlying LLM and the SAE encoder frozen, restricting the attack to a single auxiliary component at a single insertion layer. Using code generation as a case study, we demonstrate high rates of unsolicited code insertion across three language models and a wide range of insertion layers, as well as trigger-dependent behavior conditioned on a prompt cue. We further evaluate the modified SAEs using HumanEval and selected SAEBench metrics. While attack effectiveness varies across models and layers, strong backdoor behavior can coexist with relatively small changes in several conventional SAE quality measures. These results establish that SAEs can carry behavioral backdoors without modifying the language model itself and should therefore be treated as security-sensitive components.
summary:
**Central idea**
An externally supplied SAE can carry a behavioral backdoor when its reconstruction replaces an LLM activation. Updating its decoder can change downstream behavior while leaving the language-model weights and encoder frozen. Encoder preservation guarantees identical sparse codes for fixed input activations, rather than identical effects of reconstruction.

**Experiments**
The study evaluates Gemma 3 4B Instruct with Gemma Scope 2 JumpReLU SAEs, Qwen3 1.7B with Qwen-Scope TopK SAEs, and Llama 3.1 8B Instruct with Llama Scope JumpReLU SAEs. Training uses filtered teacher completions from 25 HumanEval tasks paired with ten payload-instruction variants; accepted counts are unspecified. Evaluation uses 139 held-out tasks per layer across 34, 28, and 32 layers, respectively. Reconstruction replacement starts at the final prompt position and continues through completion positions. The benign payload is `print("Hello World")`. Separate metrics measure textual insertion, observed execution, and functional correctness. Conditional experiments contrast 2024 and 2023 prefixes using the same checkpoint without an external gate. Nine manually selected, relatively successful layers receive SAEBench core, Spurious Correlation Removal (SCR), and Targeted Probe Perturbation (TPP) evaluations.

**Key results**
Unconditional textual insertion occurs at every evaluated layer, with median rates across layers of 92.4%, 87.8%, and 88.1% for Gemma, Qwen, and Llama; base models and original SAEs yield zero insertion. Median executed-print rates are 90.6%, 83.8%, and 70.1%, using all 139 tasks per layer irrespective of correctness. Median within-layer correctness changes relative to original SAEs are −1.4, −0.4, and +12.2 percentage points. Llama's modified-SAE median correctness remains 33.8%, versus 67.6% for its base model.

At the nine quality-evaluation layers, textual insertion is 85.6–98.6%. Gemma and Llama loss-recovery changes stay within 0.53 percentage points, whereas Qwen layer 19 loses 16.33 points. Across measured budgets, maximum absolute SCR and TPP changes are 0.0409 and 0.0107. Conditional Gemma layer 6 achieves 98.6% paired success with zero false triggers, but median paired success across all layers is only 9.0%, 10.1%, and 14.0% for Gemma, Qwen, and Llama.

**Limitations / open questions**
Evidence covers one benign payload, HumanEval, one SAE configuration per model, and one split and training run per layer. Checkpoint quality and architecture confound cross-model comparisons. LoRA baselines use different training budgets and 33 evaluation tasks, preventing matched superiority conclusions. Dedicated detector evasion and proposed defenses are untested. Plot images are unavailable in this rendering; numerical evidence comes from tables and prose.

title: MINAR: Mechanistic Interpretability for Neural Algorithmic Reasoning
abstract: The recent field of neural algorithmic reasoning (NAR) studies the ability of graph neural networks (GNNs) to emulate classical algorithms like Bellman-Ford, a phenomenon known as algorithmic alignment. At the same time, recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have spawned the study of mechanistic interpretability, which aims to identify granular model components like circuits that perform specific computations. In this work, we introduce Mechanistic Interpretability for Neural Algorithmic Reasoning (MINAR), an efficient circuit discovery toolbox that adapts attribution patching methods from mechanistic interpretability to the GNN setting. We show through two case studies that MINAR recovers faithful neuron-level circuits from GNNs trained on algorithmic tasks. Our study sheds new light on the process of circuit formation and pruning during training, as well as giving new insight into how GNNs trained to perform multiple tasks in parallel reuse circuit components for related tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/pnnl/MINAR.
summary:
**Central idea**

MINAR adapts edge attribution patching (EAP) and integrated-gradient EAP to neuron-level circuit discovery in graph neural networks. Clean and corrupted graphs retain identical topology while features change. Signed scores are averaged across graph nodes and probing graphs before taking absolute values. Circuit construction adds complete input–output paths containing selected edges, avoiding dangling internal components.

**Experiments**

Two-layer minimum-aggregation GNNs are trained with L1 regularization on curated graphs of at most six nodes. Evaluation uses 300 graphs, including cycles, complete graphs, Erdős–Rényi graphs, and trees, reaching 200 nodes. Predictions concern two Bellman–Ford iterations; multiplicative loss sums errors over nodes within two hops and averages across graphs. Variants add reachability prediction or remove self-loops. A second study trains a recurrent, shared two-layer maximum-aggregation GINE processor on seven SALSA-CLRS tasks. Each task has 10,000 training graphs of 4–16 nodes, 1,000 validation graphs of 16 nodes, and 1,000 test graphs of 80 nodes. Discovery uses 128 additional validation-distribution graphs and compares weights, weight gradients, EAP, and 20-step EAP-IG.

**Key results**

For Bellman–Ford, weights, EAP, and EAP-IG recover a 10-edge circuit from 18,240 computation edges. Its multiplicative loss is 0.0545 versus 0.0578 for the full model; deleting it raises loss to 21,870.6836. Sufficient extracted circuits shrink from 73 edges at epoch 1,000 to 31 at epoch 2,000 and 10 around epoch 3,000, after full-model generalization. Without self-loops, a 17-edge circuit achieves loss 0.0599 versus 0.0642 for the full model. The joint distance/reachability model admits an 11-edge circuit out of 18,432, with loss 0.0499 and reachability accuracy 98.31%, versus 0.0519 and 100% for the full model. Inspection reveals distance-thresholding rather than independent BFS computation. SALSA-CLRS circuit overlap groups weighted-path tasks and DFS-related tasks; weight gradients frequently exceed EAP variants on reported characterization scores.

**Limitations / open questions**

Minimum aggregation supplies substantial algorithmic structure. Bellman–Ford discovery uses the evaluation graphs, limiting independent validation. No regularization ablation isolates L1's causal role in refinement. SALSA-CLRS test accuracy varies widely, including 36.42% for DFS and 48.18% for Prim. Equation 17 defines prediction agreements, but the stated fidelity directions and characterization formula require disagreements. Structural information survives feature corruption, especially relevant to articulation points and bridges. Overlap does not establish causal transfer benefits. Plots are unavailable in this text rendering, and two seed-specific losses are blank.

title: Interpretability without actionability: mechanistic methods cannot correct language model errors despite near-perfect internal representations
abstract: Language models encode task-relevant knowledge in internal representations that far exceeds their output performance, but whether mechanistic interpretability methods can bridge this knowledge-action gap has not been systematically tested. We compared four mechanistic interpretability methods -- concept bottleneck steering (Steerling-8B), sparse autoencoder feature steering, logit lens with activation patching, and linear probing with truthfulness separator vector steering (Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct) -- for correcting false-negative triage errors using 400 physician-adjudicated clinical vignettes (144 hazards, 256 benign). Linear probes discriminated hazardous from benign cases with 98.2% AUROC, yet the model's output sensitivity was only 45.1%, a 53-percentage-point knowledge-action gap. Concept bottleneck steering corrected 20% of missed hazards but disrupted 53% of correct detections, indistinguishable from random perturbation (p=0.84). SAE feature steering produced zero effect despite 3,695 significant features. TSV steering at high strength corrected 24% of missed hazards while disrupting 6% of correct detections, but left 76% of errors uncorrected. Current mechanistic interpretability methods cannot reliably translate internal knowledge into corrected outputs, with implications for AI safety frameworks that assume interpretability enables effective error correction.
summary:
**Central idea**
The paper tests whether readable internal representations enable correction of clinical-triage errors. It compares concept interventions in Steerling-8B with SAE clamping, logit-lens-guided activation additions, and true-positive-minus-false-negative steering in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Strong hazard-label decodability coexists with limited correction under the tested interventions.

**Experiments**
The dataset contains 400 physician-adjudicated cases: 200 physician-created vignettes with 132 hazards and 200 Medicaid encounter messages with 12 hazards, totaling 144 hazards and 256 benign cases. Emergency/urgency keywords score free-text recommendations. Qwen probes use mean-pooled input activations, L2 logistic regression, and five-fold stratified cross-validation across 28 layers. A layer-14 ReLU SAE with 16,384 latents trains for eight epochs on 62,662 token activations from all cases. Steering clamps 20 selected latents or adds normalized TP–FN activation differences at layers 22 or 23. Steerling interventions override 20 concepts selected using leave-one-out contrasts.

**Key results**
Original-parser baseline sensitivity is 51/144 for Steerling and 65/144 for Qwen. Qwen's best probe reaches AUROC 0.982, with 95% CI 0.968–0.993. In Steerling's physician-created subset, concept suppression corrects 17/85 missed hazards but disrupts 25/47 detections; superiority over random-concept intervention is not established (reported p=0.84). The SAE averages 1,455 active latents per token and yields 3,695 hazard-associated features, but tested clamping changes none of the 79 false-negative or 65 true-positive classifications. Layer-22 addition at strength 5 corrects 16/79 misses and disrupts 5/65 detections. Layer-23 TSV addition at strength 10 corrects 19/79 and disrupts 4/65, leaving 60/79 original misses uncorrected. Refining the parser raises Qwen baseline sensitivity to 105/144.

**Limitations / open questions**
AUROC and sensitivity measure different quantities; subtracting them does not establish a calibrated 53-point knowledge deficit. Decodability establishes neither native causal use nor metacognitive awareness. Intervention construction uses the evaluation corpus; independent generalization is untested. Baselines use sampling while Arms 3–4 use greedy decoding, leaving comparison details unclear. SAE reconstruction fidelity and refined-parser intervention outcomes are unreported. The strongest TSV lacks a matched random control, although a strength-5 control favors TSV descriptively. Downstream compensation and fundamental steering limitations remain hypotheses. The conclusion's claim that only TSV achieves positive net correction conflicts with the layer-22 results. These finite recipes do not establish that effective interventions cannot exist.

title: You can remove GPT2's LayerNorm by fine-tuning
abstract: The LayerNorm (LN) layer in GPT-style transformer models has long been a hindrance to mechanistic interpretability. LN is a crucial component required to stabilize the training of large language models, and LN or the similar RMSNorm have been used in practically all large language models based on the transformer architecture. The non-linear nature of the LN layers is a hindrance for mechanistic interpretability as it hinders interpretation of the residual stream, and makes it difficult to decompose the model into circuits. Some researchers have gone so far as to name "reasons interpretability researchers hate layer norm." In this paper we show that it is possible to remove the LN layers from a pre-trained GPT2-small model by fine-tuning on a fraction (500M tokens) of the training data. We demonstrate that this LN-free model achieves similar performance to the original model on the OpenWebText and ThePile datasets (-0.05 cross-entropy loss), and the Hellaswag benchmark (-0.5% accuracy). We provide our implementation at https://github.com/ApolloResearch/gpt2_noLN, and fine-tuned GPT2-small models at https://huggingface.co/apollo-research/gpt2_noLN. Our work not only provides a simplified model for mechanistic interpretability research, but also provides evidence that the LN layers, at inference time, do not play a crucial role in transformer models.
summary:
**Central idea**

GPT2-small can be adapted to operate without LayerNorm, providing a potentially simpler model organism for mechanistic interpretability. Input-dependent normalization complicates residual-stream attribution and circuit decomposition. The method replaces normalization scales with calibrated constants while fine-tuning pretrained weights, progressively removing normalization and temporary token-specific exceptions.

**Experiments**

Average scales are estimated from 16 OpenWebText prompts. Removal schedules separately handle normalization before MLPs, attention queries/keys, attention values, and unembedding. First-position tokens receive special treatment; EOT exceptions are additionally used for attention values. Five reported schedules use 850–2,450 optimization steps, each containing 491,520 tokens. Typical runs are described as approximately 500M tokens and two hours on one A100; the best reported v4 checkpoint uses 1,200 steps, approximately 590M tokens. Evaluations measure cross-entropy on held-out OpenWebText and an uncopyrighted ThePile derivative, plus HellaSwag accuracy. Controls include the original checkpoint and additional vanilla fine-tuning, including a learning-rate-schedule-matched baseline. Reported checkpoints are selected by validation loss.

**Key results**

The best no-LN model, v4, obtains OpenWebText loss 3.000 versus 2.966 for matched vanilla fine-tuning, ThePile loss 2.900 versus 2.850, and HellaSwag accuracy 29.51% versus 30.01%. Removal therefore costs 0.034 and 0.050 cross-entropy, respectively, and 0.50 percentage points of accuracy against that control. The untouched checkpoint scores 3.095, 2.856, and 29.56%; the results prose inconsistently calls the approximately 30.0% comparator the original model. Simultaneous freezing reportedly produces NaNs or sustained loss much greater than 20 under the tested procedures. Incremental removal permits recovery, although aggressive schedules retain larger penalties. Scheduling each removal at a distinct step in v5 avoids large spikes without producing the best final model.

**Limitations / open questions**

Only GPT2-small is studied, with no reported uncertainty estimates or systematic seed replication. Aggregate predictive preservation after weight adaptation does not establish preservation of native circuits or validate fixed-scale attribution in the untouched model. Interpretability improvements and transfer of discoveries back to normalized models remain untested. Larger-model feasibility, generalization differences between corpora, and late-training loss increases under decreasing learning rates remain unresolved. Appendix generations provide only a small qualitative comparison.

title: DLM-Scope: Mechanistic Interpretability of Diffusion Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become a standard tool for mechanistic interpretability in autoregressive large language models (LLMs), enabling researchers to extract sparse, human-interpretable features and intervene on model behavior. Recently, as diffusion language models (DLMs) have become an increasingly promising alternative to the autoregressive LLMs, it is essential to develop tailored mechanistic interpretability tools for this emerging class of models. In this work, we present DLM-Scope, the first SAE-based interpretability framework for DLMs, and demonstrate that trained Top-K SAEs can faithfully extract interpretable features. Notably, we find that inserting SAEs affects DLMs differently than autoregressive LLMs: while SAE insertion in LLMs typically incurs a loss penalty, in DLMs it can reduce cross-entropy loss when applied to early layers, a phenomenon absent or markedly weaker in LLMs. Additionally, SAE features in DLMs enable more effective diffusion-time interventions, often outperforming LLM steering. Moreover, we pioneer certain new SAE-based research directions for DLMs: we show that SAEs can provide useful signals for DLM decoding order; and the SAE features are stable during the post-training phase of DLMs. Our work establishes a foundation for mechanistic interpretability in DLMs and shows a great potential of applying SAEs to DLM-related tasks and algorithms.
summary:
**Central idea**

DLM-Scope adapts sparse-autoencoder interpretation to masked diffusion language models. It collects training activations separately from masked prediction positions (Mask-SAE) and visible context positions (Unmask-SAE), and repeatedly injects decoder directions during denoising. It also compares decoding trajectories through sparse-feature overlap and examines dictionary reuse after instruction tuning.

**Experiments**

The authors train 16K-wide ReLU+TopK residual-stream SAEs at six layers of Dream-7B and LLaDA-8B, alongside Qwen-2.5-7B and LLaMA-3-8B autoregressive baselines. Reported configurations use 150M Common Pile tokens and 2,048-token contexts. Evaluation measures uncentered explained variance and insertion-induced denoising-loss changes. Dream auto-interpretation collects 5M held-out tokens and evaluates up to 1,000 eligible latents per SAE using gpt-4o-mini explanations and activation classification. Steering uses five neutral prefixes per feature, 30-token continuations, and 30 diffusion steps. Decoding-order analysis evaluates 800 GSM8K questions with Dream-7B, using 128 steps and one token decoded per step. Transfer compares Dream Base- and Instruct-trained Mask-SAEs, including instruction rollouts.

**Key results**

Reconstruction improves as more latents are retained; some shallow-layer, low-budget DLM replacements reduce masked-token cross-entropy. Four selected feature explanations score 1.00, 0.714, 0.929, and 0.286 classification accuracy; aggregate interpretation scores are absent. At L0=80, the better of the two DLM SAE variants exceeds its autoregressive comparator in 11 of 12 family–layer comparisons on concept improvement plus 0.3 times relative perplexity reduction. Dream layer-27 Unmask-SAE scores 0.38 versus Qwen’s −0.02; Qwen leads at layer 14. GSM8K accuracy is 8% for random Origin ordering, 56% for TopK-margin, and 59% for Entropy. Confidence-based orders exhibit greater early feature turnover and deeper post-decode drift, while dominant Top-1 identities remain largely stable across all orders. Base Dream dictionaries have similar transfer metrics through layer 23, with substantially worse transfer at layer 27 on Instruct.

**Limitations / open questions**

Reconstruction, explanation accuracy, steering scores, and transfer do not establish native mechanistic faithfulness or featurewise semantic invariance. Steering feature selection, evaluators, scaling, and uncertainty are insufficiently specified; equal coefficient ranges do not match functional perturbation budgets. Appendix G also describes top-activated-position selection, which differs from currently masked-position selection. Decoding dynamics are associations across three orders, without a tested SAE-guided decoding improvement. Plotted numerical values are unavailable in this rendering, and one maximal-activation example explicitly remains a placeholder.

title: Elucidating Mechanisms of Demographic Bias in LLMs for Healthcare
abstract: We know from prior work that LLMs encode social biases, and that this manifests in clinical tasks. In this work we adopt tools from mechanistic interpretability to unveil sociodemographic representations and biases within LLMs in the context of healthcare. Specifically, we ask: Can we identify activations within LLMs that encode sociodemographic information (e.g., gender, race)? We find that gender information is highly localized in MLP layers and can be reliably manipulated at inference time via patching. Such interventions can surgically alter generated clinical vignettes for specific conditions, and also influence downstream clinical predictions which correlate with gender, e.g., patient risk of depression. We find that representation of patient race is somewhat more distributed, but can also be intervened upon, to a degree. To our knowledge, this is the first application of mechanistic interpretability methods to LLMs for healthcare.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper uses activation patching to investigate demographic associations in clinical generation and predictions. It interprets compact gender-control sites and benefits from multilayer race patches as evidence about demographic localization. The revised body evaluates OLMo-7B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-it, and OLMo-2-0325-32B-Instruct; downstream clinical experiments use OLMo-7B-Instruct.

**Experiments**

Baseline vignette generation uses ten prompts and 100 samples each, yielding 1,000 vignettes per condition. Localization measures normalized demographic-token probability increases after replacing token-specific MLP activations with demographic-statement donor activations. Generation tests vary scaling and neighboring-layer replacement, including donors from prostate-cancer and preeclampsia prompts. External Llama-3.1-8B perplexity assesses generated-text likelihood. Clinical applications replace final-prompt-token residual states: depression-risk assessment uses 1,000 selected hospital courses derived from MIMIC-IV-Note, and diagnosis ranking uses one NEJM Healer case per demographic comparison.

**Key results**

OLMo generates female patients in 98% of sarcoidosis and 94% of multiple-sclerosis vignettes. Scaled layer-18 MLP replacement produces male patients in all 1,000 evaluated vignettes per condition. Table 3 reports scaled male fractions of 1.00 for both conditions in Llama, 0.85/0.92 in Gemma, and 0.96 for multiple sclerosis in OLMo-32B. Prostate-derived patches also change pronouns in 25/26 held-out profession completions at the validation-selected scale.

Selected sliding-window race configurations yield target-race fractions averaging over three alternative races of 0.96 for Llama/hepatitis B, 0.91 for Gemma/sarcoidosis, and 0.78/0.76 for OLMo-32B/hepatitis B and sarcoidosis. Benefits are not uniform across targets. The authors report little external-perplexity change for evaluated OLMo patches.

Across four depression prompts, female-source versus male-source patches increase positive predictions by 3.50 ± 2.2 percentage points; Black-source versus white-source patches increase them by 8.25 ± 5.8 points. The meaning of ± is unspecified. Diagnosis comparisons report mean rank differences of 0.24 for gender and 0.08 for race, with Mann–Whitney p-values of 0.004 and 0.02.

**Limitations / open questions**

Whole-vector replacement establishes behavioral control without demonstrating demographic specificity, exclusive natural localization, or fairer predictions. Perplexity does not establish clinical correctness or preservation of other attributes. Depression inputs originate from female patients with anxiety, excluding depression mentions and sexed conditions; no gold risk evaluation is supplied. Diagnosis evidence covers two cases. Prompt exploration and demographic categories are limited. Image-only plots prevent independent recovery of exact perplexities and rank directions. Gemma's tabulated scaling gain slightly conflicts with prose describing scaling as ineffective.

title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Antibody Language Models Using SAEs
abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a mechanistic interpretability technique that have been used to provide insight into learned concepts within large protein language models. Here, we employ TopK and Ordered SAEs to investigate autoregressive antibody language models, and steer their generation. We show that TopK SAEs can reveal biologically meaningful latent features, but high feature-concept correlation does not guarantee causal control over generation. In contrast, Ordered SAEs impose a hierarchical structure that reliably identifies steerable features, but at the expense of more complex and less interpretable activation patterns. These findings advance the mechanistic interpretability of domain-specific protein language models and suggest that, while TopK SAEs suffice for mapping latent features to concepts, Ordered SAEs are preferable when precise generative steering is required.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper distinguishes concept predictability from generative control in antibody language models. Selected TopK SAE latents predict antibody regions and germline identities through localized activations, yet selected predictive directions fail to produce reliable intended generation changes. Selected low-index Ordered SAE directions enable systematic changes, with broader activation patterns that the authors find less intuitive.

**Experiments**

The primary model is p-IgGen, a four-layer, approximately 17M-parameter autoregressive model; additional analyses examine IgLM (13M) and ProGen2-OAS (764M). SAE training draws on 1,800,545 paired OAS sequences, with Ordered training subsampled to 100,000 sequences. TopK dictionaries use 32× expansion and Ordered dictionaries 8×. Both target 32 active latents, but p-IgGen Ordered training uses BatchTopK. Concept probing uses 149,069 sequences from OAS, CoV-AbDab, and PLAbDab, partitioned by CDR-similarity clusters. Logistic regression and validation-selected activation thresholds identify concept-associated latents. Steering figures report libraries of 1,000 generated sequences.

**Key results**

At p-IgGen's final layer, CDR classification validation accuracy is 0.99 using SAE codes versus 0.98 using native activations; heavy-J classification from SAE codes reaches macro-F1 0.93. Individual-latent screening identifies features for five of six heavy-J classes, excluding IGHJ5. Three illustrated TopK IGHJ4 candidates fail to produce predictable gene-usage changes; only one passes the formal feature threshold. Selected Ordered directions yield positive and negative IGHJ4 steering-sweep Pearson correlations of 0.943 and −0.980. Separately learned Ordered directions targeting IGHJ6 yield reported correlations of 0.872 in IgLM and 0.986 in ProGen2-OAS. One selected p-IgGen steered library has diversity 0.21 versus 0.20 for natural sequences and ESM-2 likelihood −0.325 versus −0.330. All 1,000 generated sequences are ANARCI-numberable. Reported distributional comparisons are significant, with rank-biserial effect-size magnitudes below 0.2.

**Limitations / open questions**

Dictionary width, training budget, and sometimes sparsification differ between architectures, preventing attribution of steering differences specifically to ordering. Steering coverage is selective; further unsuccessful TopK searches are reported without data. Splitting and greater abstraction are proposed explanations rather than isolated mechanisms. Feature thresholds and scores use validation data, and visual readability lacks a controlled evaluation. Quality proxies do not establish binding, developability, or functional preservation. Cross-model experiments retrain the pipeline rather than transfer a dictionary or direction. Plots are unavailable as images in the supplied rendering; numerical conclusions above rely on the text and tables.

title: A Multi-Level Causal Intervention Framework for Mechanistic Interpretability in Variational Autoencoders
abstract: Understanding how generative models represent and transform data is a foundational problem in deep learning interpretability. While mechanistic interpretability of discriminative architectures has yielded substantial insights, relatively little work has addressed variational autoencoders (VAEs). This paper presents the first general-purpose multilevel causal intervention framework for mechanistic interpretability of VAEs. The framework comprises four manipulation types: input manipulation, latent-space perturbation, activation patching, and causal mediation analysis. We also define three new quantitative metrics capturing properties not measured by existing disentanglement metrics alone: Causal Effect Strength (CES), intervention specificity, and circuit modularity. We conduct the largest empirical study to date of VAE causal mechanisms across six architectures (standard VAE, beta-VAE, FactorVAE, beta-TC-VAE, DIP-VAE-II, and VQ-VAE) and five benchmarks (dSprites, 3DShapes, MPI3D, CelebA, and SmallNORB), with three seeds per configuration, totaling 90 independent training runs. Our results reveal several findings: (i) a consistent within-dataset negative correlation between CES and DCI disentanglement (the CES-DCI trade-off); (ii) that the KL reweighting mechanism of beta-VAE induces a capacity bottleneck when generative factors approach latent dimensionality, degrading disentanglement on complex datasets; (iii) that no single VAE architecture dominates across all five datasets, with optimal choice depending on dataset structure; and (iv) that CES-based metrics applied to discrete latent spaces (VQ-VAE) yield near-zero values, revealing a critical limitation of continuous-intervention methods for discrete representations. These results provide both a theoretical foundation and comprehensive empirical evaluation for mechanistic interpretability of generative models.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper combines factor-controlled input edits, latent-coordinate interventions, activation patching, and mediation analysis for image VAEs. It introduces Causal Effect Strength (CES), expected pixel-space L2 reconstruction change; specificity, inverse entropy of squared pixel changes; and modularity, one minus average absolute correlation between factor-intervention response vectors. Their interpretation as semantic strength, selectivity, and circuit specialization remains an assumption.

**Experiments**

Standard VAE, β-VAE, FactorVAE, β-TC-VAE, DIP-VAE-II, and VQ-VAE are trained on dSprites, 3DShapes, MPI3D, CelebA, and SmallNORB. Three seeds per configuration produce 90 main runs, trained for 30 epochs. Continuous models use ten latent dimensions; principal settings include β=4, FactorVAE γ=10, and β-TC-VAE decomposition weights all equal to one. VQ-VAE uses 512 codebook entries. Evaluation combines five disentanglement metrics with intervention diagnostics. Additional dSprites penalty sweeps and framework ablations use seed 0.

**Key results**

Relative to Standard VAE, β-VAE increases dSprites DCI from 0.100 to 0.305 while reducing CES from 8.231 to 5.024; corresponding 3DShapes values are 0.669 to 0.805 and 22.848 to 18.836. Significant negative CES–DCI correlations are reported for these two datasets; CelebA and SmallNORB correlations are positive and nonsignificant. The precise inclusion rule for the reported 3DShapes correlation is unclear. MPI3D DCI is numerically unstable.

Rankings depend on dataset and metric. DIP-VAE-II has the highest tabulated 3DShapes DCI, using two finite seeds, and MPI3D MIG; Standard VAE has the highest CelebA DCI. On CelebA, higher DIP-VAE-II modularity coexists with lower DCI. β-VAE has eight CES-defined active coordinates on MPI3D and seven on SmallNORB. VQ-VAE exhibits dSprites CES 0.166 and specificity above 200,000, but its CES reaches 9.424 on 3DShapes.

**Limitations / open questions**

Fixed latent width, three seeds, untuned penalties, and possible incomplete convergence restrict generalization. No dimensionality sweep or capacity-restoration intervention establishes the proposed bottleneck mechanism; the information-theoretic discussion supplies no formal CES–DCI derivation. Ablation losses largely follow metric definitions, and removing patching eliminates none of the four aggregate metrics. Input-edit construction, intervention averaging, and mediation outcomes are underspecified. Figures are unavailable visually, so interpretation relies on tables, prose, and captions. Reporting conflicts include universal-tradeoff conclusions, an MPI3D DCI difference despite invalid DCI, incorrect best-model and SAP rankings, and dimension-utilization prose contradicted by Table 8. Low VQ-VAE sensitivity does not establish that finite-difference interventions inherently require gradients or universally fail for discrete representations.

title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Structure-Aware Numerical Reasoning in LLaMA 3.1 8B
abstract: Recent work has shown that large language models (LLMs) exhibit strong numerical sequence modeling capabilities and show promise in time-series prediction. While LLMs display in-context learning capabilities, the mechanisms with which they accomplish time-series prediction remain unclear. Specifically, whether they truly understand the underlying structure, which at a minimum requires reasoning over first differences in the sequence of numbers. To study this, we investigate Llama 3.1-8B from a mechanistic interpretability point of view. Mechanistic interpretability is an emerging field concerned with the reverse engineering of the algorithms learned by neural networks such as LLMs. To assess Llamas' numerical sequence modeling capabilities and to facilitate our mechanistic interpretability analysis, we create a sequence modeling task that cannot be solved without picking up structural cues. Specifically, we sample n random numbers and repeat them with an offset. We find that Llama displays strong performance on our tasks suggesting that it can pick up on the underlying structure. To understand the mechanisms that allow it to do so, we perform probing experiments and activation patching based counterfactual analysis. Probing reveals that the model computes and stores first differences in its internal representations without explicit supervision, indicating that it tracks structural information about the sequence. Activation patching reveals that Llama retrieves the relevant first-difference with a mechanism similar to an induction circuit and subsequently adds it to the current value. Notably, our work represents one of the first studies to identify this form of concept induction in LLMs.
summary:
**Central idea**
The paper proposes that LLaMA 3.1–8B extrapolates numerical sequences through induction over internally represented first differences: it matches the final observed delta to an earlier occurrence, retrieves the following delta, and adds it to the final number. Its synthetic task repeats an irregular delta pattern while keeping sequence values unique, avoiding ordinary repeated-number copying.

**Experiments**
The authors evaluate prediction of the 30th number from 29 comma-separated integers on 10,000 sequences. Values lie between 0 and 999 and have single-token number encodings. Layerwise ordinary-least-squares probes use 4,500 training and 500 held-out examples to decode the target delta at token position 27 and the final number at position 57. Each intervention analysis uses 100 sequences selected for zero original prediction error. Experiments insert clean hidden states at individual positions into a flat sequence of 100s while restoring clean final-position queries across downstream layers; transplant individual attention-head outputs; rank positions using patching effects multiplied by attention weights and value norms; and swap keys at positions 25 and 27 while restoring values.

**Key results**
Sequence prediction achieves MAE 4.2748 and R² 0.9958. Delta decoding improves sharply after approximately layer 7, with reported R² above 0.8 through approximately layer 16; final-number decoding declines after approximately layer 8. Joint hidden-state/query patching increases probability of the counterfactual answer 100 plus the clean target delta at source position 27, beginning around layer 14. Token-importance scores rank positions 57, 33, 27, 55, and 25 highest. Key swapping shifts confidence toward the alternative-delta answer, but the original answer remains more probable in the reported comparison.

**Limitations / open questions**
Evidence covers one model and a narrow task; intervention results condition on perfect original predictions. No last-value or other forecasting baseline contextualizes the high R², and exact-match accuracy is unreported. Sustained joint patches demonstrate intervention-relative transfer without uniquely identifying the intact retrieval algorithm or its necessity. Whole-key swaps change content as well as positional information. Probe controls are inconsistently described as shuffled-label versus cross-position controls; the earlier position also cannot observe the later final number. Token/output indexing and the stated delta range contain inconsistencies, including a displayed delta of 20. Numerical intervention effect sizes and uncertainty are unavailable in the supplied text, and plot images are not accessible. The key-swap equations reference a corrupt baseline despite describing a clean-run intervention, and value-restoration layer ranges differ across descriptions.

title: Mechanistic?
abstract: The rise of the term "mechanistic interpretability" has accompanied increasing interest in understanding neural models -- particularly language models. However, this jargon has also led to a fair amount of confusion. So, what does it mean to be "mechanistic"? We describe four uses of the term in interpretability research. The most narrow technical definition requires a claim of causality, while a broader technical definition allows for any exploration of a model's internals. However, the term also has a narrow cultural definition describing a cultural movement. To understand this semantic drift, we present a history of the NLP interpretability community and the formation of the separate, parallel "mechanistic" interpretability community. Finally, we discuss the broad cultural definition -- encompassing the entire field of interpretability -- and why the traditional NLP interpretability community has come to embrace it. We argue that the polysemy of "mechanistic" is the product of a critical divide within the interpretability community.
summary:
**Central idea**

“Mechanistic interpretability” has four meanings: a narrow technical sense requiring explanations through intermediate causal mechanisms; a broad technical sense covering inspection of model internals; a narrow cultural sense identifying work from the MI community; and a broad cultural sense encompassing AI interpretability generally. The authors argue that this ambiguity reflects a historical separation between established NLP interpretability (NLPI) researchers and a newer, substantially alignment-oriented MI community.

**Experiments**

This is a historical and conceptual analysis, with no new model experiments, benchmark evaluations, datasets, or formal proofs. It draws on research publications, workshop histories, guides, public statements, and social-media exchanges. Examples involving LSTMs, BERT, transformer induction heads, probing, attention, neuron localization, and sparse autoencoders come from cited work; their experimental findings are not new tests performed here.

**Key results**

The authors distinguish causal explanation from observing representational structure. Their narrow technical definition permits partial mechanisms, whereas a stricter, less widely adopted definition requires a complete input-to-output causal pathway. Identifying induction heads alone would not satisfy that stricter definition. Causal abstraction supplies a conceptual route to faithful higher-level simplification.

The historical account traces focused NLPI analyses to 2016, BlackBoxNLP to 2018, the public introduction of MI terminology to the 2020 Circuits thread, and that thread’s shift toward language models to 2021. The authors argue that many MI methods continue earlier NLPI approaches and inherit concerns about probe baselines, correlation versus causal use, polysemantic neurons, and geometric confounds. SAE interpretation additionally inherits assumptions about linearity and naturally occurring feature sparsity. They attribute broader adoption of the MI label partly to growing resources, visibility, and research opportunities, while arguing that shared terminology has not eliminated community divisions. Appendix A connects this problem to ambiguity around explanation, faithfulness, plausibility, features, and interpretability illusions.

**Limitations / open questions**

The history is selective and classifies communities through authors’ backgrounds and networks, rather than a systematic bibliometric or sociological study. Explanations involving incentives, duplication, and community boundaries remain interpretive; their causal effects are not measured. The authors recommend engagement with prior literature and shared venues but do not evaluate an integration intervention or establish a universally accepted definition of MI.

title: Finding and using interpretable latents in a neutrino foundation model with sparse autoencoders
abstract: We present a first application of sparse-autoencoder-based mechanistic interpretability to particle physics. Studying a neutrino foundation model pretrained on IceCube data and fine-tuned for direction reconstruction, we identify a validated atlas of physical concepts in the model representation, using a strict validation protocol consisting of held-out tests, matched nuisance controls, and replication across independent dictionary trainings. Causal interventions show that the direction head barely draws on this atlas. Motivated by this underused information, we train an uncertainty head on the same event-level representation to predict the model's angular reconstruction error. Unlike the direction head, it depends causally on quality and brightness features from the atlas. At $20\%$ selection efficiency, this interpretable estimator improves the median angular resolution from $20.2^\circ$ to $3.2^\circ$. These results suggest that mechanistic interpretability can reveal learned latent physics encoded within a model's internal representation and help design downstream tasks that exploit it.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper distinguishes physical information accessible in a shared representation from information used by a particular downstream head. It studies PolarBERT, an eight-block IceCube pulse-sequence transformer, using sparse autoencoders on 256-dimensional CLS states. Clean-associated coordinates have little measured influence on direction reconstruction but substantially affect a subsequently trained angular-error predictor.

**Experiments**

A nominal million Monte Carlo events are partitioned into SAE training, reconstruction validation, concept discovery, concept validation, and causal testing, with fractions 75/10/7/6/2%. The reference BatchTopK SAE has 1,024 latents, average activation budget 16, and AuxK revival. Candidates undergo held-out AUROC evaluation, nuisance matching, input perturbations, and checks across four SAE seeds. Removal, donor writing, and scaling test latents and response-profile families against 20 firing-rate-matched controls. Comparisons include PCA, dense and sparse probes, earlier-layer dictionaries, four functional dictionaries, and head Jacobians. A frozen-backbone 256→128→1 GELU MLP predicts log angular error; linear regression provides a comparison.

**Key results**

The reference SAE achieves reconstruction R²≈0.994 and mean direction-output deviation 0.65°, versus approximately 56° under mean ablation. Bright-clean discrimination reaches AUROC 0.911 and strictest reported validation-control AUROC 0.787; layer-2 depth reaches 0.986. Complete clean-primary validation passes in three of four seeds; auxiliary validation passes only in the reference seed. Primary clean-coordinate removal remains a direction-head null across four seeds. The same removals increase uncertainty-head mean predicted log error by 0.193–0.612; clean-family removals produce shifts of 0.775–1.012. A dense brightness-associated support coordinate strongly affects direction reconstruction but fails concept selectivity. On held-out causal-test events, retaining the lowest-predicted-error 20% gives median angular error 3.15° for the MLP and 3.16° for linear regression, versus 20.2° for highest-charge selection and 51.3° without selection. This improves selected-sample resolution without changing direction predictions. The sparse bright-clean readout is ineffective as a standalone error-ranking score.

**Limitations / open questions**

Results concern one simulated-data backbone and specified interventions. Null mean error shifts do not establish absent computational use, and decoder edits do not guarantee selective, natural concept changes. Support contamination produces approximately 10° direction changes in one seed; a secondary coordinate has one isolated causal pass. Some nuisance schemes yield no usable pairs, and some single-latent shifts differ across source tables. Most latents lack validated labels. Error predictions are overconfident at intermediate predicted errors, and real-data transfer remains untested. Figure images are unavailable in the supplied rendering; numerical results above come from text and tables.

title: Findings of the BlackboxNLP 2025 Shared Task: Localizing Circuits and Causal Variables in Language Models
abstract: Mechanistic interpretability (MI) seeks to uncover how language models (LMs) implement specific behaviors, yet measuring progress in MI remains challenging. The recently released Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark (MIB; Mueller et al., 2025) provides a standardized framework for evaluating circuit and causal variable localization. Building on this foundation, the BlackboxNLP 2025 Shared Task extends MIB into a community-wide reproducible comparison of MI techniques. The shared task features two tracks: circuit localization, which assesses methods that identify causally influential components and interactions driving model behavior, and causal variable localization, which evaluates approaches that map activations into interpretable features. With three teams spanning eight different methods, participants achieved notable gains in circuit localization using ensemble and regularization strategies for circuit discovery. With one team spanning two methods, participants achieved significant gains in causal variable localization using low-dimensional and non-linear projections to featurize activation vectors. The MIB leaderboard remains open; we encourage continued work in this standard evaluation framework to measure progress in MI research going forward.
summary:
**Central idea**

The BlackboxNLP 2025 shared task extends MIB into a community comparison of circuit discovery and causal-variable localization. Four teams submitted ten methods: eight circuit methods from three teams and two DAS extensions from one team. Evaluation measures behavioral fidelity under specified interventions, without establishing complete algorithmic explanations.

**Experiments**

The benchmark uses GPT-2 Small (117M), Qwen-2.5 0.5B, Gemma-2 2B, and Llama-3.1 8B, retaining model–task combinations with at least 75% task accuracy. Tasks include IOI, synthetic color MCQA, two-digit addition/subtraction, ARC Easy/Challenge, and city-attribute RAVEL. Circuit submissions undergo private-test counterfactual ablation at nine weighted-edge budgets from 0.1% to 50%. Integrated circuit performance ratio (CPR; higher better) measures normalized task-performance recovery; integrated circuit–model distance (CMD; zero best) measures deviation from full-model answer preference. Private splits contain 1,000 examples for IOI and each arithmetic operation, 50 for MCQA, 1,188 for ARC Easy, and 586 for ARC Challenge. Arithmetic results average addition and subtraction. Variable localization measures interchange intervention accuracy, reporting means across counterfactual datasets and layers separately from best-layer results.

**Key results**

Hybrid ensembling achieves CPR 2.43 versus 1.85 for input-integrated EAP on GPT-2 IOI, 1.88 versus 1.63 on Qwen IOI, and 1.19 versus 1.16 on Qwen MCQA. The combined bootstrap sign filtering, positive/absolute-score selection, and integer-programming submission has mixed comparisons: Llama IOI CPR improves from 2.08 to 2.39, while Llama MCQA CMD worsens from 0.14 to 0.45. IPE is competitive on GPT-2 IOI but substantially weaker on its other submitted settings.

On Llama RAVEL, the simpler tanh variant raises mean continent/country/language intervention accuracy from DAS's 75/58/63% to 84/70/72%; the MLP variant scores 83/70/72%. On Qwen MCQA, the MLP variant raises answer/order means from 86/78% to 89/81%; tanh scores 90/78%. Gains are not universal: tanh scores 53% on Llama arithmetic carry versus DAS's 54%.

**Limitations / open questions**

Submission coverage is sparse, with no variable-localization submissions for IOI or ARC. Runtime comparisons, uncertainty estimates, and statistical significance tests are not supplied. Circuit rankings depend on the metric, and the combined edge-selection ingredients are not separately evaluated here. Higher interchange accuracy does not establish recovery of naturally used variables: expressive featurizers might themselves compute the target concept. The authors explicitly call for additional controls.

title: Explaining the Explainer: Understanding the Inner Workings of Transformer-based Symbolic Regression Models
abstract: Following their success across many domains, transformers have also proven effective for symbolic regression (SR); however, the internal mechanisms underlying their generation of mathematical operators remain largely unexplored. Although mechanistic interpretability has successfully identified circuits in language and vision models, it has not yet been applied to SR. In this article, we introduce PATCHES, an evolutionary circuit discovery algorithm that identifies compact and correct circuits for SR. Using PATCHES, we isolate 28 circuits, providing the first circuit-level characterisation of an SR transformer. We validate these findings through a robust causal evaluation framework based on key notions such as faithfulness, completeness, and minimality. Our analysis shows that mean patching with performance-based evaluation most reliably isolates functionally correct circuits. In contrast, we demonstrate that direct logit attribution and probing classifiers primarily capture correlational features rather than causal ones, limiting their utility for circuit discovery. Overall, these results establish SR as a high-potential application domain for mechanistic interpretability and propose a principled methodology for circuit discovery.
summary:
**Central idea**
PATCHES searches for component subsets supporting mathematical-operator prediction in NeSymReS, a pretrained symbolic-regression encoder–decoder. CMA-ES optimizes thresholded component masks using a size-plus-performance-penalty objective, followed by iterative pruning. The analyzed encoder has six induced-set-attention layers, each containing two eight-head attention blocks, with hidden width 512 and 50 inducing points. The work localizes operator-related components without reconstructing their mathematical algorithms.

**Experiments**
The authors analyze the checkpoint pretrained on 100 million equations. Each of eight operators receives 500 correctly reconstructed, constant-free expressions excluding designated related operators: 100 for discovery/evaluation and 400 for generalization. Mean patches average activations from 1,000 training equations; resample patches average operator-replacement counterfactuals; STR uses a related-operator donor. Search uses 250 generations and population 40. Evaluation measures top-1/2/3 target-token accuracy and normalized target logits, with faithfulness tolerance 0.10 and circuit-knockout cutoff 0.25. Comparators include iterative pruning, singleton-ablation-ranked restoration, and component probes trained on balanced 1,000-example datasets. Appendices extend discovery to monomial and posynomial predictions and test circuits on initially failed predictions.

**Key results**
The authors report 13 of 28 operator/configuration circuits satisfying their three operational criteria. The sine mean-functional circuit retains 57 components, achieves 100% generalization top-3 accuracy, and leaves 0% top-3 accuracy when its components are patched. Across 24 matched configurations, PATCHES yields fewer components than iterative pruning in 22, ties in one, and uses one more component in one. Mean versus resample outcomes depend on operator and objective; fully resampled addition and multiplication retain 99–100% top-3 accuracy, weakening information-removal interpretations. Complement-component probes remain accurate; only the two logarithm mean-patching comparisons have reported p<0.05. Singleton-ablation-ranked restoration reportedly requires nearly the whole model in illustrated sine/exponential cases. The monomial extension retains 69 components and 100% test top-3 accuracy; the posynomial circuit misses the top-1 tolerance.

**Limitations / open questions**
Evidence concerns one checkpoint and selected expression distributions. Minimality is operational and lacks an independent global-optimality guarantee. Printed absolute-difference definitions conflict with some reported successes, notably improved logarithm top-1 accuracy. Correctness glyphs and plotted values are unavailable in the rendering; normalized logit scores are insufficiently specified. Probe architecture and activation dimensions are inconsistently described, and the specified probes are nonlinear despite linear-decoding language. The procedure called “Direct Logit Attribution” ranks finite ablation effects, limiting conclusions about standard DLA. Dense-circuit explanations based on vocabulary size remain speculative.

title: Thinking Fast and Slow
A technical note on bilinear layers for interpretability
abstract: The ability of neural networks to represent more features than neurons makes interpreting them challenging. This phenomenon, known as superposition, has spurred efforts to find architectures that are more interpretable than standard multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) with elementwise activation functions. In this note, I examine bilinear layers, which are a type of MLP layer that are mathematically much easier to analyze while simultaneously performing better than standard MLPs. Although they are nonlinear functions of their input, I demonstrate that bilinear layers can be expressed using only linear operations and third order tensors. We can integrate this expression for bilinear layers into a mathematical framework for transformer circuits, which was previously limited to attention-only transformers. These results suggest that bilinear layers are easier to analyze mathematically than current architectures and thus may lend themselves to deeper safety insights by allowing us to talk more formally about circuits in neural networks. Additionally, bilinear layers may offer an alternative path for mechanistic interpretability through understanding the mechanisms of feature construction instead of enumerating a (potentially exponentially) large number of features in large models.
summary:
**Central idea**

Bilinear MLPs compute (W1x) ⊙ (W2x), optionally followed by an output projection. Their quadratic structure permits exact tensor accounting: B_ijk = W1_ij W2_ik, and each output coordinate contracts B with two copies of x. These contractions are linear in either input slot separately; the overall layer remains nonlinear. The note proposes using this structure to extend transformer circuit analysis and explain how features are constructed from simpler primitives.

**Experiments**

The document reports no new model training, datasets, empirical benchmarks, or interpretability measurements. Its concrete results are algebraic derivations. Language-model performance comparisons are attributed to Shazeer (2020): approximately 120M-parameter models reportedly made bilinear layers at least competitive per parameter with ReLU/GeLU and slightly less competitive than SwiGLU. These are cited prior experiments, not tests performed here.

**Key results**

For any finite input decomposition x = Σ_i a_i d_i, a single bilinear layer expands exactly as Σ_i,j a_i a_j [(W1d_i) ⊙ (W2d_j)]. Its output therefore consists of self-interactions and ordered pairwise interactions, without higher-order terms in those input coefficients. The note also develops a one-block transformer expansion distinguishing embedding-only inputs, attention contributions to either bilinear branch, and interactions between two attention contributions. Attention weights remain input-dependent.

For practical analysis, it proposes inspecting large tensor coefficients, applying higher-order singular value decomposition, and prioritizing strongly modified default output directions associated with co-occurring inputs. ICA on each branch's preactivations is suggested for selecting candidate modifier and default-feature coordinates. These analysis procedures are untested.

**Limitations / open questions**

No evidence establishes that the proposed bases recover semantic primitives, that the explanations are manageable, or that the architecture improves safety. The approach explicitly assumes that large linear transformations can be understood satisfactorily. Its argument that standard MLP feature construction is non-decomposable is informal rather than a general impossibility proof. Competitive performance at larger scales remains unresolved, and multilayer transformer expansions are left as exercises. The simplified transformer derivation omits normalization and biases; its printed full-logit expression lacks an unembedding factor on the MLP contribution, with additional apparent transpose and token-indexing inconsistencies. Understanding construction rules instead of enumerating potentially exponentially many features remains speculative.

title: Confidence Regulation Neurons in Language Models
abstract: Despite their widespread use, the mechanisms by which large language models (LLMs) represent and regulate uncertainty in next-token predictions remain largely unexplored. This study investigates two critical components believed to influence this uncertainty: the recently discovered entropy neurons and a new set of components that we term token frequency neurons. Entropy neurons are characterized by an unusually high weight norm and influence the final layer normalization (LayerNorm) scale to effectively scale down the logits. Our work shows that entropy neurons operate by writing onto an unembedding null space, allowing them to impact the residual stream norm with minimal direct effect on the logits themselves. We observe the presence of entropy neurons across a range of models, up to 7 billion parameters. On the other hand, token frequency neurons, which we discover and describe here for the first time, boost or suppress each token's logit proportionally to its log frequency, thereby shifting the output distribution towards or away from the unigram distribution. Finally, we present a detailed case study where entropy neurons actively manage confidence in the setting of induction, i.e. detecting and continuing repeated subsequences.
summary:
**Central idea**

Final-layer MLP neurons can regulate next-token distributions through two mechanisms. Entropy neurons write predominantly into low-singular-value unembedding directions, changing final normalization scaling while producing comparatively small direct logit changes. Newly identified token frequency neurons act substantially through a logit direction defined by centered log unigram probabilities. These mechanisms can alter uncertainty proxies with limited changes to the predicted token.

**Experiments**

The authors combine weight SVD with C4 neuron mean ablations, comparing ordinary absolute loss effects against effects with the clean final normalization denominator or frequency-direction logit projection held fixed. The detailed GPT-2 Small comparison uses six selected entropy neurons, 100 random neurons, and 25,600 tokens. Further entropy-neuron analyses cover GPT-2 Medium, Pythia 410M/1B, Phi-2, Gemma 2B, and LLaMA2 7B. Frequency statistics come from The Pile for Pythia and a 500-million-token OpenWebText proxy for GPT-2. Induction experiments duplicate 100-token passages and examine 1,000 natural C4 sequences containing filtered repeated six-grams. Attention-head interventions compare BOS redirection with replacement by mean induction-context outputs. A paired Pythia-160M comparison varies residual-stream dropout.

**Key results**

The reported normalization-dependence statistic, 1−DE/TE, is approximately 80% for selected GPT-2 Small, LLaMA2 7B, and Phi-2 entropy neurons, versus approximately 30–40% in Pythia and Gemma. Selected frequency neurons have loss effects that diminish when their frequency-direction projection is restored. Clipping GPT-2 Small neuron 11.2378 reduces entropy by reported maxima of 70% during synthetic induction and 20% during natural induction. Selected entropy neurons hedge incorrect predictions while increasing loss on correct ones. Frequency-neuron effects differ by context: clipping selected Pythia 410M neurons during induction instead increases entropy. Induction-head BOS interventions affect five of six examined entropy neurons; mean-output replacements preserve much of their repeated-context activation, providing preliminary evidence for generic induction information. Dropout strengthens the low-gain bottom unembedding subspace in the paired comparison.

**Limitations / open questions**

Entropy and unigram divergence are confidence proxies; task-level correctness calibration is not directly evaluated. The absolute-loss effect ratio is an operational statistic rather than an additive causal mediation fraction. The intervening induction circuit remains unresolved, and final-layer neuron analysis excludes other mechanisms. Synthetic induction sample counts conflict: Section 6.1 reports 100 sequences, whereas Appendix D reports 500. Plots are unavailable visually, so numerical reporting relies on explicit prose and captions. The supplied article is version 2, dated November 8, 2024; metadata gives the initial publication date.

title: Re-examining layernorm
Hellaswag: Can a machine really finish your sentence?
Analyzing and interpreting neural networks for nlp: A report on the first blackboxnlp workshop
Steer Like the LLM: Activation Steering that Mimics Prompting
Trojan Activation Attack: Red-Teaming Large Language Models using Activation Steering for Safety-Alignment
BackdoorLLM: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Backdoor Attacks and Defenses on Large Language Models
Gemma Scope 2: Helping the AI Safety Community Deepen Understanding of Complex Language Model Behavior
summary:
**Central idea**

Gemma Scope 2 is an open interpretability suite for the Gemma 3 family, spanning models from 270M to 27B parameters. The announcement presents sparse autoencoders (SAEs) and transcoders as tools for examining internal representations and connecting them to model behavior. It extends the original Gemma Scope, which targeted Gemma 2, with broader model coverage, tools targeting chat-tuned versions, and methods intended to help trace computations distributed across layers.

**Experiments**

This blog post announces a resource release without presenting a controlled evaluation. It reports training SAEs and transcoders on every layer of the Gemma 3 family and including skip-transcoders and cross-layer transcoders for studying multi-step computations. Matryoshka training is identified as a technique intended to obtain more useful concepts and address certain flaws in the earlier suite. Production reportedly involved storing approximately 110 petabytes of data and training over one trillion parameters in total across the interpretability tools. No training datasets, reconstruction metrics, behavioral benchmark scores, or comparative numerical evaluations are supplied.

**Key results**

The concrete contribution is the announced availability of interpretability tools across the stated model-size range and tools targeting chatbot behavior. The post points to a Neuronpedia demonstration, downloads, a technical report, and a Colab tutorial. Intended applications include investigating jailbreaks, refusal mechanisms, hallucinations, sycophancy, and discrepancies between communicated reasoning and internal processing. Previous Gemma Scope applications involving hallucinations, secret knowledge, and safer training are cited as motivation; their findings are not new tests performed in this announcement.

**Limitations / open questions**

The post does not establish feature completeness, mechanistic faithfulness, improved investigator understanding, or effective safety interventions. Claimed Matryoshka benefits and the usefulness of the transcoder variants are not evaluated here. Detailed dictionary configurations and coverage of individual variants are unspecified in the supplied article. The C2S Scale cancer-therapy example illustrates a possible future application: the post explicitly states that Gemma Scope 2 was not trained on that model.

title: Qwen-Scope: Turning Sparse Features into Development Tools for Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models have achieved remarkable capabilities across diverse tasks, yet their internal decision-making processes remain largely opaque, limiting our ability to inspect, control, and systematically improve them. This opacity motivates a growing body of research in mechanistic interpretability, with sparse autoencoders (SAEs) emerging as one of the most promising tools for decomposing model activations into sparse, interpretable feature representations. We introduce Qwen-Scope, an open-source suite of SAEs built on the Qwen model family, comprising 14 groups of SAEs across 7 model variants from the Qwen3 and Qwen3.5 series, covering both dense and mixture-of-expert architectures. Built on top of these SAEs, we show that SAEs can go beyond post-hoc analysis to serve as practical interfaces for model development along four directions: (i) inference-time steering, where SAE feature directions control language, concepts, and preferences without modifying model weights; (ii) evaluation analysis, where activated SAE features provide a representation-level proxy for benchmark redundancy and capability coverage; (iii) data-centric workflows, where SAE features support multilingual toxicity classification and safety-oriented data synthesis; and (iv) post-training optimization, where SAE-derived signals are incorporated into supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning objectives to mitigate undesirable behaviors such as code-switching and repetition. Together, these results demonstrate that SAEs can serve not only as post-hoc analysis tools, but also as reusable representation-level interfaces for diagnosing, controlling, evaluating, and improving large language models. By open-sourcing Qwen-Scope, we aim to support mechanistic research and accelerate practical workflows that connect model internals to downstream behavior.
summary:
**Central idea**
Qwen-Scope uses sparse autoencoder features as reusable interfaces for model development. Its 14 dictionary groups cover every transformer layer of seven dense and MoE Qwen3/Qwen3.5 backbones. Residual-stream TopK SAEs contain 32K–128K latents and retain 50 or 100 activations. Dictionaries use base checkpoints except Qwen3.5-27B, which uses an instruction-tuned checkpoint.

**Experiments**
Applications span qualitative language/style steering, benchmark analysis, multilingual toxicity classification, safety-data synthesis, code-switching suppression through SASFT, and repetition reduction through SAE-steered negative RL rollouts. Benchmark analysis uses 26 pretrained checkpoints and 17 benchmarks. Toxicity experiments use Qwen3-1.7B/8B and 13 languages, each with 4,000 discovery and 1,000 balanced evaluation examples. Safety synthesis uses Qwen3-8B layer-30 features and WildJailbreak. RL compares DAPO without Dynamic Sampling against one repetition-steered response per rollout group across three Qwen3 sizes.

**Key results**
Feature redundancy correlates with ranking-based redundancy at Spearman ρ≈0.85. Across 28 benchmark pairs, Pearson association between feature overlap and score-vector similarity rises from 0.684 to 0.755 after controlling benchmark-score correlations for MMLU. Sparse feature OR-rules exceed 0.90 best-layer English toxicity F1 in both models; cross-language transfer is uneven. Using 10% of discovery data retains approximately 99% of macro-averaged best-over-layers F1. Feature-targeted synthesis reaches 99.74% coverage of its selected safety-feature inventory. With 50K Alpaca examples plus 4K real and 4K synthetic safety examples, targeting raises reported safety accuracy from 72.00% to 77.75% versus random synthesis, while harmful ASR increases from 20% to 24% and benign refusal decreases from 36% to 20.5%. SASFT reduces switching versus ordinary SFT in all 12 displayed Qwen settings. Repetition-steered RL reduces repetition faster and further than vanilla RL, with task-dependent capability changes.

**Limitations / open questions**
Feature coverage and descriptions remain proxies for capabilities and supervision gaps; benchmark removal is suggested without testing removal. Feature extraction still requires backbone forward passes. SAE fidelity metrics, detailed training budgets, uncertainty estimates, and several evaluation denominators are absent. Some results select the best held-out layer or configuration. SASFT prose discusses five models, but tables show two; uniform baseline superiority and capability preservation are contradicted by some displayed comparisons. Repetition features also activate during benign repetition. Plot images are unavailable in this rendering, limiting quantitative auditing beyond reported text and tables.

title: BlackboxNLP-2025 mib shared task: exploring ensemble strategies for circuit localization methods
BlackboxNLP-2025 mib shared task: improving circuit faithfulness via better edge selection
BlackboxNLP-2025 mib shared task: ipe: isolating path effects for improving latent circuit identification
BlackboxNLP-2025 MIB shared task: exploring the impact of non-linear modules on distributed alignment search
P-IgGen: a paired antibody generative language model
IgLM: Infilling language modeling for antibody sequence design
ProGen2: Exploring the boundaries of protein language models
Enforcing Orderedness in SAEs to Improve Feature Consistency
InterPLM: Discovering Interpretable Features in Protein Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
abstract: Protein language models (PLMs) have demonstrated remarkable success in protein modeling and design, yet their internal mechanisms for predicting structure and function remain poorly understood. Here we present a systematic approach to extract and analyze interpretable features from PLMs using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). By training SAEs on embeddings from the PLM ESM-2, we identify up to 2,548 human-interpretable latent features per layer that strongly correlate with up to 143 known biological concepts such as binding sites, structural motifs, and functional domains. In contrast, examining individual neurons in ESM-2 reveals up to 46 neurons per layer with clear conceptual alignment across 15 known concepts, suggesting that PLMs represent most concepts in superposition. Beyond capturing known annotations, we show that ESM-2 learns coherent concepts that do not map onto existing annotations and propose a pipeline using language models to automatically interpret novel latent features learned by the SAEs. As practical applications, we demonstrate how these latent features can fill in missing annotations in protein databases and enable targeted steering of protein sequence generation. Our results demonstrate that PLMs encode rich, interpretable representations of protein biology and we propose a systematic framework to extract and analyze these latent features. In the process, we recover both known biology and potentially new protein motifs. As community resources, we introduce InterPLM (interPLM.ai), an interactive visualization platform for exploring and analyzing learned PLM features, and release code for training and analysis at github.com/ElanaPearl/interPLM.
summary:
**Central idea**

InterPLM applies sparse autoencoders to protein language model representations, combining biological annotations, activation visualizations, decoder-vector clustering, and automated descriptions. It introduces an annotation-based evaluation framework and an interactive platform for exploring candidate biological features. The authors interpret improved annotation alignment over native coordinates as evidence consistent with superposition.

**Experiments**

Separate L1-regularized SAEs are trained on all six layers of ESM-2-8M-UR50D using representations from five million UniRef50 proteins. Methods specify expansion from 320 coordinates to 10,240 latents. Evaluation uses 50,000 Swiss-Prot proteins shorter than 1,024 residues, divided into 25,000-protein validation and test sets, with 433 eligible concepts. A modified F1 combines residue-level precision with domain-level recall, crediting a domain when any annotated residue is detected. Validation data guide configuration and feature selection; activation thresholds are also optimized. Baselines include native coordinates and SAEs trained on weight-shuffled ESM-2 embeddings. Claude-3.5 Sonnet generates descriptions and predicts separate proteins’ maximum activations from those descriptions and extensive protein metadata. Selected interventions examine changes in residue-prediction probabilities.

**Key results**

Up to 2,548 SAE features per layer achieve concept F1 above 0.5 in both validation and test sets, versus at most 46 native coordinates per layer. Associated concepts span 143 categories across the SAEs versus 15 across native coordinates. Weight-shuffled controls produce no qualifying features for the tested biological annotations, while retaining hundreds associated with amino-acid identity. Reported zero-ablation-relative loss recovery ranges from 98.39785% to 100%. The reported 1,200-feature description analysis achieves median Pearson correlation 0.72 between predicted and measured protein-level maxima. Selected decoder neighborhoods contain biologically related features with different specificities. Two proposed Swiss-Prot annotation omissions receive protein-level corroboration from InterPro; additional binding-site suggestions remain unvalidated. Selected periodic-pattern interventions affect predictions beyond the directly modified residue, with diminishing effects over distance.

**Limitations / open questions**

Evidence concerns one small PLM and representations of unmasked residues. Annotation agreement does not establish semantic completeness, a uniquely recovered dictionary, or native computational mechanisms. Feature counts compare unequal representation widths. Description evaluation uses activation-stratified samples and metadata; eligibility exclusions are not clearly reconciled with the reported feature count. Steering covers a few constrained sequences without functional validation. Circuit organization and transfer to larger models remain open. The source inconsistently gives dictionary width as 10,420 versus 10,240, omits promised L0 values from its performance table, and disagrees on one control feature identifier. Figure images are unavailable here, so quantitative interpretation is restricted to supplied prose and tables.
