Measuring and Guiding Monosemanticity
abstract: There is growing interest in leveraging mechanistic interpretability and controllability to better understand and influence the internal dynamics of large language models (LLMs). However, current methods face fundamental challenges in reliably localizing and manipulating feature representations. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have recently emerged as a promising direction for feature extraction at scale, yet they, too, are limited by incomplete feature isolation and unreliable monosemanticity. To systematically quantify these limitations, we introduce Feature Monosemanticity Score (FMS), a novel metric to quantify feature monosemanticity in latent representation. Building on these insights, we propose Guided Sparse Autoencoders (G-SAE), a method that conditions latent representations on labeled concepts during training. We demonstrate that reliable localization and disentanglement of target concepts within the latent space improve interpretability, detection of behavior, and control. Specifically, our evaluations on toxicity detection, writing style identification, and privacy attribute recognition show that G-SAE not only enhances monosemanticity but also enables more effective and fine-grained steering with less quality degradation. Our findings provide actionable guidelines for measuring and advancing mechanistic interpretability and control of LLMs.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper introduces Feature Monosemanticity Score (FMS) and Guided Sparse Autoencoders (G-SAE). FMS combines single-coordinate concept-classification accuracy with accuracy changes after informative-coordinate removal and gains from larger coordinate combinations. G-SAE adds binary-cross-entropy supervision on designated latent coordinates to activation reconstruction. Its decoder columns provide residual-stream steering directions. These procedures operationalize label localization and redundancy; exclusive semantic meaning and recovery of native mechanisms require additional evidence.

**Experiments**

Main experiments use Llama3-8B-base residual activations after blocks 3 or 11, 24,576 latent coordinates, nominal TopK budget 2,048, and 100 training epochs. Evaluations cover RealToxicityPrompts, Shakespeare-versus-modern text, and pii-masking-300k’s 24 privacy labels; mixed toxicity/style data support two-concept experiments. Comparators include an unconditioned SAE, ICV, DiffVec, PREADD, and Model Arithmetic. Steering scores average a concept endpoint with a Llama3.1-70B-instruct quality judgment, using Perspective for toxicity, a trained classifier for style, and Presidio-detected violation reduction for privacy. Additional experiments examine other Llama/Gemma checkpoints, SAEBench metrics, and supervised adaptation of a pretrained SAE.

**Key results**

Across three equally weighted dataset summaries, with privacy first averaged over 24 concepts, FMS@1 rises from 0.27 to 0.52 and single-coordinate accuracy from 0.70 to 0.86. The text reports that vanilla SAE needs 41 features on average to match guided single-coordinate accuracy, although captions also describe node counts. All 26 evaluated targets select their designated guided coordinate as the tree root. Mean activation-separation rank-biserial correlation rises from 0.18 to 0.59. Guided steering’s composite scores are 0.98 for detoxification, 0.72 for Shakespeare style, 0.82 for combined control, and 0.53 for privacy, versus 0.95, 0.64, 0.80, and 0.47 for vanilla SAE. DiffVec ties combined control. Post-hoc guidance improves FMS, but one privacy adaptation lowers the CE score from 0.991 to 0.897 and raises MSE from 0.002 to 0.008.

**Limitations / open questions**

Evaluation counts, split procedures, and repeated-run uncertainty are insufficiently specified. Numerical pairwise win rates are absent from the supplied table rendering, and plot images are unavailable. SAEBench changes are mixed. FMS does not independently establish semantic exclusivity or causal selectivity; its chance-level assumptions, stopping rules, and remaining-feature classifier capacity need clarification. Sequence labels are broadcast to tokens, related concepts retain cross-activation, and sigmoid-after-TopK leaves zero preservation unclear. Metadata dates initial publication; the supplied body identifies December 1, 2025 v2.

title: Dissecting Jet-Tagger Through Mechanistic Interpretability
abstract: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to reverse engineer a trained neural network by identifying the minimal subset of internal components. We perform a mechanistic interpretability analysis of the Particle Transformer architecture, trained on the Top Quark Tagging reference dataset, with the goal of identifying the computational circuit responsible for jet classification and characterizing the physical content of its internal representations. Combining zero ablation, path patching with two complementary on-manifold corruption strategies and linear probing of the residual stream, we identify a sparse six-head circuit that recovers the great majority of the full model performance while admitting a clean source-relay-readout interpretation. In this circuit, a single early layer head serves as the primary causal source, a cluster of middle-layer heads acts as relays selectively attending to hard pairwise substructure and a single late-layer head reads out the aggregated signal. Linear probes show that the residual stream is preferentially aligned with the energy correlator basis over the $N$-subjettiness basis. Within the energy correlator basis, the model preferentially encodes 2-prong substructure observables over the 3-prong observables. A per-layer trained probe further reveals that the apparent single step commitment of the model to a classification decision in the first class attention block is in fact a basis rotation, with the discriminating signal already saturating in the particle attention stack. These results demonstrate that mechanistic interpretability methods developed for natural language models can be used for jet physics classifiers and indicate that gradient descent may rediscover physically meaningful aspects of jet tagging without supervision.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper applies circuit analysis to a Particle Transformer distinguishing hadronic top-quark jets from light-quark/gluon jets. It identifies selected particle-attention heads consistent with a source–relay–readout organization and compares residual representations with classical jet-substructure observables. Alignment by class attention and emphasis on the two-prong hadronic W-decay subsystem are proposed mechanistic interpretations.

**Experiments**

The approximately 1.3M-parameter model has four particle-attention layers, four heads per layer, width 128, and two additional class-attention blocks. Training/validation/test splits contain 200,000/50,000/50,000 balanced simulated jets at transverse momentum 550–650 GeV. Five seeds assess classifier performance and singleton head-ablation rankings; detailed analyses principally use seed 0. Tests combine zero masking, clean-to-corrupted head-output transplants under two replacement procedures, downstream output-change norms, 200 random six-head controls, and standardized logistic or Ridge probes. Main probes use 7,000 training and 3,000 held-out jets from the original test set. A separate energy-correlator comparison uses 5,000 jets, truncating C3 and N3 calculations to the leading 50 and 40 constituents respectively.

**Key results**

Retaining six of sixteen particle-attention heads gives AUC 0.9527, with bootstrap 95% interval [0.9510, 0.9544], versus the reported full-model reference 0.9793. The stated 97.3% retention is a raw AUC ratio; MLPs, residual paths, and class attention remain available. Eight of 200 random six-head subsets meet or exceed the reported threshold of approximately 0.953. Recovery signs agree across particle replacement and whole-jet permutation. At particle depth L4, a fitted logistic probe achieves AUC 0.977 while the final-head logit lens yields 0.111. Selected energy-correlator peak Ridge R² values are C2 0.945, D2 0.845, N3 0.804, and C3 0.672. In the separate mass-control experiment, cubic mass residualization leaves D2 more predictable than tau32: peak R² 0.807 versus 0.531. Four of six heads nevertheless have larger class contrasts for the three-particle attention proxy than the two-particle proxy.

**Limitations / open questions**

Minimality, isolated causal edges, a pure basis rotation, and identification of W-decay constituents are not established. Probe accuracy measures accessibility; downstream output-change norms include intervening pathways. Negative pairwise ablation interactions do not uniquely identify redundancy or compensation. Detailed cross-seed replication and broader kinematics remain open. Gaussian corruption reverses the recovery denominator’s sign, which alone does not invalidate normalized recovery. Source inconsistencies include seed-0 AUC attribution, ambiguous distinctions between corruption procedures, and contradictory feature-ablation sign interpretations. Figures are available here only through accompanying text and captions.

title: Interpreting Emergent Features in Deep Learning-based Side-channel Analysis
abstract: Side-channel analysis (SCA) poses a real-world threat by exploiting unintentional physical signals to extract secret information from secure devices. Evaluation labs also use the same techniques to certify device security. In recent years, deep learning has emerged as a prominent method for SCA, achieving state-of-the-art attack performance at the cost of interpretability. Understanding how neural networks extract secrets is crucial for security evaluators aiming to defend against such attacks, as only by understanding the attack can one propose better countermeasures. In this work, we apply mechanistic interpretability to neural networks trained for SCA, revealing \textit{how} models exploit \textit{what} leakage in side-channel traces. We focus on sudden jumps in performance to reverse engineer learned representations, ultimately recovering secret masks and moving the evaluation process from black-box to white-box. Our results show that mechanistic interpretability can scale to realistic SCA settings, even when relevant inputs are sparse, model accuracies are low, and side-channel protections prevent standard input interventions.
summary:
**Central idea**
The paper interprets neural classifiers of masked AES side-channel measurements by working backward from outputs. Perceived Information (PI) identifies training transitions; class-conditioned logits suggest leakage features; principal components expose candidate secret-share representations; activation interventions test their output effects. Analysis assumes an already recovered key byte, enabling intermediate-value labels, but does not initially require mask labels. Recovered quantities are share Hamming weights or partial bit clusters, rather than complete mask bytes.

**Experiments**
Three public datasets each supply 10,000 attack traces. CHES_CTF contains power measurements and 30,000 profiling traces; ESHARD contains electromagnetic measurements and 90,000 profiling traces. Both use MLPs described as four layers of 40 neurons with ReLU activations and Hamming-weight targets. Variable-key ASCAD supplies electromagnetic measurements and 200,000 profiling traces, using an MLP described as six layers of 100 neurons with ELU activations and 256 identity classes. Analyses combine checkpoint comparisons, linear probes, PCA, coordinate interventions, and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) plots conditioned on inferred shares. One ASCAD CNN extends the architectural comparison.

**Key results**
CHES_CTF exhibits PI increases around epochs 15–40 and 70–85. The first accompanies high-versus-low target Hamming-weight discrimination; the second adds parity discrimination and a clearer share-weight grid. ESHARD shows one transition around epoch four and analogous high/low geometry without parity discrimination. Interventions yield share-weight assignments with plausible physical leakage locations; extraction accuracy is not quantified. ASCAD preferentially exposes the two least significant bits of both S-box input and output. A final-layer probe over their 16 combinations achieves 0.64 accuracy; its transformed predictions achieve PI of 2.47 bits versus 2.58 for the model. The reported entropy between prediction distributions is 0.27 bits, without a precise metric definition. ASCAD interventions affect bit readouts but do not accurately recover shares. Similar four-component geometry appears in the CNN.

**Limitations / open questions**
The experiments concern structured cryptographic tasks with few expected features, manual coordinate choices, and no reported repeated-seed uncertainty. Profiling and attack measurements come from the same device. Hamming-weight extraction relies on uniform-mask frequencies, adequate score ordering, and domain knowledge. ASCAD inferred shares merge expected classes and fail to recombine correctly. Automation, cross-device applicability, transformer analysis, and transfer to general language-model interpretation remain untested. Figure images are unavailable in the supplied rendering, and several Appendix H matrices appear only as placeholders, limiting independent visual and combinatorial checks.

title: Certified Mechanistic Interpretability: Lifting Single-Input Findings to Bounded Neighbourhoods
abstract: Mechanistic interpretability reverse-engineers transformer circuits one input at a time, leaving observed mechanisms without guarantees over bounded input neighbourhoods. We address this gap with a framework based on constrained polynomial-zonotope (CPZ) propagation that lifts mechanistic-interpretability observations from a single input to certified statements over a bounded set of perturbations. Three internal-attention queries (top-$k$ stability, evidence mass, and attention entropy) are formulated as tractable programs over the simplex of attention weights, and CPZ propagation through transformer blocks is shown to preserve the softmax simplex and the LayerNorm zero-mean identity exactly. A recursive Jacobian zonotope construction extends the same certificates across layer depth by linearising the block stack at the input and avoids per-layer generator growth. We instantiate the framework on transformer attention; the resulting certificates offer a way to sharpen mechanistic statements that single-input inspection cannot resolve on its own, and to inform downstream decisions in regimes where empirical heuristics may be misleading.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper proposes extending single-input attention observations to bounded post-embedding perturbation sets using constrained polynomial zonotopes (CPZs). Three queries concern attention-target stability, minimum evidence-position mass, and entropy ranges. Shared polynomial factors retain dependencies in bilinear query–key scores; probability-simplex constraints couple attention weights. A Jacobian-zonotope connector approximates preceding transformer blocks without sequential generator growth. These are attention properties; equating their preservation with preservation of a computational mechanism requires an additional assumption.

**Experiments**

Tests cover small synthetic transformers, BERT-tiny fine-tuned on SST-2, GPT-2 Small (124M), and GPT-2 Medium (355M). Perturbations jointly affect all input-token embeddings under an L-infinity bound; structured sets enclose five paraphrases. Comparators include polynomial zonotopes, CROWN, IBP, and budget-limited Monte Carlo plus PGD. Additional studies examine 60 authored IOI prompts, output stability, connector ablations, and pruning across 20 synthetic-model seeds.

**Key results**

On the IOI prompts, GPT-2 head 0.10 receives reported top-1 certificates on 60/60 inputs at epsilon=0.0005, versus 1/60 for head 0.1; clean attention targets the duplicate on 60/60 and 36/60, respectively. BERT-tiny layer-1 Q1 passes on 74/80 head–position queries from five inputs, versus 95% empirical stability, 51.2% CROWN, and 3.8% IBP. GPT-2 Small layer-1 rates are 47.9% versus 78.1% empirical stability across 480 queries from five inputs. At epsilon=0.002, GPT-2 output checks pass on 45/50 inputs against clean top-20 candidates, falling to 20/50 with the vocabulary-tail check. Pruning averages 84.5% PGD-evaluated accuracy versus 78.5% for gradient-guided pruning across all 20 seeds; outcomes differ on eight seeds.

**Limitations / open questions**

Universal soundness of the implemented pipeline is not established. Production uses inflated sampled remainders; being smaller than an analytical upper bound does not validate them. One scalar remainder factor per token generally cannot enclose arbitrary coordinatewise errors. Further gaps concern residual-generator tightening, global-extremum claims for multistart L-BFGS-B, and claimed efficient exact entropy minimization. Table 20 explicitly describes PGD violations of Q2 certificates; Table 8 also reports a certificate rate exceeding empirical stability. Earlier 1.5-factor output bounds failed attacks; revised calibration reports no detected output contradictions across 450 input–radius pairs. Baseline implementations, attack budgets, runtimes, and some entropy descriptions vary across sections; alpha-CROWN output comparisons use a different activation function. Discrete substitutions, causal mechanism preservation, and pruning benefits in pretrained LLMs remain unestablished.

title: Discovering a Zeta Map Algorithm on Dyck Paths via Mechanistic Interpretability
abstract: Machine learning is increasingly used in mathematical discovery, but in mathematics the desired output is often not a prediction itself, but an explicit construction that can be checked independently. We study this setting through the zeta map on Dyck paths, a classical bijection in the combinatorics of the q,t-Catalan numbers. We train a deliberately small one-layer, one-head encoder-decoder transformer on this map and analyze its learned computation using mechanistic interpretability tools, including decoder cross-attention analysis, linear probing, and causal intervention. The analysis reveals a level-based mechanism: encoder representations make path levels linearly accessible, while the decoder selects and traverses input positions in a structured way. Translating these signals into combinatorics leads to the scaffolding map, an explicit peak-centered traversal algorithm for Dyck paths. We prove that this algorithm agrees with the zeta map, modulo a reversal convention in the labeling. This gives a controlled example of AI-assisted mathematical discovery in which mechanistic interpretability turns model behavior into a precise, human-verifiable combinatorial algorithm.
summary:
**Central idea**
The paper uses interpretation of a small transformer to formulate an independently verifiable combinatorial algorithm. Targets come from SageMath’s `area_dinv_to_bounce_area_map()`, corresponding to the classical Dyck-path zeta map followed by word reversal and bit swapping. Internal signals motivate the scaffolding map: compute path levels, process peaks from highest to lowest level, and traverse adjacent runs using agents, emitting symbols in decreasing position order within each level.

**Experiments**
Width-256 encoder–decoder transformers with four layers per side and eight heads reportedly exceed 99% accuracy at separately studied semilengths 11–16. The listed datasets contain the corresponding Catalan numbers of paths, ranging from 58,786 to 35,357,670; training and evaluation splits are unspecified. Selected architectural variants also reportedly achieve near-perfect accuracy. Interpretation focuses on the Minimal Dyck Transformer trained at semilength 13, whose complete task space contains 742,900 paths. It has width 128, one encoder block, one decoder block, one attention head, GELU feed-forward width 256, and learned positional embeddings. Analyses inspect cross-attention, mask attention to North-step input positions during decoding, fit linear level probes, and visualize positional embeddings using PCA.

**Key results**
The text reports recurring attention toward high-level positions and triangular shifts through East-step positions. Masking all North-step cross-attention reportedly causes negligible degradation in generated-prefix accuracy. Linear probes predict corresponding path levels with 84% accuracy. These findings motivate an approximate level-based selection and traversal interpretation, without establishing complete neural–symbolic correspondence. Theorem 6.1 and Appendix D provide a combinatorial proof identifying scaffolding queues with reversed area-sequence scans, establishing the symbolic algorithm’s equivalence to the convention-adjusted zeta map for arbitrary positive semilengths.

**Limitations / open questions**
The proof concerns the symbolic algorithm; the neural implementation remains approximate. Neither level probing nor North-step masking excludes information aggregated into unmasked East-step states, despite the text claiming otherwise. Training details, evaluation counts, uncertainty, probe baselines, and accuracy definitions are largely unspecified. Parameter counts conflict: 339,716 in Section 4 versus approximately 366,000 in Appendix B. Plots are unavailable as visual evidence in the supplied rendering, so numerical ablation effects cannot be recovered beyond the prose description. Neural length generalization is untested, small models can exhibit different internal solutions across seeds, and automation or transfer of this discovery workflow to larger models remains open.

Outliers Dimensions that Disrupt Transformers Are Driven by Frequency
abstract: While Transformer-based language models are generally very robust to pruning, there is the recently discovered outlier phenomenon: disabling only 48 out of 110M parameters in BERT-base drops its performance by nearly 30% on MNLI. We replicate the original evidence for the outlier phenomenon and we link it to the geometry of the embedding space. We find that in both BERT and RoBERTa the magnitude of hidden state coefficients corresponding to outlier dimensions correlates with the frequency of encoded tokens in pre-training data, and it also contributes to the "vertical" self-attention pattern enabling the model to focus on the special tokens. This explains the drop in performance from disabling the outliers, and it suggests that to decrease anisotropicity in future models we need pre-training schemas that would better take into account the skewed token distributions.
summary:
**Central idea**

A few unusually large, consistently indexed LayerNorm scale and bias coordinates can be disproportionately important to BERT-family models. The paper connects these disruptive coordinates to token frequency and vertical attention, where many positions attend to the same token. Skewed pre-training frequencies are proposed as a contributing cause, with causal attribution explicitly limited by confounds.

**Experiments**

Selected LayerNorm parameters are zeroed after fine-tuning BERT-base-uncased and RoBERTa-base on eight GLUE tasks. BERT results average five fine-tuning runs and include random-coordinate controls. Further experiments evaluate ViT on CIFAR-10/100 and follow one MultiBERTs seed through two million pre-training steps. MLM prediction counts are examined over 200,000 Wikipedia sentences with 15% masking. WikiText-v2 validation activations support layerwise Pearson correlations with estimated training-token frequencies; 1,500 sequences support BERT attention correlations. Three BERT-medium models share initialization and train for 327,500 steps with different separator placement or frequent-token replacement schemes.

**Key results**

Removing BERT coordinates 308 and 381 zeros 48 parameters and reduces MNLI-matched accuracy from 84.5% to 58.4%; two random removals leave it at 84.5%. RoBERTa's joint removal reduces accuracy from 87.6% to 44.9%. ViT's joint removal reduces CIFAR-100 accuracy from 92.5% to 84.9%, while CIFAR-10 changes from 98.6% to 98.5%. Exploratory screening finds no comparable outliers in the inspected protein and audio transformers, with limited methodological detail.

Outlier removal shifts MLM predictions toward frequent tokens. Selected coordinate magnitudes correlate with token frequency and received attention, including when special tokens are excluded, although relationships vary with depth and can be negative. BERT coordinate 381 has especially large disruption around layers 4–6; coordinate 308 has stronger late-layer MLM effects. Frequent-token replacement produces weaker individual-coordinate ablation effects, while lowering intact MNLI accuracy to 76.8%, versus 79.6% under SENTENCE. Reducing separator frequency alone leaves a strongly damaging outlier.

**Limitations / open questions**

Selection incorporates downstream damage. Frequency estimates use proxy corpora, especially incomplete for RoBERTa. Pre-training interventions alter linguistic structure and model quality and lack repeated-seed comparisons. Attention correlations and an illustrative ablation do not establish mediation of accuracy loss. Magnitude-based descriptions versus coordinate-value implementation details are ambiguous. Figures lack accessible plotted values; conclusions here use supplied prose and tables. Special-token frequency versus functional role and mitigation without capability loss remain unresolved.

The Misery of Mechanistic Interpretability: A Formal Perspective
abstract: Mechanistic interpretability has become the dominant lens for understanding frontier language models, as their inner workings are complex and inherently black boxes. To gain insights into these models, interpretable replacement networks (IRNs) are trained at all layers, exposing interpretable features through sparsely activated neurons. However, the faithfulness of an IRN is usually evaluated only empirically on clean data, and we show that even semantically minor input perturbations flip the dominant IRN features-and thus the human-understandable interpretation-across five open-weight model families (GPT-2 small, Gemma 2 2B, Gemma 3 1B, Llama 3.2 1B, R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B). We propose the first formal verification framework for the faithfulness of an IRN, where reachability analysis certifies a sound upper bound of the faithfulness gap in adversarial scenarios. Moreover, we show that verification-aware training of IRNs substantially tightens this certified bound, restoring a feature-level interpretation that safety auditors can act on. Together, these results give, to the best of our knowledge, the first formal guarantees for mechanistic interpretability of large language models.
summary:
**Central idea**
The paper certifies local numerical fidelity of interpretable replacement networks: an SAE approximates the identity, while a transcoder approximates its corresponding MLP throughout a specified hidden-state box. CORA reachability analysis encloses the difference network, giving a uniform infinity-norm error upper bound; PGD supplies witnessed lower bounds. These are approximation guarantees. Treating them as guarantees of preserved computational mechanisms requires an additional assumption.

**Experiments**
The evaluation selects polysemous target words in 1,000 WikiText-2 sentences, split 600/200/200 into training, validation, and test sets. Prefix perturbations replace one content word, replace all content words, or use Gemma-2-2B-it paraphrasing. Verification and PGD operate inside coordinatewise boxes enclosing resulting target-token activations. These boxes also contain points that need not represent any sentence. Nine model–dictionary configurations cover GPT-2 Small, Gemma 2 2B, Gemma 3 1B, Llama 3.2 1B, and R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B. GPT-2 SAE fine-tuning compares reconstruction training, adversarial training, reachable-set training, and LoRA variants over 50 epochs.

**Key results**
Across the nine configurations, reported worst-layer attack-derived top-20 Jaccard bounds range from 0.27–0.70 for minor regions and 0.05–0.38 for major regions. These upper-bound worst-case overlap within continuous hidden-state regions. The paper reports increasing local approximation errors with depth. Llama's layer-1 median attack/certificate error bounds are 0.055/0.225 for minor regions and 0.187/1.935 for major regions. The main GPT-2 layer-6 comparison reports approximately 90% smaller certified upper bounds after set-based training. Mean clean active-feature counts decrease from 74.4 to 13.9, whereas Set+LoRA increases them to 143.8. Benefits depend on radius: at uniform radius 0.01, Set worsens the median certified bound from 10.98 to 30.38; at radius 0.1, it improves it from 320.36 to 94.60. Only 2–3 clean top-20 features are reportedly certified to persist.

**Limitations / open questions**
Full-model compositional verification remains prospective: independently constructed hidden-state boxes do not certify coverage of all propagated input perturbations. Semantic equivalence of paraphrases, feature-label validity after fine-tuning, and safety-auditor benefits are not independently evaluated. Sparsity and numerical fidelity do not establish semantic completeness. The Jaccard derivation incorrectly presents a sufficient interval condition as necessary; activation thresholds, zero ties, and its printed survivor-set definition need qualification. Several results are accessible only through figure descriptions, without numerical plot data. Supplementary Lean checking is reported but cannot be inspected here. The descriptions of whether Std is the released baseline or a reconstruction-fine-tuned control are inconsistent.

title: Unsupervised decoding of encoded reasoning using language model interpretability
abstract: As large language models become increasingly capable, there is growing concern that they may develop reasoning processes that are encoded or hidden from human oversight. To investigate whether current interpretability techniques can penetrate such encoded reasoning, we construct a controlled testbed by fine-tuning a reasoning model (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B) to perform chain-of-thought reasoning in ROT-13 encryption while maintaining intelligible English outputs. We evaluate mechanistic interpretability methods--in particular, logit lens analysis--on their ability to decode the model's hidden reasoning process using only internal activations. We show that logit lens can effectively translate encoded reasoning, with accuracy peaking in intermediate-to-late layers. Finally, we develop a fully unsupervised decoding pipeline that combines logit lens with automated paraphrasing, achieving substantial accuracy in reconstructing complete reasoning transcripts from internal model representations. These findings suggest that current mechanistic interpretability techniques may be more robust to simple forms of encoded reasoning than previously understood. Our work provides an initial framework for evaluating interpretability methods against models that reason in non-human-readable formats, contributing to the broader challenge of maintaining oversight over increasingly capable AI systems.
summary:
**Central idea**
The paper constructs a controlled model of opaque chain-of-thought and tests whether internal vocabulary readouts recover its English content. DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B is fine-tuned to generate ROT-13 thinking followed by intelligible answers. Recovering the encoded transcript does not establish that this transcript faithfully describes all underlying computation.

**Experiments**
Training uses 85,500 LMSYS-derived examples, two epochs of 4-bit rank-8 QLoRA, and frozen embedding and unembedding matrices. Appendix B specifies 1,200-token base-model generations and clipping converted assistant responses to 2,048 tokens. Evaluation uses 50 handcrafted and Claude Sonnet 4-generated person–state–capital questions. Analyses measure English-translation vocabulary readouts across layers and cosine similarity between encoded-trace activations and baseline-subtracted English concept templates. A decoding pipeline removes repeated logit-lens words and asks Llama-8B to reconstruct readable paragraphs. Llama-70B grades similarity to cipher-decoded reference transcripts on a 0–10 scale. Comparisons include layers 40 and 58, nearby-layer logit averaging, confidence filtering, raw encoded text, and unrelated-transcript baselines.

**Key results**
The encoded model answers 72% of the 50 questions correctly. The authors report typo-tolerant intermediate-person and state identification rates of 73.5% and 83.7%; their denominators are unclear. English translation readouts peak around layer 58. Concept-versus-random alignment at encoded mentions peaks around layer 20 and subsequently declines. Layer-58 reconstructions receive higher similarity scores than layer-40 reconstructions; nearby-layer averaging adds little, while confidence filtering reportedly improves scores. Numerical transcription probabilities and grader-score means cannot be recovered from the supplied image-only plots. Examples show substantial content recovery alongside paraphraser additions, person conflations, and confusion between birth cities and state capitals.

**Limitations / open questions**
Evidence covers one adapted model, one simple cipher, and a narrow factual task. Low-rank training on transformed English traces may preserve English-aligned representations, making transfer to complex or RL-emergent encodings uncertain. No matched base-model accuracy establishes preserved reasoning quality. Decoding requires neither base-model access nor a fitted cipher-specific translator, but layer selection uses known translation performance, limiting claims of completely blind unsupervised selection. Confidence thresholds and human calibration of similarity grading are unspecified. Appendix F illustrates averaging layers 56–64, whereas the main comparison specifies 54–62. Appendix D uses inconsistent tolerance notation. These reporting and figure-access limitations do not indicate a truncated source.

title: Monet: Mixture of Monosemantic Experts for Transformers
abstract: Understanding the internal computations of large language models (LLMs) is crucial for aligning them with human values and preventing undesirable behaviors like toxic content generation. However, mechanistic interpretability is hindered by polysemanticity -- where individual neurons respond to multiple, unrelated concepts. While Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have attempted to disentangle these features through sparse dictionary learning, they have compromised LLM performance due to reliance on post-hoc reconstruction loss. To address this issue, we introduce Mixture of Monosemantic Experts for Transformers (Monet) architecture, which incorporates sparse dictionary learning directly into end-to-end Mixture-of-Experts pretraining. Our novel expert decomposition method enables scaling the expert count to 262,144 per layer while total parameters scale proportionally to the square root of the number of experts. Our analyses demonstrate mutual exclusivity of knowledge across experts and showcase the parametric knowledge encapsulated within individual experts. Moreover, Monet allows knowledge manipulation over domains, languages, and toxicity mitigation without degrading general performance. Our pursuit of transparent LLMs highlights the potential of scaling expert counts to enhance mechanistic interpretability and directly resect the internal knowledge to fundamentally adjust model behavior. The source code and pretrained checkpoints are available at https://github.com/dmis-lab/Monet.
summary:
**Central idea**

Monet builds interpretable components into transformer pretraining through 262,144 composed experts per layer. Horizontal decomposition combines shared input and output projections; vertical decomposition combines shared matrix blocks. Expert-parameter storage scales with the square root of the indexed expert count at fixed dimensions. These combinations share parameters extensively. Routing is reused across four-layer groups, with batch-normalization-based quantile estimation proposed to replace top-k sorting.

**Experiments**

Horizontal and vertical Monet models at 850M, 1.4B, and 4.1B parameters receive 100B FineWeb-Edu training tokens alongside similarly sized dense LLaMA-architecture controls. CodeMonet-1.4B receives 100B StarCoderData tokens. Evaluations cover eight knowledge and commonsense benchmarks, 14 regrouped MMLU domains, and six programming languages selected for highest baseline MultiPL-E performance. Masks select experts using routing skewness or routing–toxicity correlations. RealToxicityPrompts uses approximately 1,200 challenging prompts, each with 25 twenty-token continuations; ToxiGen uses 31,000 prompts. Instruction-tuned and vision-language derivatives supply qualitative interpretation examples.

**Key results**

Vertical Monet's zero-shot benchmark averages are 0.453, 0.478, and 0.511, versus dense controls' 0.463, 0.484, and 0.520. Vertical decomposition exceeds horizontal decomposition on every reported scale-by-shot aggregate. Domain masking produces reported target accuracy losses of 0.37–5.49 percentage points, while mean other-domain changes range from −0.51 to +0.04 points. In the six selected programming languages, target pass@100 falls 9.1–30.6 points, versus average losses elsewhere of 0.6–1.8 points, using 200 sampled completions per problem at temperature 0.8. Removing 4.1% of experts lowers RealToxicityPrompts' toxic-prompt expected maximum toxicity from 0.795 to 0.657 and its prompt-level incidence of at least one toxic continuation from 0.926 to 0.768; the rounded general benchmark average remains 0.478. On ToxiGen, removing 5.4% lowers the hate-prompt classifier score from 0.642 to 0.504 while benchmark performance falls to 0.473.

**Limitations / open questions**

Selective benchmark impairment does not establish monosemantic experts, exclusive knowledge storage, or irreversible unlearning. Displayed experts include mixed lexical associations, and self-descriptions lack quantitative evaluation. Stronger toxicity masks reduce general benchmark scores. Selection/evaluation separation, uncertainty estimates, and matched random-mask controls are unspecified. SAE replacement configurations are incompletely specified. Multimodal claims rely on qualitative illustrations whose images are unavailable in this rendering. The printed uniformity loss leaves zero-probability handling unresolved. Experiments do not isolate expert count as the cause of specialization or establish a general scaling law.

title: From Indirect Object Identification to Syllogisms: Exploring Binary Mechanisms in Transformer Circuits
abstract: Transformer-based language models (LMs) can perform a wide range of tasks, and mechanistic interpretability (MI) aims to reverse engineer the components responsible for task completion to understand their behavior. Previous MI research has focused on linguistic tasks such as Indirect Object Identification (IOI). In this paper, we investigate the ability of GPT-2 small to handle binary truth values by analyzing its behavior with syllogistic prompts, e.g., "Statement A is true. Statement B matches statement A. Statement B is", which requires more complex logical reasoning compared to IOI. Through our analysis of several syllogism tasks of varying difficulty, we identify multiple circuits that mechanistically explain GPT-2's logical-reasoning capabilities and uncover binary mechanisms that facilitate task completion, including the ability to produce a negated token not present in the input prompt through negative heads. Our evaluation using a faithfulness metric shows that a circuit comprising five attention heads achieves over 90% of the original model's performance. By relating our findings to IOI analysis, we provide new insights into the roles of specific attention heads and MLPs in LMs. These insights contribute to a broader understanding of model reasoning and support future research in mechanistic interpretability.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper investigates GPT-2 Small on templated completions involving assigned binary values. Simple Syllogisms (SS) require repeating a supplied truth value; Opposite Syllogisms (OS) require its opposite; Complex Syllogisms (CS) introduce a distractor assignment. Its central mechanistic proposal is that selected attention heads suppress the supplied truth token and downstream MLPs help favor the opposite answer. Previously identified IOI components provide reference points for interpreting these behaviors.

**Experiments**

The authors combine path patching, attention-pattern and QK/OV analysis, vocabulary projections, and retained-circuit evaluations. Table 1 reports 500 prompts per task, varying capital-letter identifiers and truth values. The outcome is correct-minus-incorrect answer logit difference; faithfulness is formally defined as the absolute difference between circuit and full-model average logit differences (ALDs). Appendix B transfers fixed SS/OS circuits to right/wrong, good/bad, positive/negative, and correct/incorrect. Appendix C compares MLP patching with and without restored attention context. Appendix D examines GPT-2 XL, Pythia-1.4B, Qwen3-1.7B, and LLaMA-3.2-1B.

**Key results**

GPT-2 Small's SS, OS, and CS ALDs are 1.8575, 1.2123, and 1.3105. The SS circuit reaches 1.9286. Head 10.7 hurts SS performance but contributes positively to OS, consistent with a suppression operation having task-dependent utility. OS inversion is reportedly more reliable from true to false than from false to true. CS analyses identify downstream suppression and modulation groups receiving shared identifier- and induction-associated inputs. Transfer fidelity varies: the OS circuit obtains 1.0113 versus the full model's 3.0032 on positive/negative. Larger-model analyses report different negative-head involvement, and Pythia is an exception to reported OS MLP dependence. Early-MLP patching effects diminish when attention context is restored.

**Limitations / open questions**

Binary margins and narrow templates do not establish general deductive reasoning, relation-sensitive computation, or complete mechanisms. Table 3 places both true and false among top post-MLP readouts, so it alone does not establish selective promotion of the opposite token. Corruption construction, final circuit membership, evaluation ablations, uncertainty, and held-out validation are insufficiently specified. The abstract's five-head, over-90% claim conflicts with the introduction's three-head SS claim and five-head/four-MLP OS claim of approximately 85%; these percentages are not reconciled with the absolute-error definition or Appendix B's ALDs. Figure contents are unavailable in this rendering and several references are unresolved; the article and appendices otherwise appear complete. Cross-model findings remain exploratory.

title: When the Coffee Feature Activates on Coffins: An Analysis of Feature Extraction and Steering for Mechanistic Interpretability
abstract: Recent work by Anthropic on Mechanistic interpretability claims to understand and control Large Language Models by extracting human-interpretable features from their neural activation patterns using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). If successful, this approach offers one of the most promising routes for human oversight in AI safety. We conduct an initial stress-test of these claims by replicating their main results with open-source SAEs for Llama 3.1. While we successfully reproduce basic feature extraction and steering capabilities, our investigation suggests that major caution is warranted regarding the generalizability of these claims. We find that feature steering exhibits substantial fragility, with sensitivity to layer selection, steering magnitude, and context. We observe non-standard activation behavior and demonstrate the difficulty to distinguish thematically similar features from one another. While SAE-based interpretability produces compelling demonstrations in selected cases, current methods often fall short of the systematic reliability required for safety-critical applications. This suggests a necessary shift in focus from prioritizing interpretability of internal representations toward reliable prediction and control of model output. Our work contributes to a more nuanced understanding of what mechanistic interpretability has achieved and highlights fundamental challenges for AI safety that remain unresolved.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper qualitatively reproduces SAE feature activation and steering demonstrations, then tests whether automated descriptions reliably characterize selected features. It distinguishes successful examples of interpretable control from evidence of dependable control suitable for safety applications.

**Experiments**

The authors use Llama-3.1-8B-Base with 32 Llama Scope residual-stream SAEs, each containing 32,768 latents. Descriptions are generated by o4-mini using SlimPajama examples. Reported generation settings include temperature 0.5, seed 16, frequency penalty 1.0, and 70 output tokens. Tests use authored passages, short contextual contrasts, and coefficient sweeps. Coffee feature 18/9463 is examined in English, German, and Japanese. Its specificity test uses 16 sentences, four per relevance category, measuring maximum and mean nonzero activation. Five layer-18 coffee features are compared on ten description-selected terms per feature; three identically labeled features are compared across layers 6, 19, and 29.

**Key results**

Feature 18/9463 activates around coffee vocabulary across the three languages and can promote or suppress coffee-related generation. Selected sadness, conditional-language, and list features also produce interpretation-consistent examples. Other descriptions obscure lexical responses: coffee-labeled feature 29/30028 activates on “coff” in coffee-related text and coffins, and negative steering changes “coffin” to “casket.” An exposure-labeled feature responds in photographic contexts outside its stated interpretation. Similar descriptions do not consistently distinguish selected features’ activation profiles, contextual requirements, or steering responses. Six selected latents have reported activation densities above 90%; eight exhibit unusually large beginning-of-text activations. These properties do not establish that the latents are functionless. Steering also produces unexpected alternatives: tennis steering yields soccer at coefficient 1 and tennis at 2; a coffee-health feature yields coffee at 5, initially tea at 6, and degraded text at 8.

**Limitations / open questions**

The selected case studies lack representative sampling, population failure rates, repeated-seed uncertainty, and systematic capability or safety benchmarks. They neither refute the existence of useful SAE interventions nor directly test Claude. Extrapolation to proprietary models assumes weak universality. Layer comparisons confound depth with feature identity and intervention magnitude. Intervention mechanics remain ambiguous: Section 4.3 describes activation scaling, whereas Appendix 8.1 describes coefficients multiplying feature vectors. The conditional-language example also has inconsistent coefficients between main text and appendix. Some image-based high-strength outputs are inaccessible in this rendering. Native reasoning faithfulness remains untested; the authors recommend prioritizing reproducible behavioral effects and side effects.

title: Circuit Tracing in Autoregressive Protein Language Models
abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) can generate novel protein sequences with properties beyond those observed in nature, yet the mechanisms underlying protein generation remain poorly understood. Existing mechanistic interpretability methods based on sparse autoencoders and transcoders primarily focus on protein representation learning models and do not capture the computation required for autoregressive generation. Here, we introduce ProGenMech, a mechanistic interpretability framework for generative protein language models that extends cross-layer transcoders (CLTs) to ProGen3, a sparse Mixture-of-Experts model trained for both causal generation and span infilling. Unlike per-layer approaches, CLTs reconstruct each layer using sparse latent variables from all preceding layers, enabling faithful recovery of inter-layer generative computation. We further develop a zero-shot circuit discovery framework to identify sparse latent circuits responsible for protein generation and fitness prediction. In causal generation and zero-shot fitness estimation tasks, ProGenMech outperforms local transcoder baselines in recovering ProGen3's probability distribution and functional scoring behavior, while matching the original model's generative distribution in span infilling tasks. Moreover, the recovered circuits reveal biologically meaningful motifs and functional regions associated with conserved sequence patterns and protein fitness landscapes, establishing a foundation for interpretable and steerable protein generation.
summary:
**Central idea**

ProGenMech adapts cross-layer transcoders (CLTs) to ProGen3-112M, a ten-layer mixture-of-experts protein language model. Sparse latents reconstruct aggregated expert outputs using contributions from the current and preceding layers, abstracting away individual experts and routing. Gradient-times-activation rankings select candidate circuits; a visualizer combines attribution edges, activating sequences, and biological annotations.

**Experiments**

CLTs and per-layer transcoders (PLTs) were trained on five million UniRef50 sequences, with 4,608 latents per layer and 64 retained activations per token per layer. Generation evaluation used 1,000 Swiss-Prot sequences clustered at 30% identity and selected so baseline generations passed a low-complexity filter. Tasks comprised continuation from an 80% prefix and short-span infilling. Generated regions were scored using original-model negative log-likelihood (NLL). Fitness evaluation covered eight ProteinGym assays with five repeated splits, each containing 256 label-balanced discovery mutants and 1,000 similarly balanced held-out mutants. Although scoring is called zero-shot, fitness labels inform circuit-size selection through discovery-set Spearman correlation.

**Key results**

For continuation, all-latent sequential CLTs achieved NLL 2.50 ± 0.42 versus PLTs' 2.57 ± 0.36 and ProGen3's 2.00 ± 0.62. CLT circuits achieved 2.54 ± 0.39 using 719 ± 339 of 46,080 available latents, under 2%. Infilling NLLs were close: all-latent CLT 2.89 ± 0.46, PLT 2.87 ± 0.43, and ProGen3 2.91 ± 0.44. Across fitness assays, mean Spearman correlations were 0.28 ± 0.12 for all-latent CLTs, 0.25 ± 0.12 for PLTs, and 0.29 ± 0.15 for ProGen3. CLT circuits achieved 0.23 ± 0.13 using 256 ± 334 latents. Selected kinase and GRB2 examples exhibited annotation-consistent activation patterns and attribution changes. Steering on four assays selected for high baseline fitness correlation did not establish improved generation.

**Limitations / open questions**

Main evaluations retain original-model attention outputs and supply original-model activations between generation steps; autonomous replacements perform worse. Generation circuits are evaluated on their discovery sequences. Similar NLL summaries establish neither distributional equivalence nor biological functionality. Qualitative annotations and frozen-linearization edges do not independently validate native causal mechanisms. Steering outputs failed the low-complexity filter, and intervention details are sparse. Evidence concerns one small backbone, lacks new laboratory validation, and supplies no inferential tests establishing the reported advantages or equivalence. CLTs have greater parameter capacity than PLTs and quadratic decoder growth with depth. Additional replacement comparisons are described in prose, but their plotted numerical values are unavailable in the supplied rendering.

title: MechELK: A Mechanistic Interpretability Framework for Eliciting Latent Knowledge in Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) frequently encode factual and reasoning knowledge in their internal representations that is not faithfully reflected in their surface-level outputs -- a phenomenon known as \emph{latent knowledge}. Existing approaches to eliciting latent knowledge, such as Contrastive Consistency Search (CCS), rely on contrastive activation patterns and struggle with complex multi-step reasoning tasks, while mechanistic interpretability tools have primarily been used to \emph{understand} model behavior rather than to \emph{extract} hidden knowledge. We present \textbf{MechELK}, a unified three-stage framework that bridges mechanistic interpretability and latent knowledge elicitation. MechELK operates through: (1) \textbf{Locate} -- using Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) feature analysis and activation patching to identify knowledge-bearing representations; (2) \textbf{Verify} -- employing causal probing to distinguish genuine latent knowledge from spurious correlations; and (3) \textbf{Elicit} -- applying representation engineering to surface hidden knowledge without modifying model weights. Evaluated on TruthfulQA, a curated Deceptive Alignment benchmark, and the Quirky LM dataset, MechELK achieves an average elicitation accuracy of 84.7\%, outperforming CCS by 6.2\% and direct linear probing by 9.1\%. Crucially, MechELK successfully identifies latent knowledge in 78.3\% of cases where the model's surface output is incorrect or evasive, demonstrating its utility for AI safety applications including deceptive alignment detection.
summary:
**Central idea**

MechELK combines mechanistic interpretability with latent knowledge elicitation. Locate contrasts SAE activations for correct and incorrect answer continuations and selects a layer by patching from the correct-answer continuation. Verify filters decoder directions using a Causal Knowledge Score (CKS). Elicit adds their CKS-weighted sum to the residual stream without updating model weights. The specified algorithm requires each query’s ground-truth answer throughout location and verification; answer-independent deployment is not described.

**Experiments**

The paper evaluates Llama-3-8B, Llama-3-70B, and Mistral-7B-v0.3 on TruthfulQA MC1 (817 questions, 38 categories), Quirky LM (1,200 questions), and a curated Deceptive Alignment Benchmark (DAB; 400 scenarios). Comparators are direct linear probing, CCS, RepE, SAE probing, and layer-level activation patching. Settings include 65,536 SAE latents, 20 candidates, perturbation magnitude 0.1, threshold 0.15, and steering strength 1.2. Threshold and strength use a 10% validation split; direct probes train on 80%. Appendix B reports three-seed accuracies. Paraphrase analysis uses 50 sets of five queries.

**Key results**

Table 5 reports higher MechELK accuracy than CCS in all nine model–dataset cells: 79.6–87.4% versus 65.9–81.2%. Equal-weight averages calculated from these cells are 83.1% and 73.6%, conflicting with the headline 84.7% versus 78.5%. On Llama-3-8B TruthfulQA, removing verification lowers accuracy from 82.3% to 76.1% and raises reported FPR from 12.7% to 24.3%. Removing layer selection produces the larger accuracy drop, to 74.8%. Reported paraphrase cosine consistency is 0.89, versus 0.68 for CCS and 0.61 for direct probing. The abstract’s 78.3% identification rate among incorrect or evasive outputs has no detailed supporting analysis.

**Limitations / open questions**

Correct-answer conditioning confounds recovery of pre-existing knowledge with answer-informed output redirection. Independent knowledge-presence labels, DAB construction, quirky checkpoint training, and evaluation denominators and splits are insufficiently specified. CKS inconsistently denotes a log-probability derivative and a probability finite difference. Proposition 1 does not establish answer dominance or candidate-state linear separation from positive local sensitivity; Theorem 1 does not derive its reconstruction-to-cosine guarantee. FPR decreasing from 28.4% to 12.7% implies approximately 55% relative reduction, contradicting the claimed 34%. The stated 8.6% elicitation-failure rate equals the complement of detection rate, rather than accuracy. The 13B scaling configuration is unspecified. Figure plots are unavailable in the supplied rendering; textual descriptions remain accessible. Fragmentation, SAE coverage, intervention disruption, and reliable deceptive-intent identification remain unresolved.

title: Disentangling Recall and Reasoning in Transformer Models through Layer-wise Attention and Activation Analysis
abstract: Transformer-based language models excel at both recall (retrieving memorized facts) and reasoning (performing multi-step inference), but whether these abilities rely on distinct internal mechanisms remains unclear. Distinguishing recall from reasoning is crucial for predicting model generalization, designing targeted evaluations, and building safer interventions that affect one ability without disrupting the other.We approach this question through mechanistic interpretability, using controlled datasets of synthetic linguistic puzzles to probe transformer models at the layer, head, and neuron level. Our pipeline combines activation patching and structured ablations to causally measure component contributions to each task type. Across two model families (Qwen and LLaMA), we find that interventions on distinct layers and attention heads lead to selective impairments: disabling identified "recall circuits" reduces fact-retrieval accuracy by up to 15\% while leaving reasoning intact, whereas disabling "reasoning circuits" reduces multi-step inference by a comparable margin. At the neuron level, we observe task-specific firing patterns, though these effects are less robust, consistent with neuronal polysemanticity.Our results provide the first causal evidence that recall and reasoning rely on separable but interacting circuits in transformer models. These findings advance mechanistic interpretability by linking circuit-level structure to functional specialization and demonstrate how controlled datasets and causal interventions can yield mechanistic insights into model cognition, informing safer deployment of large language models.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper investigates whether factual retrieval and compositional reasoning involve partially separable transformer components. It combines task-associated activation measurements with targeted interventions, interpreting selective performance losses as evidence of functional specialization. Despite broader claims in both abstracts, the experimental methods document only Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct; the conclusion identifies LLaMA and Mistral as future extensions.

**Experiments**

The reported dataset contains 60 prompts: 30 recall and 30 reasoning tasks. Sources include IOL-style linguistic puzzles and synthetic country–capital–continent questions. Synthetic pairs share factual seeds but contrast direct retrieval with inference from supplied premises; generated facts were reportedly checked against Wikidata. How naturalistic puzzles and synthetic pairs compose the final inventory is unclear.

Using nnsight, FP16 inference, temperature zero, and an A100 GPU, the authors trace final-input-token activations across 28 layers. Metrics include hidden-state norms, attention entropy and concentration, MLP magnitude, sparsity, and neuron firing probabilities. They report Mann–Whitney tests, Cohen’s d, FDR correction for layers and heads, Bonferroni correction for neurons, and five-fold classification stability. Selected components are zeroed or replaced, with equal-size random ablations as controls.

**Key results**

Recall-targeted interventions reportedly reduce recall accuracy by 15% ± 3%; reasoning-targeted interventions reduce reasoning accuracy by approximately 14% ± 4%. Table 3 gives cross-task losses of 2% and 3%, respectively, versus 2% on both tasks for controls. Relative percentages versus percentage-point changes and the meaning of the uncertainty terms are unspecified.

The paper reports approximately 74% of attention heads showing task preferences. Table 1 lists 583 consistently specialized heads: 239 recall, 219 reasoning, and 125 mixed; the denominator and relationship to the percentage are unexplained. Approximately one-third of MLP neurons reportedly meet task-specificity criteria, with activation clusters near layers 4 and 22.

**Limitations / open questions**

The claimed shallow-recall/deep-reasoning hierarchy conflicts with Table 2: reasoning-specialized layers are 1, 2, and 18, while recall-specialized layers extend through layer 25. The metadata abstract describes neuron effects as less robust, whereas the body claims strong stability. Baseline accuracies, intervention sizes, replacement donors, scoring rules, and intervention train/test separation are insufficiently specified. Task labels do not establish cognitive isolation or exclude prior puzzle exposure, information-availability differences, and prompt confounds. Plot contents are unavailable in this text rendering, so numerical conclusions rely on prose and tables. The findings provide preliminary, task-conditioned evidence rather than establishing general architectural separation.

title: Unboxing the Black Box: Mechanistic Interpretability for Algorithmic Understanding of Neural Networks
abstract: The black box nature of deep neural networks poses a significant challenge for the deployment of transparent and trustworthy artificial intelligence (AI) systems. With the growing presence of AI in society, it becomes increasingly important to develop methods that can explain and interpret the decisions made by these systems. To address this, mechanistic interpretability (MI) emerged as a promising and distinctive research program within the broader field of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). MI is the process of studying the inner computations of neural networks and translating them into human-understandable algorithms. It encompasses reverse engineering techniques aimed at uncovering the computational algorithms implemented by neural networks. In this article, we propose a unified taxonomy of MI approaches and provide a detailed analysis of key techniques, illustrated with concrete examples and pseudo-code. We contextualize MI within the broader interpretability landscape, comparing its goals, methods, and insights to other strands of XAI. Additionally, we trace the development of MI as a research area, highlighting its conceptual roots and the accelerating pace of recent work. We argue that MI holds significant potential to support a more scientific understanding of machine learning systems -- treating models not only as tools for solving tasks, but also as systems to be studied and understood. We hope to invite new researchers into the field of mechanistic interpretability.
summary:
**Central idea**

This survey defines mechanistic interpretability as studying neural networks’ internal computations and translating them into human-understandable algorithms. It connects this objective to philosophical accounts of mechanisms and organizes methods along three axes: scope of the analyzed component, interpretability task, and observational versus interventional analysis. Its task categories are feature localization, circuit discovery, and feature disentanglement.

**Experiments**

The paper conducts bibliographic searches rather than new neural-network experiments. It examines Scopus, Web of Science, and PubMed, presenting Scopus publication trends for 2015–2025, including preprints, retrieved April 17, 2025. PubMed is excluded from quantitative reporting because biomedical uses of mechanistic terminology require manual disambiguation. Web of Science provides supplementary counts. The technical review supplies pseudocode for linear probing, logit lens, and activation patching. Examples involving InceptionV1, GPT-2 Small, BERT, Pythia, Llama-2, Chinchilla, and Othello-GPT come from cited studies. Probe accuracy/F1 and patching logit differences/KL divergence are described as evaluation measures; no new model scores are reported.

**Key results**

Web of Science searches for “mechanistic interpretability” returned 3 publications for 2022, 9 for 2023, and 23 for 2024. These keyword-conditioned counts indicate growing indexed use of the term. The main conceptual contribution is a shared organization of probing and lenses, causal mediation and patching, ablation and causal scrubbing, and sparse dictionary methods. The survey adopts linear feature representations and superposition as foundations motivating sparse autoencoders, while recognizing incidental polysemanticity and disagreement about whether encouraging monosemanticity improves performance. It discusses debugging, privacy auditing, robustness, model editing, human supervision, and alignment as potential applications.

**Limitations / open questions**

The search strategy can omit relevant work that lacks MI terminology or appears only on blogs, while broader searches retrieve unrelated mechanistic research. Numerical Scopus plot values are unavailable in the supplied rendering. The Web of Science discussion alternates between “interpretability” and “interpretation” queries, and some technical citations are inconsistent: Syed et al. is described both as introducing “ACDC++” and edge attribution patching. The paper supplies no comparative method benchmark or new formal guarantee. It emphasizes intervention artifacts, semantic drift, nonunique circuit interpretations, cherry-picking, limited automation, and missing standardized evaluation. Transfer across architectures, tasks, and modalities—and comprehensive algorithmic understanding of frontier models—remain unresolved.

title: The Birth of Knowledge: Emergent Features across Time, Space, and Scale in Large Language Models
abstract: This paper studies the emergence of interpretable categorical features within large language models (LLMs), analyzing their behavior across training checkpoints (time), transformer layers (space), and varying model sizes (scale). Using sparse autoencoders for mechanistic interpretability, we identify when and where specific semantic concepts emerge within neural activations. Results indicate clear temporal and scale-specific thresholds for feature emergence across multiple domains. Notably, spatial analysis reveals unexpected semantic reactivation, with early-layer features re-emerging at later layers, challenging standard assumptions about representational dynamics in transformer models.
summary:
**Central idea**

EyeSee tracks subject-associated sparse-autoencoder coordinates across training, depth, and model size, interpreting their firing as categorical knowledge emergence. Labels are generated from ten strongly activating examples and verified on five activating and five non-activating examples. Coordinates with verification F1 >0.9 are associated with nine subjects using all-mpnet-base-v2 label–subject cosine similarity ≥0.3.

**Experiments**

The corpus combines 14,042 MMLU test questions and 12,032 MMLU-Pro questions. Each question and its candidate answers, without the correct letter, supplies one final-token residual state. The main SAE uses 512 latents and k=1, making it undercomplete relative to Pythia-12B’s 5,120-dimensional residual stream. Separate sweeps vary k at width 256 and width at k=1, selecting settings by mean label-verification F1. Temporal analysis applies a final-checkpoint SAE to 25 Pythia-12B checkpoints. Spatial analysis examines 36 blocks and selected layer-trained SAEs. Scale analysis maps ten Pythia sizes, 14M–12B, into the 12B reference space using rectangular orthogonal Procrustes fitted on the 26,074 benchmark prompts.

**Key results**

The reported global concept-activation percentage remains below 3% during the first 1,000 updates and exceeds 99% at step 143,000. Its trajectory includes a 31.8-percentage-point decline between 20,000 and 30,000 updates, followed by a 55.9-point increase. Five subjects show earlier firing than History, Biology, Chemistry, and Business. Across scale, the reported percentage increases by 92.9 points between 160M and 410M, reaching approximately 95%; models larger than 2.8B remain above 98%. Business follows a less abrupt trajectory. Early-layer probes weaken in intermediate layers and partially reactivate near the output; middle-layer probes are more localized. Cross-model linear CKA exceeds 0.90 at 14M, while cosine-matrix correlation rises from 0.34 at 14M to above 0.95 for models ≥2.8B.

**Limitations / open questions**

The activation-percentage denominator and prompt aggregation are not fully specified. These percentages do not measure benchmark accuracy or independently established knowledge. Ten verification examples offer limited label validation. Positive firing is counted despite equations specifying signed magnitude-based TopK selection. Probe transfer and reference-geometry agreement do not establish semantic invariance, knowledge absence, or causal use. No causal interventions, behavioral validation, uncertainty estimates, or independent alignment evaluation are reported. SAE training details are sparse; the spatial discussion and History scaling bullet contain unfinished sentences, and plots are unavailable as readable numerical data. The evidence therefore establishes descriptive probe behavior more directly than knowledge-acquisition thresholds.

title: BlockCert: Certified Blockwise Extraction of Transformer Mechanisms
abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aspires to reverse-engineer neural networks into explicit algorithms, while model editing seeks to modify specific behaviours without retraining. Both areas are typically evaluated with informal evidence and ad-hoc experiments, with few explicit guarantees about how far an extracted or edited model can drift from the original on relevant inputs. We introduce BlockCert, a framework for certified blockwise extraction of transformer mechanisms, and outline how a lightweight extension can support certified local edits. Given a pre-trained transformer and a prompt distribution, BlockCert extracts structured surrogate implementations for residual blocks together with machine-checkable certificates that bound approximation error, record coverage metrics, and hash the underlying artifacts. We formalize a simple Lipschitz-based composition theorem in Lean 4 that lifts these local guarantees to a global deviation bound. Empirically, we apply the framework to GPT-2 small, TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat, and Llama-3.2-3B. Across these models we obtain high per-block coverage and small residual errors on the evaluated prompts, and in the TinyLlama setting we show that a fully stitched model matches the baseline perplexity within approximately 6e-5 on stress prompts. Our results suggest that blockwise extraction with explicit certificates is feasible for real transformer language models and offers a practical bridge between mechanistic interpretability and formal reasoning about model behaviour.
summary:
**Central idea**
BlockCert packages transformer blocks in an explicit intermediate representation with replayable JSON certificates recording numerical errors, coverage policies, and SHA-256 artifact hashes. Experimental extraction copies the original architecture and weights, without fitting, pruning, or distillation. Its demonstrated contribution is reproducible implementation fidelity; it does not discover a simpler algorithm or establish human-understandable mechanisms.

**Experiments**
The paper evaluates GPT-2 small, TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat, and Llama-3.2-3B. GPT-2's baseline uses two prompts. TinyLlama uses four baseline prompts totaling 90 tokens and ten authored stress prompts totaling 251 tokens. Evaluations include a 22-layer sweep, selected-block transfer between prompt sets, multi-block replay, and fully stitched replay. Llama extraction covers blocks 0, 5, and 10. Metrics include per-token residual L2 error, thresholded activation coverage, discrete-control agreement, baseline-loss-weighted coverage of small loss changes, and perplexity. Editing experiments scale individual MLP residuals on 12 benign and 12 harmful prompts, scored using refusal and harmful-content markers.

**Key results**
GPT-2 reports mean extraction error approximately 2.32×10^-7. TinyLlama's full sweep reports activation coverage approximately 0.945–1.0; five selected blocks retain the certification thresholds after the small prompt shift. Fully stitched TinyLlama has baseline and stitched average perplexities approximately 253.1618, differing by approximately −6×10^-5 on the stress prompts. A separate multi-block replay reports mean layer MAE approximately 0.38 and maximum residual approximately 2.13. A small semantic probe reports complete next-token agreement with baseline, without a sample count.

The supplied mathematical derivation bounds final hidden-state deviation by Σ_i ε_i∏_{j>i}L_j under uniform local-error and Lipschitz assumptions. Reported hybrid block constants around 10^5–10^6 yield extremely conservative bounds. TinyLlama block-15 scaling to 0.33 raises heuristic refusal correctness from 0/12 to 3/12 while retaining approximately 12/12 benign correctness. Tested Llama edits leave these aggregate metrics unchanged.

**Limitations / open questions**
Certificates summarize finite traces. Applying the composition theorem requires compatible norms and error and Lipschitz bounds valid at the relevant states; trace maxima and selected MLP-ball bounds do not establish an all-input transformer guarantee. The Lean implementation is described as an external artifact; the supplied text contains the recurrence derivation. Block-15 coverage differs between reported stress configurations, and local per-token L2 errors and global MAE are not directly interchangeable. Small authored datasets, unvalidated refusal heuristics, and absent numerical human-label results restrict behavioral conclusions. Perplexity agreement alone does not establish identical predictions or causal mechanisms.
