Steering LLMs? Actually, Sparse Autoencoders can outperform simple baselines
abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have been seen as a promising avenue for exploring the internals of Large Language Models (LLMs) and for steering model output generation. When AxBench - a model steering benchmark - was introduced in Wu et al. (2025), SAEs did not seem to live up to their original hype due to poor steering performance relative to a set of simple baselines. This work serves as a partial rebuttal for Sparse Autoencoders and suggests that the results of Wu et al. (2025) did not do them full justice. We find that Sparse Autoencoders can, in fact, perform close to on par with the reference LoRA performance on the AxBench benchmark, when features are selected and labelled with our supervised pipeline. We also find that our pipeline selects features that are surprisingly causal of their identified labels when using only its interpretability-based components. Lastly, we present evidence that high sparsity (low l0) may not be crucial for successful steering based on interpretability, which is in contrast to the earlier findings in Wang et al. (2025).
summary:
**Central idea**

SAE steering performance depends on feature selection and labeling. This paper assigns labels to pretrained SAE features using supervised associations with Stack Exchange tags, then tests whether feature clamping induces those topics. It introduces a labeling pipeline rather than a new SAE architecture.

**Experiments**

The main experiments use Gemma-2-9b-it and 131k-wide Gemma Scope residual-stream JumpReLU SAEs at zero-indexed layers 17 and 32, with approximately 11 and 10 active features in the highest-sparsity configurations. Across eleven Stack Exchange forums, features predict tags from their fraction of positively activating tokens. The pipeline ranks feature–label pairs by threshold-optimized calibrated F1, uses a label-support threshold of 50 and an output-score threshold of 0.001, and retains the top 50 remaining pairs. Reference prevalence is 0.001. Tuning uses seven forums at layer 32; four forums and layer 17 are excluded.

Each selected pair receives 20 randomly sampled AlpacaEval instructions. Reconstruction-error-preserving clamping operates on every token, including BOS. Strengths range from 100 to 575 in increments of 25, selected separately for each pair using ten repeats of four-fold cross-validation. AxBench combines 0–2 concept, instruction-following, and fluency ratings by their harmonic mean. Comparators include prompting, 100 random Neuronpedia pairs, and published AxBench scores. Ablations vary sparsity and output-score filtering. Appendix A supplies a prevalence-invariance derivation and Gaussian probe simulations.

**Key results**

The authors report substantially improved Gemma steering ratings over Neuronpedia references. Several selected forum cohorts approach the published LoRA aggregate rating, while prompting remains stronger overall. Output-score filtering adds modest reported benefits; selection without it also improves steering over random features when both retain their original Neuronpedia labels. Sparsity ablations show no large reported advantage for the lowest-L0 dictionaries. Appendix E reports unsuccessful Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct/Llama Scope steering and notes that ordinary F1 can also perform well. Simulations show that population prevalence invariance does not eliminate low-support estimation instability.

**Limitations / open questions**

Plots are unavailable visually in the supplied rendering, preventing numerical effect-size extraction. Published LoRA comparisons use different concept populations and selection procedures; some Neuronpedia comparisons also differ in sparsity. Judge identity varies between GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini descriptions. A small student trial provides limited validation, and selected examples expose questionable concept ratings. Successful clamping demonstrates intervention effects, but does not establish exhaustive feature semantics or ordinary causal mediation. Transfer beyond the successful Gemma settings remains unresolved.

title: Sparse Autoencoders Enable Scalable and Reliable Circuit Identification in Language Models
abstract: This paper introduces an efficient and robust method for discovering interpretable circuits in large language models using discrete sparse autoencoders. Our approach addresses key limitations of existing techniques, namely computational complexity and sensitivity to hyperparameters. We propose training sparse autoencoders on carefully designed positive and negative examples, where the model can only correctly predict the next token for the positive examples. We hypothesise that learned representations of attention head outputs will signal when a head is engaged in specific computations. By discretising the learned representations into integer codes and measuring the overlap between codes unique to positive examples for each head, we enable direct identification of attention heads involved in circuits without the need for expensive ablations or architectural modifications. On three well-studied tasks - indirect object identification, greater-than comparisons, and docstring completion - the proposed method achieves higher precision and recall in recovering ground-truth circuits compared to state-of-the-art baselines, while reducing runtime from hours to seconds. Notably, we require only 5-10 text examples for each task to learn robust representations. Our findings highlight the promise of discrete sparse autoencoders for scalable and efficient mechanistic interpretability, offering a new direction for analysing the inner workings of large language models.
summary:
**Central idea**
The paper identifies task-associated attention heads using discrete sparse-autoencoder codes. A tied-weight ReLU SAE reconstructs position-averaged head outputs; post-training argmax assigns one code per head and example. Heads are ranked by positive-only codes or participation in highly ranked positive-only code-pair co-occurrences. Discovery uses constructed task contrasts without output-based importance metrics or interventions. The procedure called “edge-level” ultimately selects heads rather than identifying directed causal connections.

**Experiments**
IOI, Greater-than, and Docstring each have 250 positive and 250 corrupted negative prompts. The main recipe trains on ten balanced examples with 200 features and sparsity penalty 0.02, using remaining examples for validation and code statistics. IOI and Greater-than use GPT-2 Small. Docstring's model is inconsistently specified: the main text says GPT-2 Small, while appendices imply a smaller model and cite a four-layer attention-only reference. Evaluations compare reference-label ROC AUC with inherited ACDC/HISP/SP results and conduct new corrupted-activation retention comparisons with EAP. Further experiments vary hyperparameters, negatives, training and counting sample sizes, test four Tracr programs, and examine synthetic induction across models.

**Key results**
Fixed-parameter node AUCs are 0.853 for IOI, 0.832 for Greater-than, and 0.915 for Docstring. Tuned Table 6 scores exceed its listed baselines, but fixed settings trail the best Docstring baselines. Both reference IOI negative name movers are identified. With excluded heads replaced by corrupted activations, 40/144 IOI heads yield mean logit difference 3.62 versus 3.55 for the full model. On 100 Greater-than examples, 29/144 heads yield probability difference 76.54% versus 76.96%, and cutoff sharpness 5.76% versus 5.57%. Five to ten SAE-training prompts suffice in reported sweeps, but Greater-than code counting requires all 250 positive and 250 negative prompts. Four Tracr controls achieve AUC 1.0 under corruption explicitly informed by known weight activity. Unrelated negatives and the tested auxiliary contrastive loss reduce recovery.

**Limitations / open questions**
Code contrasts do not independently establish selective circuit deactivation, and co-occurrence does not establish communication. Position averaging removes positional specificity; MLP discovery and code semantics remain unresolved. Reference circuits may be incomplete, and standalone circuits are selected using reference-label F1. Training convergence uses evaluation data, limiting independent generalization evidence. Runtime reports cover SAE training and threshold sweeps over cached activations; activation-collection costs are unclear. Pair-budget specifications differ across sections. Figures are unavailable as images in the supplied rendering, so detailed plotted values cannot be independently assessed.

title: Does higher interpretability imply better utility? A Pairwise Analysis on Sparse Autoencoders
abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are widely used to steer large language models (LLMs), based on the assumption that their interpretable features naturally enable effective model behavior steering. Yet, a fundamental question remains unanswered: does higher interpretability indeed imply better steering utility? To answer this question, we train 90 SAEs across three LLMs (Gemma-2-2B, Qwen-2.5-3B, Gemma-2-9B), spanning five architectures and six sparsity levels, and evaluate their interpretability and steering utility based on SAEBench (arXiv:2501.12345) and AxBench (arXiv:2502.23456) respectively, and perform a rank-agreement analysis via Kendall's rank coefficients (tau b). Our analysis reveals only a relatively weak positive association (tau b approx 0.298), indicating that interpretability is an insufficient proxy for steering performance. We conjecture the interpretability utility gap may stem from the selection of SAE features, as not all of them are equally effective for steering. To further find features that truly steer the behavior of LLMs, we propose a novel selection criterion called Delta Token Confidence, which measures how much amplifying a feature changes the next token distribution. We show that our method improves the steering performance of three LLMs by 52.52 percent compared to the current best output score based criterion (arXiv:2503.34567). Strikingly, after selecting features with high Delta Token Confidence, the correlation between interpretability and utility vanishes (tau b approx 0), and can even become negative. This further highlights the divergence between interpretability and utility for the most effective steering features.
summary:
**Central idea**
The paper compares automated SAE interpretability with concept-steering utility and introduces Δ Token Confidence for feature selection. Its evidence concerns dictionary-level benchmark associations; it does not establish an intrinsic conflict between interpretability and control.

**Experiments**
The authors train 90 residual-stream SAEs: ReLU, Gated, TopK, BatchTopK, and JumpReLU at six approximate active counts spanning 50–820. Sites are Gemma-2-2B layer 12, Qwen-2.5-3B layer 17, and Gemma-2-9B layer 20. Each dictionary has 16,384 features and approximately 500 million Common Pile training tokens. Of 1,000 evaluated latents per SAE, 100 are randomly sampled into its own Concept100 inventory. Interpretability measures explanation-conditioned classification accuracy over 14 held-out windows per latent. Steering utility averages per-continuation harmonic means of gpt-4o-mini concept, instruction-topicality, and fluency ratings. Ten instructions per concept are split 5/5 for factor selection and evaluation, with six factors and 128-token continuations. The selector measures changes in negative log maximum next-token probability on “From my experience,” using amplification 10, then evaluates candidate tail subsets and retains the best.

**Key results**
Across 90 dictionaries and 4,005 pairs, reported baseline interpretability–utility Kendall correlation is 0.2979, with bootstrap interval [0.1590, 0.4191]; the conditioning aggregate is 0.2499. Unselected/output-selected/confidence-selected scores are 0.133/0.233/0.328 for Gemma-2-2B, 0.171/0.292/0.399 for Qwen-2.5-3B, and 0.142/0.255/0.289 for Gemma-2-9B. The headline 52.52% improvement over output selection is not directly recoverable from these model-level means. Interpretability versus percentage gain over each dictionary’s unselected baseline yields correlation −0.0692, interval [−0.2019, 0.0666], and conditioning aggregate −0.0568. This comparison measures selection gains, rather than final selected utility or individual-feature interpretability; it does not establish a negative population relationship.

**Limitations / open questions**
Dictionary-specific concept inventories and changing selected populations complicate comparisons. Independent evaluation for choosing the best subset and human calibration of judges are unclear. Main-text selector interventions preserve other features, whereas Appendix D zeros other codes. With k=1, the statistic measures peak-probability change rather than full-distribution divergence or semantic specificity. The displayed Kendall formula omits tie correction; subgroup intervals appear consistent with permutation-null ranges, and conditioning definitions do not match table groupings consistently. Figures are unavailable for independent visual checking, and Appendix F gives inconsistent layer identifiers for Gemma-2-2B examples. Results cover one layer per model without prefix-robustness or broad capability-retention tests.

Causal Circuit Tracing Reveals Distinct Computational Architectures in Single-Cell Foundation Models: Inhibitory Dominance, Biological Coherence, and Cross-Model Convergence
abstract: Motivation: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose foundation model activations into interpretable features, but causal feature-to-feature interactions across network depth remain unknown for biological foundation models. Results: We introduce causal circuit tracing by ablating SAE features and measuring downstream responses, and apply it to Geneformer V2-316M and scGPT whole-human across four conditions (96,892 edges, 80,191 forward passes). Both models show approximately 53 percent biological coherence and 65 to 89 percent inhibitory dominance, invariant to architecture and cell type. scGPT produces stronger effects (mean absolute d = 1.40 vs. 1.05) with more balanced dynamics. Cross-model consensus yields 1,142 conserved domain pairs (10.6x enrichment, p < 0.001). Disease-associated domains are 3.59x more likely to be consensus. Gene-level CRISPRi validation shows 56.4 percent directional accuracy, confirming co-expression rather than causal encoding.
summary:
**Central idea**
The paper maps downstream SAE activation responses to feature-contribution removal in Geneformer V2-316M and scGPT whole-human. Subtracting a decoder contribution preserves the original reconstruction residual. Biological annotations organize the resulting model interventions into candidate process-level relationships; correspondence to cellular regulatory mechanisms requires separate evidence.

**Experiments**
Geneformer has 18 layers, hidden width 1,152, and 4,608-feature TopK dictionaries; scGPT has 12 layers, width 512, and 2,048-feature dictionaries. Both use k=32. Four conditions combine Geneformer K562-only or mixed K562/Tabula Sapiens dictionaries with K562 or Tabula Sapiens inputs, plus scGPT on Tabula Sapiens. Each uses 200 cells and 90–120 annotation-selected source features. Retained responses require |d|>0.5 and sign consistency>0.7. The paper reports 80,191 forward passes and 96,892 aggregate edges, followed by annotation, cross-model, and existing CRISPRi-data analyses.

**Key results**
Across conditions, 65.5–89.4% of retained responses are downstream activation decreases after source removal; mean retained-edge |d| ranges from 0.72 to 1.40. Early-source effects persist across network depth. Geneformer K562-only coherence is 16,507/31,176 doubly annotated edges (52.9%), versus reported fractions of 68.8% for mixed dictionaries on K562, 68.5% on Tabula Sapiens, and 53.0% for scGPT. Cross-model analysis finds 1,142 shared directed domain pairs, including 303 with mean |d|>1 in both models; reported enrichment is 10.6-fold against 1,000 label permutations. Immune-label enrichment is OR=3.18 in multi-tissue-specific versus shared pairs. Broad disease-labelled domains have higher reported centrality and consensus. However, 282,250 evaluated gene pairs yield only 56.4% directional agreement and Spearman rho=0.038 with CRISPRi responses; 36/599 source genes show nominal, uncorrected target enrichment.

**Limitations / open questions**
Sources favor richly annotated features, K562 evaluation cells overlap dictionary training, layer coverage differs, and only singleton ablations are tested. Aggregate and per-source-layer edge totals conflict; scGPT's claimed 95.7% coverage divides multilayer target counts by one layer's dictionary width. Negative removal responses indicate positive source support, despite the paper's “inhibitory” terminology. Responses include mediated effects rather than isolated direct connections. Shared annotations and broad PMI target overlap do not establish selective mechanisms or matching causal edges. Forward-only tracing cannot independently validate biological temporal order, and dictionary-dependent coherence undermines the proposed universal 53% constant. Several supposedly novel domain links report shared-gene counts exceeding the stated known-link threshold.

title: Sparse autoencoders reveal organized biological knowledge but minimal regulatory logic in single-cell foundation models: a comparative atlas of Geneformer and scGPT
abstract: Background: Single-cell foundation models such as Geneformer and scGPT encode rich biological information, but whether this includes causal regulatory logic rather than statistical co-expression remains unclear. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can resolve superposition in neural networks by decomposing dense activations into interpretable features, yet they have not been systematically applied to biological foundation models. Results: We trained TopK SAEs on residual stream activations from all layers of Geneformer V2-316M (18 layers, d=1152) and scGPT whole-human (12 layers, d=512), producing atlases of 82525 and 24527 features, respectively. Both atlases confirm massive superposition, with 99.8 percent of features invisible to SVD. Systematic characterization reveals rich biological organization: 29 to 59 percent of features annotate to Gene Ontology, KEGG, Reactome, STRING, or TRRUST, with U-shaped layer profiles reflecting hierarchical abstraction. Features organize into co-activation modules (141 in Geneformer, 76 in scGPT), exhibit causal specificity (median 2.36x), and form cross-layer information highways (63 to 99.8 percent). When tested against genome-scale CRISPRi perturbation data, only 3 of 48 transcription factors (6.2 percent) show regulatory-target-specific feature responses. A multi-tissue control yields marginal improvement (10.4 percent, 5 of 48 TFs), establishing model representations as the bottleneck. Conclusions: These models have internalized organized biological knowledge, including pathway membership, protein interactions, functional modules, and hierarchical abstraction, yet they encode minimal causal regulatory logic. We release both feature atlases as interactive web platforms enabling exploration of more than 107000 features across 30 layers of two leading single-cell foundation models.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper builds sparse-autoencoder atlases to investigate biological associations and regulatory information in single-cell foundation models. It reports 82,525 alive features across Geneformer V2-316M’s 18 layers and 24,527 across scGPT whole-human’s 12 layers. Its central negative result concerns a particular Geneformer perturbation-response assay; regulatory specificity was not tested in scGPT.

**Experiments**

Layerwise TopK SAEs use fourfold dictionary expansion and retain 32 coefficients per position. Geneformer training uses one million sampled positions per layer from 2,000 K562 control cells; scGPT training uses approximately 3.56 million positions per layer from 3,000 Tabula Sapiens cells spanning immune, kidney, and lung tissues. Analyses include top-20-gene ontology enrichment, comparison with 50 SVD axes, cross-layer decoder matching, PMI-based Leiden communities, and cell-type enrichment. Reconstruction-based interventions evaluate 50 selected annotated features per model. Geneformer perturbation mapping tests 100 CRISPRi targets, including 48 TRRUST transcription factors, with 20 perturbed cells per target. Additional Geneformer dictionaries pool K562 and multi-tissue activations at four layers.

**Key results**

Mean reconstruction variance explained is 81.7% for Geneformer and 90.2% for scGPT. Ontology annotations cover 52.4% and 31.0% of alive features; co-activation analysis identifies 141 and 76 layerwise communities. Geneformer annotation rates dip and recover with depth, while scGPT’s pattern is weaker and irregular. Only 189/82,525 Geneformer decoder directions exceed cosine 0.7 with any top-50 SVD axis; corresponding detailed scGPT counts are absent. Selected Geneformer layer-11 edits yield median annotated-position specificity 2.36, with 30/50 exceeding two; scGPT’s proxy-expression experiment yields median 0.98 and 0/50 exceeding two. Geneformer features respond to 92/100 perturbations, but target-specific responses occur for only 3/48 transcription factors. The best pooled-data layer reaches 5/48, with disjoint gains and losses. Cross-layer PMI links are common, although reported coverage uses different source, target, and conditional denominators.

**Limitations / open questions**

Nonalignment with 50 axes does not establish invisibility to linear methods or superposition. Summed feature counts across layers do not count distinct concepts simultaneously represented in one vector. PMI associations do not establish directed information flow. Interventions replace entire states with modified SAE reconstructions; a reconstruction-only control is unspecified. scGPT interventions use uniform proxy expression. Regulatory conclusions depend on incomplete TRRUST coverage, position-level statistics, one SAE configuration, and limited layer sampling. The pooling comparison does not exclude extraction or assay limitations. Co-membership of unannotated features in large communities does not validate their biology. Figure images are unavailable in the supplied rendering, but substantial methods, results, and supplementary tables are present.

Interpretable Steering of Large Language Models with Feature Guided Activation Additions
abstract: Effective and reliable control over large language model (LLM) behavior is a significant challenge. While activation steering methods, which add steering vectors to a model's hidden states, are a promising approach, existing techniques often lack precision and interpretability in how they influence model outputs. We introduce Feature Guided Activation Additions (FGAA), a novel activation steering method that leverages insights from Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) and Sparse Autoencoder-Targeted Steering (SAE-TS). By operating in the latent space of a Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) and employing optimization techniques to select desired SAE features, FGAA constructs precise steering vectors that provide better steering effects while maintaining coherence of steered model outputs. In this regard, evaluations on Gemma-2-2B and Gemma-2-9B models across various steering tasks demonstrate that FGAA outperforms existing steering methods of CAA, SAE decoder steering, and SAE-TS. Our results also highlight important trade-offs between steering scale and general model capabilities that are consistent across all tested steering methods.
summary:
**Central idea**

Feature Guided Activation Additions (FGAA) contrasts mean SAE activations on desired and undesired texts, removes features with activation density above 0.01 and BOS-associated features, and selects a sparse feature target. The evaluated recipe retains 1–8 positive contrast features and no negative features. A pretrained affine effect approximator supplies a steering direction by combining separately normalized target and bias-correction terms.

**Experiments**

Experiments use Gemma-2-2B and Gemma-2-9B with layer-12 residual-stream Gemma Scope SAEs containing 16,384 features and pretrained effect approximators. Baselines are CAA, single-feature SAE decoder steering, and SAE-TS targeting that same feature. L2-normalized directions are added at every token position. Evaluations sample 100 completions per condition, each 33 tokens long, from `<bos>I think`. Nine targets cover anger, Christianity, conspiracy, French, London, love, praise, wanting to die, and weddings. GPT-4o-mini rates target expression and coherence; the product of rescaled ratings is the Behavioral-Coherence Score (BCS). Feature-count sweeps use 30 samples per count; exploratory positive/negative-count grids for anger and praise use ten samples per combination.

Capability checks use Gemma-2-2B only: the first 100 OpenWebText records with all nine task vectors, the first five questions per MMLU subject, and the first ten questions per MMLU-Pro category. Benchmark checks use only anger, Christian evangelist, and conspiracy vectors.

**Key results**

FGAA has the highest reported average BCS: 0.4702 versus SAE-TS’s 0.3650 on 2B, and 0.3979 versus 0.3467 on 9B. It leads on 8/9 and 4/9 tasks, respectively. Mean cosine similarities to SAE-TS are 0.8919 and 0.9284. Negative-feature inclusion is reported to worsen or destabilize results. Capability measurements remain relatively close to baseline at smaller coefficients and deteriorate at larger coefficients; these thresholds concern the tested intervention settings.

**Limitations / open questions**

Evidence covers two models, one layer, short generations, and one evaluation prefix. Table 1’s precise aggregation over steering scales and independent hyperparameter validation are unclear. Judge ratings lack human calibration and do not establish selective semantic control or native causal mechanisms. Density and BOS filtering lack isolated quantitative ablations. Plot images are unavailable, limiting numerical verification of curves. Appendix F’s reported L1-versus-L2 target-normalization advantage is unexplained by Equation 5: positive scalar rescaling cancels in its normalized target term. Safety applications remain prospective.

Why Linear Interpretability Works: Invariant Subspaces as a Result of Architectural Constraints
abstract: Linear probes and sparse autoencoders consistently recover meaningful structure from transformer representations -- yet why should such simple methods succeed in deep, nonlinear systems? We show this is not merely an empirical regularity but a consequence of architectural necessity: transformers communicate information through linear interfaces (attention OV circuits, unembedding matrices), and any semantic feature decoded through such an interface must occupy a context-invariant linear subspace. We formalize this as the \emph{Invariant Subspace Necessity} theorem and derive the \emph{Self-Reference Property}: tokens directly provide the geometric direction for their associated features, enabling zero-shot identification of semantic structure without labeled data or learned probes. Empirical validation in eight classification tasks and four model families confirms the alignment between class tokens and semantically related instances. Our framework provides \textbf{a principled architectural explanation} for why linear interpretability methods work, unifying linear probes and sparse autoencoders.
summary:
**Central idea**

The paper attributes linear interpretability to transformer communication interfaces. Its Invariant Subspace Necessity argument begins with an assumed exact linear semantic readout and derives a context-independent readout geometry. The stronger Self-Reference Property proposes that a class name's activation supplies its semantic direction. The valid kernel and projection identities do not establish that architecture itself makes semantic features linearly decodable, or that whole token states are proportional to individual feature directions.

**Experiments**

Eight classification tasks cover animals, countries, cartoon characters, authors, languages, emotions, fruits, and companies in LLaMA3-8B, LLaMA3.2-3B, Mistral-7B, and GPT2-Small. Individual attention-head outputs are classified using centered class-name prototypes, a contrastive linear transformation trained only on class names, or TopK SAEs trained on implicit instance activations without class names. Table 2 reports each method's single best-performing head separately for every model–task combination. The text baseline sums conditional class-name token log-likelihoods. Additional tests examine prototype–instance cosine alignment, shared SAE coordinates, Apple polysemy, and division modulo 97 in a two-layer transformer with an MLP output head.

**Key results**

LLaMA3-8B best-head zero-shot accuracy is 84.22% on animals, 82.97% on countries, and 89.12% on languages. The class-name-only transformation improves animals to 94.32% and authors from 62.95% to 75.13%; it improves 25 of 32 model–task comparisons, rather than uniformly improving performance. GPT2-Small performs substantially worse on several tasks. Figure 3's caption reports greater same-class than other-class alignment in 91.5%, 97.6%, 86.0%, and 89.6% of LLaMA3-8B heads for countries, animals, cartoon characters, and emotions. Class names and instances share 15/32 leading SAE coordinates for mammals, 23/32 for fish, 25/32 for reptiles, and 22/32 for birds. A modular-division run reaches approximately 95% MLP-head validation accuracy versus approximately 20% linear-probe accuracy without the reported Fourier-circle geometry.

**Limitations / open questions**

Independent head-selection data, SAE evaluation splits, uncertainty estimates, and modular-training details are unspecified. Dataset counts and some class definitions conflict between Table 1 and Appendix D.1; Figure 3's percentages conflict with the prose range. Image-only plots limit verification beyond textual reports and captions. The dimensional-bound and semantic-factorization arguments do not establish their advertised conclusions. Self-reference additionally assumes a dominant target-feature component. Classification and coordinate overlap do not establish native causal mechanisms, exact feature recovery, selective steering, or superposition of Apple meanings. Nonlinear QK routing and higher-dimensional representations remain unresolved.

title: Temporal Sparse Autoencoders: Leveraging the Sequential Nature of Language for Interpretability
abstract: Translating the internal representations and computations of models into concepts that humans can understand is a key goal of interpretability. While recent dictionary learning methods such as Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) provide a promising route to discover human-interpretable features, they often only recover token-specific, noisy, or highly local concepts. We argue that this limitation stems from neglecting the temporal structure of language, where semantic content typically evolves smoothly over sequences. Building on this insight, we introduce Temporal Sparse Autoencoders (T-SAEs), which incorporate a novel contrastive loss encouraging consistent activations of high-level features over adjacent tokens. This simple yet powerful modification enables SAEs to disentangle semantic from syntactic features in a self-supervised manner. Across multiple datasets and models, T-SAEs recover smoother, more coherent semantic concepts without sacrificing reconstruction quality. Strikingly, they exhibit clear semantic structure despite being trained without explicit semantic signal, offering a new pathway for unsupervised interpretability in language models.
summary:
**Central idea**

Temporal Sparse Autoencoders (T-SAEs) introduce a sequential prior into dictionary learning: semantic and contextual information should persist across nearby tokens, while local syntactic properties can change rapidly. Nested reconstruction losses divide the dictionary into a high-level prefix and a low-level remainder. A symmetric contrastive loss aligns adjacent-token high-level codes against other batch examples. This encourages specialization without proving identification of native semantic variables.

**Experiments**

The main experiments use Pythia-160m layer 8 and Gemma2-2b layer 12, nominally 16k features, BatchTopK k=20, a 20:80 split, and temporal-loss weight 1.0. Dictionaries train and test on the Pile. Comparisons include BatchTopK, Matryoshka, and raw activations. Sparse probes using 1, 5, 10, or 20 features and dense logistic probes evaluate MMLU, Wikipedia, and FineFineWeb. MMLU targets are question category, question identity, and spaCy part of speech. Other tests assess reconstruction, smoothness, automated explanation detection, absorption, HH-RLHF preference associations, Gemma steering, and training ablations. A preliminary Llama-3.1-8b-Instruct experiment provides t-SNE evidence after 20% of training steps.

**Key results**

The authors report improved semantic/contextual probing with little syntactic loss. High-partition adjacent-change scores are lower than Matryoshka's: 0.09 versus 0.12 for Pythia and 0.10 versus 0.15 for Gemma. Full-dictionary smoothness does not uniformly improve. Reconstruction FVE is 0.94 versus 0.95 for both Pythia baselines; Gemma scores are 0.75 versus 0.75 and 0.76. Automated explanation-detection means are similar. The reported selected-feature steering comparison favors T-SAEs on concept-expression/coherence frontiers using Llama3.3-70b ratings. In the first 1,000 HH-RLHF examples, rejected responses average 49.243 tokens versus 37.844 for chosen responses, a difference of 11.399 tokens (two-sided t-test p=9e-10). Selected activation contrasts also associate with length differences.

**Limitations / open questions**

Probe accuracy, smoothness, and readable labels do not establish semantic exclusivity or native mechanisms. Numerical probing and steering curves are unavailable in this text rendering; split protocols, training budgets, and repeated-run uncertainty are insufficiently specified. Steering descriptions differ across dictionaries, potentially affecting ratings; the text reports 30 features but Table 8 lists 29 correspondences. No downstream replacement-loss evaluation is reported. Temporal pairing increases memory requirements. Absorption prose contradicts Table 10: T-SAEs have higher reported mean absorption metrics and more split features, 2.19 versus 1.96. State tracking and benefits beyond lexical persistence remain untested.

title: Persistent Sparse Autoencoders: Learning Feature-Specific Timescales in Language Model Representations
abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose language model activations into sparse features, yet these models traditionally encode each token independently, failing to expose information that persists across a sequence. We first show that temporal persistence can naturally emerge in standard SAE features: after a feature activates, the hidden state remains aligned with its direction, and past activations help reconstruct later hidden states. How long this lasts varies widely across features. We therefore introduce Persistent Sparse Autoencoders (Persistent SAEs), an extension of standard SAEs that learns a persistence coefficient for each feature, allowing the model to learn feature-specific timescales from reconstruction alone. Our experiments show that Persistent SAEs retain competitive reconstruction quality while learning a spectrum of timescales: short-timescale (fast) features stay locally interpretable, whereas long-timescale (slow) features accumulate information that identifies the current context. Moreover, we show in a prompt-injection monitoring case study that slow features preserve injection-related signals and remain causally effective over long contexts. These results suggest that Persistent SAEs offer new opportunities for interpreting and monitoring language models via persistent sparse features.
summary:
**Central idea**
Persistent SAEs add a learned exponential moving average to each sparse feature: h_j(t)=λ_jh_j(t−1)+(1−λ_j)a_j(t). Reconstruction uses the accumulated state, while BatchTopK constrains token-wise updates. Timescales are learned without predefined temporal groups or an auxiliary temporal objective; the accumulated state need not be sparse.

**Experiments**
The study evaluates Pythia-160M-deduped layer 8 and Gemma-2-2B layer 12. Persistent, BatchTopK, Matryoshka, and Temporal SAEs have 16,384 features, nominal average update budget 20, and approximately 500 million Pile Uncopyrighted activation tokens. Standard-feature persistence is compared between natural documents and cross-document concatenations of intact sentences. Other tests include GPT-4o-mini activation-explanation scoring, token-category update frequencies, and linear subject probes on spliced text from five MMLU subjects with source-document-held-out testing. Injection monitoring replays Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct AgentDojo banking, travel, and workspace trajectories through an external Gemma monitor. Positives contain failed important_instructions or direct attacks; negatives contain no injection.

**Key results**
Eligible standard-SAE features retain elevated decoder-aligned projections through lag 512, whereas shuffled controls approach zero at long lags. Actual-history corrections remove 0.61–0.89% of Pythia’s baseline reconstruction error at lag one and approximately 0.40% of Gemma’s; unrelated-history controls do not improve reconstruction. Persistent versus BatchTopK FVE is 0.93 versus 0.94 in Pythia and 0.66 versus 0.72 in Gemma. Higher learned λ groups exhibit slower empirical decay. The lowest-λ 50% score 0.93/0.89 on local autointerpretation, versus 0.84/0.79 for the highest-λ 1%, respectively. The lowest quintile receives relatively more noun updates; the highest receives more punctuation and conjunction updates. Selecting the slowest 1% yields high subject-probing AUC approaching supervised selection. Injection probes trained at the untrusted-span endpoint retain more distant signal through slow states, evaluated up to 350 tokens later. Slow-state probe-weighted decoder directions produce the largest consistently positive shifts in the external monitor’s yes/no margin under interventions scaled to 10% of hidden-state norm.

**Limitations / open questions**
Only two model-layer sites and one principal width/update budget are evaluated. Fixed diagonal recurrence excludes feature interactions and context-dependent resets. The auxiliary encoder introduces memory, so probing and steering do not identify native memory mechanisms or exclude lexical recurrence. Interventions affect the replay monitor, whose unmodified query-margin AUC is 0.51, rather than the original agent’s actions or demonstrated detection accuracy. Monitoring sample counts, detailed split construction, and numerical probing/intervention curves are unspecified; figure images are unavailable in the supplied rendering.

title: Unveiling A Core Linguistic Region in Large Language Models
abstract: Brain localization, which describes the association between specific regions of the brain and their corresponding functions, is widely accepted in the field of cognitive science as an objective fact. Today's large language models (LLMs) possess human-level linguistic competence and can execute complex tasks requiring abstract knowledge and reasoning. To deeply understand the inherent mechanisms of intelligence emergence in LLMs, this paper conducts an analogical research using brain localization as a prototype. We have discovered a core region in LLMs that corresponds to linguistic competence, accounting for approximately 1% of the total model parameters. This core region exhibits significant dimension dependency, and perturbations to even a single parameter on specific dimensions can lead to a loss of linguistic competence. Furthermore, we observe that an improvement in linguistic competence does not necessarily accompany an elevation in the model's knowledge level, which might imply the existence of regions of domain knowledge that are dissociated from the linguistic region. Overall, exploring the LLMs' functional regions provides insights into the foundation of their intelligence. In the future, we will continue to investigate knowledge regions within LLMs and the interactions between them.
summary:
**Central idea**
The paper proposes a small multilingual linguistic core in LLaMA models, identified through parameter stability during language fine-tuning. Parameters changing little across six language-specific runs form the “Bottom” region. The authors interpret its perturbation sensitivity and recovery behavior as evidence of shared linguistic machinery, by analogy with brain localization.

**Experiments**
LLaMA2-7B and LLaMA2-13B undergo next-token fine-tuning on Arabic, Spanish, Russian, Chinese, Korean, and Vietnamese, normally using 100,000 samples per language; selected 13B conditions use 10,000. Perplexity is evaluated across 30 languages, with evaluation sizes ranging from 630 Swahili tokens to 7,598,161 Portuguese tokens. Interventions target least-changing, most-changing, or random parameters, selected matrix dimensions, and individual RMSNorm weights. Recovery experiments use up to 50,000 Chinese Zhihu samples, testing Chinese Wechat and English Falcon text. Separate checkpoint comparisons evaluate C-Eval, Gaokao-Bench, AGI-Eval, and MMLU.

**Key results**
Approximately 0.981% of parameters change by at most 3% across all six localization runs. Perturbing the bottom-ranked 1% raises Chinese Wechat perplexity to 71,137.844 in 7B and 62,191.785 in 13B, versus roughly 6–7 for matched-count top-ranked or random perturbations. Bottom-ranked 3% perturbations severely increase perplexity in all 30 languages. After 1% Bottom perturbation and 50,000 recovery samples, freezing the region yields Chinese/English perplexities of 7.151/1,276.354; allowing updates yields 5.698/18.961. Selected matrix dimensions are disproportionately sensitive. Resetting LLaMA2-13B’s L1 input_layer_norm coordinate 2100 to one raises perplexity from 5.865 to 83,224.078; multiplying it by ten yields 4,363.462. Chinese-LLaMA-7B and Open-Chinese-LLaMA-7B, continued-pretrained on 30B and 100B Chinese tokens, reportedly improve Chinese competence without substantial gains on three Chinese examination benchmarks.

**Limitations / open questions**
Perturbation sensitivity does not establish a uniquely linguistic module rather than general computational fragility. General perturbation magnitudes, training details, and repeated-run uncertainty are underspecified. The approximately 1% stability-threshold set differs from the ranked perturbation budgets. Recovery checkpoint identity and several evaluation-corpus assignments are unclear. Figures are unavailable beyond captions and textual descriptions, preventing independent inspection of plotted benchmark scores and qualitative outputs. Checkpoint comparisons do not localize a separate knowledge region or isolate causal effects of model size and pretraining. The proposed training recommendations are untested.

Priors in Time: Missing Inductive Biases for Language Model Interpretability
abstract: Recovering meaningful concepts from language model activations is a central aim of interpretability. While existing feature extraction methods aim to identify concepts that are independent directions, it is unclear if this assumption can capture the rich temporal structure of language. Specifically, via a Bayesian lens, we demonstrate that Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) impose priors that assume independence of concepts across time, implying stationarity. Meanwhile, language model representations exhibit rich temporal dynamics, including systematic growth in conceptual dimensionality, context-dependent correlations, and pronounced non-stationarity, in direct conflict with the priors of SAEs. Taking inspiration from computational neuroscience, we introduce a new interpretability objective -- Temporal Feature Analysis -- which possesses a temporal inductive bias to decompose representations at a given time into two parts: a predictable component, which can be inferred from the context, and a residual component, which captures novel information unexplained by the context. Temporal Feature Analyzers correctly parse garden path sentences, identify event boundaries, and more broadly delineate abstract, slow-moving information from novel, fast-moving information, while existing SAEs show significant pitfalls in all the above tasks. Overall, our results underscore the need for inductive biases that match the data in designing robust interpretability tools.
summary:
**Central idea**
Temporal Feature Analysis (TFA) combines a context-associated code obtained through attention over preceding encoded states with a sparse residual code, reconstructed through a shared dictionary. It places the proposed temporal independence prior on residual innovations. The paper argues that ordinary SAE objectives omit temporal structure useful for exposing contextual geometry.

**Experiments**
ReLU, TopK, BatchTopK, and TFA dictionaries are trained on one billion Pile-Uncopyrighted activation tokens. Experiments primarily use Gemma-2-2B, with supplementary Llama-3.1-8B evaluations. Diagnostics include normalized second-moment effective dimension, lagged cosine similarity, context-subspace projection, reconstruction NMSE, explained variance, Fourier-separated kernel comparisons, clustering, and UMAP tortuosity. Tasks cover TinyStories, 50 GPT-5-generated and event-labeled stories, 50 generated garden-path sentences with matched controls, random walks on a 3×3 grid, and the first 350 tokens of 1,000 Ultrachat conversations processed by Gemma-2-2B-IT using base-trained dictionaries.

**Key results**
Activation effective dimension increases with position, while temporal similarities vary by position. Projection onto a 500-token context retains up to approximately 80% of the reported variance metric. TFA story/web/code NMSE is 0.139/0.139/0.152 versus BatchTopK's 0.152/0.139/0.149; explained variance is 0.73/0.79/0.75 versus 0.72/0.79/0.75. Predictive-code CKA with slow activation components is 0.75 versus 0.35–0.37 for standard SAEs. Predictive codes show stronger within-event similarity and more consistent garden-path/control phrase similarities. Grid interventions succeed for 4/9 nodes using predictive codes; an appendix reports novel-code success for two of those nodes. The illustrated dialogue trajectory has UMAP tortuosity approximately 2 versus 25–30 for SAE/novel codes. Selected novel features support conventional interpretation cards. Appendix G reports largely separated dictionary usage and substantially lower effective rank for predictive codes.

**Limitations / open questions**
Semantic conclusions largely rely on geometric proxies, synthetic labels, and selected visualizations; parsing accuracy and broad causal fidelity are not established. The attention query uses the current activation, so the contextual component is not forecast from history alone, and exact orthogonality is not guaranteed. Effective dimension does not directly count concepts. Separable penalty factors do not imply independent learned codes; exact BatchTopK budgets couple samples. The support-switching proof lacks a quantitative error argument and inconsistently uses strict versus non-strict dimension thresholds. Gemma layers are inconsistently reported as 12 and 15; supplementary Llama baselines have unfinished training. Training competition can undermine stream separation. Downstream replacement loss and systematic intervention evaluations are absent. Image-only plots limit access to numerical results, but the supplied article and appendices are complete.

Time-Aware Feature Selection: Adaptive Temporal Masking for Stable Sparse Autoencoder Training
abstract: Understanding the internal representations of large language models is crucial for ensuring their reliability and safety, with sparse autoencoders (SAEs) emerging as a promising interpretability approach. However, current SAE training methods face feature absorption, where features (or neurons) are absorbed into each other to minimize $L_1$ penalty, making it difficult to consistently identify and analyze model behaviors. We introduce Adaptive Temporal Masking (ATM), a novel training approach that dynamically adjusts feature selection by tracking activation magnitudes, frequencies, and reconstruction contributions to compute importance scores that evolve over time. ATM applies a probabilistic masking mechanism based on statistical thresholding of these importance scores, creating a more natural feature selection process. Through extensive experiments on the Gemma-2-2b model, we demonstrate that ATM achieves substantially lower absorption scores compared to existing methods like TopK and JumpReLU SAEs, while maintaining excellent reconstruction quality. These results establish ATM as a principled solution for learning stable, interpretable features in neural networks, providing a foundation for more reliable model analysis.
summary:
**Central idea**

Adaptive Temporal Masking (ATM) selects SAE features using statistics accumulated across training steps. Importance multiplies exponential moving averages of activation magnitude and absolute reconstruction-loss gradient. Mean importance plus a standard-deviation multiplier determines a threshold for stochastic masking. Training retains an L1 penalty, starts with unrestricted activation during warmup, periodically increases pruning, and guarantees minimum feature retention. Temporal tracking concerns optimization history rather than explicit memory across language tokens.

**Experiments**

The comparison uses Gemma-2-2B layer 12, hidden dimension 2,304, and 16,384 SAE latents. ATM, TopK, JumpReLU, and standard L1 SAE recipes are evaluated after five million WikiText-103 training tokens, using 128-token sequences and a reported learning rate of 3×10⁻⁴. Evaluation includes first-letter absorption through probe projections, reconstruction metrics, zero-ablation-normalized cross-entropy recovery, and single-latent probing. The probing suite reportedly contains 35 binary tasks across Bias in Bios, Amazon Reviews, Europarl, GitHub, and AG News, with 4,000 training and 1,000 test examples per task.

**Key results**

ATM's mean absorption score is 0.0068, versus 0.1402 for TopK, 0.0114 for JumpReLU, and 0.0161 for the standard SAE: approximately 40% below JumpReLU. ATM achieves MSE 0.5508, explained variance 0.9102, cosine similarity 0.9727, and cross-entropy recovery 0.9967. These reconstruction results exceed TopK and JumpReLU but trail the standard SAE. Average active-latent counts differ substantially: ATM 3,280, TopK 40, JumpReLU 2,666, and standard SAE 8,724. Top-one probing accuracy is 0.7161 for ATM, below TopK's 0.7698, close to JumpReLU's 0.7154, and above the standard SAE's 0.6379.

**Limitations / open questions**

The results do not establish superiority at matched sparsity. Only one model, layer, width, and short training budget are evaluated; repeated-run uncertainty, component ablations, and direct cross-seed or longitudinal feature-stability measurements are not reported. First-letter absorption is a restricted diagnostic rather than comprehensive semantic validation. The conclusion's probing-superiority statement conflicts with TopK's higher table score. Method details remain unresolved: EMA decay is 0.9 in Section 3 but 0.99 experimentally; frequency tracking lacks a specified role; and the masking formula yields negative probabilities above a positive threshold unless additional handling is applied. Generalization, computational costs, optimal temporal scales, and targeted editing remain open.

title: What’s in my human feedback? Learning interpretable descriptions of preference data
SAFER: Probing Safety in Reward Models with Sparse Autoencoder
abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) is a key paradigm for aligning large language models (LLMs) with human values, yet the reward models at its core remain largely opaque. In this work, we present Sparse Autoencoder For Enhanced Reward model (\textbf{SAFER}), a novel framework for interpreting and improving reward models through mechanistic analysis. Leveraging Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), we uncover human-interpretable features in reward model activations, enabling insight into safety-relevant decision-making. We apply SAFER to safety-oriented preference datasets and quantify the salience of individual features by activation differences between chosen and rejected responses. Using these feature-level signals, we design targeted data poisoning and denoising strategies. Experiments show that SAFER can precisely degrade or enhance safety alignment with minimal data modification, without sacrificing general chat performance. Our approach contributes to interpreting, auditing and refining reward models in high-stakes LLM alignment tasks. Our codes are available at https://github.com/xzy-101/SAFER-code. \textit{This paper discusses topics related to reward model safety and may include discussions or examples that highlight potential risks or unsafe outcomes.}
summary:
**Central idea**

SAFER uses sparse autoencoders to identify safety-associated reward-model representations and rank preference pairs for modification. Features receive normalized chosen–rejected activation-contrast scores; GPT-4o filters highly contrasting features for safety relevance. A signed, length-normalized aggregation over 32 selected features scores each pair. High-scoring pairs are label-flipped for poisoning; low-scoring pairs are removed for denoising.

**Experiments**

The authors train Llama-3.2-1B and 3B reward models on approximately 102,000 PKU-SafeRLHF and WildGuardMix preference pairs. TopK SAEs use 16,384 latents and k=64 at approximately three-quarters depth, initially training on 100 million OpenWebText2 tokens before safety-domain adaptation. RewardBench Safety and Chat scores evaluate retrained reward models against random and reward-margin data selection. Additional tests compare human/GPT-4o ratings of 500 random features, contrast-ranked versus random groups of 100 features, training and hyperparameter variants, decoder-direction UMAP visualizations, and amplification of one feature.

**Key results**

Over 80% of sampled features receive identical human and GPT-4o relevance ratings. Contrast-ranked features receive higher relevance ratings than random features. At 5% label flipping, SAFER reduces Safety from 92.30 to 71.76 in 1B and from 94.86 to 75.14 in 3B; Chat changes from 89.39 to 91.34 and 89.11 to 90.50, respectively. Reward-margin poisoning damages Chat substantially more. Removing 4% of pairs raises Safety to 94.20 and 96.46. Safety-domain adaptation and sentence-final training improve several outcomes, with exceptions and Chat tradeoffs. Fivefold amplification of feature #3389 increases chosen-response rewards by an average of 1.04 across 20 safety pairs versus 0.02 across 20 chat pairs.

**Limitations / open questions**

Main data interventions cover two small reward models and one benchmark; no downstream policy training tests assistant safety or capability preservation. Repeated-run uncertainty and statistical-test details are absent. Semantic ratings, UMAP separation, and dataset interventions do not establish dictionary-wide monosemanticity or native causal mechanisms. Steering covers one feature at an unspecified checkpoint without matched perturbation controls. Low pair scores are not independently validated as annotation errors; examples include benign requests rejected through over-refusal. Tables 3–6 disagree on several denoising values. Sentence-final selection versus token aggregation and length normalization is incompletely specified. Figure images are unavailable, limiting independent assessment of plotted distributions and geometry. Supplied metadata dates initial publication to July 2025; the text identifies the analyzed revision as v3, January 30, 2026.

title: Cross-Layer Discrete Concept Discovery for Interpreting Language Models
abstract: Interpreting language models remains challenging due to the existence of residual stream, which linearly mixes and duplicates features across adjacent layers, causing single-layer analyses to miss this cross-layer structure. Cross-layer sparse autoencoders (SAEs) address layer mixing but operate in continuous space, where concepts split across many neurons without clear boundaries. We introduce Cross-Layer Vector Quantized-Variational Autoencoder (CLVQ-VAE), a novel framework which maps representations from a lower layer to a higher layer through a discrete vector-quantization bottleneck, collapsing duplicated residual-stream features into compact, interpretable concept vectors. Our approach combines top-k temperature-based sampling with exponential moving average (EMA) codebook updates, providing controlled exploration of the discrete latent space while maintaining codebook diversity. Across both encoder- and decoder-based models on ERASER-Movie, Jigsaw, and AGNews, CLVQ-VAE outperforms clustering, single-layer vector quantized-variational autoencoder (VQ-VAE), and sparse autoencoder (SAE) baselines across three evaluation axes: removing identified concepts drops downstream probe accuracy by up to 93%, LLM judges rank our concepts first in 66.7% of comparisons, and human annotators recover model predictions from our visualizations with 78% accuracy versus 54% for clustering.
summary:
**Central idea**

CLVQ-VAE learns discrete token-level codes while predicting higher-layer activations from lower-layer activations. An adaptive residual encoder feeds a 400-entry codebook using temperature-controlled sampling among five nearest entries and exponential moving-average updates. A six-layer bidirectional transformer decoder reconstructs target states using both quantized codes and unquantized encoder outputs through cross-attention. The discrete channel therefore is not the sole reconstruction bottleneck. The supplied body identifies itself as the September 2026 v4 revision.

**Experiments**

Task-fine-tuned BERT-base and RoBERTa-base, plus prompted LLaMA-2-7B and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct without task fine-tuning, are evaluated on ERASER-Movie, Jigsaw, and AGNews. Reported layer pairs are 8–12 for the encoders, 28–32 for LLaMA, and 32–36 for Qwen. Baselines include hierarchical clustering, an otherwise matched single-layer VQ-VAE, and single-layer/cross-layer SAEs. Layer Integrated Gradients selects a salient token; its assigned code direction is projected out of the lower-layer sentence representation. Frozen two-layer MLP probes, evaluated through 20-fold stratified cross-validation, measure task-label accuracy. Encoders use CLS states; decoder models use mean pooling. Further evaluations examine label-associated routing, four LLM judges, human prediction from word clouds, and architectural ablations.

**Key results**

CLVQ-VAE obtains the lowest perturbed probe accuracy in 5/12 model–dataset settings, beats the cross-layer SAE in 10/12, and beats single-layer VQ-VAE in 9/12. Its largest relative reduction is 93.2%, from 0.8777 to 0.0594 for RoBERTa/ERASER-Movie. Salient-code removal exceeds degradation from distance-weighted alternative active codes in 8/9 tested settings, excluding LLaMA. LLM judges give CLVQ-VAE the highest aggregate rating, 1.890/3, and a 66.7% win rate over configuration-level pairwise mean-rating comparisons; this is not a first-place frequency. Overall judge agreement is moderate, W=0.533. Fourteen annotators evaluating 19 stratified ERASER sentences achieve 78.20% agreement with model predictions versus 54.14% for clustering, with κ=0.864 versus 0.59. Cross-attention lowers perturbed accuracy in 7/9 settings and code-vector cosine similarity in 8/9. Initialization preferences differ between probe disruption and judge ratings.

**Limitations / open questions**

Probe disruption does not establish native model reliance, selective semantic erasure, or recovery of computation. Label-sensitive routing does not establish atomic concepts or elimination of residual-stream duplication. Human evidence covers only 19 sentences; LLM sample allocation is unclear. Comparisons are not compute-matched, and the layer sweep does not establish uniform optimality of layers 8–12. Usage perplexity measures assignment entropy rather than semantic diversity. Separate training is required for each layer pair, and the contextual decoder adds quadratic sequence-length cost.

abstract: Reward models (RMs) are at the crux of successfully using RLHF to align pretrained models to human preferences, yet there has been relatively little study that focuses on evaluation of those models. Evaluating reward models presents an opportunity to understand the opaque technologies used for alignment of language models and which values are embedded in them. Resources for reward model training and understanding are sparse in the nascent open-source community around them. To enhance scientific understanding of reward models, we present RewardBench, a benchmark dataset and code-base for evaluation. The RewardBench dataset is a collection of prompt-chosen-rejected trios spanning chat, reasoning, and safety, to benchmark how reward models perform on challenging, structured and out-of-distribution queries. We create specific comparison datasets for RMs that have subtle, but verifiable reasons (e.g. bugs, incorrect facts) why one answer should be preferred to another. On the RewardBench leaderboard, we evaluate reward models trained with a variety of methods, such as the direct MLE training of classifiers and the implicit reward modeling of Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). We present many findings on propensity for refusals, reasoning limitations, and instruction following shortcomings of various reward models towards a better understanding of the RLHF process.

Rethinking Sparse Autoencoders: Select-and-Project for Fairness and Control from Encoder Features Alone
abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are widely employed for mechanistic interpretability and model steering. Within this context, steering is by design performed by means of decoding altered SAE intermediate representations. This procedure essentially rewrites the original activations as a weighted sum of decoder features. In contrast to existing literature, we forward an encoder-centric alternative to model steering which demonstrates a stronger cross-modal performance. We introduce S&P Top-K, a retraining-free and computationally lightweight Selection and Projection framework that identifies Top-K encoder features aligned with a sensitive attribute or behavior, optionally aggregates them into a single control axis, and computes an orthogonal projection to be subsequently applied directly in the model's native embedding space. In vision-language models, it improves fairness metrics on CelebA and FairFace by up to 3.2 times over conventional SAE usage, and in large language models, it substantially reduces aggressiveness and sycophancy in Llama-3 8B Instruct, achieving up to 3.6 times gains over masked reconstruction. These findings suggest that encoder-centric interventions provide a general, efficient, and more effective mechanism for shaping model behavior at inference time than the traditional decoder-centric use of SAEs.
summary:
**Central idea**
S&P Top-K suppresses attributes using selected SAE encoder directions directly in native activations. It optionally combines directions using logistic-regression weights and attenuates their span without running the SAE at inference. “Retraining-free” concerns the target model: classifiers are fitted, and the vision experiments train an SAE.

**Experiments**
Vision experiments use CLIP ViT-B/16 and a 16,384-feature JumpReLU SAE trained on approximately 37 million images. CelebA measures retrieval gender balance and hair-color worst-group ROC-AUC; FairFace measures gender balance in stereotype-query retrieval. Evaluation uses five-fold cross-validation, with 50% held out as a reference set. KL divergence and MaxSkew compare gender proportions among the top 500 retrieved images with dataset proportions. The default selection budget is 16 features. Ablations compare selectors, aggregation rules, direct CAVs, and prompt debiasing. The masking baseline preserves reconstruction residuals by subtracting selected decoder contributions from original embeddings.

Llama-3-8B-Instruct experiments use the SAELens dictionary at blocks.25.hook_resid_post. Discovery uses 100 target-style and 100 contrasting opinions per behavior, approximately 55,000 tokens. Evaluation produces 100 opinions per behavior and intervention under explicit aggressive or sycophantic instructions; an unspecified LLM judge assigns 1–10 intensity scores.

**Key results**
On CelebA, interpolated S&P changes KL from 0.113880 to 0.079235 and worst-group AUC from 0.754743 to 0.752426. Its approximately 3.3-fold KL advantage over LP-selected masking uses that baseline’s KL of 0.260455. With the same Stylist selector, masking achieves lower KL, 0.061290, but AUC falls to 0.527940. Full-span encoder removal achieves KL 0.035051 with AUC 0.629358, showing that aggregation exchanges some fairness improvement for utility. Selector rankings differ between datasets. Adding S&P to BendVLM changes KL from 0.0186 to 0.0101 on CelebA and from 0.0100 to 0.0080 on FairFace. The prose reports a 1.6-point aggressiveness reduction and a sycophancy reduction 3.6 times the masking reduction.

**Limitations / open questions**
Evidence covers one vision backbone and one LLM, without broad generation-quality tests, judge validation, or FairFace task-utility measurements. Opinion examples include awkwardness, sarcasm, and templates. Binary aggregation, suppression-only control, and amplification of other biases remain limitations. Native-space editing does not establish mechanistic faithfulness or complete attribute removal. Equation 1 requires full column rank and gives exact orthogonality only at alpha=1; the subsequent single-axis formula has an inconsistent denominator. Figure plots are unavailable in the supplied rendering; aggregate LLM findings rely on prose. Metadata dates initial publication; the text identifies version 2 dated December 5, 2025.

title: Auxiliary losses for learning generalizable concept-based models
Incorporating Hierarchical Semantics in Sparse Autoencoder Architectures
abstract: Sparse dictionary learning (and, in particular, sparse autoencoders) attempts to learn a set of human-understandable concepts that can explain variation on an abstract space. A basic limitation of this approach is that it neither exploits nor represents the semantic relationships between the learned concepts. In this paper, we introduce a modified SAE architecture that explicitly models a semantic hierarchy of concepts. Application of this architecture to the internal representations of large language models shows both that semantic hierarchy can be learned, and that doing so improves both reconstruction and interpretability. Additionally, the architecture leads to significant improvements in computational efficiency.
summary:
**Central idea**

Hierarchical Sparse Autoencoders (H-SAEs) attach a low-dimensional expert SAE to each feature of a top-level TopK SAE. Selected parent features gate expert execution, and reconstruction adds parent contributions and expert-specific refinements. The design draws on previously proposed parent-vector and low-dimensional child-increment geometry. Training combines full reconstruction, top-level-only reconstruction, bi-orthogonality, and L1 penalties.

**Experiments**

The main comparison uses one billion unit-normalized layer-20 residual-stream vectors from Gemma 2-2B, collected from multilingual Wikipedia article prefixes. Models train for four epochs with batch size 32,512 and top-level k=32. Experts contain 16 or 64 sublatents, using subspaces of dimension four or eight. Baselines are standard TopK SAEs. Evaluation measures explained variance, SAEBench-normalized replacement cross-entropy, and first-letter feature absorption. A multilingual test translates 1,000 training-derived English sequences of 16–48 tokens into French, Spanish, and German using Gemini-2.0-Flash, then compares the eight strongest last-token features. Separate qualitative ablations use 186,032 retained Gemma unembedding vectors and a 2,048-expert, 32-sublatent H-SAE with k=5.

**Key results**

The text reports improved reconstruction and replacement-loss curves and reduced first-letter absorption relative to the tested baselines. Across all six language pairs, top-eight feature symmetric differences are smaller: English–French decreases from 9.772 to 8.448, and French–Spanish from 7.170 to 5.748, on a 0–16 scale. Selected examples show parent/refinement associations involving marriage, airports, and question words. Qualitative unembedding ablations find no obvious hierarchy advantage from either auxiliary regularizer, while whitening improves the apparent coherence of selected features. The authors report slightly faster training than their naive baseline auxiliary-loss implementation, without numerical timing benchmarks.

**Limitations / open questions**

Evidence centers on one backbone and residual-stream site. Hierarchy assessments use selected examples without quantitative semantic validation; some relationships are lexical or contextual rather than strictly taxonomic. Cross-language overlap and first-letter absorption do not establish general compositionality or native causal feature recovery. Matching parent k does not match total parent-plus-child activity or parameter count. The fourfold compute claim ambiguously identifies its comparator as having “32 top-level features.” Algorithm 1 omits the stated expert TopK₁ step and uses DE where Equation 3.4 uses ED; the prose and algorithm also differ on which activations receive L1 regularization. Plot images are unavailable, so precise reconstruction and absorption values cannot be recovered. Repeated-run uncertainty is not reported.

title: When Trees Are Not Enough: Learning Mixed-Topology Feature Graphs with Adaptive Graph Sparse Autoencoders
abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) expose interpretable features in large language model activations, yet existing structured SAEs impose single-parent trees or forests, while post-hoc graphs permit multiple parents but neither guide feature learning nor ensure reliable relation recovery. We introduce the Adaptive Graph Sparse Autoencoder (AG-SAE), a structure-guided training paradigm that treats each feature's complete parent set as an atomic structural hypothesis and lets evidence select zero, one, or multiple parents. By competing complete parent sets against null, subset, and alternative explanations, AG-SAE identifies jointly necessary multi-parent relations while rejecting redundant or spurious alternatives and verifying that each child contributes beyond its parents. The induced topology over SAE features then defines a differentiable structural loss that guides SAE training, while topology-guided refinement mitigates feature absorption and uses persistent reconstruction gaps exposed by the learned structure to initialize new features. The entire graph is then induced again from the revised dictionary by reassessing every feature's complete parent set, closing the dictionary-graph self-consistency cycle. Experiments demonstrate exact mixed-topology recovery in a controlled toy model, greater relational reliability and semantic validity than structured and post-hoc baselines on real LLM activations, and stronger feature-level causal interventions than conventional SAE features. AG-SAE thereby turns recovered mixed-topology feature structure into an unsupervised training signal that improves the dictionary, enables reliable feature organization beyond the topological limitations of trees, and exhibits stronger causal control beyond reconstruction.
summary:
**Central idea**

Adaptive Graph Sparse Autoencoder (AG-SAE) alternates sparse dictionary optimization with feature-graph induction allowing zero, one, or multiple parents. Complete parent sets compete against null, proper-subset, and equal-cardinality alternatives using activation coverage, decoded-contribution support, and additional child reconstruction value. Selected relations guide structural training, graph-conditioned decoder refinement, and residual-based feature initialization before full re-induction. The implemented LLM search retrieves 24 candidates, searches a pool of 12, and permits at most three parents.

**Experiments**

A controlled benchmark uses 24 generating directions in 24 dimensions, eight features each with zero, one, and two parents, and 32 predefined hard negatives. Main experiments use Gemma-2-2B block-13 MiniPile residual activations, a shared 100M-activation training cache, and dictionary scales totaling 30,720 features. Comparators include Vanilla SAE Post-hoc, Matryoshka DAG/tree projections, HSAE, and Tree SAE. Frozen outputs undergo separate report-only predictive structural validity (PSV), nonredundancy (NR), and blinded Qwen3-30B-A3B semantic validity (SV) evaluation. Mixed-topology Joint scores pool 800 single-parent, 400 two-parent, and 400 three-parent relations from each method; single-parent-only methods use 800. Additional settings evaluate Gemma/PubMed and Qwen3.5-2B-Base layer 18/MiniPile. Interventions use 416 held-out prompts across 26 first-letter concepts.

**Key results**

AG-SAE recovers all 24 toy features and complete parent sets and rejects 32/32 hard negatives. Vanilla also recovers all features at R²=1.00, separating feature recovery from relation recovery. In Gemma/MiniPile, 1,670/7,091 parented features have multiple parents. AG-SAE achieves 69.56% Joint validity versus 40.63% for Vanilla Post-hoc, with EV 0.670 and L0 50.13. Fixed-dictionary complete-set induction raises multi-parent PSV from 34.80% to 66.13%. One realignment update reduces absorption fraction from 42.08% to 28.11% with negligible EV and L0 changes. Leading-feature addition and ablation increase target-letter margin effects from 4.22 to 4.79 and 3.23 to 3.91 logits, respectively; 21/26 concepts improve in both directions. Matched continuation controls on 13 fixed features do not reproduce the bidirectional improvement.

**Limitations / open questions**

Real-model graph ground truth is unavailable. Predictive relations, reconstruction gains, and model-judged labels do not establish native causal dependencies or exhaustive semantics. Interventions concern probe-selected first-letter features at dictionary-specific native scales, without comprehensive off-target evaluation. Budget matching does not establish equal computation; additional model/domain settings lack baseline comparisons. Formal proofs establish local graph stability and eventual stopping under explicit nondegeneracy and convergence assumptions, without proving optimization convergence.

title: On the Interpretability of Whisper Encodings Using Sparse Autoencoders
abstract: While deep transformer-based models have advanced rapidly, their internal mechanisms remain largely a mystery. Recent work has prioritized understanding text-based transformer models, leaving ASR systems largely unexplored. In order to address this gap, we examine the internal representations of Whisper's encoder using a sparse autoencoder. We find diverse monosemantic features across linguistic and non-linguistic boundaries, spanning a hierarchy from phonetic to semantic representations, and conduct a causal feature-steering campaign across this hierarchy, including cross-lingual steering. We further find that steering is more reliable for higher-level features than lower-level ones, an asymmetry that may reflect redundant encoding of lower-level information. Altogether, this work demonstrates that Whisper's encoder represents a surprisingly rich hierarchy of linguistic information that extends well beyond what is strictly necessary for transcription.
summary:
**Central idea**
The paper investigates linguistic information in frozen Whisper base's final encoder output using a TopK sparse autoencoder. The SAE maps 512-dimensional audio frames into 16,000 latents, retains K=45 coefficients, and reconstructs frames using MSE. The proposed hierarchy concerns abstraction levels at one activation site, not a progression across encoder layers.

**Experiments**
Training uses 646,769 audio files, approximately 200 million unpadded frames, and nine epochs. Data include English and Spanish speech, environmental sounds, and internal recordings; French is absent from SAE training. The analysis set is reported as 28,414 files, although its listed components sum to 28,745. Selected linguistic latents receive occurrence-level precision/recall evaluations using phone or word alignments. Steering modifies individual coefficients within one word's frame span before reconstruction and transcription. GPT-OSS 120B labels the entire dictionary from activation-marked transcript examples; 76% of 100 randomly sampled labels pass manual evaluation.

**Key results**
Selected latents associate with R–UW1 phones (87.8% precision, 68.4% recall), “nothing” (86.9%, 100%), third-person pronouns (74.8%, 41.5%), “-ly” (78.4%, 15.7%), and numbers (93.5%, 37.7%). Two profanity-associated latents jointly achieve 3.9% precision and 89.9% recall; reported word-level profanity prevalence is 0.11%. Among the six selected families in Table VI, positive steering succeeds for five, while negative steering succeeds only for profanity. Neither direction cleanly steers the phonetic example. Selected Spanish and French transcripts also lose profanity under negative steering, sometimes with substantial collateral corruption. Separately, a noise-only detector achieves 98.1% precision and 99.8% recall. A language-associated latent discriminates Spanish from English but fails to flip Whisper's language classification under positive steering. Three other latents show narrowly timed activations.

**Limitations / open questions**
Steering lacks trial denominators, systematic dose specifications, confidence intervals, and WER/CER preservation measurements. Selected associations and output interventions do not establish exhaustive monosemanticity, native causal mediation, or language-independent semantics. Phonetic controls and broader model, layer, and dictionary comparisons are absent. Analysis partly overlaps SAE training; Appendix D acknowledges possible decomposition overfitting and asserts held-out generalization without a numerical split breakdown. Its fixed-encoder image argument does not establish feature recovery or make overlap inconsequential. K=45 is outside the stated preliminary search grid, and final-model reconstruction fidelity is not reported. Redundancy and compensatory decoding remain proposed explanations for steering asymmetry. The text is complete, but figure images are unavailable in this rendering.
